meta-radio-clock.title: The 45-Minute Contract: RADIO as a Time Budget
objectives: Allocate a defensible minute budget across the five RADIO phases for a given prompt archetype and say why the split differs from the default.
Decide mid-phase whether to continue or cut, and name the cut aloud in one sentence.
Distinguish overruns that are recoverable by compression from ones that invalidate every later phase.
claims: RADIO names five phases of a frontend system design round: Requirements, Architecture, Data model, Interface (API), Optimizations.

In a 45-minute frontend design round a workable default budget is ~2 min framing, ~8 min Requirements, ~10 min Architecture, ~5 min Data model, ~5 min Interface, ~10 min Optimizations/deep dive, ~5 min for the candidate's questions.
Skipping Requirements costs more than overrunning it, because every later phase is then scored against a scope the interviewer never agreed to.
Announcing the intended time split in the first two minutes transfers the burden of interrupting to the interviewer and is itself a scored communication signal.
Data model and Interface are the compressible phases — each can be delivered as a 3-minute typed sketch — whereas Requirements and the deep dive lose their signal entirely when compressed.
Reaching zero minutes with no deep dive anywhere caps a senior-level score regardless of how correct the earlier phases were.
Time pressure in a round is produced by unbounded scope, not by speaking speed; the recovery lever is naming a cut aloud, never talking faster.

viz.title: Where the 45 Minutes Actually Go
viz.whatIsDrawn: One 45-minute horizontal track segmented by RADIO phase. The learner's dragged allocation is the solid track; a ghost track beneath shows the reference budget for the selected prompt archetype. Inside each segment a signal meter fills as minutes are added and visibly saturates at that phase's ceiling, so extra minutes past the ceiling produce no further fill. All labels and deltas are anchored inside the track band.
viz.predictPrompt: Candidate A spends 14 minutes on requirements and reaches the deep dive with 6 minutes left. Candidate B spends 3 minutes on requirements and reaches the deep dive with 20 minutes left. Both are technically correct throughout. Which one scores lower — and which of the two overruns is recoverable without losing points?
controls: drag phase boundaries to re-allocate minutes
step the playhead minute by minute
switch prompt archetype (infinite feed / collaborative editor / analytics dashboard) to see the reference budget shift
viz.insight: Signal per phase saturates. Minutes past a phase's ceiling are dead minutes, and the phases with the lowest ceilings — data model and interface — are the ones you compress when you are late.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds the saturating signal curve per phase and a pure allocation -> total-signal function, unit-tested against the claim that a non-uniform allocation dominates an even one and that zero requirements minutes multiplies down every later phase. viz.tsx is hand-rolled SVG: two stacked rows of rects, ghost at 40% opacity. Deterministic — no RNG, no clock; the playhead is a controlled index. prefers-reduced-motion renders the committed allocation with static per-segment deltas and a text narration of the total-signal comparison in an aria-live region.

drills.prompt: Reorder these seven moves into a defensible first twelve minutes of a 45-minute round.
drills.answerSketch: Restate prompt -> announce time plan -> state 3 assumptions for correction -> ask the 2 questions that change the architecture -> write the scope statement -> name one exclusion -> commit 2-3 NFR targets with numbers.

drills.prompt: The round is 30 minutes instead of 45, and the interviewer hands you the requirements outright. Which two phases absorb the cut, and which phase's budget must not shrink?
drills.answerSketch: Data model and Interface compress to a combined ~5 min typed sketch; the deep dive budget is held, because it is the only phase that produces senior signal.

drills.prompt: Here is a minute-by-minute log of a round that ended in a no-hire. Click the minute at which the round became unrecoverable.
drills.answerSketch: Minute 4 — scope was never bounded, so the architecture phase kept expanding; the visible symptom at minute 38 is downstream.

drills.prompt: You are at minute 33. The data model is undrawn and your virtualization argument is half-finished. Choose one to finish and write a two-sentence justification. 90 seconds, locked.
drills.answerSketch: Either choice can score; the criteria are: names what is being given up, ties the choice to a stated requirement or NFR, and says the cut aloud rather than silently dropping it.

failureModes: Treats RADIO as a checklist to complete, narrating all five phases shallowly and going deep nowhere.
Starts drawing boxes within 90 seconds of hearing the prompt.
Silently overruns requirements, then rushes architecture without ever telling the interviewer a trade was made.
Believes speaking faster recovers time, when the only real lever is cutting scope out loud.
Spends the last five minutes on a phase nobody was going to score instead of a closing summary.
interviewProbes: We have 45 minutes — how do you want to use them?
We're at the halfway mark. Where are you?
You have ten minutes left. What's the most valuable thing you can tell me in that time?

meta-requirements-negotiation.title: The First Eight Minutes: Requirements as Negotiation
objectives: Produce a written scope statement from an open prompt containing the primary user action, the device/network floor, the data volume and one explicit exclusion.
Convert questions into assumptions stated aloud for correction, and choose the small number of questions worth spending minutes on.
Scope down explicitly, with a reason, without asking permission.
claims: For an open prompt such as 'design a news feed', producing the scoped problem statement is the candidate's job; interviewers withhold scope deliberately to see whether you bound it.
Stating an assumption aloud and pausing for correction extracts constraint faster than an open question, because the interviewer only has to say yes or no.
A usable frontend scope statement names four things: the primary user action, the device and network floor, the data volume per screen, and at least one explicitly excluded feature.
Scoping down is positive signal when the cut is named aloud with a reason, and negative signal when it happens silently.
A clarifying question is only worth asking if at least two of its possible answers lead to different frontend architectures.
'How many users do we have' is a backend-framed question in a frontend round; the frontend-relevant translations are items per screen, payload bytes per item, update frequency, and session length.
Requirements must leave three visible artifacts on the board — a scope list, an assumption list, and non-functional targets — because the rest of the round is scored against them.

viz.title: Question Value Tree
viz.whatIsDrawn: The open prompt sits at the root of a tree whose branches are candidate opening moves (a question, or an assumption offered for correction). Branch thickness encodes how much of the remaining design space that move eliminates; a minute meter runs inside the tree's header. As moves are chosen, surviving architectures at the leaves are pruned away in place, and a ghost path shows the reference opening for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: 'Design a news feed.' Which opening extracts more usable constraint per minute — six clarifying questions asked back to back, or three assumptions stated aloud and offered for correction? And which single move eliminates the largest share of the design space?
controls: pick the next move from a menu of eight questions and assumptions
reset and try a different first move
viz.insight: Requirements is a search over design space, not an information dump. The best move is the one that prunes the most alternative architectures per minute, and that is usually an assumption offered for correction rather than a question.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models the design space as a set of candidate architectures with predicates; each move is a pure predicate filter with a fixed minute cost. Unit test asserts the reference opening prunes more per minute than the six-question opening, so the pedagogical claim is enforced by the test, not by prose. Layout for the tree is precomputed at build time (no runtime layout library). reduced-motion: static pruned tree with the pruning counts labelled inside each branch.

drills.prompt: Twelve statements about a team inbox app. Sort each into: functional requirement / non-functional requirement / assumption to state aloud / out of scope / not the frontend's problem.
drills.answerSketch: Message threading = functional; 'INP under 200 ms while typing' = NFR; 'web only, no native shell' = assumption; 'billing' = out of scope; 'spam scoring model' = not frontend.

drills.prompt: Four clarifying questions for 'design a photo-sharing feed'. Pick the only one that has two answers leading to genuinely different frontend architectures, and say what each answer forces.
drills.answerSketch: 'Does the feed update live while the user is reading it?' — yes forces a subscription plus a merge/insert strategy; no allows a pull-to-refresh cursor list.

drills.prompt: The interviewer answers: 'it must remain usable offline for 24 hours.' Which two of your scope items become non-negotiable, and which planned exclusion is no longer available to cut?
drills.answerSketch: Local persistence and a write queue with conflict handling become in scope; the data model can no longer be waved off, because offline requires a durable client-side shape.

drills.prompt: Assemble a scope statement from slots: primary action / device and network floor / data volume per screen / one explicit exclusion.
drills.answerSketch: Slot fill from a fixed vocabulary, graded against a canonical set with synonym tolerance.

drills.prompt: The interviewer refuses to say whether offline is required. Write the assumption you will state aloud and exactly what you would change if you are wrong. 90 seconds, locked.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: assumption is falsifiable, the consequence of being wrong is named, and the change is localized to one part of the design rather than a restart.

failureModes: Asks 'how many DAU?' and 'do we need to handle 10 million users?' — backend framing that signals the wrong round.
Collects answers but never writes a scope statement, then designs against a scope the interviewer never confirmed.
Asks permission to scope down instead of scoping down and giving the reason.
Burns twelve minutes on questions whose answers could not have changed the design.
Lists functional requirements only, then has to be prompted for non-functional ones.
interviewProbes: What do you need to know before you start?
Assume anything you like — just tell me what you assumed.
That's a large surface. What are you going to leave out, and why?

meta-nfr-checklist.title: Non-Functional Requirements: Six Axes, Two That Matter
objectives: Select the two or three load-bearing NFR axes for a given product and defend the omission of the rest.
Convert each selected axis into a target with a number, a percentile and a measurement method.
Re-surface each committed NFR in the optimizations phase paired with the mechanism that satisfies it.
claims: The reusable frontend NFR axes are performance, accessibility, internationalization, security, offline/resilience and observability; regulated products add a seventh, privacy/compliance.
Reciting all six axes scores lower than selecting two or three and stating why the others are noise for this product.
An NFR is not stated until it has a number, a percentile and a measurement method: 'INP under 200 ms at p75 on mid-tier Android, measured by RUM' is a requirement; 'it should feel fast' is not.
The Core Web Vitals 'good' thresholds at p75 are LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms and CLS <= 0.1; INP above 500 ms is classified 'poor'.

Accessibility is the axis candidates skip most often and the one most likely to be contractually binding (WCAG 2.2 AA is the common target), which makes skipping it a visible senior-level gap even for internal tools.

Frontend observability means client-side error reporting, RUM for the vitals you committed to, and a release version tag on every event; without it none of your other NFR targets can be verified in production.

Claiming i18n commits you to naming its architectural consequences: CSS logical properties for RTL, ICU MessageFormat for plurals and gender, locale-split bundles, and roughly 30% text expansion from English into German.
An NFR stated in minute six and never mentioned again reads as a memorized list; each committed axis must reappear later attached to a mechanism.

viz.title: Which Axes Are Load-Bearing
viz.whatIsDrawn: A six-axis by four-product criticality grid (consumer feed, internal analytics dashboard, checkout, collaborative editor). Reference criticality is the cell fill; the learner's own assignment is drawn as a border overlay on the same cell, so the disagreement is visible without a side panel. Selecting a cell expands it in place to show the measurable target and the single mechanism that satisfies it.
viz.predictPrompt: An internal analytics dashboard used by 40 employees on managed desktop Chrome. Rank the six axes. Which axis that engineers routinely dismiss for internal tools is actually load-bearing here, and which axis that feels important is genuinely noise?
controls: reveal the reference weighting and the delta
expand a cell to see its measurable target and mechanism
viz.insight: Prioritizing the axes is the signal; reciting them is not. Internal tools do not escape accessibility, and dashboards fail on render cost rather than on bytes.
viz.buildNotes: This module ships the reusable NFRChecklist component consumed by every case study and by the mock rubric, so the reference weighting table lives in typed content, not in the viz. sim.ts is a scoring function over (product, axis) -> criticality plus the learner delta; unit-tested so the reference table cannot drift from the prose. Static SVG grid, one CSS transition on fill. reduced-motion: identical grid, transitions disabled, aria-live announces each delta as text.

drills.prompt: For a checkout flow, assign a criticality to each of the six axes, and for every axis you rate 2 or higher supply a measurable target chosen from the bank (units are checked).
drills.answerSketch: Security and performance at 3 (payment data, LCP <= 2.5 s at p75); a11y at 3 (WCAG 2.2 AA, keyboard path through payment); offline at 0-1 with the reason stated; i18n at 2-3 if multi-market.

drills.prompt: Fill in: 'The Core Web Vitals good thresholds at p___ are LCP <= ___ s, INP <= ___ ms and CLS <= ___; INP above ___ ms is poor.'
A transcript states five NFRs at minute six. In the optimizations phase, click the NFR the candidate never attached to any mechanism.
drills.answerSketch: Observability — stated as a target, never revisited with error reporting or RUM.

drills.prompt: The internal dashboard is now sold to EU customers. Which two axes jump in criticality and which mechanism does each newly require?
drills.answerSketch: i18n (locale-split bundles, ICU messages, RTL via logical properties) and privacy/compliance (consent-gated analytics, data residency of client telemetry); a11y moves from should to must under EU accessibility legislation.

drills.prompt: You have 40 seconds of NFR airtime for a real-time collaborative editor. Name the two axes you will state and defend omitting the others. Locked, then self-score against five criteria.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: each stated axis has a number and a measurement, each omission has a product-specific reason, and no axis is named that you cannot later attach to a mechanism.

failureModes: Recites all six axes as a list, with no numbers and no prioritization.
States 'it should be fast and accessible' and moves on, giving the interviewer nothing to score.
Drops accessibility because the tool is internal.
Never mentions observability, so no NFR is verifiable after launch.
Claims i18n support without naming a single architectural consequence of it.
interviewProbes: What are the non-functional requirements here?
You said it should be fast. Fast how, measured where, at what percentile?
How would you know in production whether you hit that target?

meta-frontend-estimation.title: Back-of-the-Envelope for Frontends: Bytes, Nodes, Frames, Heap
objectives: Compute order-of-magnitude estimates for wire bytes, DOM node count, per-frame milliseconds and heap for a described screen.
State which of the four budgets saturates first and explain why, using the threshold each is compared against.
Recognize and refuse backend-denominated estimation (QPS, shards, replication) as a scope error in a frontend round.
claims: Frontend estimation is denominated in bytes over the wire, DOM nodes, milliseconds per frame and megabytes of heap — not in QPS, shard counts or replication factors.
Lighthouse's default mobile profile is 'Slow 4G': 1,638.4 Kbps down, 675 Kbps up, 150 ms RTT, plus a 4x CPU slowdown, so 1 MB of transferred bytes costs roughly 5 seconds of download alone.
Text-like payloads (JSON, HTML, JS, CSS) compress roughly 3-5x under gzip and slightly better under Brotli, so a usable shortcut is to estimate uncompressed size and divide by about four.

The frame budget is 16.7 ms at 60 Hz and 8.3 ms at 120 Hz; after browser overhead your script should stay under roughly 10 ms per frame, and any single task longer than 50 ms is a Long Task by the Long Tasks API definition.

Lighthouse's DOM size audit warns around 800 elements in the body and fails around 1,400; since Lighthouse 13 (October 2025) it is an 'Optimize DOM size' insight that triggers on style recalculation plus layout exceeding roughly 40 ms rather than on raw node count alone.

A 10,000-row table at about 8 elements per row is roughly 80,000 elements — some 50x the failing DOM threshold — which is why virtualization is a requirement rather than an optimization above a few thousand rows.
On the frontend, DOM construction, style recalculation and layout typically dominate before network transfer or JSON.parse do, which inverts the backend instinct that bytes are the bottleneck.

A number is not an estimate until it is compared to a budget: '4 MB of JSON' is a number, '4 MB uncompressed is about 1 MB on the wire is about 5 s on Slow 4G against a 2.5 s LCP target' is an estimate.

viz.title: What Blows Up First
viz.whatIsDrawn: Four stacked budget bars — wire bytes, parse milliseconds, DOM nodes, heap megabytes — each carrying its own threshold line drawn inside the bar. Sliders for row count, columns per row, bytes per row and compression ratio drive all four simultaneously. The first bar to cross its threshold is outlined in place, and a ghost bar behind each shows the same design with virtualization enabled.
viz.predictPrompt: A table renders 10,000 rows by 8 columns from a 4 MB JSON response on a mid-tier Android over Slow 4G. Rank these by how far each exceeds its own budget: network transfer, JSON.parse, DOM construction, heap. Most engineers put the wrong one in first place.
viz.insight: Bytes are rarely the binding frontend constraint; node count and the layout work it implies are. Virtualization moves three of the four bars and barely touches network — which tells you where the remaining minutes of the round should go.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is pure arithmetic over the committed constant table (Slow 4G throughput, RTT, compression ratios, DOM thresholds, frame budgets) with no clock and no RNG; unit tests assert the constants match the cited sources and that the ranking for the canonical 10k-row case puts DOM first. viz.tsx is hand-rolled SVG bars (no chart library per the cut list). Threshold lines and crossing labels sit inside each bar. reduced-motion: bars render at final height with numeric deltas; aria-live narrates 'DOM nodes exceed budget by 57x; wire bytes by 2x'.

drills.prompt: A feed item is about 1.2 KB of JSON and 14 DOM elements. 50 items per page, user scrolls 20 pages. Give the order of magnitude for wire bytes and for total DOM nodes if nothing is recycled, and pick the bucket for each.
drills.answerSketch: 1.2 MB uncompressed, about 300 KB on the wire; 14,000 DOM nodes, roughly 10x the Lighthouse failing threshold — recycling, not compression, is the lever.

drills.prompt: Fill in: Lighthouse Slow 4G is ___ Kbps down at ___ ms RTT with a ___x CPU slowdown; a Long Task is any task over ___ ms; the 60 Hz frame budget is ___ ms.
The product changes from 10,000 static rows to 200 rows, each with a live sparkline updating at 4 Hz. Which budget becomes binding, and which one stops mattering?
drills.answerSketch: Frame milliseconds becomes binding (800 updates/sec across 200 components); DOM node count and wire bytes stop mattering at 200 rows.

drills.prompt: In this transcript excerpt, click the first sentence where the candidate leaves frontend scope, then choose the frontend-equivalent question they should have asked.
drills.answerSketch: 'We'll see about 50k QPS so we should shard the read replicas' — the frontend equivalent is 'how many items per screen, at what payload size, refreshed how often?'

drills.prompt: Which single change reduces the largest number of the four budgets at once for the 10k-row table, and which budget does it leave untouched?
drills.answerSketch: Windowing/virtualization reduces DOM nodes, layout milliseconds and heap; it leaves wire bytes untouched unless pagination is added too.

failureModes: Estimates QPS, storage and shard counts — the backend script — in a frontend round.
Produces numbers with no threshold attached, so nothing follows from them.
Assumes network transfer is the bottleneck and optimizes payload while shipping 80,000 DOM nodes.
Confuses uncompressed payload size with bytes on the wire, overestimating transfer by ~4x.
Cannot state the frame budget, so 'it might drop frames' stays an adjective.
interviewProbes: Roughly how much data are we shipping to render that screen?
How many DOM nodes is that, and does it matter?
What's your per-frame budget here, and what fits inside it?

meta-component-hierarchy.title: From Requirements to Component Tree: Deriving Boundaries, Not Copying the Mock
objectives: Derive a component hierarchy from state ownership and update frequency rather than from the visual layout.
Label each box with its inputs, outputs and owned state so the diagram is a design rather than decoration.
Name one extension point in the tree before the interviewer adds a requirement.
claims: A component boundary is justified by state ownership, update frequency or reuse — never by the existence of a visual box in the mock.
The first architecture artifact in a frontend round is a boxes-and-arrows diagram with three named layers: view components, a client store or cache, and a server-communication layer.
A tree derived from data ownership survives curveballs like 'add optimistic likes with rollback' because the state already lives at the level that has to roll back.
Components that update at very different frequencies belong in different subtrees, since a shared parent forces the slow subtree to reconcile at the fast subtree's rate.
Labelling each box's inputs, outputs and owned state converts a drawing into a design; an unlabelled box diagram produces no scoreable evidence.
The component tree and the render tree diverge whenever content is composed through children or slots, so any claim that 'this parent re-render is cheap' must say which of the two trees it refers to.
A senior answer names at least one extension point ('new post types plug in here as a renderer registry'), because interviewers routinely add a requirement around minute 30.

viz.title: Two Trees for the Same Screen
viz.whatIsDrawn: The same feed screen drawn as two trees: one derived from visual layout, one from state ownership. Ownership regions are shaded inside each tree. When a curveball is applied, the nodes that must change light up in place and each tree's header shows a live count of changed nodes, so the comparison never leaves the diagram.
viz.predictPrompt: Two candidates draw component trees for the same feed — one mirroring the visual layout, one mirroring state ownership. The interviewer then says 'add optimistic likes with rollback.' How many nodes does each tree have to change, and is there any curveball for which the layout-derived tree is the better answer?
controls: apply a curveball (optimistic like / new post type / live comment count / offline draft)
step the change propagation node by node
swap which tree is shown on the left
viz.insight: Boundaries drawn from state ownership localize change; boundaries drawn from layout distribute it across the tree. The layout tree only wins when the screen is genuinely static.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds both trees as data plus a pure propagate(curveball, tree) -> changed node set; unit tests assert the ownership tree's changed-set is a strict subset for three of the four curveballs and NOT for the static-screen case, so the module's honest caveat is test-enforced. Tree layout precomputed at build time and committed. reduced-motion: both trees static with changed nodes marked and the counts stated in text.

drills.prompt: Given eight requirement lines, place the components and mark which component owns each of five state slices.
drills.answerSketch: Graded against a canonical ownership map with naming tolerance; the load-bearing checks are that draft state is not at the root and that the like state sits at the item level.

drills.prompt: New requirement: the like count updates live over a websocket for every visible post. Which boundary in your tree breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Any boundary where the list owns per-item counts — the whole list reconciles at the socket's update rate; the fix is per-item subscription at the leaf.

drills.prompt: This tree places the composer's draft text in the App root. Click the two consequences that follow.
drills.answerSketch: Every keystroke reconciles the entire app subtree, and the draft can no longer be persisted or discarded per-composer when multiple composers exist.

drills.prompt: Order the derivation from requirements to boundaries.
drills.answerSketch: Requirements -> entities -> state slices -> ownership per slice -> component boundaries -> update-frequency split -> extension points.

drills.prompt: Defend in two sentences why pagination state belongs to the feed list rather than to the route component. 90 seconds, locked.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the reuse case, names what breaks if it lives at the route (two feeds on one route), and names the condition under which the route is right (pagination reflected in the URL).

failureModes: Redraws the mock's visual boxes and calls it a component hierarchy.
Draws boxes with no labels for inputs, outputs or owned state.
Puts all state at the root 'for simplicity', then cannot answer any performance question.
Cannot say which boundary would change when a requirement is added, because none of them were derived from anything.
Talks about the component tree and the render tree interchangeably when arguing about re-render cost.
interviewProbes: Walk me through your component hierarchy — and why is that a boundary?
Which component owns that piece of state, and who else needs it?
If I add a new post type next quarter, what changes?

meta-api-contract.title: Designing the Client Contract Live: Shape, Pagination, Errors
objectives: Design a client-facing list and mutation contract in the room: field set, pagination scheme, error shape, idempotency.
Choose a pagination scheme from the mutability of the underlying list and state the failure it prevents.
Justify request granularity against over-fetching bytes and under-fetching round trips.
claims: The Interface phase designs the contract the client needs — endpoint or query shape, field set, pagination, error shape — not the server's storage schema.

Cursor (keyset) pagination is stable under concurrent inserts and deletes; offset pagination duplicates or skips items whenever the underlying list changes between page fetches, which is the default failure of an infinite feed.
A list response needs items, a next cursor and an explicit has-more flag; inferring 'no more pages' from a short page is a bug whenever the server filters after applying the limit.

Over-fetching wastes bytes on fields the screen never renders; under-fetching produces a waterfall of dependent requests costing one RTT each, which is about 150 ms per hop on Lighthouse's Slow 4G profile.
A mutation contract must state its idempotency story: a client-generated request id, or an Idempotency-Key header, is what makes a retried like or purchase safe.

A typed error shape with a machine-readable code alongside a human message is what lets the UI branch between retry, re-auth and inline validation; an HTTP status code alone is not enough to branch on.
An optimistic write contract must define what identifies the pending entity before the server assigns an id — normally a client-generated temporary id reconciled on response.

Choosing REST, GraphQL or RPC only produces signal when tied to a stated requirement: many heterogeneous screens over one dataset favors GraphQL, a single well-known screen favors a purpose-built endpoint.

viz.title: Offset vs Cursor Under Live Inserts
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two lanes — server list state and the client's rendered list — advancing over time. Page fetches are arrows between lanes; head inserts and deletions are marked events on the server lane. Items that end up duplicated or skipped in the client list are outlined where they appear, with the running duplicate/skip counts printed inside the client lane's header.
viz.predictPrompt: A feed uses ?offset=20&limit=20. Between the page-1 and page-2 fetches, three new posts are inserted at the head. Exactly what does the user see? And does switching to cursor pagination fix the duplicates, the skips, or both?
controls: insert or delete items at the head between fetches
toggle the ghost 'no concurrent writes' baseline
viz.insight: Offset pagination is only correct over an immutable list. Cursor pagination removes duplicates and skips but not staleness — an item you already rendered can still be gone.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a deterministic list-mutation model with a seeded event schedule (no Math.random, no Date.now); unit tests assert offset pagination yields exactly N duplicates for N head inserts and that cursor pagination yields zero duplicates and zero skips under the same schedule — the claim is the test. Code snippets are pre-baked with Shiki at build time. reduced-motion: final-state comparison table drawn as two annotated lists with counts.

drills.prompt: Here is a response payload and the screen that renders it. Click the three fields the screen never uses, and the one field the screen needs that is missing.
drills.answerSketch: Unused: full author bio, raw EXIF block, internal ranking score. Missing: hasMore / nextCursor.

drills.prompt: The feed becomes personalized and re-ranked on every request. Which pagination scheme still works, and what must the contract add?
drills.answerSketch: Neither pure offset nor a value-keyed cursor survives re-ranking; the contract needs a server-issued opaque cursor bound to a session-pinned ranking snapshot, plus a snapshot expiry error code.

drills.prompt: Complete the list response type: `{ items: Post[]; ____: string | null; ____: boolean }` and say which field is not derivable from the other.
drills.answerSketch: nextCursor, hasMore — hasMore is not safely derivable from a short page when filtering happens after the limit.

drills.prompt: Fill the two missing lines in this optimistic mutation handler so that a failed request rolls back correctly and a retry stays idempotent.
drills.answerSketch: Capture the previous entity before mutating for the rollback path, and send a stable client-generated request id reused across retries.

drills.prompt: Order the Interface-phase moves.
drills.answerSketch: Enumerate each screen's data needs -> choose request granularity -> shape the list response -> pagination scheme -> mutations and idempotency -> error shape -> caching/staleness note.

failureModes: Designs database tables and indexes instead of the client contract.
Reaches for offset pagination on an infinite feed and cannot say what goes wrong.
Returns a raw HTTP status and expects the UI to branch on it.
Proposes optimistic updates with no rollback story and no temporary id.
Picks GraphQL because it is modern, with no requirement attached to the choice.
interviewProbes: What does the response for that screen look like?
How do you paginate, and what happens if someone posts while I'm scrolling?
The like request fails. What does the user see, and what happens if it's retried?

meta-tradeoff-defense.title: The One-Sentence Trade-off and the Condition That Flips It
objectives: State a trade-off in one sentence containing the axis, the choice, what is given up, and the flip condition.
Locate a design decision as a point in a parameter space and identify which parameter moves the boundary most.
Respond to a challenge by restating the flip condition rather than defending or capitulating.
claims: A complete trade-off statement names four things: the axis traded, the option chosen, what is given up, and the condition under which the choice flips.
'X is better than Y' with no named condition scores as an opinion; the flip condition is what proves the comparison was reasoned rather than memorized.
Most frontend trade-offs reduce to one of five axes: latency vs freshness, bytes vs interactivity, complexity vs correctness, memory vs recomputation, and control vs platform leverage.

Optimistic UI trades correctness for perceived latency; its value shrinks as server latency approaches the ~100 ms perceptual threshold while its rollback complexity stays constant, so the flip is governed by failure rate and the user cost of a wrong rollback rather than by latency alone.
Naming the option you rejected earns more than elaborating the one you chose, because it shows the size of the space you searched.
A trade-off defended with a number from your own estimate is scored differently from the same claim defended with an adjective.
When challenged, restating the flip condition ('you're right if writes fail more than about 2% of the time — then I'd drop optimism here') outperforms both defending the choice and abandoning it.

viz.title: Where the Decision Flips
viz.whatIsDrawn: A two-axis plane: server p99 mutation latency on x, write failure rate on y, with a decision boundary separating 'optimistic UI wins' from 'explicit pending state wins'. The learner's committed choice is plotted as a point inside the plane; dragging the parameters moves the point across the boundary, and the governing inequality is written inside the plot region rather than in a legend.
viz.predictPrompt: Optimistic UI versus an explicit pending state for a 'like' button. As p99 mutation latency falls from 2 s to 80 ms, at what point does optimistic UI stop being worth its rollback complexity — and which variable moves the boundary more, latency or failure rate?
controls: switch the action (like / send message / purchase) to change the cost of a wrong rollback
viz.insight: A trade-off is a boundary in a parameter space, not a preference. The sentence that scores names the parameter you would have to be wrong about.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts computes expected user cost for both options from (latency, failure rate, rollback cost) and derives the boundary analytically; unit tests assert the boundary moves further under a 10x change in failure rate than under a 10x change in latency for the 'purchase' action, which is the module's central non-obvious claim. This module also hosts the shared TradeoffDefense component (forced choice -> locked timed justification -> model answer decomposed into 5 criteria with three-level anchors -> self-score with token-absence flagging -> re-surface own answer at 14 days). Self-scores feed the confidence axis and the scheduler only, never mastery.

drills.prompt: Choose: virtualize the 5,000-row table, or paginate at 50 per page. Two-minute locked written justification, then self-score against five criteria with anchor answers at three quality levels. Your own answer re-surfaces at 14 days.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the axis, names what is given up (deep-linking and Ctrl-F for virtualization; interaction cost for pagination), cites one number from your own estimate, names the flip condition, and names the rejected option.

drills.prompt: Complete the template: 'I'd choose ___ over ___, giving up ___; I'd flip if ___.'
drills.answerSketch: Any completion where all four slots are filled with concrete, checkable content; the grader checks for a conditional clause in slot four.

drills.prompt: Four candidate sentences about server rendering versus client rendering. Pick the only one that names a flip condition, and say what is wrong with each of the other three.
drills.answerSketch: The winner names a measurable condition (e.g. 'if the page is behind auth and personalized, the SSR cache hit rate goes to zero and the argument flips'); the others are adjectives, appeals to popularity, or restated definitions.

drills.prompt: The action changes from 'like' to 'transfer money'. Which side of the boundary does the choice move to, and which parameter did not change at all?
drills.answerSketch: It moves to explicit pending state because the cost of a wrong rollback rises by orders of magnitude; latency did not change.

drills.prompt: In this 40-second answer, click the three adjectives that should have been numbers.
drills.answerSketch: 'huge payload', 'a bit slow', 'quite a lot of DOM' — each has an estimate available from the estimation module.

failureModes: Presents a choice with no alternative considered, so there is no trade-off to score.
Says 'it depends' without ever naming what it depends on.
Defends the choice with adjectives when a number from their own estimate was available.
Capitulates instantly when challenged, which reads as no conviction, or refuses to move, which reads as no reasoning.
Lists trade-offs generically ('more complexity') without tying them to this design's requirements.
interviewProbes: Why that and not the alternative?
What would have to be true for you to make the other choice?
I disagree — convince me, or tell me what would change your mind.

meta-deep-dive-steering.title: Steering the Deep Dive: Choosing Depth, Absorbing Curveballs
objectives: Select a deep-dive topic against three tests: bound by a committed NFR, frontend-owned, and carryable three levels deep.
Route interviewer interruptions between absorb now, park with a promise, and decline with a reason.
Deliver a closing summary in the final three to five minutes.
claims: The deep dive is where senior signal is produced; a round that covers every phase evenly and goes deep nowhere reads as mid-level.
The strongest deep-dive opening is a 20-second breadth index followed by an explicit choice and a reason for that choice.
A good deep-dive topic passes three tests: it is bound by an NFR you already committed to, it is frontend-owned, and you can carry it three levels — mechanism, measurement, failure mode.
An interviewer's interruption is a steering signal, not an attack: a question about a subsystem you skipped means they want it, and returning to your prepared thread instead is a scored failure.
A curveball changes exactly one requirement, so the correct first move is to state which parts of the existing design survive before proposing anything new.
'I don't know' followed by how you would find out — the API to check, the measurement to run, the baseline to look up — scores above a confidently wrong mechanism.

Reserving the final three to five minutes for a summary of scope, the two key decisions and the one thing you would do next is disproportionately valuable, because it is the last thing the interviewer hears before writing feedback.

viz.title: The Cost of a Tangent
viz.whatIsDrawn: The final fifteen minutes as a single track, reusing the phase-budget-timeline primitive with interviewer interruptions as event markers on the track. For each marker the learner routes it — absorb now, park with a promise, decline with a reason — and depth achieved on the chosen topic is drawn as a three-rung ladder filling inside the track. A ghost run beneath shows the candidate who absorbed every interruption immediately.
viz.predictPrompt: Twelve minutes left. The interviewer asks 'how would you make this feel fast on a three-year-old Android?' Is it better to list six optimizations or to pick one and go three levels deep? And where does the ghost run — the candidate who answered every interruption the moment it arrived — end up?
controls: change the number of interruptions from 1 to 5
viz.insight: Depth is produced by parking or declining, out loud. A 20-second breadth index is what buys the right to spend the remaining minutes on exactly one thing.
viz.buildNotes: Reuses the meta-radio-clock timeline primitive with an interrupt-event layer, which is the point: archetypes are shared across the app. sim.ts computes depth reached from the routing decisions; unit test asserts that absorbing all five interruptions never reaches rung three, and that the pure-depth strategy loses to index-then-depth when interruptions exceed two. reduced-motion: static final track with routing decisions and rungs labelled inline.

drills.prompt: Four deep-dive candidates for a collaborative editor. Pick the one satisfying all three selection tests and say which test each rejected option fails.
drills.answerSketch: Conflict resolution and cursor rendering under load passes all three; 'database replication' fails frontend-ownership, 'CSS architecture' fails NFR-binding, 'CRDT internals proof' fails carryability under time.

drills.prompt: At minute 35 the interviewer adds 'this must also work offline for a day.' Select every part of your existing design that survives unchanged.
drills.answerSketch: Component boundaries and the render path survive; the API contract gains a queue and conflict policy; the cache moves from memory to durable storage.

drills.prompt: Order the response to a curveball.
drills.answerSketch: Acknowledge -> state what survives -> name which committed NFR the new constraint binds on -> propose the change -> name its cost -> confirm the interviewer wants this before spending minutes on it.

drills.prompt: In this transcript the interviewer raises caching twice and the candidate returns to their prepared thread each time. Click both misses.
drills.answerSketch: Minute 28 and minute 33 — the second is worse, because a repeated question is an explicit steer.

drills.prompt: Ten minutes left and two viable deep dives. Choose one and justify in 90 seconds, locked.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: applies all three selection tests explicitly, names the rejected dive, and states what the chosen dive will demonstrate.

failureModes: Lists eight optimizations at one level of depth and calls it the deep dive.
Continues the prepared narrative after the interviewer has asked twice about something else.
Answers a curveball by redesigning from scratch instead of stating what survives.
Bluffs a mechanism rather than saying how they would find out.
Runs the clock to zero mid-sentence, with no summary.
interviewProbes: Pick one area and go deeper.
How would you make this feel fast on a low-end device?
Suppose it also has to work offline. What changes?
We have two minutes left — summarize.

meta-scoring-rubric.title: What the Interviewer Is Actually Writing Down
objectives: Score a transcript on separable rubric dimensions and justify each score with a quoted line.
Calibrate against below-bar / at-bar / above-bar anchors rather than against a feeling.
Distinguish evidence that appears in written feedback from thinking that stayed in the candidate's head.
claims: Frontend design rounds are scored on separable dimensions — problem framing, technical breadth, depth in at least one area, trade-off articulation, communication and steering, and frontend-specific judgment — not on a single 'was the design right' verdict.
Depth in at least one area behaves as a gate: strong scores everywhere else with no depth anywhere converges on mid-level or no-hire for a senior role.

Coverage is a floor and signal is the score: a transcript that skips a phase but produces a measured, defended decision often outranks a complete but shallow one, unless the skipped phase was load-bearing for the stated requirements.
Interviewers write down sentences, not diagrams, so a decision you drew but never verbalized usually does not appear in the feedback at all.
The most common written negatives are 'did not state trade-offs' and 'needed prompting to consider non-functional requirements' — both process failures rather than knowledge failures.
Self-calibration requires anchors: a below-bar, at-bar and above-bar answer per dimension turns self-scoring into a comparison instead of a feeling.
Self-scored long-form answers are evidence about your calibration and must never advance mastery, because self-ratings correlate weakly with interviewer ratings.

viz.title: Scoring Two Rounds Side by Side
viz.whatIsDrawn: Six rubric dimensions as paired horizontal bars for transcripts A and B. Below-bar, at-bar and above-bar anchors are tick marks drawn inside each bar. The learner sets every bar before the reference score is revealed; the difference between their score and the reference then appears as a bracket inside the same bar, with the justifying transcript line quoted beneath it.
viz.predictPrompt: Transcript A covers all five RADIO phases evenly with no technical errors. Transcript B never draws a data model, but derives a virtualization design with numbers and names the condition under which it would flip. Which one gets the senior offer, and on which single dimension does the gap open?
controls: set your own score per dimension
reveal the reference score and its anchor quotes
switch between transcript A and B
jump to the transcript line that justifies a dimension
viz.insight: The rubric is not additive across phases. It is dominated by depth-in-one-area and trade-off articulation — even coverage is the characteristic shape of a mid-level round.
viz.buildNotes: The rubric is typed content shared with the mock round and with the TradeoffDefense self-score, so there is one rubric definition in the codebase. sim.ts scores a transcript from tagged evidence spans; unit-tested so that transcript B outranks A only when the skipped phase is not load-bearing, preventing the module from teaching an over-general rule. Learner scores write to the confidence axis and the scheduler; they never touch mastery.

drills.prompt: Given this six-line excerpt, which rubric dimension does it produce evidence for — and which dimension does it sound like it covers but does not?
drills.answerSketch: It shows technical breadth; it sounds like trade-off articulation but names no alternative and no condition.

drills.prompt: Click the three moments in this transcript where good thinking produced no written evidence.
drills.answerSketch: Three points where the candidate draws or gestures without a sentence: the cache layer, the retry path, and the decision to drop notifications.

drills.prompt: Sort ten lines of real interviewer feedback into: process failure / knowledge gap / communication / scope error.
drills.answerSketch: 'Needed prompting for NFRs' = process; 'thought cursor pagination required a sorted numeric id' = knowledge; 'hard to follow the order of the design' = communication; 'spent eight minutes on database indexes' = scope.

drills.prompt: Score your own saved answer from the trade-off module against the six dimensions, flagging every dimension whose concept tokens are absent from what you actually wrote.
drills.answerSketch: Self-score with evidence highlighting; absence of tokens for 'alternative' or a conditional clause auto-flags the trade-off dimension for review.

failureModes: Assumes the score is 'did I get the right design', and optimizes for a correct answer instead of visible reasoning.
Assumes covering all five phases is the win condition.
Draws the decision and never says it, then is surprised by 'did not state trade-offs' in the feedback.
Self-rates generously with no anchors, and treats that rating as progress.
Reads a rubric as a checklist to recite rather than as the dimensions their sentences must generate evidence for.
interviewProbes: If you were the interviewer, what would you write down about that answer?
Which part of your design are you least confident about?
What would a stronger version of this answer have included?

meta-failure-transcript.title: The Five Ways Rounds Die: Annotated Transcript Diagnosis
objectives: Identify the seeding move that caused a failure, not the minute at which the symptom appeared.
Name the canonical failure mode and produce its verbalized recovery move.
Move up the ladder from a worked case to a faded case to a 12-15 minute mini-case before attempting a full timed mock.
claims: The five canonical failure modes are: drawing components before scoping, never stating non-functional requirements, drifting into backend territory (sharding, replication, QPS), asserting choices without trade-offs, and running out of time before any deep dive.
Failure modes are seeded twenty or more minutes before they become visible: a round that runs out of time at minute 40 was decided by unbounded scope at minute 4.
The recovery for 'I jumped straight to components' is to stop, state the assumption set your boxes already imply, and get it confirmed — not to erase the diagram.
The recovery for backend drift is an explicit handoff sentence ('I'll assume the server returns a ranked page; on the client that means...'), which converts a scope error into a boundary statement.
Backend drift is usually caused by pattern-matching a familiar prompt rather than by ignorance of the frontend, which is why it survives even in strong candidates.
A recovery only scores if it is verbalized; silently correcting course reads to the interviewer as inconsistency.

Attempting a full 45-minute round before you can complete one subsystem in twelve minutes measures panic rather than skill; the ladder is worked example, then faded case, then a 12-15 minute mini-case, then a full mock on a structurally analogous but different problem.
The independent stage must use a different case from the walkthrough, otherwise it measures recall of the walkthrough rather than design ability.

viz.title: Where This Round Actually Died
viz.whatIsDrawn: A 45-minute transcript rendered as a scrubbable strip. The learner drags a marker to the minute they believe the round became unrecoverable and must commit before any annotation unlocks. Annotations then appear anchored to the transcript lines themselves, never in a side panel, and a second track shows accumulating rubric signal with the divergence point from a ghost 'recovered' run marked in place.
viz.predictPrompt: This transcript ends with the candidate rushing the last ten minutes into a no-hire. Scrub to the minute at which the round became unrecoverable — before or after they drew their first box? Most learners choose a minute in the thirties; the reference answer is far earlier.
controls: commit a fatal-minute marker before annotations unlock
viz.insight: Rounds die from process decisions made in the first ten minutes and only appear to die in the last ten. Diagnose the seeding move, not the symptom.
viz.buildNotes: Transcripts are original authored content in typed MDX with tagged spans (failure mode, seeding move, recovery opportunity, rubric evidence) so linting can assert every failure mode has both a seeding tag and a recovery tag. sim.ts computes the accumulating rubric signal from tagged spans, unit-tested so the divergence point precedes the visible symptom by more than fifteen minutes. Prediction is gated: the scrubber will not reveal annotations until a marker is committed. reduced-motion: full annotated transcript as a static document with the signal track rendered as inline per-minute values.

drills.prompt: In this twelve-line excerpt, click the first line where the candidate leaves frontend scope and select which of the five failure modes it is.
drills.answerSketch: The line introducing read replicas — backend drift, seeded by pattern-matching 'feed' onto a backend prompt.

drills.prompt: The candidate drew components before scoping, at minute 6. Order the four sentences of the recovery.
drills.answerSketch: Name what you did -> state the assumptions the boxes already imply -> ask for confirmation of those assumptions -> state the one exclusion you are taking, then continue from the diagram.

drills.prompt: Same transcript, but the round is 30 minutes. Which failure mode becomes most likely, and which becomes essentially irrelevant?
drills.answerSketch: Running out of time before a deep dive becomes near-certain; over-long requirements gathering becomes irrelevant because the interviewer supplies scope in a shorter round.

drills.prompt: Three transcripts arrive at the same wrong final design. Which candidate is hired, and what distinguishes the diagnosis?
drills.answerSketch: The one who named the assumption that made the design wrong and the measurement that would have caught it — the design was wrong, the reasoning was auditable.

drills.prompt: Faded case: requirements and architecture are pre-filled for an analogous product. Complete the data model, interface and one deep dive in twelve minutes.
drills.answerSketch: Graded on the structural checks only — pagination scheme matches list mutability, one NFR is bound to a mechanism, one trade-off carries a flip condition.

drills.prompt: Run the 12-minute mini-case on one subsystem, then diagnose your own transcript against the five failure modes and name your seeding move.
drills.answerSketch: Not auto-gradable; self-diagnosis is scored against anchors and feeds the confidence axis and the scheduler only.

failureModes: Diagnoses the symptom minute ('they rushed at the end') instead of the seeding move.
Believes the fatal error was technical when it was a process decision made twenty minutes earlier.
Recovers silently and assumes the interviewer noticed.
Jumps straight from module study to a full 45-minute mock, panics, and concludes they are bad at design rather than untrained at pacing.
Reruns the same case for the independent attempt, measuring recall of the walkthrough.
interviewProbes: Looking back, what would you do differently in the first ten minutes?
You spent a while on the server side there — what was the frontend consequence?
You changed your mind mid-way. Talk me through why.

ds-api-shapes.title: Four API Shapes: Configuration, Composition, Slots, Render Props
objectives: Distinguish the four API shapes by what each one lets the consumer change and what it costs the maintainer.
Predict which shape a given requirement change breaks first.
Compute the type-permitted state space of a props-configured component and identify the single refactor that shrinks it most.
claims: A component with N independent boolean props exposes 2^N type-permitted states, almost all of which the design never specified; collapsing the mutually exclusive ones into a single discriminated variant union makes the invalid states unrepresentable rather than merely undocumented.

Configuration (props) keeps layout decisions inside the library and is cheap at the call site; composition (children) moves them to the consumer and is cheap to extend — the trade is consistency for flexibility, and it is a permanent one.

A slot prop typed as ReactNode (icon, footer, action) is a fixed hole in a layout the library still owns; children is an unbounded hole the consumer owns. Choosing a slot is choosing to keep responsibility for the arrangement.
A render prop exists only to hand internal state back to the consumer; if the consumer needs none of the component's internal state, a render prop is strictly worse than children.

Every prop on a shared component is a permanent commitment paid repeatedly by the maintainer at each future refactor and paid once by the consumer who used it — which is why prop count is a maintenance metric, not an ergonomics metric.
The reliable signal that a component needs composition rather than another prop is a prop whose only job is to change whether another prop is honoured.

A shared component should offer both a configured default path and a composed escape hatch; offering only configuration produces forks, and offering only composition produces forty inconsistent call sites for the same button.

viz.title: Prop Explosion: 6 Booleans, 64 States
viz.whatIsDrawn: An 8x8 grid where each cell is one combination of six boolean props on a Button (primary, destructive, ghost, loading, disabled, iconOnly). Cells are shaded three ways: specified by design, never specified, or internally contradictory. A ghost baseline overlays the 9 combinations the design spec actually defines. Annotations are anchored on the grid cells themselves; a counter strip sits inside the diagram frame.
viz.predictPrompt: Button has primary, destructive, ghost, loading, disabled and iconOnly as six independent booleans. Design specified 9 valid appearances. Before you run this: how many states does the type signature permit, roughly what fraction will your stories ever render, and which single API change deletes the largest number of invalid states?
controls: add/remove a boolean prop (watch the grid double or halve)
collapse the three appearance booleans into one variant union
step through contradictory combinations one at a time
viz.insight: Prop count grows linearly while the state space grows exponentially, and the untested region is precisely where bug reports come from. A discriminated union does not document invalid states — it deletes them.
viz.buildNotes: Pure SVG grid, no chart library. sim.ts enumerates combinations and classifies each against a declared spec set — unit-test that the count is 2^N and that collapsing k booleans into a union yields 2^(N-k)+k-1 states, which is the claim the visual makes. Scrub, never autoplay; reduced-motion renders the final grid with the same anchored annotations.

drills.prompt: You shipped Button with a `variant: 'primary' | 'destructive' | 'ghost'` union. Product now needs a destructive button that also reads as low-emphasis — 'destructive ghost'. What breaks first, and what are your two options?
drills.answerSketch: The union forbids the combination by construction — that was the point, and now it is the cost. Options: (a) extend the union with 'destructive-ghost' (states stay enumerable, name space grows combinatorially if this recurs); (b) split into two orthogonal axes (`tone` x `emphasis`) and re-enumerate which of the resulting products are valid. Wrong option: re-add booleans alongside the union, which gives you both failure modes at once.

drills.prompt: Six requests land on your Card component in one sprint. Label each: (1) add a footer with two buttons; (2) add `elevated` prop; (3) let one team put the image on the right; (4) add `headerAlign: 'left' | 'center'`; (5) let a team render the whole card as an <a>; (6) add `showDivider` which is only honoured when a footer exists. For each, say prop / slot / children / not-this-component.
drills.answerSketch: 1 slot or children; 2 prop (variant axis); 3 composition — a layout permutation is not a prop; 4 prop, but a smell if it grows; 5 not a prop at all, this is polymorphism (asChild); 6 the tell from claim 6 — a prop that gates another prop means the footer should be a composed part that owns its own divider.

drills.prompt: A team asks for `renderHeader={(state) => ...}` on your Accordion. Which single question decides whether a render prop is right here — and what is the answer if the header needs nothing but the open/closed flag?
drills.answerSketch: The question is: does the consumer need internal state that has no other route out? If the only need is open/closed, a compound `Accordion.Header` reading context, or a `data-state` attribute on the trigger for CSS, is simpler and does not force a function at every call site. Render prop earns its place when the consumer needs several internal values and must interleave them into arbitrary markup.

drills.prompt: An internal Table component has 34 props, of which 11 are booleans. Estimate the number of type-permitted boolean combinations, and estimate how many distinct configurations your 40 story files can plausibly cover. State the ratio.
drills.answerSketch: 2^11 = 2048 boolean combinations before the other 23 props multiply it further; 40 stories cover at most 40. Roughly 2% of the boolean space at best. The point of the estimate is that no test budget closes that gap — only a smaller state space does.

failureModes: Answers every new requirement with 'add a prop', and never notices the state space.
Says composition is always better, then produces a 40-line call site for a Button.
Conflates a slot prop (ReactNode in a fixed position, library owns layout) with children (consumer owns layout).
Counts 6 states for 6 booleans instead of 64.
Adds a boolean that gates another boolean and calls it backwards-compatible.
interviewProbes: Your Button has grown to 22 props. Walk me through how you'd cut it in half without breaking consumers.
When would you deliberately choose a slot prop over children?
How do you make an invalid combination impossible rather than documented?

ds-compound-context.title: Compound Components: Context Wiring, and Why cloneElement Fails
objectives: Design a compound component whose parts work at any depth and survive being wrapped by the consumer.
Justify when a compound API is over-engineering for the component in question.
Split a compound root's context so a volatile value does not re-render every part.
claims: Compound parts share state through a React context created by the root, so a part continues to work when the consumer wraps it, reorders it, or nests it inside another component.

Wiring compound children with React.Children.map plus cloneElement breaks as soon as a consumer wraps a child in any element, a Fragment, a conditional, or a motion component, because the mapped child is no longer the component the root expected.

A compound part rendered outside its root must throw a named error from its context hook; the alternative is a silent render with undefined context that surfaces much later as a mysterious layout bug.

Dot-notation parts obtained via a namespace import (import * as Select) stay separate named exports and remain tree-shakeable; attaching parts onto the root function with Object.assign makes the entire namespace reachable from one binding and defeats tree-shaking.

A compound API costs the consumer more call-site code, so it earns its keep only when the parts are genuinely rearrangeable or independently styleable; parts that always appear in the same order in the same place should be props.

Context propagates by identity: a root that recreates its context value each render re-renders every part, so the root must memoize, and volatile values (highlighted index, hover) belong in a separate context from stable callbacks.

Accessibility wiring between parts needs stable ids generated once in the root with useId and distributed through context — ids generated inside each part cannot reference each other, and hand-rolled counters break under React's concurrent rendering and SSR hydration.

A compound root that renders no DOM (a pure provider) keeps the consumer's layout free, but then the root cannot own focus or keyboard handling — that responsibility must move to a part that does render an element.

viz.title: Two Wirings, One Wrapper
viz.whatIsDrawn: The same Tabs JSX tree rendered twice side by side — left wired by React.Children.map + cloneElement, right wired by context. Each node is annotated in place with whether it actually received the selected state. A perturbation control injects a wrapper around one child. Ghost baseline: the unperturbed tree, drawn faintly behind each version.
viz.predictPrompt: A consumer wraps <Tabs.Tab> in <Tooltip> to add a hint. In the cloneElement-wired Tabs, what exactly does the root clone, and what is the first user-visible symptom: a crash, a tab that disappears, or a tab that renders correctly but never becomes selected?
controls: move a part one level deeper
toggle 'root memoizes context value' and watch re-render highlights
viz.insight: cloneElement wiring couples the API to the consumer's JSX shape; context wiring couples it only to the tree. Every 'why doesn't it work when I wrap it' bug report is this one bug.
viz.buildNotes: Two static tree diagrams; the only animated channels are (1) the state-received highlight propagating and (2) the re-render flash count. Annotations anchored on nodes. sim.ts models 'does this node receive state' as a pure function of wiring strategy and tree shape, unit-tested against the claim that cloneElement reaches depth-1 element children only.

drills.prompt: Given a 20-line Tabs implementation using React.Children.map + cloneElement, and a consumer call site where one <Tab> is wrapped in a permission check that returns a Fragment: identify the exact line where the wiring is lost and state the runtime symptom precisely.
drills.answerSketch: The Children.map callback clones the Fragment, so the injected props land on the Fragment (which ignores unknown props, and warns for non-key/children props); the inner Tab renders with its own defaults. Symptom: the tab renders and is clickable but never reports selected — no crash, no warning that names the real cause.

drills.prompt: Design the part list and context shape for a Combobox compound component that must support: a trigger, a filterable input, grouped options, an empty state, and a footer action. State which contexts exist and what is in each, and where useId is called.
drills.answerSketch: Root provider (no DOM) holds: stable context {ids, open/setOpen, select(value), refs} memoized once; volatile context {activeIndex, query} separate. Parts: Root, Trigger, Input, List, Group, Item, Empty, Footer. useId once in the root produces listboxId/inputId/labelId; Item ids derive from the root id plus value. Empty is a part, not a prop, because it needs the query.

drills.prompt: Your compound Select is tree-shakeable today. A consumer asks for `<Select>` to also work as a single-import shorthand: `<Select options={...} />`. What does adding that do to the bundle for consumers who only import the compound parts?
drills.answerSketch: If the shorthand is attached to the same root binding (Object.assign) or the root imports every part to implement the shorthand, every consumer of Select now pulls in all parts plus the shorthand's logic. Keep the shorthand as a separate module/export (`SelectField`) that imports the parts, so the dependency arrow points the safe way.

drills.prompt: Order these steps for converting a props-configured Dialog into a compound one without a breaking change: (a) ship parts as new exports; (b) reimplement the props API as a thin wrapper over the parts; (c) add a deprecation warning to the props API; (d) publish the codemod; (e) remove the props API in the next major.
drills.answerSketch: a → b → d → c → e. Parts first, then re-express the old API in terms of them so both are one implementation, then ship the codemod so the warning is actionable, then warn, then remove at the next major. Warning before the codemod exists generates noise nobody can act on.

failureModes: Reaches for cloneElement because it makes the demo call site shorter, then treats the wrapper bug as a consumer error.
Puts every value in one context object rebuilt each render, then blames React context for being slow.
Makes everything compound, including a Badge, and calls the resulting verbosity 'flexibility'.
Generates ids with a module-level counter, which breaks SSR hydration and duplicates across roots.
interviewProbes: Why does your Tabs break when I wrap a tab in a tooltip?
Where do the aria-controls ids come from, and who generates them?
When would you not make something compound?

ds-controlled-uncontrolled.title: State Ownership: Controlled, Uncontrolled, and the Hybrid
objectives: Diagnose which ownership mode a broken input is actually in, from its symptom.
Implement the hybrid ownership test correctly, including the null-vs-undefined case.
Explain why debouncing a controlled value is a defect and what to do instead.
claims: A controlled component renders exactly what its value prop says; if the parent ignores onChange the control appears frozen, and that is correct behavior rather than a bug in the component.
An uncontrolled component owns its state internally and takes defaultValue; changing defaultValue after mount has no effect, and the supported reset is remounting the subtree with a new key.

A hybrid decides ownership once, at mount, from whether the value prop is undefined; switching modes after mount is what produces React's warning about changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled.
The ownership test must be `value !== undefined`, not a nullish check, because null is a legitimate controlled empty value for a Select or a date picker.
A hybrid must call onChange on every user interaction regardless of mode, because consumers subscribe to onChange for validation, analytics and dirty-tracking without wanting to own the value.

Between an onChange and the parent's state landing, the text on screen belongs to the browser, not to React; any re-render in that window snaps the field back to the stale prop, which is why a debounced controlled input drops characters and jumps the caret.

Debouncing expensive work is correct; debouncing the value prop of a controlled input is not. Keep the field uncontrolled or locally controlled, and debounce only the derived effect (search, validation, persistence).

Copying a value prop into state inside an effect creates a second source of truth and one frame of stale UI; the fixes are to render from the prop directly or to reset the subtree with key, not to add another effect.
For a design system, every form primitive ships the hybrid because the consumer must be free to choose; an internal, single-use component should pick one mode and document it.

viz.title: Who Owns The Value?
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three stacked tracks over one keystroke event stream: the DOM/internal value, the prop value, and what is actually painted. Divergences between tracks are hatched and annotated inline at the moment they occur. Ghost baseline: the uncontrolled track, always drawn faintly for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: A controlled <Input> whose parent debounces setValue by 300ms. The user types 'react' in 150ms, and an unrelated context update re-renders the parent at t=100ms. What is on screen at t=100ms, what is on screen at t=400ms, and why is this a different failure from the field simply feeling laggy?
controls: parent behaviour: echoes onChange / ignores it / debounces 300ms
inject an unrelated re-render at a chosen time
viz.insight: Controlled means the painted value is a pure function of the prop. Latency the parent inserts between onChange and the new prop is not slowness — it is a window in which any render deletes the user's typing.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes an injected clock and an event list and returns the three tracks; unit-test the specific claim that with a 300ms debounce and a re-render at t=100ms, the painted track reverts to the last committed prop value. viz.tsx draws timelines in SVG with anchored callouts. Reduced motion: full timeline rendered statically with the same callouts.

drills.prompt: `const isControlled = value ?? false;` then `const current = isControlled ? value : internal;`. A consumer renders <Select value={null} onChange={...} /> to mean 'nothing selected'. Describe the bug the user sees and fix the line.
drills.answerSketch: null is falsy, so the component decides it is uncontrolled and renders internal state — the consumer's clear-to-null never clears the field, and selections stick after the parent resets them. Fix: `const isControlled = value !== undefined;` decided once at mount (or asserted stable across renders).

drills.prompt: Complete the hybrid hook: `const isControlled = ____; const [internal, setInternal] = useState(defaultValue); const value = isControlled ? controlledValue : internal; const setValue = (next) => { if (____) setInternal(next); ____?.(next); };`
drills.answerSketch: `controlledProp !== undefined`; `!isControlled`; `onChange`. onChange fires in both modes; internal state is only written when uncontrolled.

drills.prompt: Your search input is uncontrolled with a debounced onSearch. Product now needs a 'clear all filters' button elsewhere on the page to empty it. What breaks, and what are the two fixes with their costs?
drills.answerSketch: Nothing in the input can be told to clear — the parent has no handle on its value. Fix (a): go controlled and pay the per-keystroke re-render, keeping the debounce only on the search effect. Fix (b): stay uncontrolled and remount with a changing key, which is one line but also discards caret position, composition state (IME) and any local validation.

drills.prompt: A team reports: 'your Input drops characters when typing fast.' Rank these three hypotheses by likelihood and state the one-line check for the top one: (1) the parent debounces the controlled value; (2) the input re-renders too slowly; (3) onChange is attached with the wrong event.
drills.answerSketch: 1 is by far the most likely — check whether the value prop is derived from a debounced/throttled state, or whether the parent uses a transition that defers the value update. 2 almost never drops characters (React keeps the DOM value until a render). 3 would drop everything, not some.

failureModes: Uses `value ?? internal`, which silently breaks null-as-empty.
Adds a useEffect to sync the value prop into state and calls it 'supporting both modes'.
Debounces the controlled value to 'fix performance' and ships a caret-jumping field.
Claims a frozen controlled input is a bug in the component rather than the parent ignoring onChange.
Changes defaultValue at runtime and expects the field to reset.
interviewProbes: A consumer says your Select won't clear. Where do you look first?
Why does React warn about switching between controlled and uncontrolled, and what is the actual harm?
How would you support server-side-owned sorting state in a component that sorts internally today?

ds-polymorphism-refs.title: Polymorphism and Refs: asChild, Slot Merging, and React 19 ref-as-prop
objectives: Explain, per prop key, how a Slot-style merge resolves collisions between the primitive's props and the child's.
Explain why asChild beat the `as` prop in the ecosystem, in terms of type cost rather than taste.
State what a composable primitive must do with ref and rest props, and what breaks when it doesn't.
claims: asChild renders the element the consumer passed instead of the primitive's own default element and merges the primitive's props into it, so <Tooltip.Trigger asChild><a/></Tooltip.Trigger> emits a single <a> rather than an anchor nested inside a button.
A Slot requires exactly one React element child; a string or multiple children throws, and a Slottable marker exists to designate which of several children is the slot target.

In Radix's Slot merge, the child's own props win on collision, className values are concatenated, style objects are shallow-merged with the child's keys applied last, and event handlers are composed so that the child's handler runs first and the primitive's runs after it.

Radix's composeEventHandlers, used inside primitives, runs the consumer's handler first and skips the primitive's own handler if the event was default-prevented — a different rule from Slot's plain prop merge, and the reason 'my preventDefault didn't stop the dialog' depends on which mechanism is in play.

asChild composes refs so that both the primitive's internal ref and any ref the consumer put on the child receive the node; a naive cloneElement(child, { ref: ours }) silently discards the consumer's ref.

An `as`/polymorphic prop pushes element choice into the type system, forcing generic components whose props must union the target element's attributes — expensive in inference, error messages, and .d.ts size; asChild keeps the primitive's own prop types monomorphic and moves the choice into JSX, which is why the ecosystem converged on it (Base UI expresses the same idea as a `render` prop).

In React 19 a function component receives ref as an ordinary prop; forwardRef still works but is retained for compatibility, and `npx codemod react/19/remove-forward-ref` performs the mechanical migration.

Any primitive meant to be composed must forward its ref and spread unrecognized props onto its root element; without that, consumers cannot attach a tooltip, measure it, or add a data-testid, and they fork the component instead.

asChild changes which element carries the primitive's semantics, so it can silently destroy accessibility: passing a <div> to a Trigger produces a control with no role, no keyboard activation, and no focusability unless the consumer restores all three.

viz.title: asChild: Who Wins Each Key?
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two prop bags (the primitive's, the consumer's child's) flowing into one resolved element. Rows for className, style, onClick, ref, id, aria-*, data-state reveal one at a time, each annotated in place with the rule applied and the resulting value. The resolved DOM element is drawn below with its final attributes labelled on it.
viz.predictPrompt: <Dialog.Trigger asChild onClick={A}><button onClick={B} className="btn" /></Dialog.Trigger>. Which handler runs first, does the dialog still open if B calls event.preventDefault(), and what is the final className?
controls: step through prop keys one at a time
swap the child element: button / a / div / custom component that ignores ref
switch merge strategy: Slot merge vs naive cloneElement
viz.insight: asChild is a per-key prop merger, not a wrapper. Knowing that className concatenates, style shallow-merges, refs compose and handlers chain child-first is the whole difference between using it and debugging it.
viz.buildNotes: Static two-column table plus a rendered element; the animated channels are the row-by-row reveal and the resolved-value highlight. sim.ts implements the merge rules as a pure function over two prop bags and is unit-tested key by key against the documented Slot behaviour — this sim's correctness is the module's correctness.

drills.prompt:
A consumer writes
Open
. Mouse users report it works fine. Name three things that are now broken and the minimum fix.
drills.answerSketch: No role (nothing is announced as a control), not focusable (no tabindex, so keyboard users cannot reach it), and no Enter/Space activation (div has no default activation behaviour). Minimum fix is to pass a real <button>; the 'restore it by hand' path requires role, tabIndex and key handling for both Enter and Space, which is three chances to get it wrong.
