drills.prompt: React 19 primitive, no forwardRef: `function Trigger({ ref, asChild, ...rest }: Props) { const Comp = asChild ? ____ : 'button'; return <Comp ref={____} {...rest} />; }` — fill both blanks and state what breaks if `...rest` is dropped.
drills.answerSketch: `Slot`; `ref`. Dropping `...rest` means consumers cannot pass data-testid, aria-describedby, event handlers, or anything the primitive did not anticipate — the standard cause of a fork.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when a click lands on an asChild trigger whose child has its own onClick: (a) primitive's onClick runs; (b) child's onClick runs; (c) Slot composes the two into one handler at render time; (d) React dispatches the synthetic click.
drills.answerSketch: c (at render) → d (on click) → b (child first) → a (primitive after). The composition happens once at render, not per event; the child-first order is what makes 'my handler ran but the popover still opened' expected rather than surprising.

drills.prompt: Your library is on React 18 with forwardRef everywhere. The org upgrades to React 19 and a consumer's custom component is passed to asChild but is a plain function component that never accepted ref. What happens, and what changes about this after React 19?
drills.answerSketch: On 18, the ref is dropped and React warns that function components cannot be given refs — the primitive silently loses its node handle (positioning, focus management fail). On 19, ref arrives as a normal prop, so the child only needs to spread it onto an element; the failure becomes 'the consumer forgot to spread props' rather than 'the API forbids it'.

failureModes: Believes asChild wraps the child rather than replacing the rendered element, then wonders why there is no extra button in the DOM.
Assumes the primitive's onClick wins the collision or runs first.
Reaches for an `as` prop and discovers the generic signature two days later.
Ships a primitive that neither forwards ref nor spreads rest props and calls the resulting forks 'customization'.
Passes a div to asChild and considers keyboard support somebody else's problem.
interviewProbes: A consumer needs your Button to be a Next.js Link. Show me the API.
Both the trigger and the child define onClick. What is the contract?
What has to be true of a component before it can be passed to asChild?

ds-headless-a11y.title: Headless Primitives: Behavior Without Style, Accessibility Not Bolted On
objectives: Diagnose which of the five modal mechanisms a hand-rolled dialog is missing, from a keyboard trace.
Choose between roving tabindex and aria-activedescendant for a given widget and justify it.
Argue the headless split in terms of where accessibility cost is paid once versus forty times.
claims: A headless primitive owns behavior — focus management, keyboard interaction, ARIA wiring, portal/top-layer placement, dismiss semantics — and owns no visual styling, which is what lets one behavior implementation serve every brand and every product in the org.

A modal dialog needs five separate mechanisms: focus moved in on open, focus trapped while open, focus restored to the trigger on close, the background made inert, and Escape closing it. A hand-rolled div-with-a-role typically implements none of them.

The native <dialog> element opened with showModal() provides top-layer stacking, background inertness, Escape-to-close and focus containment without JavaScript, which removes the z-index war a portaled dialog fights.

inert and aria-hidden are not interchangeable: aria-hidden removes content from the accessibility tree but leaves it keyboard-focusable, so a background hidden only with aria-hidden produces focus that lands on announced-as-nothing controls.
aria-modal="true" is a declaration to assistive technology, not a mechanism: it does not move focus, does not trap it, and does not make the background inert.

A listbox or combobox has two legitimate focus models — roving tabindex, where real DOM focus moves between options, and aria-activedescendant, where DOM focus stays on the input and an attribute points at the active option. A combobox that must keep typing working requires the second.

An accessible name must be computed on the element that carries the role; putting aria-label on a wrapper div does not name the inner control, so the durable pattern is a label/aria-labelledby pair using an id generated in the component root.

Automated axe-style checks find roughly a third to a half of WCAG issues — contrast, missing names, invalid attribute combinations — and structurally cannot detect broken focus order, a missing focus restore, or a trap. That asymmetry is the argument for spending the accessibility budget inside primitives, where it is fixed once and inherited by every consumer.

Retrofitting accessibility onto styled components is expensive because correct roles constrain DOM structure: once forty teams have written CSS against the wrong structure, fixing it is a breaking change to all of them.

viz.archetype: focus-trajectory trace over a DOM outline, with ghost baseline
viz.title: Tab Path Through A Dialog
viz.whatIsDrawn: A static outline of the page DOM with an open dialog. A focus marker steps along the actual tab order, annotated in place at each stop. The ghost baseline traces the same key presses on a naive portaled div-with-role dialog. A live region inside the diagram prints what a screen reader would announce at the current stop.
viz.predictPrompt: A dialog is a portaled <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true"> with no focus trap and the background left visible. The user presses Tab from the last button inside the dialog. Where does focus go, what does a screen reader announce there, and does aria-modal="true" prevent any of it?
controls: step Tab / Shift+Tab / Escape one key at a time
enable each mechanism independently: move focus in, trap, restore, inert background, Escape
switch implementation: portaled div / native <dialog> showModal()
viz.insight: aria-modal is a promise. Only moving focus, trapping it, and making the background inert make the promise true — and the trace shows exactly which promise each missing mechanism breaks.
viz.buildNotes: Two animated channels only: the focus marker position and the announcement text. Everything else is static with anchored labels. sim.ts computes tab order from a declarative DOM model plus the set of enabled mechanisms, unit-tested for the specific claim that without a trap, Tab from the last dialog control lands on the next focusable node in document order behind the dialog.

drills.prompt: Keyboard trace of a custom Select: Tab reaches the trigger; Enter opens the list; ArrowDown moves a highlight; Enter selects and closes; focus is now on <body>. Name the defect, name the user it hurts most, and give the one-line fix.
drills.answerSketch: Focus restore is missing. It hurts keyboard and screen-reader users hardest: after closing, the next Tab starts from the top of the document, so the user is teleported. Fix: capture the trigger element on open and call .focus() on it after the close transition (and before unmount, or restore in a cleanup that runs after the element is back in the tree).

drills.prompt: You are building a filterable combobox whose input must stay typable. Choose roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant, and state the one symptom that would prove the other choice was wrong.
drills.answerSketch: aria-activedescendant. With roving tabindex, DOM focus leaves the input to land on the option, so keystrokes stop reaching the text field — the proof symptom is that typing after pressing ArrowDown either does nothing or is swallowed by option typeahead.

drills.prompt: Your dialog uses native <dialog> showModal(). Design now requires an exit animation and a dialog that can spawn a second dialog on top. What still works for free, and what do you now have to own?
drills.answerSketch: Free: top-layer stacking (the second dialog lands above the first without any z-index), background inertness, Escape. You now own: keeping the element mounted through the exit (::backdrop and display need allow-discrete transitions or a JS-held close), and deciding focus-restore ordering across two stacked dialogs so closing the inner one returns focus to the outer one, not the page trigger.

drills.prompt: Forty teams each build their own dropdown. Estimate the accessibility defect count if each implementation independently has a 50% chance of missing each of four mechanisms (focus restore, Escape, typeahead, correct roles). Then state what the number becomes with one shared primitive, and what it does NOT become.
drills.answerSketch: Roughly 40 x 4 x 0.5 = 80 defects, spread across forty places to fix. A shared primitive reduces the behavior defects to at most 4, fixed once. What it does not fix: contrast, incorrect labels supplied by consumers, and consumers who pass a div to asChild — a primitive can guarantee behavior, not the content or markup consumers hand it.

failureModes: Believes aria-modal or role="dialog" does anything mechanically.
Uses aria-hidden on the background and leaves it in the tab order.
Chooses roving tabindex for a combobox and then fights the input for keystrokes.
Names the dialog by putting aria-label on the portal wrapper.
Treats an axe pass as accessibility complete, having never pressed Tab.
Says 'accessibility is a design system concern' without being able to name a single mechanism a primitive owns.
interviewProbes: Walk me through everything that has to happen when your modal opens and closes.
Where does focus go when this closes, and how do you know?
Which parts of accessibility can a primitive guarantee, and which can it never guarantee?

ds-tokens-theming.title: Design Tokens in Three Tiers and CSS-Variable Theming
objectives: Assign a given value to the correct token tier and defend the boundary.
Design a theming setup where a brand swap and a dark mode swap are the same operation at different tiers.
Explain why a token whose value is another variable behaves differently under @theme and @theme inline.
claims: Tokens come in three tiers: primitive (--blue-600, a raw value with no meaning), semantic (--color-danger-foreground, meaning with no component), and component (--button-danger-bg, one component's contract). A component that reads a primitive directly cannot be re-themed without editing the component.

Runtime theming needs CSS custom properties because they inherit and cascade: a theme swap is one class on an ancestor, with no React re-render, no stylesheet reload, and no flash while a new sheet loads.

A custom property's value is substituted on the element where it is declared, and the computed result is what inherits. So --color-bg: var(--bg) declared at :root computes once against the light value and inherits unchanged into a .dark subtree that redefines --bg.

Tailwind v4 declares tokens in CSS with @theme, which both registers utilities and emits the variables; @theme inline substitutes the referenced variable directly into the generated utility, which is what makes a token defined as var(--background) respond to a .dark override — the reason shadcn/ui's Tailwind v4 setup uses @theme inline.

Dark mode is not an inversion of the light palette: elevation reverses (surfaces get lighter with depth rather than casting shadows), and saturated brand colors must be lightened or desaturated to keep contrast against dark surfaces.

Semantic token names must encode role, not appearance: --color-danger survives a rebrand, --color-red-button does not, and --color-brand-2 gives the next engineer no basis for choosing it over --color-brand-3.

Contrast is a property of a token pair, not of a token, so the verification surface grows with the number of foreground/background pairs a theme permits — an argument for fewer, more opinionated semantic pairs rather than a large palette.
shadcn/ui's Tailwind v4 themes express color in OKLCH, whose lightness channel is perceptually uniform, so stepping L produces ramp steps of even visual weight where the equivalent HSL steps do not.

A component tier is worth introducing only where a component genuinely needs an override point that the semantic tier cannot express; adding a component token for every property is how a token system becomes a second, worse stylesheet.

viz.archetype: three-tier dependency graph with theme flip
viz.title: Where The Theme Actually Changes
viz.whatIsDrawn: A DAG of primitive → semantic → component tokens feeding one rendered button, drawn together in a single frame with values labelled on the edges. Flipping to dark highlights precisely which edges change value and which do not. A toggle rewires the button to read a primitive directly, drawing the now-dead edge.
viz.predictPrompt: Your Button reads --blue-600 directly. Marketing ships a second brand, and the same button must also work in dark mode. Which tier do you edit for each change, how many components does each edit touch, and is one of the two changes free under a semantic tier while the other is only cheaper?
controls: rewire the button to read primitive / semantic / component tier
reveal the computed value at each node
viz.insight: The semantic tier is the only place a theme can be swapped. A component that skips it converts a one-line theme change into a codemod — and the same graph shows why a variable resolved at :root cannot see a .dark override.
viz.buildNotes: Static DAG; animated channels are the value-change highlight travelling down edges and the rendered swatch. sim.ts resolves the token graph as a pure function of (tier wiring, theme) and must be unit-tested for the substitution-site claim: a node whose value is a reference resolved at the root does not update when a descendant scope redefines its target.

drills.prompt: globals.css defines --background in :root and again in .dark. The Tailwind block is `@theme { --color-background: var(--background); }`. In the app, `bg-background` never changes in dark mode even though --background is clearly overridden. Explain the mechanism and give the one-word fix.
drills.answerSketch: --color-background is declared at :root, so var(--background) is substituted there against the light value; the computed result inherits into .dark unchanged, and the utility resolves to var(--color-background). Fix: `@theme inline`, which emits the utility as var(--background) directly so substitution happens on the element inside .dark.

drills.prompt: Assign each to a tier (primitive / semantic / component / not a token): (1) #0B57D0; (2) the background of a destructive button's hover state; (3) 4px; (4) the page's default text color; (5) the width of the sidebar; (6) the focus ring color used by every interactive element; (7) the border radius of the Card only.
drills.answerSketch: 1 primitive; 2 component (only if the semantic tier genuinely cannot express it — otherwise semantic danger-bg-hover); 3 primitive (spacing scale step); 4 semantic; 5 layout constant, not a design token — it is a component/layout concern; 6 semantic; 7 component, and a smell worth questioning before adding.

drills.prompt: You have 60 semantic tokens and a passing contrast audit. Marketing adds a third brand whose primary is a light yellow. What breaks first, and which decision made two years ago determines how bad it is?
drills.answerSketch: Foreground-on-primary pairs break first: white text on a light yellow fails contrast, and everything that hardcoded a light foreground on brand surfaces is now unreadable. The determining decision is whether the system exposes --color-primary-foreground as its own semantic token per theme (fixable in one theme file) or whether components assumed white — in which case it is a code change across every component.

drills.prompt: Your team proposes a component token for every CSS property of every component ('maximum themability'). Take a position in 150 words, timed, before seeing the model answer.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer decomposes into: (1) each component token is an API commitment that can never be removed without a breaking change; (2) themability nobody uses still costs review, docs and naming debate; (3) the semantic tier is what makes themes coherent — per-component tokens let two buttons legitimately diverge, which is the thing a design system exists to prevent; (4) the defensible rule is to add a component token when a real second consumer needs the override, not in anticipation; (5) the counter-position worth conceding: a small set of deliberate component tokens (surface, border, radius) genuinely prevents forks.

failureModes: Names tokens after colors, then cannot rebrand.
Skips the semantic tier because 'we only have one theme', then discovers dark mode is a codemod.
Assumes any CSS variable indirection automatically reacts to a .dark scope.
Adds a component token per property and calls the resulting sprawl a system.
Builds dark mode by inverting lightness and ships unreadable saturated brand colors.
interviewProbes: Add a second brand to this system. What files change?
Why does your dark mode not apply to this one utility?
Which of these three values should not be a token, and why?

ds-distribution-versioning.title: Distribution: Copy-In vs Installed Package, Semver, and Codemods
objectives: Judge which distribution model fits a given org, in terms of who pays the upgrade cost.
Classify a proposed change as patch / minor / major, including the cases semver does not cover.
Specify the full deprecation ladder for a breaking change, including what makes it actually land.
claims: The shadcn/ui model copies component source into the consumer's repository: consumers own and may edit every line, and there is no installed version to bump — which also means upstream fixes never arrive unless someone re-applies them.
An installed component package makes an upgrade one version bump for every consumer and makes local edits impossible without a fork. That is the inverse trade of copy-in, not a strictly better one.

shadcn's registry is a JSON contract, so an organization can host its own registry of copy-in components at its own URL and distribute them with the same CLI — the model does not require depending on the public library.

As of 2026 shadcn/ui defaults new projects to Base UI primitives while continuing to support Radix, which means the copy-in model's ownership promise now has to absorb an underlying-primitive migration — a concrete instance of the upgrade cost the model defers to consumers.

Semver on a component package encodes only the TypeScript API surface. Rendered DOM structure, class names, and visual appearance are not represented in any version number, so a patch release can break a consumer's CSS override without violating semver.
Adding an optional prop is a minor; adding a required prop, removing a prop, or narrowing an accepted union is a major; widening an accepted union is a minor.
Changing a default value is a breaking change even when no type changes, because the rendered output of every existing call site changes.

A migration is cheap only if it ships with its codemod: publish the major together with an ast-grep or jscodeshift transform, keep the old export working behind a runtime deprecation warning for one window, and delete it in the following major.

The honest cost of copy-in is the upgrade story: fund an internal registry and a codemod per breaking change, or accept that consumers' copies diverge permanently. 'Teams can just re-run the CLI' stops being true the moment a team edits the file, which is the model's entire selling point.

viz.archetype: propagation over a dependency graph (blast radius)
viz.title: Push One Fix, Count The Diffs
viz.whatIsDrawn: One design-system node surrounded by twelve consumer repositories, each labelled with whether it has locally edited the component. Injecting a change propagates along edges under the selected distribution model; counters inside the frame track repos fixed, repos still on old behavior, and person-hours spent.
viz.predictPrompt: A focus-trap bug is fixed in your Dialog. Under copy-in, how many of twelve consumer repos get the fix by doing nothing? Under an installed package on a caret range, how many get it — and which model carries the higher risk of an unrelated visual break landing in the same week?
controls: distribution model: copy-in / installed caret range / installed pinned
change type: bug fix / new required prop / DOM structure change / default value change
set how many repos have locally edited the component
viz.insight: Copy-in trades upgrade cost for edit freedom: the fix arrives everywhere or nowhere. You are not choosing the model with no failure, you are choosing the failure you can staff.
viz.buildNotes: Force-free fixed layout (positions committed, no runtime layout library). Animated channels: propagation highlight along edges, and the counter values. sim.ts is a pure propagation function over (graph, model, changeType, editedSet, codemod) — unit-test that under copy-in a fix reaches zero repos without action, and that under a caret range an edited-fork repo does not receive it either.

drills.prompt: Classify each as patch / minor / major, or 'semver cannot express this': (1) add optional `size` prop; (2) change default `size` from 'md' to 'sm'; (3) rename a wrapper div's class from .ds-btn to .ds-button; (4) widen `variant` to accept a new value; (5) narrow `align` from string to a union; (6) fix a focus-restore bug; (7) swap the underlying primitive library.
drills.answerSketch: 1 minor; 2 major (rendered output changes everywhere); 3 semver cannot express it — types unchanged, consumer CSS breaks, so it needs a communicated major by policy; 4 minor; 5 major; 6 patch by types, but behavior-changing, so it is worth a minor with release notes; 7 major regardless of whether props are identical, because DOM, data attributes and behavior all shift.

drills.prompt: A 400-engineer org with 30 product repos and a strong brand asks you to pick copy-in or an installed package. Commit to one and defend it in 200 words, timed, before seeing the model answer.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names who pays the upgrade cost under each; (2) reckons with fan-out — 30 repos means a security or a11y fix under copy-in requires 30 PRs and a codemod, which is a staffing question not a preference; (3) notes the compromise position (installed package for behavior/primitives, copy-in registry for composed app-level patterns); (4) states the guard that makes the choice survivable (private registry + codemod per major, or a caret range + visual gates); (5) does not claim one model is objectively correct.

drills.prompt: Order the steps for landing a breaking rename of `onSelect` to `onValueChange` across 30 repos: (a) delete the old prop; (b) publish the codemod; (c) accept both props, old one warns; (d) run the codemod across repos and merge PRs; (e) announce the deprecation window with a date; (f) release the major.
drills.answerSketch: c → b → e → d → a → f. Support both first so no consumer is blocked, ship the codemod so the warning is actionable, announce with a date, land the mechanical PRs yourself, then remove and cut the major. Cutting the major first, or warning before the codemod exists, converts your migration into thirty teams' backlog items.

drills.prompt: You chose copy-in. Security reports a prototype-pollution bug in a utility that was copied into 30 repos eight months ago, and 9 of them have edited the file. How does the fix land, and what does this change about your original decision?
drills.answerSketch: Codemod handles the 21 unedited copies mechanically; the 9 edited ones need individual review because the transform cannot assume the surrounding code. The lesson is not 'copy-in was wrong' but that copy-in requires an inventory: without knowing which repos hold which copy at which revision, you cannot even scope the fix. That inventory (a registry with recorded versions) is the thing that has to exist before choosing copy-in at scale.

failureModes: Treats copy-in as strictly better because it 'has no lock-in', with no answer for how a security fix reaches consumers.
Calls a default-value change non-breaking because the types did not change.
Believes semver protects consumers from visual and DOM changes.
Ships a major with a migration guide and no codemod, then wonders why adoption stalls at 40%.
Publishes a deprecation warning before there is a way to act on it.
interviewProbes: You just fixed an accessibility bug. Who has it in production tomorrow?
Is renaming an internal class name a breaking change? Defend it.
How do you land a required-prop addition across thirty repos?

ds-quality-gates.title: Quality Gates: Stories, Interaction Tests, axe, and What Visual Regression Actually Costs
objectives: Match each defect class to the cheapest gate that can actually detect it.
Judge whether a visual regression suite is worth its cost for a given system, with numbers.
Identify the four dominant sources of snapshot flake and the deterministic fix for each.
claims: Stories are a design system's executable specification: each story pins one state, which is what makes the same artifact addressable by interaction tests, automated a11y checks and visual snapshots at once.

A visual regression suite's cost is snapshots x viewports x browsers x commits; the highest-leverage reduction is snapshotting components rather than pages, because a page snapshot re-flags every component it contains on every unrelated change.

Snapshot flakiness has four dominant sources — unloaded webfonts, in-flight animations and transitions, non-deterministic data such as dates and generated ids, and image decoding — each with a deterministic fix. Raising the pixel-difference threshold is not a fix; it is a setting that hides real regressions.

Change-detection modes such as Chromatic's TurboSnap only snapshot stories whose module graph the commit touched, which is what makes visual testing affordable — and which silently misses regressions from a global CSS or token change unless those files are configured to force a full run.

Automated axe checks belong in the story runner but cannot verify focus order, focus restoration, or announcement quality; those require an interaction test with explicit keyboard assertions, or a manual pass.

Component tests should assert through the accessible interface — getByRole, keyboard events, announced names — because that is the contract both consumers and assistive technology depend on; asserting class names re-breaks on every refactor and proves nothing about behavior.

Documentation for a design system fails on findability before it fails on completeness: the pages that get used are 'which component do I use for X', do/don't pairs, and a copyable snippet. An exhaustive props table is table stakes and should be generated from types.

The right gate for a defect is the cheapest one that can see it: types for wrong props, unit and interaction tests for behavior, axe for attribute-level accessibility, visual snapshots for unintended CSS changes, and human review for whether the API is a good idea at all.

A visual regression suite pays for itself in proportion to how much shared CSS the system has: a token or base-layer change is exactly the class of defect no other gate can see, and exactly the change type teams make most nervously.

viz.archetype: defect-class x gate coverage matrix with cost meter
viz.title: Which Gate Would Have Caught This?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A matrix: rows are six real defects (wrong ARIA role, focus not restored on close, a 3px padding shift, a class rename that broke a consumer override, a dark-theme contrast failure, a misspelled prop), columns are gates (types, unit, interaction, axe, visual snapshot, review). Cells read caught / missed / flaky, annotated inline. A cost meter inside the frame sums CI minutes and monthly snapshot count as gates are toggled on.
viz.predictPrompt: You may enable exactly two automated gates. Which two cover the largest number of the six defect classes, and which defect class remains uncovered by every automated gate you could buy at any price?
controls: switch to a token-change commit and watch which cells flip
change team size / commits per day and watch the cost meter
viz.insight: Gates are not ranked by rigor, they are ranked by the defect class they can see. Two well-chosen gates cover most of the matrix — and 'is this a good API' is covered by none of them, which is what review is for.
viz.buildNotes: Static matrix; animated channels are the cell-state flip and the cost meter. sim.ts holds the defect x gate detection table and the cost model as data, and is unit-tested so that the pedagogical claim (visual snapshot is the only automated gate that sees the padding shift; nothing automated sees the API-quality defect) cannot silently drift when the table is edited.

drills.prompt: Your visual suite reports 40-80 changed snapshots on roughly one commit in four, and the team now approves diffs without reading them. List the three most likely causes in order and the specific fix for the top one.
drills.answerSketch: (1) Snapshots taken at page level rather than component level, so one shared component re-flags everything — fix by snapshotting stories, not routes. (2) Fonts loading after capture, producing metric shifts — fix by inlining/preloading the font and waiting on document.fonts.ready. (3) Animations in flight — fix by forcing reduced motion and zeroing durations in the snapshot environment. The team's rubber-stamping is the real defect: a suite nobody reads has negative value because it also gives false assurance.

drills.prompt: For each defect, name the cheapest gate that can detect it: (1) Button renders role="presentation"; (2) closing the dialog leaves focus on body; (3) a token change dropped contrast on secondary text in dark theme; (4) a consumer passed `varient` instead of `variant`; (5) padding changed from 12px to 9px; (6) the new API needs six props to render a link.
drills.answerSketch: 1 axe; 2 interaction test with explicit focus assertions (axe cannot); 3 axe run against the dark-theme story, or a contrast check across the token pair matrix; 4 TypeScript; 5 visual snapshot; 6 human review — no automated gate has an opinion about this.

drills.prompt: 180 components, 4 stories each, 2 viewports, 2 browsers, 20 commits per weekday. Estimate monthly snapshot volume with and without change-detection, and state the assumption change-detection makes that your token file violates.
drills.answerSketch: 180 x 4 = 720 stories; x2 viewports x2 browsers = 2,880 snapshots per full run; x ~440 runs/month = roughly 1.27M snapshots — clearly unaffordable. Change detection cuts this to the stories touched by each commit, typically one to two orders of magnitude less. The assumption it makes is that the module graph captures the blast radius, which a global token or base-layer CSS change violates — those must be configured to force a full run.

drills.prompt: Leadership wants the visual regression suite cut to fund headcount. Take a position in 150 words, timed, before seeing the model answer.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names the defect class that becomes invisible without it — unintended CSS/token regressions, the class no other gate sees; (2) quantifies rather than asserts, using snapshot volume and diff-review time; (3) offers a scoped middle position (keep it on the base layer, tokens and 20 highest-fan-in components; drop it elsewhere) rather than all-or-nothing; (4) admits the honest cost, including review fatigue and flake; (5) states the leading indicator that would prove the cut was wrong — a rise in CSS regressions reported by consumers rather than caught in CI.

failureModes: Treats an axe pass as accessibility done, having never asserted a focus order.
Raises the pixel threshold until the suite is quiet and calls the flake solved.
Snapshots whole pages and drowns; concludes visual testing does not work.
Asserts on class names in component tests, so every refactor is a red build.
Enables change detection and does not force a full run on token or base CSS changes.
Answers 'more tests' instead of naming which gate sees which defect.
interviewProbes: What does your visual regression suite catch that nothing else does — and what does it cost per month?
How do you test that focus is restored?
Your snapshot suite is flaky. Walk me through the diagnosis.

ds-adoption-migration.title: Adoption and Migration: Strangler Fig, Lint Ratchets, and Build vs Buy
objectives: Judge a migration plan by its probability of surviving a mid-flight org change, not by its best-case date.
Specify how adoption is measured such that the number cannot be gamed by intent.
Take a defensible build-vs-buy position with the cost curve, not the component count.
claims: Strangler-fig migration keeps both systems running and converts one surface at a time behind a boundary; the freeze-and-rewrite alternative fails because product work does not stop for it, and the rewrite is cancelled at the first re-prioritization.

Adoption must be measured from the import graph in CI — legacy versus design-system imports per repository, trended over time — because component counts and surveys measure intent and inventory, not use.

A no-restricted-imports rule on the legacy path with a per-file allowlist that may only shrink converts migration from a campaign into a ratchet: new violations become impossible and existing ones become a visible, monotonically decreasing countdown.

Dual-running requires the two systems to be visually coexistable on the same page; if the new tokens make adjacent old components look broken, teams will refuse partial migration and the strangler stalls at the page boundary.

A design system is a product whose users can decline it: the adoption blockers that actually bind are a missing component, a slow contribution path, and unanswered support questions — not documentation polish.

Build-versus-buy is not settled by component count. Buying (MUI, Ant) is cheaper until the design requirements diverge from the vendor's model, at which point override cost grows faster than linearly; the durable middle path is buying behavior (headless primitives) and building appearance.

The recurring cost of a design system is support, review and migration, not authoring — so a system with no funded owner degrades into a component graveyard regardless of how good the components were on day one.
A migration deadline shipped without a codemod and an enforcing lint rule is a request, and product teams correctly deprioritize requests against their own roadmaps.

Migration progress must be legible to leadership in the same units they fund — repos converted, violations remaining, and support hours — or the funding is withdrawn at the first budget review, which is the most common cause of half-migrated systems.

viz.archetype: two-strategy adoption curve with a velocity-tax channel
viz.title: Big Bang vs Strangler, Through One Re-Org
viz.whatIsDrawn: Adoption percentage over eight quarters for two strategies drawn on one set of axes, with a second, lower channel showing the velocity tax each imposes on product teams. Disruption events are marked on the timeline itself. Ghost baseline: the do-nothing curve.
viz.predictPrompt: Two quarters in, a rebrand lands and a re-org moves two of the four design-system engineers. Which strategy is further ahead at quarter eight — and which one is more likely to be cancelled at quarter three, and why is that second number the one that decides the answer?
controls: inject an event: rebrand / re-org / a new required component / a hiring freeze
turn the lint ratchet on or off
set team count and legacy surface size
viz.insight: Migration strategies are judged by their probability of surviving a mid-flight org change, not by their best-case completion date. A strategy that delivers value every quarter keeps its funding; one that delivers at the end has to survive every budget review before it delivers anything.
viz.buildNotes: Hand-rolled SVG line chart (no chart library, per the cut list). Animated channels: the two curves advancing quarter by quarter, and the velocity-tax band. Events are static markers with anchored labels. sim.ts is a seeded, deterministic model — no Math.random at render — unit-tested so that injecting a cancellation event at Q3 produces the documented divergence.

drills.prompt: You inherit a 6-year-old app with three UI libraries and 30 product engineers. Leadership offers either two engineers for four quarters, or eight engineers for one quarter. Commit to one and defend it in 200 words, timed.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) recognizes the eight-for-one-quarter offer is a rewrite in disguise and cannot include adoption, only authoring; (2) names what two-for-four-quarters buys that the burst cannot — a ratchet, codemods, and support presence during the quarters teams actually migrate; (3) concedes the real case for the burst (a hard external deadline such as a rebrand launch or an accessibility ruling); (4) states the first thing built either way — the import-graph metric — because neither plan is steerable without it; (5) commits, rather than hedging.

drills.prompt: Order the first five moves of a strangler migration: (a) publish the codemod for the top-3 most-imported legacy components; (b) instrument the import graph in CI; (c) add no-restricted-imports with a full allowlist of current violations; (d) make old and new visually coexistable on one page; (e) convert one high-traffic surface end to end as the reference.
drills.answerSketch: b → c → d → e → a. Measure before you move; ratchet immediately so the hole stops getting deeper while you are still planning; make coexistence possible or nothing can be partial; prove it once on a real surface so the reference exists; then scale with codemods on the highest-fan-in components. Shipping the codemod first optimizes the step that is not the bottleneck.

drills.prompt: A migration dashboard shows 'components migrated: 84/90 (93%)' while consumers still report the old library everywhere. What is the metric measuring, what should it measure, and what is the one query that gives the real number?
drills.answerSketch: It measures authoring — how many replacements exist in the design system — not use. The real metric is per-repo import counts of the legacy package versus the new one, weighted by call sites, trended weekly. The query is a CI job that parses imports across all repos (or reads the lint allowlist size) and publishes the count; the allowlist length is itself a serviceable proxy that cannot be gamed.

drills.prompt: Your strangler plan assumes both systems coexist on a page. A new brand ships mid-migration and makes the legacy components look visibly wrong beside the new ones. What breaks first, and what are your two options?
drills.answerSketch: Partial migration breaks: teams will not ship a page that looks half-broken, so they either wait for a full-page conversion (slow, and now blocking) or revert to legacy for the whole page (regression). Options: (a) back-port the new tokens into the legacy components so they are visually neutral — cheap if legacy reads variables, expensive if it hardcodes values; (b) redraw the migration unit from component to whole-page/route, which raises the batch size and slows the ratchet but restores visual coherence.

failureModes: Proposes a freeze-and-rewrite and cannot say what ships in quarter one.
Reports adoption as 'components built' and is surprised nobody is using them.
Announces a deadline with no codemod and no lint rule, then blames product teams.
Answers build-vs-buy with component counts instead of a divergence cost curve.
Never funds ongoing support, then attributes the graveyard to poor component quality.
interviewProbes: How do you know how much of the org is actually on your system?
A team says they can't migrate this quarter. What do you do?
When would you buy MUI instead of building on headless primitives?

ds-case-table-select.title: Capstone: Design the API for a Table (then a Select)
objectives: Design a Table API that separates data model, interaction state, and rendering before naming a prop.
Predict which earlier API decision a late requirement (virtualization, server-side sorting) turns into a breaking change.
Run the same method independently on a structurally analogous but different component (Select) under time pressure.
claims: A Table API has three separable surfaces — the data and column model, the interaction state (sorting, selection, expansion, pagination), and the rendering — and the staff-level answer separates them so any one can be replaced without the other two.

Column definitions belong in a data structure rather than in <Column> children as soon as columns are computed, reordered, or persisted, because JSX children cannot be serialized into a saved view or a user preference.

Every piece of table interaction state must be optionally controllable (sorting / onSortingChange, and the same for selection and pagination), because server-side sorting means the parent owns that state — a table that can only sort internally cannot do server-side sorting at all.

Row virtualization constrains the API upstream: it rules out intrinsic-height rows without measurement, forces the sticky header out of the scrolling container, and breaks native browser find-in-page. Those constraints must be visible in the API rather than discovered after adoption.

Cell rendering must be a slot — a render function per column — because the alternative, a `type: 'currency' | 'date' | ...` enum, grows a new case for every product need forever and eventually reimplements formatting inside the design system.
The Table, Modal and Select probes all score the same underlying thing: whether the candidate separates state ownership, behavior and presentation before naming a single prop.

The correct first move in an API-design interview is to enumerate the consumers and the escape hatches each one requires, then choose the API shape; starting from the prop list is the specific move that produces a forty-prop component in twenty-five minutes.

A component's compatibility surface is everything a consumer can observe — props, DOM structure, class names, focus behavior, and announced text — so deciding which of those you promise is itself part of designing the API.
A staff-level answer states what it will not support and why, because an API that claims to support everything has made no design decisions and will absorb every future requirement as a prop.

viz.archetype: requirement-arrival timeline against two candidate APIs
viz.title: Five Requirements, Two APIs
viz.whatIsDrawn: A timeline of five requirements arriving in order (server-side sorting, selection persisted to the URL, expandable rows, a sticky action column, 50,000 rows) run against two candidate Table APIs drawn side by side: props-configured, and headless model plus composed rendering. Each arrival marks, in place, whether the API absorbs it, needs a new prop, or needs a breaking change. Running prop count is annotated on each candidate.
viz.predictPrompt: Requirement five is '50,000 rows'. Which of the four earlier decisions — server-side sorting, URL-persisted selection, expandable rows, sticky action column — becomes a breaking change once virtualization arrives, and which API shape had already paid for it without knowing virtualization was coming?
controls: step requirements one at a time
toggle the third candidate: fully-composed table with no model
reveal running prop count and breaking-change count
viz.insight: An API is not evaluated against today's requirements but against the one that arrives after you ship. The shape that absorbs virtualization is the one that separated the data model from rendering on day one — not because it anticipated virtualization, but because it never coupled row height to cell content.
viz.buildNotes: Static two-column comparison; animated channels are the requirement marker advancing and the prop/breaking-change counters. sim.ts encodes each API shape's absorption rule per requirement as data and is unit-tested against the module's claims — especially that the props-configured shape requires a breaking change at virtualization while the model-plus-slots shape does not.

drills.prompt: WORKED then FADED. Stage 1 shows a complete worked walkthrough of the Table API (consumers, three surfaces, controllable state, cell slots, what is explicitly unsupported). Stage 2 gives you the same case with the consumer list and the three surfaces pre-filled — you supply the controllable-state list, the slot boundaries, and the two things you refuse to support.
drills.answerSketch: Controllable: sorting, selection, expansion, pagination, column sizing — each as value + onChange, each optional. Slots: header cell, body cell per column, empty state, loading state, row actions. Explicitly unsupported: nested/grouped headers in v1, and per-cell editing — both stated with the reason (each doubles the interaction-state surface) and a composition escape hatch instead.

drills.prompt: INDEPENDENT (12-15 min, timed, one subsystem). Design the API for a Select that must support: single and multiple selection, async-loaded options, free-text creation of new options, and a form library owning the value. Do not look at the Table answer. State the three surfaces, the controllable state, the slots, and one thing you refuse to support.
drills.answerSketch: Structurally analogous, deliberately different content. Surfaces: option/value model (option shape, value identity — id not object reference), interaction state (open, query, highlighted index, value), rendering (trigger, option, group, empty, loading, create-new row). Controllable: value (hybrid, undefined-test, null is a valid empty), open, and query — because async loading means the parent owns fetching keyed off query. Slots: option renderer and empty/loading, not a `type` enum. Refuse: arbitrary nesting depth of groups. Graded against a rubric, not an exact answer.

drills.prompt: Your Table API ships. Six months later a team needs each row to expand into an arbitrary detail panel of unbounded height, and another team needs 50k rows virtualized. Which requirement makes the other one expensive, and what would you have had to decide on day one to keep both cheap?
drills.answerSketch: Variable-height expandable rows and virtualization conflict: virtualization needs to know or measure row height, and an arbitrary detail panel is unmeasurable until rendered. Day-one decision: make row height an explicit, declared part of the model (fixed, estimated + measured, or unvirtualizable) rather than an emergent property of cell content — so the expanding row declares 'measured' and pays only a measurement pass instead of forcing a rewrite of the row renderer.

drills.prompt: Twenty minutes into a Table design round the interviewer adds five things at once: CSV export, column reordering by drag, i18n of headers, row-level permissions, and printing. Triage into: belongs in this API / belongs to the consumer / belongs to a different layer entirely. Justify each in one line.
drills.answerSketch: CSV export — consumer's, it needs the source data not the table's view state (though the table should expose the sorted/filtered row model to make it possible). Column reordering — this API, because it is column-model state and must be controllable to be persisted. i18n of headers — consumer's, headers are already slots/strings the consumer supplies. Row-level permissions — different layer, a data concern that should shape the rows before they reach the table. Printing — different layer (CSS + a non-virtualized render path), and worth explicitly refusing in a virtualized table.

drills.prompt: The interviewer says: 'TanStack Table already exists. Why are you designing this at all?' Answer in 150 words, timed, before seeing the model answer.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) distinguishes the headless model (which you should buy) from the design system's presentational contract (which you must own, because it encodes tokens, a11y and DOM structure); (2) states what wrapping costs — the wrapper's API is now your compatibility surface even though the model is someone else's; (3) names the specific risk of exposing the vendor's types directly through your API (their major becomes your major); (4) does not answer with NIH pride or with pure deference; (5) concludes with an explicit boundary: vendor model internal, your props and DOM public.

failureModes: Starts listing props at minute two and has forty by minute twenty-five.
Makes sorting internal-only, then cannot answer the server-side sorting follow-up.
Puts columns in JSX children, then cannot persist or reorder a user's saved view.
Adds a `type` enum for cell formatting and owns currency formatting forever.
Claims the API supports everything and therefore has decided nothing.
Rebuilds the walkthrough's Table answer for the Select prompt instead of re-running the method.
interviewProbes: Design the API for a Table. Start wherever you want — but tell me why you started there.
The parent now owns sorting. What changes in your API?
What will this component deliberately not do, and how do consumers handle those cases?
Same exercise, Select instead. Ten minutes.

found-nav-lifecycle.title: Navigation, End to End
objectives: Narrate the phases from user gesture to interactive in fixed order, naming the boundary event and the observable metric at each phase.
Localise a symptom (slow TTFB vs slow LCP vs slow INP) to the phase that must own it, before proposing any fix.
Distinguish the three navigation classes — cold navigation, back/forward restore from bfcache, and SPA soft navigation — by what work each skips.
claims: Navigation Timing exposes the phases in a fixed order — startTime, redirect, service worker start, DNS, TCP connect, TLS, request, responseStart, DOM processing, load — and while any phase can be zero-length, none can be reordered.
TTFB is responseStart minus navigation start, so it includes redirects, DNS, TCP, TLS and server think time; a server that responds in 40ms can still produce a 1s TTFB.
The HTML response is parsed incrementally as bytes arrive: the browser builds DOM and dispatches subresource requests before the document has finished downloading.
DOMContentLoaded fires once the HTML is parsed and all deferred scripts have executed; the load event additionally waits for images, stylesheets and iframes.
A back/forward navigation served from bfcache issues no network request and performs no parse: the page resumes with its existing JS heap and DOM and fires pageshow with persisted === true.

Cache-Control: no-store on the document response makes the page ineligible for bfcache in Chrome and Firefox, so a blanket 'no-store everything' security policy silently deletes the largest available back-navigation win.

103 Early Hints lets an origin send Link: rel=preload headers before the final response status, overlapping server think time with subresource fetching — it is the supported replacement for HTTP/2 Server Push.
A client-side route change in an SPA creates no Navigation Timing entry, so soft navigations are invisible to field data unless explicitly instrumented.

viz.title: One Navigation, Every Phase
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single horizontal navigation timeline segmented into labelled phases (redirect, DNS, connect, TLS, request, TTFB, parse, first paint), each phase filling as the playhead advances. A ghost baseline of the same navigation restored from bfcache is drawn directly underneath on the same time axis. Phase labels and durations are anchored inside each segment, never in a side panel; at most 7 labels are visible at once because sub-phases collapse until the playhead enters them.
viz.predictPrompt: Your team cuts server render time from 400ms to 40ms. Field p75 TTFB moves from 1.15s to 1.10s. Before running the sim: commit to where the missing second is spent, and to whether any change the backend team can make will recover it.
controls: Step / scrub the playhead one phase at a time (no autoplay)
Toggle a 301 apex-to-www redirect into the chain
Toggle connection state: cold vs warm socket
Toggle navigation type: fresh load vs bfcache restore vs SPA soft navigation
viz.insight: TTFB is a sum of phases that mostly do not belong to the server, and a bfcache restore deletes nearly the entire timeline — which is why the biggest available win on a repeat-visit journey is usually a header, not code.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure phase-duration reducer taking an injected clock and a seeded RNG for jitter; unit tests assert phase ordering invariants and that the bfcache variant produces zero network phases. prefers-reduced-motion renders the fully-revealed static timeline with all annotations. Live region announces 'Phase 4 of 8: TLS, 92ms, cumulative 310ms'.

drills.prompt: Order the phases of a cold cross-origin navigation with one redirect, from user gesture to first contentful paint. Distractors include 'CSSOM construction' and 'service worker start', which must be placed correctly rather than discarded.
drills.answerSketch: gesture -> SW start -> DNS -> TCP -> TLS -> request -> 301 -> DNS/TCP/TLS for new host (or reuse) -> request -> responseStart -> incremental parse -> CSSOM -> render tree -> FCP.

drills.prompt: Given a five-row phase table for a p75 navigation (redirect 340ms, DNS 0ms, connect 210ms, TLS 190ms, request+response 90ms, parse 120ms), select the single phase to attack first and the one proposed fix that cannot possibly help.
The requirement changes: security asks for Cache-Control: no-store on all HTML. Select every consequence that follows, and name which metric regresses on the back button specifically.
Complete: 'DOMContentLoaded fires after the HTML is parsed and all ____ scripts have run; a bfcache restore fires ____ with persisted === ____.'

Your RUM shows healthy p75 LCP but users complain the site 'feels slow'. In 150 words, defend a hypothesis about which navigation class your instrumentation is failing to see, and state the one measurement that would confirm it. (Timed, locked, then self-scored against 5 criteria.)

failureModes: Treats TTFB as 'how fast the server is' and sends a latency problem caused by redirects and cold handshakes to the backend team.
Claims DOMContentLoaded waits for images, or that load fires before deferred scripts execute.
Assumes RUM 'page views' include SPA route changes, so a 900ms client-side transition never appears in any dashboard.
Describes bfcache as 'the HTTP cache for the back button' rather than a frozen in-memory page with its heap intact.
interviewProbes: Walk me from pressing Enter to first paint. Where exactly would you place a probe that distinguishes a slow origin from a slow network?
p75 LCP is 1.9s on desktop and 5.4s on mobile against the same origin. What is your first hypothesis and what single number would falsify it?
Your site's back button feels instant on one page and slow on another. Same framework, same server. What differs?

found-connection.title: The Cost of the First Response: Round Trips and Bytes
objectives: Account for the latency of a cold HTTPS request in round trips rather than in milliseconds or bytes.
Explain why the first ~14KB of a response is privileged, and what compression has to do with it.
Judge when preconnect, dns-prefetch and connection reuse actually pay, and when they cost.
claims: A cold HTTPS request over TCP costs roughly three round trips before the first request byte is sent: about 1 RTT for DNS if it missed cache, 1 RTT for TCP's SYN/SYN-ACK, and 1 RTT for the TLS 1.3 handshake.
TLS 1.3 completes a full handshake in 1 RTT and a resumed handshake in 0 RTT, versus 2 RTT for TLS 1.2 — so the version bump is a latency change, not only a security change.
TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data is replayable by an on-path attacker, so it may only carry idempotent requests and never a state-mutating POST.

TCP begins with an initial congestion window of about 10 segments (RFC 6928), roughly 14KB of payload, so any response larger than that waits at least one extra round trip before its remainder arrives, regardless of available bandwidth.

Once bandwidth exceeds a few Mbps, page load time is dominated by latency rather than throughput, because handshakes and congestion-window growth are counted in round trips that bandwidth cannot shorten.

rel=dns-prefetch resolves DNS only; rel=preconnect performs DNS, TCP and TLS and then holds an idle socket that browsers close after roughly 10 seconds — so preconnecting to origins you will not use immediately spends the work twice.

HTTP/2 connection coalescing lets a browser reuse one connection for a different hostname when it resolves to the same IP and the existing certificate covers that host, which is why domain sharding can silently collapse to a single connection.

Text responses are compressed via Content-Encoding — gzip, Brotli (br) or Zstandard (zstd) where supported; Brotli typically beats gzip by roughly 15-20% on JS and CSS, while already-compressed formats (JPEG, WebP, WOFF2, MP4) gain nothing and should be excluded from compression.

viz.title: Counting Round Trips
viz.whatIsDrawn: A client column and a server column with arrows for each exchange, plotted against a cumulative-time axis on the left. Each arrow is annotated in place with what it carries (SYN, ClientHello, GET, first 14KB). A ghost baseline ladder for the warm-connection case is drawn behind at reduced opacity so the deleted round trips are visible as absence.
viz.predictPrompt: Your users are on a 100 Mbps link with 120ms RTT. You double their bandwidth to 200 Mbps. Predict how much sooner a 30KB gzipped HTML document finishes arriving, and state the mechanism behind your number, before the sim will run.
controls: Handshake: TLS 1.2 / TLS 1.3 full / TLS 1.3 resumed (0-RTT)
Connection state: cold / warm / coalesced from another origin
Response size slider crossing the ~14KB initcwnd boundary, with a compression toggle (none / gzip / brotli) that moves the same source file across it
viz.insight: Round trips, not bytes, are the unit of cost on a cold connection — and compression matters most exactly where it moves a response across the initial congestion window boundary.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts computes an RTT ledger from a pure model (handshake RTTs by config + ceil-based cwnd growth); unit-tested against the claim that a 30KB body at 120ms RTT gains nothing from a bandwidth doubling but ~120ms from crossing under 14KB. Deterministic, no Date.now.

drills.prompt: RTT is 80ms. Cold connection, uncached DNS (one RTT to resolver), TLS 1.3 full handshake, server think time 30ms, 9KB brotli response. Estimate TTFB in milliseconds.
drills.answerSketch: DNS 80 + TCP 80 + TLS 80 + request/response 80 + 30 think = ~350ms; body fits in initcwnd so no extra RTT. Accept 320-380.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: assets must move to a separate cookieless subdomain to shrink request headers. Under HTTP/2 on the same CDN IP and certificate, select what actually happens to connection count, and what you have paid for.

found-http-multiplexing.title: Multiplexing and Head-of-Line Blocking: H1.1 to H2 to H3
objectives: Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 by the layer at which each still suffers head-of-line blocking.
Identify the network regime in which HTTP/2 loses to six parallel HTTP/1.1 connections.
Reject era-obsolete advice (sharding, spriting, server push) with the mechanism that made it obsolete.
claims: HTTP/1.1 carries one request at a time per connection, so browsers open up to six connections per origin and everything beyond six queues in the browser before it ever touches the network.

HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, removing application-layer head-of-line blocking but not transport-layer: a single lost TCP segment stalls delivery for every stream on that connection until it is retransmitted.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP with independent per-stream loss recovery, so a lost packet stalls only the stream whose bytes it carried.
QUIC combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into one exchange, so a cold HTTP/3 connection costs about 1 RTT versus about 2 RTT for TCP plus TLS 1.3.
A QUIC connection is identified by a connection ID rather than the source-IP/port 4-tuple, so a client switching from Wi-Fi to cellular keeps the connection instead of re-handshaking.

HTTP/2's advantage over HTTP/1.1 is largest on high-latency low-loss links and can invert on lossy links, where TCP head-of-line blocking makes a single H2 connection slower than six independent H1.1 connections.

HPACK (HTTP/2) and QPACK (HTTP/3) compress request headers against a shared dynamic table, so repeated headers cost near-zero after the first request — which is why many small files stopped being catastrophic, though per-request framing and cache-entry overhead is still not zero.
HTTP/2 Server Push was removed from Chrome in 2022 because it routinely pushed resources the client already had; 103 Early Hints is the supported replacement.

viz.title: Where the Line Blocks
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three stacked transports carrying the same 12-asset workload: HTTP/1.1 as six parallel lanes, HTTP/2 as one lane with interleaved coloured frames, HTTP/3 as one lane with per-stream recovery. viz.insight: Multiplexing pushed head-of-line blocking down a layer rather than deleting it; only QUIC's per-stream loss recovery actually removes it, which is why the ranking is regime-dependent and not absolute.

found-parse-block.title: Parser, Preload Scanner, and What Blocks What
objectives: Judge the correct loading strategy for each resource on a page against a stated LCP budget, and defend each choice by what it blocks.
Predict which resources the preload scanner can and cannot discover, and price the difference in round trips.
Distinguish parser-blocking from render-blocking from execution-blocking, and name the transitive case.
claims: A classic <script> with no attributes is parser-blocking: the HTML parser stops at that position, fetches if external, executes, and only then resumes.

defer downloads in parallel and executes in document order after parsing completes, immediately before DOMContentLoaded; async executes as soon as it arrives, in arrival order, and can interrupt parsing — so async is unsafe for scripts with dependencies on each other.
<script type=module> is deferred by default, and adding async to a module makes it behave like a classic async script.

The preload scanner is a second lightweight tokenizer that runs ahead of a blocked main parser and starts fetches for discoverable subresources — which is why an present in the initial HTML is requested early while a script-injected one is not.
A stylesheet does not block the HTML parser but does block rendering, and a pending stylesheet blocks execution of any following classic script — so CSS can transitively block parsing.

Resources referenced only from CSS — background-image, @import, font files — are invisible to the preload scanner and are requested only after the CSSOM is built; @import in particular serialises an additional round trip behind the stylesheet that contains it.

rel=preload makes a late-discovered resource discoverable early but does not raise it above the critical path, so preloading many resources starves the ones it was meant to accelerate; fetchpriority is the separate control for priority.

A font file is not fetched until a rendered element actually matches its @font-face rule, so fonts are late by construction; rel=preload fixes discovery time while font-display fixes what the user sees during the gap — they solve different halves.

viz.title: Two Cursors Down One Document
viz.whatIsDrawn: The HTML source as a vertical token list on the left. Two cursors descend it: the main parser (which stalls visibly on blocking tags) and the preload scanner running ahead. Each fetch the scanner spawns draws a request bar on a timeline to the right, aligned to the source line that caused it, with the causing line highlighted in place. A ghost baseline shows the same document with every script marked defer.

viz.insight: Blocking is a property of the parser cursor, not of the network — and everything the preload scanner cannot see (CSS-referenced, JS-injected) pays a full extra serial round trip that no amount of bandwidth removes.

found-render-pipeline.title: Style, Layout, Paint, Composite
objectives: Diagnose a janky animation by identifying which pipeline stage the changed property invalidates.
Explain mechanically why compositor-driven animation survives a busy main thread, without saying 'GPU accelerated'.
Detect forced synchronous layout in code and restructure a read/write loop to remove it.
claims: The rendering pipeline runs style, layout, paint, composite in that order, and a changed property re-runs the pipeline from the earliest stage it affects: width costs layout, paint and composite; background-color costs paint and composite; opacity and transform cost composite alone.

transform and opacity can be animated on the compositor thread, so they keep advancing while the main thread is blocked; animating top, left or width cannot, and visibly stutters under main-thread load.

Reading a layout-dependent property such as offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect or scrollTop after a style write forces a synchronous layout; alternating reads and writes in a loop produces N forced layouts instead of one, which is layout thrashing.
Promoting an element with will-change: transform trades main-thread work for GPU memory and a new layer; applying it broadly can cost more than it saves and is not a general-purpose optimisation.
Paint cost is bounded by the invalidated region, not the viewport, so one full-width fixed header repainting on every scroll frame can cost more than many small elements repainting rarely.
content-visibility: auto lets the browser skip style, layout and paint for off-screen subtrees, but without contain-intrinsic-size the scrollbar jumps as content is realised.

A non-passive wheel or touchstart listener forces the compositor to wait for the main thread before it may scroll, because the handler might call preventDefault; browsers therefore default these to passive on window, document and body, and an explicit {passive: false} reintroduces the stall.
The compositor thread can scroll and composite existing layers without the main thread, which is why a page can scroll smoothly while being completely unresponsive to clicks.

viz.title: Which Stages Did You Just Buy?

found-event-loop.title: The Event Loop and the Rendering Steps
objectives: Explain the fixed ordering of task, microtask drain, and rendering steps, and place any given callback in it.
Predict how many paints a given sequence of callbacks produces.
Explain why an unbounded microtask chain hangs a page that contains no infinite loop.
claims: The event loop runs one task to completion, then drains the entire microtask queue, then may run the rendering steps; a microtask queued from within a microtask is drained in the same checkpoint, so an unbounded microtask chain starves rendering indefinitely.
queueMicrotask, promise reaction callbacks and MutationObserver callbacks enter the microtask queue; setTimeout, MessageChannel/postMessage and I/O completions enter task queues.
setTimeout(fn, 0) is clamped to a minimum of 4ms once timers are nested five deep, so chained timers cannot serve as a fast yield primitive.

Within the rendering steps the order is fixed: requestAnimationFrame callbacks run first, then scroll/resize and IntersectionObserver steps, then style, layout and paint — so DOM written inside a rAF callback is painted in that same frame.

The browser renders when it chooses to, typically once per display refresh (about 16.7ms at 60Hz), so several tasks completing inside one frame interval produce exactly one paint rather than one paint each.

requestIdleCallback runs in the gap after a frame's work with a deadline of at most 50ms of reported idle time, and on a permanently busy main thread it never runs at all unless given a timeout option.

Rendering and rAF are throttled or suspended for background tabs and off-screen cross-origin iframes, so animation logic that counts rAF callbacks silently loses time; state that must advance in real time should read wall-clock time and listen for visibilitychange.
await on an already-resolved promise resumes in a microtask, not a task, so awaiting inside a hot loop does not yield to the browser and does not allow a paint.

viz.title: One Step at a Time
viz.whatIsDrawn: A discrete machine with four in-place regions: the current call stack, the task queue, the microtask queue, and a frame boundary marker with a paint counter. Stepping executes exactly one unit of work and moves one labelled chip; each chip carries its source line inside it. A ghost baseline shows where the paint would have landed in the alternative snippet.
viz.predictPrompt: Inside one click handler you call setTimeout(A, 0), then Promise.resolve().then(B), then requestAnimationFrame(C), then synchronously log D. Commit to the execution order of D, A, B and C — and to how many paints occur — before you may step the machine.

viz.insight: Microtasks are not 'slightly later' — they run before the browser is ever permitted to paint, which is why a microtask loop freezes a page that has no loop in it.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is an actual miniature event-loop interpreter over a pre-parsed instruction list with an injected clock; unit tests assert the D, B, C, A ordering and a paint count of exactly 1 for the canonical snippet. Live region announces each step ('microtask drain: B, no paint yet').

found-responsiveness.title: Long Tasks, Yielding, and INP
objectives: Decompose a reported INP into input delay, processing time and presentation delay, and attribute it to a cause.
Diagnose why reducing handler duration failed to move field INP.
Choose between yielding, virtualising, debouncing and moving work off-thread based on which component dominates.
claims: A task occupying the main thread for more than 50ms is a Long Task; any input arriving during it must wait, which is the mechanical cause of poor responsiveness.

INP measures the whole interaction as input delay (waiting for the main thread to become free) plus processing time (your handlers) plus presentation delay (waiting for the next frame to paint); the reported value is a high percentile of a page's interactions, and the thresholds are 200ms or less for good and above 500ms for poor.
Optimising only handler duration frequently fails to move INP because most of a bad interaction is input delay caused by work that was already running and has nothing to do with the handler.

scheduler.yield() yields to the browser and resumes with continuation priority, so the remainder of your work is not sent to the back of the queue the way setTimeout(fn, 0) sends it; it ships in Chromium and Firefox but not Safari, so it is not Baseline and needs a feature check with a fallback.
scheduler.postTask() exposes three priorities — user-blocking, user-visible and background — and is the only standard way to communicate priority to the browser's own scheduler.
The Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API attributes a slow frame to the specific scripts, their source locations and the rendering work involved, which the Long Tasks API could not do.
Yielding after every item is itself costly; the useful pattern is to yield when the elapsed slice exceeds a budget of roughly 5ms, not on a fixed item count.
Debouncing improves INP only when the expensive work lives in the handler; if the cost is in the render the handler triggers, the interaction is still long and only the frequency of the pain changes.

viz.title: What Was Already Running When They Clicked
viz.whatIsDrawn: A horizontal main-thread occupancy tape of task blocks. A draggable input arrow lands at a chosen instant; the resulting interaction is decomposed into three coloured segments drawn directly on the tape beneath the arrow — input delay, processing, presentation — each labelled in place with its milliseconds. A ghost tape underneath shows the identical workload chunked with yields.

viz.insight: INP is mostly decided by what was already occupying the main thread when the user clicked, not by how fast your handler is — which is why handler micro-optimisation is the most common wasted effort in this area.

found-workers.title: Off the Main Thread: Workers and the Message Boundary
objectives: Judge whether a given workload belongs on a worker, on the main thread, or nowhere, and justify by the ratio of work to data crossing the boundary.
Account for structured-clone cost as main-thread cost, not worker cost.
Recognise the organisational cost of cross-origin isolation before proposing SharedArrayBuffer.
claims: A Web Worker has no DOM, no window and no synchronous access to layout, so any work that must read or write the DOM cannot be moved off the main thread.

postMessage copies its payload using the structured clone algorithm, and the cost scales with object size and graph complexity — that serialisation and deserialisation is charged to the sending and receiving threads, so a chatty worker can cost more main-thread time than it saves.
Transferables — ArrayBuffer, MessagePort, ImageBitmap, OffscreenCanvas — move ownership in constant time instead of copying, but the sender loses access because the buffer becomes detached.
Workers reduce main-thread occupancy, not total CPU: the work still runs, on cores that may already be saturated, so spawning eight workers on a four-core phone makes every thread slower.

SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation (COOP: same-origin plus COEP: require-corp), which breaks embedding of any third party that does not send CORP or CORS headers — that is a product and vendor decision, not a code change.
Good worker candidates are pure, chunky and infrequent: parsing or validating large payloads, compression, diffing, building a search index, crypto, and image decode via OffscreenCanvas.
Module workers (new Worker(url, { type: 'module' })) support static import, which is what makes sharing typed code between the main thread and the worker practical.
A worker's startup cost — spawning the thread and evaluating its module graph — is on the order of tens of milliseconds, so a worker created per interaction usually loses to doing the work inline.

viz.title: Where the Clone Cost Lands
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two stacked occupancy tapes, main thread and worker, for the same job, with message arrows between them. Crucially, the structured-clone block is drawn on the main-thread tape (both directions), labelled with its size and milliseconds in place. A ghost tape shows the all-on-main-thread version, so the actual saving is read as the difference in main-tape occupancy, not worker occupancy.

Worker count vs simulated core count
viz.insight: The message boundary is the cost centre; a worker wins only when the work per message is large relative to the bytes crossing it, and cloning a big result back can erase the entire saving.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models clone cost as a pure function of payload shape with a calibrated constant documented in the module prose; unit test asserts the pedagogical claim that a 12MB clone-back can exceed the parse it replaced. No real workers in the sim — determinism matters more than realism here, and the constants are cited.

found-memory.title: Memory, GC, and the Leak Taxonomy
objectives: Diagnose a suspected leak by identifying the retainer path rather than the growth curve.
Classify a leak into one of four archetypes and name the specific line that retains.
Distinguish normal allocation churn from genuine retention using a repeated-action snapshot comparison.
claims: JavaScript engines collect by reachability from GC roots, not by reference counting, so reference cycles are collected; a 'leak' in JS always means something is still reachable that you believed was gone.

V8 uses a generational heap: most objects die young in a fast scavenged young generation and survivors are promoted to old space, which is why heavy allocation shows up as frequent cheap minor GCs rather than as growth.
The four leak archetypes are detached DOM held by a JS reference, event listeners never removed, closures capturing more than they need, and timers, observers or subscriptions never cancelled.
A detached DOM subtree stays alive if any single node in it is still referenced, so caching one child element retains the whole removed tree including its siblings and ancestors.

A listener added to window or document from a component outlives that component unless explicitly removed, and removeEventListener only works with the identical function reference; passing { signal } from an AbortController removes a whole group in one call.

WeakMap, WeakSet and WeakRef hold values without preventing collection, which makes WeakMap the correct store for per-node metadata; FinalizationRegistry callbacks are not guaranteed to run and must never be relied on for correctness.
A leak is diagnosed by repeating an action, taking heap snapshots between repetitions, and comparing retained size and the retainer path — a single snapshot or a single rising graph proves nothing.

A sawtooth memory graph that returns to its previous baseline after GC is normal churn; monotonically rising baselines and a rising detached-node count across repeated identical actions are the leak signal.

viz.title: One Reference, One Retained Tree
viz.whatIsDrawn: A small object graph: GC roots (window, a module-scope Map), a component object, a DOM subtree of six nodes, a listener closure and an interval handle. Running a GC sweep greys everything unreachable in place and leaves retained nodes lit, drawing the retainer path as a highlighted chain of edges inside the graph with the responsible source line labelled on the edge. A retained-bytes counter sits inside the diagram, not beside it.
viz.predictPrompt: A modal removes its root node from the DOM on close, but the component kept `this.body = root.querySelector('.body')` and added a window resize listener. After 50 open/close cycles, predict how many DOM subtrees are retained and which single line, removed, frees all of them.
controls: Toggle each of four retention causes independently (child reference, window listener, closure capture, uncancelled interval)
Switch the metadata store between Map and WeakMap
viz.insight: Retention is a path, not a size: one surviving reference to one child node holds an entire removed subtree, so the diagnostic question is always 'who points at this', never 'how big is this'.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure mark-and-sweep over a declared graph with an injected 'cycle' counter; unit-tested against the claim that a single child reference retains the full subtree and that switching Map to WeakMap drops retention to zero. Reduced motion renders the post-sweep graph with the retainer path pre-highlighted.

drills.prompt: Pre-baked React code: a useEffect adding a window scroll listener with no cleanup, a module-scope Map keyed by DOM element, and a setInterval started in a ref callback. Mark every leaking line and name each archetype.
Fill in AbortController-based cleanup for three listeners and an observer, plus the WeakMap replacement for the element-keyed cache.
Order the steps of a heap-snapshot leak investigation, including the distractor 'take a snapshot immediately on page load and compare to now'.
