Classify five memory-over-time curves as leak, churn, expected cache growth, GC pressure, or measurement artefact, with a one-clause reason each.

The requirement changes: a route-level data cache must survive navigations for the whole session. Select the structure and the eviction policy that keep it from becoming an unbounded leak, and say what makes WeakMap the wrong choice here.
drills.answerSketch: WeakMap is wrong because the keys are route strings, not objects with independent lifetimes — nothing would ever be collected. Needs a bounded LRU with an explicit max entry count and a size or age policy.

failureModes: Says 'JavaScript is garbage collected, so you can't leak'.
Uses reference-counting language and claims cycles leak in modern engines.
Declares a leak from one rising memory graph without checking whether it returns to baseline after GC.
Calls removeEventListener with a freshly created arrow function and believes cleanup happened.
Reaches for FinalizationRegistry to release resources deterministically.
interviewProbes: An SPA grows 8MB per route change. Walk me through your investigation, naming the exact tool view at each step.
Why can caching a single DOM node be more expensive than caching a hundred plain objects?
When is WeakMap the right answer, and when is it useless?

found-http-cache.title: HTTP Caching Semantics
objectives: Design a complete Cache-Control policy for a build's set of response types and defend each directive.
Distinguish storage, freshness, revalidation and cache-key concerns, which are four separate mechanisms.
Diagnose the classic 'deploy didn't go out' failure to the specific header on the specific resource.
claims: no-cache means the response may be stored but must be revalidated before every reuse; no-store means it must not be written down at all — only no-store disables storage, and the two are routinely swapped.
Freshness is computed from max-age against the response's age, and a shared cache prefers s-maxage over max-age when both are present.

Conditional revalidation sends If-None-Match derived from ETag, or If-Modified-Since derived from Last-Modified; a 304 Not Modified saves the response body but still costs a full round trip, so it is cheap in bytes and expensive in latency.
immutable tells the browser not to revalidate even on an explicit reload, which is only safe for content-addressed URLs where changing the bytes changes the URL.

stale-while-revalidate=N allows a cache to serve a stale response immediately and refresh it in the background for N seconds past expiry, converting a blocking revalidation into a background one at the cost of one guaranteed-stale response per window.

Vary names the request headers that become part of the cache key; Vary: Accept-Encoding is necessary and normal, while Vary: User-Agent fragments the key across effectively unbounded values and destroys hit rate.

The correct default for a modern hashed build is long-lived assets behind a short-lived pointer: hashed static files get public, max-age=31536000, immutable and the HTML entry point gets no-cache so it revalidates every time.

A response with no explicit freshness information may still be cached heuristically — commonly around 10% of the elapsed time since Last-Modified — so omitting Cache-Control does not mean 'not cached'.

viz.title: Who Answered This Request?
viz.whatIsDrawn: One URL's life across repeated requests as a horizontal trace. For each request the trace shows, annotated inline: which layer answered (memory cache, disk cache, shared/CDN cache, origin), whether it was fresh, stale-served, or revalidated, and the bytes and round trips spent. A freshness clock is drawn on the response itself. A ghost trace shows the same sequence under a different header preset.
viz.predictPrompt: main.a1b2c3.js is served with max-age=31536000, immutable. You ship a fix; the content hash and filename change. Users still hit the old bug for hours. Predict where the stale copy lives and which header, on which resource, is actually at fault — before revealing the trace.
controls: Header preset: no-cache HTML / max-age=600 HTML / immutable assets / SWR / no-store everything
Actions: navigate, soft reload, hard reload, deploy, wait N minutes
Toggle a shared CDN cache into the path
Toggle Vary: Accept-Encoding vs Vary: User-Agent and watch the key fragment count in place
viz.insight: Cache the pointer differently from the thing it points at — nearly every 'stale deploy' incident is a cacheable HTML document, not a cacheable asset.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts implements RFC 9111 freshness and revalidation as a pure reducer over (headers, action, clock); unit tests assert no-cache still stores, that immutable skips revalidation on soft reload, and that SWR serves exactly one stale response before refreshing. This sim doubles as the correctness oracle for the drills.

drills.prompt: Assign Cache-Control (and Vary where needed) to seven responses: HTML entry point, hashed JS bundle, unhashed vendor.js, a user's avatar, an authenticated /me JSON response, a public price list that must be fresh within 60s, and a WOFF2 font.

A response carries `Cache-Control: no-cache, max-age=31536000` and `Vary: *` on the HTML document, and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` on hashed assets. Identify all three defects and state the user-visible symptom of each.
Complete: '____ permits storage but forces revalidation; ____ forbids storage. A 304 response saves the ____ but not the ____. A shared cache prefers ____ over max-age.'

The requirement changes: prices may never be more than 60 seconds stale, but p99 latency must stay under 100ms and the origin cannot take the load of a revalidation per request. Select the directive combination and state exactly what correctness you gave up.
drills.answerSketch: s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=60 at the edge with a short browser max-age; the concession is that up to one request per window sees a response up to 120s old.

drills.prompt: A colleague wants `immutable` on assets served from a path with no content hash, arguing 'we bump a query string on deploy'. In 150 words, defend or reject, naming the specific failure mode. (Timed, locked, criteria self-score, re-surfaced at 14 days.)

failureModes: Uses no-cache believing it prevents storage, then adds no-store 'to be safe' and destroys bfcache.
Puts a long max-age on the HTML document and cannot explain why the deploy 'didn't go out'.
Adds Vary: User-Agent for a mobile variant and collapses CDN hit rate.
Treats a 304 as free and optimises byte size while ignoring the round trip.
Assumes a response with no Cache-Control header is never cached.
interviewProbes: Design the caching headers for a hashed-asset SPA and tell me which one line, if wrong, causes a stale deploy.
Give me the exact case where stale-while-revalidate is unacceptable.
What does ETag buy you that Last-Modified does not, and when is that difference worth the CPU?

found-cdn-edge.title: CDNs: Cache Keys, Tiering, and Invalidation
objectives: Design a cache key and TTL split (browser vs edge) for a mixed personalised/public site.
Predict origin load after a purge under different topologies, and choose the topology that bounds blast radius.
Choose an invalidation strategy that matches the publishing model rather than the URL structure.
claims: A CDN's cache key is by default method plus host plus path plus query string, extended by whatever the response's Vary names; anything absent from the key cannot produce a different cached response, and anything added to it fragments the cache.
Unnormalised query strings such as utm_source fragment one asset into thousands of distinct cache entries unless the CDN is configured to strip or allowlist parameters.
A CDN is not one cache but N independent POP caches, so a cold object is fetched from the origin once per POP unless a mid-tier exists.

Tiered caching or an origin shield inserts a mid-tier cache between the POPs and the origin, so a cold or newly purged object costs roughly one origin fetch instead of one per POP — this is the primary defence against a post-purge thundering herd.
Request coalescing at the edge collapses concurrent misses for the same cache key into a single origin request; without it, purging a hot object can take the origin down.

Purge-by-URL is precise but must fan out to every POP and is not instantaneous; surrogate keys or cache tags (Surrogate-Key, Cache-Tag) let one publish event invalidate every cached page that contains the changed entity, which is what content-driven sites actually need.

s-maxage and Surrogate-Control let the edge hold an object far longer than the browser does, so the standard pattern is a short browser TTL plus a long edge TTL plus tag-based purge — fresh and cached at the same time.

Serving personalised responses from a shared cache requires either splitting the personalised fragment out of the cached document or deliberately adding the varying dimension to the key; Cache-Control: private prevents shared caching entirely, and Vary: Cookie usually reduces hit rate to near zero.

viz.title: Blast Radius of a Purge
viz.whatIsDrawn: A static topology drawn once — clients, four POPs, an optional shield, the origin — with hit/miss counters rendered inside each node. Running a scenario animates request dots along the edges and increments the counters in place; a purge flashes the affected nodes and the origin's request counter is the headline number inside the origin box. A ghost counter shows the same scenario without a shield.
viz.predictPrompt: One hot asset, 40 POPs, 100,000 requests per second globally. You purge it. With request coalescing at every edge but no origin shield, predict how many requests reach the origin in the next second: about 1, about 40, or about 100,000? Commit before running.
controls: Toggle query-string normalisation and watch the key count
Purge button (by URL vs by surrogate key) and a traffic-rate slider
viz.insight: The cache key decides your hit rate and the topology decides your origin's blast radius — and a purge is the moment both get tested simultaneously.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure discrete-event model over POPs with a seeded arrival process; unit-tested against the claim that shield + coalescing yields ~1 origin fetch, coalescing alone yields ~N_pops, and neither yields a herd proportional to RPS. Numbers shown are model outputs, and the prose states the model's assumptions explicitly.

drills.prompt: Estimate origin requests in the first second after purging a hot object under three topologies: (a) no shield, no coalescing; (b) coalescing only; (c) shield plus coalescing. 40 POPs, 100k rps.

The requirement changes: every page must display the viewer's currency. Select what must enter the cache key, estimate the hit-rate consequence, and pick the alternative that keeps the document cacheable.
drills.answerSketch: Either Vary on a normalised currency header/cookie (key multiplied by currency count, tolerable if small) or, better, keep the document keyless and inject currency client-side or via an edge-side personalisation fragment.

drills.prompt: A CDN config sets Vary: Cookie on a public marketing page, forwards the full query string, and sets a browser max-age of 86400 on the HTML. Identify each defect and its symptom.

Design edge caching for a news site: home page, article pages, a personalised recommendation rail, image assets, and an editorial correction that must be live globally in under 30 seconds. Specify keys, TTLs (browser and edge), and invalidation mechanism per surface.

Your CMS can either purge by URL on publish or tag every response with surrogate keys. In 200 words, defend one, including the failure mode you accept. (Timed, locked, criteria self-score, re-surfaced at 14 days.)

failureModes: Treats the CDN as a single cache and cannot explain why a purge causes an origin spike.
Assumes purge is instant and globally atomic.
Forwards cookies or the full query string into the cache key, then reports a 12% hit rate as a CDN problem.
Cannot separate browser TTL from edge TTL, and so ships either a permanently stale site or an effectively uncached one.
Reaches for 'cache everything at the edge' on a page with per-user content and leaks one user's data to another.
interviewProbes: Your hit rate is 45% on an asset that never changes. Give me four causes in order of likelihood.
How do you make a page both personalised and edge-cached?
Publish-to-live must be under 30 seconds worldwide, and the origin can serve 500 rps. Design it.

found-origins-credentials.title: Origins and Credentials: CORS, Preflight, Cookies
objectives: Diagnose a cross-origin failure to the specific gate that rejected it and the specific missing header.
Predict whether a given request triggers a preflight, and what the preflight costs at scale.
Judge cookie attributes against a stated threat and deployment topology, distinguishing XSS defences from CSRF defences.
claims: CORS does not protect the server: for a non-preflighted request the browser sends it and the server executes it — CORS decides only whether the calling page is permitted to read the response.

A request avoids preflight only if it uses GET, HEAD or POST, sets no headers outside the CORS-safelisted set, and carries a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain; Content-Type: application/json alone forces a preflight.

The preflight is an OPTIONS request carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers; the result is cached per origin, URL and method for Access-Control-Max-Age seconds, which Chromium clamps to 2 hours (7200s) and Firefox to 24 hours regardless of a larger value.

With credentials: 'include', Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is rejected: the server must echo the exact origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and must therefore also send Vary: Origin or a shared cache will hand one origin's ACAO to another.
Response headers are invisible to JavaScript unless named in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, which is why a correct 200 response can still surface as undefined in the client.

SameSite=Lax — Chrome's default when the attribute is absent — sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations but not on cross-site subresource requests or cross-site POSTs; genuine third-party use requires SameSite=None, which is only accepted together with Secure.
HttpOnly removes a cookie from document.cookie and so blocks its exfiltration by XSS, but provides no protection against CSRF, which is addressed by SameSite plus anti-forgery tokens.
The Partitioned attribute (CHIPS) gives a third-party cookie a separate jar per top-level site, so an embed keeps per-site state without being usable for cross-site tracking.

viz.title: The 200 You Are Not Allowed To Read
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single fetch drawn as a token moving left to right through five gates: origin check, simple-vs-preflight decision, preflight response evaluation, credentials gate, expose-headers gate. Each gate shows pass/fail in place; a failing gate expands inline to show the exact console error text and the precise header that is missing or wrong. The server's actual 200 response and its side effect are drawn beyond the gates, so the 'it succeeded and you still cannot read it' case is visible in one picture.
viz.predictPrompt: fetch('https://api.example.com/me', { credentials: 'include' }) shows a 200 with a visible JSON body in the Network panel, but your code catches a TypeError. Commit to which gate failed, and to whether changing the server's status code would help — before stepping the trace.
controls: Content-Type: text/plain / application/json; custom header on/off
Server response: ACAO * / ACAO echoed origin / plus Allow-Credentials / plus Vary: Origin
Cookie attributes: SameSite Lax / None+Secure / Partitioned; step gate by gate
viz.insight: A green 200 in the network panel says nothing about whether your code may read it — CORS failures happen after a successful, side-effect-producing response.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure implementation of the fetch CORS check plus the cookie SameSite decision, taking (request config, response headers, site context) to a verdict and an error string; unit-tested against every claim in this module, since a wrong CORS rule here would actively mislead. Reduced motion shows all gates resolved with the failing one expanded.

drills.prompt: Four server configurations, each with exactly one CORS defect (ACAO * with credentials; missing Vary: Origin behind a CDN; missing Access-Control-Expose-Headers for X-Total-Count; OPTIONS handled by an auth middleware that 401s it). Name the defect and the client-visible symptom for each.

For six requests, decide preflight or no preflight, and for each preflight name the attribute that triggered it. Includes a POST with text/plain, a GET with an Authorization header, and a POST with FormData.
Order the full exchange for a credentialed cross-origin POST of JSON, from the preflight through the cookie decision to the expose-headers check.

The requirement changes: the API moves from api.app.com to a different registrable domain, and sessions remain cookie-based. Select everything that must change on the client and the server, and the one thing that will silently keep working in Safari's dev build but fail in production.

A teammate proposes eliminating CORS entirely by proxying all API traffic through the app origin. In 200 words, defend or reject, addressing preflight cost, cookie scope, caching, and the new failure domain you introduce. (Timed, locked, criteria self-score, re-surfaced at 14 days.)

failureModes: Says 'CORS blocked my request' when the request was sent and the server already mutated state.
Sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * alongside credentials and cannot explain why it still fails.
Believes HttpOnly prevents CSRF, or that SameSite prevents XSS.
Sets SameSite=None without Secure, or assumes Lax blocks all cross-site sending including top-level navigation.
Sets a large Access-Control-Max-Age and assumes preflights are gone, unaware of the browser clamp.
Reads a response header in JS without Access-Control-Expose-Headers and reports it as a backend bug.
interviewProbes: Your DELETE request shows 200 in the network panel and a CORS error in the console. What happened on the server?
You are adding a widget embedded on 500 customer sites that must remember a per-site preference. Which cookie attributes, and why each one?
Preflights are adding 90ms to every API call on a high-latency connection. Give me three ways to remove them, ranked.

api-view-model.title: Response Shapes for Screens, Not Resources
objectives: Derive a response contract from a screen's render requirements rather than from the backend's entity model.
Quantify over-fetching (unused bytes) against under-fetching (extra dependent round trips) for a candidate shape on a given network.
Remove a client-side N+1 by choosing deliberately among expansion parameters, compound documents, field selection, or an aggregation layer.
claims: Under-fetching is paid in latency and over-fetching is paid in bandwidth; on a high-latency link one extra DEPENDENT round trip usually costs more than several kilobytes of unused fields.
A client-side N+1 occurs when a list response returns only identifiers and the UI fetches each row separately, so request count scales with page size rather than with the number of screens.
A response shape that mirrors database entities pushes the join into components at render time, where it cannot be cached, cannot be tested, and is re-implemented by every new screen.

Expansion parameters such as `?include=author,comments` let one endpoint serve several screens, but each distinct include-set is a distinct HTTP cache entry, so cache hit rate falls as include combinations multiply.

Derived fields whose RULE must stay identical across clients — permission flags like `canEdit`, currency formatting, eligibility — belong in the response even when they are cheap for the client to compute.
Making a response field nullable is a contract change for every consumer, because each must now render an absent state; nullability is part of the contract, not an implementation detail.

Only requests that are dependent — where request 2's URL or body comes from request 1's response — are removable by reshaping; independent requests are already concurrent and reshaping them saves bytes, not time.

viz.title: Screen ↔ Payload Binding
viz.whatIsDrawn: A wireframe of one product screen on the left and the JSON response tree on the right. Every field the wireframe actually reads is joined by a line drawn inside the diagram to the element that reads it; unread fields grey out and their byte cost accumulates in an inline bar directly under the tree. Beneath both sits a request timeline for the selected shape, with the previously selected shape's timeline retained as a ghost outline to compare against.
viz.predictPrompt: Shape A is three REST calls totalling 12 KB, where call 3 needs an id from call 1. Shape B is one compound endpoint returning 48 KB, of which the screen reads 9 KB. On a 150 ms RTT / 5 Mbps link, which shape paints the screen first — and at roughly what RTT does the answer flip?
controls: screen: list, detail, or list-with-detail prefetch
network profile: 30 ms LAN, 80 ms 4G, 300 ms far-edge
step through the request timeline one round trip at a time
viz.insight: Round trips are priced in latency and bytes are priced in bandwidth; the shape you should ship depends on which of the two your users actually pay — and only DEPENDENT round trips can be reshaped away.
viz.buildNotes: Pure `sim.ts`: given (shape, screen, networkProfile) return {requests[], bytesTransferred, bytesUsed, firstPaintMs} with an injected clock and no Math.random. Unit-test the crossover RTT asserted by the predictPrompt so the teaching claim is CI-verified. prefers-reduced-motion renders the completed timeline with anchored labels and no sweep. Live region announces e.g. 'Shape B: 1 round trip, 48 KB transferred, 9 KB used, paints at 412 ms'.

drills.prompt: Nine screen requirements for an order-detail page are listed. Tag each as MUST be in the first response, CAN be lazily fetched after paint, or BELONGS to a different endpoint entirely. Justify any 'must' that is not visible above the fold.
drills.answerSketch: Above-the-fold identity, status and price must be in the first response. Comment threads, audit history and recommendations are lazy. Address-book search and payment-method management are separate endpoints because their lifecycle and permissions differ from the order's.

drills.prompt: A component tree is shown alongside a devtools network panel with 1 + 24 requests. Identify the exact line that causes the N+1 and name the two contract-level fixes (not the client-level ones).
drills.answerSketch: The row component calls useUser(row.authorId). Contract fixes: an `?include=author` expansion, or a compound list response that embeds a normalized `users` map keyed by id. Client-level batching/coalescing is a mitigation, not a fix.

drills.prompt: The same list endpoint must now also serve a mobile card that shows only title and avatar. Which property of your `?include=` design breaks first, and what is the cheapest contract change that does not fragment the cache further?
drills.answerSketch: Cache cardinality: a second include-set halves hit rate and mobile still over-fetches. Cheapest fix is a small fixed number of named projections (`?view=card|full`) rather than open-ended include combinations.

drills.prompt: Given RTT 220 ms, 3 Mbps throughput, and two candidate shapes with stated dependency graphs and payload sizes, compute time-to-render for each and state the RTT at which they cross over.

From a fixed palette of endpoints, include parameters and embedded maps, assemble a contract serving three screens. Graded on total dependent round trips per screen and unused-field ratio, against a stated budget.

failureModes: Enumerates the backend's database tables, calls each one a resource, and then re-joins them in components.
Reaches for GraphQL before establishing whether the problem is round trips, bytes, or team ownership.
Adds `?include=` for every relation and never notices the response has become uncacheable per variant.
Says 'we'll just fetch it in the component' and never counts the resulting requests for a 50-row list.
Treats over-fetching as always bad, and cannot say when 4× the bytes is the correct trade.
interviewProbes: Here is the screen. Design the response. Now the PM adds a 'last commenter' avatar to every row — what changes in your contract?
How do you decide whether `canEdit` is computed on the server or in the client?
The backend already returns entity-shaped resources and will not change them this quarter. What do you do?

api-paradigm-choice.title: REST, GraphQL, tRPC, gRPC-Web: What Actually Changes for the Client
objectives: Contrast the four paradigms along client-relevant axes: cache key location, coupling, type-safety mechanism, streaming story, bundle cost, and devtools observability.
State, for a given organisational constraint, what each paradigm buys and what it takes away — without appealing to popularity.
claims: GraphQL sent as a POST body cannot be served by the browser HTTP cache or a CDN, because the cache key is the URL and the operation is in the body; persisted queries issued as GET restore both layers at the cost of a build-time query registry.
gRPC-Web cannot speak to a gRPC server directly because browsers expose neither HTTP/2 frames nor trailers to JavaScript; it requires a translating proxy such as Envoy in front of the service.

The Connect protocol carries unary RPCs as ordinary HTTP requests with JSON or binary bodies, so a browser client needs no proxy and the calls are readable in devtools — which is the practical reason teams pick it over gRPC-Web.

tRPC produces no schema artifact: its type safety is a TypeScript type import, so both ends must be TypeScript and usually in one repository, and no third-party or non-TypeScript consumer can be served at all.

GraphQL moves the shape decision to the client and moves the cost-control problem to the server: without depth limits, complexity scoring or persisted queries, any client can issue an arbitrarily expensive query.
REST with expansion parameters and GraphQL solve the same under-fetching problem; the substantive difference is who may change the response shape without a backend deploy.

GraphQL's incremental delivery directives `@defer` and `@stream` are still outside the ratified specification as of 2026 and remain experimental in graphql-js v17, so a design that depends on them is a bet, not a plan.
Paradigm choice is also a bundle decision: a normalizing GraphQL client costs tens of kilobytes gzipped that a fetch-plus-generated-types REST client does not.

viz.title: The Same Request, Four Ways
viz.whatIsDrawn: One requirement — 'load a post with its author and first ten comments' — rendered as the literal bytes on the wire in four stacked lanes: method, URL, the headers that matter, and the body. Inside each lane, four cache stops (browser HTTP cache, CDN, service worker, client normalized store) light green or grey with the REASON written in the lane itself, never in a side legend.
viz.predictPrompt: The same operation is `GET /posts/1?include=author,comments` in REST and `POST /graphql` in GraphQL, and the response bytes are identical. A CDN sits in front of both. How many of the four cache layers can serve the GraphQL version — and name the single change to the REQUEST that moves that number.
controls: toggle persisted queries served over GET
toggle 'translating proxy present' for the gRPC-Web lane
reveal the response frame and its trailers
viz.insight: Nothing about GraphQL forbids caching — sending it as an opaque POST body does. Each paradigm's real client-side cost is decided by where its cache key can be computed and who owns the shape.
viz.buildNotes: Sim returns, per paradigm, the exact request line plus a boolean-with-reason per cache layer; assert in tests that POST /graphql yields cacheable=false for browser cache and CDN and that enabling persisted-GET flips both. Static reduced-motion variant shows all four lanes fully revealed.

drills.prompt: A team wants CDN caching of read operations, a public third-party API, and a Kotlin mobile client. Which paradigm is eliminated first, and by which single property? Select and state the eliminating property, not the general vibe.
drills.answerSketch: tRPC — it emits no language-neutral schema artifact, so the Kotlin client and the third party cannot be served at all. GraphQL survives only with persisted queries over GET.

drills.prompt: You have shipped GraphQL. The requirement changes: 90% of traffic is one read-only screen and the CDN bill is now the top cost line. What breaks first, and what is the smallest change that fixes it?
drills.answerSketch: POST-based operations are uncacheable at the edge. Smallest fix: automatic/registered persisted queries issued as GET with a hashed operation id, plus Cache-Control on the read operations.

drills.prompt: Complete: gRPC-Web requires a ______ proxy because browsers do not expose HTTP/2 ______ to JavaScript; the ______ protocol avoids this by carrying unary calls as ordinary HTTP requests.
drills.answerSketch: translating (e.g. Envoy); trailers/frames; Connect.

drills.prompt: Six constraints are given (polyglot consumers, one monorepo team, offline cache, streaming updates, public API, strict bundle budget). For each, mark which paradigms remain viable and which are eliminated, with the eliminating property named.

You are told 'we should adopt GraphQL so the frontend stops waiting on backend endpoint changes'. Take a position in 200 words, timed, before seeing the model answer. Your justification must address cache location, server-side query cost control, and bundle size.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer decomposed into criteria: (1) names the real bottleneck as team ownership rather than protocol; (2) prices the loss of URL-keyed caching and the persisted-query remedy; (3) names query cost control as a new server obligation; (4) prices the normalizing client bundle; (5) names the cheaper alternative (named projections or a BFF) and says under what condition it is insufficient.

failureModes: Argues GraphQL 'has no over-fetching' without mentioning that the cache key moved out of the URL.
Believes gRPC-Web works browser-to-service with no proxy.
Proposes tRPC for an API that must serve a mobile team or an external partner.
Compares paradigms on 'developer experience' only and cannot name one runtime cost of each.
Assumes @defer/@stream are production-ready spec features.
interviewProbes: Your CDN hit rate went to zero after the GraphQL migration. Why, and what do you do?
When is tRPC's type safety a liability rather than an asset?
What does Connect give a browser client that gRPC-Web does not?

api-bff.title: Owning the Aggregation Layer: BFF, Gateway, or Neither
objectives: Decide, with latency arithmetic rather than intuition, whether a BFF is justified for a given screen and dependency graph.
Distinguish an API gateway's cross-cutting responsibilities from a BFF's per-client view-shaping, and say what goes wrong when they are merged.
Price the ownership cost — deploy pipeline, on-call, partial-failure policy — against the alternative of asking the backend team for one compound endpoint.
claims: A BFF reduces wall-clock time only for DEPENDENT request chains; independent requests already run concurrently over one HTTP/2 connection, so relocating them behind a BFF saves close to nothing.

Collapsing three sequential dependent calls into one BFF call saves roughly two client round trips — about 2×RTT on the user's link — while adding datacenter-internal hops that are typically one to two orders of magnitude cheaper.

A BFF is code you own with a deploy pipeline, an on-call rotation and its own failure modes; the honest comparison is against 'ask the backend team for one compound endpoint', not against 'do nothing'.
One BFF per client type is the pattern's actual definition; a single BFF shared by web, iOS and Android degenerates into a general-purpose gateway with a misleading name and a shared release train.

A BFF can exchange a browser cookie session for downstream service tokens, keeping access tokens out of JavaScript-reachable storage entirely — this token-boundary benefit is often a stronger justification than latency.

An API gateway handles cross-cutting concerns for every client (authn, rate limiting, routing, TLS); a BFF handles view-shaping for one. Putting view logic in the gateway makes every client's release depend on the gateway's.

A BFF that fans out to N services must publish its own partial-failure contract: whether a slow non-critical dependency degrades the response or fails it is a product decision that must be written down, not a framework default.
A BFF inherits the tail latency of its slowest dependency unless it sets per-dependency timeouts and a total budget; without a budget it converts one slow service into a screen that never renders.

viz.title: Where the Round Trips Go
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three lanes — browser, BFF, and three backend services — with request tokens travelling along them. The client's RTT is drawn to scale against the datacenter RTT so the asymmetry is visible rather than asserted. A wall-clock budget bar underneath fills as the scenario steps, with the no-BFF run retained as a ghost bar directly beneath it. Per-dependency timeout markers are drawn on the lanes themselves.
viz.predictPrompt: Client RTT is 180 ms; service-to-service RTT inside the datacenter is 4 ms. Screen A needs three calls that can all start immediately. Screen B needs three calls where each depends on the previous one's response. Which screen does introducing a BFF actually speed up, and by roughly how many milliseconds?
controls: dependency mode: fully parallel / fully chained / mixed
inject one slow dependency (p99 = 2 s) and toggle a per-dependency timeout
viz.insight: A BFF buys round trips on dependent chains, control of the response shape, and a token boundary. It does not make parallel requests faster, and it costs you a service to run and be paged for.
viz.buildNotes: Sim takes {clientRttMs, dcRttMs, depGraph, bffEnabled, slowDep, timeoutMs} and returns total wall clock plus per-lane spans. Unit-test the predictPrompt: parallel saving ≈ 0, chained saving ≈ 2×clientRtt − 2×dcRtt. Reduced motion draws the finished spans; live region reads the two totals and the delta.

drills.prompt: Client RTT 200 ms, DC RTT 5 ms. Screen needs: A, then B(A), then C(A) — B and C are independent of each other. Compute wall clock with and without a BFF, and state the saving.
drills.answerSketch: Without BFF: 200 (A) + 200 (B and C in parallel) = 400 ms. With BFF: 200 + 5 + 5 = ~210 ms. Saving ≈ 190 ms — one round trip, not two, because B and C were already parallel.

drills.prompt: Seven stated motivations for building a BFF are listed. Mark each as SOLVED by a BFF, solved more cheaply by a compound endpoint, or not solved by a BFF at all.
drills.answerSketch: Solved: token boundary, per-client shaping, dependent-chain collapse, cross-team shape ownership. Cheaper elsewhere: single-screen over-fetching, response caching. Not solved: backend service slowness, schema drift.

drills.prompt: A BFF handler awaits four service calls with no timeouts and returns 500 if any rejects. Describe the incident this produces when one non-critical service degrades to p99 = 8 s, and name the two contract changes that prevent it.
drills.answerSketch: Every screen render blocks on the slowest dependency and then fails entirely; the BFF's own request pool saturates and takes down unrelated screens. Fixes: per-dependency timeout inside a total budget, and a declared partial-success shape marking the non-critical section as degraded.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the same BFF must now serve the iOS app, which ships on a six-week cycle. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The BFF stops being per-client: its release train now serves two clients with different cadences, so any shape change must be additive and versioned, which is exactly the coupling the pattern existed to remove.

drills.prompt: Timed, 250 words: the backend team offers to build you one compound endpoint within a quarter. Argue for or against building a BFF instead. You must address latency arithmetic, ownership cost, and the token boundary.

failureModes: Proposes a BFF for a fan-out that is already parallel, and cannot state what it saves when pushed.
Cannot distinguish a BFF from an API gateway, and puts view logic in the gateway.
Ignores that the BFF is a new production service with an on-call rotation.
Forgets timeouts and a total latency budget, so the BFF inherits the worst dependency's tail.
Never mentions the token-exchange benefit, which is often the strongest real justification.
interviewProbes: Your screen makes six parallel calls and is slow. Does a BFF help? Show me the arithmetic.
Who owns the BFF, and what happens at 3am when it's down?
When would you deliberately NOT build a BFF even though the shape is wrong?

api-pagination.title: List Contracts: Pagination, Filtering, and Stable Order
objectives: Specify a list contract — cursor semantics, sort key, filter grammar, count strategy — for a stated product requirement.
Predict the exact duplication and skip behaviour of offset pagination over a mutating dataset.
Choose a count and deep-linking strategy that the product requirement actually needs rather than the one that is conventional.
claims: Offset pagination is correct only over a dataset that does not change between page requests: an insert before the current window makes the client see an item twice, and a delete before it makes the client skip one entirely.
Keyset (cursor) pagination anchors the window to the last row's sort key, so inserts and deletes elsewhere cannot shift it — the cost is that it cannot jump to an arbitrary page N.

A keyset cursor must include a unique tiebreaker, normally the primary key, because a non-unique sort column alone does not define a total order and rows with equal values will be duplicated or skipped at page boundaries.
Opaque (base64-encoded) cursors are a versioning device: because clients only echo them back, the server can change the underlying sort key or encoding without a breaking change.
Exact total counts are expensive at scale — a `COUNT(*)` over a filtered set — and are frequently the reason a list endpoint is slow; fetching `limit + 1` rows yields `hasNextPage` at almost no cost.
Infinite scroll and deep linking conflict: a cursor identifies a window, not a position, so a shareable 'jump to item 400' URL needs a separate anchor parameter or a fixed page-size contract.
A cursor is only valid under the filter and sort it was issued for; a cursor presented with different filter parameters must be rejected with an explicit error rather than silently reinterpreted.

Every distinct combination of filter, sort and page size is a distinct cache key, so a filter grammar with free-form operators such as `?filter[price][gte]=` has effectively unbounded cache cardinality.

viz.title: What the Window Sees When the List Moves
viz.whatIsDrawn: A vertical dataset of rows with visible sort keys. The current page window is a bracket drawn over the rows. Mutations injected by the learner appear as rows sliding in or out at a chosen position. When the next page is requested, rows the user sees twice are outlined and counted inline; rows never shown are hatched and counted inline. The keyset run is retained as a ghost bracket for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: You are viewing page 3 of a newest-first list, 20 per page, using `?offset=40`. While you read it, 5 items are inserted at the top and 2 items on page 1 are deleted. When you request page 4, how many items will you see twice, and how many will you never see?
controls: inject N inserts or deletes, at head / inside window / after window
viz.insight: Offset pagination's correctness is a property of the dataset, not of your client code. Cursors trade random access for stability — decide which one the screen actually needs before choosing.
viz.buildNotes: Sim is a pure function over an ordered array with a mutation log: given (mode, pageSize, cursorOrOffset, mutations) return {rows, duplicates[], skipped[]}. Unit-test the predictPrompt arithmetic (net shift +3 → 3 duplicates, 0 skips) and the equal-sort-key case with no tiebreaker. Reduced motion shows before/after states side by side with the same inline counts.

drills.prompt: Newest-first list, page size 25, currently at `?offset=75`. Between requests, 9 items are inserted at the head and 4 items above the window are deleted. How many duplicates and how many skips on the next page?
drills.answerSketch: Net downward shift of 5 → 5 duplicates, 0 skips. Had deletes exceeded inserts, the sign flips to skips.

drills.prompt: A cursor encodes only `{createdAt}` and the list is sorted by `created_at DESC`. Twelve rows share the same second-granularity timestamp. Describe exactly what the user observes, and give the one-field fix.
drills.answerSketch: Rows with the tied timestamp are duplicated or dropped at the boundary, non-deterministically per query plan. Fix: include the primary key in the cursor and sort by (created_at DESC, id DESC).

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the product wants a jump-to-page control and a 'showing 41–60 of 12,847' label on a 40-million-row table. What breaks first, and what do you offer instead?
drills.answerSketch: Keyset cannot address page N and the exact count is a full filtered scan. Offer: keyset plus an approximate/capped count ('10,000+') and a sequential pager, or accept offset with a hard depth cap and stale-count tolerance.

drills.prompt: From a fixed palette (cursor field, sort keys, filter operators, count strategy, page-size bounds, error codes), assemble a list contract for a stated feed requirement. Graded on total order completeness, cursor/filter binding, and count cost.

Complete: to return `hasNextPage` without a COUNT query, fetch `limit + ___` rows and ______ the extra one before responding. A cursor presented with a changed ______ must be ______ rather than reinterpreted.
drills.answerSketch: 1; discard/trim; filter (or sort); rejected with an explicit error code.

failureModes: Defaults to offset pagination for a live feed and is surprised by duplicate rows in infinite scroll.
Builds a cursor from a non-unique sort column with no tiebreaker.
Promises an exact total count on an unbounded dataset without pricing it.
Exposes a raw database key as the cursor, then cannot change the sort without breaking clients.
Lets the client change the filter while reusing an old cursor, and silently returns nonsense.
interviewProbes: Design the pagination contract for a chat history that grows at both ends.
The list is sorted by a user-editable 'priority' field. What does that do to your cursor?
Product wants deep-linkable 'page 7'. How do you answer without lying about cost?

api-errors.title: The Error Contract: Codes, Partial Success, Retryability
objectives: Specify an error envelope that a UI can branch on without parsing prose.
Separate transport-level status from application-level machine codes, and decide which failures must be individually addressable.
Design the partial-success shape for a batch or fan-out endpoint, and signal retryability explicitly.
claims: RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` — which obsoletes RFC 7807 — provides a standard envelope with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance` plus extension members, so a client parses one shape rather than one per endpoint.

HTTP status codes are too coarse to route a UI: a single 409 can mean 'already exists', 'version conflict', or 'idempotency key reused with a different body', so the contract needs a stable machine code alongside the status.
Machine codes are consumed by code and must be stable identifiers; human-readable messages may be rewritten at any time, so a client branching on message text is broken by a copy edit.

Field-level validation errors need a machine-addressable pointer to the offending input — a JSON Pointer such as `/items/2/quantity` — or the UI cannot attach the message to the control that caused it.

Retryability is a server-side fact the client cannot infer: a 500 may be permanently fatal and a 400 may be transient, so the contract should state it explicitly, and throttling responses should carry `Retry-After`.

Partial success needs its own shape: a batch where half the items succeeded is neither 200 nor 500. WebDAV's 207 Multi-Status is a borrowed convention, so the per-item result array — not the status code — is the load-bearing part of the contract.
GraphQL signals partial failure as HTTP 200 with a top-level `errors` array beside partial `data`, so a client that treats HTTP 200 as success will silently render an incomplete screen.
Every error response should carry a correlation identifier the UI can surface, because without one the user is the only link between the screen they saw and the server logs.

viz.title: Where Does This Failure Land?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A real HTTP failure response — status line, headers, body — enters at the left and flows through the client's routing gates (auth? retryable? field-scoped? user-actionable?), each gate drawn with the deciding field highlighted INSIDE the gate. It exits into one of five UI outcomes drawn as small screen thumbnails: silent retry, inline field error, toast, blocking dialog, full-page error. A ghost path shows where status-code-only routing would have sent the same response.
viz.predictPrompt: A 409 arrives with body `{"code":"INVENTORY_RESERVED","retryable":true,"retryAfterMs":800}`. Status-code routing sends every 409 to a 'conflict' dialog. Where should this one actually land, and name the single field that decides it.
controls: choose one of eight canned real responses
step through the gates one at a time
viz.insight: The UI's branching is driven by fields you have to design on purpose; HTTP status alone routes at most three of the five outcomes correctly, and the two it gets wrong are the ones users complain about.
viz.buildNotes: Sim: (response, routingMode) → {gatePath[], outcome}. Unit-test that at least two canned responses route differently under status-only vs code-aware mode — that difference IS the pedagogical claim. Reduced motion renders the full path statically with the deciding field boxed.

drills.prompt: Client code branches with `if (err.message.includes('already exists'))`. Name three distinct ways this breaks in production and give the contract change that fixes all three at once.
drills.answerSketch: Breaks on copy edits, on localisation, and on any backend refactor of the message. Fix: a stable `code` field in a problem+json envelope, with the message reserved for humans.

drills.prompt: From a constrained palette of envelope members, design the error contract for a checkout endpoint that can fail on validation, inventory, payment authorisation, and downstream timeout. Graded on: stable code present, field pointer present, retryability explicit, correlation id present, and no overloading of one status for two outcomes.
The endpoint becomes a batch endpoint accepting 100 items. What in your single-item error envelope breaks first, and what do you add?
drills.answerSketch: A single top-level status/code cannot express 97 successes and 3 failures. Add a per-item result array with index/id, per-item code and pointer, and define whether the write is atomic — the atomicity statement is part of the contract.

drills.prompt: For each of six failures, choose 400, 409, 422, 429 or 503 and state the machine code you would pair with it. Selecting the right status with no code, or a code with an implausible status, scores zero.
Timed, 200 words: argue for a small closed set of generic error codes versus a large specific set. You must address UI branching, client version skew, and who is allowed to add a code.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) recognises that every code is a contract clients may branch on; (2) names the version-skew problem — new codes reach old clients that must have a default branch; (3) proposes a hierarchy or category prefix so unknown codes degrade to a known category; (4) says who owns adding codes; (5) states the failure mode of the option not chosen.

failureModes: Returns 500 with a stringified stack trace and calls it an error contract.
Uses HTTP status codes as the only taxonomy, then discovers three meanings of 409.
Puts the user-facing sentence in the code field, so localisation breaks branching.
Treats a batch endpoint as all-or-nothing without ever saying so in the contract.
Handles GraphQL responses by checking `res.ok` and renders partial data as complete.
interviewProbes: Design the error contract for checkout. Now the payment provider starts returning soft declines — what changes?
How does the client know whether to retry? Don't say 'it's a 5xx'.
Half the batch succeeded. What is the response?

api-retry-safety.title: Retry Safety: Idempotency Keys, Backoff, and Coalescing
objectives: Diagnose duplicate-write and retry-storm incidents down to the specific client-side decision that caused them.
Trace an idempotency key through a lost-response scenario, including the changed-body case.
Distinguish client-side in-flight coalescing from server-side idempotency and say which incident each one prevents.
claims: A lost response is indistinguishable from a lost request at the client, so any timeout on a non-idempotent POST leaves the client unable to know whether the write happened; automatic retry is safe by default only for the methods HTTP defines as idempotent (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE).

An idempotency key makes the server store the ORIGINAL response against the key and replay it, so the correct behaviour of a retry is to return the first response — not merely to skip the write and return a bare success.
Reusing an idempotency key with a different request body must be rejected with a 4xx rather than silently ignored, because ignoring the new body loses a write the user believes they made.

The client must generate the idempotency key once, before the first attempt, and reuse it for every retry of that same user intent; generating it inside the retry loop defeats the mechanism completely.

`Idempotency-Key` is a widely copied Stripe convention rather than a ratified standard — as of 2026 it exists only as an IETF Internet-Draft (`draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header`) — so its scope, TTL and conflict semantics must be read from each vendor's documentation, not assumed.

Exponential backoff without jitter re-synchronises exactly the clients it was meant to spread out; full jitter — sleep = random(0, base·2^attempt) — is the variant that actually flattens the retry spike.

A retry budget, capping retries at a small fraction of total requests (commonly around 10%), prevents a client fleet from converting a partial outage into a full one; per-request retry counts alone cannot, because they multiply across the fleet.

In-flight request coalescing — returning one shared promise to concurrent identical GETs — removes duplicate work inside a single page session, but it is not a substitute for server-side idempotency, which is what covers retries across reloads, tabs and devices.

viz.title: The Response That Never Came Back
viz.whatIsDrawn: Client, network and server lifelines. A POST travels down; the learner chooses where it is dropped. The server's idempotency ledger is drawn as rows appearing on the server lifeline itself, each showing key, body fingerprint and stored response. A duplicate-side-effect counter sits anchored beside the ledger, and the no-key run is retained as a ghost ladder.
viz.predictPrompt: The client's 10-second timeout fires. The server actually committed the write at 9.8 s and its response was dropped by a proxy. The client retries with the SAME Idempotency-Key, but the user edited the amount in between so the body differs. What should the server return — and what does a naive 'have I seen this key before?' implementation return instead?
controls: drop point: request in flight / response in flight / none
body changed between attempts: yes / no
key TTL expired before the retry: yes / no
viz.insight: The key protects the RESPONSE, and it must be bound to a fingerprint of the request body — otherwise a changed body silently returns the wrong result and the user's real intent is lost.
viz.buildNotes: Split strictly into sim.ts (injected clock, seeded RNG for the drop) and viz.tsx. Unit-test all four corner cases: drop-request+key, drop-response+key, drop-response+no-key (duplicate side effect = 1), and same-key-different-body (must yield a 4xx, not a replay). This is the module where a wrong sim teaches a genuinely dangerous belief.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of a correct client-side retry for a payment POST: generate key, attach key, send, classify error, consult retry budget, sleep with full jitter, resend with the same key, surface terminal failure with correlation id.

An interceptor generates `crypto.randomUUID()` inside its retry wrapper, immediately before each attempt. Describe the incident this produces during a 30-second gateway degradation, and state the one-line fix.
drills.answerSketch: Each attempt is a distinct key, so every retry is a fresh write: one user intent becomes N charges. Fix: generate the key at the call site, once per user intent, and pass it into the retrying transport.

drills.prompt: Fill the blanks in a pre-baked retry helper: the full-jitter sleep expression, the predicate deciding whether a response is retryable, and the line that must NOT be inside the loop.
drills.answerSketch: sleep = Math.random() * base * 2 ** attempt; retryable comes from the server's explicit flag / 429 / 503 plus Retry-After, not from status class alone; the key generation must sit outside the loop.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: requests now pass through a queue with at-least-once delivery and three competing workers. What breaks first, and which of your existing mechanisms already covers it?
drills.answerSketch: Duplicate delivery, not client retry, becomes the dominant duplicate source; client-side coalescing does nothing here. Server-side idempotency with a key that survives across workers — plus a uniqueness constraint at the storage layer — is what covers it.

drills.prompt: 1,000 clients hit a 15-second outage. Each retries up to 4 times with base 500 ms exponential backoff and no jitter. Sketch the request-per-second profile at the moment the service recovers, then repeat with full jitter and state the peak reduction.

failureModes: Says 'we retry with exponential backoff' and cannot explain why it made the outage worse.
Generates a new idempotency key per attempt.
Believes an idempotency key means 'do nothing on retry' rather than 'replay the stored response'.
Retries POSTs automatically with no key and no server guarantee.
Adds client-side request deduplication and believes duplicate writes are now impossible.
interviewProbes: The user was charged twice. Walk me from the symptom to the line of code.
Where exactly do you generate the idempotency key, and why there?
Your retries are correct per-request. Explain how they still took the service down.

api-transport-choice.title: Choosing a Transport: Polling, SSE, WebSocket, WebTransport
objectives: Walk an explicit decision tree from stated requirements to a transport, naming the eliminating constraint at each branch.
Account for the browser's per-origin connection limits and for intermediary behaviour, not just protocol semantics.
Specify the auth, resume and heartbeat parts of the contract that the transport itself does not give you.
claims: Browsers cap HTTP/1.1 at roughly 6 connections per origin, so a page holding several SSE streams to one origin can starve every other request to that origin; over HTTP/2 those streams multiplex on one connection, bounded instead by the server's max-concurrent-streams setting, commonly around 100.
`EventSource` cannot set request headers, so bearer-token auth over SSE requires a cookie, a URL parameter, or a fetch-based SSE implementation rather than the native API.

`EventSource` reconnects automatically and resumes position by sending `Last-Event-ID`, and the server tunes the delay with a `retry:` field — so resumability is part of the SSE contract and costs the client no code.

The browser `WebSocket` constructor cannot set an `Authorization` header, so WebSocket auth uses cookies, a short-lived ticket in the URL, or an application-level auth message sent after connect — each with different leak, revocation and log-exposure properties.

SSE carries UTF-8 text only and is strictly server-to-client; client-to-server messages need a second ordinary HTTP channel, which keeps normal caching, proxies and observability working and is usually simpler than it sounds.

Intermediaries terminate idle connections — many load balancers default to about 60 seconds — so any long-lived transport needs application-level heartbeats and a reconnect-with-resume story, not merely an open socket.

Polling's cost is clients × payload ÷ interval and is entirely predictable: polling a 2 KB response every 5 s for 10,000 users is roughly 4 MB/s of egress, which is often cheaper to run and reason about than stateful sockets.

WebTransport reached Baseline browser support in 2026 once Safari shipped it, but it requires HTTP/3 over QUIC end to end, which many corporate proxies and load balancers still will not pass — so it is a considered v2 option, not a default.
Proxies and CDNs that buffer responses break SSE silently: events arrive in a burst at connection close instead of streaming, which looks like a server bug and is a configuration one.

viz.title: The Transport Decision Tree, With the Connection Ledger
viz.whatIsDrawn: A fixed decision tree drawn once — direction, update frequency, per-client fan-out, resume needed, intermediary constraints. Constraint controls light exactly one satisfied path; every pruned branch carries its disqualifying reason written on the branch itself. A second lane shows the browser's per-origin connection ledger filling as streams open, switchable between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.
viz.predictPrompt: A dashboard tab opens 8 SSE streams to the same origin over HTTP/1.1, then issues an ordinary GET for a chart. What happens to that GET — and what changes if the only difference is that the origin serves HTTP/2?
viz.insight: Transport choice is decided by connection accounting, auth mechanics and intermediary timeouts far more often than by 'is it real-time enough'.
viz.buildNotes: Sim: (constraints) → {chosenTransport, prunedBranches[{branch, reason}], connectionLedger}. Unit-test that 7+ streams on HTTP/1.1 yields a blocked request and that the same input on HTTP/2 does not. Reduced motion renders the highlighted path and a filled ledger statically.

drills.prompt: Six features are listed (live cursor positions, order status changes, a build log, a stock ticker for 50k viewers, collaborative text editing, a slow report that finishes eventually). Assign a transport to each and name the ONE constraint that eliminated the runner-up.
You shipped SSE. Ops puts a response-buffering CDN in front of the origin. What breaks, how does it present to users, and what is the fix?
drills.answerSketch: Events are buffered and delivered in a burst at stream close, so the UI looks frozen then jumps. Fix: disable buffering for that path (e.g. an explicit no-transform / streaming passthrough route) rather than changing client code.

drills.prompt: A team authenticates their WebSocket by appending `?token=<jwt>` to the URL. List three concrete exposure paths and give the standard replacement.
drills.answerSketch: Tokens land in load-balancer and proxy access logs, in browser history/referrer surfaces, and in APM traces. Replacement: a single-use short-TTL ticket exchanged over normal HTTP, or a post-connect auth message before any subscription is honoured.

drills.prompt: 25,000 concurrent users, 3 KB payload, 10-second polling interval. Compute steady-state egress and request rate, then compute what changes if you move to SSE with an average of 1 event per user per minute.
Timed, 250 words: defend polling over WebSockets for an order-status screen. You must address cost, operational complexity, reconnection semantics and what would change your answer.

failureModes: Reaches for WebSockets for a server-to-client-only feed and inherits reconnection, auth and scaling problems for nothing.
Does not know EventSource and WebSocket cannot send an Authorization header.
Opens one stream per widget and hits the per-origin connection cap on HTTP/1.1.
Never plans heartbeats, then blames 'random disconnects' on the browser.
Names WebTransport as the answer without checking HTTP/3 reachability through the customer's proxies.
interviewProbes: Design the update mechanism for a live order-status page. Now make it work for 100k concurrent viewers.
How does your client authenticate the stream, and how do you revoke it mid-session?
The connection drops after exactly 60 seconds every time. Where do you look?

api-uploads.title: Upload Contracts: Multipart, Presigned, Resumable
objectives: Contrast the three upload strategies on bandwidth ownership, failure cost, progress reporting, and CORS/auth surface.
State what each strategy does NOT give you, and design the post-upload processing contract that direct-to-storage forces on you.
claims: Proxying uploads through your own API costs you full ingress and egress bandwidth and holds a server request open for the duration of the slowest client; presigned URLs move that traffic directly to object storage and off your bill.

A presigned single PUT is not resumable: a failure at 90% re-sends the entire object. Resumability requires either the storage provider's own multipart-upload API (S3 parts are minimum 5 MB except the last, maximum 10,000 parts) or a resumable protocol.
`multipart/form-data` survives because it is the only body a plain HTML form can send; it is a poor fit for large binaries because the body is framed and typically buffered somewhere along the path.

Resumable upload is being standardised as `draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload`, the IETF successor to tus 1.0, introducing the `104 Upload Resumption Supported` interim response and an upload resource the client queries for its current offset.

`fetch()` reports no upload progress: streaming a request body requires a `ReadableStream` with `duplex: 'half'` over HTTP/2 and is still not universally supported, which is why `XMLHttpRequest`'s `upload.onprogress` remains in production upload code in 2026.

A presigned PUT from the browser is a cross-origin request to the storage host, so the bucket needs its own CORS configuration; sending a `Content-Type` header triggers a preflight that must be allowed, and the signature only covers the headers that were signed.

Presigned URLs are bearer credentials with an expiry — up to 7 days for S3 SigV4, and further bounded by the session lifetime when signed with temporary credentials — so their TTL should be minutes, they should be minted per upload, and they must never be logged or emailed.

Because a direct-to-storage upload bypasses your API entirely, completion, validation, virus scanning and transcoding become a separate asynchronous contract: the client must be told explicitly how it learns the file is actually usable.

viz.title: What Gets Re-Sent When It Fails
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three lanes — multipart through your API, presigned single PUT to storage, resumable chunks — each drawn as a progress bar over a byte axis, with your API server drawn in or out of the data path per lane. A failure marker is placed by the learner; the bytes that must be re-sent are overlaid as a hatched region on each bar with the byte total written inside the bar. Your server's bandwidth meter sits inline on the lanes that traverse it.
viz.predictPrompt: A 2 GB upload fails at 90% on a flaky connection. How many bytes must be re-sent under (a) multipart/form-data through your API, (b) a presigned single PUT to S3, (c) 5 MB resumable chunks? Two of these three have the same answer — say which, and why that surprises people.
controls: chunk size for the resumable lane
retry policy: none / resume from offset
viz.insight: Presigned URLs solve YOUR bandwidth problem; resumable protocols solve the USER'S failure cost. They are different problems, and choosing one does not give you the other.
viz.buildNotes: Sim: (sizeBytes, failAtFraction, strategy, chunkBytes) → {bytesSent, bytesResent, serverBytes}. Unit-test that presigned-single-PUT and multipart-through-API both resend 100% while resumable resends at most one chunk — the whole point of the module. Reduced motion draws final bars with hatched resend regions and inline totals.

drills.prompt: 1.5 GB file, fails at 70%. Compute bytes re-sent and bytes that crossed your own servers for: multipart through your API; presigned single PUT; S3 multipart with 8 MB parts; resumable with 5 MB chunks.

Seven requirements are listed (mobile users on trains, 50 GB video masters, an HTML form fallback with no JS, virus scanning before sharing, a hard 25 MB cap, per-file audit logging, no egress budget). Map each to a strategy and mark the requirements that force a hybrid.
A presigned PUT works in curl and fails in the browser with a CORS error before any bytes are sent. Choose the cause and state the exact fix.
drills.answerSketch: The browser preflights the PUT because of a non-simple header (Content-Type or x-amz-*). The bucket's CORS configuration must allow the method, the origin and that request header — and the header must be among those covered by the signature.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: uploaded files must be virus-scanned and transcoded before the user may share the link. What breaks in a naive presigned design, and what do you add to the contract?
drills.answerSketch: The client believes 'PUT returned 200' means done, but the object is unscanned and unusable. Add a server-side completion step, an explicit asset state machine (uploaded → scanning → ready → rejected), and a defined way for the client to learn the state — poll or push — with a terminal rejected state the UI can render.

drills.prompt: A team mints presigned GET URLs with a 7-day TTL and puts them in email notifications and in their APM traces. Name the two distinct problems and the design change that removes both.
drills.answerSketch: The URL is a long-lived bearer credential that is now in mail archives and third-party telemetry, and it cannot be revoked before expiry. Fix: short-TTL URLs minted on demand behind an authenticated redirect endpoint, and scrubbing signed URLs from logs.

failureModes: Believes 'direct to S3' automatically means resumable.
Sends 2 GB through the API server and only discovers the memory profile in production.
Uses fetch() and then cannot explain why there is no progress bar.
Mints presigned URLs with day-long TTLs and treats them as harmless links.
Never defines what happens between 'PUT succeeded' and 'the file is usable'.
interviewProbes: Design the upload contract for 4 GB video files from mobile clients on poor networks.
Where does the byte stream actually go, and who pays for it?
The upload returns 200 but the user says the file is missing. Where is the gap in your contract?

api-evolution.title: Evolving the Contract: Breaking Changes, Codegen, Contract Tests
objectives: Judge whether a specific change is breaking, for a specific named consumer, with a stated parser discipline.
Sequence an expand-and-contract migration with in-band deprecation signalling.
Decide where compile-time codegen and consumer-driven contract tests each earn their cost.
claims: Request and response compatibility run in opposite directions: a server may safely ACCEPT more (new optional request fields) and may safely RETURN more only if consumers ignore unknown fields — so 'additive is safe' is a claim about the client's parser, not about the schema.

Adding a value to an enum, or making a response field nullable, are both breaking changes even though nothing was removed, because each introduces a case the consumer's parser and UI have never handled.
Tightening a constraint is breaking on requests and safe on responses; loosening a constraint is safe on requests and breaking on responses — this asymmetry is the whole of compatibility reasoning.

Native mobile clients pin a build for months, so 'we deployed the new version' does not exist for them; the real question for any change is the oldest client still in the wild and what share of traffic it carries.
Expand-and-contract — add the new field, migrate consumers, verify usage has fallen to zero, then remove the old field — is the mechanism that lets you make a breaking change without a version bump.

The `Deprecation` response header field (RFC 9745) and `Sunset` (RFC 8594) announce a removal date in-band, which is observable in client telemetry and in tests — unlike a changelog entry, which is observable by nobody.
GraphQL has no versioning: fields are marked `@deprecated` and removed once per-field usage telemetry shows nobody reads them, which only works if the server actually records per-field usage.

Generated clients — from OpenAPI 3.1, which aligns with JSON Schema 2020-12, or from a GraphQL schema — convert a contract change into a compile error instead of a runtime one; that is the entire value, and it evaporates the moment anyone hand-writes the types alongside them.

Consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) assert the fields THIS client actually reads, so the provider can prove a change is safe before deploying — something schema diffing alone cannot do, because a diff does not know who reads what.

viz.title: Breaking For Whom?
viz.whatIsDrawn: Schema v1 and v2 side by side with changed lines marked. Below, a matrix whose rows are real consumers — web (current), web (tab open since yesterday), iOS build 4.2 pinned, a partner's server-side integration — and whose columns are the individual changes. Each cell reads safe or breaks with the reason written inside the cell. A parser-strictness control rewrites the cells live, keeping the previous state as a ghost layer.
viz.predictPrompt: You add one optional field to a response and add one value to an existing enum. Which of the four consumers break, and which of the two changes is the more dangerous one?
controls: change set: pick from ten real diffs
consumer parser discipline: ignore-unknown / strict validation / exhaustive switch
viz.insight: Breaking-ness is a property of the consumer's parser and its deploy cadence, not of the diff. You cannot answer 'is this breaking?' without first naming the consumer.
viz.buildNotes: Sim: (change, consumerProfile) → {breaks: boolean, reason: string}. This table is the module's factual core, so every cell must be unit-tested against the stated compatibility rules — a wrong cell teaches a wrong belief that a candidate will repeat in an interview. Reduced motion shows the full matrix with no ghost transition.

drills.prompt: Eight schema changes are listed. For each, mark breaking or safe AND name the consumer it breaks. Marking 'safe' without qualifying the parser discipline scores zero.
drills.answerSketch: e.g. new optional response field — safe for ignore-unknown, breaks strict validators and snapshot tests; new enum value — breaks exhaustive switches; response field made nullable — breaks everyone; request field made required — breaks all existing callers; renamed field — breaking; widened numeric range on a response — breaking for narrowly typed clients.

drills.prompt: Order an expand-and-contract migration that renames `customer_name` to `billing.name` with a pinned mobile client in the field: add new field, dual-write, emit Deprecation and Sunset, instrument old-field reads, migrate web, wait out the mobile version tail, verify zero reads, remove.
The requirement changes: a partner integration you cannot contact consumes this endpoint. Which of your migration steps become impossible, and what replaces them?
drills.answerSketch: You cannot 'migrate the consumer'. Replace with: indefinite dual-support behind a media-type or explicit version, usage telemetry keyed by API credential to detect the tail, and Sunset headers plus contractual notice as the only lever.

drills.prompt: A generated TypeScript client is regenerated after a new enum value is added. The build passes. Explain why, and why that is worse than a compile error.
drills.answerSketch: The handling code used a default/fallback branch (or the generated type is a string union that is only checked where exhaustiveness was asserted), so the new case silently falls into the default path and is rendered as an unknown or dropped. Compile errors are the mechanism you paid for; a default branch opts out of it.

drills.prompt: Timed, 250 words: URL path versioning (/v2/) versus header or media-type versioning. Take a position. You must address CDN cache keys, the pinned-mobile-client problem, and the operational cost of maintaining two code paths.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) notes URL versioning gives distinct cache keys and trivially debuggable requests; (2) notes header/media-type versioning keeps one resource identity but is invisible in logs and easy to omit; (3) prices maintaining N live versions against expand-and-contract; (4) names the pinned-client tail as the actual constraint; (5) states what would change the answer.

failureModes: Says 'additive changes are always backwards compatible' without naming a consumer or a parser.
Forgets that adding an enum value breaks exhaustive handling.
Assumes every client updates when the server deploys.
Adds /v2/ for a change that expand-and-contract would have absorbed, then maintains both forever.
Treats generated types as proof of compatibility while hand-writing an override next to them.
interviewProbes: Is adding a field to a response a breaking change? Defend your answer.
How do you remove a field that a two-year-old mobile build still reads?
How would you prove to the backend team that their change is safe for you, before they deploy it?

api-auth-contract.title: Auth Inside the Contract: 401, Refresh, and the Race
objectives: Diagnose auth incidents — refresh loops, mass logouts, redirect storms — down to the client decision that caused them.
Specify the refresh contract: single-flight, queued replay, retry-once, and cross-tab coordination.
State the token-transport trade-off as a choice between two attack classes rather than a security ranking.
claims: 401 means the request lacked valid authentication and the response is required to carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header; 403 means the identity is known and still not permitted, so retrying it with a fresh token cannot help.
A client that refreshes and retries on 403 turns an authorisation bug into an infinite loop; the refresh-and-retry path must be reachable only from 401, and only once per originating request.

With three requests in flight when the access token expires, a naive per-request refresh issues three refresh calls; the correct contract is single-flight — one shared refresh promise, with the 401'd requests queued and replayed once it resolves.

Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection — the OAuth 2.1 direction — revokes the entire token family when an already-consumed refresh token is presented, so a concurrent-refresh race does not merely waste a call: it logs the user out.

Access tokens should be treated as expired slightly early, using a 30–60 second skew buffer against `exp`, because client clocks drift and a token that expires in flight produces an entirely avoidable 401 round trip.

Keeping the access token in JavaScript-reachable memory or storage makes it exfiltratable by XSS; keeping the session in an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookie makes it CSRF-exposed instead — the decision is between two attack classes, not between insecure and secure.

An `Authorization` header makes a cross-origin request non-simple, so every call incurs a CORS preflight unless it is cached, and browsers cap `Access-Control-Max-Age` — Chromium at 2 hours, Firefox at 24 — so the preflight returns on a schedule you do not control.

Tabs share cookies and storage but not memory, so refresh must be coordinated across tabs — a lock in storage or a `BroadcastChannel` — or every open tab races the same rotation and one of them loses.

viz.title: Three Requests, One Expiring Token
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three tab lifelines plus a server lifeline that holds the refresh-token family as visible rows with their consumed/valid state. The access token's validity is a bar that runs out mid-flight. Requests that receive 401 are drawn parked in a queue box inside the diagram; each refresh call is a distinct arrow so the count is countable by eye. The single-flight version of the same timeline is retained as a ghost ladder underneath.
viz.predictPrompt: Three requests are in flight when the access token expires, and each independently refreshes on its 401. The server uses refresh-token rotation with reuse detection. How many refresh calls are made, and what is the user's final state?
controls: rotation with reuse detection: on / off
viz.insight: Concurrency is what breaks auth clients. Single-flight refresh with a replay queue is the contract; rotation with reuse detection turns getting it wrong into a forced logout rather than a wasted request.
viz.buildNotes: Sim: (inFlight, strategy, rotation, tabs, skewMs) → {refreshCalls, replayedRequests, finalSessionState}. Unit-test that per-request refresh with rotation yields sessionState='revoked' and that single-flight yields exactly one refresh call regardless of in-flight count. Reduced motion draws the completed ladder with the refresh arrows numbered.

drills.prompt: An HTTP interceptor refreshes the token on any response where `status >= 400 && status < 500`. Name the two distinct incidents this produces and give the two-line fix.
drills.answerSketch: 403 (genuine authorisation failure) and 429 both trigger refresh loops — the 403 case loops forever, the 429 case amplifies a throttle. Fix: refresh only on 401, and only once per originating request, then surface a terminal error.

drills.prompt: Order the single-flight refresh sequence: receive 401, check a refresh is not already in flight, start or join the shared refresh promise, park the original request, await resolution, replay the original request once with the new token, on second 401 abandon and log out.
Fill the blanks in a pre-baked refresh helper: the memoised in-flight promise, the line that clears it in a finally block, the retry-once guard flag, and the cross-tab lock acquisition.
drills.answerSketch: A module-scoped `let inFlight: Promise|null`; `finally { inFlight = null }`; a per-request `hasRetried` flag rather than a global counter; a navigator.locks or BroadcastChannel-coordinated leader for the refresh.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: users routinely keep four tabs of your app open. What breaks first under your current design, and what do you add?
drills.answerSketch: Four independent single-flight refreshers still race each other; with rotation, three of them present a consumed refresh token and the family is revoked.
