Add cross-tab coordination (a lock or a leader tab) plus a storage-event listener so followers adopt the new token instead of fetching their own.

drills.prompt: For six scenarios, choose 401, 403 or 404 and state whether the client should refresh, re-authenticate, or surface a terminal error. Choosing the right status with the wrong client action scores zero.

failureModes: Treats 401 and 403 as interchangeable and refreshes on both.
Fires one refresh per 401'd request, then reports 'random logouts' as a backend bug.
Never considers a second tab.
Argues localStorage tokens are 'fine because we have a CSP' without naming the attack class they accepted.
Fails to buffer against clock skew and ships an avoidable 401 on every token boundary.
interviewProbes: Ten requests are in flight when the token expires. Walk me through your client, exactly.
When would you deliberately return 404 instead of 403?
Cookie or Authorization header? Name the attack you are choosing to accept.

ui-cascade-architecture.title: Cascade Layers and the Modern Selector Model
objectives: Design a cascade architecture for a design system consumed by multiple product teams, using @layer to make override order explicit and independent of selector shape
Predict the winner of a cascade conflict by walking origin/importance, layer order, specificity and source order in the correct sequence
Choose between :is(), :where(), :has() and nesting based on the specificity each contributes, not on how the selector reads
claims: Cascade layers are compared before specificity: a declaration in a later layer beats a declaration in an earlier layer no matter how specific the earlier selector is.
Unlayered declarations act as an implicit final layer, so unlayered styles beat all layered styles in the normal (non-!important) cascade.
For !important declarations the layer order is inverted: the earliest layer's !important wins, and layered !important beats unlayered !important.
@layer statement order (e.g. `@layer reset, base, components, utilities;`) fixes precedence once at the top of the stylesheet, so later @import or file order cannot change it.
`revert-layer` rolls a property back to the value it would have had from previous layers, whereas `revert` rolls back to the previous cascade origin.
:where() contributes zero specificity and :is() contributes the specificity of its most specific argument; :has() follows the :is() rule, so :has(#id) is id-specific.
Logical properties (margin-inline-start, block-size, inset-inline) resolve against writing-mode and direction, so one rule serves LTR and RTL without a mirrored stylesheet.
Cascade layers replace convention-based specificity control (BEM depth, ITCSS import order, !important ladders) because they encode override order in the language rather than in a naming agreement.

viz.title: Cascade Resolution Trace
viz.whatIsDrawn: Five competing `color` declarations for one element are drawn as cards in a single column. A stepper walks the cascade algorithm — (1) origin and importance, (2) layer order, (3) specificity, (4) order of appearance — and at each step the losing cards are struck through in place, with a short reason printed on the card itself, not in a margin. The surviving card is boxed. A ghost column to the right shows the outcome of the same five declarations with all @layer assignments removed, so the learner sees exactly what layering changed.
viz.predictPrompt: A stylesheet starts `@layer base, components;`. `@layer base { .btn { color: red !important } }` and `@layer components { .btn { color: blue !important } }`. Both selectors have identical specificity, base is declared first. Which colour wins — and would your answer change if neither declaration were !important?
controls: assign each declaration to a layer (or unlayered)
step forward/back through the four cascade stages
viz.insight: Layer order outranks specificity entirely, and !important inverts layer order — which is why dropping !important into a late 'overrides' layer silently makes it lose to an early layer it was meant to beat.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure cascade resolver: takes an array of {origin, important, layer, specificity, sourceIndex} and returns the winner plus a per-stage elimination trace. Unit-test it against a table of WPT-derived cases, especially the important-inversion and unlayered cases — this sim IS the pedagogical claim. viz.tsx renders the trace; no animation library needed beyond an opacity/strike transition on card elimination. Reduced-motion: render the final trace fully expanded with all four stages stacked.

drills.prompt: Order the stages the cascade uses to pick a winner, most decisive first: specificity · order of appearance · origin and importance · layer order.
drills.answerSketch: origin and importance → layer order → specificity → order of appearance.

drills.prompt: Your design system ships in `@layer ds` and product teams write unlayered CSS, which currently overrides it — that is intentional. The requirement changes: brand colours must now be unoverridable by product teams, but everything else in the DS must stay overridable. What is the minimum change?
drills.answerSketch: Split the DS into two layers, declare the forced one first (`@layer ds.brand, ds.base;`) and mark the brand declarations !important. Because !important inverts layer order and layered !important beats unlayered !important, product CSS — layered or not, !important or not — cannot win. Raising specificity or adding !important to unlayered DS rules does not achieve this.

drills.prompt: A team adds `:is(#app, .root) .card { padding: 8px }` to a utilities layer to 'keep specificity low with :is'. Their `.card--tight { padding: 4px }` utility stops working. Identify the defect in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: :is() takes the specificity of its MOST specific argument, so the selector is (1,1,0) — id-weighted. They wanted :where(), which contributes zero. (Layer order would also have solved it without touching the selector.)

drills.prompt: Complete: to reset a property back to whatever value earlier cascade layers would have given it, use ______; to reset it back to the previous cascade origin (e.g. the UA stylesheet), use ______.
drills.answerSketch: revert-layer; revert

drills.prompt: You are designing the CSS architecture for a component library consumed by three product apps with different Tailwind configs. Choose ONE: (a) zero-specificity everything via :where(), (b) an explicit @layer stack, (c) shadow DOM encapsulation. Write a 120-word justification naming what each rejected option would have cost you.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer decomposes into: does the choice make override order explicit rather than accidental; does it survive a consumer adding an unlayered utility; what happens to theming/custom properties; what is the debugging story in devtools; what does the consumer have to know. :where() makes everything overridable including things that should not be; shadow DOM solves encapsulation but breaks global theming and page-level layout; layers make order explicit but require consumer cooperation on the @layer statement.

failureModes: States that specificity is evaluated before layer order.
Assumes the last layer's !important wins, so puts escape-hatch overrides in a final 'overrides' layer where they lose to earlier !important rules.
Believes :has() has zero specificity because it resembles :where().
Proposes a new naming convention (BEM depth, ITCSS ordering) to solve an override-order problem that layers solve in the language.
Uses physical properties (margin-left, right) throughout and then adds an RTL stylesheet.
interviewProbes: A product team says the design system is 'too hard to override'. Walk me through what you'd change and what you'd deliberately keep hard to override.
Two rules, same specificity, different layers, both !important. Which wins and why?
Where does an unlayered rule sit in the cascade, for normal and for !important declarations?
When would you use :where() over :is(), concretely?

ui-layout-intrinsic.title: Layout Systems: Grid, Flex, Subgrid and Content-Length Variance
objectives: Compare flex and grid on the axis that actually decides it — whether alignment must hold across independent siblings — rather than on one-dimensional vs two-dimensional folklore
Predict and defeat the automatic min-content floor that makes 'equal width' items unequal
Design layouts that hold at 1 character and at 2.5x string expansion, and truncate without removing text from the accessibility tree
claims: Flex items size from their content by default (`flex-basis: auto`) so item sizes depend on what is inside them; grid tracks are sized by the track definition, independently of which item lands in them.

A flex item's default `min-width: auto` floors it at its min-content size, so `flex: 1` does not produce equal widths when one item contains a long unbreakable string; `min-width: 0` removes the floor.
The grid equivalent of that floor is the `auto` minimum in `1fr` (which means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`); `minmax(0, 1fr)` is what actually allows the track to shrink below its content.
Subgrid lets a nested grid adopt its parent's track lines, which is the only way to align content across sibling cards without giving every card a fixed row height.

CSS `text-overflow: ellipsis` requires a constrained inline size plus `overflow: hidden` and only truncates one line; the interoperable multi-line clamp is still `display: -webkit-box` with `-webkit-line-clamp`.

CSS truncation leaves the full string in the DOM and the accessibility tree; JavaScript truncation that rewrites textContent destroys it, which is why measuring-and-slicing in JS is the wrong default.

Intrinsic sizing keywords (`min-content`, `max-content`, `fit-content()`) size a box from its content without JS measurement; `fit-content(20ch)` grows to content but caps at a content-relative bound.

Content length is a first-class constraint, not an edge case: layouts must be verified at one character and at roughly 2.5x the English string length, because that is the realistic expansion for German and Finnish UI strings.

viz.title: Layout Stress Rig
viz.whatIsDrawn: One row of three cards rendered simultaneously in three strips: (1) `display:flex; flex:1`, (2) `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)`, (3) the same grid with `minmax(0,1fr)` plus subgrid for the internal rows. All three are fed the identical content. Overflow is marked with a red edge tick drawn on the offending card. A faint ghost outline of the 1x-content layout stays pinned behind each strip so the learner can see displacement rather than guess it.
viz.predictPrompt: Three cards in a flex row, each with `flex: 1`, each containing one long unbroken URL. Predict: are the cards equal width? Now predict what changes if you add `min-width: 0` to the items — and separately, what changes if instead you only add `overflow: hidden`.
controls: toggle subgrid on the card internals
viz.insight: 'Equal width' is a lie until you defeat the automatic min-content floor; and once you do, only subgrid keeps internal rows aligned across cards as their content lengths diverge.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure 1-D track solver: given item min-content/max-content sizes, flex factors and a min floor, return final widths and overflow flags. Unit-test the min-width:auto vs 0 divergence and the minmax(0,1fr) case — those two are the module's core claims. viz.tsx draws pure SVG boxes; no real layout engine, so results are deterministic and testable. Reduced-motion: replace the scrubber animation with three static snapshots at 1x/2x/3x.

drills.prompt: `.row { display:flex } .row > * { flex: 1; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap }`. Cards containing long URLs are still wider than the others. What is missing and why does the existing `overflow: hidden` not help?
drills.answerSketch: `min-width: 0` on the flex items. `overflow: hidden` controls what happens to content that exceeds the box; it does not lower the box's automatic min-content minimum, so the item is still floored at the URL's min-content width.

drills.prompt: Complete: `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, ______)` is required instead of `1fr` when a track must be allowed to shrink below its content, because `1fr` expands to `minmax(______, 1fr)`.
drills.answerSketch: minmax(0, 1fr); auto

drills.prompt: For each, pick flex, grid, or grid+subgrid: (1) a tag list of unknown length that should wrap and pack tightly; (2) a card deck where every card's title, body and footer must sit on the same baseline row across cards; (3) a toolbar with a left group, a spacer and a right group; (4) a dashboard where widgets span 1-3 columns and 1-2 rows; (5) a definition list where the term column sizes to the longest term but never exceeds 20ch; (6) a page shell with header, sidebar, main, footer.
drills.answerSketch: 1 flex (wrap, content-sized, unknown count) · 2 grid+subgrid (alignment across independent siblings) · 3 flex (one axis, distribute) · 4 grid (two-dimensional spans) · 5 grid with `fit-content(20ch)` track · 6 grid (named areas).

drills.prompt: Your card deck uses `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr))` and looks correct. The requirement changes: card footers must now align horizontally across every card in a row, and card bodies have variable length. What breaks first, and what is the fix that does NOT involve fixed heights or JS measurement?
drills.answerSketch: Nothing breaks visually at the deck level — the failure is inside each card, whose internal rows are sized independently, so footers land at different y positions. Fix: give the deck explicit row tracks (`grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto`), make each card `grid-row: span 3` and `display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid`, so all cards share the deck's row lines. Fixed heights and JS equal-height loops are the wrong answers.

drills.prompt: A designer hands you a comparison table where each cell must truncate to two lines. Choose ONE: `-webkit-line-clamp`, a JS measure-and-slice with a tooltip, or letting the row grow. Write 120 words defending it, and name explicitly what a screen reader user and a German-locale user experience under your choice.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: is the full string preserved in the DOM/a11y tree; does the layout hold at 2.5x expansion; is there an affordance to read the full value; does it force a synchronous layout read; does it survive font loading. line-clamp preserves text and needs no measurement but is a -webkit-prefixed box model with quirks; JS slicing destroys the accessible text and forces reflow; growing rows is honest but breaks the comparison scan the table exists for.

failureModes: Adds `overflow: hidden` to fix a blown-out flex row instead of `min-width: 0`, and is confused when it does not help.
Writes a JS equal-height / measure-and-truncate loop for a problem subgrid or fit-content() solves in CSS.
Uses grid for a wrapping tag list of unknown length, producing ragged empty tracks.
Only tests with short English placeholder text, so the layout ships broken in German and with one-character values.
Truncates by rewriting textContent, removing the full string from the accessibility tree and from find-in-page.
interviewProbes: Three items, `flex: 1` each, one has a long URL. Why aren't they equal, and what's the one-property fix?
When would you reach for subgrid over just nesting a grid?
How do you keep a comparison table readable when one locale's strings are 2.5x longer?
What's the difference between `1fr` and `minmax(0, 1fr)`?

ui-container-queries.title: Container Queries and Responsive Strategy Beyond Breakpoints
objectives: Design a component whose responsiveness is owned by its container, so the same instance works in a 240px sidebar and a 900px main column with no props and no breakpoint knowledge
Decide correctly which responsive requirements are container-scoped, which are genuinely viewport- or device-scoped, and which are neither
Place `container-type` on the right element and explain the containment cost that placement incurs
claims: A container query resolves against the nearest ancestor that declared `container-type`, not against the viewport, so one component can render differently in a sidebar and in a main column without props.
An element cannot query its own size: `container-type` must be on an ancestor of the queried rules, which is why the wrapper-plus-component split exists.
`container-type: inline-size` applies size containment in the inline axis, so the container's inline size must come from its context; an element sized by its own content stops being able to do that.
`container-type: size` requires both axes to be containment-independent and will collapse an auto-height element, so `inline-size` is the correct default.
Container query units (cqi, cqb, cqw, cqh) resolve against the query container, letting type and spacing scales be component-relative rather than viewport-relative.
Style queries — `@container style(--density: compact)` — branch on a custom property value set anywhere up the tree, so a parent can switch a mode without adding a class to every descendant.

Container queries do not replace media queries for things that are genuinely page- or device-scoped: print, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-color-scheme`, `pointer: coarse`, and top-level page layout switching.

Naming containers (`container-name`) matters once containers nest, because an unnamed `@container` binds to the nearest eligible ancestor — which can silently change when someone adds a container higher or lower in the tree.

viz.title: Same Card, Two Containers
viz.whatIsDrawn: One card component is instantiated twice on a single simulated page — once inside a resizable sidebar, once inside a resizable main column. Both instances read from the same rule set. Each card carries an in-diagram badge showing the container width it is currently resolving against and which `@container` branch matched. A ghost overlay on each card shows what a viewport `@media` version of the identical rules would have rendered at the current page width.
viz.predictPrompt: You put `container-type: inline-size` directly on the card element itself (not a wrapper) and write `@container (min-width: 400px)` inside it. The card is a grid item in a `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr))` deck. Predict what renders — and now predict what happens if you use `container-type: size` instead.
controls: set `--density` on the page root (style query)
viz.insight: Responsiveness belongs to the container, not the page — and the query container must be a wrapper whose size arrives from outside, because nothing can both be sized by its content and answer questions about its own size.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts resolves container-query matching purely: given a tree of {containerType, name, resolvedInlineSize} and a set of queries, return which branch each component takes. Test the self-query case and the nested-unnamed-container case explicitly. viz.tsx uses real CSS container queries for the live cards (dogfooding) but drives the ghost overlay from sim.ts so the comparison is deterministic in tests. Reduced-motion: three fixed sidebar widths as static side-by-sides.

drills.prompt: `.card { container-type: inline-size; display: grid } @container (min-width: 400px) { .card__media { grid-column: 1 } }`. In a masonry-ish deck the cards render at zero-ish width and the query never matches. One sentence: why?
drills.answerSketch: `container-type: inline-size` applies inline-axis size containment to the card, so the card can no longer be sized by its own content — and nothing else is giving it an inline size. The container must be a wrapper whose width comes from the deck's track.

drills.prompt: Classify each as container query, media query, or neither: (1) a product card switches to horizontal layout when its column is wider than 420px; (2) hit targets grow to 44px on touch devices; (3) the print stylesheet hides the nav; (4) the whole app switches from a rail to a bottom bar; (5) a chart's font scales with the widget it's in; (6) mirroring the layout for Arabic.
drills.answerSketch: 1 container · 2 media (`pointer: coarse`) · 3 media (print) · 4 media (viewport — this is genuinely page-scoped) · 5 container (cqi units) · 6 neither — logical properties, not a query.

drills.prompt: Your card already responds to its container. New requirement: an app-wide 'dense mode' toggle must make every card compact regardless of container width, and the card component must not receive a new prop. What is the minimum-CSS answer, and what is the fallback if style queries are unavailable?
drills.answerSketch: Set a custom property at the app root (`--density: compact`) and add `@container style(--density: compact)` rules to the card. Fallback: a `:root[data-density=compact] .card` rule in a later cascade layer, or `:has()` on an ancestor. Adding a prop or a class to every card is the wrong answer.

drills.prompt: Complete: to scale a heading with the width of its query container rather than the viewport, use ______ units; the viewport equivalent would be ______. In a vertical writing mode, ______ still tracks the inline axis while cqw does not.
drills.answerSketch: cqi; vw; cqi

drills.prompt: A team proposes deleting all media queries from the component library and using only container queries. Take a position in 120 words. Name at least two requirements that would regress and one that would genuinely improve.
drills.answerSketch: Regressions: device/user-preference conditions (print, reduced-motion, colour scheme, pointer coarseness) have no container analogue; page-level layout switching is legitimately viewport-scoped; every component now needs a wrapper, which is real DOM and real containment cost. Improvement: components become portable — the same card works in a sidebar, a modal and a dashboard cell with no props and no breakpoint contract between component and page.

failureModes: Puts `container-type` on the component root and cannot explain why the component collapsed.
Uses `container-type: size` by default and loses auto height.
Replaces every media query with a container query, losing print, reduced-motion and pointer conditions.
Uses cqw where cqi is meant, breaking in vertical writing modes.
Leaves containers unnamed, so an `@container` silently rebinds when someone adds a container in between.
interviewProbes: Same card in a 280px sidebar and a 900px column, no props. How?
Why can't an element query itself?
Which responsive behaviours should still be media queries in 2026?
What does `container-type: inline-size` actually cost you?

ui-stacking-context.title: Stacking Contexts, Containing Blocks, and Why Your Overlay Is Clipped
objectives: Diagnose a mis-painted or clipped overlay by locating the stacking context that contains it, rather than by escalating z-index
Identify which CSS properties silently create a stacking context and which additionally make an ancestor the containing block for `position: fixed`
Explain precisely what a portal fixes and what it leaves untouched
claims: z-index only orders elements within their own stacking context; a descendant with z-index: 9999 cannot paint above an element that outranks its stacking-context root.

Stacking contexts are created by far more than positioning: `opacity` < 1, any `transform`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, `mix-blend-mode` other than normal, `isolation: isolate`, `contain: paint` (or layout), and `will-change` naming any of those properties.

`transform`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, `contain: layout|paint`, and `will-change` on those properties make the element the containing block for `position: fixed` descendants — so a fixed overlay inside a transformed card is positioned and clipped relative to the card, not the viewport.
`isolation: isolate` creates a stacking context with no other visual effect, which makes it the correct tool for fencing a component's internal z-index range.

Within one stacking context, paint order is fixed: the root's background and borders, then negative z-index children, then in-flow block-level boxes, then floats, then inline content, then z-index: 0/auto positioned children, then positive z-index children.

Portalling to document.body escapes ancestor clipping and containing-block problems, but does not change DOM tab order, does not change React's synthetic event bubbling (which follows the React tree, not the DOM tree), and does not create any aria relationship.

`overflow: hidden|auto|scroll` on an ancestor clips descendants — including absolutely positioned ones, unless the descendant's containing block is outside the clipper — which is the other half of 'my dropdown is cut off'.
The top layer (a modal `<dialog>` or an open popover) paints above every stacking context in the document and is the only mechanism that reliably escapes both clipping and ordering.

viz.title: Stacking Context Tree with Paint Order
viz.whatIsDrawn: The page is drawn as nested rectangles (header, content, card, modal). Every rectangle that forms a stacking context gets a badge printed inside its top-left corner naming the property that created it and its z-index within its parent context. A paint-order counter walks the tree and stamps an ordinal number inside each box in the order it paints. When `position: fixed` is active, an arrow drawn inside the diagram points from the fixed element to whichever box is currently its containing block.
viz.predictPrompt: A sticky site header has `z-index: 10`. Deep inside the page, a card has `transform: translateZ(0)` (added months ago 'for GPU acceleration'). A modal rendered inside that card is `position: fixed; inset: 0; z-index: 9999`. Predict two things: where the modal's backdrop actually covers, and whether the modal paints above the header.
viz.insight: z-index is a local sorting key, not a global one — the ancestor chain decides who wins, and a transform added for performance silently redefines what 'fixed' is fixed to.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure paint-order + containing-block resolver over a small declarative tree: input {tag, styles}, output an ordered paint list plus, for each fixed element, its resolved containing block and clip rect. Unit-test against the transform-creates-containing-block case and the overflow-clip case — these are the two claims the module lives or dies on. viz.tsx is SVG only. Reduced-motion: render all paint ordinals at once instead of sweeping.

drills.prompt: A modal is `position: fixed; inset: 0; background: rgba(0,0,0,.5)`. It covers only a 400x300 region in the middle of a card and scrolls away with the page. The modal's own CSS is correct. Name the ancestor property causing it and the one-line diagnostic you'd run in devtools.
drills.answerSketch: An ancestor has a transform (or filter / backdrop-filter / contain / will-change on one), making it the containing block for fixed descendants. Diagnostic: walk up the chain checking computed `transform !== none`, `filter !== none`, `contain`, `will-change` — or in Chrome devtools inspect the fixed element's 'containing block' badge.

drills.prompt: Order these from painted first to painted last within a single stacking context: floats · positive z-index children · the context root's background and borders · inline content · negative z-index children · in-flow block-level boxes · z-index:0/auto positioned children.
drills.answerSketch: root background/borders → negative z-index → in-flow block-level → floats → inline content → z-index:0/auto positioned → positive z-index.

drills.prompt: Select every property value below that creates a stacking context: `position: relative` (no z-index) · `opacity: 0.99` · `will-change: transform` · `overflow: hidden` · `isolation: isolate` · `contain: paint` · `mix-blend-mode: multiply` · `filter: none`.
drills.answerSketch: opacity: 0.99, will-change: transform, isolation: isolate, contain: paint, mix-blend-mode: multiply. `position: relative` without z-index does not; `overflow: hidden` clips but does not create one; `filter: none` does not.

drills.prompt: Your dropdown works today because it is `position: absolute` inside a card. New requirement: the card must scale up on hover with `transform: scale(1.02)`, and the card sits in a container with `overflow: hidden`. What breaks first, and which of these fixes it without JS positioning: portal to body · isolation: isolate on the card · popover attribute on the dropdown · raising z-index?
drills.answerSketch: The dropdown is now clipped by the overflow ancestor and (if it were fixed) reparented to the transformed card. `popover` fixes it: the dropdown is promoted to the top layer, escaping both the clip and the ordering. Portal-to-body also escapes the clip but costs you focus order and positioning. isolation and z-index do nothing about clipping.

drills.prompt: In 120 words, explain to a teammate why 'just portal it to body' is an incomplete fix for a dropdown menu. Name three things the portal does not do.
drills.answerSketch: It does not restore DOM tab order (the menu is now at the end of the document, so Tab from the trigger goes elsewhere); it does not establish any programmatic relationship for assistive tech (aria-controls/aria-expanded and, if needed, aria-activedescendant are still your job); and it does not solve positioning — you have inherited a manual measure-and-reposition loop on scroll and resize that CSS anchor positioning would have handled. React's event bubbling also still follows the React tree, which surprises people writing outside-click handlers.

failureModes: Escalates z-index (999 → 9999 → 999999) instead of locating the stacking-context root that is actually losing.
Adds `will-change: transform` 'for performance' and creates both a stacking context and a containing block for fixed descendants.
Believes `position: fixed` is unconditionally viewport-relative.
Thinks a portal also fixes tab order and screen-reader relationships.
Blames overflow clipping when the real cause is paint order, or vice versa, because they never draw the tree.
interviewProbes: My modal renders behind the sticky header even at z-index 9999. Walk me through your diagnosis.
Name five properties that create a stacking context that aren't position + z-index.
What exactly does portalling to body fix, and what does it leave broken?
When would you use `isolation: isolate`?

ui-overlay-layer.title: The Top Layer: dialog, popover, anchor positioning and focus
objectives: Design an overlay system by deciding, per overlay, which of the four modality guarantees it needs — paint order, focus containment, assistive-tech containment, dismissal
Choose between `<dialog>.showModal()`, `<dialog>.show()`, `popover=auto`, `popover=manual` and a plain element from a requirement, not from habit
Replace a JS positioning loop with CSS anchor positioning and state honestly when the JS library is still required
claims: `<dialog>.showModal()` does four things `.show()` and a styled div do not: promotes the element to the top layer, renders `::backdrop`, makes the rest of the document inert, and moves focus into the dialog — and on close it returns focus to the previously focused element.
The top layer is a document-level painting layer above every stacking context; only a modal `<dialog>` and an open popover put content there, and no z-index value can reach it.

`popover` (the attribute) gives top-layer promotion, Escape dismissal and — for `popover=auto` — light dismiss on outside click, but deliberately does NOT trap focus or make the page inert; `popover=manual` drops light dismiss and Escape-driven auto-close.

`inert` removes an entire subtree from tab order, from pointer events and from the accessibility tree, which is why it is the correct replacement for hand-rolled focus traps plus `aria-hidden` on siblings.

`aria-modal="true"` plus a JS focus trap does not reliably contain a screen reader's virtual/browse cursor; only removing the background from the accessibility tree (inert, or the implicit inertness of a modal dialog) does.

CSS anchor positioning — `anchor-name`, `position-anchor`, `anchor()`, `position-area`, `position-try-fallbacks` — performs the flip-and-shift work JS positioning libraries did; it reached Baseline in 2026 when Firefox 147 shipped it, after Chrome 125 (2024) and Safari 26 (2025).

Anchor positioning works across the top-layer boundary: a popover in the top layer can still be positioned against an anchor in normal flow, which is what makes the portal-plus-measure-on-scroll loop unnecessary.
A modal `<dialog>` blocks scrolling of the page behind it, but `overscroll-behavior: contain` is still needed on the dialog's own scroll container to stop scroll chaining out of it.

viz.title: Four Guarantees of Modality
viz.whatIsDrawn: An exploded side-on view of one document: the normal-flow plane at the bottom, stacking contexts stacked above it, and the top layer floating clear above everything. The chosen overlay variant is drawn into whichever plane it actually occupies. Overlaid on the same figure — not beside it — are three status ticks drawn inside the overlay's box: focus contained / AT contained / dismissible. A focus token walks the tab chain, drawn as a path through the boxes it can reach, so an escaping focus is visible as a line leaving the overlay.
viz.predictPrompt: Your modal is a div: `position: fixed`, `z-index: 9999`, `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, and a JS focus trap on Tab and Shift+Tab. A VoiceOver user opens it and swipes right past the last control. Predict what they reach next — and predict which single line of code would change that answer.
controls: choose overlay: styled div | portal | popover=auto | popover=manual | dialog.show() | dialog.showModal()
step the focus token forward/back through the tab chain
toggle anchor positioning vs fixed coordinates
viz.insight: Modality is four separate guarantees — paint order, focus containment, assistive-tech containment, and dismissal — and a div with z-index and a focus trap buys you at most two of them.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models each overlay variant as a record of the four guarantees plus a tab-order graph, and returns the sequence of reachable nodes. Unit-test that the aria-modal-only variant reaches background nodes in AT-cursor mode while the inert variant does not — this is the claim most likely to be disputed, so cite the ARIA APG and WebKit/Chromium behaviour in the prose. viz.tsx is SVG with an optional real live demo below it. Reduced-motion: render the focus path as a numbered static polyline.

drills.prompt: Pick the right primitive for each: (1) a tooltip on a truncated cell; (2) a combobox listbox; (3) a destructive 'delete workspace' confirmation; (4) a toast stack; (5) a nav drawer on mobile that must be dismissible by tapping the page; (6) a colour picker that must stay open while the user interacts with the canvas behind it. Options: dialog.showModal() · dialog.show() · popover=auto · popover=manual · plain element.
drills.answerSketch: 1 popover=auto (or popover=hint) · 2 popover=auto positioned to the input, listbox stays owned by the combobox, focus stays in the input · 3 dialog.showModal() · 4 plain element in the top layer only if needed; toasts must not steal focus — a live region, not a popover · 5 dialog.showModal() (needs inertness) or popover=auto if the page must stay usable · 6 popover=manual.

drills.prompt: Order what `showModal()` does: renders ::backdrop · makes the rest of the document inert · promotes the element to the top layer · moves focus to the first focusable element (or the dialog itself).
drills.answerSketch: promote to top layer → render ::backdrop → make the rest of the document inert → move focus in. (And on close: remove from top layer, un-inert, return focus to the invoker.)

drills.prompt: A hand-rolled modal sets `aria-hidden="true"` on the page wrapper while open. Screen-reader users report the modal itself is unreachable roughly half the time. What is the defect?
drills.answerSketch: The modal is rendered inside the wrapper that just got aria-hidden, so it is hidden from AT along with everything else — or, if portalled out, focus is still inside an aria-hidden subtree at the moment of the toggle, which is a spec violation. `inert` on the siblings (or a real modal dialog) is the correct mechanism; aria-hidden on an ancestor of the focused element is never valid.

drills.prompt: Your dropdown uses CSS anchor positioning with `position-area: block-end span-inline-start` and works. New requirement: the dropdown must not float detached when the user scrolls its anchor out of the scrollport. What breaks, and which CSS handles it without a scroll listener?
drills.answerSketch: By default the positioned element stays put and appears orphaned once the anchor leaves the viewport. `position-visibility: anchors-visible` (with `position-try-fallbacks` for flipping) hides it when the anchor is no longer visible. A JS scroll listener is the answer to avoid.

drills.prompt: Your component library must support Firefox ESR for another 12 months. In 120 words, decide between shipping CSS anchor positioning with a fallback, keeping Floating UI, or shipping both behind a feature detect. Name the bundle, correctness and maintenance cost of your choice.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: what does the fallback render when anchor positioning is unsupported (a statically positioned menu is often acceptable; a detached one is not); `@supports (anchor-name: --x)` gives a clean detect; shipping both means paying Floating UI's bytes for everyone unless it is dynamically imported behind the detect, which adds a request on first open; maintenance means two positioning code paths and two sets of visual tests. Strong answers name the concrete bytes and pick a date to delete the fallback.

failureModes: Sets `aria-hidden` on background siblings instead of `inert`.
Believes `aria-modal="true"` plus a Tab-key focus trap contains a screen reader.
Reaches for Floating UI without checking that CSS anchor positioning is now Baseline.
Forgets to restore focus to the invoking element on close.
Uses a popover for a destructive confirmation, so the user can click straight past it.
Uses `overflow: hidden` on body for scroll lock and loses scroll position on iOS.
interviewProbes: Build me a modal. Now tell me everything `<dialog>.showModal()` gives you for free that your div didn't.
What is the difference between a focus trap and inert?
Where does a popover paint, and why can no z-index reach it?
How would you position a dropdown against its trigger in 2026, and what's your fallback?

ui-declarative-motion.title: Browser-Driven Motion: View Transitions and Scroll Timelines
objectives: Explain the snapshot-freeze-animate lifecycle of a view transition precisely enough to predict what a user sees during a slow update callback
Explain why a scroll timeline can run off the main thread while a scroll event listener cannot, and what that means for jank
Explain what the view-transition pseudo-element tree is, where it paints, and why page z-index does not apply to it
claims: `document.startViewTransition(cb)` captures the old visual state, runs your DOM update inside `cb`, captures the new state, then animates between them; rendering is suspended between the two captures, so anything slow inside `cb` shows the user a frozen page.

The update callback has a ~4 second timeout: if it has not settled by then the transition is skipped and the DOM update still applies, so a network fetch inside the callback is a correctness bug as well as a UX one.

View transitions animate a pseudo-element tree — `::view-transition` > `::view-transition-group(name)` > `::view-transition-image-pair(name)` > `::view-transition-old(name)` / `::view-transition-new(name)` — that is rendered above all page content, so page z-index and ancestor clipping do not apply to the animation.
A `view-transition-name` must be unique in the document at capture time; two elements sharing a name skips the transition, which is why list items need per-id names generated from data.

The default group animation interpolates only position and size between the old and new boxes; the old state is a captured image and the new is live content, so non-uniform aspect-ratio changes stretch unless you tune `object-fit`/`height` on the old/new pseudo-elements.

Cross-document view transitions require `@view-transition { navigation: auto }` in BOTH documents and are same-origin only; they are supported in Chromium (126+) and Safari (18.2+), with Firefox still catching up as of 2026 — so they must be treated as a progressive enhancement.

Scroll-driven animations bind an animation's progress to scroll offset via `animation-timeline: scroll()` or `view()` rather than to a clock, which means the browser can run them off the main thread — something a `scroll` event listener plus rAF fundamentally cannot do.
A `view()` timeline exposes named ranges (`cover`, `contain`, `entry`, `exit`) describing the subject's passage through the scrollport, and `animation-range` selects the slice the animation occupies.

Both APIs animate by default, so `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` must be handled explicitly — skip the transition and apply the DOM update directly, or neutralise the pseudo-element animations in a media block.

viz.title: Snapshot Stepper
viz.whatIsDrawn: A four-cell filmstrip across the top: old state captured · DOM updated (rendering suspended) · new state captured · pseudo-element tree animating. Directly beneath, a main-thread frame track where the suspended window is shaded and labelled inside the shading with its duration. A ghost track below shows the equivalent JS/FLIP crossfade for the same visual result, with its extra layout reads marked in place. Everything is scrubbed; nothing autoplays.
viz.predictPrompt: Inside `startViewTransition(async () => { const data = await fetch(...); setState(data) })` the fetch takes 800ms. Predict exactly what the user sees for those 800ms. Then predict what happens if the fetch takes 6 seconds.
controls: toggle two elements sharing one name
viz.insight: A view transition is a snapshot-and-freeze, not a tween — everything you do inside the callback happens while the user is staring at a still image, and past ~4s the browser gives up on you.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure state machine over the transition lifecycle: inputs {callbackDuration, namesUnique, reducedMotion, timeoutMs}, outputs the ordered phase list with durations and a terminal outcome (animated | skipped-timeout | skipped-duplicate-name | skipped-reduced-motion). Unit-test the 4s timeout and the duplicate-name skip against spec text; cite the CSS View Transitions spec in the prose. viz.tsx renders the filmstrip in SVG and, separately, a small real view transition demo gated behind feature detection so the page degrades where unsupported. Reduced-motion: static filmstrip, no scrub animation.

drills.prompt: Order the phases of a same-document view transition: run the update callback · capture the new state · animate the pseudo-element tree · capture the old state · suspend rendering · remove the pseudo-element tree and resume normal rendering.
drills.answerSketch: suspend rendering → capture old state → run the update callback → capture new state → animate the pseudo-element tree → remove it and resume.

drills.prompt: A photo grid sets `view-transition-name: card` in a shared CSS rule for every `.card`. Navigating to detail works the first time on a one-item grid but does nothing on the real grid. One sentence: why, and what is the fix?
drills.answerSketch: view-transition-name must be unique per document at capture time; with many cards the names collide and the transition is skipped. Fix: generate a per-item name from a stable id (a style attribute or `--vt-name: --card-<id>` fed into `view-transition-name`), or only name the one card being navigated from.

drills.prompt: Complete: cross-document view transitions require the at-rule ______ with `navigation: auto` in ______ document(s), and only work between pages of the same ______.
drills.answerSketch: @view-transition; both; origin

drills.prompt: You ship a route transition with `startViewTransition`. New requirement: users with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` must get no animation, but the navigation must still happen instantly. Which is correct — (a) `@media (prefers-reduced-motion) { ::view-transition-group(*) { animation: none } }`, (b) branch in JS and call the update function directly without startViewTransition, (c) set `animation-duration: 0.01ms` on the pseudo-elements?
drills.answerSketch: (b) is the robust answer: skipping the API entirely avoids the rendering suspension and any capture cost. (a) is an acceptable belt-and-braces addition for CSS-declared cross-document transitions, where there is no JS entry point. (c) still pays the snapshot cost and can produce a visible flash.

drills.prompt: This app already ships framer-motion via LazyMotion. In 120 words, decide whether a route change should use framer-motion's layout animation or the View Transitions API, and name what each costs at the moment of the transition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: does the animation need to survive a full DOM replacement (VT does; layout animation needs both trees mounted); who pays the bytes (VT is 0kb, layout animation is already bundled); what happens to interactivity mid-transition (VT suspends rendering and is not interruptible in the same way); what is the fallback where VT is unsupported; can it cross a document boundary. A strong answer commits and names the one scenario that would flip the decision.

failureModes: Awaits a network request inside the update callback and freezes the page — then blames the API for feeling slow.
Applies one shared `view-transition-name` to every item in a list.
Tries to z-index page content above the transition, not realising the pseudo tree paints above everything.
Uses a scroll event listener with rAF for a parallax effect that a `view()` timeline would run off the main thread.
Makes scroll-driven animation the only way content becomes visible, so it never appears where the feature is unsupported or reduced-motion is on.
Assumes cross-document view transitions work cross-origin.
interviewProbes: Walk me through what the browser does between calling startViewTransition and the animation starting.
Why can a scroll-driven animation stay smooth when the main thread is busy, but a scroll listener can't?
Where does the view-transition pseudo tree render relative to page stacking contexts?
How do you make a list-to-detail morph work when there are 200 list items?

ui-interaction-patterns.title: Drag, Resize, Gesture and Multi-Select — Accessibly, Without a Library
objectives: Design a pointer-driven drag as an explicit state machine over one captured pointer, with no document-level listeners
Design the keyboard and assistive-tech equivalent of every pointer gesture, as a first-class path rather than a fallback
Choose between roving tabindex and aria-activedescendant for a composite widget and justify it from the widget's behaviour
claims: Pointer Events unify mouse, touch and pen; `setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)` retargets all subsequent events for that pointer to the capturing element, which removes the need for document-level mousemove/mouseup listeners and for cleanup on pointer exit.

`touch-action: none` on the draggable surface is required to stop the browser's own scroll and zoom gestures from claiming the pointer; without it the browser fires `pointercancel` mid-drag and `preventDefault` in a passive touch listener is ignored.

The HTML5 drag-and-drop API (`dragstart`/`dragover`/`drop`) is not keyboard operable, cannot be styled consistently, and has poor touch support — which is why production drag is built on pointer events, and why that choice creates an explicit obligation to build a keyboard path.

An accessible drag needs a non-pointer equivalent: a keyboard grab mode (Space or Enter to lift, arrows to move, Space to drop, Escape to cancel) with each move announced in an `aria-live="assertive"` region, or a 'Move to…' menu command that reaches the same state.

Multi-select follows a convention users already have: plain click sets the anchor and replaces the selection, Shift+click extends from the anchor, Ctrl/Cmd+click toggles one item — and the anchor must not move on a toggle, or ranges feel random.

A composite widget (grid, listbox, tree, toolbar) must be a single tab stop and manage focus internally with roving `tabindex` or `aria-activedescendant`; making every row focusable turns a 500-row list into 500 tab stops.

Roving tabindex moves real DOM focus (correct when each item should receive focus events and be scrolled into view by the browser); `aria-activedescendant` keeps DOM focus on the container and names the active item (correct when a text input must retain focus, as in a combobox).

Drag positions must be derived from pointer deltas against a rect captured once at `pointerdown`; calling `getBoundingClientRect()` on every `pointermove` forces synchronous layout and couples drag smoothness to the rest of the page.

`ResizeObserver` is the correct source of element size changes (window `resize` misses container-driven changes), and its 'loop completed with undelivered notifications' error is a genuine infinite-loop guard fired when a callback writes layout that re-triggers itself.

viz.title: Pointer Trace
viz.whatIsDrawn: A small drag surface at the top with one draggable chip. Beneath it, four synchronised lanes — pointer events (down/move/up/cancel), capture state, touch-action, and the chip's committed transform — with each notable event labelled inline on its lane, not in a legend. A ghost lane underneath replays the same gesture without pointer capture, so the drop-out point where events stop arriving is visible as a gap rather than described in text. Playback is scrubbed.
viz.predictPrompt: You implement drag with pointerdown/pointermove/pointerup bound only to the handle element, no pointer capture. Predict the exact moment it breaks on a desktop mouse. Then predict what still breaks on a touchscreen even after you move the listeners to `document`.
controls: switch input model: mouse | touch | keyboard grab mode
step through the recorded event trace
viz.insight: A drag is a state machine over exactly one captured pointer — and every pointer gesture you ship owes a keyboard command that reaches the identical state without a pointer.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure drag state machine: feed it a recorded pointer event sequence plus {captureEnabled, touchActionNone, inputKind} and it returns the resulting state trace and final position, including the pointercancel path. Unit-test that capture-off + a fast desktop drag loses events, and that touch-action:auto injects pointercancel — those are the two claims. viz.tsx renders the lanes in SVG and drives a real drag demo from the same reducer, so the demo and the diagram cannot disagree. Reduced-motion: the trace renders fully; the chip jumps rather than tweens.

drills.prompt:
```js
handle.addEventListener('pointerdown', e => { dragging = true; startX = e.clientX })
handle.addEventListener('pointermove', e => { if (dragging) move(e.clientX - startX) })
handle.addEventListener('pointerup', () => { dragging = false })
```
The chip sometimes sticks to the cursor after release, and on a phone it barely moves. Name both defects.
drills.answerSketch: (1) No `handle.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)` — a fast drag moves the pointer off the handle, so pointermove and pointerup go elsewhere and `dragging` is never cleared. (2) No `touch-action: none` on the handle, so the browser claims the gesture for scrolling and fires pointercancel (which is also unhandled).

drills.prompt: Order the keyboard grab-mode state machine for reordering a list item: announce the new position in a live region · Space lifts the item and announces 'grabbed, position 3 of 12' · Escape restores the original position and exits grab mode · arrow keys move the item one position · Space drops and commits.
drills.answerSketch: Space lifts and announces → arrow keys move → announce new position after each move → Space drops and commits (Escape at any point restores and exits).

drills.prompt: For each widget, pick roving tabindex, aria-activedescendant, or individual tab stops: (1) a toolbar of formatting buttons; (2) a combobox whose text input must keep focus while the user arrows through options; (3) a 10,000-row data grid; (4) a tab list; (5) a form with five text inputs.
drills.answerSketch: 1 roving tabindex · 2 aria-activedescendant (DOM focus must stay in the input) · 3 roving tabindex (grid cells take real focus; the container is one tab stop) · 4 roving tabindex · 5 individual tab stops — a form is not a composite widget.

drills.prompt: Your pointer-based reorder works on a 50-item list. New requirement: the same list is now virtualized at 5,000 rows. Name what breaks first among: the dragged row unmounting when it scrolls out of the window · indices used as drop targets going stale · the absence of auto-scroll at the viewport edge · the live-region announcement.
drills.answerSketch: The dragged row unmounting is first and fatal — it takes the captured pointer with it, so the drag dies mid-gesture. Fix: render the dragged item outside the virtual window (a floating clone driven by the same state), key drop targets by stable id rather than index, and add edge auto-scroll. The live region needs the total count from the data, not from rendered rows.

drills.prompt: dnd-kit is off the table. In 130 words, justify shipping drag-to-reorder with no library: name the three things you must build yourself, the one you would cut from v1, and the acceptance test that proves the feature is done.
drills.answerSketch: Must build: the captured-pointer state machine with pointercancel handling; the keyboard grab mode with live-region announcements; the collision/drop-target model keyed by stable id. Reasonable v1 cut: multi-item drag, or cross-container drag, or drag auto-scroll — but not the keyboard path. Acceptance test: the reorder can be completed end to end with keyboard only and a screen reader announces start, each move and the commit; plus a pointercancel test that leaves no stuck state.

failureModes: Uses the HTML5 drag-and-drop API and asserts it is accessible because it is 'native'.
Adds document-level mousemove/mouseup instead of `setPointerCapture`, then hunts leaked listeners.
Omits `touch-action: none` and cannot reproduce the touch bug on a desktop.
Makes every row in a long list focusable.
Ships pointer drag with no keyboard path and puts an `aria-label` on the drag handle as the accessibility story.
Calls `getBoundingClientRect()` inside pointermove.
Moves the multi-select anchor on every click, so Shift+click ranges behave unpredictably.
interviewProbes: Implement drag-to-reorder. Now make it work for a keyboard-only user — walk me through the announcements.
Why setPointerCapture instead of listening on document?
Roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant for a combobox listbox, and why?
What breaks when you put drag-to-reorder on a virtualized list?

ui-perceived-speed.title: Skeletons, Spinners and Optimistic UI
objectives: Judge, per interaction, whether to show nothing, a delayed indicator, a skeleton, or an optimistic result — from the latency distribution and the reversibility of the action, not from house style
Judge when optimistic UI is a correctness hazard rather than a polish win, and specify its rollback contract
Judge a loading design by whether it holds layout and reaches assistive technology, not by whether it looks busy
claims: The classic response-time thresholds still hold: under ~0.1s feels instantaneous, under ~1s preserves the user's flow with no indicator needed, and beyond ~10s the user's attention leaves the task entirely.

An indicator shown immediately for work that usually completes in ~200ms makes the UI feel slower, because the flash itself is a perceived event; delaying the indicator by roughly 200-500ms removes it for the common case.
Once an indicator has appeared it needs a minimum display duration (commonly ~300-500ms), otherwise a fast response produces a flicker that reads as a glitch rather than as speed.

A skeleton beats a spinner only when it accurately predicts the final layout; a skeleton whose shape differs from the loaded content causes a layout shift, which the user experiences as a second wait.

Reserving space for asynchronous content — `aspect-ratio`, `contain-intrinsic-size`, fixed skeleton dimensions — is what keeps Cumulative Layout Shift low; CLS is rated 'good' at 0.1 or below at the 75th percentile.

Optimistic UI is a correctness decision: it is appropriate when the action has a high success rate, is cheap to reverse, and the user can be shown what was undone — and it is wrong for payments, destructive actions, and anything whose server-computed result the user must trust.

An optimistic update needs a defined reconciliation path: the server response replaces the optimistic entity by stable id, and a failure must both restore the prior state and tell the user specifically what was rolled back.
Loading state must reach assistive technology: a skeleton is invisible to a screen reader, so the region needs `aria-busy` while pending and a polite live-region announcement when it settles.
Streaming a shell and filling regions as data arrives generally beats one whole-page skeleton, because the user begins reading before the slowest region resolves.

viz.title: Two Timelines
viz.whatIsDrawn: For a single request, four horizontal strips run in parallel on one shared time axis: no indicator, immediate spinner, delayed spinner with minimum display, and skeleton. Perceived events — flash, layout shift, settle — are stamped inside the strip where they occur, with the millisecond offset printed next to the stamp. A ghost strip pinned above shows the actual server timing, so the gap between real and perceived is a visible distance rather than a claim.
viz.predictPrompt: Your endpoint's median is 180ms and its p95 is 2.4s. You add a spinner that appears immediately. Predict: what fraction of users see a spinner, whether the median user perceives the app as faster or slower than with no indicator at all, and whether raising the delay to 400ms helps or hurts the p95 user.
controls: toggle skeleton-shape mismatch (to show the shift)
viz.insight: An indicator's job is not to show that work is happening — it is to keep the user's model of the system correct, which means appearing late enough to skip the common case and staying long enough to be read.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {actualMs, delayMs, minDisplayMs, strategy} and an injected clock and returns the ordered list of perceived events with timestamps plus a derived 'flash' / 'flicker' / 'shift' flag. Unit-test the flicker case (actual just over delay, below delay+minDisplay) and the no-indicator case — these are exactly the claims. viz.tsx renders strips in SVG on a scrubbed playhead; no autoplay. Reduced-motion: strips render complete with all stamps, playhead becomes a static marker the learner steps.

drills.prompt: Classify each as optimistic, pending indicator, or blocking confirm-then-wait: (1) like a post; (2) transfer $4,000 between accounts; (3) rename a file; (4) delete an account; (5) add to cart; (6) submit a support ticket that returns a ticket number.
drills.answerSketch: 1 optimistic · 2 blocking (high stakes, must trust server result) · 3 optimistic · 4 blocking with explicit confirmation · 5 optimistic · 6 pending indicator — the ticket number is server-computed, so it cannot be optimistically invented.

drills.prompt: A card list shows three generic grey bars as a skeleton. The real cards are 180px tall with an image, two lines and a footer. Users report the page 'jumps'. Name the metric this regresses and the specific fix.
drills.answerSketch: CLS — the skeleton's height does not match the loaded content, so content below it moves when data arrives. Fix: make the skeleton the exact dimensions of the loaded card (or reserve the box with `aspect-ratio` / `contain-intrinsic-size`); the skeleton's job is to hold the layout, and holding it is more important than looking like the content.

drills.prompt: You chose a 300ms delayed spinner with a 400ms minimum display for a median-180ms endpoint. The backend regresses: median 1.2s, p95 9s. What changes? Choose: (a) nothing, the strategy still fits; (b) drop the delay to 0 and add progress or streaming; (c) go optimistic; (d) remove the minimum display.
drills.answerSketch: (b). Past ~1s the user needs immediate feedback, and past several seconds a determinate or staged signal (streaming regions, skeletons that fill in, progress) is required to hold attention. The delay existed only to skip the fast common case, which no longer exists. Going optimistic does not fix a read; removing minimum display is irrelevant once every request exceeds it.

drills.prompt: Complete the thresholds: responses under ~____ feel instantaneous; under ~____ the user stays in flow without an indicator; beyond ~____ their attention leaves the task. Cumulative Layout Shift is 'good' at or below ____ at the 75th percentile.

A PM insists every mutation must show a spinner because 'users need feedback'. Your median mutation is 240ms. In 120 words, defend showing no indicator at all for that path, and name the one measurement that would change your mind.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: the sub-1s threshold means flow is preserved without an indicator; a flash at 240ms is itself a perceived event and reads as slower; the real feedback is the state change (the row updates, the toggle flips), which is stronger than a spinner. What would change my mind: a p90 above ~1s, an action whose visible result is off-screen, or a failure rate high enough that silent success is ambiguous. Strong answers propose measuring the latency distribution, not the median alone.

failureModes: Adds a spinner to every async call and calls it feedback, producing a page that flashes on every interaction.
Uses a generic three-grey-bars skeleton unrelated to the real layout, trading a spinner for a layout shift.
Makes deletes or payments optimistic.
Designs against the median latency only and never looks at p95.
Implements optimistic UI with no rollback message, so a failed action silently reverts and the user believes they made a mistake.
Never adds `aria-busy` or a live region, so screen-reader users get silence during loading.
interviewProbes: Median 180ms, p95 2.4s. Design the loading state and defend the numbers you pick.
When is optimistic UI actually wrong?
Your skeleton improved perceived speed but CLS got worse. What happened?
How does a screen-reader user know something is loading?

ui-data-grid.title: Data Grids at Scale: virtualization, sticky headers, resize and sort
objectives: Design a 100k-row grid whose DOM cost is a function of viewport size rather than dataset size, and state where the remaining cost actually lives
Design the accessibility contract of a virtualized grid, where the DOM holds only a window of the real data
Design column resize and sort so neither work is proportional to rendered rows
claims: Row virtualization renders only the rows intersecting the scrollport plus an overscan margin, making DOM node count O(viewport) rather than O(dataset) — which is what keeps style and layout cost flat as the dataset grows.

Virtualization does not make scrolling smooth on its own: the remaining cost is per-row render work on the main thread between the scroll event and the next paint, which is why blank bands appear on slow devices and why overscan exists.

Variable-height rows require measurement: the virtualizer estimates total height, corrects it as rows render, and must cache measurements keyed by stable row id — keying by index makes the scrollbar drift when data reorders.

Column virtualization uses a different mechanism from row virtualization: rather than absolutely positioning cells, it renders leading and trailing spacer cells whose widths sum the hidden columns, so table/grid layout stays valid.

A virtualized grid is invisible to assistive technology unless it declares the real size: `role="grid"` with `aria-rowcount`/`aria-colcount` on the grid and `aria-rowindex`/`aria-colindex` on every rendered row and cell, because the DOM only contains a window.

With `auto` table layout, column widths are computed from the cells currently in the DOM, so widths visibly jump as the virtual window scrolls; `table-layout: fixed` or a CSS grid with explicit tracks is required.

`position: sticky` silently fails when any ancestor between the sticky element and the scroll container has `overflow` other than `visible`, or when the sticky element's nearest scrolling ancestor is not the one the user is scrolling.
Column resize must not re-render rows per pointermove: write the width to a CSS custom property on the grid container so only track sizing changes, and commit to React state once on pointerup.

Sorting or filtering 100k rows on the main thread blocks input; sort an array of indices rather than row objects, and move non-trivial comparators to a worker or a chunked scheduler so the frame budget is not consumed in one task.
Selection must be stored as a set of stable ids (or an inverted set for 'select all'), never as rendered-row state — otherwise the selection is destroyed the moment a row scrolls out of the window.

viz.title: The Virtual Window
viz.whatIsDrawn: A tall schematic column represents 100,000 rows. A viewport rectangle sits over it, with the overscan margin drawn as a lighter band above and below and labelled inside itself. To the right, a live DOM-node counter with a ghost horizontal line marking what the non-virtualized count would be, drawn on the same scale so the two are comparable at a glance. When the device-speed control is throttled, the region the compositor painted before React committed is hatched in place on the window — the blank band, shown rather than described.
viz.predictPrompt: A virtualized 100k-row list with overscan 0 scrolls smoothly on your laptop but shows white bands on a mid-tier Android. Predict which of these actually fixes it — bigger overscan · `content-visibility: auto` on rows · moving row rendering to a Web Worker · `will-change: transform` on the scroller — and say what the white band physically is.
viz.insight: Virtualization trades a memory problem for a latency problem: the window has to be filled before the compositor paints again, so overscan and per-row render cost — not row count — decide whether it feels smooth.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts computes the visible range, overscan range, measured-offset corrections and DOM node count from {scrollTop, viewportHeight, rowHeights, overscan}, with an injected clock modelling the render-commit deadline so the blank-band condition is derived, not faked. Unit-test the variable-height offset correction and the blank-band predicate — the blank-band claim is the pedagogically load-bearing one. viz.tsx is SVG plus a small real virtualized list for the demo, both driven by the same range calculation. Reduced-motion: stepped scroll positions instead of continuous scrub.

drills.prompt: 50,000 rows x 12 columns, ~3 DOM nodes per cell, 32px rows, 900px viewport, overscan 10 above and below. Estimate DOM node count with and without row virtualization. Give both to one significant figure.
drills.answerSketch: Without: 50,000 x 12 x 3 = 1,800,000. With: ceil(900/32)=29 visible + 20 overscan ≈ 49 rows x 12 x 3 ≈ 1,760. Roughly a 1000x reduction. Accept 1.8M ±10% and 1,500-2,500.

drills.prompt: A sticky table header (`position: sticky; top: 0`) works in isolation but not inside the app shell. The shell is `.layout { display: grid; overflow: hidden } .main { overflow-y: auto }` and the table sits in a `.card { overflow: hidden; border-radius: 12px }`. Name the exact cause.
drills.answerSketch: `.card { overflow: hidden }` sits between the sticky header and the scroll container, so the header is sticky within the card's (non-scrolling) box and never sticks. Fix: move the overflow/rounding off the direct ancestor chain (clip with a wrapper that is not between the sticky element and the scroller, or use `overflow: clip` with `overflow-clip-margin` carefully), or make the card itself the scroll container.

drills.prompt: Your grid works at 100k rows. New requirement: 'select all matching the current filter' with a live count, where the filter matches 84,000 rows. What breaks first, and what is the data shape that fixes it?
drills.answerSketch: Selection stored as a set of selected ids breaks — you would materialise 84,000 ids, and rows outside the window were never rendered so a rendered-row model has nothing to select. Fix: an inverted selection model — {mode: 'all-matching-filter', filterHash, excludedIds: Set} — so the count is derived from the filter's total and the payload stays O(exclusions). The mutation API must accept the filter, not the id list.

drills.prompt: Complete the virtualized grid ARIA contract: the container declares role="grid" plus ______ and ______; each rendered row declares ______ (1-based, against the full dataset) and each cell declares ______.
drills.answerSketch: aria-rowcount; aria-colcount; aria-rowindex; aria-colindex

drills.prompt: Order a column resize from grab to commit: commit the final width to store and persist it · pointerdown on the divider, setPointerCapture, record startX and startWidth · pointermove writes `--col-3-width` on the grid container via a rAF-throttled handler · pointerup releases capture · the CSS grid track re-sizes with no React re-render.
drills.answerSketch: pointerdown + capture + record → pointermove writes the custom property (rAF-throttled) → the grid track resizes with no re-render → pointerup releases capture → commit the width to store and persist.

drills.prompt: In 130 words, decide between TanStack Virtual plus your own table layer and a full commercial grid for an internal admin tool with 40 screens. Name the bundle cost, the accessibility position, and the one requirement that would flip your answer.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: what fraction of the 40 screens need anything beyond sort/filter/virtualize; who owns the ARIA contract (a commercial grid usually ships it, a hand-rolled one is your obligation and your most likely defect); bundle and lazy-loading story; how much of the grid's API surface leaks into 40 screens; licence. The flip is typically a requirement the hand-rolled layer would take months to reach — pivoting, grouping with aggregation, Excel-fidelity export, or frozen column groups.

failureModes: Claims virtualization fixes scroll jank without accounting for per-row render cost, then cannot explain the blank bands.
Ships a virtualized grid with role="grid" but no aria-rowcount/aria-rowindex, so the screen reader reports 30 rows out of 100,000.
Caches row measurements by index, so heights are wrong after a sort.
Stores selection as rendered-row state and loses it on scroll.
Leaves `table-layout: auto` and gets columns that resize as the user scrolls.
Sorts by mutating and re-rendering the whole row array on the main thread.
Puts `overflow: hidden` on a card between the sticky header and the scroller and calls sticky broken.
interviewProbes: Design a grid for 100k rows. Now tell me exactly what is still on the main thread after virtualization.
How does a screen reader know there are 100,000 rows when only 30 are in the DOM?
Implement column resize without re-rendering rows.
'Select all' across a filtered 84k rows — what does the selection state look like?

ui-beyond-dom.title: When to Leave the DOM: 10k nodes, canvas and WebGL
objectives: Judge whether a UI's problem is node count or per-frame cost, and exhaust the DOM-side levers before proposing canvas
Judge the full price of leaving the DOM — accessibility tree, text selection, find-in-page, hit testing — and specify what you would rebuild
Judge when WebGL/WebGPU is justified over 2D canvas, and when neither is
claims: Style and layout cost scales with the number of elements the browser must consider, so the first levers are always fewer nodes and less invalidation — virtualization, `content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size`, and `contain: layout paint` — before any decision to leave the DOM.

`content-visibility: auto` skips rendering work for off-screen subtrees without removing them from the DOM or the accessibility tree; it needs `contain-intrinsic-size` (ideally `auto <length>`) or the scrollbar jumps as content renders and un-renders.

A canvas draws pixels, not elements: it contributes nothing to the accessibility tree, supports no text selection, no find-in-page, no browser zoom reflow and no hit testing — rebuilding those is the actual cost of leaving the DOM, and it is large.

The accepted pattern for accessible canvas is a parallel DOM mirror: real focusable elements describing each interactive object, visually hidden but present, kept in sync with the scene, with keyboard interaction driving the same state the pointer does.

Canvas hit testing is done by geometry (a spatial index) or by an offscreen 'pick' buffer that encodes object ids as colours; reading that buffer back with `getImageData` is a GPU-to-CPU synchronisation and must never run on every pointermove.

The threshold for leaving the DOM is a cost per frame, not a node count: leave when thousands of independent items must update every frame (maps, timelines, node graphs, waveforms, spreadsheets with live cells); stay when items are discrete, text-bearing and individually interactive.
WebGL/WebGPU beats 2D canvas when the same geometry is redrawn at high instance counts, because instanced draw calls batch on the GPU while a 2D canvas redraw is a serial main-thread CPU loop.
`OffscreenCanvas` transferred to a worker moves the draw loop off the main thread, so canvas rendering can hold frame rate while the main thread is busy — a property no DOM-based UI can have.

Hybrid is usually the right answer: render the dense field on canvas and keep the interactive, text-bearing chrome (labels, selection handles, menus, the focused item) in the DOM, so accessibility and text rendering come from the platform.

viz.title: Cost-Per-Frame Ladder
viz.whatIsDrawn: The same scatter of N items rendered four ways, one per row: plain DOM · DOM plus content-visibility · 2D canvas · WebGL instanced. Each row is a horizontal frame-cost bar segmented into style, layout, paint and composite, with each segment's millisecond cost printed inside it. A single ghost line at 16.7ms is drawn straight across all four rows, so crossing the budget is a spatial fact rather than a number to compare. Rows that lose a capability (a11y tree, text selection, find-in-page) carry a struck-through capability chip inside the row.
viz.predictPrompt: 10,000 absolutely-positioned divs, each with only `transform` changing every frame. Predict which pipeline stages actually run per frame. Then predict whether replacing them with 10,000 `fillRect` calls on a 2D canvas is faster or slower — and why your answer might flip at 100,000 items.
controls: interaction model: static | hover-only | animate every frame
viz.insight: You leave the DOM for per-frame cost, not for node count — and the bill you pay is the accessibility tree, which you then have to rebuild by hand.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a cost model, not a benchmark: per-renderer per-stage cost coefficients calibrated once from real traces (record the numbers and their capture device in the prose so the model is honest), returning a frame budget breakdown for a given item count and interaction model. Unit-test the crossover points against the recorded traces so the claim 'canvas overtakes DOM around N' cannot silently drift. Do not run live 100k-node benchmarks in the page — it would make the module itself the slowest page in the app. Reduced-motion: bars render at their final lengths with no growth animation.

drills.prompt: Choose DOM · DOM+virtualization · 2D canvas · WebGL for each: (1) a Kanban board with ~200 cards; (2) a Gantt chart with 20,000 bars and live drag; (3) an infinite chat log; (4) a stadium seat map with 45,000 selectable seats; (5) a code editor; (6) 400 dashboard sparklines.
drills.answerSketch: 1 DOM · 2 canvas (per-frame cost during drag; hybrid with DOM chrome for the dragged bar) · 3 DOM+virtualization · 4 canvas or WebGL with a parallel DOM mirror for the seats in the current zoom/section · 5 DOM (text, selection, IME, a11y — the platform must own it) · 6 DOM, one small inline SVG or canvas per sparkline; no chart library.

drills.prompt: A canvas node-graph editor calls `ctx.getImageData(x, y, 1, 1)` inside its pointermove handler to identify the node under the cursor. Hover feels sluggish on every machine. Name the mechanism and the two standard fixes.
drills.answerSketch: getImageData forces a GPU-to-CPU readback and flushes the pending draw queue, synchronously, on every pointermove. Fixes: (a) hit-test with geometry against a spatial index (quadtree/R-tree) instead of pixels; or (b) keep the pick-buffer approach but read it at most once per frame from a rAF handler, or use `willReadFrequently: true` on a dedicated offscreen pick context.

drills.prompt: The frame budget is 16.7ms. React and app logic already consume 6ms of it. You must draw 5,000 items per frame. Estimate the per-item draw budget, and say whether a 2D canvas `fillRect` per item (roughly 0.5-2µs each in practice) fits.
drills.answerSketch: (16.7 - 6) / 5000 ≈ 2.1µs per item. fillRect at ~0.5-2µs sits inside that but with almost no headroom for state changes (fillStyle switches, transforms, text) — so a naive per-item style change will blow it. Accept 1.8-2.5µs and a conclusion of 'fits only if per-item state changes are batched'.

drills.prompt: Your canvas timeline ships. New requirement from legal: users must be able to Ctrl+F for any event label, and the view must pass an accessibility audit. Which of your options survive: keep canvas and add an aria-label · keep canvas plus a parallel focusable DOM mirror of visible events · move to virtualized DOM · render text in DOM and only the dense bars in canvas?
drills.answerSketch: An aria-label on the canvas does not survive — it satisfies nothing (no per-object semantics, and find-in-page still finds nothing). The parallel DOM mirror satisfies the audit but only makes text findable if the mirror is real text in the DOM (visually hidden text is still findable by Ctrl+F in most browsers — verify per target browser). Virtualized DOM and the hybrid both satisfy it directly; the hybrid is usually the right trade because it keeps the per-frame win.

drills.prompt: Your PM wants the node-graph editor rewritten on canvas 'so it feels smooth'. In 140 words, argue the position you actually hold. Name the DOM-side levers you would try first, the exact accessibility work canvas would add to the estimate, and the measurement that would settle it.
drills.answerSketch: Levers first: virtualize to the viewport, `content-visibility: auto` + `contain`, promote only the dragged node, batch transform writes, stop reading layout in the drag loop. Canvas adds: a parallel focusable DOM mirror, keyboard navigation over nodes and edges, hit testing via a spatial index, text rendering and zoom handling, and its own test strategy — realistically weeks, not days.
