The settling measurement is a profile of the actual slow case on the actual target device, split by pipeline stage: if style+layout dominate, DOM levers win; if paint at high instance counts dominates, canvas is justified.

failureModes: Proposes canvas at ~1,000 nodes when virtualization or content-visibility would have solved it.
Ships a canvas UI with an `aria-label` on the `<canvas>` element and presents that as the accessibility story.
Believes `content-visibility: auto` removes nodes from the DOM or the accessibility tree.
Asserts WebGL is always faster than 2D canvas without reference to instance counts or draw-call batching.
Calls getImageData per pointermove for hit testing.
Rewrites the whole surface in canvas instead of keeping text and chrome in the DOM.
interviewProbes: 10,000 items on screen and it's janky. Walk me through what you check before proposing canvas.
What exactly do you lose the moment you draw to canvas, and what do you have to rebuild?
How do you hit-test 50,000 canvas objects on hover?
When does WebGL beat a 2D canvas here?

perf-field-vs-lab.title: Field, Lab, and the p75 You Actually Ship
objectives: Choose the correct evidence source (CrUX, first-party RUM, Lighthouse, WebPageTest) for a specific performance question, and state what each one cannot answer
Explain how a lab score and a field score can disagree without either being wrong
Reason quantitatively about how a change affecting a subset of sessions moves a 75th percentile
claims: Core Web Vitals are assessed at the 75th percentile of a page's real-user distribution, not at the mean or median.
CrUX reports Chrome-only field data over a rolling 28-day window, so a shipped fix takes up to 28 days to be fully reflected in the reported number.
Lighthouse is a single lab run under simulated throttling on one device profile: it cannot produce a p75, and it cannot measure INP because a lab run performs no real interactions.
LCP and CLS are measurable in the lab; INP is a field-only vital because it depends on which interactions real users perform.
CrUX segments by device class, and an origin-level assessment can pass while individual page groups fail.
Improving the median of a distribution can leave p75 unchanged; p75 moves only when the sessions between p75 and the worst case move.
RUM answers 'what is happening to real users' and is the correct input for prioritisation; synthetic answers 'did this specific scenario change' and is the correct input for regression detection.

The web-vitals library reports final INP and CLS values only at page hide, so field beacons must be flushed on visibilitychange rather than on unload (an unload listener also disqualifies the page from bfcache).

viz.title: Who Moves p75?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A histogram of ~1000 real LCP session values for one page, with the p75 line drawn vertically through it and labelled in place. Applying a fix redraws the bars while a ghost outline of the original distribution stays behind them, and the p75 delta is annotated inside the plot area next to the marker.
viz.predictPrompt: You ship a fix that makes the fastest 60% of sessions 40% faster and leaves every other session untouched. Does p75 LCP improve — and if so, roughly by how much?
controls: which slice of sessions the fix applies to (fastest 60% / middle 40% / slowest 25% / all)
viz.insight: p75 is a tail statistic. Making already-fast sessions faster is completely invisible to Core Web Vitals — the only sessions that count are the ones at and beyond the 75th percentile, which are almost never the ones you develop on.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds a seeded log-normal sample of LCP values plus applyFix(slice, factor) and percentile(); no Date.now/Math.random. Unit test asserts the pedagogical claim directly: a 40% improvement to the fastest 60% moves p75 by <2%, while the same improvement applied to the slowest 25% moves it by >25%. Reduced-motion: static before/after pair of histograms with the delta annotated between them; live region announces 'p75 moved from X to Y'.

drills.prompt: Tag each of these six questions with the only evidence source that can answer it — CrUX, first-party RUM, Lighthouse/lab, or none of them: (1) Did last Tuesday's release regress INP on the checkout route? (2) Is our competitor's homepage LCP worse than ours? (3) Which third-party script contributes most to our long tasks? (4) What fraction of our Android users experience CLS above 0.25? (5) Did this PR add 40KB to the settings route? (6) Why is the hero image discovered late?
drills.answerSketch: 1 = first-party RUM (per-release, per-route, field-only metric). 2 = CrUX (the only public field data for an origin you do not own). 3 = lab/trace (attribution needs a profile; LoAF in RUM can also do it, accept either with justification). 4 = first-party RUM segmented by device (CrUX gives phone/desktop buckets but not your OS split). 5 = lab/CI byte measurement. 6 = lab/trace waterfall.

drills.prompt: A teammate reports: 'Lighthouse gives us 99 on mobile and our average load time dropped 31% after the CDN migration, but Search Console still flags the product page as failing Core Web Vitals.' Select every statement that is a real defect in this reasoning.
drills.answerSketch: Correct selections: Lighthouse score is not the CWV assessment and cannot measure INP; an average is not a p75; CrUX lags up to 28 days so the migration may not be reflected yet; the failing vital may be INP, which no Lighthouse run reports; page-level CrUX data may differ from the origin-level number they looked at. Distractors that are NOT defects: 'Lighthouse throttles the CPU' (that is correct behaviour), 'CDNs do not affect LCP'.

drills.prompt: Core Web Vitals are graded at the ____th percentile of field data. CrUX aggregates over a rolling ____-day window. The 'good' thresholds are LCP <= ____ s, INP <= ____ ms, CLS <= ____.

Your p75 LCP is 2.4s and passing. Product launches in a market where 20% of sessions arrive on a 3G-class connection and a sub-$150 Android device. Which vital crosses into failure first, and why does p75 make this worse than the 20% share suggests?
drills.answerSketch: LCP fails first for most content sites (TTFB + load duration both stretch), but INP is the more common real-world casualty on low-end CPUs — accept either with the mechanism. The p75 point: adding 20% very slow sessions shifts which session sits at the 75th percentile, so the reported number can move far more than 20% of the way toward the slow cohort's value; the previously-passing majority provides no cushion.

drills.prompt: Your team proposes gating deploys on 'Lighthouse performance score >= 90'. In 120 words or fewer, argue for or against, and name what you would gate on instead.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names lab run-to-run variance as the reason the gate flakes; (2) notes the composite score is weighted and can be gamed without helping any user; (3) notes it cannot see INP; (4) proposes gating hard on deterministic byte/count budgets and treating lab timings as trend signals over N runs; (5) proposes a field p75 alarm as the actual user-facing guard.

failureModes: Quotes the Lighthouse performance score as if it were the Core Web Vitals assessment.
Says 'we cut average load time 30%' and assumes p75 followed.
Believes Lighthouse measures INP, or reports a lab INP number.
Optimises the fast path — fast device, warm cache, local network — because that is the environment they develop in.
Does not know CrUX lags, and declares a fix failed three days after shipping it.
interviewProbes: Our Lighthouse score is 98 and CrUX says the page is failing. Walk me through how both can be true.
We shipped a caching change and the median LCP dropped a lot but p75 barely moved. What does that tell you about who the change helped?
How would you decide whether to spend the next sprint on LCP or on INP?

perf-inp.title: INP: Where the 200ms Actually Went
objectives: Decompose a slow interaction into input delay, processing duration and presentation delay from a trace
Attribute each segment to a plausible cause and rule out causes that cannot explain the observed shape
Explain why FID passed almost everywhere and INP does not
claims: INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital on 12 March 2024; FID measured only the input delay of the first interaction, which is why the overwhelming majority of pages passed it.
INP thresholds at p75 are: good <= 200ms, needs improvement 200-500ms, poor > 500ms.
INP reports approximately the worst interaction latency observed on the page, discounting roughly one interaction per 50 so that a single outlier on a long-lived page does not define the score.

An interaction's latency splits into input delay (from the input event until the first handler runs), processing duration (all event handlers for that interaction), and presentation delay (from the last handler returning until the next frame is painted).
INP counts only clicks, taps and key presses; scrolling and hovering are excluded.
Input delay is caused by the main thread being occupied when the input arrives — usually by work the interaction did not cause, such as a third-party script or a hydration task.
Presentation delay is dominated by style, layout and paint over a large DOM, and by rendering work the handler scheduled synchronously; moving handler logic to a Web Worker does not reduce it.
The Long Animation Frames API (PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming, Chrome 123+) attributes a slow frame to specific script entry points, which the older Long Tasks API cannot do.

viz.title: Anatomy of a 420ms Click
viz.whatIsDrawn: One horizontal interaction timeline from pointerdown to the next paint, split into three labelled segments. The main-thread tasks responsible are drawn as blocks inside the input-delay segment, and the style/layout/paint work is drawn inside the presentation-delay segment. A ghost bar beneath shows a 90ms 'good' interaction at the same scale for comparison. All numbers annotated inside their own segment.
viz.predictPrompt: A profiler shows the click handler executing 8ms of JavaScript. The page's INP for that interaction is 420ms. Before you look at the breakdown: which segment holds most of the remaining 412ms, and what code is responsible for it?
controls: toggle the third-party analytics task on/off
handler mode: synchronous setState vs startTransition
viz.insight: The handler is rarely the problem. INP is mostly paid before your code runs — input delay from work the interaction did not cause — and after it returns, rendering the update over a large DOM.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models a task queue with injected clock: given (competing tasks, handler cost, DOM size, transition on/off) it returns the three segment durations. Unit test asserts the claim the module teaches: with an 8ms handler, a 250ms competing task and 40k nodes, processing duration is under 5% of total INP. Reduced-motion: static three-segment bar with the ghost baseline; live region reads 'input delay 240ms, processing 8ms, presentation 172ms, total 420ms'.

drills.prompt: Order these events for a single tap, earliest first: next frame painted; pointerdown dispatched; event handlers run; browser finishes the task already in progress; style and layout recalculated; input queued by the compositor.
drills.answerSketch: input queued by compositor -> browser finishes the task already in progress -> pointerdown dispatched -> handlers run -> style and layout recalculated -> next frame painted. The first two boundaries are input delay; the last two are presentation delay.

drills.prompt: A click handler calls setSelected(id), then loops over 200 rows calling row.getBoundingClientRect() and writing an inline style to each. Which INP segment does this inflate, and which one does it leave untouched?
drills.answerSketch: It inflates processing duration (the read/write loop forces synchronous layout 200 times inside the handler) and, via the enlarged dirty tree, presentation delay. Input delay for THIS interaction is untouched — but the resulting long task inflates input delay for the NEXT interaction, which is what the field data usually reports.

drills.prompt: You move the handler's 300ms of computation into a Web Worker. INP drops from 520ms to 480ms. Which segment is now dominant, and name two changes that would actually reduce it.
drills.answerSketch: Presentation delay dominates: the result still commits to the DOM and pays style/layout/paint on the main thread over a large tree. Valid fixes: reduce the number of nodes committed (virtualise/paginate), use CSS containment or content-visibility to bound the recalculated subtree, split the update so the visible part commits first (transition/deferred value), or avoid re-rendering unaffected siblings.

drills.prompt: INP replaced ____ in March 2024. The p75 'good' threshold is ____ ms and 'poor' begins above ____ ms. INP counts clicks, taps and ____ presses, but not ____.
drills.answerSketch: FID; 200; 500; key; scrolling (hover also accepted)

drills.prompt: A PM asks why the old dashboards said responsiveness was 'all green' for two years and the new metric says the app is poor. Explain in 120 words or fewer, without saying 'the metric changed'.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) FID measured only the FIRST interaction, which usually lands before the app is busy; (2) FID measured only input delay, excluding the handler and the rendering — i.e. everything the app itself does; (3) INP takes near-worst-case across all interactions, so it catches the slow list filter nobody profiled; (4) the app did not get worse — the measurement stopped ignoring the expensive part; (5) states what they would look at first to confirm (RUM breakdown by interaction target).

failureModes: Optimises the event handler, because it is the only part visible in a naive flame chart.
Treats INP as 'FID with a new name' and still quotes the 100ms threshold.
Moves work to a Web Worker when the cost is DOM commit and rendering, then reports that workers 'did not help'.
Counts scroll jank as bad INP.
Debounces the input handler, which hides the work from the profiler but leaves the same long task landing later.
interviewProbes: Our p75 INP is 480ms. Where do you look first, and what would each of the three possible answers make you do differently?
A single interaction on a page takes 900ms but INP reports 260ms. How?
Why does a large DOM hurt INP even when your handler is fast?

perf-longtask-yield.title: Breaking Up Long Tasks: Yielding, Priority and Starvation
objectives: Design a chunking and yielding strategy for a long synchronous workload against a stated latency target
Choose between scheduler.yield, scheduler.postTask, setTimeout and a Web Worker with a defensible reason
Predict the throughput cost that a given yielding strategy pays for its latency win
claims: A long task is any main-thread task longer than 50ms; input arriving during it cannot be dispatched until it finishes, so the task's remaining duration becomes input delay.
Yielding with `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` places the continuation at the back of the task queue, behind anything that arrived meanwhile — including a third-party script.

`scheduler.yield()` yields to the browser but resumes the continuation ahead of newly-queued work of the same priority, so you do not lose your place; it ships in Chromium and Firefox but not Safari as of 2026, so it needs a scheduler.postTask / setTimeout fallback chain.

`scheduler.postTask()` accepts priority 'user-blocking' | 'user-visible' | 'background' and a TaskSignal for cancellation; `requestIdleCallback` is not a substitute for user-visible work because idle callbacks may never run on a busy page.

`navigator.scheduling.isInputPending()` lets a loop yield only when input is actually waiting, but yielding solely on pending input still starves rendering, so animation frames are dropped even though input feels responsive.
Yielding increases total wall-clock duration while reducing worst-case latency — it is a throughput-for-latency trade, not a free improvement.

A Web Worker removes computation from the main thread, but any result that must reach the DOM still pays style, layout and paint on the main thread, and structured-cloning a large result can itself block.
React's `startTransition` marks an update as interruptible by React's own scheduler; it does not chunk a synchronous loop you wrote.

viz.title: Yield Points and the Input That Waits
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single main-thread lane of tasks across 600ms, drawn as blocks with durations printed inside them. An input arrow lands at a draggable time; the resulting input delay is bracketed and labelled in place on the lane. A ghost lane directly above shows the unchunked baseline at identical scale.
viz.predictPrompt: A 300ms task is split into six 50ms chunks with `await setTimeout(0)` between them. A competing 200ms third-party task arrives just after chunk 2. Does worst-case input delay go down — and does your total work finish sooner or later than it did unchunked?
controls: yield strategy: none / setTimeout / scheduler.yield / postTask('background')
arrival time of the competing task
step forward one task at a time
viz.insight: Chunking bounds input delay to roughly one chunk, but a naive setTimeout yield hands your place in the queue to whoever showed up — which is exactly how a 'fixed' page ends up finishing later and still feeling slow.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a deterministic task-queue simulator with an injected clock and seeded arrival times; it exposes run(strategy, chunkMs, competitors) -> {maxInputDelay, totalDuration, taskCount}. Unit tests assert both halves of the pedagogical claim: setTimeout chunking reduces maxInputDelay below chunkMs + competitor overlap, AND increases totalDuration relative to unchunked; scheduler.yield reduces maxInputDelay with a much smaller totalDuration penalty. Reduced-motion: static two-lane comparison with the input-delay bracket annotated.

drills.prompt: Complete a feature-detecting yieldToMain() helper that prefers scheduler.yield, falls back to scheduler.postTask at user-visible priority, and finally to setTimeout(0), returning a promise in every branch.
drills.answerSketch: Checks `'scheduler' in globalThis && 'yield' in scheduler` first, then `'postTask' in scheduler` with `{priority:'user-visible'}`, then `new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))`. Grader checks the ordering of the branches and that each returns a thenable; a common wrong answer puts postTask first or forgets that setTimeout's clamp makes it the worst option.

drills.prompt: Your chunked import loop keeps input delay under 50ms. The requirement changes: the whole import must also complete within 500ms of wall-clock time, and the page loads three third-party tags. Which yield strategy breaks first and what do you change?
drills.answerSketch: setTimeout chunking breaks first: each yield costs clamping plus whatever third-party work is queued, so total duration blows past 500ms. Move to scheduler.yield (keeps your place in line, so total duration stays near the unchunked time) and/or increase chunk size to trade a little input delay back for throughput; consider a worker for the pure computation and only chunk the DOM commit.

drills.prompt: Identify the defect: a search-as-you-type feature schedules its filtering work with requestIdleCallback(runFilter, {timeout: 2000}) so it 'never blocks the user'.
drills.answerSketch: requestIdleCallback is for non-user-visible work; on a busy page it fires only at the 2000ms timeout, so results appear up to two seconds late — and when the timeout fires the work runs as one unchunked task, producing exactly the long task it was meant to avoid. Correct approach: scheduler.postTask at 'user-visible' or a transition, chunked with scheduler.yield.

drills.prompt: Order these by the input delay each would produce for an input arriving at t=100ms into a 400ms workload, lowest first: (a) one unchunked task, (b) eight 50ms chunks with setTimeout yields, (c) eight 50ms chunks with scheduler.yield, (d) the workload in a Web Worker with a single DOM commit at the end.
drills.answerSketch: d (near zero until the commit) < c ~= b (bounded by one chunk; b is slightly worse when competing tasks are queued) < a (up to 300ms). Grader accepts b and c as tied or c before b, but not b before c when competitors are present.

drills.prompt: You must parse a 12MB CSV and render the first 100 rows of a table. Argue for either 'worker + chunked commit' or 'main-thread chunking with scheduler.yield', in 120 words or fewer, and name the specific cost your choice pays.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) separates the parse (pure computation, worker-friendly) from the commit (DOM, main thread only); (2) names transfer cost — structured clone of a 12MB result, and the mitigation (transferable ArrayBuffer, or stream rows in batches); (3) names the latency each option gives during parse; (4) states which one is simpler to ship and whether that matters here; (5) commits to one answer rather than describing both.

failureModes: Reaches for a Web Worker for work that is 80% DOM manipulation.
Uses requestIdleCallback for user-visible work and it never fires under load.
Chunks with setTimeout and is surprised that total duration nearly doubled from clamping and queue contention.
Believes startTransition chunks a synchronous for-loop.
Yields between every item instead of on a time budget, so scheduling overhead exceeds the work.
interviewProbes: You have a 400ms synchronous formatting pass on the main thread. Walk me through your options and what each one costs.
Why might splitting a long task make the page slower overall?
When would you NOT move work to a worker?

perf-lcp.title: LCP: Four Subparts and the Discovery Problem
objectives: Decompose an LCP measurement into TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration and element render delay from a waterfall
Identify which subpart a proposed fix actually targets, and reject fixes that target a subpart that is already small
Explain why the LCP element's discoverability, not its size, is usually the binding constraint
claims: LCP thresholds at p75 are: good <= 2.5s, poor > 4.0s. The candidate element is the largest image, video poster frame, or block-level text node rendered in the initial viewport.

LCP decomposes into four subparts: time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load duration, and element render delay. On most real sites load delay and render delay dominate — not the number of bytes.
Resource load delay is the gap between TTFB and the LCP resource's request actually starting; it is a discovery and prioritisation problem, not a bandwidth problem.

An LCP image declared as a CSS `background-image` is invisible to the preload scanner and is discovered only after the stylesheet has downloaded and been parsed, adding at least one round trip to load delay.
`loading="lazy"` on the LCP image is a guaranteed regression; `fetchpriority="high"` raises an in-viewport `` from the browser's default Low initial priority to High.
Render-blocking stylesheets and synchronous scripts in `<head>` extend render delay even when the LCP image has already fully downloaded.
When the LCP element is client-side rendered, its render delay includes the time to download, parse, execute and hydrate the JavaScript that creates it — the element does not exist until then.
The LCP value is not final until the first user interaction or page hide, because a late-arriving larger element can replace the earlier candidate.

viz.title: Why 70% Fewer Bytes Bought You 40 Milliseconds
viz.whatIsDrawn: A request waterfall for a page with the LCP resource highlighted, and directly above it a four-segment LCP bar (TTFB | load delay | load duration | render delay) whose segment boundaries align vertically with the waterfall events that cause them. Each segment's duration is printed inside it. A ghost bar shows the pre-change measurement at the same scale.
viz.predictPrompt: You replace a 900KB hero JPEG with a 260KB AVIF — a 71% byte reduction. Which of the four LCP subparts changes, by roughly how much, and what would you have to change to move each of the other three?
controls: hero declared as vs CSS background-image
fetchpriority: auto / high, and loading: eager / lazy
step through the four subparts one at a time
viz.insight: Byte size only shortens load duration. If the browser does not start requesting the hero until 2.1s, no amount of compression will save you — you have to fix when it is discovered and at what priority it is fetched.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models a simplified network + parser with an injected clock and a fixed bandwidth: given (markup shape, hints, byte size, render-blocking count) it returns the four subpart durations. Unit test asserts the headline claim: with the hero as a CSS background on a 5 Mbps link, a 71% byte reduction improves LCP by under 10%, while converting it to a preloaded improves it by over 35%. Reduced-motion: static aligned waterfall + subpart bar with the ghost baseline drawn as a dashed outline.

drills.prompt: Given this head and hero markup, name every change that delays LCP and rank them by expected impact: the hero is a div with a CSS background-image; there are two render-blocking stylesheets from a different origin with no preconnect; the hero div carries loading="lazy" via a data attribute picked up by a JS lazy-loader; a synchronous analytics script sits above the stylesheets.
drills.answerSketch: Ranked: (1) the JS-driven lazy loader means the image is not even requested until the bundle executes — this is pure load delay and usually the largest; (2) CSS background-image defeats the preload scanner, adding a stylesheet round trip before discovery; (3) cross-origin render-blocking stylesheets with no preconnect add DNS+TCP+TLS to render delay; (4) the synchronous analytics script blocks parsing. Note that image bytes appear nowhere in this list.

drills.prompt: Marketing replaces the static hero with a client-side-rendered carousel whose first slide is the LCP element. Which subpart absorbs the change, and which of your existing fixes (preload, fetchpriority, AVIF) stop helping?
drills.answerSketch: Render delay absorbs it: the element does not exist until the JS bundle is fetched, parsed, executed and the component mounts. Preload and fetchpriority still get the bytes early — so the image is sitting in cache doing nothing — and AVIF still shrinks load duration, which is now irrelevant. The real fixes are server-rendering the first slide, or rendering slide 1 as plain markup and hydrating the carousel afterwards.

drills.prompt: Order the browser's steps for discovering and painting an LCP image referenced by a CSS background-image, earliest first: paint; stylesheet downloaded; HTML response begins; CSSOM built and matched to the element; image request issued; layout computed; image bytes arrive.
drills.answerSketch: HTML response begins -> stylesheet downloaded -> CSSOM built and matched to the element -> layout computed -> image request issued -> image bytes arrive -> paint. The key ordering insight is that the request cannot be issued until layout proves the element exists and is visible.

drills.prompt: LCP is 'good' at or below ____ s and 'poor' above ____ s, at the ____th percentile. Its four subparts are ____, resource load ____, resource load ____, and element ____ delay.
drills.answerSketch: 2.5; 4.0; 75; TTFB (time to first byte); delay; duration; render

drills.prompt: You have one engineering day. p75 LCP is 3.6s: TTFB 700ms, load delay 1400ms, load duration 900ms, render delay 600ms. Choose exactly one intervention and defend it in 120 words or fewer.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) identifies load delay as the largest single subpart; (2) proposes a discovery fix — preload with fetchpriority=high, or converting a background-image to an , or removing a JS lazy-loader — rather than compression; (3) estimates the expected gain and says what it would NOT fix; (4) names how they would verify in the field, including the CrUX lag; (5) explicitly rejects the tempting-but-wrong option (image compression targets the 900ms, and a 40% saving there is worth ~360ms versus a potential ~1.2s).

failureModes: Compresses the hero image, reports 'LCP optimised', and never looks at the subpart breakdown.
Applies loading="lazy" site-wide, including above the fold.
Confuses LCP with First Contentful Paint or with the load event.
Preloads the hero but leaves it as a CSS background, causing a mismatched double fetch.
Assumes a CDN fixes LCP when TTFB is already 200ms and load delay is 1.4s.
interviewProbes: p75 LCP is 3.9s. What are the first three numbers you ask for, and what does each one rule out?
Why can a smaller image fail to improve LCP at all?
Your LCP element is text rendered by React on the client. What is the ceiling on how fast LCP can be, and what raises it?

perf-cls.title: CLS: Session Windows and the Shifts You Never See
objectives: Compute a layout shift score from element geometry and displacement
Explain why the reported CLS is not the sum of a page's shifts
Identify the shifts a developer's own manual testing structurally cannot reproduce
claims: CLS is 'good' at or below 0.1 and 'poor' above 0.25, at p75 of the field distribution.

A single shift's score is impact fraction x distance fraction: impact fraction is the union of the unstable elements' visible area before and after, as a fraction of the viewport; distance fraction is the greatest distance any unstable element moved, divided by the viewport's larger dimension.

Reported CLS is the largest session window, where a session window is a run of shifts separated by gaps of no more than 1 second and capped at 5 seconds total — it is not the sum of every shift on the page.
A shift occurring within 500ms of a discrete user input is flagged hadRecentInput and excluded from CLS, which is why 'it does not shift when I click around' is not evidence of anything.

Setting width and height attributes on images (or aspect-ratio in CSS) lets the browser reserve the correct box before the bytes arrive; with `width: 100%; height: auto` these act as a ratio, not a fixed size.
`font-display: swap` guarantees a text reflow when the web font arrives, unless the fallback's metrics are adjusted with size-adjust, ascent-override and descent-override.
Content injected above existing content — banners, consent dialogs, A/B test variants — shifts everything below it; reserving the slot or using position: fixed/sticky avoids the shift.
Animating top, left, height or margin produces layout shifts; animating transform does not, because transform changes are explicitly not counted as layout shifts.

viz.title: Which Shift Scores Worse?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A phone viewport outline containing two candidate shifts drawn as before/after rectangles. The impact-fraction union is shaded and its fraction printed inside the shaded region; the distance is drawn as an arrow with its fraction printed on the arrow. The multiplication is written inside the viewport next to the result. Below the viewport, a 5-second strip groups shifts into session windows with the 1s gaps marked.
viz.predictPrompt: Shift A: a full-width hero occupying 60% of the viewport moves down 8px. Shift B: a 40px-tall notice occupying 5% of the viewport moves down the entire viewport height. Which produces the larger CLS contribution, and by roughly what factor?
controls: place the shifts in time to form or split session windows
step: shift A score -> shift B score -> window total
viz.insight: Large elements moving slightly usually outscore small elements moving far, because impact fraction is area-based while distance fraction is capped by the viewport. And only the worst 5-second window counts — three small shifts inside one burst can beat one large isolated shift.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts implements scoreShift(rectBefore, rectAfter, viewport) and sessionWindows(shifts) exactly per spec, including the 1s gap and 5s cap. Unit tests assert the predict answer numerically (A ~= 0.6 x 0.01 = 0.006; B ~= 0.10 x 1.0 = 0.10 — note B's impact fraction is the union of before and after, so ~10%, not 5%) and assert that summing shifts overstates CLS on a fixture with two windows. Reduced-motion: static before/after rectangles with the arithmetic annotated; live region reads the computed score.

drills.prompt: Viewport is 400x800. A 400x200 banner is inserted at the top, pushing a 400x300 card from y=0 down to y=200. Compute the impact fraction, the distance fraction and the shift score. (Tolerance +/-0.02.)
drills.answerSketch: The unstable element is the card. Before: y 0-300. After: y 200-500. Union of visible area = 400x500 = 200,000 of 320,000 viewport px = 0.625 impact fraction. Distance = 200px moved / 800px (larger viewport dimension) = 0.25. Score = 0.625 x 0.25 = 0.156 — a single shift already in 'poor' territory.

drills.prompt: A developer reports 'zero CLS on my machine' after testing a page that injects a cookie banner at the top of the DOM 400ms after load, loads three unsized images from an ad slot, and swaps a web font at ~800ms. Name every reason their manual test failed to reproduce the field CLS.
drills.answerSketch: (1) They interacted with the page within 500ms of each shift, so hadRecentInput excluded them. (2) Warm cache — fonts and images were already local, so no swap and no unsized-image reflow. (3) Fast connection compressed everything into a window they scrolled past. (4) The ad slot may not have been filled locally (ad blocker, or no ad inventory in dev). (5) Desktop viewport, while the field data is p75 across mobile where the same shift has a larger distance fraction.

drills.prompt: Which of these six shifts count toward CLS? (1) A modal opening 200ms after the user clicks a button. (2) An image loading and pushing content down 1.2s after load with no interaction. (3) A CSS transform: translateY animation on a card. (4) A sticky header changing height on scroll. (5) A font swapping at 900ms. (6) An accordion expanding 300ms after a keypress.
drills.answerSketch: Count: 2 and 5. Excluded: 1 and 6 (within 500ms of discrete input -> hadRecentInput), 3 (transforms are not layout shifts). 4 is a judgement call — scroll is not a discrete input, so a scroll-triggered layout change DOES count; this is the trap in the set and the one most candidates get wrong.

drills.prompt: Reported CLS is the largest ____ ____, defined as shifts separated by gaps of at most ____ second(s) and capped at ____ seconds. A shift within ____ ms of a discrete user input is excluded via the ____ flag.
drills.answerSketch: session window; 1; 5; 500; hadRecentInput

drills.prompt: Legal requires a consent banner rendered at the top of the DOM, above all content, and it may not be position: fixed. Your CLS budget is 0.05. Design the fix.
drills.answerSketch: Reserve the banner's slot at the top of the initial HTML with a known min-height matching the banner's rendered height (measure at the widest and narrowest breakpoints), so the banner fills a box that already existed rather than inserting one. If the height is genuinely unknown, render the banner server-side in the same response as the page so no shift occurs after paint. Fall back to position: sticky within a reserved spacer. Explicitly wrong: animating the banner in, which shifts on every frame.

failureModes: Sums every layout shift on the page and reports a number several times the real CLS.
Tests by clicking around, gets zero, and concludes the page is clean (hadRecentInput exclusion).
Fixes CLS with guessed min-height values that break at other aspect ratios instead of using intrinsic dimensions or aspect-ratio.
Blames a transform-based animation for CLS.
Fixes only the shift they can see on desktop, where the distance fraction is smallest.
interviewProbes: Reproduce the arithmetic: what is the score of a shift where a 50%-of-viewport element moves 100px on an 800px-tall screen?
Why is CLS a session window rather than a sum, and what behaviour does that choice make acceptable?
Your CLS is 0.31 in the field and 0.00 in every lab run. What are you going to do?

perf-images.title: Image Strategy: Format, Selection, Priority, Reserved Space
objectives: Write srcset/sizes that selects the correct candidate at each device profile, and predict the bytes each profile transfers
Decide format, loading, decoding, fetchpriority and dimension attributes per image role rather than site-wide
Explain why the preload scanner's evaluation order makes `sizes` a correctness problem, not a tuning knob
claims: AVIF is typically 20-30% smaller than WebP at comparable quality but far slower to encode; `<picture>` with typed `<source>` elements ships AVIF with a WebP or JPEG fallback. Both AVIF and WebP are Baseline widely available in 2026.

With `w` descriptors in srcset, the browser picks a candidate using device pixel ratio and the layout width declared in `sizes` — and the preload scanner evaluates `sizes` before layout exists, so it trusts your declaration rather than measuring.

A `sizes="100vw"` declaration on an image that actually renders 400px wide on a 3x device makes the browser select a ~1200px-or-larger candidate; the wasted bytes routinely exceed everything the format choice saved.
`sizes="auto"` lets the browser use the real layout size, but it is only valid together with `loading="lazy"`, which makes it unusable for the LCP image.
width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) reserve the box before the bytes arrive; combined with `width: 100%; height: auto` they behave as a ratio, so they do not lock the rendered size.
`loading="lazy"` below the fold saves bytes, but above the fold it delays LCP because the request is deferred until layout proves the image is near the viewport.
`decoding="async"` affects when the decode blocks the main thread; it does not change network priority and does not substitute for fetchpriority.
LQIP and blur-up placeholders improve perceived speed but add bytes to the critical path and introduce a shift if the placeholder's aspect ratio differs from the final image.

viz.title: The Byte Cost of a Wrong `sizes`
viz.whatIsDrawn: A grid of device profiles (viewport width x DPR) against the candidate list from one srcset. The cell for the selected candidate is highlighted and its transferred bytes are printed inside the cell. A ghost overlay marks which cell would have been selected under a corrected `sizes`, with the byte delta annotated between the two cells.
viz.predictPrompt: A card image renders 400px wide on a 3x phone. The markup declares `sizes="100vw"`. You then switch the format from JPEG to AVIF, saving 30% of bytes. Is the AVIF-with-wrong-sizes image larger or smaller on the wire than the JPEG-with-correct-sizes one?
viz.insight: `sizes` is a promise the browser trusts before layout exists. Getting it wrong costs a multiple of the bytes; getting the format wrong costs a percentage. Fix the declaration before you fix the codec.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts implements candidate selection per the HTML spec (effective pixel density = candidate width / sizes-resolved CSS width, pick the smallest candidate >= DPR) plus a byte model per format at a fixed quality. Unit test asserts the predict answer: at 400px rendered on 3x, sizes=100vw on a 390px viewport selects a 1200px+ candidate whose AVIF bytes still exceed the 1200px-correct JPEG. Static SVG grid; the only animated channel is the selection highlight, so reduced-motion just removes the transition.

drills.prompt: Write the sizes attribute for an image in a grid that is 1 column below 640px, 2 columns between 640px and 1024px, and 3 columns above 1024px, inside a max-width 1200px container with 24px gaps and 16px page padding.
drills.answerSketch: Something equivalent to: sizes="(min-width: 1024px) 384px, (min-width: 640px) calc(50vw - 32px), calc(100vw - 32px)". Grader checks the media-query ordering (largest first), that the fixed value is used once the container caps out, and that gaps/padding are subtracted rather than ignored.

drills.prompt: srcset offers 400w, 800w, 1200w and 1600w candidates at roughly 30KB, 95KB, 190KB and 320KB. The image renders 400px wide. Give the transferred bytes for (a) a 3x phone with correct sizes, (b) the same phone with sizes="100vw" on a 390px viewport. State the ratio.
drills.answerSketch: (a) needs 1200 effective px -> 1200w -> 190KB. (b) sizes=100vw resolves to 390 CSS px, x3 DPR = 1170 effective px -> also 1200w. The trap: on THIS device the wrong sizes happens to agree. Repeat for a 1x desktop at 1440px viewport: correct sizes picks 400w (30KB), sizes=100vw picks 1600w (320KB) — a 10.7x overspend. Full credit requires noticing that the penalty is device-dependent and worst where the element is smallest relative to the viewport.

drills.prompt: Review this hero: ``. List every defect and the vital each one damages.
drills.answerSketch: (1) loading="lazy" on the LCP element defers the request until layout — damages LCP, the largest defect here. (2) No width/height and no aspect-ratio — damages CLS. (3) No sizes with w descriptors — the browser assumes 100vw, over-fetching on most devices. (4) No fetchpriority="high" — the hero starts at Low priority. (5) decoding="async" is harmless but is not a fix for any of the above and is often cited as one.

drills.prompt: Design changes so the hero is full-bleed on mobile only and a 480px-wide inset on desktop. Which of your existing attributes become wrong, and does this change your format decision?
drills.answerSketch: sizes must invert its usual shape: `(min-width: 1024px) 480px, 100vw`. The aspect ratio also changes between breakpoints, so a single width/height pair no longer reserves the right box — either use <picture> with per-source dimensions, or set aspect-ratio per breakpoint in CSS. Format decision is unchanged: format is orthogonal to selection.

drills.prompt: Your product accepts user-uploaded images and serves them to a feed. Someone proposes AVIF for everything. In 120 words or fewer, defend or reject, naming the specific cost.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names AVIF encode time (often seconds per image at good settings) as a pipeline and cost problem, not a client problem; (2) proposes a tiered strategy — WebP immediately on upload, AVIF generated asynchronously and swapped in via <picture> once ready; (3) notes AVIF's advantage narrows on photographic content at high quality and is largest at low quality/flat graphics; (4) notes decode cost on low-end devices; (5) commits to a decision.

failureModes: Ships srcset with w descriptors and no sizes, assuming the browser measures layout first.
Applies loading="lazy" globally, including to the LCP image.
Optimises format while serving a 2400px asset into a 300px slot.
Uses a fixed min-height instead of aspect-ratio, so non-standard ratios still shift.
Treats decoding="async" and fetchpriority as interchangeable.
interviewProbes: Explain what the browser knows and does not know at the moment the preload scanner reads your img tag.
We have 4x more image bytes than budget and the formats are already AVIF. Where do you look?
When is loading=lazy actively harmful?

perf-fonts.title: Font Loading: Invisible Text, Reflow, and Metric-Matched Fallbacks
objectives: Choose a font-display value by naming which failure mode it accepts, rather than by default
Trace the discovery chain for a font referenced only from CSS and identify where to intervene
Judge when metric overrides beat preloading, and when neither is worth the complexity
claims: With the default font-display, browsers apply roughly a 3 second block period during which text using the font is invisible (FOIT), followed by an indefinite swap period — so a text LCP element can be blocked on a font.

`font-display: swap` renders fallback text immediately and swaps when the font arrives: no invisible text, but a guaranteed reflow. `font-display: optional` gives roughly a 100ms block period and no swap period, so if the font is not ready it is simply not used for that page view — which is why optional produces no layout shift.

`<link rel="preload" as="font">` requires the crossorigin attribute even for same-origin fonts, because fonts are always fetched in CORS mode; omitting it causes a second, separate fetch of the same file.
A font referenced only from a stylesheet is discovered after the stylesheet is downloaded and parsed and after the matching text is laid out — two dependencies behind the HTML response.
size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override on an @font-face fallback let a local system font match the web font's metrics, driving the swap reflow toward zero shift.
Splitting a face with unicode-range means a Latin-only page never downloads Cyrillic or Greek glyph data; a single variable font typically costs less than three static weights of the same family.

Since browser HTTP cache partitioning (Chrome 86, 2020), a font served from a shared third-party CDN gets no cross-site cache reuse, so self-hosting removes a cross-origin connection with no cache downside.
`document.fonts.ready` lets you gate rendering on font load, but blocking paint on it re-creates FOIT by hand — with none of font-display's timeouts.

viz.title: Block, Swap, or Never
viz.whatIsDrawn: A timeline of the font request with the block period, swap period and failure period drawn as labelled regions. A small live text block above the timeline re-renders at each phase boundary, and an accumulating CLS counter is printed inside the diagram beside the text. A ghost row shows the same timeline with a metric-matched fallback, whose CLS counter stays at zero.
viz.predictPrompt: You add `font-display: swap` and `<link rel=preload>` for the hero font. LCP improves by 300ms. What happens to CLS — and why does making the font arrive *faster* not make the resulting shift any smaller?
controls: font-display: auto / block / swap / fallback / optional
fallback metric overrides: off / size-adjust only / full override set
step through block -> swap -> failure phases
viz.insight: font-display chooses which failure you accept — invisible text or a reflow. Only a metric-matched fallback (or `optional`, which declines to swap) removes the shift; preloading merely makes the same shift happen sooner.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds the phase model (block/swap/failure durations per font-display value) plus a text-metrics model that computes reflow distance from size-adjust and ascent-override values, feeding the real CLS scoring function shared with perf-cls. Unit test asserts the predict answer: preloading reduces the time-to-swap but leaves the shift score identical, while size-adjust tuned to the fallback reduces it by >90%. Reduced-motion: static phase diagram with three text renderings side by side.

drills.prompt: Find every defect: `<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/brand.woff2" as="font">` followed by six more preloads for brand-300, brand-400, brand-500, brand-600, brand-700 and brand-italic, with @font-face rules using font-display: block.
drills.answerSketch: (1) Missing crossorigin on every preload -> each font is fetched twice. (2) Seven preloads saturate the connection and compete with the LCP resource. (3) Six static weights should be one variable font. (4) font-display: block means up to 3s of invisible text, which is worse than the shift it avoids for body copy. (5) No unicode-range subsetting is implied but not shown — accept as a raised question, not a defect.

drills.prompt: Order the discovery chain for a web font used by body text, earliest first: text laid out and the face matched; font file requested; HTML response begins; stylesheet requested; CSSOM constructed; stylesheet response arrives.
drills.answerSketch: HTML response begins -> stylesheet requested -> stylesheet response arrives -> CSSOM constructed -> text laid out and the face matched -> font file requested. The point: the font is three dependencies deep, which is what preload short-circuits.

drills.prompt: `font-display: swap` accepts a ____ and avoids ____. `font-display: optional` uses a ~____ ms block period and a ____ swap period. A font preload must carry the ____ attribute even same-origin.
drills.answerSketch: reflow (layout shift); invisible text / FOIT; 100; zero (no); crossorigin

drills.prompt: Brand requires the exact typeface visible on first paint for the hero headline, and the CLS budget is 0.02. What combination gets you there, and what does it cost?
drills.answerSketch: Subset the hero headline's glyphs into a tiny woff2 (often <5KB), preload it with crossorigin and fetchpriority, and use font-display: block for that one face only — the block period is short enough that the font wins. Body text stays on a metric-matched swap or optional. Cost: a build step for the subset, a second face definition, and a hard dependency on the preload succeeding.

drills.prompt: A brand-heavy marketing site must choose between font-display: swap and font-display: optional for body copy. Argue one side in 120 words or fewer and state what you would measure to confirm.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) frames it as reflow-vs-wrong-typeface rather than fast-vs-slow; (2) notes optional's outcome depends on cache state, so returning visitors get the brand font and first-time visitors often do not; (3) notes swap + metric overrides can get most of optional's stability without abandoning the font; (4) names the measurement — p75 CLS split by cache state, plus a qualitative brand check; (5) commits.

failureModes: Assumes swap is strictly better and never considers optional.
Preloads fonts without crossorigin and silently doubles every font fetch.
Preloads six weights of a family that should be one variable font.
Treats self-hosting vs a font CDN as a shared-cache question, which cache partitioning ended in 2020.
Believes preloading the font eliminates the swap shift.
interviewProbes: Walk me through what a user sees, second by second, on a 3G connection with font-display: block, swap and optional.
Why does a font preload need crossorigin when the file is on your own origin?
How would you get a web font with zero layout shift and no invisible text?

perf-bundles.title: Bundle Anatomy: Splitting, Tree Shaking, and the Barrel Trap
objectives: Explain why a specific module was retained in a chunk, using reachability and side-effect analysis rather than intuition
Attribute bundle growth to a cause from a treemap or module-graph report
Choose split points that reduce time-to-interactive rather than merely increasing chunk count
claims: Tree shaking is dead-code elimination over a statically analysable ES module graph: it requires import/export rather than CommonJS, and it can only remove a module the bundler can prove has no needed side effects.

`"sideEffects": false` in package.json is a promise that importing a module purely for its top-level effects is never necessary; asserting it falsely silently deletes needed code, with global CSS imports the classic casualty — the safe form is `"sideEffects": ["*.css"]`.

A barrel file (an index that re-exports everything) causes a single deep import to pull the whole re-exported graph into the same chunk whenever any re-exported module has side effects, and it slows dev-server module resolution even when tree shaking eventually succeeds.
`import()` creates a split point, but a dynamic import of a module that is also statically imported anywhere in the graph does not remove that module's static cost.
Route-level splitting is the highest-yield split; splitting components below roughly 20KB usually costs more in request overhead and waterfall depth than it saves.
Compare dependencies by compressed transfer size AND by parse/execute cost: a 40KB library that runs work at startup can cost more INP than a 120KB one that is only touched lazily.
Polyfills and transpile targets are often the largest invisible cost — a browserslist that still includes dead browsers forces helper and regenerator output into every chunk.

The correct question for a dependency is 'how many bytes does removing this import actually delete from my graph', which a bundle-visualiser's retained-size attribution answers and a package's published npm size does not.

viz.title: What Does This Import Actually Cost?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A module DAG for a small app with a build-time-computed layout. Selecting an import edge shades every module that becomes reachable through it, and the retained-byte total is printed inside the shaded region. A ghost outline shows the same graph when the barrel import is replaced by a deep import.
viz.predictPrompt: You import one 2KB `formatCurrency` helper from `@acme/ui`, whose entry is a barrel index.ts. The bundle grows by 180KB. The package ships pure ESM and declares `"sideEffects": false`. Name a mechanism that still explains the growth.
controls: inject a side-effectful module (a global CSS import, a polyfill, a registry auto-register)
step: reachable set -> side-effect proof -> retained bytes
viz.insight: Bytes are attributed by graph reachability plus a side-effect proof, not by which symbols you named. One re-export whose module registers something on import anchors its whole subtree into the chunk.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds a fixture module graph (nodes with byte weights, edges, sideEffect flags) and implements reachableSet() and retainedBytes() with the same reachability rule bundlers use. Graph layout is computed at build time and committed as JSON — no layout library in the bundle. Unit test asserts the predict answer: a side-effectful CSS-importing sibling behind the barrel retains 180KB even with sideEffects:false honoured for the rest, and switching to a deep import drops it to 2KB.

drills.prompt: A team adds `"sideEffects": false` to their internal design-system package to improve tree shaking. Production builds now render unstyled in some routes but not others. Explain the mechanism and give the minimal fix.
drills.answerSketch: Components import their own CSS (`import './button.css'`) purely for the side effect. sideEffects:false tells the bundler those imports can be dropped when no binding is used from them — CSS files export nothing, so they are always droppable. It is route-dependent because some routes also pull the CSS in through a used sibling. Minimal fix: `"sideEffects": ["*.css", "*.scss"]`.

drills.prompt: Your splitting plan assumes each route's CSS ships with its JS chunk. The design system switches from imported CSS files to runtime CSS-in-JS. Which of your budgets and split points stop meaning what they meant?
drills.answerSketch: CSS bytes move from a separate, parallel-loadable, cacheable stylesheet into the JS chunk, so the JS budget absorbs them while the CSS budget reads as improved — the total is worse, not better. Style insertion now happens at render time on the main thread, adding to INP and to LCP render delay. Route-level CSS splitting stops existing; shared styles are duplicated per chunk unless the runtime dedupes. Budgets must be restated as total critical-path bytes rather than per-type.

drills.prompt: For each, say split / do not split / already free: (1) a 240KB rich-text editor used on one admin route, (2) a 6KB date formatter used on every page, (3) a 45KB charting module used below the fold on the dashboard, (4) a 30KB i18n bundle for the user's single active locale, (5) a 90KB PDF viewer opened from a button, (6) a 12KB modal component used on 3 of 40 routes.
drills.answerSketch: 1 split (route-level, huge, rare). 2 do not split (tiny, universal — a request costs more). 3 split, ideally on intersection or idle rather than on route entry. 4 already free if locales are separate chunks selected at runtime; splitting per-locale is the point, not splitting i18n itself. 5 split, loaded on the button's pointerdown. 6 do not split — 12KB is below the overhead threshold; put it in a shared chunk.

drills.prompt: Rewrite these three barrel imports as deep imports, and complete the Vite manualChunks function that isolates the vendor charting library into its own chunk while leaving everything else to the default strategy.
drills.answerSketch: Deep imports target the concrete module path rather than the package index. manualChunks(id) returns 'charts' when id includes the charting package's node_modules path and returns undefined otherwise — the common wrong answer returns 'vendor' for all node_modules, which recreates one giant chunk and destroys cache granularity.

drills.prompt: A table needs 8 date/time formats. Argue for date-fns, dayjs with plugins, or Intl.DateTimeFormat with hand-written wrappers, in 120 words or fewer, naming the bytes and the risk.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) reaches for Intl first and says why (zero bytes, locale-correct, in every browser) and names its real limitation (parsing and arithmetic, which Intl does not do); (2) gives approximate retained bytes for the alternatives under tree shaking rather than published package size; (3) notes dayjs plugins are side-effectful and resist shaking; (4) names the risk of hand-written wrappers (timezone and DST edge cases); (5) commits to one.

failureModes: Quotes a package's published or bundlephobia size instead of the retained bytes in their own graph.
Sets sideEffects:false on their own package and loses global CSS in production only.
Lazy-loads a component that a sibling still imports statically, then reports that code splitting 'did nothing'.
Splits at component granularity and creates a deep request waterfall that is slower than the monolith.
Treats a treemap's largest rectangle as the thing to remove, without checking whether anything actually depends on it.
interviewProbes: Our main chunk grew 180KB from a one-line import. Walk me through how you find out why.
When does code splitting make a page slower?
What exactly does sideEffects:false authorise the bundler to do?

perf-hints.title: Resource Hints and Speculative Loading
objectives: Select the correct hint for a resource given when it is needed and which origin serves it
Predict when adding a hint makes the page slower, and say which hint you would delete first
Judge whether speculative prerendering is worth its bandwidth and correctness cost for a given product
claims: `preconnect` performs DNS, TCP and TLS ahead of time and typically saves 100-300ms on a cross-origin critical resource; `dns-prefetch` does only the DNS step. Browsers hold few speculative connections open, so preconnecting to more than about four origins is counterproductive.

`preload` is a discovery-and-priority instruction for a resource needed on the *current* page; its `as` attribute determines both the assigned priority and the CORS mode, and a mismatched `as` causes a duplicate fetch plus a console warning.
Preload is zero-sum under bandwidth constraint: preloading several resources reorders them ahead of the LCP resource and can make LCP worse even though every hint is syntactically correct.

`prefetch` fetches at the lowest priority for a *future* navigation; `modulepreload` preloads an ES module and its dependency graph and also parses and compiles it, which `preload as="script"` does not.
`fetchpriority="high" | "low" | "auto"` adjusts priority on img, link, script and fetch(); it reached Baseline when Firefox 132 shipped it in October 2024 (Chrome 101, Safari 17.2).

Speculation Rules (`<script type="speculationrules">`) express prefetch and prerender with an eagerness of immediate | eager | moderate | conservative, where moderate triggers on roughly 200ms of hover and conservative on pointerdown.

Prerendering fully runs the target page — its JavaScript, analytics and side effects — in a hidden state, so code must check `document.prerendering` and listen for `prerenderingchange` or it will log phantom pageviews and fire mutations early.

Speculation Rules are effectively Chromium-only in 2026 (Safari has an implementation behind a flag; Firefox has not shipped), and unsupported browsers ignore the script tag entirely — so it is a progressive enhancement, never a load strategy you depend on.

An unconditional `unload` listener or a `Cache-Control: no-store` response disqualifies a page from bfcache, and losing instant back/forward restoration usually costs more real navigations than any prefetching gains.

viz.title: Preload Everything, Regret Everything
viz.whatIsDrawn: A bandwidth-constrained waterfall where each request's bar width equals bytes divided by available bandwidth, with a priority label printed inside each bar. Connection setup (DNS/TCP/TLS) is drawn as a distinct leading segment. The LCP moment is a vertical line drawn through the waterfall and labelled in place. A ghost waterfall behind shows the no-hints baseline.
viz.predictPrompt: You add rel=preload to five resources — the hero image, two web fonts, the analytics script and a below-the-fold video poster. Every hint is syntactically correct. On a 5 Mbps connection, what happens to LCP, and which single hint would you delete first?
controls: add or remove each hint independently
fetchpriority on the hero: auto / high
toggle preconnect for the cross-origin font host
viz.insight: Hints redistribute a fixed pipe rather than widening it. Preload competes against your own LCP resource; preconnect is the only hint that creates time instead of moving it, because it overlaps latency you would have paid serially.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models a shared-bandwidth scheduler with per-request priority classes and a connection-setup cost per new origin, on an injected clock. Unit test asserts the predict answer: five correct preloads on a 5 Mbps link delay LCP versus preloading only the hero, and that adding preconnect for the font origin improves LCP without consuming bandwidth. Reduced-motion: static side-by-side waterfalls with the LCP line on each.

drills.prompt: Assign the single best hint (or none) to each: (1) the hero image on this page, (2) a font used only in the footer, (3) the JS bundle for the page users visit next 70% of the time, (4) a payments iframe origin contacted 3s after load, (5) an ES module entry point for the current route, (6) an analytics endpoint on a third origin.
drills.answerSketch: 1 fetchpriority="high" on the img (preload only if it is not discoverable in markup). 2 none — preloading it competes with the hero for no LCP benefit. 3 speculation-rules prefetch, or rel=prefetch. 4 preconnect (or dns-prefetch if you want it cheaper). 5 modulepreload. 6 dns-prefetch at most; preconnect wastes a socket on something non-critical.

drills.prompt: Find the defects: `<link rel=preload href="/f/brand.woff2" as="font">`, `<link rel=preload href="/next-page.js" as="script">`, and a speculation-rules block prerendering every same-origin link with eagerness "immediate" on a site whose analytics fires on module load.
drills.answerSketch: (1) Font preload missing crossorigin -> double fetch. (2) preload (not prefetch) for a next-page resource -> fetched at high priority now, competing with this page's critical path, and warned as unused. (3) eagerness "immediate" on every link prerenders potentially dozens of pages — huge bandwidth cost, especially on metered connections — and the analytics module will fire pageviews for pages nobody visited because nothing checks document.prerendering.

drills.prompt: Speculation Rules eagerness values are ____, ____, ____ and ____. `moderate` triggers on roughly ____ ms of hover; `conservative` triggers on ____. During prerender, `document.____` is true and the page fires a ____ event when activated.
drills.answerSketch: immediate; eager; moderate; conservative; 200; pointerdown; prerendering; prerenderingchange

drills.prompt: Your hint strategy was designed for a multi-page site. The product becomes a client-routed SPA. Which hints stop mattering, which start mattering more, and what replaces prerender?
drills.answerSketch: prefetch/prerender of documents largely stop mattering — there is one document. modulepreload and route-chunk prefetching start mattering much more: prefetch the next route's JS chunk (and its data) on hover/pointerdown, which is the SPA analogue of speculative navigation. preconnect to API origins matters more because data, not documents, is now on the critical path. bfcache stops helping in-app navigation, so back/forward must be handled by your own state restoration.

drills.prompt: Argue for or against enabling prerender with eagerness "moderate" across a news site's article links, in 120 words or fewer. Name who pays.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) quantifies the wasted-bandwidth risk — a hover-triggered prerender loads a full page including its images and third parties; (2) names the metered-connection and battery cost on mobile, and Save-Data / connection-type gating as the mitigation; (3) names the correctness work required (document.prerendering guards on analytics, ads, and anything that mutates); (4) notes it is Chromium-only so it cannot be the plan, only a bonus; (5) commits, with a scope limit such as 'top 3 links only, desktop only'.

failureModes: Preloads everything above the fold and regresses LCP while every hint is syntactically valid.
Uses prefetch for a current-page resource, or preload for a next-page one.
Ships prerendering without guarding analytics, then reports inflated pageviews and cannot explain them.
Adds preconnect to eight origins and exhausts the browser's speculative connection budget.
Breaks bfcache with an unload handler while optimising forward navigation, and never measures the back-navigation loss.
interviewProbes: What is the difference between preload and prefetch, and what happens if you swap them?
We added preloads and LCP got worse. How is that possible if every preload is for a resource we genuinely need?
What has to be true about a page's code before you can safely prerender it?

perf-react-render.title: React Render Cost: Reconciliation, Context Storms and Transitions
objectives: Determine, from a profile, whether a slow update is caused by too many components rendering, by one expensive render, or by the browser's commit and paint
Identify the data-flow shape that causes a re-render fan-out, and pick the fix that addresses the shape rather than masking it
State precisely what React Compiler does and does not eliminate
claims: Re-rendering is not re-committing: React re-runs the component function, diffs the result, and writes to the DOM only where the output changed. 'Renders are bad' is the wrong model; expensive renders and large commits are the actual costs.
A change to a Context value re-renders every consumer regardless of which field that consumer reads, because context propagation is not field-granular.
React Compiler 1.0 (stable since October 2025) memoises computation inside components automatically; it does not change context propagation, so it does not fix a context storm.

The fix for a context storm is to change the data-flow shape: split the stable dispatch from the changing value into separate contexts, or move the state into a store read through selectors via useSyncExternalStore.

Using array index as a key is only safe for lists that are append-only, never reordered or filtered, and whose items hold no uncontrolled DOM or component state; otherwise React reuses the wrong instance and state follows the wrong item.
React.memo compares props shallowly, so a new inline object, array or closure defeats it — which is why hand-memoisation frequently does nothing measurable.
startTransition and useTransition mark an update as interruptible so that urgent input can preempt it; they reduce input delay on subsequent interactions but do not make the render itself any faster.

useDeferredValue renders the previous value at urgent priority and schedules the expensive render at transition priority — the same trade as startTransition, expressed at a value rather than at a setter.

viz.title: The Context Storm the Compiler Will Not Fix
viz.whatIsDrawn: A component tree of about 24 nodes. A state change lights the set of components that re-render, and the count plus the total render cost is printed at the root, inside the diagram. A ghost overlay shows the same tree after the chosen fix, with its own count printed alongside.
viz.predictPrompt: React Compiler 1.0 is enabled across the whole app. A theme context's value object is recreated on every keystroke in an unrelated search box. How many of the 24 components re-render — and does enabling the compiler change that number?
controls: change source: context value / prop drill / store selector
step one commit at a time
viz.insight: Automatic memoisation removes redundant computation inside a component. It cannot stop a context value from notifying every consumer — that is a data-flow shape problem, and only re-shaping the data flow fixes it.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models the tree, the subscription edges, and per-node render costs, exposing propagate(changeSource, options) -> {renderedIds, totalCost}. Unit test asserts the pedagogical claim: with the compiler on, the rendered-node count for a context change is identical to compiler-off, while the count for a prop-drill change drops. Reduced-motion: static before/after tree pair with the two counts; live region announces 'renders: 24 -> 3'.

drills.prompt: `<ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>` inside a component that also holds unrelated search state. Explain the mechanism by which a keystroke in the search box re-renders every theme consumer, and give two structurally different fixes.
drills.answerSketch: The provider component re-renders on every keystroke; the object literal is a new reference each time, so every consumer's context subscription fires even though theme itself never changed. Fix A: split into ThemeValueContext and ThemeDispatchContext, and memoise the value object on [theme]. Fix B: hoist search state out of the provider component so it does not re-render. Fix C (structural): move theme into a store and read it with a selector. Naming useMemo alone is partial credit — it fixes the identity but not the fan-out when theme genuinely changes.

drills.prompt: Your list uses index as key and has been fine for two years. The requirement changes: rows become reorderable by drag, and each row has an uncontrolled text input. What breaks, and exactly why?
drills.answerSketch: React matches children by key, so after a reorder the element at index 3 is still key 3 — React reuses that fiber and its DOM node, keeping the previous row's uncontrolled input value and any focus/scroll/animation state while the props change to a different row's data. Users see typed text follow the position, not the item. Fix: stable domain ids as keys.

drills.prompt: Convert a component that reads `const { user, notifications, theme } = useContext(AppContext)` but only uses `user.name` into a selector subscription over a Zustand store, so it re-renders only when the name changes.
drills.answerSketch: `const name = useAppStore(s => s.user.name)` — the grader checks that the selector returns a primitive (or uses a shallow/equality comparator if it returns an object), since returning `s.user` re-renders on any user field change and returning a new object literal from the selector re-renders every time.

drills.prompt: Order what happens after setState on an urgent update, earliest first: browser paints; component functions re-run; DOM mutations applied; style and layout recalculated; React diffs the new tree; layout effects run.
drills.answerSketch: component functions re-run -> React diffs the new tree -> DOM mutations applied -> layout effects run -> style and layout recalculated -> browser paints. The teaching point: everything from 'DOM mutations applied' onward is presentation delay in INP terms and is invisible in the React Profiler.

drills.prompt: A filter box over a 5,000-row table freezes while typing. Choose between useDeferredValue, a 250ms debounce, and virtualising the table. Defend one in 120 words or fewer and state what it does not fix.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) identifies that debounce hides the work but still runs it as one unchunked task later — the long task and the INP hit remain; (2) identifies that useDeferredValue keeps the input responsive by rendering the stale list at low priority, but the expensive render still happens and still costs a large commit; (3) identifies virtualisation as the only option that reduces the actual work, and that it is complementary rather than alternative; (4) picks virtualisation as the root fix with useDeferredValue as the responsiveness layer; (5) names what remains unfixed (server-side filtering if the dataset grows).

failureModes: Wraps everything in memo/useMemo/useCallback and declares victory without measuring.
Assumes React Compiler removes the need to think about context shape or data-flow.
Uses index keys on a reorderable list and blames React for 'losing state'.
Debounces to hide a render cost, which then arrives as one giant long task and a worse INP.
Reads the React Profiler's render times and concludes the browser's layout and paint cost is React's fault, or vice versa.
interviewProbes: A keystroke in one corner of the app re-renders 200 components. Walk me through your diagnosis before you change any code.
What does React Compiler actually memoise, and name something it cannot help with.
When is a re-render genuinely fine, and how do you tell?

perf-virtualization.title: Windowing: DOM Nodes, Frame Budget and Measurement Thrash
objectives: Decide whether a given list needs virtualisation, pagination, or nothing, using node counts and frame budget rather than row counts
Design a windowing configuration (overscan, measurement, keys, offsets) that holds the frame budget during fast scrolling
Specify the accessibility and find-in-page equivalents that a virtualised list destroys
claims: Cost scales with DOM nodes, not with rows: 5,000 rows at 8 nodes each is 40,000 nodes, and style recalculation and layout over that tree exceed the ~16.7ms frame budget at 60Hz (~8.3ms at 120Hz).
Virtualisation renders only the visible window plus an overscan buffer; overscan trades extra render work for the blank rows a user sees during a fast flick.

Fixed row heights make total height and every row offset an O(1) computation; variable heights require measurement, and measuring inside a scroll handler interleaves reads and writes and forces synchronous layout every frame.
Row heights should be measured with ResizeObserver into a cached measurement map — the approach TanStack Virtual and react-window v2 take — rather than reading offsetHeight per row per frame.
Positioning rows with `transform: translateY` keeps the offset change on the compositor path; setting `top` per row forces layout on every scroll frame.

A virtualised list is invisible to browser find-in-page, breaks anchor links to offscreen items, and reports the wrong item count to assistive technology unless you supply aria-setsize and aria-posinset (or an equivalent role) — and it still needs a non-virtualised print and export path.

Using the array index as the row key while the window slides causes React to remount rows instead of reusing them, converting cheap prop updates into DOM creation and destruction on every scroll frame.

`content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size` skips rendering work for offscreen sections with no JavaScript, but it does not reduce DOM node count or memory, and a wrong intrinsic size estimate makes the scrollbar jump.

viz.title: Fewer Nodes, Worse Scroll
viz.whatIsDrawn: A scrollable list mock with the rendered window highlighted and the overscan buffer outlined. Live counters for DOM node count and last-frame milliseconds are printed inside the panel, beside the list. Below, a frame-time strip with the 16.7ms budget line drawn across it; a ghost strip shows the unvirtualised baseline.
viz.predictPrompt: You virtualise a 10,000-row table down to 20 rendered rows. Node count drops 99% and first paint is dramatically faster. Scrolling on a trackpad becomes *choppier* than the unvirtualised version was. Name the mechanism.
controls: row heights: fixed / measured per row
key strategy: stable id / array index
scrub the scroll position frame by frame
viz.insight: Windowing converts a one-time layout cost into a per-frame cost. If each frame re-measures rows or remounts them because the keys moved, you have traded a slow first paint for permanent jank.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models per-frame cost as a function of (rows rendered, nodes per row, measurement mode, key stability, offset method) with an injected clock and a seeded scroll-velocity trace. Unit tests assert both halves of the predict answer: index keys plus per-frame measurement produce a higher p95 frame time than the unvirtualised baseline, while stable keys plus cached measurement plus transform offsets stay under budget. Reduced-motion: static frame-time strips for the four configurations side by side.

drills.prompt: Review: rows are keyed by their index within the visible window; each row's height is read with `ref.current.offsetHeight` inside the scroll handler and written back into state; rows are positioned with `style={{ top: offset }}`. Name each defect and the per-frame cost it adds.
drills.answerSketch: (1) Window-relative index keys change identity for every row on every scroll -> full remount of 20 rows per frame instead of prop updates. (2) offsetHeight inside the scroll handler after a state write forces synchronous layout, once per row, every frame — classic thrash. (3) setState inside a scroll handler schedules a render per scroll event. (4) `top` forces layout instead of staying on the compositor. Correct: stable item ids, ResizeObserver into a measurement cache, transform: translateY, and rAF-throttled scroll state.

drills.prompt: Which of these need virtualisation? (1) a 60-item settings list, (2) a 3,000-row admin table where users rely on Ctrl+F, (3) a 200-message chat log with images, (4) a 50,000-point log viewer, (5) a 400-row report that is printed, (6) an infinite feed of 30-node cards.
drills.answerSketch: 1 no — 60 items is nothing. 2 conditionally: virtualise but you must replace Ctrl+F with an in-app search, or paginate instead — the honest answer names the requirement conflict. 3 probably not for 200 rows; use lazy images and content-visibility. 4 yes, unambiguously. 5 no — printing needs the full DOM; if you virtualise you need a separate print path. 6 yes, and the node count per card is why.

drills.prompt: Rows render 11 DOM nodes each. Measured style+layout cost is approximately 0.4ms per 1,000 nodes on the target device. Give the frame cost for 500 unvirtualised rows and for a 25-row window with overscan 10, and say which fits a 120Hz budget.
drills.answerSketch: 500 rows x 11 = 5,500 nodes -> ~2.2ms of style+layout per full recalculation (and the initial layout of 5,500 nodes is far worse than one incremental recalculation — credit for noting the distinction). 35 rows x 11 = 385 nodes -> ~0.15ms. Both fit an 8.3ms budget for a steady-state recalculation; the real 120Hz risk is the per-frame remount and measurement work, not the node count. Full credit requires that conclusion, not just the arithmetic.

drills.prompt: Rows must become expandable to arbitrary height, and the expanded state must survive scrolling away and back. What changes in your windowing design?
