drills.answerSketch: Fixed-height O(1) offsets are gone; you need a measurement cache keyed by stable item id, seeded with an estimate, updated via ResizeObserver, with the total height and offsets recomputed incrementally (prefix sums / a segment tree, not a full re-scan). Expanded state must live outside the row component (in the list's state keyed by item id) because unmounted rows lose local state. Scroll anchoring must be handled explicitly so expanding a row above the viewport does not jump the scroll position.

drills.prompt: A 3,000-row admin table must support browser find-in-page, which virtualisation breaks. In 120 words or fewer, choose virtualise-plus-in-app-search, paginate, or content-visibility, and name who is worse off.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) states that content-visibility keeps all nodes in the DOM so find-in-page keeps working — often the correct answer at this scale and the one candidates forget; (2) names its limits (memory, and that it does not reduce node count); (3) if choosing virtualisation, commits to shipping in-app search with keyboard parity and says explicitly that power users lose a habit; (4) names pagination's cost (loses cross-page scanning, adds server round trips); (5) commits and names the measurement that would change their mind.

failureModes: Virtualises a 60-row list because 'lists should be virtualised'.
Ships a virtualised list that breaks find-in-page and screen-reader item counts, with no equivalent provided.
Measures every row on every frame and concludes the virtualisation library is slow.
Uses the window-relative index as the key, so every scroll frame remounts the whole window.
Never considers content-visibility, which would have solved the problem with three lines of CSS and no accessibility regression.
interviewProbes: When would you NOT virtualise a long list?
Your virtualised list is janky on scroll but the React Profiler shows tiny render times. Where is the time going?
How do you keep a virtualised list accessible and searchable?

perf-animation.title: Compositor-Only Animation and FLIP
objectives: Name which rendering pipeline stages a given animated property triggers, and predict the per-frame cost
Explain why some animations keep running while the main thread is blocked and others freeze
Implement a layout change as a FLIP animation and state what FLIP cannot do
claims: The rendering pipeline is style -> layout -> paint -> composite; animating a property that affects only compositing skips layout and paint entirely.
`transform` and `opacity` are the two properties that are reliably compositor-only across engines; animating width, height, top, left or margin forces layout on every frame, on the main thread.

Compositor-driven animations continue running while the main thread is blocked; a layout- or JavaScript-driven animation freezes during a long task and then jumps — this is the difference users describe as jank.
FLIP animates a layout change with transforms: measure First, apply the Last layout, compute the Inverted transform, then Play it to identity — so the browser lays out once instead of on every frame.

`will-change` promotes an element to its own compositor layer in advance; every layer costs GPU memory, so leaving will-change applied permanently across many elements can make scrolling worse rather than better.
Layout thrash is interleaved reads and writes within one frame — reading offsetHeight after writing a style forces a synchronous layout each time; batching all reads before all writes removes it.
requestAnimationFrame callbacks run before paint in the same frame, so a 20ms rAF callback drops that frame at 60Hz — rAF is not a way to make work cheap, only a way to align it with the frame.

`element.animate()` (Web Animations API) with transform/opacity keyframes gets the same compositor path as an equivalent CSS animation; the API choice does not determine the pipeline cost, the property does.

viz.title: Which Stages Does This Property Wake Up?
viz.whatIsDrawn: Four stacked pipeline stages (style, layout, paint, composite). Animating the selected property lights the stages it triggers and draws that frame's cost bar against a 16.7ms line, with the milliseconds printed inside the bar. A 'block the main thread' toggle shows the compositor animation continuing while the layout-driven one freezes. A ghost bar shows the transform version at the same scale.
viz.predictPrompt: Two visually identical slide-in animations: one animates `left`, one animates `translateX`. Mid-animation, you block the main thread with a 400ms task. Predict what each animation looks like *during* those 400ms — and what each looks like immediately *after*.
controls: property: transform / opacity / left / width / box-shadow
will-change on / off, with a layer-memory readout
viz.insight: Compositor-only animations survive a blocked main thread; layout-driven ones freeze and then jump to catch up. The property you animate decides whether your animation is a hostage to your JavaScript.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts maps property -> triggered stages -> per-frame cost, and models a blocked main thread as frames the main thread cannot produce while the compositor continues. Unit test asserts the claim: with a 400ms block, the transform animation's position at t+400ms is on-schedule while the `left` animation's is unchanged from t, then discontinuous. Reduced-motion: static filmstrip of five sampled frames for each property with positions annotated.

drills.prompt: Find the layout thrash: a loop over 100 cards that reads `card.offsetTop`, then writes `card.style.transform = translateY(...)`, then reads `card.getBoundingClientRect().height`, then writes a class. State how many synchronous layouts this forces and give the batched rewrite.
drills.answerSketch: Each read after a write invalidates and forces layout: roughly 200 forced synchronous layouts (two read-after-write boundaries per card, 100 cards). Batched rewrite: one pass collecting all offsetTop and rect values into an array, then a second pass applying all transforms and classes — 1 layout instead of 200.

drills.prompt: Complete a FLIP helper: given an element and a callback that mutates the DOM into its final layout, animate the change using only transforms. Fill in the First measurement, the Last measurement, the Invert transform, and the Play call.
drills.answerSketch: First: `const first = el.getBoundingClientRect()`. Run the mutation. Last: `const last = el.getBoundingClientRect()`. Invert: `const dx = first.left - last.left; const dy = first.top - last.top; const sx = first.width / last.width`. Play: `el.animate([{transform: \`translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px) scaleX(${sx})\`}, {transform: 'none'}], {duration, easing})`. Grader checks the subtraction direction (first minus last) and that the final keyframe is identity, the two most common errors.

drills.prompt: Order the rendering pipeline stages and mark which ones `opacity`, `width` and `box-shadow` each trigger: composite, layout, paint, style.
drills.answerSketch: style -> layout -> paint -> composite. opacity: style + composite only. width: all four. box-shadow: style + paint + composite (no layout — this is the one candidates usually get wrong in both directions).

drills.prompt: An accordion must animate its height to fit dynamic content, so `height: auto` cannot be replaced with a fixed value. How do you keep it off the layout path, and what do you give up?
drills.answerSketch: Measure the target height once (or use a scaleY FLIP on a wrapper with a counter-scale on the content to avoid distortion), then animate transform rather than height. Alternatives worth naming: CSS `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` / `calc-size()` where supported, or animating a clip-path/max-height with an accepted approximation. What you give up: exact reflow of surrounding content during the animation (siblings do not move until the end unless you FLIP them too), and content-distortion artefacts with naive scaleY.

drills.prompt: A 200-card grid animates a hover lift. Someone adds `will-change: transform` to every card. In 120 words or fewer, defend or reject, and name the number you would look at.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names the GPU memory cost — 200 layers, each roughly card-area x 4 bytes per pixel, which on a large screen runs to tens or hundreds of MB; (2) notes that on low-memory devices this causes layer eviction and worse scrolling than no promotion at all; (3) proposes applying will-change on pointerenter and removing it on transition end, or omitting it entirely since transform animations promote on their own; (4) names the number: layer count and GPU memory in the browser's layers panel, plus scroll frame times before and after; (5) commits.

failureModes: Applies will-change: transform to every card and reports worse scrolling without connecting the two.
Animates height for an accordion and describes the resulting per-frame layout as unavoidable.
Reads offsetTop inside a rAF loop after writing styles, then blames rAF.
Assumes all CSS animations are automatically GPU-accelerated because they are 'CSS not JS'.
Believes moving an animation to requestAnimationFrame makes it cheaper.
interviewProbes: Why does a CSS transform animation keep going while a long task blocks the main thread, and what does the user see when a `left` animation does not?
Walk me through FLIP and tell me when it does not work.
When is will-change a mistake?

perf-budgets-ci.title: Budgets, Regression Detection, and the Noise Floor
objectives: Design a performance gate whose detection threshold is defensible against the measured noise of the signal it gates
Assign each performance signal to the right role: prioritisation, diagnosis, or enforcement
Specify the escape hatch and ownership model that keeps a gate alive past its first blocked launch
claims: A budget is only real if a violation blocks a merge; a dashboard nobody is accountable for is documentation, not a budget.

Byte budgets (size-limit, Lighthouse budget.json) are near-deterministic and can be gated hard; lab timing metrics vary run to run by roughly 10-20% on shared CI hardware and must be gated on a median of several runs or on a trend, never a single run.

Detection power is the ratio of the effect size to the measurement noise: a 5% threshold on a metric with 12% run-to-run noise produces frequent false failures and still misses real regressions, which trains the team to ignore the alarm.
Budgets belong per route entry and per incremental chunk, not as one app-wide total, or the largest route's headroom hides every later regression.
Compare against the merge base rather than a hardcoded constant, so the budget cannot be silently ratcheted upward by unrelated PRs; ratchet the constant downward deliberately as a separate commit.

Lighthouse CI on a shared runner is noisy because of CPU contention with other jobs; either pin a dedicated runner, use a hosted lab with controlled devices, or restrict the gate to byte- and count-based audits.

Field regressions are detected by comparing p75 per release and per route over a rolling window in RUM; no lab suite can detect a regression that only affects low-end Android devices, because no lab suite runs on the user's device.

Every gate needs a named owner and a time-boxed override with an expiry, or the team deletes the check the first time it blocks a launch — which is the most common way performance budgets actually die.
The signal chain is: RUM tells you what to work on, traces and lab profiles tell you why, and CI gates tell you it stays fixed. Using any one of the three for another's job is the underlying error.

viz.title: How Small a Regression Can You Actually Detect?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A per-commit time series of one metric with a shaded band representing measurement noise and a horizontal threshold line. False alarms and missed real regressions are marked with in-chart labels at the commits where they occur, and running counts of each are printed inside the plot. A ghost series shows the same commits measured by bytes instead of by lab timing.
viz.predictPrompt: Your CI runs one Lighthouse pass per PR and fails the build on a greater-than-5% LCP regression. Measured run-to-run noise on your shared runner is about 12%. Roughly what fraction of clean PRs get failed, and how large does a real regression have to be before you reliably catch it?
controls: metric: compressed bytes / lab LCP / field p75
viz.insight: A gate's usefulness is the effect size divided by the noise, not the strictness of its threshold. Gate hard on bytes, which barely move on their own; gate softly and on trends for timings, which move constantly.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts generates a deterministic commit series with a seeded RNG, injected noise sigma per metric, and injected regressions at known commits; it returns falseAlarmRate and detectionRate for a given threshold and run count. Unit test asserts the predict answer to within tolerance (5% threshold at 12% sigma with n=1 gives a false-alarm rate above 30%; averaging 5 runs cuts sigma by sqrt(5) and brings it under 10%). Reduced-motion: static chart with the marks and the two counters.

drills.prompt: A metric has ~12% run-to-run standard deviation. Your gate fails any PR above +5% versus the merge base, from a single run. Estimate the false-failure rate on clean PRs, then estimate it again if you take the median of 5 runs. (Tolerance is generous — the reasoning is what is graded.)
drills.answerSketch: Single run: +5% is about 0.42 standard deviations, so roughly 34% of clean PRs fail. Median of 5 reduces the effective spread by roughly sqrt(5) (~2.2x), putting +5% near 0.93 sigma, so roughly 18%... still unacceptable — full credit requires concluding that the threshold, not just the run count, has to change, or that the metric should not be a hard gate at all.

drills.prompt: Classify each as hard gate (blocks merge), soft signal (comment or trend alert), or field alarm: (1) gzipped bytes of the entry chunk, (2) Lighthouse performance score, (3) number of render-blocking requests, (4) lab LCP on a shared runner, (5) p75 INP per route from RUM, (6) total image bytes on the home route.
drills.answerSketch: Hard gate: 1, 3, 6 (deterministic counts and bytes). Soft signal: 2 and 4 (both noisy composites; 2 additionally rewards things users do not feel). Field alarm: 5 (cannot be measured in CI at all, and needs a rolling-window comparison per release).

drills.prompt: Review this CI config: a single budget of 'total JS < 900KB gzipped' for the whole app, compared against a constant in the repo, with a `[skip-perf]` commit-message escape hatch and no owner. Name every structural defect.
drills.answerSketch: (1) One app-wide total means a small route can grow 200KB while the total stays under budget — no per-route or per-incremental limit. (2) Comparing against a constant lets anyone bump the constant in the same PR that breaks the budget; comparing against the merge base plus a deliberate ratchet is correct. (3) An unlogged, unexpiring, self-service skip flag means the gate is optional in practice. (4) No owner means nobody investigates a failure. (5) 900KB gzipped is far above any reasonable landing budget — the number itself has no justification tied to a device or connection target.

drills.prompt: Your gate design assumed 5 PRs a day. The team grows and now ships 60 PRs a day into a trunk. What breaks, and what do you change?
drills.answerSketch: False-alarm cost scales linearly: a 15% false-failure rate is one annoyance a day at 5 PRs and nine a day at 60, which guarantees the check gets disabled. Lab runs also become a CI cost and queue-time problem. Changes: move all noisy timing checks off the blocking path into a post-merge trend job on a dedicated runner; keep only deterministic byte/count gates blocking; add automatic bisection on the post-merge series so a regression is attributed without blocking anyone; alert on the trend, not the commit.

drills.prompt: Argue for either blocking the merge or posting a bot comment when a route exceeds its byte budget by 8%. 120 words or fewer; name the failure mode of the option you rejected.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) recognises bytes are deterministic, so the usual anti-blocking argument (flakiness) does not apply here; (2) argues for blocking with a documented, owner-approved, expiring override; (3) names the rejected option's failure mode explicitly — comments are ignored within weeks and the budget silently becomes a historical artefact; (4) names the social cost of blocking and how the override mitigates it; (5) commits.

failureModes: Gates on the Lighthouse performance score and spends the following month triaging flakes until someone deletes the check.
Sets one total-bundle budget and never notices per-route regressions.
Compares against a hardcoded constant that gets bumped in whichever PR first fails it.
Has no field signal at all, so a regression affecting only low-end Android ships and is discovered by a support ticket.
Builds an elaborate perf dashboard with no owner and no gate, and calls it a performance culture.
interviewProbes: Design the performance gates for a team shipping 40 PRs a day. What blocks a merge and what does not?
Your CI fails a PR for a 6% LCP regression. How do you decide whether to believe it?
How would you catch a regression that only affects users on 4-year-old Android phones?

arch-render-matrix.title: The Rendering Decision Matrix
objectives: Given a route's SEO, TTFB, personalization, freshness and infrastructure constraints, choose a rendering strategy and name the single constraint that decided it.
Identify which constraints eliminate which strategies, and recognise a constraint set that no single strategy satisfies.
Decompose a route so that one personalized fragment does not force the whole document to be dynamic.
claims: Build-time rendering can only produce HTML for content knowable without the request — no cookies, no headers, no per-user data.
Time to First Byte is bounded below by whatever data the server awaits before its first byte, so adding SSR to a static route strictly increases TTFB.
A CDN-served static document's TTFB is dominated by network round-trip time to the edge PoP, not by application compute.

Personalization and shared caching are in direct conflict: a document that varies per user cannot be served from a shared cache unless the varying parts are deferred — streamed, client-fetched, or composed at the edge.
A freshness requirement is a tolerable staleness window; if that window is greater than zero, stale-while-revalidate / ISR is available and per-request SSR is not required.
Server rendering imposes a running server or serverless function per request, which is an operational and cost constraint, not only a latency one.
Streaming SSR is the right answer when a page has a fast frame and one slow data dependency, not when every region is slow.
The rendering strategy is chosen per route and, within a route, per Suspense boundary — one application normally mixes static, streamed and client-rendered routes.

viz.title: The Constraint Grid
viz.whatIsDrawn: A 5x5 grid: rows are strategies (static, ISR/SWR, streamed SSR, per-request SSR, client-rendered), columns are constraints (indexability, TTFB budget, personalization, staleness budget, infra you will operate). Moving a constraint control greys out the cells it eliminates and stamps the eliminating reason INSIDE the greyed cell (e.g. 'varies per user — not shareable'). A ghost outline marks the strategy the learner predicted.
viz.predictPrompt: A product page must be indexable and shareable in Slack, shows a per-user 'recently viewed' rail, and its inventory count may be at most 60 seconds stale. Which single constraint eliminates the most strategies — and does the personalized rail force the whole document to per-request SSR?
controls: infrastructure toggle (static host only / functions available)
viz.insight: Constraints eliminate strategies; they almost never select one. The winning move is usually to push the personalized fragment out of the cacheable document, not to drag the document into SSR.
viz.buildNotes: Pure derived state: strategies x constraints is a static predicate table in sim.ts, unit-tested claim by claim (e.g. 'personalization=per-user eliminates shared-cache strategies'). No timers, no RNG. Elimination is staged — one constraint applied per step — so at most the grey-flood channel and the reason-label fade animate. Reduced-motion: render the fully-eliminated grid with all reasons visible.

drills.prompt: Six routes from one e-commerce app, each with a one-line requirement set (marketing home, category listing, product detail, cart, order history, admin report). Assign a rendering strategy to each and tag the one constraint that decided it.
drills.answerSketch: Home: static (no personal data, on-publish freshness). Category: ISR (shared, staleness budget minutes). PDP: ISR + deferred personalized rail (indexable + shareable + 60s staleness). Cart: client-rendered or per-request SSR (per-user, not indexable). Order history: per-request SSR behind auth, noindex. Admin report: client-rendered (per-user, no SEO, low traffic).

drills.prompt: You chose ISR with a 60-second revalidation for a product page. Legal now requires that the displayed price be correct at the instant of render, with zero tolerable staleness. What breaks first, and what is the cheapest fix that does not move the whole page to per-request SSR?
drills.answerSketch: The cached document breaks: any shared cache can serve a stale price. Cheapest fix is to remove the price from the cached document — stream it behind a Suspense boundary or fetch it client-side — leaving the rest of the page static. Moving the whole page to SSR pays for the 95% that did not need it.

drills.prompt: A team switches a route from client-rendered to server-rendered with identical data and identical JS bundle. Select every metric that gets worse, and say why.
drills.answerSketch: TTFB gets worse (the server now awaits data before the first byte). Server cost gets worse. LCP improves substantially; interactivity readiness barely moves because the same bundle must still download, parse and hydrate.

drills.prompt: You have a documentation site with 40,000 pages, edited by 200 authors, where an edit must be live within two minutes. Argue for static-with-on-demand-revalidation over per-request SSR in under 150 words, then name the specific number at which your answer flips.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer decomposes into: shared content so shareable cache; two-minute window > 0 so revalidation qualifies; 40k pages makes full rebuild-per-edit the failure mode, so on-demand/incremental revalidation not full rebuild; TTFB and cost both favour cached HTML; flips when per-page personalization appears or when the freshness window reaches zero.

drills.prompt: A route is statically generated at build time and reads a request cookie to decide which currency to display. Nothing errors in development. What is wrong and when does it surface?
drills.answerSketch: At build time there is no request, so the cookie read resolves to a default and is baked into HTML shared by all users. It surfaces as every user seeing the build machine's default currency — or worse, a cached response from the first user leaking to others.

failureModes: Reaches for SSR reflexively because 'SEO' without asking which crawlers matter.
Lets one personalized widget force the entire document to per-request rendering.
Cannot state the staleness budget in seconds, so cannot see that ISR/SWR is available.
Says 'SSR is faster' without separating TTFB, LCP and interactivity.
Ignores that choosing SSR means committing to operate a server.
interviewProbes: What would have to change about this product for you to pick a different rendering strategy?
How stale is the data allowed to be, in seconds, before a user is materially harmed?
Which parts of this page are the same for every user, and which are not?

arch-streaming-suspense.title: Streaming SSR, the Shell, and Suspense Boundary Placement
objectives: Place Suspense boundaries so that the fast parts of a page are not held hostage by the slow ones.
Identify what belongs in the shell and what a data dependency in the shell costs.
Decide when a static shell with resumed dynamic holes beats streaming the whole document.
claims: renderToString produces the whole document before sending a byte; renderToPipeableStream (Node streams) and renderToReadableStream (Web streams) can flush the shell before slow data resolves.
The shell is everything outside the outermost Suspense boundary, so any awaited data in the shell blocks the entire response — no bytes flush until the shell renders.
React streams boundaries out of order and repositions late content with inline script/template pairs, so a boundary's position in the DOM does not determine when it arrives.
A Suspense fallback whose geometry differs from its resolved content causes layout shift on swap, so fallbacks should reserve the final dimensions.

Selective hydration lets React hydrate a boundary as soon as its HTML has arrived and prioritises the boundary the user just interacted with, so streaming and hydration interleave rather than running in phases.
Streaming does not reduce total bytes or total work; it re-orders when the user sees them, which moves FCP and LCP but not interactivity readiness.
Once the first byte has flushed, the HTTP status and headers are fixed, so a failure inside a late boundary cannot become a 500 or a redirect — it must be recoverable in the client.

Partial pre-rendering (React 19.2's prerender producing a prelude plus postponed state, then resume / resumeToPipeableStream) lets a static shell be served from a CDN while only the postponed holes are rendered per request.

viz.title: The Stream Playhead
viz.whatIsDrawn: Top lane: the HTTP response as a byte ribbon with flush markers. Bottom: a wireframe page preview showing exactly what is painted at the playhead. Suspense boundaries are drawn as brackets over the wireframe with their resolve time labelled inside the bracket. A dashed ghost ribbon shows the same page rendered with renderToString for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Boundary A resolves at 200ms and B at 1200ms, and B appears BEFORE A in the DOM. When does the user first see A's content? Now suppose you wrap A and B in one shared boundary instead — what is the user-visible cost, and does total bytes change?
controls: move one data fetch into the shell
scrub the playhead / step flush by flush
viz.insight: Every Suspense boundary is a promise that the rest of the page will not wait for this. Boundary placement is a scheduling decision, and one boundary around everything is the same as no streaming at all.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models flushes as a sorted event list from injected latencies — no real timers, no Date.now. Unit tests assert: shell-blocking fetch delays first flush by exactly its latency; merged boundaries resolve at max(latencies); DOM order does not affect arrival order. Only the playhead and the preview fill animate. Live region narrates 'at 640ms: shell painted, boundary A resolved, boundary B still pending'.

drills.prompt: Order the bytes the client receives for a page with a 50ms shell, boundary A (in DOM position 2) resolving at 900ms, and boundary B (DOM position 1) resolving at 150ms.
drills.answerSketch: Shell HTML with both fallbacks in DOM order (B's fallback first) → B's content chunk + repositioning script at ~150ms → A's content chunk + repositioning script at ~900ms.

drills.prompt: A page streams, but TTFB is 1.4s. The code awaits getUserPreferences() in the root layout component and renders three Suspense boundaries below it. Name the defect in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: The await is in the shell — outside every boundary — so nothing can flush until it resolves; streaming below it is irrelevant. Fix: move the preference read behind a boundary or pass it as a promise consumed inside one.

drills.prompt: The route must return HTTP 404 for a product that does not exist. Currently the product fetch lives inside a Suspense boundary and the shell flushes at 40ms. What breaks, and what has to move?
drills.answerSketch: The status is already sent as 200 by the time the fetch resolves, producing a soft 404. The existence check must move into the shell (before the first flush) even though the rest of the product data can stay behind a boundary.

drills.prompt: Complete the boundary placement for a page with a nav (instant), a product summary (80ms), and a reviews list (1100ms) so that first paint is not delayed beyond ~80ms and reviews do not cause layout shift.
drills.answerSketch: Nav and summary in the shell (or summary behind a boundary if 80ms matters); reviews wrapped in Suspense with a fallback that reserves the reviews list's height; no await above the shell.

drills.prompt: Defend, in under 150 words, prerendering a static shell to the CDN and resuming only the personalized holes per request, versus streaming the whole document from a server on every request — for a homepage at 200 requests/second.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: TTFB source (CDN RTT vs server compute), cost per request, cache hit ratio, blast radius when the origin is slow, operational complexity of a two-phase render, and what happens on shell content change (needs a rebuild/invalidation).

failureModes: Wraps the whole page in one Suspense boundary and calls it streaming.
Claims streaming improves time-to-interactive; it improves paint order only.
Leaves an await above the outermost boundary and wonders why TTFB did not move.
Assumes DOM order determines arrival order.
Expects a late error to produce a 500 after bytes have been flushed.
interviewProbes: Where exactly does your first byte get sent, and what is it waiting on?
If this fetch fails at 900ms, what does the user see and what status code did they already get?
Which regions of this page are worth their own boundary, and which are not?

arch-hydration.title: Hydration: What It Costs and How It Breaks
objectives: Predict hydration cost from what was rendered rather than from what is interactive.
Diagnose a hydration mismatch from a symptom and name its true cause.
Choose the correct fix for intentionally-divergent server and client output.
claims: Hydration re-executes component render functions on the client to build the fiber tree and attach listeners; the DOM is reused but the JavaScript work is not saved.
Hydration cost scales with the number of components rendered and the JS that must be downloaded and parsed, not with the number of interactive elements on the page.

A hydration mismatch is any difference between the server HTML and the first client render; React 19 logs a diff of the offending subtree and recovers by client-rendering it, discarding the server HTML for that subtree.

The usual mismatch causes are locale- or timezone-dependent formatting, Math.random, `typeof window` branching during render, reading localStorage or matchMedia during render, and browser extensions mutating the DOM before hydration.
suppressHydrationWarning silences the warning for one element's text content; it does not reconcile the values and it does not apply to arbitrary attribute or subtree differences.

The correct fix for values that legitimately differ is to render the server value on the first client render and update in an effect, or to use useSyncExternalStore with a getServerSnapshot that matches what the server emitted.
useId generates identifiers that are stable across server and client renders; counters or random ids generated during render will mismatch.

HTML that has been streamed but not yet hydrated is visible and non-interactive; React prioritises hydrating the boundary the user interacts with, but an interaction before that boundary begins hydrating is not reliably delivered to React handlers.

viz.title: The Hydration Bill
viz.whatIsDrawn: A component tree on the left with a live count of rendered nodes. On the right, a stacked cost bar — download / parse+compile / hydrate walk — with the numbers printed inside each segment. A dashed ghost bar shows the same page as inert server HTML (zero hydration). A 'inject mismatch' control paints the discarded subtree red inside the tree itself.
viz.predictPrompt: A page renders 3,000 static list rows and exactly one interactive button, all through React on the server. You delete the button. By roughly what percentage does hydration time drop?
controls: inject mismatch at a chosen node
viz.insight: Hydration is proportional to what you rendered, not to what is interactive. That asymmetry — 3,000 rows and one button cost almost the same — is the entire motivation for islands, resumability and RSC.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts computes cost from node count, bytes and a CPU multiplier with an injected clock; unit test asserts that changing interactive count alone moves total hydration cost by <2%, which is the module's core claim. Animated channels: the tree-walk cursor and the growing cost bar. Reduced-motion shows the completed walk with per-segment numbers.

drills.prompt: `function Timestamp({iso}) { return {new Date(iso).toLocaleString()} }` renders correctly in dev and produces a mismatch warning in production for some users. Name the cause and the class of user affected.
drills.answerSketch: Locale and timezone differ between the server process and the browser, so the formatted string differs. Affects every user whose locale/timezone is not the server's. Fix: format on the server with an explicit locale+timeZone, or render the raw value and localise in an effect.

drills.prompt: React encounters a hydration mismatch inside a deeply nested component. What actually happens, and what is the user-visible consequence?
drills.answerSketch: React logs a diff and re-renders that subtree on the client, throwing away the server HTML for it — so the content flashes/reflows and the work of server-rendering that subtree is wasted. It is not a silent warning and not a whole-page crash.

drills.prompt: A header must show 'Good morning/afternoon' based on the visitor's local time. Fill in the implementation so that hydration does not mismatch and the correct greeting still appears.
drills.answerSketch: Render a deterministic server value (or nothing) on first render, then set the local-time-derived greeting in useEffect — or useSyncExternalStore with a getServerSnapshot returning the same server value. Not `typeof window !== 'undefined'` in render.

drills.prompt: Your team halves the bundle by lazy-loading half the components, and hydration time barely moves. Why, and what would actually move it?
drills.answerSketch: The lazy components are still rendered and hydrated once their chunks load — the walk still covers the whole tree, and parse cost moved rather than disappeared. What moves it: rendering fewer components on the client at all (islands / server components), not deferring them.

drills.prompt: Given 2,400 rendered components, 180KB gz of JS, and a 4x-throttled mid-tier phone, estimate hydration-blocked interactivity and state which of the two inputs dominates.
drills.answerSketch: Parse/compile of 180KB gz (~700KB parsed) plus the render walk over 2,400 components — on 4x throttle both land in the hundreds of ms, with JS parse+execute typically dominating until component counts get very large. Accept a range; grade on identifying the dominant term and the throttle multiplier.

failureModes: Silences a mismatch with suppressHydrationWarning and considers it fixed.
Branches on `typeof window` during render, which moves the mismatch rather than removing it.
Believes a mismatch is a harmless dev-only warning.
Assumes hydration cost tracks the number of buttons and inputs on the page.
Ships code-splitting as a hydration fix.
interviewProbes: This page is visible at 400ms and clickable at 2.1s — where did the 1.7s go?
What exactly does React do when the server HTML and the first client render disagree?
How would you make a 3,000-row table cheap without giving up server rendering?

arch-islands-resumability.title: Islands, Progressive Hydration, and Resumability
objectives: Compare islands, lazy hydration and resumability by what each does to the startup cost and where it moves it.
Predict the cross-cutting costs each model imposes — shared state, first-interaction latency, framework lock-in.
Match a product shape to the model whose trade-off it can absorb.
claims: Islands architecture ships zero JavaScript for non-interactive regions; each island is an independent hydration root with its own entry chunk and its own hydration trigger.

Astro's client directives choose the trigger, not the amount of code: client:load hydrates immediately, client:idle on requestIdleCallback, client:visible on IntersectionObserver, client:only skips server rendering entirely.
Lazy or progressive hydration defers hydration cost without removing it — the same JavaScript still runs, just later — and an interaction during the deferral must be queued or is lost.
Islands cannot share React context across island boundaries because each island is a separate root; cross-island state requires an external store, custom events, or URL/DOM state.

Resumability (Qwik) serialises the listener references and reactivity graph into the HTML so that no component code executes on load; the code for a handler is fetched at the moment of the first interaction.
Resumability converts a fixed startup cost into a per-interaction network cost, which is the wrong trade when the first interaction must feel instant on a slow or offline-ish network.

Islands, lazy hydration, RSC and resumability all attack the same number — component code executed on the client — but islands do it at the page-composition layer while RSC does it inside a single React tree.
client:visible on above-the-fold interactive UI is a self-inflicted delay: the element is already in the viewport, so the trigger fires immediately but only after the observer's setup work.

viz.title: Three Ways Not To Hydrate
viz.whatIsDrawn: One identical page (85% article, 15% interactive widget) rendered under four engines shown as four stacked horizontal strips. Each strip plots JS bytes executed over time, with a user-click marker the learner can drag onto the timeline. A ghost strip (full hydration) sits behind all four. The response-to-click latency is annotated inside each strip at the click marker.
viz.predictPrompt: On a page that is 85% article and 15% interactive widget, islands cut startup JS by roughly 85%. Under resumability, what is the startup JS — and what happens to the latency of the very first click on the widget on a 200ms-RTT connection?
controls: engine: full hydration / islands / lazy hydration / resumability
drag the first-click marker along the timeline
viz.insight: Every 'no hydration' technique moves cost somewhere. The only question that matters is whether you moved it off the user's critical path or merely just past it — and a first click that arrives during 'just past it' pays the whole bill at the worst moment.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is one pure function (engine, interactiveFraction, rtt, clickTime) -> event list; unit-tested against the claims (lazy hydration's total executed bytes equals full hydration's; resumability's startup bytes are ~0 but click latency includes one RTT). Animated: the playhead and one strip's fill at a time. Reduced-motion: all four strips fully drawn with click-latency labels.

drills.prompt: Four products: a documentation site, an internal analytics dashboard, a news homepage with a live-updating ticker, and a kiosk app on a slow captive-portal network. Pick islands, lazy hydration, resumability or full hydration for each and name the deciding property.
drills.answerSketch: Docs: islands (mostly static). Dashboard: full hydration/SPA (everything interactive, islands buy nothing). News homepage: islands with the ticker as an eagerly-hydrated island. Kiosk on bad network: full hydration or islands — never resumability, because first-interaction fetches are the failure mode.

drills.prompt: A marketing site uses three separate islands: a cart badge in the header, an 'add to cart' button in the hero, and a mini-cart in the footer. Product now requires all three to reflect the same cart count instantly. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: React context/state cannot cross island roots, so the three islands have three independent states. Fix: an external store (or custom DOM events / a shared signal module) imported by all three islands, at the cost of that store's JS being in every island's chunk.

drills.prompt: Which statement about client:visible is correct for a hero CTA that is above the fold? Justify in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: It is strictly worse than client:load here: the element is already visible so the IntersectionObserver fires almost immediately, but only after observer setup — you paid complexity for no deferral and risked a click landing before hydration.

drills.prompt: A team reports that switching from full hydration to lazy hydration cut Total Blocking Time in the lab but users complain that early clicks 'do nothing'. Explain both observations with one mechanism.
drills.answerSketch: The hydration work moved after the measurement window — total work is unchanged, only rescheduled. Early clicks land on non-hydrated DOM and are dropped unless events are recorded and replayed. Lab metric improved; real interaction got worse.

failureModes: Says islands 'reduce bundle size' without saying which bundle or when it executes.
Assumes React context or a provider works across island boundaries.
Treats resumability as strictly better rather than as a different cost placement.
Uses client:visible for above-the-fold interactive UI.
Presents lazy hydration as removing work rather than rescheduling it.
interviewProbes: Under this model, what runs on the client before the user touches anything?
Two widgets on this page need the same piece of state — how do they get it?
Where does the cost you removed from startup actually show up?

arch-waterfalls.title: Request Waterfalls and How to Kill Them
objectives: Identify from code or a trace the exact line that makes request N+1 wait for request N.
Distinguish client-side, server-side and code-then-data waterfalls, including the ones the browser network panel cannot show.
Choose the fix that shortens the critical path rather than the one that hides it.
claims: A waterfall exists whenever request N+1 cannot start until request N returns, so the page's latency is the sum of those requests rather than the max.
The most common client waterfall is a child component fetching in an effect after the parent's data decided whether to render it.
Nested routes fetch in parallel only if the framework knows every matched route's data requirement before rendering; render-driven fetching serialises them by construction.
A fetch inside a lazily-loaded component cannot start until that component's chunk has downloaded, so code splitting inserts a chunk download in front of a request.
Sequential awaits inside nested Server Components create a server-side waterfall that never appears in the browser network panel and shows up only as TTFB or in server traces.

Hoisting both requests to the nearest component that knows about both and issuing them with Promise.all removes a waterfall; wrapping the second one in Suspense only changes what is shown while waiting.

Preloading — starting a request before the component that needs it renders, via react-dom's preload/preinit, a Link rel=preload response header, or a route-level data declaration — converts a serial dependency into an overlap.
The two waterfalls most often left in production are a bootstrap config or feature-flag fetch that gates every other request, and a 401-then-refresh-then-retry authentication round trip.

viz.title: Waterfall Surgery
viz.whatIsDrawn: A hand-rolled SVG request waterfall where the dependency ARROWS between bars are the subject, not the bars. The critical path is stroked heavier and its total is printed inside the chart. A ghost row beneath shows the same requests fully parallelised. Applying a surgical move (hoist / preload / parallelise / Suspense-wrap) redraws the arrows in place.
viz.predictPrompt: Feature flags 90ms → auth check 120ms → user profile 150ms → recommendations 300ms, strictly chained. You wrap the recommendations component in Suspense with a nice skeleton. What is the new critical path in milliseconds?
controls: apply move: hoist fetch / preload / Promise.all / wrap in Suspense
viz.insight: Suspense changes what the user looks at while waiting. Only changing when a request starts changes how long they wait — and the fix is almost always to move a fetch upward, not to move a spinner downward.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a DAG of {id, latency, dependsOn} with a pure critical-path solver and an injected clock; unit tests assert that the Suspense-wrap move leaves critical path unchanged and that the hoist move reduces it by exactly the overlapped amount — the module's central pedagogical claim. Animated: the bar-fill playhead and the critical-path highlight. Reduced-motion: fully drawn chart with numeric annotations.

drills.prompt: Requests: config 90ms (no deps), auth 120ms (needs config), profile 150ms (needs auth), recommendations 300ms (needs profile), avatar image 60ms (needs profile). Give the current critical path in ms, then the best achievable if only config truly gates auth.
drills.answerSketch: Current: 90+120+150+300 = 660ms (avatar overlaps recommendations). Best: config 90 → auth 120 → then profile and recommendations in parallel if recommendations only needs the user id from auth = 90+120+300 = 510ms; if recommendations can be keyed off the auth token alone, closer to 90+120+max(150,300)=510ms.

drills.prompt: `const {data: user} = useUser(); if (!user) return <Spinner/>; return <Orders userId={user.id}/>` where Orders fetches in its own effect. One sentence: what is the defect and what is the cheapest fix that keeps the component structure?
drills.answerSketch: Orders' fetch cannot start until the user request resolves AND the early return stops rendering it — a render-gated waterfall. Cheapest fix: start the orders request at the same level as the user request (both depend only on the session), and pass the promise down.

drills.prompt: Put these in the order the browser actually performs them for a lazily-loaded route whose component fetches its data in an effect: route match, chunk request, chunk parse, component render, data request, data render.
drills.answerSketch: route match → chunk request → chunk parse → component render → data request → data render. The point: the data request is fifth, not first.

drills.prompt: You move all data fetching into Server Components and the browser network panel now shows a single document request. TTFB is 1.9s. Where is the waterfall and how do you see it?
drills.answerSketch: Sequential awaits in nested server components — invisible to the browser. You see it in server tracing/spans or by instrumenting each await. Fix: hoist the independent fetches to a common server ancestor and Promise.all them, or start them and pass promises down.

drills.prompt: Which of these actually shortens the critical path: (a) adding Suspense, (b) adding a loading skeleton, (c) preloading the second request when the first starts, (d) switching the fetch library? Justify.
drills.answerSketch: (c) only. (a) and (b) change perceived waiting, not duration; (d) changes nothing about ordering. This is the module's whole thesis in one item.

failureModes: Answers a waterfall question with 'add Suspense' or 'add a caching library'.
Only opens the browser network panel and therefore misses server-side await chains entirely.
Parallelises requests that genuinely depend on each other and introduces a correctness bug.
Blames the backend for latency that is actually serialisation on the client.
Leaves a feature-flag or config fetch gating every other request.
interviewProbes: Point at the exact line that makes this second request wait.
This page makes six requests totalling 900ms of server time and takes 2.4s — where is the rest?
How would you detect a waterfall that never appears in the network panel?

arch-route-loading.title: Route-Level Code Splitting with Co-located Data
objectives: Choose split points that match navigation rather than component structure.
Design a navigation so that code and data for the next route start together, not in sequence.
Handle the failure modes that route-level splitting introduces: stale chunks, shared-chunk duplication, request amplification.
claims: Route boundaries are the highest-value split points because they match what the user navigates between; splitting at arbitrary component boundaries mostly adds requests without removing bytes from the critical path.
React.lazy starts the chunk request during render, so that route's data fetch cannot begin until the chunk has downloaded unless the fetch is started outside the component.
Preloading on intent — pointerenter, touchstart or focus on the link — typically buys 100–300ms before the click and costs nothing when the user does not navigate.

The Speculation Rules API (script type=speculationrules) can prefetch or prerender whole documents in Chromium browsers; Firefox does not implement it and Safari has it disabled by default as of 26.x, so it is an enhancement layered on top of a working navigation, never the strategy itself.

A dependency imported by two lazy routes should be hoisted by the bundler into a shared chunk; the same library appearing in both route chunks is a bundler configuration failure, not an inevitability.

Dynamic imports fail permanently after a deploy removes the previously hashed chunks, so every lazy boundary needs a chunk-load error path that forces a full reload rather than showing a broken route forever.
Route-level splitting increases request count per navigation; on HTTP/2 that is usually acceptable, but each un-preloaded chunk still costs at least one round trip.
Declaring a route's data requirement alongside the route definition, rather than inside its components, is the property that makes parallel fetching across nested routes possible at all.

viz.title: The Navigation Budget
viz.whatIsDrawn: Reuses the waterfall chart, framed around one navigation: a route tree on the left, and on the right the chunk request, data request and render bars for the clicked route plus its nested children. A ghost run shows the same navigation with intent-preloading applied. Hover time before click is drawn as a shaded pre-roll region on the same timeline.
viz.predictPrompt: The user hovers a link 400ms before clicking. The route chunk is 40KB gz and its data query takes 260ms on a 100ms-RTT link. If you can only preload one thing on hover — the code or the data — which produces the shorter time-to-content, and by how much?
viz.insight: Splitting by route is free; splitting without preloading is not. The chunk is usually the shorter pole — preloading only the code leaves the data waterfall exactly where it was.
viz.buildNotes: Same sim.ts DAG solver as arch-waterfalls with a different scenario fixture — this is the archetype reuse that makes the second module cheap. Unit tests assert code-only preload leaves total unchanged when data latency exceeds chunk latency. Reduced-motion: both runs drawn with deltas labelled.

drills.prompt: Two weeks after a deploy, a subset of users see a blank panel and 'Failed to fetch dynamically imported module' in logs. They had the tab open before the deploy. Name the mechanism and the fix.
drills.answerSketch: Their loaded app references old hashed chunk filenames that the new deploy removed. Fix: an error boundary around lazy routes that catches chunk-load errors and triggers location.reload() once (guarded against reload loops), plus retaining previous chunk versions for a grace period.

drills.prompt: Fill in a Link component so that hovering (and keyboard focus) starts both the route chunk import and the route's data fetch, with the preload deduplicated so repeated hovers do not re-request.
drills.answerSketch: onPointerEnter/onFocus → a memoised preload() that calls the same import() promise (import() is cached) and the route's data loader keyed by URL, both guarded by a Set of already-preloaded routes.

drills.prompt: Your app splits at every route and averages 11 chunk requests per navigation on a 3G-like connection. Product now requires navigation under 1s at the 75th percentile. What breaks first, and what do you change?
drills.answerSketch: Request count amplification: each un-preloaded chunk costs an RTT, so 11 serial-ish requests blow the budget. Change: coarsen split points (split per route group, not per route), hoist shared deps into one common chunk, and preload on intent so the chunks overlap the hover window.

drills.prompt: Given a route tree (shell → dashboard → {overview, reports → report detail}), mark the split points and mark where each route's data requirement is declared, such that navigating shell→reports→detail issues no serial code-then-data pairs.
drills.answerSketch: Split at dashboard, reports, and report-detail; declare each route's data requirement at the route definition so a navigation to /reports/:id can start reports' and detail's data with the chunk requests. No split inside overview's components.

drills.prompt: Your analytics show 60% of Safari users get no benefit from your prefetch strategy. Which strategy did you likely ship, and what should it have been layered on?
drills.answerSketch: Speculation Rules (Chromium-only; Safari has it off by default, Firefox unimplemented). It should sit on top of intent-based preloading via pointerenter/focus with import() and a data prefetch, which works everywhere.

failureModes: Splits at component granularity and ships thirty requests per navigation.
Preloads the route chunk on hover but not the route's data, leaving the waterfall intact.
Ships no recovery path for dynamic-import failure after a deploy.
Assumes Speculation Rules prefetching works across all browsers.
Declares data requirements inside components, making parallel nested fetching structurally impossible.
interviewProbes: When the user hovers this link, what starts? What starts only on click?
What happens to a user with the tab open across a deploy?
Two of your routes both import the charting library — is it downloaded once or twice, and how do you know?

arch-rsc-model.title: React Server Components: the Boundary and the Payload
objectives: Explain what a Server Component is, where its code goes, and what crosses the boundary.
Distinguish the RSC payload from HTML, and RSC from SSR.
Explain 'use client' and 'use server' as module-graph directives rather than component labels.
claims: A Server Component executes once, on the server or at build time, and its module is never included in the client bundle; it has no state, no effects and no event handlers.
The RSC payload is not HTML: it is a streamed serialised description of the rendered UI tree that the client runtime can fetch again later and merge into a live React tree without a full page reload.
SSR and RSC are separate mechanisms that usually run together — RSC produces the tree and SSR turns it into initial HTML — and each can exist without the other.
'use client' marks a module boundary, not a component: that module and everything reachable through its import graph become client code.

Props crossing the server-to-client boundary must be serialisable, so functions, class instances and symbols cannot cross — but an already-rendered Server Component can, when it is passed as children or as a prop element.
A Client Component cannot import a Server Component; it can only render one that a server ancestor passed to it as children or as an element prop.
'use server' marks Server Functions, which the client invokes over the network; each one is a publicly reachable endpoint that must authenticate and authorise every call on its own.
Because the payload is streamed UI rather than JSON, re-rendering a server subtree after a mutation transfers new UI instead of data plus the client code to render it.

viz.title: The Boundary Paint
viz.whatIsDrawn: A module import graph of about a dozen real-looking modules (layout, nav, search-box, product-grid, price-formatter, analytics-hook, db-client). Clicking a module to add 'use client' floods its entire import-reachable subgraph with the client colour, in place. A client-bundle byte counter sits inside the graph frame, with a ghost value for the all-client baseline. A red badge appears on any module that also imports the db client.
viz.predictPrompt: To fix one hook error, a developer adds 'use client' to the root layout module. Which modules end up in the client bundle — and does the page still server-render HTML and appear to work?
controls: click any module to toggle 'use client'
apply the 'pass as children' refactor to one edge
step the flood one edge at a time
viz.insight: 'use client' is a cut in the import graph, not a label on a component — and the application still renders and still works after you cut it in the wrong place, which is exactly why the cost stays invisible until someone measures the bundle.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure graph reachability function over a fixture import graph plus a bytes-per-module map; unit-tested that marking the root floods ~all descendants and that the children-refactor removes a specific subtree from the client set. Animated: the flood front and the byte counter. Reduced-motion: the final flooded graph with a diff list.

drills.prompt: Which of these is true of the RSC payload? Justify in one sentence: (a) it is HTML, (b) it is JSON data for client components to render, (c) it is a serialised UI tree that can be re-fetched and merged, (d) it replaces the need for SSR.
drills.answerSketch: (c). It is a UI description, not HTML and not raw data; SSR is still what turns it into the first paint's HTML, so (d) is false.

drills.prompt: A Client Component file does `import { ProductTable } from './product-table.server-logic'` where that module reads from the database. It builds. What has actually happened?
drills.answerSketch: The database module has been pulled into the client graph — its code, and any secrets it reads at module scope, are now bundled and shipped. Adding the `server-only` package to that module turns this into a build error instead of a leak.

drills.prompt: A server page must render a client-side <Tabs> component whose panels are server-rendered content. Fill in the composition so the panel content stays out of the client bundle.
drills.answerSketch: The server page renders <Tabs><ServerPanel/></Tabs>, passing already-rendered server elements as children; Tabs (a client module) renders {children} without importing ServerPanel.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when a client button calls a Server Function that mutates data and the UI updates: handler fires, POST to the function endpoint, server executes and authorises, server re-renders the affected tree, RSC payload streams back, client merges the new tree.
drills.answerSketch: handler fires → POST to the endpoint → server authorises and executes → server re-renders the affected server tree → RSC payload streams back → client reconciles it into the existing tree, preserving client state outside that subtree.

drills.prompt: A Server Component passes an onSelect callback down to a Client Component. It fails. What is the rule, and what is the standard way to express the same intent?
drills.answerSketch: Functions are not serialisable across the boundary. Express it as either a Server Function ('use server') passed as an action, or by moving the interactive state into the client component and passing serialisable data down.

failureModes: Describes RSC as 'SSR but better' or as 'SSR that caches'.
Reads 'use client' as 'this one component is interactive' rather than as a graph cut.
Passes a function or class instance across the boundary and concludes RSC is broken.
Assumes a Server Function is safe because it is only invoked from an authenticated page.
Thinks importing a Server Component into a Client Component is merely discouraged rather than impossible.
interviewProbes: Where does this component's code live at runtime, and how do you prove it?
What does the client receive when this server subtree re-renders after a mutation?
This module has a database import and a 'use client' three levels up — what shipped?

arch-rsc-boundary.title: Designing the Server/Client Boundary
objectives: Place client boundaries at the leaves by rearranging composition rather than relabelling components.
Design server data access that avoids server-side waterfalls and duplicate fetches.
Decide which state must live on the client and which can be server-owned and refreshed.
claims: Push client boundaries downward: the leaf that owns state carries 'use client', and its server-rendered siblings are handed to it as children.
A provider that must wrap the whole application is itself a client module, but rendering {children} inside it does not make those children client modules.
Server Components can await data directly, removing the client-server-client round trip, but sequential awaits down a nested server tree create a server-side waterfall that shows up only as TTFB.
Data needed by two sibling server components should be fetched once through a request-scoped memo (React's cache) rather than threaded through props or fetched twice.
Anything read inside a Server Component is a value the client cannot re-read; if the UI must change without a navigation or a server round trip, that state belongs on the client.

After a mutation, revalidating a server subtree re-streams UI, so client state living outside that subtree survives while state inside a re-rendered client component may be reset — that boundary has to be chosen deliberately.
Secrets stay safe only because the module never ships; importing that module from a client module is what leaks it, and the server-only package makes that a build-time error.
A third-party library that uses hooks or browser APIs should be wrapped in a thin 'use client' adapter module, so the boundary sits at the adapter instead of spreading to every consumer.

viz.title: Pushing the Boundary Down
viz.whatIsDrawn: The same flood graph, now in edit mode over a realistic page: layout, theme provider, nav with a search box, product grid, add-to-cart button, reviews. Two meters live inside the frame: client bytes and server round trips per interaction. Two named refactor moves (hoist-to-children, extract-client-leaf) can be applied and their effect on both meters is annotated in place. A ghost outline shows the pre-refactor client set.
viz.predictPrompt: A root layout imports a client-only theme provider and renders {children}. Are those children in the client bundle? Now the nav module imports an analytics hook that requires 'use client' — what changes, and by how much?
controls: toggle server-only guard on the data module
viz.insight: The boundary is designed by rearranging composition, not by relabelling components — {children} is the primitive that lets a client shell wrap server content without swallowing it.
viz.buildNotes: Reuses arch-rsc-model's graph engine and renderer with a new fixture plus two scripted refactor transforms — the reason this expert module costs 16h rather than 24h. Unit tests assert the children-refactor strictly reduces the client-reachable set and that a server-only import from a client module is flagged.

drills.prompt: Given a page tree (RootLayout → ThemeProvider → Nav[SearchBox] → ProductGrid[ProductCard[AddToCartButton]] → Reviews), select exactly the modules that should carry 'use client' for a minimal client bundle, and mark any composition change required.
drills.answerSketch: 'use client' on: ThemeProvider, SearchBox, AddToCartButton. Required change: ThemeProvider must render {children} passed from the server layout; AddToCartButton must be a leaf extracted out of ProductCard so ProductCard stays a Server Component.

drills.prompt: Two sibling Server Components each call getCurrentUser(), which hits the database. Server traces show two identical queries per request and TTFB is 340ms. Name the fix and why prop-drilling is not the best one.
drills.answerSketch: Wrap the accessor in a request-scoped memo (React cache) so both calls dedupe within the request. Prop-drilling works but couples the components to a common ancestor and breaks the moment a third consumer appears deeper in the tree.

drills.prompt: The reviews section is a Server Component reading from the database. Product now requires a client-side sort control that reorders reviews instantly with no network round trip. What has to move, and what is the cost of the alternative?
drills.answerSketch: Either the review list becomes a client component receiving the data as serialisable props (client bundle grows by the list renderer), or the sort becomes a server round trip via search params (bundle stays small, but each sort costs a network trip and cannot be instant). Choose on interaction frequency.

drills.prompt: A charting library uses useLayoutEffect and window. Write the adapter module so that the boundary stops at the adapter and the page that uses the chart remains a Server Component.
drills.answerSketch: A separate module with 'use client' at the top that imports the library and re-exports a thin wrapper component taking serialisable props; the server page imports only the wrapper.

drills.prompt: In under 180 words, defend keeping a product filter's state in URL search params handled by the server, versus in client state — for a catalogue where users change filters roughly six times per session.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: shareability/back-button correctness, client bundle size, per-interaction latency (a round trip per filter change), server load at six changes/session, whether the filtered result set is cacheable per URL, and the perceived-latency mitigation available (optimistic UI / transitions).

failureModes: Adds 'use client' to a layout or page to fix one hook error and ships the whole tree to the client.
Believes wrapping {children} in a client provider makes those children client components.
Threads shared data through props instead of deduping the fetch, or fetches it twice.
Awaits sequentially down a nested server tree and blames the database for TTFB.
Adds 'use client' to every consumer of a browser-only library instead of writing one adapter.
interviewProbes: Show me the smallest set of modules that must be client modules for this page.
This mutation refreshes the server tree — what happens to the text the user had typed in the unrelated search box?
How would you keep this page's TTFB flat as the number of server data reads grows?

arch-resilience.title: Partial Failure: Error Boundaries, Degradation and Progressive Enhancement
objectives: Place error boundaries so that a failure costs the user one region rather than the page.
Distinguish what an error boundary can and cannot catch, and wire the errors it cannot.
Design a realistic degradation ladder for an authenticated application rather than an all-or-nothing no-JS argument.
claims: An error boundary catches errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods and in constructors of its subtree; it does not catch errors thrown in event handlers, in async callbacks, or after the response has begun streaming on the server.
Boundary granularity is a product decision: one boundary per page yields an all-or-nothing page, one boundary per independently valuable region yields a page that loses only the failed region.
React 19 surfaces render errors through the root options onUncaughtError, onCaughtError and onRecoverableError, which is where error reporting belongs rather than relying on window.onerror alone.
Every lazy boundary needs both a Suspense fallback and an error fallback, because a chunk that fails to download throws rather than suspending forever.
A retry affordance must reset the boundary's state — a key change or an explicit reset — since re-rendering the same failed tree reproduces the error immediately.

Progressive enhancement means the core task completes through a plain HTML form submission that the server accepts; it is a claim about the server's endpoints, not about how the page looks without CSS.

The realistic degradation ladder for an authenticated app is: HTML streamed but not yet hydrated (content readable), one region's JS failed (that region shows a fallback, the rest works), a third-party script failed (the feature is absent, the page is intact) — full no-JS support is worth building only where the audience or a crawler path demands it.

A failure inside a Suspense boundary after the HTTP status has been sent cannot become a 5xx or a redirect, so the fallback must be renderable on the client or the user gets a broken region with a 200.

viz.title: Blast Radius
viz.whatIsDrawn: A page component tree where the learner can drop error boundaries onto nodes. Injecting a failure at any node shades everything the user loses, with the lost regions labelled by what they meant to the user ('cannot check out', 'cannot read the article'). A ghost overlay shows the same failure under a single root boundary. A toggle marks whether the failure occurs before or after the first byte flushed, which changes whether a 500 was possible.
viz.predictPrompt: The recommendations widget throws during render on a product page whose only error boundary is at the root. What does the user lose? Now the same error happens 900ms into a streamed response — what status code did the user already receive, and does the answer change?
controls: toggle error type: render / event handler / chunk load
viz.insight: Resilience is a placement decision measured in what the user loses, not in how many try/catches exist — and after the first byte flushes, your only remaining recovery is client-side.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models the tree, boundary set, error type and flush state as a pure function returning the lost-node set; unit tests encode the catchability matrix (event-handler errors are never caught; chunk-load errors are catchable at the lazy boundary). Animated: the shading spread and the ghost comparison. Reduced-motion: static shaded tree plus a lost-regions list.

drills.prompt: `<ErrorBoundary><button onClick={async () => { await save(); }}>Save</button></ErrorBoundary>` — save() rejects and the UI shows nothing. Explain in one sentence why the boundary did not catch it and give the fix.
drills.answerSketch: Error boundaries do not catch errors in event handlers or async callbacks. Fix: handle the rejection in the handler and render an error state, or set it into state (or use a transition/action) so a subsequent render can surface it.

drills.prompt: Given a checkout page (header, cart summary, address form, payment widget from a third party, order total, promotional banner), place the minimum set of error boundaries so that no single failure prevents the user from paying.
drills.answerSketch: Boundaries around the third-party payment widget (must degrade to a fallback method or a retry), the promotional banner, and the recommendations/upsell region. No boundary should be able to hide the cart summary and total together with the address form; the payment path needs its own explicit fallback rather than a generic 'something went wrong'.

drills.prompt: Your app is fully streamed with a 40ms shell. Compliance now requires that a user without permission to view an order never receives any part of that order's page, and gets a 403. What breaks, and where does the check have to move?
drills.answerSketch: The status is already committed at 40ms, so a permission failure inside a boundary cannot produce a 403. The authorisation check must run in the shell before the first flush, even though the order's data can still stream.

drills.prompt: Complete a lazy route boundary that shows a skeleton while loading, an error fallback with a Retry button on failure, and forces one full reload when the error is a chunk-load failure after a deploy.
drills.answerSketch: Suspense fallback = skeleton; error boundary with a reset via key or resetErrorBoundary for retry; inside the error handler, detect the dynamic-import failure message/type and call location.reload() once, guarded by a sessionStorage flag to avoid a reload loop.

drills.prompt: In under 150 words, argue for or against making an authenticated internal admin dashboard work with JavaScript disabled. Name the specific audience or requirement that would change your answer.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: who the users are and whether any of them disable JS, whether crawlers or link unfurlers need the content (they do not, it is authenticated), the cost of maintaining two submission paths, what the realistic failure is (JS fails to load, not JS disabled), and the requirement that would flip it — a regulated accessibility mandate, a government/kiosk audience, or a public unauthenticated surface.

failureModes: Puts a single error boundary at the root and calls it resilience.
Expects an error boundary to catch a rejected promise in a click handler.
Confuses a Suspense fallback with an error fallback and leaves lazy routes with no error path.
Renders a retry button that re-renders the same failed tree without resetting the boundary.
Argues for full no-JS support in an authenticated dashboard while having no story for a failed chunk.
interviewProbes: This third-party widget is down. Draw me exactly what the user still sees and can still do.
Your response already sent a 200 and then the data layer failed — what now?
Which failures in this page should page someone, and which should degrade silently?

arch-seo.title: Crawlability, Indexing and Metadata Architecture
objectives: Decide how much server-rendered HTML a route actually needs by identifying which consumers must see it.
Diagnose indexing failures that rendering strategy alone does not explain.
Place metadata, status codes and canonical signals where the consumers that matter can act on them.
claims: Googlebot executes JavaScript with an evergreen Chromium, but rendering happens in a deferred queue, so client-rendered content is indexed later and less reliably than server-rendered content.

Social and chat link unfurlers (Slack, X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Discord) and most AI crawlers do not execute JavaScript, so Open Graph and title tags injected by client-side JavaScript never appear in shared previews.
A single-page app that returns HTTP 200 with 'not found' UI creates a soft 404; removal from an index requires a real 404 or 410 status from the server.

rel=canonical deduplicates near-identical URLs such as tracking parameters and sort orders; it is a hint, and conflicting canonical, sitemap, redirect and internal-link signals let the search engine choose for you.
Content that only enters the DOM after a user interaction is generally not indexed, whereas content present in the DOM but hidden with CSS generally is.
Every indexable view needs a real URL that the server answers directly; a view reachable only through client-side state change cannot be indexed, linked or shared.
The X-Robots-Tag response header controls indexing before any rendering happens and works for non-HTML resources, unlike a robots meta tag injected by JavaScript.
Core Web Vitals are a real but small ranking input, and no amount of LCP improvement makes an unindexable page rank.

viz.title: What the Crawler Sees
viz.whatIsDrawn: One HTTP response feeding three lanes: Googlebot (fetch → render queue → rendered DOM), a link unfurler (fetch → raw HTML only), and an AI crawler (fetch → raw HTML only). Each lane shows the exact <head> and body snippet that consumer acts on, with missing tags struck through inside the lane. The render-queue delay is drawn as a labelled gap in the Googlebot lane.
viz.predictPrompt: A product page sets its title and Open Graph tags in a useEffect. It ranks fine on Google and the team concludes the setup is correct. What is broken, and why did Google not reveal it?
controls: metadata source: server head / injected in effect
status code for a missing entity (200 / 404)
viz.insight: 'Google can render JavaScript' is true and mostly irrelevant. The consumers that break your metadata are the ones that never run your JavaScript at all — and they are the ones your growth team actually notices.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts maps (strategy, metadataSource, status) to what each consumer lane observes — a pure lookup with unit tests per claim (unfurler never sees effect-injected OG tags; a 200 with not-found UI is a soft 404 in all lanes). Animated: the lane playhead and the strike-through reveal. Reduced-motion: all three lanes rendered complete.

drills.prompt: Marketing reports that pasting product links into Slack shows the site name and no image, even though the page's title and og:image are correct in the browser. Name the mechanism in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: The tags are being set by client JavaScript after load; Slack's unfurler reads the raw HTML response and never executes JS, so it sees only the static shell's head.

drills.prompt: For each route decide indexable or not, and what status/metadata it needs: public product page, faceted search results with 40,000 parameter combinations, user profile set to private, an /account/orders page, and a paginated blog archive.
drills.answerSketch: Product: indexable, server HTML, canonical to the clean URL. Faceted search: index a curated subset, canonical the rest to the base facet, or noindex-follow — avoid 40k crawlable combinations. Private profile: X-Robots-Tag noindex plus real authorisation. /account/orders: noindex, authenticated, never in the sitemap. Blog archive: indexable with self-referencing canonicals per page.

drills.prompt: A discontinued product's URL returns 200 with a 'This product is no longer available' component. Six months later it is still in the index and ranking for the brand. Which single change fixes it, and why do the others not?
drills.answerSketch: Return a real 404/410 (or 301 to the replacement) from the server. A JS-injected noindex is applied only after rendering and may never be processed; removing internal links does not deindex; robots.txt disallow actually prevents the crawler from seeing the noindex.

drills.prompt: The site is client-rendered and ranks acceptably. The company now depends on links being shared into Slack and LinkedIn, and on being cited by AI answer engines. What is the minimum change — and is full SSR required?
drills.answerSketch: Minimum: server-render the head (title, description, OG/Twitter tags, canonical) and enough body content to be summarisable, for the shareable routes only. Full SSR of the app is not required; per-route static or streamed HTML for the public surface is enough.

drills.prompt: Indexing signals that must exist in the initial HTTP response rather than being applied by client JavaScript include the ____ status code, the ____ header for non-HTML resources, and ____ tags consumed by link unfurlers.
drills.answerSketch: 404/410 (real status code); X-Robots-Tag; Open Graph / meta description / title.

failureModes: 'Google runs JavaScript now, so client rendering is fine for SEO' — with no thought for unfurlers or AI crawlers.
Sets Open Graph tags in an effect and verifies them in DevTools rather than in curl.
Returns 200 for missing entities and then tries to deindex with a meta tag.
