Blocks the JS bundle in robots.txt and wonders why rendered content is missing.
Treats Core Web Vitals as the SEO lever on a page that is not reliably indexed.
interviewProbes: What does `curl` on this URL return, and is that enough for every consumer you care about?
This product was deleted — what does the URL return, and for how long?
Which of your routes should be indexable, and how does a crawler discover them?

arch-edge.title: Edge vs Origin Rendering
objectives: Decide whether moving compute to the edge helps a given route by counting the round trips it removes.
Recognise the runtime constraints an isolate-based edge imposes on application code.
Identify the request-shaped work that belongs at the edge and the rendering work that does not.
claims: Edge rendering shortens the network portion of TTFB by putting compute near the user; it does nothing for the data portion when the database is still one region away.

Moving compute to the edge while the data stays at the origin can make total latency worse, because every data round trip is now made across the long link instead of from a server sitting next to the database.

Edge runtimes are V8 isolates rather than Node processes: no filesystem, no native modules, a restricted Node API surface, and a hard CPU-time budget per request, so a large fraction of npm dependencies simply cannot run there.
Isolate-based functions have effectively no cold start, compared with roughly 100–500ms for container or Lambda cold starts, which matters most on low-traffic routes.

The highest-value edge work is cheap and request-shaped: geo and locale routing, A/B bucket assignment, auth-cookie checks, header and path rewriting, and patching cached HTML — not full application rendering.
A CDN cache hit beats any edge computation, so edge rendering is only interesting for responses that genuinely cannot be shared between users.
Edge personalisation is usually done by caching one shared document and rewriting it per request rather than by rendering a whole page per user.
Deploying application logic to many regions fragments logs, traces and incident response, so edge is an operational commitment rather than a configuration flag.

viz.title: Where the Milliseconds Live
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single request drawn as labelled distance segments: user → PoP → origin → database, each segment carrying its own RTT number inside the bar. A round-trip counter multiplies the data segment. A ghost bar shows the origin-rendered version of the same request. Moving the database marker redraws both bars.
viz.predictPrompt: A user in Sydney hits a route rendered at a Sydney PoP that makes three sequential queries to a database in Virginia. The origin-rendered alternative runs in Virginia, next to that database. Which is faster, and by roughly how much?
controls: number of sequential data round trips
viz.insight: Latency is round trips multiplied by distance. The edge only removes the trips it can actually terminate — and if your data did not move, you multiplied the long ones.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts computes total = clientToRender + roundTrips * renderToData, using a small fixed inter-region RTT table (documented as approximate, cited); unit test encodes the Sydney/Virginia case so the module's headline claim cannot silently break. Animated: the request marker traversing segments and the total counter. Reduced-motion: both bars drawn with numeric totals.

drills.prompt: Client→PoP 15ms RTT, PoP→origin region 200ms RTT, origin→DB 2ms RTT. The route needs three sequential data reads. Compute TTFB for edge rendering and for origin rendering, ignoring compute time.
drills.answerSketch: Edge: 15 + 3*200 = ~615ms. Origin: 200 + 3*2 = ~206ms. Origin wins by roughly 400ms; edge only wins here if the data is replicated to the edge or the response is cacheable.

drills.prompt: Assign each to edge or origin and say why: geo-based currency redirect, A/B bucket assignment cookie, rendering a personalised dashboard with five queries, serving a cached marketing page, and an image-resizing endpoint using a native binary.
drills.answerSketch: Edge: geo redirect (no data), A/B bucket (cheap, cookie only), cached marketing page (CDN, not compute). Origin: personalised dashboard (five data round trips), image resizing with a native binary (no native modules in an isolate).

drills.prompt: You moved SSR to the edge and p75 TTFB improved 30% in Europe but regressed 60% in Asia. What is the most likely cause and what is the cheapest fix?
drills.answerSketch: Data lives in one region: European PoPs are close to it, Asian PoPs are not, so Asian requests pay long data round trips. Cheapest fixes: pin rendering for Asian traffic to the origin region, replicate/read-replica the data, or make the response cacheable so PoPs serve it without compute.

drills.prompt: A team ports their SSR handler to an edge runtime. It builds locally and fails at deploy or at runtime with module resolution errors mentioning fs and a native dependency. Explain in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: Edge isolates have no filesystem and no native module support, so any dependency reaching for fs or a compiled binary cannot run there — the runtime is not a smaller Node, it is a different one.

drills.prompt: In under 150 words, defend serving a personalised homepage as one cached shared document patched at the edge, versus rendering it per user at the origin. State the traffic level at which your answer flips.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: cache hit ratio and origin load, how much of the document is actually personal, TTFB for the shared part, complexity/observability of the rewriting layer, correctness risk of patching HTML, and the flip point — low traffic or heavily personal documents make per-user origin rendering simpler and cheap enough.

failureModes: Offers 'deploy it to the edge' as a generic latency answer.
Forgets that the database did not move with the compute.
Assumes Node APIs and native modules are available in an edge runtime.
Uses edge rendering for a response that could simply have been CDN-cached.
Ignores the operational cost of debugging a failure that only occurs in one region.
interviewProbes: How many round trips does this request make after it reaches your rendering code, and where do they go?
What in this response actually varies per user?
How would you debug a 3x latency regression that only affects users in one region?

arch-monorepo.title: Monorepo and Package-Boundary Architecture
objectives: Design package boundaries and layering rules that a tool can enforce, not merely a convention document.
Predict what rebuilds and re-tests from the shape of the dependency graph.
Identify the graph shapes that destroy incremental builds and caching.
claims: A monorepo provides atomic cross-package changes and a single dependency version; it does not by itself provide module boundaries, which come from package boundaries plus an enforced dependency graph.
The exports field in package.json is a package's enforceable public API: paths not listed cannot be imported, which is what stops deep-import coupling from spreading.
The package dependency graph must be acyclic; cycles break topological build ordering and incremental caching even when the bundler tolerates them at runtime.
Task caching in Turborepo or Nx is only correct if each task declares its inputs completely — an undeclared input produces a stale cache hit, which is more damaging than having no cache.
TypeScript project references give per-package incremental type checking and enforce that a package can only see what it declares as a reference.

Layering rules — features may depend on shared packages but never the reverse, and features may not import each other — must be enforced by lint (eslint-plugin-boundaries, Nx tags) rather than by convention.
A catch-all shared package that most packages import becomes a rebuild-everything bottleneck and a de facto cycle in change-propagation terms; splitting it by purpose is the fix.
Monorepo versus polyrepo is a build-and-ownership trade-off rather than an architecture: both layouts can have good or terrible boundaries, and the boundaries are defined by the dependency rules.

viz.title: What Rebuilds When
viz.whatIsDrawn: Packages arranged in layer bands (apps, features, shared, infra) with dependency edges drawn between them. Selecting a package to 'edit' floods the affected set upward and prints the rebuild and test cost inside the flooded region. A ghost total shows the no-boundaries baseline where everything rebuilds. Illegal edges (a shared package importing a feature) are drawn in the violation colour with the rule named on the edge.
viz.predictPrompt: A 40-package monorepo has one @app/utils imported by 32 packages. You change one line in a date helper inside it. How many packages must rebuild and re-test — and does remote task caching save you?
controls: add or remove one dependency edge
viz.insight: Your CI time is a function of your dependency graph's shape, not of your repo layout — and one catch-all shared package converts every change into a full rebuild.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure reverse-reachability computation over a fixture graph with per-package build/test costs; unit tests assert that splitting the catch-all package reduces the affected set for a targeted change and that a rule violation is detected on the exact edge. Animated: the upward flood and the cost counter. Reduced-motion: final flooded graph plus an affected-package list.

drills.prompt: `packages/shared/ui` imports a type from `packages/features/checkout` 'just for the OrderSummary props'. Builds are green. Name the two things this breaks.
drills.answerSketch: It inverts the layering (shared now depends on a feature) and creates a change-propagation cycle: any checkout change rebuilds shared, which rebuilds every feature. Fix: move the type into a shared contracts package or invert with a generic prop.

drills.prompt: Given nine packages (web app, admin app, checkout feature, catalogue feature, design system, api client, analytics, date utils, eslint config), assign layer tags and list the allowed dependency directions.
drills.answerSketch: Layers: apps (web, admin) → features (checkout, catalogue) → shared (design system, api client, analytics, date utils) → tooling (eslint config, referenced by all but importing none). Rules: apps may import features and shared; features may import shared only, never each other; shared may import shared but never features or apps.

drills.prompt: CI is 26 minutes and remote caching is enabled, but hit rates are near zero on main. What are the two most likely causes, given the caching claim in this module?
drills.answerSketch: Either task inputs are over-declared (every task depends on the repo root or on a lockfile/env that changes each run, so hashes never repeat), or a catch-all shared package is edited constantly so the affected set is everything. Both are graph/input-declaration problems, not caching-tool problems.

drills.prompt: A package's public API is enforced by the ____ field in package.json; per-package incremental type checking is enabled by TypeScript ____; and cross-layer import rules are enforced at ____ time by lint rather than at review time.
drills.answerSketch: exports; project references; lint/CI (build) time.

drills.prompt: In under 150 words, argue whether a 6-person team building one product should adopt a monorepo with four packages or keep a single application package. Name the signal that would make you split.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: cost of the boundary tooling versus the coupling it prevents, whether any code is genuinely reused, CI time today, ownership overlap at 6 people (essentially none), and the split signal — a second deployable artefact, a second consumer of the same code, or a build time dominated by unrelated work.

failureModes: Equates 'monorepo' with 'shared code' and ships no boundaries at all.
Creates a `common` or `utils` package that everything imports and then blames CI.
Assumes task caching is free of complete input declaration.
Enforces layering in a README instead of in lint.
Argues for polyrepo isolation while publishing untyped, deep-importable shared packages.
interviewProbes: Draw the dependency direction between your feature packages — what stops one importing another?
One line changes in your shared package. What rebuilds, and what does that cost?
How is a package's public surface defined, and what happens if someone deep-imports past it?

arch-microfrontends.title: Micro-Frontends: the Org-Topology Test
objectives: Judge whether a stated problem is actually deployment coupling, and therefore whether micro-frontends can address it at all.
Compare the four integration points by isolation, cost and the failure they permit.
Identify the cheaper organisational fix that solves most cases presented as micro-frontend problems.
claims: Micro-frontends buy independent deployment; when teams can already ship independently, they buy nothing and cost a shared runtime.
The decisive question is deployment coupling — can team A ship without waiting on team B's release — not repository count, framework diversity, or bundle size.

Integration happens at one of four points: build time via versioned packages, server or edge composition of fragments, runtime module loading via module federation or import maps, or in the browser via iframes and web components.

Route-level ownership behind a reverse proxy, with separately deployed apps and a full page load between them, is the cheapest micro-frontend that works, because navigation resets shared state and isolates failure.
Running multiple frameworks — or multiple copies of one framework — on a single page multiplies runtime cost and is the most common way micro-frontends make performance worse.
Shared concerns such as the design system, authentication, analytics and routing become versioned distributed contracts requiring deprecation policies, and that ongoing tax is the real cost.
Micro-frontends do not decompose a coupled domain: if two teams edit the same screen, splitting the deployment converts a code dependency into a runtime contract rather than removing the coupling.

Iframes still provide the strongest isolation of CSS, JavaScript and crashes, which makes them correct for third-party or untrusted embedded UI despite duplicated runtime and awkward sizing and navigation.

viz.title: The Release Train
viz.whatIsDrawn: Teams as rows against a two-week deploy timeline. Blocked deploys are drawn as stalled blocks with the blocking reason named inside them (failing shared test, waiting on a design-system version, shared release train). A ghost timeline shows the same fortnight after splitting deployment, including the new blocks that appear — contract version negotiations and a duplicated runtime cost banner.
viz.predictPrompt: Four teams, one repo, one pipeline, 25-minute CI. Team D's flaky tests block everyone about once a week. Do micro-frontends remove those blocks — and what new blocks appear on the split timeline?
controls: integration point: build / server / runtime / iframe
viz.insight: Micro-frontends solve a deployment-coupling problem. Most teams reaching for them have a CI, test-ownership or code-ownership problem — which is an order of magnitude cheaper to fix.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models deploys as a queue with blocking rules derived from contract edges and flake probability using a SEEDED RNG and injected clock, so the two timelines are reproducible and unit-testable; the test asserts that splitting removes CI-flake blocks but introduces contract-version blocks. Animated: the timeline playhead and one row's block shading. Reduced-motion: both fortnights rendered statically with block counts.

drills.prompt: For each, decide whether micro-frontends are justified: (a) 8 engineers, one product, one deploy; (b) 60 engineers across 6 domains, one 45-minute pipeline, weekly release train; (c) a platform embedding third-party vendor widgets; (d) a team that wants to try Svelte.
drills.answerSketch: (a) No — no deployment coupling to break. (b) Plausibly yes, but fix CI and code ownership first; if the release train is the constraint, route-level split by domain. (c) Yes, and iframes specifically, for isolation and untrusted code. (d) No — framework curiosity is never the justification.

drills.prompt: You split a product into four runtime-composed micro-frontends on one page. The design system then ships a breaking token change. What happens, and what would have happened under build-time integration?
drills.answerSketch: At runtime, whichever version loads first may win the singleton and the other three render with mismatched tokens, or two copies load and styles conflict — a live visual break with no build signal. Under build-time integration each app pins its version and upgrades on its own schedule; the mismatch is visible but contained per deployable and caught at build.

drills.prompt: Which single fact would most change your recommendation against micro-frontends for a 60-engineer org? Justify.
drills.answerSketch: That teams currently cannot deploy without a shared release train and that CI/ownership fixes have been attempted and failed — i.e. the coupling is organisational and durable. Bundle size, framework diversity and repo count would not change it.

drills.prompt: In under 180 words, defend route-level ownership behind a reverse proxy over runtime module federation for a 6-team product, and name the requirement that would force you to federation.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: isolation (full page load resets state and contains crashes), no shared-singleton class of bugs, independent tech choices per route, simple rollback per app, versus the cost of losing client-side navigation between routes and duplicating shell chrome. Forced to federation when two teams' UI must appear on the SAME screen simultaneously with shared client state.

drills.prompt: A micro-frontend migration is justified in a design doc with: 'each team picks its own framework, teams stop stepping on each other's code, and bundles get smaller'. Name what is wrong with each of the three claims.
drills.answerSketch: Framework diversity multiplies runtime bytes and hiring/maintenance cost, it is a cost not a benefit. 'Stepping on code' is a code-ownership problem solvable with CODEOWNERS and package boundaries. Bundles get larger, not smaller, because shared runtime and duplicated dependencies are now per-remote.

failureModes: Proposes micro-frontends for a small single-product team.
Justifies the split with framework diversity or repository hygiene rather than deployment coupling.
Ignores the shared design-system and auth contract versioning tax.
Never mentions independent deployment at all — the only thing the pattern actually buys.
Assumes the split makes bundles smaller.
interviewProbes: What specifically can a team not do today that this would let them do?
Two of these teams need to change the same screen next quarter — what happens?
What is the cheapest change that removes the blocking you just described?

arch-module-federation.title: Module Federation: Runtime Composition and Its Failure Modes
objectives: Diagnose runtime failures that depend on load order rather than on any single build.
Explain what shared, singleton and strictVersion actually do at resolution time.
Design the containment a runtime remote requires: pinning, rollback, error isolation and style scoping.
claims: Module Federation loads a remote's manifest or remoteEntry at runtime and resolves the remote's modules in the host process, so a remote's new deploy changes the host's behaviour without the host deploying — that is simultaneously the feature and the risk.

Declaring a dependency as shared with singleton true forces a single instance across host and remotes; without it React can be instantiated twice, producing invalid-hook-call errors that appear only when two particular remotes are on the page together.
strictVersion turns an incompatible shared version into a load-time failure instead of a warning plus a silently loaded second copy.

Version skew is the dominant failure class because the singleton instance is chosen at runtime by whichever consumer loads first, so the failure depends on navigation order and cannot be reproduced from any single build.

Every remote is a runtime dependency with no build-time type checking unless types are published; Module Federation 2.0 adds cross-bundler type sharing and a manifest protocol shared by webpack, Rspack and Vite implementations.

A remote that fails to load must be caught by an error boundary around the dynamic import and degrade to an absent feature, because nothing at the bundler level guarantees the remote will be reachable.
Remotes must be pinnable and rollback-able by the host; consuming 'whatever is at latest' makes a remote team's bad deploy an outage the host cannot roll back itself.

Global CSS, font loading and design tokens leak across federated boundaries because every remote shares one document, so isolation requires scoped styles or a single versioned design-system singleton.

viz.title: Who Wins the Singleton
viz.whatIsDrawn: Host and two remotes as columns with their declared shared ranges printed under each. A step-by-step resolution trace runs down the middle showing which version was registered first, what each subsequent consumer received, and where the incompatibility surfaces — with the resulting error message rendered inline at the step that causes it. A ghost trace shows the alternate navigation order.
viz.predictPrompt: Host declares react ^18.2 shared singleton, remote A ^18.2 singleton, remote B ^19.0 singleton, and strictVersion is off. A user lands on a page using A and then navigates to a page using B. What happens? Now what if they land on B first?
viz.insight: Federation moves dependency resolution from build time to runtime, where it becomes order-dependent. 'Works on my machine' becomes 'works in that navigation order', and the bug report will not contain the order.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts implements a small semver-range resolver over the declared shared config with a deterministic step log — no RNG, no clock. Unit tests pin each documented outcome (singleton off ⇒ two instances; strictVersion on ⇒ load error at the incompatible consumer; order swap ⇒ different winner). This is the module whose sim MUST be tested, because the claim is subtle enough to teach wrong. Animated: the trace cursor and the winner highlight.

drills.prompt: 'Invalid hook call' appears only for users who visit the reports page and then the billing page, never in isolation, and never in either remote's own test app. Name the mechanism in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: React is not configured as a shared singleton (or the ranges are incompatible), so the second remote loads its own copy; two React instances on one page break hooks. It only reproduces in that navigation order because that is when both copies coexist.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when a host renders a federated remote component for the first time: manifest/remoteEntry fetched, shared scope negotiated, remote chunk fetched, module factory executed, component rendered, error boundary catches on failure.
drills.answerSketch: manifest/remoteEntry fetched → shared scope negotiated (versions registered/resolved) → remote chunk fetched → module factory executed → component rendered; a failure at any of the first four surfaces at the error boundary wrapping the dynamic import.

drills.prompt: Complete the shared configuration for react and react-dom so that a version incompatibility fails loudly at load time rather than silently loading a second copy, and so that only one instance can ever exist.
drills.answerSketch: shared: { react: { singleton: true, strictVersion: true, requiredVersion: '^18.2.0' }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true, strictVersion: true, requiredVersion: '^18.2.0' } } — plus eager loading only where the host must render before any remote.

drills.prompt: Compliance now requires that any production defect be rollback-able by the owning host team within 10 minutes. Your hosts consume remotes at 'latest'. What breaks, and what is the minimum change?
drills.answerSketch: A remote's bad deploy instantly affects every host with no host-side rollback path. Minimum change: hosts consume pinned, immutable versioned remote entries (versioned URLs or a manifest with a pinned version), with promotion as an explicit host-side change that can be reverted.

drills.prompt: A remote's CDN returns 503 for two minutes. With no error boundary around the dynamic import, what does the user experience, and what should it have been?
drills.answerSketch: The import rejects during render and, uncaught, takes down the nearest ancestor that has a boundary — often the whole page. It should have been a caught failure degrading to the feature being absent or a retry affordance, with the rest of the host intact.

failureModes: Forgets singleton for React and attributes the hook error to a React bug.
Assumes remote module types are checked at build time.
Wraps no error boundary around the dynamic import of a remote.
Consumes remotes at 'latest' with no pinning or rollback path.
Debugs an order-dependent failure by rebuilding one remote in isolation, where it cannot reproduce.
interviewProbes: Remote B ships a breaking change at 2pm. Who finds out, how, and who can roll it back?
Two remotes declare different React ranges — what determines which one runs?
What does the user see when a remote's CDN is down?

state-taxonomy.title: The Five States: Server Cache, Client UI, URL, Form, Ephemeral
objectives: Classify any piece of application state into one of five ownership buckets by asking who owns the truth and which lifecycle events it must survive.
Predict the specific class of bug that appears when a piece of state is placed in the wrong bucket.
Defend a placement decision when a requirement changes (shareability, multi-tab, offline, reload).
claims: Server-cache state has an authoritative copy elsewhere, so it can always be discarded and refetched; client-UI state has no other copy, so discarding it destroys information.
Copying a fetched response into a Zustand or Redux store converts a cache into a fork, and a fork has no invalidation policy attached to it.
State that must survive a reload and be reproducible from a pasted link belongs in the URL, not in a store.
Form state is client-owned but seeded from server state at mount, which is why 'stale defaults' bugs appear when the underlying record changes mid-edit.
Ephemeral state (hover, focus, in-flight drag, transient toast) must never be persisted, because rehydrating it renders UI describing an interaction that is not happening.
The number of copies of a fact in an app is the number of places that fact can be wrong, so deduplicating to a single owner is the primary fix for 'the sidebar count disagrees with the table'.
'Global vs local' is the wrong first question; 'who owns the truth' is the right one, because server-cache state is often global and client-UI state is often app-wide.
Placement is testable: for each bucket there is a known answer to what happens on reload, in a second tab, on a shared link, and when the server changes underneath you.

viz.title: Where does this state live?
viz.whatIsDrawn: One fact (for example `unreadCount`) is drawn with its authoritative source on the left and four candidate homes as labelled slots. Dropping the fact into a slot traces a highlighted path through four lifecycle events drawn inline along the path — reload, second tab, shared link, server-side change — and stamps a red badge directly on the event where the value goes wrong, with the wrong and right values written inside the badge.
viz.predictPrompt: A dashboard fetches `unreadCount` once and stores it in a Zustand store so the sidebar and the header both read it. Exactly one of these breaks FIRST in production: (a) the sidebar and header disagree with each other, (b) the count is stale after another tab marks messages read, (c) the count is wrong after the user reloads. Pick one and say why the other two do not fire first.
controls: choose the fact: unread count / selected row id / active filter / draft comment / drag offset
choose a home slot: server cache / client store / URL / form / ephemeral
step through the four lifecycle events
viz.insight: The bug a misplaced piece of state causes is predictable: it is whichever lifecycle event the value survives that it should not, or fails to survive that it should.
viz.buildNotes: Static SVG board; the only motion is the trace path drawing (channel 1) and the value badge changing (channel 2). Reduced-motion renders the full trace with all four badges stamped at once. Live region announces 'unread count in client store: after event server-change, displayed 4, actual 0 — stale'. Ghost baseline = the same fact placed in its correct bucket, drawn as a dimmed parallel trace with no red badges.

drills.prompt: A spec for a support-ticket console lists 10 pieces of state (current ticket id, agent's saved filter preset, active filter, unsent reply draft, ticket list, unread badge, sort direction, sidebar collapsed, hovered row, in-flight assignment). Assign each to one of the five buckets.
drills.answerSketch: URL: current ticket id, active filter, sort direction. Server cache: ticket list, unread badge, saved filter preset (server-owned). Form: unsent reply draft. Client UI persisted: sidebar collapsed. Ephemeral: hovered row, in-flight assignment.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: 'any filtered view must be shareable by link, and reopening the link must show the same rows'. Select every item from your previous assignment whose bucket now moves, and name the item that looks like it should move but must not.
drills.answerSketch: Active filter and sort move to the URL if they were not already there; page/cursor joins them. The reply draft must NOT move — putting an unsent draft in a shared link leaks it.

drills.prompt: Select the line that creates a second copy of a fact with no invalidation policy: 1) `const { data } = useQuery(...)` 2) `useEffect(() => { setUsers(data) }, [data])` 3) `const users = useStore(s => s.users)` 4) `<Table rows={users} />`
drills.answerSketch: Line 2. It forks the query cache into a store; the store now holds server data with no staleTime, no revalidation trigger and no invalidation edge. The fix is to delete lines 2 and 3 and render `data` directly.

drills.prompt: An internal admin tool's tech lead wants the active filter kept in a Zustand store, not the URL, because 'nobody shares links to an internal tool'. Take a position and justify it in under 150 words. You will be scored against criteria covering: reload behaviour, back-button semantics, support/debugging workflows, and the cost of moving it later.
drills.answerSketch: Strongest answer concedes the sharing argument is weak internally but wins on reload persistence, back-button correctness, and the fact that support engineers reproduce bugs by pasting URLs. Also notes the migration cost is near-zero now and non-trivial later, once components read the store directly.

drills.prompt: State that can always be thrown away and refetched is ____-owned; state whose only copy lives in the browser is ____-owned. The first needs a ____ policy; the second needs a ____ policy.
drills.answerSketch: server; client; freshness/invalidation; persistence

failureModes: Answers a placement question with a library name ('I'd put it in Redux') without asking who owns the truth.
Syncs server data into a store with a useEffect, then spends the interview debugging the sync instead of deleting it.
Puts the active tab or open detail panel in a store, then cannot explain why deep links to it do not work.
Dismisses URL state as 'just routing' and never considers it a storage bucket.
Treats 'global vs local' as the classification axis, which produces the right shape for the wrong reason and collapses under the first requirement change.
interviewProbes: Walk me through every piece of state on this screen and tell me who owns each one.
The sidebar unread count and the inbox list disagree. Where do you look first?
We want any view in this dashboard to be shareable as a link. What moves?

state-server-cache.title: Server State Is a Cache: Freshness, Staleness, and the SWR Machine
objectives: Explain the fresh → stale → inactive → collected lifecycle of a cache entry and which parameter governs each transition.
Explain why stale-while-revalidate removes a loading state and what it costs in correctness.
Map the loading/fetching/error state machine onto UI affordances without producing impossible states.
claims: `staleTime` controls whether a cached value is reused without a network request; `gcTime` controls how long an unused entry is retained in memory — they are independent, and gcTime greater than staleTime is the normal relation.
TanStack Query v5 defaults to `staleTime: 0` and `gcTime: 5 minutes`, so by default every mount revalidates while still rendering cached data instantly.
Stale-while-revalidate serves the stale value immediately and revalidates in the background, trading a bounded window of incorrectness for the removal of a loading state.
HTTP has the same primitive: `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` (RFC 5861) permits a cache to serve a response up to 600 seconds past expiry while it refetches.
Two booleans (`isLoading`, `isError`) encode four states but only three are reachable; a status enum plus a separate `isFetching` flag makes the impossible fourth unrepresentable.

`isLoading` (no data yet) and `isFetching` (a request is in flight, data may already exist) must drive different UI — a skeleton versus a subtle refresh indicator — and conflating them is what causes content to flash back to a spinner on every revalidation.
Revalidation triggers (mount, window focus, network reconnect, polling interval) are policies, not correctness mechanisms: none guarantees freshness, each only shrinks the staleness window.
A cache entry's identity is its key, so any input that changes the response — locale, tenant, auth scope, feature flag — must appear in the key or the cache will serve one context's data in another.

viz.title: Fresh → Stale → Inactive → Collected
viz.whatIsDrawn: One cache entry's life along a horizontal time axis. Fresh and stale intervals are drawn as bands with their boundary labelled inline with the staleTime value; mount and unmount markers sit on the axis; each network request is a tick below the axis annotated in place with why it fired (mount / focus / interval). A dimmed ghost track directly beneath shows the identical event sequence with `staleTime: 0`.
viz.predictPrompt: A component mounts, unmounts after 10 seconds, and remounts at 4 minutes. `staleTime` is 30s, `gcTime` is 5 minutes. How many network requests fire in total, and does the remount show a skeleton or show data immediately? Commit to both answers before scrubbing.
viz.insight: staleTime decides whether you refetch; gcTime decides whether the user sees a skeleton while you do.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the scrub playhead. Channel 2 = the entry's state colour band. Nothing else moves; request ticks appear statically as the playhead passes them. Reduced-motion renders the full timeline with every tick and label present. Live region: 'at 4:00, remount — entry is stale but within gcTime: data rendered immediately, isFetching true, request 2 of 2'. sim.ts is a pure reducer over (events, staleTime, gcTime) returning the request log; unit-tested against claim 1 and the predictPrompt's answer (2 requests, no skeleton).

drills.prompt: `____` decides whether cached data is reused without a request. `____` decides how long an unused entry survives in memory. In TanStack Query v5 their defaults are ____ and ____.
drills.answerSketch: staleTime; gcTime; 0; 5 minutes

drills.prompt: A list is on screen with data. The user switches tabs and comes back; refetchOnWindowFocus fires. Which flags are true, and what should the UI do?
drills.answerSketch: `isLoading` false, `isFetching` true, `status: 'success'`. UI keeps rendering the current rows and shows a non-blocking refresh indicator. Rendering a skeleton here is the content-flash bug.

drills.prompt: Order the state transitions for a focus-triggered revalidation that fails, starting from a successful cached render.
drills.answerSketch: success + isFetching false → focus event → success + isFetching true (data still rendered) → response errors → status error, but previous data retained (errored-with-data) → retry or manual refetch → success.

drills.prompt: `useQuery({ queryKey: ['invoices', status], queryFn: () => fetchInvoices({ status, tenantId }) })`. The app supports tenant switching. What is the bug, when does it appear, and what is the minimal fix?
drills.answerSketch: `tenantId` is a queryFn input but not part of the key, so switching tenants serves the previous tenant's invoices from cache. Appears only on tenant switch, not on reload. Fix: `['invoices', tenantId, status]`.

drills.prompt: staleTime is 0. Six components mount in the same render pass and all call the same query key. How many network requests are issued, and why?
drills.answerSketch: One. The cache deduplicates by key: the first call starts the request, the other five subscribe to the same in-flight promise.

failureModes: Says 'cacheTime/gcTime controls how long data stays fresh' — collapsing the two independent parameters into one.
Renders a full-page skeleton on every background revalidation because the code branches on `isFetching`.
Claims refetchOnWindowFocus 'keeps the data fresh', as if it were a guarantee rather than a heuristic that shrinks a window.
Confuses the browser HTTP cache with the in-memory query cache and cannot say which one `staleTime` touches.
Leaves a request input out of the query key and only discovers it during a tenant/locale switch.
interviewProbes: What is the difference between staleTime and gcTime, and what does the user see when each expires?
How long is this screen allowed to be wrong, and what makes it right again?
Why did the page flash back to a spinner when I switched browser tabs?

state-normalization.title: Document Cache vs Normalized Entity Cache
objectives: Compare document and normalized caching on write amplification, read cost, and invalidation surface.
Judge from entity-overlap evidence which cache shape a given product needs.
Explain why partial entities and missing ids are the two failure sources unique to normalization.
claims: A document cache stores whole responses keyed by request; a normalized cache splits responses into entities keyed by type and id, and stores each query as an ordered list of references.

In a document cache, one entity appearing in three responses exists as three independent copies, so a mutation must invalidate three keys; in a normalized cache it is one record and every view updates from a single write.
Normalization moves cost from write time to read time: every read must denormalize by re-joining references, and that join runs on every render unless it is memoized.
A normalized cache requires a stable, globally unique id per entity; a list endpoint that omits the id, or reuses per-page indices as ids, silently corrupts the cache rather than erroring.
Partial entities are the hard problem: a list response carrying 3 fields and a detail response carrying 20 must merge such that the list write does not erase the detail fields.
TanStack Query and SWR are document caches by design; Apollo Client and Relay are normalized; Redux Toolkit Query is a document cache that you normalize yourself with `createEntityAdapter`.
Relay's fragment masking exists because normalization alone does not stop a component from reading a field it never declared, which is how one component breaks when an unrelated query changes.

The deciding variable is entity overlap between queries and mutation frequency, not app size: high overlap plus frequent mutation favours normalization; mostly disjoint read-heavy views favour a document cache.

viz.archetype: side-by-side mechanism comparison with shared input
viz.title: One rename, two caches
viz.whatIsDrawn: The same three query results rendered twice: on the left as a document cache (three boxes each containing a duplicated copy of user 42), on the right as a normalized cache (a query→reference index above a single entity table). A rename mutation is applied once; affected cells highlight in place, and a counter drawn inside each panel shows writes performed and views currently stale.
viz.predictPrompt: User 42 is rendered in three places: a table row, a comment author line, and the header avatar. A rename succeeds and the server returns the updated user. In a document cache with correct tag invalidation, how many network requests follow? In the normalized cache, how many? And which design can show two of those three views disagreeing with each other — for how long?
viz.insight: Duplication is not a storage problem, it is an invalidation problem: every copy is a view that can be wrong independently of the others.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the highlight sweep over affected cells. Channel 2 = the stale-view counter. Both panels are static SVG otherwise. Reduced-motion shows before/after states side by side with all highlights applied. Live region: 'document cache: 3 keys invalidated, 3 refetches, 2 views disagreed for 240ms; normalized cache: 1 entity write, 0 refetches, 0 disagreement'. sim.ts models both caches as pure data structures and is unit-tested against claim 2.

drills.prompt: A trading dashboard renders the same 40 instruments across a watchlist, a positions table, and a chart legend, and a websocket updates prices continuously. Which cache shape, and what is the single strongest reason?
drills.answerSketch: Normalized. Entity overlap is near-total and update frequency is high, so a document cache would require invalidating or patching every overlapping response on every tick.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the server now pushes per-field patches for entities instead of returning whole resources. Which cache design breaks first, and what specifically breaks?
drills.answerSketch: The document cache. A per-field patch has no response key to write into, so you either invalidate and refetch every containing query (losing the point of the push) or hand-merge into N copies and risk them diverging.

drills.prompt: `entities[user.id] = user` runs inside the list-response handler. The detail endpoint returns 20 fields; the list endpoint returns 3. Describe the exact user-visible symptom and where it appears.
drills.answerSketch: Assignment replaces rather than merges, so any list refetch strips the 17 detail-only fields from an already-loaded entity. Symptom: the open detail panel blanks out fields when a background list revalidation lands. Fix: `entities[user.id] = { ...entities[user.id], ...user }`, plus a per-field null-vs-absent policy.

drills.prompt: Complete the merge that preserves existing fields and treats an explicit `null` as a real value while treating an absent key as 'unknown'.
drills.answerSketch: Merge only keys present in the incoming payload (`Object.keys(incoming)`), spreading over the existing record; do not iterate the union of keys, and do not use a truthiness check that would drop `null`, `0` or `''`.

drills.prompt: You inherit a TanStack Query app and a teammate proposes adding a normalized entity layer underneath it. Argue for or against in under 150 words. Criteria cover: entity overlap evidence, denormalization cost at read time, who maintains the merge rules, and whether tag/key invalidation would solve it more cheaply.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer demands the overlap measurement first, notes that normalization on top of a document cache means maintaining two caches and a merge policy by hand, and proposes hierarchical keys plus write-through from mutation responses as the cheaper intermediate step.

failureModes: Says 'always normalize' as a reflex, with no reference to entity overlap or mutation frequency.
Assumes normalization removes the need for invalidation, when it only reduces its blast radius.
Denormalizes inside render without memoizing, then reports that normalization 'made it slower'.
Uses an array index or a per-page position as the entity id.
Shallow-overwrites entities on merge, silently deleting fields that only the detail query supplies.
interviewProbes: The same user object appears in six queries. What happens when their name changes?
Would you normalize this cache? What evidence would change your answer?
How does a partial response from a list endpoint interact with a fully-loaded entity?

state-invalidation.title: How a Cache Learns It Is Wrong: Invalidation and Live Patching
objectives: Design a tag or key graph whose invalidation set covers every server-side effect of a mutation, including unmodelled ones.
Decide per event type whether a pushed message should patch the cache or trigger a refetch.
Design gap detection and resynchronisation for a versioned event stream.
claims: A cache has exactly three ways to learn it is wrong: it expires (time), you tell it (mutation-driven invalidation), or the server tells it (a pushed event) — every freshness design is a mix of these three.

Mutation-driven invalidation is a graph problem: correctness requires the invalidated set to be a superset of everything the mutation could have changed server-side, including side effects the client never modelled.

Redux Toolkit Query expresses the graph as `providesTags` on queries and `invalidatesTags` on mutations; TanStack Query expresses the same graph as hierarchical query keys with prefix matching in `invalidateQueries` — the notation differs, the obligation does not.

Hierarchical keys make invalidation cheap only when the hierarchy matches the server's ownership hierarchy: `['todos', filters]` is invalidated by the prefix `['todos']`, but `['user', userId, 'todos']` is not.

`invalidateQueries` marks entries stale and refetches only the ones currently mounted; unmounted entries refetch on their next mount, which is why an invalidation bug can appear only after a back navigation.

Over-invalidation is a performance bug and is safe; under-invalidation is a correctness bug that stays invisible until a user reports it — so default to over-invalidating and narrow only with measurement.

A pushed event can be applied as a patch (zero extra round trips, risks drift) or treated purely as an invalidation signal (one round trip, always consistent); patching is safe only when the event carries the complete post-state of the fields it touches.

Push delivery is not globally ordered once the server fans out from multiple producers, so events need a monotonic per-resource version; a version gap means the client has missed state and must resynchronise from a snapshot rather than apply the next event.

viz.title: Blast radius of a mutation
viz.whatIsDrawn: A static graph of query nodes, each labelled with the tags it provides, plus one mutation node and one push-event node. Firing either propagates a single highlight wave along tag edges. Each node is stamped in place with its outcome — refetched / marked stale but unmounted / not reached — and any node that is factually wrong but unreached gets a red badge drawn on the node itself. A request counter sits inside the canvas.
viz.predictPrompt: `createOrder` declares `invalidatesTags: ['Order']`. The cart badge query provides `['Cart']`, and the server empties the cart as a side effect of creating an order. A websocket then pushes `cart.updated` carrying only `{ id }` with no field values. Point at the exact interval during which the badge is wrong, and say which of the two mechanisms actually fixes it — and what would fix it if the user never switched browser tabs.
controls: push an event: full payload / id-only / delta
viz.insight: You do not invalidate what changed; you invalidate what you modelled as changed — and a pushed event only helps if its payload is complete enough to trust.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the propagation wave along edges. Channel 2 = the request counter. Node badges appear statically as the wave passes. Reduced-motion draws the final propagation state with every badge and the counter at its terminal value. Live region names each node's outcome in order. sim.ts is a pure graph-propagation function over (tags, edges, event) with a seeded ordering; unit-tested against claims 2, 5 and 8 (including a dropped-version case).

drills.prompt: Given six queries with their tags and four mutations, build the invalidation map. The server's documented side effects are listed separately and deliberately exceed what the endpoint names suggest.
drills.answerSketch: Each mutation must invalidate the tags of every query touching a resource in its documented side-effect list, not only the resource it is named after. `createOrder` invalidates Order, Cart, Inventory and LoyaltyBalance.

drills.prompt: A dashboard shows an aggregate 'open tickets: 42' from `['stats','tickets']`. Closing a ticket invalidates `['tickets']`. Select the symptom and the fix.
drills.answerSketch: The aggregate is a separate key not covered by the `['tickets']` prefix, so the count stays 42 until an unrelated remount or focus refetch. Fix: invalidate `['stats','tickets']` too, or restructure so the aggregate lives under the `['tickets']` prefix.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the same list must stay correct with four tabs of the app open, and each tab issues its own mutations. Select everything in a tag-only design that is now insufficient.
drills.answerSketch: Tag invalidation is per-tab and in-memory, so mutations in tab A never reach tabs B–D. You need either server push, a BroadcastChannel invalidation signal between tabs, or a refetch-on-focus floor. Focus refetch alone leaves background tabs wrong indefinitely.

drills.prompt: For each of four pushed events — `order.created` (full resource), `cart.updated` (id only), `price.tick` (delta, 20/second), `document.patch` (JSON Patch with a version) — choose patch, invalidate, or bypass-the-cache.
drills.answerSketch: order.created → patch (complete payload). cart.updated → invalidate (payload insufficient). price.tick → bypass the durable cache, coalesce per frame. document.patch → patch, but only after a version-contiguity check; a gap forces a snapshot resync.

drills.prompt: A dashboard has 20 active queries, all with staleTime 0 and refetchOnWindowFocus enabled. A user alt-tabs 15 times in a working session. How many requests does focus revalidation alone generate, and what is the smallest change that cuts it by roughly 90%?
drills.answerSketch: 300 requests. Setting a staleTime floor (say 60s) collapses nearly all of them, since focus refetch only fires for entries that are already stale.

failureModes: Calls `queryClient.invalidateQueries()` with no arguments and calls that a strategy.
Assumes the mutation's own resource is the only thing the server changed.
Believes marking a query stale immediately refetches it even when nothing is mounted.
Applies an id-only or delta event as if it were a full-state patch, leaving the cache permanently diverged.
Assumes one websocket connection implies globally ordered delivery, so never adds a version or gap check.
Writes cursor/presence/ticker events into the query cache and then wonders why every subscriber re-renders 20 times a second.
interviewProbes: This mutation succeeded but the badge in the header is still wrong. Walk me through why.
How do you know your invalidation set is complete?
The server can push updates now. Do you patch the cache or refetch? Defend it per event type.
Your websocket reconnects after 30 seconds offline. What do you do before applying the next event?

state-optimistic.title: Optimistic Updates, Rollback, and Reconciliation
objectives: Diagnose rollback bugs caused by snapshots taken from a racing cache.
Identify which parts of a mutation result may be predicted and which must be reconciled from the server.
Judge whether a given action should be optimistic at all.
claims: An optimistic update has exactly three obligations: apply the predicted change, restore the previous value on failure, and replace the prediction with the server's authoritative value on success.
Rollback requires the snapshot to be taken after cancelling in-flight refetches for that key, otherwise a refetch landing mid-mutation becomes the 'previous' value you restore to.

React 19's `useOptimistic` reverts automatically when the transition owning the action settles, which scopes it to a single action rather than to a store — so it cannot express a mutation queue that outlives the component.
Two concurrent optimistic mutations on the same entity make rollback order-dependent: restoring the first mutation's snapshot while the second is still pending erases the second.

An optimistic update is only safe where the client can compute the same result as the server; anything the server derives — ids, timestamps, totals, ordering, permission outcomes — must be reconciled, not predicted.

Optimistic UI pays off when the action's success rate is high and its latency is user-visible (roughly above 200ms); for low-success-rate actions it converts an honest wait into a lie followed by a correction.

Silent reversion is the failure users report as 'it didn't save and didn't tell me', so a failed optimistic write needs a visible, non-destructive affordance — especially when the item has scrolled out of view.
Rollback correctness depends on the request being idempotent or carrying an idempotency key: if a retry can apply the mutation twice, the value you restore is a state the server never held.

viz.title: Predicted vs actual
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two stacked tracks over one time axis: what the user sees, and what the server holds. Mutations are drawn as arrows between them; the region where the tracks disagree is shaded and labelled inline with its duration. A dimmed ghost track underneath shows the same interaction without optimism. A failure can be injected on any request, drawn as a break in that arrow.
viz.predictPrompt: A like button is optimistic. The user taps like, then taps again to unlike 200ms later. The FIRST request fails; the second succeeds. Each mutation independently snapshots before it fires and restores its own snapshot on error. What does the UI show once both have settled, and is that state correct?
controls: toggle single shared snapshot vs per-mutation snapshot
viz.insight: Rollback is not 'undo my change', it is 'restore a snapshot' — and a snapshot taken from a cache that is still racing is the wrong value to restore.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the playhead. Channel 2 = the divergence shading growing/collapsing. Arrows are static. Reduced-motion renders the final timeline with the divergence region measured and labelled. Live region: 'request 1 failed at 620ms, restored snapshot liked=false, overwriting the pending unlike; final UI liked=false, server liked=false — correct by accident'. sim.ts models the cache, the mutation queue and the server as pure functions with an injected clock; unit-tested against claim 4.

drills.prompt: Order the six steps of a correct optimistic mutation lifecycle: setQueryData with the prediction; invalidate on settled; cancel in-flight queries for the key; restore the snapshot on error; capture the snapshot; fire the request.
drills.answerSketch: cancel in-flight queries → capture snapshot → setQueryData with the prediction → fire request → restore snapshot on error → invalidate on settled.

drills.prompt: An `onMutate` handler reads the current cache value and stores it as `previous`, then writes the optimistic value. There is no `cancelQueries` call. Describe the exact sequence that makes the rollback restore a wrong value.
drills.answerSketch: A background refetch started before onMutate resolves between the snapshot and the failure. Its response overwrites the cache; the failure then restores `previous`, which is now older than the refetched truth. The user sees data regress to a value the server has already superseded.

drills.prompt: The entity now gets a server-generated id and a server-computed `position` in an ordered list. Select everything in your optimistic path that breaks.
drills.answerSketch: The temporary client id must be reconciled to the real id when the response lands (any code holding the temp id needs remapping); the predicted list position may differ from the server's, so the item can visibly jump on reconciliation; any child mutation issued against the temp id before reconciliation will 404.

drills.prompt: Complete the `onError` handler so that it restores only if this mutation's snapshot is still the latest one for the key.
drills.answerSketch: Compare a per-mutation sequence/token against the key's current owner before writing; if a newer mutation has since taken ownership, skip the restore and let the newer mutation's own settlement reconcile.

drills.prompt: Should 'submit expense report' be optimistic? Answer in under 150 words. Criteria cover: success rate, latency visibility, cost of being wrong, reversibility, and what the user does next.
drills.answerSketch: No. Server-side validation and approval routing mean a meaningful failure rate; the user's next action depends on the submission having succeeded; and an incorrect success is expensive to retract. Show honest pending state instead; reserve optimism for high-success, low-consequence, high-frequency actions.

failureModes: Takes the snapshot after firing the request, or without cancelling in-flight refetches.
Predicts a server-generated id, then cannot match the mutation response back to the optimistic row.
Treats `useOptimistic` as a general-purpose optimistic cache and is surprised when the value reverts on unmount.
Reverts a failed write silently, with no affordance and no way for the user to recover their input.
Cannot say what happens when two optimistic mutations on the same entity are in flight at once.
interviewProbes: Make this optimistic. Now the request fails — what exactly do you restore, and where did that value come from?
The user taps twice quickly and the first request fails. Walk me through the final state.
Which fields would you refuse to predict optimistically, and why?

state-races.title: Out-of-Order Responses, Cancellation, and Request Deduplication
objectives: Diagnose which response a racing UI actually renders, and name the guard that makes the outcome deterministic.
Explain precisely what AbortController does and does not cancel.
Reconcile deduplication with cancellation without aborting a request another subscriber still needs.
claims: Concurrent requests for the same logical slot resolve in completion order, not issue order, so with no ordering guard the UI ends up showing whichever response happened to be slowest.
Aborting a fetch does not cancel the server's work: `AbortController` only detaches the client, so cancellation prevents a stale render, never a stale write.
The React-documented fix for fetching in an effect is a cleanup-scoped `ignore` flag; abort is an optimization layered on top, because an aborted request still rejects and must be handled.

`fetch` rejects with a `DOMException` whose `name` is `AbortError` on abort, so treating every rejection as a real error is how 'network error' toasts appear when the user simply typed another character.

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives a per-request deadline and `AbortSignal.any([...])` composes an unmount signal with a timeout signal; both shipped across all major engines during 2024 and are safe to use today.

Request deduplication keys in-flight promises by request identity and hands the same promise to every caller, collapsing N simultaneous identical requests into one — a correctness feature for render fan-out, not merely a bandwidth optimization.
Deduplication and cancellation conflict directly: if two components share one in-flight promise, one component unmounting must not abort it, so shared requests need subscriber reference counting.
Debouncing reduces how often races occur but never eliminates them; only an explicit ordering rule — a sequence number, latest-request-wins, or abort — makes the final render deterministic.

viz.archetype: request lane timeline with adjustable latency
viz.title: Type 'react' fast
viz.whatIsDrawn: One horizontal lane per keystroke-triggered request, each drawn as a bar from issue time to completion with an individually adjustable duration. Beneath the lanes sits a single 'rendered results' cell whose contents are labelled in place as each response lands. A dimmed ghost lane set shows the same run under latest-request-wins.
viz.predictPrompt: The user types r-e-a-c-t, one request per keystroke. Request 3 takes 900ms; the other four take 150ms each. With no guard at all, what is displayed one second after the last keystroke — and would a 300ms debounce have prevented it?
viz.insight: The last request issued is not the last response received; only an explicit ordering rule makes the final render deterministic.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the playhead sweeping the lanes. Channel 2 = the rendered-results cell contents. Bars are static once drawn. Reduced-motion shows the completed run with each lane's completion order numbered and the final cell contents labelled. Live region announces each completion and what it did to the rendered cell. sim.ts is a pure scheduler over (issueTimes, latencies, guard) with an injected clock and seeded latency jitter; unit-tested to prove the no-guard run renders request 3's result and the debounced run still can.

drills.prompt: `useEffect(() => { fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(setData) }, [url])`. Name the bug, the exact user action that triggers it, and the two-line fix.
drills.answerSketch: No cleanup, so a slow earlier response can setState after a newer one. Triggered by changing `url` faster than the slowest response. Fix: `let ignore = false; ... .then(d => { if (!ignore) setData(d) }); return () => { ignore = true }`.

drills.prompt: Complete the effect so it (a) ignores stale responses, (b) aborts on unmount, and (c) does not surface AbortError to the user.
drills.answerSketch: Create a controller in the effect; pass `controller.signal` to fetch; return `() => controller.abort()`; in the catch, `if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;` before any error handling.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of a deduplicating fetcher that also supports cancellation: increment subscriber count; return the shared promise; check the in-flight map; on unsubscribe decrement; abort only when the count reaches zero; create the controller and store the promise.
drills.answerSketch: check the in-flight map → (miss) create the controller and store the promise → increment subscriber count → return the shared promise → on unsubscribe decrement → abort only when the count reaches zero.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: results for several independent filters must now stream in and be displayed as each arrives, rather than one slot showing the latest. Select every guard that is now wrong.
drills.answerSketch: Latest-request-wins and a single shared ignore flag are wrong — they discard results that are still needed. The correct model is one slot per filter key, each with its own ordering guard; only requests for the SAME key race.

drills.prompt: Classify five rejections — a user navigating away mid-request, an offline DNS failure, `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` firing, a 500 response, a 401 — as AbortError, network error, or a resolved response that is not `ok`.
drills.answerSketch: Navigate-away and timeout → AbortError (timeout rejects with a TimeoutError DOMException specifically). Offline DNS → TypeError network error. 500 and 401 → resolved responses with `ok === false`; fetch does not reject on HTTP error status.

failureModes: Says 'debounce it' and stops, without any ordering guard.
Believes AbortController cancels the server's processing or rolls back a write.
Aborts a shared, deduplicated request when a single subscriber unmounts.
Surfaces AbortError to the user as a network error toast.
Cannot describe what the UI actually renders in the race — only that 'there's a race condition'.
interviewProbes: Search-as-you-type. Show me what the user sees when the third request is slow.
What does AbortController actually cancel?
Six components request the same thing in one render pass. What do you do, and what happens when one of them unmounts?

state-lists.title: Pagination and Infinite Lists: Offset, Cursor, Keyset
objectives: Compare offset, cursor and keyset pagination on stability, jumpability, cost and countability.
Predict the exact corruption (duplicates vs skips) a concurrent write produces under offset pagination.
Compare refetch strategies for an infinite list against the user's scroll position.
claims: Offset pagination (`LIMIT n OFFSET k`) is stateless and jumpable but unstable: an insert or delete before the current offset shifts every later page.
Under offset pagination, an insert ahead of your position causes items to appear twice and a delete causes items to be skipped entirely — the direction of the error identifies which write happened.
Cursor pagination is stable across concurrent writes because the cursor names a position in a total order, but it cannot answer 'jump to page 40' and usually cannot supply a cheap total count.

Keyset pagination is cursor pagination with the sort key exposed, as in `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?)`, and it requires a strict total order: a non-unique sort column must be tie-broken by a unique id or rows are silently skipped at page boundaries.

Offset cost grows with the offset because the database still scans the skipped rows, while keyset cost is constant per page — which is why deep pagination is the query that falls over first under load.
An infinite list's client state is an ordered array of pages plus a cursor, not a flat array; keeping pages distinct is what allows a single page to be refetched in place without discarding the rest.
Refetching an infinite list by discarding all pages and refetching page one destroys the user's position; refetching each loaded page in place preserves it at a cost of N requests.

Scroll restoration requires the list to occupy the same height it did before, so with virtualised rows the app must set `history.scrollRestoration = 'manual'` and restore explicitly once the target item is measurable — otherwise the browser restores a position in a list that has not been rendered yet.

viz.archetype: side-by-side mechanism comparison with shared input
viz.title: Someone posts while you scroll
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single ordered source list in the centre, with two readers walking it: an offset reader on the left and a keyset reader on the right. As items are inserted at the head or deleted mid-list, each reader's accumulated pages are drawn beneath it, with duplicated items outlined and skipped items marked by a gap glyph placed inline where the item should have been.
viz.predictPrompt: You have read pages 1 and 2 (20 items) from a newest-first feed using offset pagination. Three new items are posted. When you fetch page 3, how many items do you see twice, and how many do you never see at all? Give both numbers before running it.
controls: toggle a non-unique sort key with no tiebreaker
viz.insight: Offset pagination duplicates on insert and skips on delete; keyset trades away jump-to-page for the guarantee that neither happens.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the reader position markers advancing. Channel 2 = the newly-fetched page appearing in each reader's stack. Reduced-motion draws every fetched page at once with duplicate outlines and gap glyphs in place. Live region: 'offset reader page 3: 3 items duplicated from page 2, 0 skipped; keyset reader page 3: 0 duplicated, 0 skipped'. sim.ts is a pure list-walker over (source, mutations, strategy); unit-tested to prove the insert→duplicate and delete→skip claims exactly.

drills.prompt: Pick the pagination scheme for each: an admin table with 'jump to page 40' and a total count; a social feed with constant inserts; an audit log with 40 million rows and no jump requirement; a leaderboard where rank must be shown next to each row.
drills.answerSketch: Admin table → offset (jumpability and count are the requirements; instability is tolerable). Feed → cursor/keyset. Audit log → keyset (offset scan cost is the killer). Leaderboard → offset or a server-computed rank column, since rank is inherently positional.

drills.prompt: Product adds 'jump to page 40' to a cursor-paginated table. Select every honest option and mark the one that is a trap.
drills.answerSketch: Honest: switch to keyset with a seekable index, precompute page-boundary cursors, or replace paging with a filter/search affordance. The trap is fetching 39 pages client-side to synthesise page 40 — it works in the demo and collapses on real data volume.

drills.prompt: `WHERE created_at < $cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Twelve rows share the same `created_at` at a page boundary. Name the symptom and the fix.
drills.answerSketch: Rows sharing the boundary timestamp are silently skipped or duplicated depending on the comparison. Fix: make the sort a strict total order — `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` with the cursor as a `(created_at, id)` tuple compared row-wise.

drills.prompt: Order the steps to restore scroll position into a virtualised infinite list after a back navigation.
drills.answerSketch: set `history.scrollRestoration = 'manual'` → on leave, persist the last visible item's id plus its offset within the viewport → on return, rehydrate the cached pages up to that item → render enough rows for the item to exist and be measured → scroll to the item's measured position → only then re-enable normal scroll handling and further page loads.

drills.prompt: A user has scrolled through 10 pages of 25 items. A mutation invalidates the list. How many requests does 'refetch every loaded page in place' cost, and what does 'reset to page 1' cost the user instead?
drills.answerSketch: 10 requests, position preserved. Reset costs 1 request but throws away 250 rendered rows and the user's scroll position — the classic 'I lost my place' complaint. Choose per interaction cost, not per request count.

failureModes: Uses offset pagination on a real-time feed and cannot explain the duplicate rows users see.
Sorts by a non-unique timestamp with no id tiebreaker in a keyset cursor.
Resets an infinite list to page one on every invalidation.
Adds scroll restoration without stable item heights, so the browser restores into an empty list.
Treats infinite scroll as a styling choice rather than a state design that makes the footer unreachable and individual items unlinkable.
interviewProbes: Someone posts a new item while I am on page 3. What do I see?
Design pagination for a 40-million-row audit log. Now product wants a total count.
I hit back from a detail page. Put me exactly where I was.

state-url.title: The URL as Shareable State
objectives: Design the URL schema for a view so that a pasted link reproduces exactly what the sender saw.
Design push vs replace semantics so the back button behaves as users expect.
Design the boundary that parses and validates untrusted search params.
claims: Any state that determines what the page shows and that a user would expect to survive a reload or a paste into a chat belongs in the URL: filters, sort, page or cursor, selected tab, open detail panel, and query text.
Search params are strings from an untrusted source, so every read must parse and validate — a schema at the boundary is what stops a hand-edited URL from crashing the view or rendering `NaN`.

`push` creates a history entry and `replace` does not, so continuous input must replace while committed navigation pushes; a push per keystroke makes the back button take thirty presses to leave the page.
Back-button semantics are a product decision encoded in push vs replace: closing a modal with the back button only works if opening it pushed an entry.

Browsers throttle history writes — Safari throws a `SecurityError` after roughly 100 `replaceState` calls in 30 seconds, and Chrome and Firefox throttle similarly — so URL-synced typing must be debounced rather than written per keystroke.
URLs have a practical interoperability ceiling around 2,000 characters, so state larger than that must be reduced to an id resolved from durable storage rather than serialised into the query string.
React Router v7 in library mode supplies `useSearchParams`, whose setter accepts the same `{ replace: true }` option — with no loaders, the component reads params and drives its own fetch from them.
Deriving the cache key from the parsed params object makes back and forward navigation a cache hit instead of a refetch, which is why URL state and query keys should share one derivation function.

viz.title: Thirty back presses
viz.whatIsDrawn: A vertical history stack that grows upward as the learner types into a mock filter input, each entry showing its full URL. A back-button control pops entries one at a time with the current entry highlighted in place. A dimmed ghost stack alongside shows the identical interaction under debounced-replace, with its final depth labelled.
viz.predictPrompt: A filter input syncs to the URL with `push` on every change, debounced at 300ms. The user types a 12-character query in one continuous burst, then clicks a result. How many history entries exist when they land on the detail page, and how many back presses return them to the page they arrived from?
viz.insight: The history stack is a user-visible data structure, and push vs replace is the only API you have for editing it.
viz.buildNotes: Channel 1 = the stack growing/popping. Channel 2 = the current-entry highlight. Reduced-motion renders both final stacks with depths labelled. Live region: 'push mode: 5 entries after typing, 6 after navigation; 5 back presses to leave the results page. replace mode: 1 entry, 1 back press'. sim.ts is a pure reducer over (keystrokes, debounceMs, mode) returning the resulting stack; unit-tested against the predictPrompt answer.

drills.prompt: For an analytics dashboard, decide URL vs store vs neither for: date range, selected metric, chart type, comparison mode toggle, sidebar collapsed, an in-progress CSV export, the hovered data point, an open 'share' modal, the drag-selected brush region, and the auth token.
drills.answerSketch: URL: date range, selected metric, chart type, comparison mode, brush region (if it defines the view). Store/localStorage: sidebar collapsed. Neither/ephemeral: in-progress export, hovered point. Modal: URL only if it must be linkable — the share modal usually should be. Auth token: never in the URL.

drills.prompt: Complete the `useSearchParams` setter call so that typing does not pollute history but selecting a result does.
drills.answerSketch: `setSearchParams(next, { replace: true })` for the debounced typing path; the same call without the option (push) on result selection.

drills.prompt: `const page = Number(params.get('page'))`. Name three inputs that break the view and the one-line fix.
drills.answerSketch: An absent param yields 0, `'abc'` yields NaN, and `'-5'` or `'1e9'` yields an out-of-range page. Fix: parse through a schema with a coercion, a positive-integer bound and a default, at a single boundary, not at each call site.

drills.prompt: The filter set grows to 40 fields including free-text. Select everything about a naive query-string encoding that now breaks.
drills.answerSketch: URL length hits the ~2,000 character ceiling; the URL becomes unreadable and unshareable in chat clients that truncate; and the cache key derived from it churns on every character. The fix is a saved-view id persisted server- or client-side, with only the id plus a few hot params in the URL.

drills.prompt: Should an open modal be URL state? Under 150 words. Criteria cover: linkability, back-button expectation, refresh behaviour, and the cost when the modal's content depends on unshareable local state.
drills.answerSketch: Yes when the modal is a destination — a detail view, a shareable dialog, anything a user would send someone. No when it is a transient confirmation over unsaved local state, because a reload would restore a modal whose underlying context no longer exists.

failureModes: Pushes a history entry per keystroke, then blames the framework when the back button stops working.
Reads search params with `Number()` or a raw cast and no validation.
Serialises a large filter object as JSON into the query string until it exceeds the URL length ceiling.
Duplicates URL state into a store and then writes a two-way sync effect between them.
Cannot say what the back button should do when a modal is open, because push/replace was never a deliberate decision.
interviewProbes: Make this filtered view shareable. What goes in the URL and in what shape?
I typed a query and pressed back. What should happen?
Someone hand-edits the URL to `?page=-1`. What does your app do?

state-store-choice.title: Choosing a Global Store, and the Context Re-render Trap
objectives: Compare Context, external stores, atoms and signals on update granularity and on what each one actually costs.
Explain precisely why memoizing a context value and wrapping consumers in React.memo does not stop context-driven re-renders.
Judge a store choice from the shape of the client-owned state rather than from library preference.
claims: React Context is a dependency-injection mechanism, not a store: every consumer re-renders when the provider's value identity changes, regardless of which field that consumer reads.
There is no per-field bail-out in Context, so the only real mitigations are splitting one context into several, or moving the value into an external store read through `useSyncExternalStore`.
`React.memo` on a consumer does not prevent a context-driven re-render, because the context read happens inside the component rather than arriving as a prop.

Zustand, Redux Toolkit and Jotai all escape the context trap the same way: components subscribe to an external store and re-render only when their selected slice changes under the store's equality check.

Zustand compares selector results with `Object.is`, so a selector returning a new object or array re-renders on every store change; `useShallow` is the supported fix in v5, where passing an equality function as a second argument to the hook was removed.

Jotai inverts the model: state is defined bottom-up as atoms and derived atoms whose dependency graph is discovered at read time, so a component subscribes to exactly the atoms it reads without anyone writing a selector.

Signals move the update boundary below the component: a signal read inside JSX can update that DOM node without re-rendering the component, which React does not do because React's unit of update is the component.
React 19's compiler removes most hand-written `memo` and `useMemo`, but it does not make Context per-field — an unchanged field inside a changed context value still notifies every consumer.

Server-cache state should not live in the global store at all, so the store-choice question only concerns the client-owned slice, which in most apps is small enough that the choice matters far less than the taxonomy decision did.

viz.title: Who re-rendered, and why
viz.whatIsDrawn: A fixed component tree of about twelve nodes.
