drills.answerSketch: 1 -> script injection. 2 -> image-URL exfiltration (and only 2, or proxying/no-remote-images). 3 -> javascript: link. 4 -> 'call the delete tool'. 5 -> the impersonation payload, which no sanitizer addresses because nothing about it is malformed.

drills.prompt: Exfiltration through a rendered markdown image is closed at the ____ boundary, using the ____ CSP directive or by ____ images through your own origin. It is not closed by HTML ____, because the image is ____ markdown.
drills.answerSketch: network; img-src; proxying; escaping/sanitizing; valid (legitimate)

drills.prompt: Two citation UIs: (A) a superscript marker linking to a URL the model produced in its answer; (B) a superscript marker resolving to a stored character range in a specific retrieved chunk, which opens that chunk with the range highlighted. Both look identical to a user. State which is provenance and what failure mode B prevents that A cannot.
drills.answerSketch: B is provenance. A cannot detect the case where the model's sentence is unsupported by any retrieved text — the URL may be real, reachable and irrelevant, so a plausible link launders a fabricated claim. B fails loudly instead: a claim with no resolvable span has no marker.

drills.prompt: An internal engineering assistant renders remote images from model output because engineers paste diagram URLs constantly. Defend keeping or removing that, given the assistant also reads internal tickets and source. Under 150 words.
drills.answerSketch: Remove auto-loading of arbitrary remote images; the assistant reads attacker-influenceable content (tickets, code comments, dependency READMEs), which makes the image tag a zero-click exfiltration channel for anything in the transcript. Keep the capability by allowlisting internal image hosts through img-src, or by proxying and stripping query strings. 'Internal tool' argues for the mitigation, not against it — the data at risk is exactly the data worth taking.

failureModes: Says 'we sanitize the HTML' and considers the question closed, missing that the dangerous primitive is markdown they chose to support.
Treats model output as trusted because it came from their own backend.
Answers prompt injection with 'better system prompt' instead of reducing what a tool call can do without a human.
Ships citation chips that link wherever the model said, and calls it grounding.

ai-compute-boundary.title: Where Does the Compute Run: WASM and WebGPU as a Payload Decision
objectives: Judge a proposal to move work into WASM or WebGPU by its fixed entry cost and the workload size that amortizes it.
State the conditions under which in-browser inference beats a server call, and reject it where it does not.
claims: Moving work to WASM or WebGPU is a decision about crossing a boundary: the cost is the payload you must ship plus the data you must copy across, not the instruction count once you are there.
WASM wins on numeric, allocation-heavy inner loops with little crossing; for DOM-bound or string-bound work the JS-to-WASM call and copy overhead usually exceeds the gain.

A WASM module and its runtime are a bundle cost paid before any speedup, so it must be lazily loaded on the route that needs it — a multi-megabyte tokenizer shipped in the initial bundle degrades the very metric it was added to improve.

WebGPU reached Baseline in January 2026 — Chrome and Edge since 113 in 2023, Safari 26 in September 2025, Firefox 141 on Windows in July 2025 — but Linux and Intel-Mac Firefox coverage still lags, so a WebGL2 or CPU fallback path is a requirement rather than a nicety.
GPU work is asynchronous and buffer-based: uploading and reading back data has its own cost, so a pipeline that round-trips per frame can be slower than a CPU implementation that never leaves memory.

In-browser inference removes the network round trip and the per-token price but substitutes a multi-hundred-megabyte model download, device memory limits, and thermal throttling that turns a fast first run into a slow tenth run on a laptop or phone.
The only argument for local inference that a bigger server model cannot answer is the privacy boundary: data that never leaves the device.

The honest default for an assistant UI is server inference with a client that is fast at rendering; local compute earns its place in narrow, offline or privacy-bound tasks such as embedding search over local files or on-device transcription, not as the main chat model.

viz.archetype: crossover chart (fixed cost + marginal cost lines)
viz.title: When does the boundary pay for itself?
viz.whatIsDrawn: Total end-to-end time on the y-axis against workload size on the x-axis. Four lines: plain JS (zero intercept, steep slope), WASM (intercept = module download plus instantiate, shallow slope), WebGPU (higher intercept including adapter request and buffer upload, shallowest slope), and server round trip (large flat intercept, near-zero slope). Crossover points are marked and labelled inline with the item count at which each line wins; a cold/warm cache toggle drops the WASM intercept and visibly moves the crossover.
viz.predictPrompt: A 1.2MB WASM module makes a per-item computation 8x faster. Your page processes 500 items once, on load, over a typical 4G connection. Roughly what item count does WASM start winning end to end — and is 500 above or below it?
viz.insight: Every boundary has a fixed entry price; the only real question is how many items amortize it — and on a cold cache the answer is usually larger than the workload you actually have.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure cost model: (workload, moduleBytes, bandwidth, speedup, cacheState) -> per-strategy total ms and crossover points, computed analytically — no benchmarking at runtime. Unit test asserts the crossover formula against hand-computed fixtures and that warm cache strictly lowers the WASM crossover. Reduced motion shows the final chart with crossovers labelled.

drills.prompt: A 1.2MB gzipped WASM module downloads on a link delivering ~1.5MB/s and takes ~40ms to instantiate. It makes a 0.9ms-per-item JS computation 8x faster. Compute the break-even item count on a cold cache, then on a warm cache.
drills.answerSketch: Cold: fixed cost ~800ms download + 40ms instantiate ≈ 840ms; saving per item ≈ 0.9 - 0.11 ≈ 0.79ms; break-even ≈ 1,060 items. Warm: fixed cost ≈ 40ms; break-even ≈ 50 items. The same proposal is obviously right or obviously wrong depending only on cache state — which is why the answer must name it.

drills.prompt: Four candidate workloads in an assistant UI: (a) exact client-side token counting for a 30k-token transcript, (b) fuzzy search over 50k locally stored messages, (c) syntax highlighting of streamed code blocks, (d) on-device transcription of a 3-minute voice note. For each, choose JS, WASM, WebGPU or server, and name the deciding constraint.
drills.answerSketch: (a) Server — a real tokenizer is megabytes for a number the server must own anyway; estimate on the client. (b) WASM or plain JS with an index; deciding constraint is index size and how often it is queried, not raw speed. (c) Neither — highlight at build time and ship pre-rendered tokens; the runtime cost is avoidable entirely. (d) WASM/WebGPU on device is defensible if privacy is the requirement; otherwise server, because the model download dwarfs the audio.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the feature that justified your WASM module must now also work on the first page load for a new user on a mid-range Android phone. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The cold-cache intercept lands on the critical path — the module download and instantiate compete with the initial bundle and are paid before anything is faster, so the measured first-load metric regresses even though steady-state throughput improved. Fix: keep the module off the initial route, run the JS path for the first, small workload, and upgrade in the background.

drills.prompt: 'We should run the model in the browser with WebGPU — it's free, private, and there's no latency.' Identify which of the three claims survives scrutiny and what the other two actually cost.
drills.answerSketch: Only privacy survives, and only if nothing else about the request leaves the device. 'Free' relocates cost to a several-hundred-megabyte download, device memory and battery. 'No latency' is false after the first run on sustained load, where thermal throttling and a smaller model make time-to-first-token and quality both worse than a server call.

drills.prompt: You need semantic search over a user's locally stored conversations, with no server. Defend running embeddings on-device versus not shipping the feature. Under 150 words.
drills.answerSketch: On-device is the right call precisely here: the corpus never leaves the machine, embedding a message is a small, amortizable one-off at write time rather than a per-query cost, and the model needed is small enough to lazy-load on the search route. The honest constraint is first-use: the initial backfill over an existing history is the expensive moment, so it runs in the background, is resumable, and the feature degrades to substring search until it completes.

failureModes: Proposes WASM for a speedup without ever naming the module size or when it is downloaded.
Treats WebGPU availability as a binary and ships no fallback, on the strength of 'it's Baseline now'.
Argues for in-browser inference on cost grounds without pricing the model download or the device memory.
Benchmarks the hot loop and reports the win, ignoring transfer and copy costs across the boundary.

incl-a11y-tree.title: The Accessibility Tree and Accessible Name Computation
objectives: Trace how the DOM plus computed style produce the accessibility tree that assistive technology actually consumes.
Apply the accessible-name computation precedence ladder to predict what a screen reader announces for a given element.
Explain why a native element beats a role, and state the specific behaviours a role does not give you.
claims: The accessibility tree is derived from the DOM plus computed style, so `display:none` and `visibility:hidden` remove a node from it while `opacity:0`, `clip-path` and off-screen positioning do not.

Accessible name computation resolves in precedence order: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then the host-language labelling mechanism (`<label for>`, `alt`, `<caption>`, `<legend>`), then descendant text content for roles that support name-from-content, then `title` as a last resort.
`aria-labelledby` replaces the element's content-derived name entirely — it does not append to it — and it can reference the element's own id to reassemble a name from parts.

The accessible description (from aria-describedby or `title`) is announced after the name and often after a delay or on demand, so anything the user must hear to act belongs in the name, not the description.

Adding a `role` replaces an element's native semantics but adds none of its native behaviour: `<div role="button">` gets no Enter/Space activation, no focusability, no disabled state and no form participation.
`aria-hidden="true"` removes a subtree from the accessibility tree but leaves it focusable, so any focusable descendant becomes a phantom tab stop that AT cannot name.

Only roles that support name-from-content (button, link, heading, cell, menuitem, option, tab) derive their name from descendant text; `role="region"`, `role="group"` and generic containers require an explicit aria-label or aria-labelledby.
Most ARIA states are booleans mirrored from real application state, so any code path where `aria-expanded` and the DOM it controls diverge tells AT a lie that no visual or snapshot test will catch.

viz.archetype: layered transform diagram (source → derived tree) with staged reveal and in-place strike-through
viz.title: DOM → Accessibility Tree
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two columns anchored in one frame. Left: a small real card markup — an icon-only `<button>` wrapping an `<svg aria-hidden="true">` plus a visually-hidden `<span class="sr-only">` and a `title` attribute; a `<div role="button" tabindex="0">`; a decorative wrapper. Right: the computed accessibility tree, one node per line showing role · name · description · states. Connector lines run between the columns inside the frame; pruned nodes are struck through in place on the left with the pruning reason printed on the connector, never in a side panel. Max 7 labels.
viz.predictPrompt:
This icon button contains an `Close`, and carries `title="Dismiss"`. Next to it sits a `
` inside a wrapper marked `aria-hidden="true"`. Before running: which of these five nodes reach the accessibility tree, what is the button's computed name, and how many tab stops does a keyboard user encounter?
controls: Step through the five computation stages: prune → role → name → description → state
Toggle each hiding mechanism independently: display:none / visibility:hidden / opacity:0 / aria-hidden / inert
Swap the button's labelling source (aria-label vs sr-only text vs title vs alt) and watch the name recompute up the precedence ladder
Toggle the ghost baseline: the same markup as a naive dev imagines the tree looks (1:1 with the DOM)
viz.insight: AT does not read your DOM; it reads a derived tree in which role, name and state are computed by a precedence ladder — and CSS is an input to that computation, which is why 'it looks right' proves nothing.
viz.buildNotes: Pure `axtree.ts`: takes a serialized {tag, attrs, computedStyle, children} tree and returns AX nodes; no DOM dependency, no clock, no RNG. Unit-tested against accname 1.2 worked examples including the aria-labelledby self-reference case and the title-as-last-resort case. This sim is reused by incl-forms-errors and incl-complex-widgets — build it well once. prefers-reduced-motion → all five stages rendered at once, numbered, with connector labels static.

drills.prompt: Given `<button aria-label="Close" title="Dismiss">×</button>`, the computed accessible name is ______ and the accessible description is ______.
drills.answerSketch: Name: "Close" (aria-label outranks both content and title). Description: empty — title is consumed as the name only when nothing higher wins; here aria-label won, and title then falls through to description in most implementations, so accept "Dismiss" with a note. Grade the name strictly.

drills.prompt: Put the accessible-name computation sources in precedence order, highest first: descendant text content · aria-label · title · aria-labelledby · native label mechanism (`<label for>` / `alt` / `<caption>`).
drills.answerSketch: aria-labelledby → aria-label → native label mechanism → descendant text content (roles supporting name-from-content) → title.

drills.prompt:
Select every defective line. A card renders: `
`, `🗑`, `
e.key === 'Enter' && submit()}>Submit
`.
drills.answerSketch: Line 1: focusable button inside aria-hidden subtree → phantom tab stop. Line 2: aria-label on a `<span>` with no role is ignored by most AT; also not focusable, not activatable. Line 3: role=button with no tabindex (unfocusable), no Space handling, no preventDefault on Space, no disabled semantics.

drills.prompt: Which hiding technique keeps a node in the accessibility tree while removing it visually, and why does that distinction matter for a skip link? (a) display:none (b) visibility:hidden (c) clip-path + 1px box (d) aria-hidden="true" (e) inert
drills.answerSketch: (c). The skip link must be reachable and announceable while invisible until focused; a/b/e remove it from the tree and focus order, d removes it from the tree while leaving it focusable — the worst of both.

drills.prompt: The design changes: icon buttons lose their visually-hidden text and get a hover tooltip instead. Name the first three user groups this breaks and the one WCAG criterion it most cleanly fails.
drills.answerSketch: Screen reader users (name now depends on title, unreliably exposed and never on touch), voice-control users (no spoken label to say), touch users (no hover). Cleanest failure: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value; 2.5.3 Label in Name becomes relevant once a visible label exists at all.

failureModes: Reaches for `role` and `aria-*` before reaching for a native element — adds `role="button"` to a div, then hand-rolls keyboard handling and misses Space, preventDefault on Space, and form submission.
Believes `aria-label` works on any element, and puts it on a `<span>` or `<div>` with no role where most AT ignores it entirely.
Assumes `aria-hidden="true"` also removes the subtree from the tab order, shipping focusable elements AT cannot name.
Describes the mechanism as 'screen readers read the DOM top to bottom', which mispredicts roles, names, virtual cursor navigation and everything downstream.
interviewProbes: Walk me through exactly what a screen reader announces when focus lands on this icon-only button. Then tell me what it announces after you add a tooltip.
When is `role="button"` on a div actually the right call, and what do you owe the user if you make it?
Your design system exposes labels only through Tooltip. Is that conformant? What is the first thing that breaks, and for whom?

incl-keyboard-model.title: Keyboard Interaction Model: Tab Stops, Roving Tabindex, Skip Links
objectives: Decide which elements in a composite widget are tab stops and which are arrow-key targets, and justify the tab-stop budget.
Choose between roving tabindex and aria-activedescendant from the widget's focus requirements, not from habit.
Design bypass mechanisms — skip link, landmarks, heading structure — that measurably reduce keystrokes to the primary task.
claims: The tab sequence contains only elements that are focusable, rendered and not inert; `tabindex="-1"` makes an element programmatically focusable while removing it from the tab sequence.
A composite widget — toolbar, menu, menubar, tablist, listbox, radiogroup, grid, tree — must expose exactly ONE tab stop, with movement inside it handled by arrow keys.

Roving tabindex moves real DOM focus, setting `tabindex="0"` on the active item and `tabindex="-1"` on all others; `aria-activedescendant` leaves DOM focus on the container and names the active item by id instead.

`aria-activedescendant` is mandatory when the focused element must remain a text input — combobox, editable grid, tag input — because moving DOM focus away from the input would break typing and IME composition.
A positive `tabindex` (>0) creates a separate tab sequence that runs ahead of all document-order tab stops, and is a defect in essentially all application code.

A skip link must be the first focusable element in the document, may be visually hidden only until focused, and must MOVE FOCUS — typically to a `tabindex="-1"` `<main>` — because changing `location.hash` alone scrolls without moving focus in several browser/AT combinations.

WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order requires focus order to preserve meaning, and CSS reordering (`order`, `grid-area`, `flex-direction: row-reverse`) does not change the tab sequence — so visual and focus order silently desynchronize.

WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap forbids any focus state a keyboard user cannot leave with standard keys; a modal's deliberate focus trap is conformant only because Escape or a always-reachable close control releases it.

viz.archetype: annotated path overlay on a live layout (focus-order visualizer) with ghost baseline and keystroke counter
viz.title: Focus Order Visualizer: Tab Stops vs Arrow Keys
viz.whatIsDrawn: A realistic app screen — a 12-button toolbar, a 40-card product grid where each card has 3 controls, and pagination at the bottom. A numbered SVG polyline is drawn over the layout connecting tab stops in order; arrow-key movement inside the composite widget is drawn as a dashed loop that stays inside the widget's bounding box. A faint ghost polyline shows the naive 'every control is a tab stop' path. Keystroke count is rendered inside the frame next to the current focus ring, not in a side panel.
viz.predictPrompt: A keyboard user wants to reach the pagination control at the bottom of this page. The naive implementation makes every control a tab stop; the APG implementation gives the toolbar and the grid one tab stop each. Before running: how many Tab presses does each cost? And which implementation is WORSE for a screen-magnifier user at 400% zoom — the answer is not the one you expect.
controls: Step forward/back through the tab sequence one keystroke at a time
Flip CSS `order` / `flex-direction: row-reverse` on the toolbar to desynchronize visual and DOM order
Toggle the skip link and watch the keystroke count to `main` collapse
Inject a `tabindex="3"` on one control and watch it jump to the front of the sequence
viz.insight: Tab moves between widgets; arrows move within one. The cost of confusing them is measured in keystrokes to the thing the user actually came for — and CSS can silently make the path visually incoherent without changing the count at all.
viz.buildNotes: `focusorder.ts` computes the tab sequence from a serialized element list (tabindex, disabled, inert, hidden, contenteditable) — pure, no DOM, no clock. Unit-tested against browser-captured fixture sequences including the positive-tabindex ordering rule and the disabled-in-tab-order rule. Path is an SVG polyline anchored to element rects computed at build time so it never needs layout measurement at runtime. Reduced motion → static numbered badges on every tab stop with both paths shown.

drills.prompt: Given this markup (a header with skip link, a `tabindex="2"` search box, a toolbar with roving tabindex, a disabled Save button, and a footer link), list the tab stops in the order they are reached.
drills.answerSketch: Positive tabindex first (search box), then document order: skip link, toolbar's single tabindex=0 item, footer link. Disabled Save is not in the sequence.

drills.prompt: You are building a tag input: a text field where typing filters a list of suggestions and arrow keys highlight one. Roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant? Give the deciding reason, not the tradeoff list.
drills.answerSketch: aria-activedescendant. DOM focus must stay on the input or the user cannot keep typing and IME composition breaks. Roving tabindex requires moving real focus, which is disqualifying here.

drills.prompt:
Select every defect: `Skip to content` where `.skip { display: none }` until `:focus`, `
` with no tabindex, a nav using `tabindex="1"`…`tabindex="6"` to 'fix ordering', and a grid where each of 120 cells is `tabindex="0"`.
drills.answerSketch: display:none removes the skip link from the tab order entirely (use clip/transform instead). `<main>` needs tabindex="-1" to receive focus. Positive tabindex creates a competing sequence. 120 tab stops violate the one-tab-stop rule for grid.

drills.prompt: Complete the roving-tabindex keydown handler: on ArrowRight, set `tabindex` to ____ on the outgoing item, ____ on the incoming item, and then call ____ so that focus actually moves.
drills.answerSketch: -1 on outgoing, 0 on incoming, `incoming.focus()`. Also expect `event.preventDefault()` to stop page scroll on arrow keys.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the toolbar must remember its last-active item across route changes, and must also be reachable from a global keyboard shortcut. What changes in your roving-tabindex implementation, and what new WCAG risk did you just create?
drills.answerSketch: Persist activeIndex outside the component; on shortcut, focus the item at activeIndex, not index 0. New risk: a shortcut that steals focus mid-typing (2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts requires the shortcut be disableable, remappable, or active only on focus), plus a focus jump that violates 3.2.1/3.2.2 expectations if unannounced.

failureModes: Makes every cell or control in a grid or toolbar a tab stop — technically 'keyboard accessible', practically 200 tabs deep — and reports it as done.
Ships a skip link that only sets `location.hash`, so focus never moves and the next Tab returns to the top of the page.
Uses positive `tabindex` to patch a focus-order problem instead of fixing DOM order.
Handles only Enter on a custom control, so Space does nothing — or handles Space without preventDefault, so the page scrolls on every activation.
interviewProbes: How many Tab presses does it take a keyboard user to reach the primary action in this design? Show me your arithmetic.
This toolbar is visually right-to-left because of `flex-direction: row-reverse`. What is the tab order, and is that a WCAG failure?
Where does roving tabindex stop being the right tool?

incl-focus-lifecycle.title: Focus Management Across Route Changes, Overlays and Async Updates
objectives: Design a focus contract for a client-side route change that works for both keyboard and screen-reader users.
Choose the correct overlay primitive (`showModal`, popover, custom) from its focus and inertness guarantees rather than from styling convenience.
Specify a focus restore target that survives the opener being unmounted.
claims: A client-side route change does not move focus and does not reset the screen reader's virtual cursor, so without explicit handling the user remains focused on a link inside a view that no longer exists.

The standard SPA route-change remedy is to move focus to a `tabindex="-1"` heading or main landmark of the new view AND update `document.title`; a live-region announcement is an addition to that, never a substitute for moving focus.

Of `<dialog>.showModal()`, `dialog.show()` and the Popover API, only `showModal()` makes the rest of the document inert and confines focus; popovers give light-dismiss and Escape but leave the page fully interactive behind them.

The `inert` attribute removes a subtree from focus, hit-testing and the accessibility tree in one declaration, which is why it is the correct backdrop mechanism rather than a JS keydown loop that re-queries focusable selectors.

Focus must be restored to the element that opened an overlay; if that element was unmounted while the overlay was open, focus must fall back to a stable ancestor, or the browser resets focus to `<body>` and the keyboard user is silently returned to the top of the page.
Focus set on an element that is later removed from the DOM reverts to `<body>` with no event you can rely on, so any async render that replaces the focused subtree must re-establish focus explicitly.

Autofocusing the first focusable element inside a dialog is wrong when that element is destructive or when the dialog is long; focus the dialog container or its heading so the user hears the dialog's name before its controls.
Scrolling an element into view is not focusing it, and `element.focus({ preventScroll: true })` exists precisely because the two responsibilities are separable and often need to be separated.

viz.archetype: event timeline with a single focus-owner track and ghost baseline
viz.title: Where Did Focus Go?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A horizontal event timeline (click Delete → dialog mounts → data loads → row removed → dialog closes → route changes) drawn above a single 'focus owner' track that names the currently focused element at every instant. A miniature of the app UI sits above with the focus ring drawn in its actual position for the scrubbed instant. A ghost focus-owner track underneath shows the unmanaged implementation collapsing to `<body>` and staying there. All annotations sit on the track itself.
viz.predictPrompt: A user tabs to a table row's Delete button, opens the confirm dialog, confirms, and the row is removed from the DOM while the dialog is closing. Before running: name the element that holds focus 100ms after the dialog closes in (a) a naive implementation and (b) an implementation that saved `document.activeElement` on open and restores it on close. One of these two answers is the same in both cases — which, and why?
controls: Scrub the event timeline forward and back
Toggle managed vs unmanaged focus (ghost track)
Switch the overlay primitive: native showModal + inert / popover / hand-rolled keydown trap
Delete the opener element while the dialog is open and watch the restore chain
Insert an async data load that re-renders the focused subtree mid-dialog
viz.insight: Focus has exactly one owner at every instant, and every unmount, route change and async swap is a moment where that owner can silently become `<body>` — the bug is never visible on screen, only in the next keystroke.
viz.buildNotes: `focuslife.ts` is a pure reducer over an event log producing the focus owner at each tick, with an explicit restore-target fallback chain (opener → opener's stable ancestor → view root). Injected clock, no Date.now. Unit tests assert the opener-unmounted case lands on the table container and never on body, and that the hand-rolled trap variant fails the shift+Tab-from-first-element case. Reduced motion → the full timeline rendered statically with every focus owner labelled.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of a correct modal open/close cycle: restore focus to the saved opener · render the dialog · save `document.activeElement` · move focus to the dialog heading · mark the background inert · remove inert · close the dialog.
drills.answerSketch: save activeElement → render dialog → mark background inert (or use showModal which does both) → move focus to heading → [user acts] → remove inert → close dialog → restore focus to saved opener (with fallback).

drills.prompt: Select every defect in this React modal: it queries `querySelectorAll('a, button, input')` on mount to build a focus loop, listens for `keydown` on Tab only, sets `overflow: hidden` on body, autofocuses the 'Delete permanently' button, and on close calls `document.body.focus()`.
drills.answerSketch: Stale selector list misses [tabindex], summary, contenteditable, audio/video controls, and includes disabled/hidden ones. Tab-only handling misses Shift+Tab wrap and Escape. overflow:hidden is not inertness — background stays focusable and hit-testable. Autofocusing a destructive action. body.focus() is a no-op-shaped reset that loses the opener.

drills.prompt: Of `dialog.show()`, `dialog.showModal()` and `[popover]`, only ______ makes the rest of the document inert. The declarative attribute that achieves the same effect on an arbitrary subtree is ______.
drills.answerSketch: showModal(); inert.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the dialog is now opened from a row that the confirm action deletes, and the table may be empty afterwards. Define your restore-target fallback chain precisely, including the empty-table case.
drills.answerSketch: opener (if still connected via `.isConnected`) → the next/previous sibling row's equivalent control → the table container with tabindex=-1 → the view's h1. Empty table: focus the container, and announce the empty state so the user knows why there is nothing to move to.

drills.prompt: For a three-pane email client, choose ONE route-change strategy: move focus to the new view's h1, or announce the new view via a polite live region and leave focus alone. Commit, then write a timed justification naming the user group each choice hurts.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names that focus movement is what resets the virtual cursor; (2) recognises the three-pane case is special — moving focus to h1 on every list→detail transition destroys list navigation for keyboard users; (3) proposes a hybrid: focus move on full-view navigation, live region + preserved focus on in-pane detail change; (4) names document.title update as required either way; (5) names the group hurt by each: SR users lose context with announce-only, keyboard power users lose their place with focus-always.

failureModes: Hand-rolls a focus trap with a keydown listener over a `querySelectorAll` focusable-selector string, which drifts out of date and misses shadow DOM, iframes, disabled and inert — instead of using `inert` plus `showModal()`.
Announces route changes with a live region but never moves focus, so keyboard users continue tabbing from the previous view's link position.
Puts `autoFocus` on the primary destructive action in a confirm dialog because it 'saves a keystroke'.
Answers 'React handles focus for us', or 'we use a modal library, so it's handled', with no account of what the library actually does on close.
interviewProbes: The user is on page 3 of a list, opens an item, then hits back. Where is focus? Where should it be?
You need a dropdown that must not trap focus and a confirm dialog that must. What do you build each from, and what do you get for free?
Your modal library restores focus on close. The opener was deleted by the modal's own action. What happens?

incl-live-regions.title: Screen Reader Mental Model and Announcement Strategy
objectives: Judge, per event, whether the correct response is a focus move, a polite announcement, an assertive announcement, or silence.
Explain why a live region is a lossy single-lane channel and design throttling accordingly.
State what varies across AT/browser/mode combinations and what that means for a test plan.
claims: Screen reader users navigate primarily by structure — headings, landmarks, links list, form-controls list — rather than linearly, which makes heading hierarchy and landmark labels navigation UI rather than decoration.
A live region only announces mutations that occur after the region element is already present in the accessibility tree; inserting the region and its text in the same tick usually announces nothing.

`aria-live="polite"` queues behind the current utterance while `aria-live="assertive"` interrupts it, so assertive is reserved for content the user must hear immediately — submission failure, session timeout, data loss.
`role="alert"` is equivalent to `aria-live="assertive"` plus `aria-atomic="true"`, and `role="status"` is equivalent to `aria-live="polite"` plus `aria-atomic="true"`.
`aria-atomic="true"` re-reads the entire region on any change, which is right for an 'N of M results' counter and wrong for an append-only log where only the new entry should be spoken.

High-frequency updates must be coalesced before reaching a live region: speech is real-time and single-lane, no AT guarantees delivery of every mutation, and an unthrottled region either floods the user or silently drops most updates.

Screen reader behaviour is a product of AT × browser × interaction mode (virtual/browse vs forms/focus), so verifying a pattern in VoiceOver/Safari is not evidence it works in NVDA/Chrome or JAWS/Chrome.
Moving focus to new content announces it reliably; a live region does not — so prefer focus movement for changes the user initiated, and reserve live regions for changes the user did not initiate.

viz.archetype: single-lane event queue simulator with preemption and drop marking
viz.title: The Announcement Queue
viz.whatIsDrawn: App events (keystrokes in a filter, results-count updates, a toast, a form error) fall from an upper event track into one speech lane below. Each utterance is a block whose width is its spoken duration at the configured speech rate; a polite utterance queues, an assertive one truncates the block it interrupts (drawn as a clipped block with the cut edge marked), and mutations that arrive while the queue is saturated are marked dropped in place. A ghost lane shows the unthrottled implementation for the same event stream.
viz.predictPrompt: A search filter updates a `role="status"` region with 'N results' on every keystroke while the user types 'accessible' — 10 characters in about 1.6 seconds — and a `role="alert"` toast fires at t=1.2s. Before running: how many of the 10 count updates does the user actually hear, does the toast get through, and does the user ever hear the FINAL count?
controls: Type into the filter at a chosen words-per-minute
Switch the region between polite / assertive / role=alert / role=status
viz.insight: The live region is a single lane with a real-time speech budget: announcing more does not mean the user hears more, and the update they most need — the final state — is the one most likely to be lost.
viz.buildNotes: `announce.ts`: injected clock, no Math.random. Models utterance duration from character count at a configurable rate (default ~180 wpm), polite queueing, assertive preemption, and a bounded queue that drops. Unit test asserts the pedagogical claim directly — that at 0ms debounce the final count is NOT the last thing spoken, and that at ≥500ms it is. If the test fails, the teaching claim is wrong and the module must not ship.

drills.prompt:
Select the defect: `{error &&
{error}
}` inside a form component that re-renders on submit.
drills.answerSketch: The region does not exist in the accessibility tree before the message appears, so the mutation that would trigger the announcement is the insertion of the region itself — commonly silent. Fix: render the empty region unconditionally and mutate its text content.

drills.prompt: For each event, choose: move focus · polite live region · assertive live region · say nothing. (1) autosave completed (2) session expires in 60s (3) filter results count changed while typing (4) payment declined after submit (5) a background job finished that the user started 5 minutes ago (6) an optimistic UI update rolled back.
drills.answerSketch: 1 polite (debounced, or nothing if a persistent visible indicator exists). 2 assertive. 3 polite + debounce ≥500ms. 4 move focus to the error summary (focus move beats announcement — the user must act). 5 polite. 6 assertive or focus move — silent rollback is data-loss-shaped.

drills.prompt: `role="status"` is equivalent to `aria-live="______"` plus `aria-atomic="______"`. `role="alert"` is equivalent to `aria-live="______"` plus `aria-atomic="______"`.
drills.answerSketch: polite/true; assertive/true.

drills.prompt: An append-only chat transcript is wrapped in `<div role="log" aria-atomic="true">`. What does the user hear on the 40th message, and what is the one-attribute fix?
drills.answerSketch: The entire transcript is re-read from the top on every new message. Fix: aria-atomic="false" (which is role=log's default — the bug is the explicit override).

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: search results now stream in over 8 seconds instead of arriving at once. Redesign the announcement strategy, and say what you announce at t=0, during, and at completion.
drills.answerSketch: t=0: polite 'Searching'. During: silence — do not announce partial counts. Completion: polite final count, or focus move to the results heading if the user submitted explicitly. Add aria-busy="true" on the results container during the stream so AT can suppress intermediate reads.

failureModes: Wraps every important message in `aria-live="assertive"`, producing an experience of constant interruption that users disable.
Conditionally renders the live region together with its message and cannot work out why nothing is ever announced.
Treats a live region as a substitute for focus management after a user-initiated action, leaving the keyboard user's focus stranded on the submit button.
Tests once with VoiceOver on macOS, declares the pattern verified, and ships something NVDA reads twice and JAWS not at all.
interviewProbes: The results count updates as the user types. What does a screen reader user hear? What do you want them to hear?
When would you deliberately announce nothing?
Your toast system uses role=alert for everything including 'Copied to clipboard'. Defend or fix it.

incl-forms-errors.title: Accessible Forms, Validation and Error Messaging
objectives: Design the labelling, description and error-association wiring for a control so that its full announcement string is correct.
Choose a validation timing strategy and defend it against the 'instant feedback' request.
Map form requirements onto the specific WCAG 2.2 criteria that govern them.
claims: Every control needs a programmatically associated label; `<label for>` or a wrapping `<label>` is preferred over `aria-label` because it also enlarges the click target and gives voice-control users a visible word to speak.
Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears on input, commonly fails 4.5:1 contrast, and is exposed as the accessible name only as a last-resort fallback.

Error text must be associated to its control with `aria-describedby` AND the control marked `aria-invalid="true"`, so a user who tabs back to the field hears the error again rather than only once when it appeared.

An error summary at the top of the form — a focusable container listing each error as a link to its field, focused on failed submit — is the pattern that serves screen-reader and screen-magnifier users alike, because per-field errors are invisible when the field is off-screen at 400% zoom.
Multiple ids in `aria-describedby` are announced in the order of the id list, not in DOM order, so hint/counter/error ordering is something you control and must decide.
Validate on submit, and on blur only after the first submit attempt; validating on every keystroke announces errors for input the user has not finished typing.
WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A) forbids requiring the same information twice within a single process unless re-entry is essential or the field is auto-populated.

WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) forbids a cognitive function test as the only authentication factor and requires that password fields permit paste and support password managers — in practice, correct `autocomplete` tokens and no paste-blocking.

viz.archetype: association-wiring overlay on a live form, with the computed announcement string rendered in place
viz.title: Form Wiring: What the Control Actually Announces
viz.whatIsDrawn: A real checkout form. Connector lines are drawn from each control to its name source and each of its description sources, entirely inside the form's frame. Directly beneath each control, the computed announcement string is rendered in announcement order: role · name · required/invalid state · description. A ghost overlay shows the same form built with placeholders-as-labels and red-border-only errors, whose announcement strings are visibly empty.
viz.predictPrompt: A field has a visible `<label>`, a hint paragraph, a live error message and a character counter, all wired through one `aria-describedby="hint err counter"`. Before running: in what order are these read, what happens to that order when the error appears and then clears, and what does a user hear if you instead re-order the ids to `"err hint counter"` only while invalid?
controls: Toggle each association independently: label / each describedby id / aria-invalid / required / autocomplete
Trigger a submit with three errors and watch the summary appear and take focus
Switch validation timing: on-change / on-blur / on-blur-after-first-submit / on-submit
viz.insight: The announcement string is assembled from associations in a fixed order — an error the user can see but that is not referenced by `aria-describedby` does not exist for anyone who is not looking at that pixel.
viz.buildNotes: Reuses `axtree.ts` from incl-a11y-tree for name/description computation rather than reimplementing it — this is the payoff for building that sim properly. Adds `formstate.ts` for validation timing (pure reducer, injected clock for debounce). Unit test asserts describedby order follows the id list, not DOM order. Reduced motion → all wires and announcement strings rendered at once.

drills.prompt:
Select every defect: an email input with `placeholder="Email address"` and no label; an error rendered as `

Invalid email

` immediately after it with no id; `aria-required="true"` but no `required`; and a password field with `onPaste={e => e.preventDefault()}`.
drills.answerSketch: Placeholder-as-label (no reliable name, disappears, contrast). Error not associated via aria-describedby and control not marked aria-invalid. aria-required without required (state duplicated, native validation lost). Paste blocking fails SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication and breaks password managers. Bonus: colour-only error signalling fails 1.4.1.

drills.prompt:
Wire this input for an error state. `` and `

…

`. Then name the one additional element that must exist on failed submit.
drills.answerSketch: aria-invalid="true"; aria-describedby="email-err email-hint". Additional element: a focusable error summary at the top of the form linking to #email.

drills.prompt: Map each requirement to the WCAG 2.2 success criterion it satisfies, or to 'none': (1) shipping address is pre-filled from the billing address entered two steps earlier (2) the password field supports paste (3) the 'Country' select has a visible label (4) error text says 'Enter a date in the format DD/MM/YYYY' not just 'Invalid' (5) a Help link sits in the same place on every step (6) autocomplete="family-name" on the surname field.
drills.answerSketch: 1 → 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A). 2 → 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (AA). 3 → 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions / 1.3.1. 4 → 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA). 5 → 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A). 6 → 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (AA).

drills.prompt: The PM wants inline validation on every keystroke for 'faster feedback'. Name what breaks for a screen-reader user, what breaks for a user with a motor impairment, and write the counter-proposal you would actually ship.
drills.answerSketch: SR: the live region announces 'invalid email' after the third character of every email address, repeatedly, and floods the queue. Motor: errors appear and vanish under the cursor mid-entry. Counter-proposal: validate on submit; after first submit, validate that field on blur; allow keystroke validation only for positive-progress affordances (password strength meter) that are not announced assertively.

drills.prompt: A 40-field insurance form on mobile. Choose: error summary at top, or inline-only errors with scroll-to-first-error. Commit, then write a timed defence.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) names that inline-only + scroll does not move focus, so keyboard/SR users are not taken there; (2) recognises the magnifier case — at 400% zoom the inline error is off-screen; (3) accounts for the mobile constraint where a top summary may require scrolling back; (4) proposes both — summary that receives focus, each entry linking to its field, plus inline errors; (5) names the cost: two places to keep in sync, and a summary that must be re-rendered not re-mounted to announce correctly.

failureModes: Signals errors with a red border and red text only, failing both 1.4.1 Use of Color and every non-visual user simultaneously.
Uses the placeholder as the label to fit a compact design, then adds `aria-label` with different text, breaking 2.5.3 Label in Name for voice control.
Puts the error in a live region but never in `aria-describedby`, so it is announced once and is then unreachable when the user tabs back.
Sets `aria-invalid="true"` on every untouched required field at mount, so the whole form announces as invalid before the user types anything.
interviewProbes: Submit fails with three errors. Describe every single thing that happens in the next 500ms, for a keyboard-only user.
Your design has no visible labels — floating placeholders only. What do you do?
Why is `aria-describedby` and not just a live region the right home for error text?

incl-perception.title: Contrast, Non-Colour Affordances, Zoom and Motion
objectives: Judge whether a colour pair passes for a given text size or UI role, and state which threshold applies and why.
Identify colour-only information and specify the second affordance that fixes it.
Judge a layout against reflow, text-spacing and target-size criteria without a tool.
claims: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) requires 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text, where large means at least 24px (18pt) regular or 18.66px (14pt) bold.

WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast requires 3:1 for the parts of a UI component needed to identify it — an input's boundary, a focus indicator, a toggle's on-state, a chart's data line — not for the component's entire surface.

WCAG contrast is a ratio of relative luminance and is blind to hue, so it passes some pairs that are unreadable for colour-vision-deficient users and fails some that read fine; APCA is the perceptual successor being developed for WCAG 3 but is not a conformance requirement in 2026.

SC 1.4.1 Use of Color forbids colour as the ONLY visual means of conveying information — a red-only error, a colour-only chart series, or a link distinguished from surrounding text by colour alone unless that pair is at least 3:1 against the body text AND another cue appears on hover and focus.

SC 1.4.10 Reflow requires content to be usable at 320 CSS px wide (equivalently 400% zoom on a 1280px viewport) with no two-dimensional scrolling, which makes fixed-width tables and `100vw` sticky bars real failures rather than polish items.

SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing requires no loss of content when the user forces line-height 1.5×, paragraph spacing 2×, letter-spacing 0.12em and word-spacing 0.16em — fixed-height containers with `overflow: hidden` fail it.
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA) requires pointer targets of at least 24×24 CSS px, or enough spacing that 24px-diameter circles centred on adjacent targets do not overlap.

`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` means removing large-scale movement — parallax, slide transitions, autoplay, spin — not removing all feedback; cross-fades and opacity changes are the accepted substitute, and the preference must be honoured by JS-driven animation too, not only by CSS transitions.

viz.archetype: parameter-space explorer with threshold contours and an in-plot sample swatch
viz.title: The Contrast Plane
viz.whatIsDrawn: A 2D plane of foreground lightness × background lightness with WCAG threshold contours drawn as bands (3:1, 4.5:1, 7:1). The currently selected token pair is plotted as a point, and a live text sample is rendered inside the plot at that point so the swatch and its coordinates are never separated. A ghost set of APCA Lc contours can be overlaid on the same plane so the disagreement between the two models is visible in place. Max 7 labels.
viz.predictPrompt: Your design system's body text is #767676 on #FFFFFF — the classic 'lightest grey that passes AA'. Before running: (a) what is its exact ratio, (b) does it still pass when the same grey sits on a #F5F5F5 card, and (c) does a deuteranopia simulation change either verdict? Two of these three have answers most engineers get wrong.
controls: Drag the foreground/background pair anywhere on the plane
Toggle WCAG 2.x contours vs the APCA ghost contours
Apply a colour-vision simulation: deuteranopia / protanopia / tritanopia
Switch the sample between 16px regular, 24px regular and 14px bold to move the applicable threshold band
Switch the sample from text to a 1px input border to jump to the 1.4.11 threshold
viz.insight: Contrast is a luminance ratio with hard thresholds and no notion of hue — passing it is necessary but never sufficient, and which threshold applies depends on text size and on whether the pixel is text or a component boundary.
viz.buildNotes: `contrast.ts` implements WCAG 2.x relative luminance and ratio, plus APCA Lc. Deterministic, no clock, no RNG. Unit tests pin the reference values: #767676 on #FFFFFF = 4.54:1 (passes AA body), #767676 on #F5F5F5 ≈ 4.15:1 (fails), #808080 on #FFFFFF ≈ 3.95:1 (fails). If those tests drift, the module's central teaching example is wrong. Reduced motion → static plane with the contours and three worked example points pre-plotted.

drills.prompt: Rank these five pairs by contrast ratio, highest first, without a tool: #767676/#FFFFFF · #FFFFFF/#0066CC · #595959/#FFFFFF · #767676/#F5F5F5 · #949494/#FFFFFF. Then state which pass AA for 16px body text.

Map each design-review comment to the SC it violates, or to 'no SC': (1) required fields are marked only by red label text (2) the focus ring is #C7C7C7 on #FFFFFF (3) the pricing table needs horizontal scrolling at 400% zoom (4) chips truncate at a fixed 32px height when line-height is increased (5) the 20×20px close button in the toast (6) the hero video autoplays with a parallax scroll.
drills.answerSketch: 1 → 1.4.1 Use of Color. 2 → 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (≈1.4:1). 3 → 1.4.10 Reflow. 4 → 1.4.12 Text Spacing. 5 → 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum). 6 → 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA) plus 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide; honour prefers-reduced-motion.

drills.prompt: Select every defect in this status component: statuses are shown as coloured dots (green/amber/red) with a `title` attribute; the amber dot is #F0B429 on #FFFFFF; the tooltip appears on hover only; and the component is 16×16 CSS px.
drills.answerSketch: Colour-only information (1.4.1). Amber on white ≈ 1.9:1 fails 1.4.11 for a meaningful graphic. title-on-hover is unavailable to touch and keyboard (and fails 1.4.13 Content on Hover expectations). 16×16 fails 2.5.8 if it is an interactive target.

drills.prompt: Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, which is the correct treatment for a 300ms slide-in panel? (a) remove the transition entirely (b) cross-fade over the same duration (c) keep the slide but halve the duration (d) disable all transitions app-wide via `* { transition: none !important }`
drills.answerSketch: (b). The preference targets large-scale movement, not feedback. (a) and (d) remove the state-change cue that helps users with cognitive disabilities; (d) additionally breaks focus-ring transitions and any transitionend listener.

drills.prompt: Marketing mandates the brand green #4CAF50 for primary buttons with white label text, at 16px. Compute the problem, then state exactly what you change and what you refuse.
drills.answerSketch: #FFF on #4CAF50 ≈ 2.8:1 — fails AA for 16px body and even for large text. Options: darken the brand green for the button surface only (a shade token, not the brand colour), or use dark text on the green, or reserve the brand green for non-text surfaces where 3:1 against adjacent colour is the only requirement. Refuse: shipping white 16px on the untouched brand green.

failureModes: Checks contrast for text only, then ships a 1.6:1 input border and a focus ring that vanishes on the branded surface.
Treats AAA (7:1) as the target everywhere and destroys the visual hierarchy, or treats AA as optional for 'secondary' and 'disabled-looking' text.
Implements reduced motion as `* { animation: none; transition: none }`, removing every state-change cue and breaking transitionend-dependent logic.
Cites the inactive-component exemption to justify disabled text that no one can read, and never checks whether the control is actually inactive.
interviewProbes: Your PM says the grey secondary text 'looks fine'. How do you settle it in 30 seconds without opening a tool?
Give me three ways to signal 'error' that are not colour, and say which one you'd pick for a data table with 40 rows.
What breaks in this layout at 400% zoom, and which criterion is that?

incl-complex-widgets.title: Complex Widgets: Combobox, Tree, Grid and Drag Alternatives
objectives: Implement a named APG pattern's full keyboard contract as an explicit state machine rather than ad-hoc handlers.
Identify what virtualization, filtering and async loading break in a widget's ARIA, and specify the fix.
Design a single-pointer, non-dragging alternative for any drag interaction.
claims: The APG combobox pattern places `role="combobox"` on the text input with `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` referencing the popup, and `aria-activedescendant` naming the highlighted option — DOM focus never leaves the input.
Arrow-key traversal in a combobox must not commit a selection; commit happens on Enter or click, and Escape closes the listbox without committing.

Virtualized listboxes report the wrong size to AT unless `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` are set explicitly on each rendered option, because AT counts the rendered DOM children — a 10,000-row virtual list otherwise announces 'option 3 of 20'.

`role="grid"` and `role="treegrid"` change the keyboard contract to a 2D arrow-key model with Home/End and Ctrl+Home/End and require every cell to be reachable; a table that is merely sortable and filterable should remain a plain `<table>` with no grid role.

A data `<table>` needs `<th scope="col">` / `<th scope="row">` and a `<caption>`; adding ARIA table roles on top of a real table almost always destroys correct native table semantics rather than improving them.

WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA) requires a single-pointer alternative to any drag operation — a 'Move to…' menu, or a select-then-place interaction — which is a separate obligation from the keyboard requirement in 2.1.1.

Natively disabled controls are removed from the tab sequence and are often skipped entirely by AT; for controls the user must be able to discover and interrogate — toolbar buttons, menu items — `aria-disabled="true"` with suppressed activation keeps them focusable and announceable.

A widget should adopt a named APG pattern and its keyboard contract wholesale; inventing a hybrid produces a widget whose announced role sets expectations the implementation does not meet, which is worse than an unlabelled div.

viz.archetype: explicit state machine driven by real keystrokes, with the ARIA attributes projected onto the rendered widget
viz.title: Combobox State Machine
viz.whatIsDrawn: A state chart (closed · open-none-active · open-active · committed) with the current state highlighted and every transition edge labelled with the key that causes it, drawn directly beside a live combobox. The combobox's live ARIA attribute values are rendered as small inline badges pinned to the element they sit on, and the announcement string appears as an inline caption anchored under the input — nothing in a side panel.
viz.predictPrompt: In an autocomplete combobox, the user types 'ca', presses ArrowDown twice, presses Escape, then presses Tab. Before running: what value is committed to the input, what is `aria-expanded` at each of those four moments, and at which step (if any) does the user hear an option name?
controls: Press keys — ArrowDown/Up, Enter, Escape, Tab, Home/End, printable characters — and watch the machine transition
Switch combobox variant: autocomplete none / list / both (inline autocomplete)
Toggle virtualization on the listbox to expose the aria-setsize/aria-posinset break in place
Toggle an async 'loading results' state and watch aria-busy and the announcement
viz.insight: A widget's ARIA role is a public promise about its keyboard contract; the state machine IS that contract, and every ARIA attribute is a projection of current state — which is why divergence between them is a category of bug, not a detail.
viz.buildNotes: `combobox.ts` is a pure reducer (state, key) → {state, aria, announcement}. Unit tested row by row against the APG combobox keyboard table, including the inline-autocomplete selection-range behaviour and the Escape-twice case. The viz renders the machine and the widget from the same state object so they structurally cannot diverge — this is the point of the module and the point of the sim/viz split. Reduced motion → machine and widget rendered statically with a key-log the learner steps through.

drills.prompt: Select every defect in this combobox: `onArrowDown` calls `options[i].focus()`; the popup is `role="menu"` with `role="menuitem"` children; the input has `aria-owns` but no `aria-expanded`; and each rendered option has no `aria-posinset` in a windowed list of 8 over 4,000 items.
drills.answerSketch: Moving DOM focus to options breaks typing and inline autocomplete — use aria-activedescendant. menu/menuitem is the wrong pattern (menus are for commands, not value selection) — use listbox/option. Missing aria-expanded means the user is never told the popup opened. Missing setsize/posinset makes a 4,000-item list announce as 8.

drills.prompt: Order the tree pattern's keyboard contract for a collapsed parent node with focus on it: ArrowRight expands · ArrowRight moves to first child · ArrowLeft moves to parent · ArrowLeft collapses. Give the sequence of effects for ArrowRight, ArrowRight, ArrowLeft, ArrowLeft.
drills.answerSketch: ArrowRight expands (node now open, focus stays). ArrowRight moves to first child. ArrowLeft moves to parent (child had no children to collapse). ArrowLeft collapses the parent.

drills.prompt: The option list grows from 200 to 50,000 and must be virtualized. Select every ARIA guarantee that breaks first: (a) aria-activedescendant referencing an unrendered id (b) aria-setsize/posinset (c) aria-expanded (d) the listbox's accessible name (e) Home/End reaching the true first/last option (f) type-ahead matching across unrendered items.
drills.answerSketch: a, b, e, f. aria-activedescendant must reference a rendered element, so the window must always contain the active option. setsize/posinset must be explicit. Home/End must scroll-and-render the true endpoints. Type-ahead must run against the full data set, not the window. (c) and (d) are unaffected.

drills.prompt: Complete the option update on ArrowDown: set `aria-activedescendant` on the ______ to the id of the new active option; set `aria-selected` to ______ on it; and set `aria-selected` to ______ on the previous one. Which of these three is wrong for a single-select listbox where arrow keys do not commit?
drills.answerSketch: input (combobox); the aria-selected toggling is the trap — in a combobox where traversal does not commit, use only aria-activedescendant for the highlight and reserve aria-selected for the actual committed value.

drills.prompt: A Kanban board where dragging cards between columns IS the product. The PM says a non-drag alternative is scope creep. Commit to a position, then write a timed defence.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) names SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements as AA, distinct from 2.1.1 keyboard; (2) proposes a concrete alternative — a 'Move to…' menu on each card, or select-then-place — not 'add keyboard support'; (3) notes the alternative also serves trackpad-averse, tremor and touch users, i.e. it is not a niche build; (4) estimates cost honestly against the drag implementation already needed; (5) states what the announcement is when a card moves (polite live region: 'Card X moved to Column Y, position 3 of 7').

failureModes: Puts `role="grid"` on a plain data table because it 'sounds more accessible', then fails to implement 2D navigation, leaving a widget that promises a contract it does not honour.
Moves DOM focus into the listbox options, which breaks typing, inline autocomplete and IME composition all at once.
Ships drag-only reordering and schedules keyboard support as a follow-up that never lands.
Announces 'option 3 of 20' from an 8-row window over a 10,000-item virtual list and never notices because axe reports zero violations.
interviewProbes: Draw me the state machine for your combobox. Now tell me what happens on Escape in each state.
This listbox has 50,000 options and is virtualized. What did you have to do that a naive implementation would not?
Your board supports drag-and-drop. Walk me through the same task with one finger and no dragging.

incl-a11y-nfr.title: Accessibility as an NFR: Conformance Target, Test Strategy, CI Gates
objectives: State a conformance target as a testable NFR: standard, level, and scope.
Judge what an automated tool can and cannot license you to claim, and place each detection method where it earns its cost.
Design a CI gate that survives a legacy codebase without being disabled in week one.
claims: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023, is backward compatible with 2.1, added 9 success criteria, obsoleted SC 4.1.1 Parsing, and moved SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible from Level AA to Level A.

A conformance target is a triple — standard + level + scope (which flows, which viewports, which AT/browser pairs) — and 'we are WCAG compliant' without all three is not a testable NFR and cannot be gated.

Automated tooling such as axe-core detects on the order of a third of WCAG issues and is structurally silent on focus order, announcement quality, whether alt text is meaningful, and whether a widget's keyboard contract matches the role it announces.

The efficient ladder is axe in component tests (jest-axe / @axe-core/playwright) → a keyboard-only pass per critical flow → a screen-reader pass on changed flows → a periodic external audit; each rung catches a class the rung below structurally cannot.

A CI gate must fail on NEW violations against a committed baseline of known ones; a gate that fails on all existing violations in a legacy codebase is disabled within a week and then provides nothing.

Component-level axe runs attribute a violation to an owner and run before composition hides it, but only page-level runs catch landmark structure, heading-order and duplicate-id problems that exist solely in the composition.

European Accessibility Act obligations applied from 28 June 2025 to consumer-facing digital products and services in the EU, with EN 301 549 — which incorporates at least WCAG 2.1 Level AA — as the harmonised standard, making a named conformance level a legal, not aspirational, artifact.

The design system is where the accessibility budget compounds: a keyboard and ARIA contract fixed once in a shared Dialog or Combobox propagates to every consumer, whereas the same fix applied per-feature must be re-applied per-feature forever.

viz.archetype: detection-coverage matrix with staged fill and an in-frame catch-rate counter
viz.title: What Automation Cannot See
viz.whatIsDrawn: A matrix. Rows are nine real defect classes shipped in one release: missing alt, colour-only error, wrong focus order, unnamed icon button, div-as-button, phantom tab stop inside aria-hidden, misleading heading level, unannounced route change, drag-only reorder. Columns are detection methods: axe in component tests, axe on pages in E2E, keyboard-only pass, screen-reader pass, external audit. Cells fill as each method is enabled. The running catch-rate is printed inside the matrix beside the last enabled column, with a ghost line marking the axe-only level.
viz.predictPrompt: You add axe-core to every component test and to every page in the E2E suite, and the whole suite is green. Before running: of these nine defect classes, how many does that suite catch? Then name which single ADDITIONAL method has the highest marginal yield — and which uncaught defect is the one most likely to generate a legal complaint.
controls: Switch gate policy: fail on any violation vs fail on new violations against a baseline
Inject a new defect class and see which column, if any, catches it
Set team size and per-method cost to see the catch-rate-per-hour ranking change
viz.insight: Automation is a regression floor, not a measurement of accessibility. The gate's job is to stop new debt; the keyboard-only pass is the highest marginal yield per hour, and no amount of axe coverage substitutes for it.
viz.buildNotes: The defect → detectable-by mapping is a typed table validated at build time against the axe-core rule catalogue, so if a future axe release gains a rule, the build fails rather than the module silently teaching a stale claim. No RNG, no clock. This is the cheapest viz in the domain — it is a matrix, not a simulation — which is why buildCost is lower here.

drills.prompt: An external audit returns 8 findings. Assign each to the CHEAPEST method that would have caught it before release: (1) an icon button with no accessible name (2) a modal you cannot Escape out of (3) alt text reading 'image1.png' (4) the checkout error summary is never announced (5) a duplicate id after two components composed (6) 2.1:1 focus ring on the primary CTA (7) tab order jumps from the header to the footer and back (8) the date picker announces role=grid but has no 2D navigation.
drills.answerSketch: 1 axe component. 2 keyboard pass. 3 human review/audit (axe flags empty alt, not meaningless alt). 4 screen-reader pass. 5 axe page-level. 6 axe component (colour-contrast rules cover focus indicators only partially — accept axe page or design review). 7 keyboard pass. 8 screen-reader pass or manual widget review.

drills.prompt: Your CI reports 'axe: 0 violations across 47 pages'. Which claim is licensed? (a) the app is WCAG 2.2 AA conformant (b) the app has no known automatically-detectable violations in tested states (c) screen reader users can complete all flows (d) the app meets EN 301 549
drills.answerSketch: (b), and note the phrase 'in tested states' — axe sees only the DOM state the test rendered, so a closed modal, an error state, or a hover-only tooltip is untested by construction.

drills.prompt: Legal moves the target from WCAG 2.1 AA to 2.2 AA. Select the criteria that are new at Level A or AA in 2.2, and name the two most likely to be expensive in an existing product: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) · 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) · 2.4.13 Focus Appearance · 2.5.7 Dragging Movements · 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) · 3.2.6 Consistent Help · 3.3.7 Redundant Entry · 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) · 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) · 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
drills.answerSketch: New at A/AA in 2.2: 2.4.11 (AA), 2.5.7 (AA), 2.5.8 (AA), 3.2.6 (A), 3.3.7 (A), 3.3.8 (AA). 2.4.12, 2.4.13 and 3.3.9 are AAA. 1.4.13 is from 2.1, not new. Most expensive in an existing product: 2.5.8 Target Size (touches every dense table/toolbar) and 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (requires a whole alternative interaction).

drills.prompt: Select every defect in this CI setup: axe runs nightly, only on `/` and `/pricing`, fails the job on any violation, has no baseline, and its failures notify a shared #frontend channel with no owner.
drills.answerSketch: Nightly not per-PR (feedback arrives after merge). Two static pages, no authenticated or error states. Fail-on-any with no baseline on a legacy app → disabled within a week. No component-level runs → no attribution. Shared channel with no owner → alerts become noise.

drills.prompt: A legacy app with 4,000 existing axe violations and a hard EAA deadline. Design the gate you would ship on Monday, commit to it, then defend it in writing under time.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) baseline the 4,000 and fail only on new violations, per PR, per component; (2) rank the existing 4,000 by user-flow criticality, not by rule count; (3) put a keyboard pass into the definition of done for the 5 revenue-critical flows immediately — it is the highest yield and needs no tooling; (4) name the conformance target as a triple and get it written down; (5) put the spend in the design system first so fixes compound; (6) state what you will NOT do: a full remediation sprint that regresses the moment it ends.

failureModes: Answers 'we run axe in CI' as the whole accessibility strategy, with no account of the two-thirds axe cannot see.
Sets the gate to fail on any violation in a legacy codebase, watches it get disabled, and concludes gating does not work.
Says 'WCAG AA compliant' with no scope — no flows, no viewports, no AT/browser matrix — and cannot say how it would be verified.
Runs axe only on the default rendered state, so every error state, modal and hover-only affordance is untested by construction.
interviewProbes: Write the accessibility NFR for this system as one sentence a QA engineer could test.
You inherit an app with thousands of violations and a deadline. What ships Monday?
Where in the org do you spend the accessibility budget for the best compounding return, and why there?

incl-i18n-arch.title: i18n Architecture: Messages, ICU MessageFormat and Locale Bundles
objectives: Design a message pipeline from source extraction through translation to runtime formatting, and name what each stage protects.
Write ICU messages with correct plural, select and rich-text interpolation for languages with more than two plural categories.
Specify locale resolution, bundle splitting and a pseudo-localization gate.
claims: Translatable strings must live in extractable message files keyed by a stable id, not inline in JSX with concatenation, because concatenated fragments cannot be reordered by a translator and produce ungrammatical output in languages with different word order.

ICU MessageFormat `plural` is required because plural categories are language-specific: English has 2 (one, other), Russian has 4 (one, few, many, other), Arabic has 6 (zero, one, two, few, many, other) — an `n === 1` ternary is wrong for most of the world's users.

ICU `select` handles grammatical gender and other enumerated variants, and `selectordinal` handles ordinals ('1st', '2nd', '3rd'), which follow a different rule set from cardinal plurals in the same language.
Rich text inside a message must be expressed as tags interpolated by the runtime (`You have {count} items left`) rather than by splitting the sentence into three strings around a React component.

MessageFormat 2.0 reached stable status in Unicode LDML 47/48 during 2025, but the TC39 `Intl.MessageFormat` proposal is still at Stage 2 and the mainstream React libraries (FormatJS/react-intl, Lingui) remain on ICU MessageFormat 1 — so in 2026 you plan for MF1 with an eventual migration, not for a native runtime.

Locale message bundles must be code-split per locale and loaded on demand; shipping every locale in the main bundle multiplies the translation payload by the locale count for zero benefit to any individual user.

Locale resolution has a defined precedence — persisted explicit user choice > URL path or subdomain > `Accept-Language` / `navigator.languages` > default — and the resolved locale must appear in the URL so links are shareable and pages are crawlable.

Build-time pseudo-localization (`[!!! Ŧĥîš îš ŧȩẋŧ !!!]`) catches hard-coded strings, concatenation and length-fragile layout before a single translator is hired, and is the cheapest i18n gate that exists.

viz.archetype: pipeline with an inspectable payload at each stage and a failing ghost lane
viz.title: The Message Pipeline
viz.whatIsDrawn: A left-to-right pipeline: JSX source → extracted ICU message with id and translator description → per-locale catalogue → compiled AST → formatted output. One real message travels through it and its representation is drawn at each stage. A ghost lane beneath carries the same sentence built by string concatenation and visibly fractures at the Russian and Arabic stages, with the break annotated on the stage where it occurs.
viz.predictPrompt: The message `{count} items selected` is translated by pluralizing the word 'items' alone. It renders correctly in English and German. Before running: name the first locale where it breaks, the exact grammatical reason, and what the count value 21 does in Russian that 2 does not.
controls: Switch target locale: en / de / ru / ar / ja
Set count to 0, 1, 2, 5, 21, 100 and watch the selected plural category change per locale
Toggle pseudo-localization on the source stage
viz.insight: A message is a function of (locale, arguments), not a string. Every stage upstream in the pipeline exists to preserve that function through a process — translation — that would otherwise destroy it.
viz.buildNotes: `plural.ts` wraps `Intl.PluralRules` rather than hand-rolling category tables. Unit tests pin: ru → 1:one, 2:few, 5:many, 21:one, 100:many; ar → 0:zero, 1:one, 2:two, 3:few, 11:many, 100:other; ja → all:other. A tiny ICU-subset formatter handles plural/select/tag interpolation and is tested against a golden file. Catalogue fixtures are original translations, not copied from any product's message files. Reduced motion → all five stages rendered simultaneously with the payloads visible.

drills.prompt:
Select every defect: `

{t('you.have')} {count} {count === 1 ? t('item') : t('items')} {t('in.cart')}

`, where the keys are `you.have = "You have"`, `item = "item"`, `items = "items"`, `in.cart = "in your cart"`.
drills.answerSketch: Sentence split into four un-reorderable fragments (word order differs in Japanese, German subordinate clauses, Arabic). Ternary pluralization ignores few/many/zero/two categories. Fragment keys give the translator no context. The bold tag position is fixed in English structure. Fix: one ICU message with a plural argument and a `<b>` tag placeholder.

drills.prompt: Write the ICU message for 'N results found' handling zero as a special case: `{count, ______, =0 {No results found} ______ {# result found} ______ {# results found}}`.
drills.answerSketch: plural, one, other. Note `=0` is an exact match distinct from the `zero` category, and `#` interpolates the formatted number.

drills.prompt: Russian has ______ plural categories. The browser API that reports which category a number falls into for a given locale is `Intl.______`. Ordinals like '3rd' require the ICU keyword ______, not `plural`.
drills.answerSketch: 4 (one, few, many, other); Intl.PluralRules; selectordinal.

drills.prompt: For each string decide: plain · plural · select · selectordinal · none-of-these-it-needs-restructuring. (1) 'Delete' (2) '3 files uploaded' (3) 'Alex added you to her team' (4) 'You finished 2nd' (5) 'Showing 1-20 of 4,312' (6) 'Last edited by Sam 3 minutes ago'.
drills.answerSketch: 1 plain. 2 plural. 3 select (gender of the actor) — and the name must be an argument, never concatenated. 4 selectordinal. 5 plain with number args, but the range needs Intl.NumberFormat.formatRange and the whole string must be one message. 6 select/plural combined with Intl.RelativeTimeFormat — the 'ago' part must not be a separate string.

drills.prompt: Product adds Japanese, which has exactly one plural category. Plurals are therefore a non-issue. Name three problems Japanese introduces that plural rules do not cover at all.
drills.answerSketch: Counters (the classifier changes with the noun: 3枚 vs 3本 vs 3人 — one plural category, many count words). No spaces between words, so word-boundary line breaking and truncation need Intl.Segmenter, not a space split. Vertical text and different line-height/ruby needs. Also: name order (family name first) and no capitalisation, so any text-transform or 'sort by first name' logic is wrong.

failureModes: Writes `count === 1 ? 'item' : 'items'` and considers pluralization solved.
Splits sentences around React components: `t('you.have')` + `{count}` + `t('items')`, producing four untranslatable fragments.
Uses the English source string as the message key, so a copy edit silently invalidates every existing translation.
Loads all 24 locale bundles eagerly because 'the JSON is only 40KB each' — 960KB of payload for one user's one locale.
interviewProbes: Show me how you'd write '{n} people liked this' so it works in Russian and Arabic.
Where does the locale live — URL, cookie, header, store — and what breaks with each choice?
How do you find hard-coded strings before a translator does?

incl-intl-format.title: Intl, Time Zones and the Data Model for Dates and Money
objectives: Diagnose date bugs by locating where the code confused an instant with a wall-clock reading.
Choose the correct storage representation for each kind of temporal value.
Replace ad-hoc formatting and sorting with the correct `Intl` API and cache it correctly.
claims: `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `NumberFormat`, `ListFormat`, `RelativeTimeFormat`, `PluralRules`, `Collator` and `Segmenter` ship CLDR data inside the browser, so a formatting library adds bundle weight for behaviour the platform already provides.

`Intl.*` constructors are expensive relative to their `format` calls; construct once per (locale, options) and cache — constructing a formatter inside a render or inside a list `.map()` is a measurable performance defect on large tables.
