A point in time must be stored and transported as an absolute instant (UTC or epoch) with the time zone kept separately as an IANA identifier such as `Europe/Berlin`; a fixed offset like `+02:00` is not a time zone and cannot survive a DST transition or a political offset change.

'Today' is a function of the viewer's time zone, so any server-computed day boundary — daily digest, streak, report bucket — is wrong for users outside the server's zone unless the boundary is computed in the user's zone.

`Intl.NumberFormat` with `style: 'currency'` derives symbol, position and fraction digits from the currency code rather than the locale: JPY has 0 fraction digits and KWD has 3, which is why money must not be stored as a float or formatted with a hard-coded two decimals.

Sort order is locale-dependent: `Intl.Collator` places 'ä' with 'a' in German and after 'z' in Swedish, so `localeCompare` or a cached `Collator` must replace `<` on strings anywhere the user sees the resulting order.

Locale and language are separable preferences: `en-GB` and `en-US` differ in date order, first day of week, and quotation marks, and a user may legitimately want an English UI with de-DE formatting — so the formatting locale must be a distinct setting from the translation language.

Temporal shipped in Firefox 139 (May 2025) and Chrome 144 (January 2026) but is not Baseline while Safari lags, so a 2026 production app either polyfills it or keeps a date library — while still modelling instants and zoned date-times the way Temporal does.

viz.archetype: absolute-time axis with multiple wall-clock lanes and in-lane day boundaries
viz.title: One Instant, Many Clocks
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single horizontal absolute-time (UTC) axis at the top. Below it, three zone lanes — America/Los_Angeles, Europe/Berlin, Asia/Kolkata — each showing its local wall-clock reading and drawing its own day boundary as a vertical rule inside the lane. A DST transition appears as a visible step in the Berlin lane. One event marker sits at a chosen instant and projects a line down into all three lanes so the same instant's three different day labels are readable at once.
viz.predictPrompt: A daily report job runs at 00:05 UTC and buckets events with `new Date(ts).toISOString().slice(0,10)`. A user in Asia/Kolkata (UTC+5:30) acts at 04:00 their local time. Before running: which day's report does that event land in, and how many hours of that user's day are misfiled every single day? Now add a Berlin user during the autumn fall-back — what additionally breaks that a fixed offset would not have exposed?
controls: Drag the event marker along the UTC axis
Jump to a DST transition — spring-forward gap and fall-back repeated hour
Switch the bucketing rule: UTC day vs viewer-local day
Toggle a ghost lane showing a fixed `+05:30` offset instead of the IANA zone
viz.insight: There is one instant and many wall clocks. Every date bug you have ever shipped is a place where the code treated one as the other — and the ones that only appear twice a year are the expensive ones.
viz.buildNotes: `zones.ts` derives offsets via `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with a `timeZone` option rather than shipping a tz database. Injected clock — no `Date.now()` anywhere. Unit tests pin the 2026 US and EU DST transition dates, the Kolkata +05:30 offset, and assert the exact misfiled-hours figure the viz claims (5.5 hours/day for Kolkata under UTC bucketing). Reduced motion → static three-lane diagram at three pinned instants including the DST step.

drills.prompt: Select every defect: `const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10)` used to label a user-facing 'Today' header; `items.sort((a,b) => a.name < b.name ? -1 : 1)` on a localized list; `` `$${(cents/100).toFixed(2)}` `` for prices; and `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale).format(row.date)` inside a 5,000-row table cell renderer.
drills.answerSketch: toISOString is UTC, not the viewer's day. Raw `<` comparison ignores collation (ä, å, ß, accented Latin, CJK). Hard-coded $ and 2 decimals breaks JPY (0), KWD (3) and every non-USD currency's symbol position. Formatter constructed per cell — hoist and cache per (locale, options).

drills.prompt: Choose the storage representation for each: (a) an audit-log entry (b) a user's birthday (c) a recurring 09:00 standup in Europe/Berlin. Options: UTC instant · plain calendar date, no zone · local wall-clock time + IANA zone id · fixed offset timestamp.
drills.answerSketch: (a) UTC instant — it happened at one moment. (b) plain calendar date with no zone — a birthday is not an instant and must not shift when the user flies. (c) local wall-clock time + IANA zone — the meeting stays at 09:00 Berlin across DST, so the derived instant must be recomputed, not stored. Fixed offset is never correct for any of them.

drills.prompt: `Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'JPY' }).format(1234.5)` produces ______ fraction digits, because fraction digits come from the ______ and not from the ______.
drills.answerSketch: 0 fraction digits (¥1,235); from the currency code; not from the locale.

drills.prompt: Refactor for performance: move `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, opts)` out of the row renderer and into a ______ keyed by ______, then call only `.______()` per row.
drills.answerSketch: A module-level Map (or useMemo), keyed by `${locale}|${JSON.stringify(opts)}`, calling `.format()` per row.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes from 'show when this happened' to 'count down to the next standup, which is 09:00 every weekday in Europe/Berlin'. Storing a UTC instant no longer suffices. Explain precisely why, and what you store instead.
drills.answerSketch: A future recurring event is defined in wall-clock terms; its UTC instant changes when Berlin crosses DST, and would change again if the EU abolished DST. Storing the instant freezes a decision the calendar has not made yet. Store: local time-of-day + recurrence rule + IANA zone, and compute the instant at read time from the current tz database.

failureModes: Stores a local date string with no zone, or stores `+05:30` and calls that the user's time zone.
Formats money with `.toFixed(2)` and a prefixed symbol, then discovers JPY, KWD and the fact that many locales put the symbol after the number.
Sorts a localized list with default `Array.prototype.sort()` and ships an alphabet that is wrong in Swedish, German and Turkish simultaneously.
Constructs `new Intl.NumberFormat(...)` inside a table cell renderer and blames React's reconciler for the slow list.
interviewProbes: The daily-summary email is arriving with the wrong day's data for users in Asia. Where do you look first?
How do you store a birthday? How do you store a meeting? Why are they different?
You need to display 40,000 formatted currency cells. What is the first thing you'd check?

incl-rtl-bidi.title: RTL, Logical Properties and Locale-Driven Layout
objectives: Diagnose which components break under RTL, and distinguish direction bugs from expansion bugs.
Specify a logical-property CSS strategy that makes RTL a `dir` change rather than a second stylesheet.
Budget for text expansion and script coverage before translation begins.
claims: CSS logical properties — `margin-inline-start`, `padding-block`, `inset-inline-end`, `border-start-start-radius`, `text-align: start` — resolve against the element's writing mode and direction, so an RTL build becomes a `dir` attribute change rather than a mirrored stylesheet.
`dir="rtl"` belongs on `<html>` together with the matching `lang`, and `dir="auto"` should be applied to any element rendering user-generated text whose direction is unknown at build time.

Bidi text mixes directions within a single line, so an untrusted LTR fragment — a username, a filename, a number range — embedded in RTL text can visually reorder the surrounding punctuation; the fix is isolation with `<bdi>` or `unicode-bidi: isolate`, never manual reordering.

Icons encoding a direction or a sequence — back/forward, undo/redo, indent, progress, reply — must mirror under RTL, while icons encoding a physical object or a fixed convention — clock faces, checkmarks, media transport controls, logos — must not.

Text expansion is inversely proportional to source length: W3C/IBM guidance budgets roughly 200% extra for strings under 10 characters and roughly 30% for strings over 70, which is why buttons, tabs and chips break before paragraphs do.

Locale-driven layout shift is both a design and a CLS problem: a component whose width was derived from its English label will overflow or truncate in de-DE, and the mitigation is intrinsic sizing plus a pseudo-localized visual-regression pass, not `text-overflow: ellipsis` applied everywhere.

Font strategy must cover the target scripts: a Latin-only webfont silently falls back for Arabic, Devanagari, Thai and CJK, changing metrics and line height mid-page, so `unicode-range` subsetting with per-script fallback stacks is part of the i18n plan, not a later optimisation.

Arabic and Indic scripts need more vertical room than Latin at the same `font-size` because of taller ascenders, descenders and diacritics, so fixed px `line-height` and fixed-height rows clip glyphs in precisely the locales added last.

viz.archetype: side-by-side locale comparison with a ghost outline of the source layout and an expansion slider
viz.title: The Same Component in Four Locales
viz.whatIsDrawn: One card component rendered four times across a row — en-US, de-DE, ja-JP, ar-EG. Inside each instance the inline and block axes are annotated with arrows, mirrored icons are circled, and overflow is marked where it occurs. A faint ghost outline of the en-US box is overlaid on each of the other three so expansion is measurable in place. A toggle swaps the whole row between physical and logical CSS.
viz.predictPrompt: This card uses `margin-left: 12px`, `text-align: left`, a right-pointing chevron, and a button whose width was set to fit the word 'Save'. Switch it to ar-EG. Before running: list, in order, the first three things that visibly break — and identify the one that a pseudo-localization pass would NOT have caught.
controls: Switch locale: en / de / ja / ar / he
Toggle physical vs logical CSS properties
Drag a text-expansion slider from 0% to 200% independently of locale
Toggle icon mirroring rules on and off
Insert an LTR username into an RTL sentence with and without `<bdi>`
viz.insight: RTL is not a mirror image of your CSS; it is a different resolution of the inline axis. And the component that breaks is always the one whose size was derived from an English string — which pseudo-localization catches, but direction bugs it does not.
viz.buildNotes: No runtime i18n library; per-locale strings are original pre-baked fixtures. `expansion.ts` maps source string length to the W3C/IBM expansion band and is unit tested against that table. The bidi reordering demo uses real Unicode bidi behaviour via the browser rather than a reimplementation — the sim's job is to pick the fixtures, not to reimplement UBA. Reduced motion → the four-up comparison with all annotations pre-revealed and the expansion slider replaced by three pinned positions.

drills.prompt: Select every defect: `.card { padding-left: 16px; border-left: 3px solid; text-align: left }`, `.btn { width: 88px }`, `` used for 'next', ``, and `{user.displayName} commented` inside an Arabic paragraph.
drills.answerSketch: Physical properties on card (use padding-inline-start, border-inline-start, text-align: start). Fixed 88px button will overflow in German. chevron-right must mirror in RTL. Clock must NOT mirror. displayName is untrusted-direction UGC inside RTL text — wrap in `<bdi>` or the punctuation reorders.

drills.prompt: For each icon mark mirror / do-not-mirror under RTL: back arrow · checkmark · undo · clock · play (media) · list-indent · magnifying glass with a handle · company logo · progress bar direction · reply arrow.
drills.answerSketch: Mirror: back arrow, undo, list-indent, progress direction, reply arrow, and the magnifier (handle direction is a layout convention, mirror it). Do not mirror: checkmark, clock, media play, logo.

drills.prompt: In a `horizontal-tb` document, the logical equivalent of `padding-left` is `padding-______-______`, and the logical equivalent of `text-align: left` is `text-align: ______`. RTL is enabled by setting the ______ attribute on `<html>`, not by setting `direction` in CSS on a wrapper div.
drills.answerSketch: padding-inline-start; text-align: start; dir.

drills.prompt: Your longest primary-button label is 6 characters in English ('Delete'). Using the W3C/IBM expansion guidance, what width band must the button accommodate for de-DE, and what does that imply about `width: 88px`?
drills.answerSketch: Strings under 10 chars budget up to ~200% expansion, so plan for up to ~18 characters ('Dauerhaft löschen' is 17). A fixed 88px is roughly 2.5× too narrow. Use intrinsic sizing with a min-width, never a fixed width.

drills.prompt: You add Hebrew. Your app contains charts with axis labels, code blocks, phone-number inputs and a file-path breadcrumb — all of which are LTR content sitting inside an RTL page. Decide what you do to each of the four, and justify the one where you deliberately do NOT flip.
drills.answerSketch: Charts: mirror the layout/axis order but keep numeric labels LTR-isolated. Code blocks: force `dir="ltr"` — code is always LTR regardless of UI direction. Phone inputs: `dir="ltr"` on the input with the label following page direction, and isolate the value where it is displayed. Breadcrumb: file paths are LTR content; keep the path LTR-isolated while the separators and chrome follow page direction. The deliberate non-flip is the code block — mirroring it makes it wrong, not localized.

failureModes: Ships a separate `rtl.css` generated by a flipper tool, then spends every subsequent sprint keeping two stylesheets in sync.
Mirrors every icon indiscriminately, so the clock runs backwards and the logo is reversed.
Tests RTL by setting `direction: rtl` on a wrapper div rather than `dir` on `<html>`, missing form controls, scrollbar side, and bidi text resolution.
Says 'the designer will handle German' — so no length budget exists until QA files the first overflow bug, at which point every fixed-width component is already shipped.
interviewProbes: You are asked to add Arabic support to an existing app. What is the first PR, and what is in it?
Which icons in your design system mirror, and where is that decision recorded?
A username renders with the punctuation in the wrong place inside an Arabic sentence. What is happening and what is the fix?

sec-xss-sinks.title: XSS: Sinks, Sanitization, Trusted Types
objectives: Classify a given XSS by where the payload is stored and where it executes, including DOM-based XSS that never reaches the server.
Identify the DOM sinks in a real React codebase and explain which React defaults do and do not cover them.
Diagnose why a sanitizer placed on the wrong side of the boundary can be bypassed (mutation XSS).
Explain how Trusted Types converts a diffuse code-review problem into a small auditable set of policies.
claims: XSS is classified by injection point and execution point: reflected (the server echoes the current request into the response), stored (the server persists it and serves it later), and DOM-based (client JS moves attacker-controlled data into a sink, and the payload may never reach the server at all).

React escapes interpolated text in JSX, so {userInput} rendered as a child is not an XSS vector; the vectors are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, attacker-controlled href/src, props spread onto a raw element, and any direct DOM manipulation outside React.

React sanitizes javascript: URLs in href/src (warning since 16.9, rendered inert since 18), but this covers only JSX attributes — a URL passed to window.location, window.open, or a DOM node React does not own is unprotected.

The core DOM XSS sinks are innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, iframe.srcdoc, eval, new Function, setTimeout/setInterval with a string argument, and setAttribute used to set an on* handler.

Escaping is context-dependent: an escaping function correct for HTML text is not sufficient inside an attribute value, inside a <script> block, inside a URL, or inside CSS, so 'we escape all output' is not a complete answer.

Sanitization must be performed with the same parser that will later render the string; a server-side sanitizer can be defeated by mutation XSS (mXSS), where the browser's HTML parser re-interprets a sanitizer-approved string — particularly inside foreign content such as <svg> and <math> — into nodes the sanitizer never inspected.

Trusted Types enforced via Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script' makes injection sinks throw a TypeError on a plain string, accepting only objects produced by a named policy; this moves review from 'audit every assignment' to 'audit the policies'. It reached Baseline in February 2026 (Chrome/Edge since 83, Safari 26, Firefox in early 2026).

A feature that must render user-authored markup should be isolated in a sandboxed iframe on a separate hostname rather than sanitized into the main document, because sanitizer bypasses are discovered continuously and the main document holds the session.

viz.title: From source to sink: which transform actually stops it
viz.whatIsDrawn: A left-to-right data-flow graph: a SOURCE node (location.hash, fetched JSON, or a form field), one or two TRANSFORM nodes the learner can place (server-side sanitizer, client-side sanitizer, escape function), and a SINK node (innerHTML / textContent / dangerouslySetInnerHTML). A single tainted payload token travels the path; each node stamps the token with what it did to it, and the sink node shows the resulting parsed DOM inline beneath it — with the executable node highlighted in place. A Trusted Types gate can be dropped just before the sink and visibly rejects an unstamped token.
viz.predictPrompt: A markdown comment is sanitized on the server with a jsdom-based sanitizer, stored, and later assigned to innerHTML on the client. The sanitizer's output contains no <script>, no on* attribute, and no javascript: URL — it verifiably parsed the string and approved every node. Name the single browser behaviour that can still turn that approved string back into executable markup before any of your JavaScript runs.
controls: Source: location.hash / stored JSON / form field
Payload: plain <script> / img onerror / svg-foreign-content mXSS / javascript: href
Transform placement: none / server-side / client-side (same parser)
viz.insight: A sanitizer is only sound when it runs on the parser that will render the output. Server-side sanitization plus client-side innerHTML is two different parsers, and the gap between them is mutation XSS — which is why the durable fix is to remove the raw-string sink (Trusted Types) rather than to filter harder.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models a tiny deterministic parse/serialize pipeline over a fixed payload table — do NOT attempt a real HTML parser; ship a hand-authored table of {payload, serverSanitized, reparsedDom, executes} verified against real browser behaviour once during authoring and unit-tested as fixtures. The unit test IS the claim: assert the mXSS payload has executes=false under client-side sanitization and executes=true under server-side sanitization. Render the resulting DOM as an inline tree inside the sink node, with the executing node ringed — never in a side panel. Reduced motion: static three-column comparison of the three transform placements.

drills.prompt:
Pre-baked React component (Shiki-rendered). Five candidate lines are marked. Identify every line that is an XSS sink and, for each, say what the attacker controls: (a)

{comment.body}

, (b) , (c)
, (d) useEffect(() => { window.location = params.get('next') }), (e) .
drills.answerSketch: (a) safe — JSX child interpolation is escaped. (b) covered by React's javascript: neutralisation, but still an open-redirect / data: URL problem, so validate the scheme against an allowlist. (c) sink — depends entirely on renderMarkdown; a markdown renderer with raw-HTML passthrough is a full XSS. (d) sink — React's URL sanitisation does not apply to window.location; javascript: executes. (e) sink — a spread can land dangerouslySetInnerHTML or an on* prop onto the element.

drills.prompt: Complete the Trusted Types policy so that this legacy innerHTML assignment keeps working under require-trusted-types-for 'script', without becoming a rubber stamp. trustedTypes.createPolicy('____', { ____: (input) => ____ });  ...  el.innerHTML = policy.____(userHtml);
drills.answerSketch: createPolicy('sanitize-html', { createHTML: (input) => DOMPurify.sanitize(input, {RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE: false}) }); then el.innerHTML = policy.createHTML(userHtml). A policy whose createHTML is the identity function compiles and passes CSP while providing zero protection — that is the rubber stamp the drill is testing for.

drills.prompt: Today your app renders only plain-text comments. The requirement changes: enterprise customers may now author rich HTML email templates that other users preview in-app. What breaks first, and what is the smallest architecture change that keeps the blast radius bounded?
drills.answerSketch: Escaping stops being an option, so a sanitizer becomes load-bearing and a single bypass yields session compromise. Smallest bounded change: render the preview in <iframe sandbox="allow-same-origin" is WRONG — render it on a separate hostname (e.g. usercontent-example.net) in an iframe with sandbox="allow-popups" and no allow-same-origin, communicate by postMessage with an exact targetOrigin, and set frame-ancestors on that host. Sanitization becomes defense in depth rather than the only wall.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of a Trusted Types rollout on a large existing app so that you never break production.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Ship Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types 'allow-duplicates' and collect violations. 2) Triage reports into: framework-internal sinks, our own sinks, third-party sinks. 3) Adopt a framework/library default policy where one exists; replace our own sinks with textContent or a real component. 4) Create a small number of named policies for the sinks that must stay, each with a real sanitizer. 5) Restrict trusted-types to the named policy list. 6) Move to the enforcing header. 7) Keep report-only running with the next-stricter policy.

drills.prompt: Name six DOM XSS sinks and, for each, the safe replacement.
drills.answerSketch: innerHTML -> textContent; outerHTML -> replaceChildren; insertAdjacentHTML -> insertAdjacentText; document.write -> DOM construction; eval / new Function -> JSON.parse or a real parser; setTimeout('str') -> setTimeout(fn); iframe.srcdoc -> a sandboxed src on a separate origin; setAttribute('onclick', ...) -> addEventListener.

failureModes: "React escapes everything, so we can't have XSS" — ignoring dangerouslySetInnerHTML, prop spreads, URL sinks and non-React DOM code.
"We use DOMPurify" as a complete answer, with no statement of where it runs or what it is defending.
Listing only reflected and stored XSS and never mentioning DOM-based — which is the dominant class in an SPA.
Proposing a regex or a blocklist of dangerous strings.
Escaping at input time rather than at output time, producing both double-escaped display bugs and context-wrong output.
Treating CSP as the fix for the injection rather than as containment for the ones that get through.
interviewProbes: Our SPA has no server-rendered HTML at all. Can we still have XSS? Show me where.
You have DOMPurify running on the server before storage. I claim I can still get script execution. How?
What would you have to be true about a codebase before you could turn on require-trusted-types-for 'script' tomorrow?

sec-csp-rollout.title: A CSP You Can Actually Ship
objectives: Design a nonce-or-hash based script-src with strict-dynamic instead of a host allowlist, and justify the choice against the deployment model.
Sequence a report-only rollout that produces signal rather than noise.
Name the supporting directives without which a nonce policy is bypassable.
State precisely what CSP does and does not buy, so it is never offered as an XSS fix.
claims: A host-allowlist policy such as script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com is weak in practice: any JSONP endpoint, user-upload path, open redirect, or outdated library on an allowlisted host becomes a script source, which is why Google's CSP research moved the recommendation to nonces and hashes.

A CSP nonce must be unpredictable (at least 128 bits from a CSPRNG) and regenerated per response; a nonce baked into a cached static HTML file is not a nonce, which is why a statically hosted SPA must either use hashes or inject the nonce at an edge/CDN worker.

strict-dynamic propagates trust from an already-trusted script to scripts it creates programmatically, and it causes browsers that support it to ignore host allowlists, 'self', and 'unsafe-inline' in the same directive — so those entries remain only as a fallback for older parsers.
A parser-inserted <script src> written directly in the HTML does not inherit strict-dynamic trust and needs its own nonce or hash; only script-created (document.createElement) scripts inherit it.

Content-Security-Policy enforces and Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only only reports; both headers can be sent simultaneously, which is the standard rollout — enforce today's policy while report-only measures tomorrow's stricter one.

Violation reports arrive via the Reporting API using the Reporting-Endpoints header plus the report-to directive; the older report-uri directive is deprecated but still worth sending alongside for coverage.

CSP reports are deliberately lossy — cross-origin and inline violations collapse to blocked-uri values like 'inline' or a stripped origin — and browser extensions inject scripts that generate high-volume false positives, so a report pipeline needs filtering by document URL, effective-directive and known extension schemes before it is a signal.

A nonce policy is bypassable without object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' (or 'self'): an injected <base href> redirects every relative script URL to the attacker's host while the nonce still matches.

CSP is containment, not a fix: it converts a working XSS into a blocked-script violation report. The injection still has to be repaired, and unsafe-inline in script-src removes essentially all of the protection.
wasm-unsafe-eval permits WebAssembly compilation without granting the far broader unsafe-eval, so a WASM dependency is not a reason to open eval.

viz.title: Which of these six scripts loads?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A page skeleton on the left with six candidate scripts pinned inside it (nonced inline bootstrap, parser-inserted CDN script, script-created CDN script, inline event handler, eval call, dynamically imported chunk). A single policy string sits at the top as an editable token row. Stepping evaluates each script in document order; each script node turns allowed or blocked IN PLACE with the deciding directive token drawn as a short leader line to the policy string above it. A ghost column shows the same six under the previous policy for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Policy: script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic' https://cdn.example.com 'unsafe-inline'. Your nonced bootstrap script calls document.createElement('script') and loads https://cdn.example.com/analytics.js. Separately, the HTML contains a hardcoded <script src="https://cdn.example.com/widget.js"> with no nonce. Which of the two loads — and does 'unsafe-inline' let an injected inline handler run?
controls: Toggle each policy token: 'strict-dynamic', 'unsafe-inline', host allowlist, 'self', nonce present
Toggle: script insertion method for the CDN script (parser-inserted vs script-created)
Step through the six scripts in document order
viz.insight: strict-dynamic deliberately makes your host allowlist dead text, and a nonce makes 'unsafe-inline' dead text. The tokens that survive in a modern browser are almost never the ones a team thinks it is relying on — so the policy must be read as 'what does the newest browser see', with everything else being legacy fallback.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a small, honest CSP script-src evaluator over a fixed script inventory: inputs {tokens, scriptKind, hasNonce, url}, output {allowed, decidingToken, ignoredTokens}. Unit-test the four claims that matter: nonce present => 'unsafe-inline' ignored; strict-dynamic present => host allowlist and 'self' ignored; parser-inserted script does not inherit strict-dynamic; script-created script does. Leader lines from the script node to the deciding policy token keep annotation inside the diagram. Reduced motion: a static decision table (6 scripts x 4 preset policies) with the same leader-line colouring.

drills.prompt: Inventory: one bundled app entry, code-split dynamic imports from your own origin, Google Tag Manager, a Stripe.js widget, an inline JSON-LD block, and a runtime CSS-in-JS library that injects <style> tags. Your app is deployed as static files to a CDN with no server rendering. Produce the minimal script-src and style-src, and state which item forces the biggest concession.
drills.answerSketch: No per-response HTML means no nonce without an edge worker, so: hashes for the inline JSON-LD (or move it to a file), strict-dynamic + a hash on the bootstrap so dynamic imports work, 'self' as fallback. GTM is the big concession — it wants unsafe-inline and often unsafe-eval; either put it behind an edge-worker nonce, or move it to a separate origin/iframe, or accept the concession explicitly and document it. Stripe.js is a plain script-src entry (and requires frame-src for its iframes). Runtime CSS-in-JS forces style-src 'unsafe-inline' unless the library supports nonces — which is a real reason to prefer build-time CSS. Correct answer names the edge worker as the unlock for the whole policy.

drills.prompt: Policy shipped to production: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https: data:; img-src *. The team reports 'CSP is done'. List every way an attacker with an HTML injection still achieves script execution.
drills.answerSketch: 'unsafe-inline' permits injected <script>...</script> and on* handlers outright — that alone ends it. https: permits any script from any HTTPS host on the internet. data: permits <script src="data:text/javascript,...">. No object-src means <object>/<embed> plugin vectors fall back to default-src 'self' (acceptable) but no base-uri means <base href> hijacks every relative script URL. No frame-ancestors means the page is still clickjackable. The policy provides essentially zero XSS containment.

drills.prompt: Order a report-only-to-enforce rollout for a strict nonce policy on a live app.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Stand up a report collector and add Reporting-Endpoints + report-to (and report-uri for coverage). 2) Ship the strict policy in Report-Only ONLY, changing nothing else. 3) Filter reports: drop extension schemes (chrome-extension:, moz-extension:), group by effective-directive and document URI, ignore known-noisy blocked-uri 'inline' from injected toolbars. 4) Fix real violations in app code; obtain nonce/hash support from vendors or move them off. 5) Watch the violation rate flatten across a full weekly traffic cycle including mobile webviews. 6) Move the policy to the enforcing header and simultaneously start a NEW report-only header with the next-stricter policy. 7) Alert on a violation-rate step change as a deploy regression signal.

drills.prompt: Your SPA is deployed as immutable static files behind a CDN. Choose: (a) hash-based script-src, or (b) add a CDN edge worker purely to inject a per-response nonce. You have 6 minutes. Commit to one, then justify against caching, developer ergonomics, third-party scripts, and what happens when a vendor updates their inline snippet.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer criteria: (1) names that hashes preserve full-page cacheability while nonces require the HTML to be uncacheable or worker-rewritten; (2) names that hashes break on any inline content that varies per response and on vendor snippet changes, creating a silent breakage class; (3) recognises that strict-dynamic works with either, and is what makes dynamic imports viable; (4) prices the edge worker honestly — an extra deploy artifact, a cold-start cost, a new failure mode; (5) states a decision rule, e.g. 'hashes if inline content is build-time-static and vendor-free, worker-injected nonce as soon as a third-party inline snippet exists'; (6) states what would change their mind.

drills.prompt: Your strict nonce policy is live and clean. Marketing now requires Google Tag Manager with the ability for non-engineers to add arbitrary tags. What breaks first, and what are your three options ranked by residual risk?
drills.answerSketch: Breaks first: GTM's custom HTML tags need unsafe-inline or a nonce it cannot see, so tags silently fail to fire. Options: (1) lowest risk — no GTM in the app origin; run it on a separate hostname in a sandboxed iframe, pass only whitelisted events by postMessage; (2) medium — GTM with server-side tagging and a nonce propagated by the edge worker, custom-HTML tags disabled by GTM policy; (3) highest — grant strict-dynamic trust to the GTM loader, which effectively hands anyone with GTM access remote code execution in your origin. The honest framing is that option 3 makes the marketing team's account a production credential.

failureModes: Claiming CSP protection while shipping 'unsafe-inline' in script-src.
Relying on a host allowlist and not knowing that strict-dynamic makes browsers ignore it.
Putting a nonce in a statically cached HTML file, producing a constant 'nonce' that is not a nonce.
Omitting base-uri and object-src, leaving the nonce policy bypassable.
Offering CSP as the fix for an XSS rather than as containment.
Turning on enforcement first and rolling back after the first outage, then abandoning CSP entirely.
interviewProbes: Write me a script-src for this app. Now tell me which tokens a Chrome from last month actually honours.
How do you ship a nonce-based CSP on a fully static deploy?
You have 40,000 CSP reports from yesterday. How many are real, and how do you find out?

sec-cookies-csrf.title: Cookies, SameSite, and CSRF
objectives: Predict whether a cookie is attached to a given request, from its attributes and the request context.
Judge which CSRF defense is appropriate for a given deployment, including when none is needed.
Explain what SameSite does not protect against, especially the subdomain case.
Choose cookie attributes deliberately, including the __Host- prefix.
claims: Chrome and Firefox treat a cookie with no SameSite attribute as SameSite=Lax, which blocks it on cross-site POSTs and subresource requests but still sends it on top-level cross-site GET navigations.

SameSite=None requires the Secure attribute, and in Chrome a third-party cookie should also carry Partitioned (CHIPS) so it is keyed to the embedding top-level site; Safari and Firefox block third-party cookies by default, while Chrome does not, after Google reversed the deprecation in April 2025.
SameSite is evaluated at the site boundary (scheme + eTLD+1), so a compromised or attacker-controlled subdomain is same-site with your app and SameSite gives zero protection against it.

HttpOnly blocks document.cookie reads, which prevents exfiltration of the session value, but an XSS can still issue authenticated same-origin fetches from the victim's page, so HttpOnly removes theft, not abuse.

Cookies are scoped by (Domain, Path) and ignore the port, so cookies are not origin-scoped and the same-origin policy does not govern them; http://example.com:3000 and https://example.com share a cookie jar in ways the SOP would never permit for storage.
The __Host- name prefix forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute, which pins the cookie to the exact host and makes it unsettable by a sibling subdomain — the strongest available cookie scoping.

The synchronizer-token pattern requires server-side state per session; the double-submit-cookie pattern is stateless but is broken by any subdomain that can set cookies unless the cookie value is cryptographically bound to the session (signed double-submit).

Checking the Origin header is a cheap and effective CSRF defense because browsers send it on all cross-origin requests and on same-origin POSTs; checking Referer is not equivalent because referrer policies routinely strip or truncate it.

CSRF remains a live risk under SameSite=Lax for any state change reachable by a top-level GET, for clients that do not apply the Lax default (some webviews and older browsers), and for attacks originating from a same-site subdomain.

If the app authenticates exclusively with an Authorization header, classic CSRF does not apply, because the browser never attaches that header automatically — which is a genuine argument for bearer tokens that must then be weighed against the storage question.

viz.archetype: attribute matrix with a live request probe
viz.title: Is the cookie attached?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A grid: rows are cookie configurations (no attribute / Lax / Strict / None+Secure / None+Secure+Partitioned / __Host- prefixed), columns are request contexts (same-origin fetch, same-site subdomain fetch, cross-site top-level GET nav, cross-site form POST, cross-site fetch with credentials, cross-site ). The learner drags a probe onto any cell; that cell expands in place into a miniature request diagram showing the decision and the deciding rule as pinned text. A ghost layer shows the pre-2020 'no default' behaviour behind the current grid so the learner sees exactly which cells the Lax default changed.
viz.predictPrompt: Your session cookie is set with no SameSite attribute at all. Which of these three attacker-initiated requests carries it in current Chrome: (a) a cross-site auto-submitted <form method="POST">, (b) a cross-site top-level GET navigation opened with window.open, (c) a cross-site fetch with credentials:'include'? Then: does your answer change if the attacker's page is hosted on a subdomain of your own site?
controls: Toggle: attacker page is same-site subdomain vs cross-site
Toggle: browser third-party cookie policy (Chrome default / Safari-Firefox blocking)
viz.insight: The Lax default removed the easiest CSRF (cross-site POST) and nothing else. Top-level GET navigations and same-site subdomains are both still fully open, which is exactly the gap that a same-site-scoped defense cannot close and an Origin check or synchronizer token can.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure attachment predicate: (cookieAttrs, requestContext, browserPolicy) -> {attached, reason}. Unit-test it against the specific claims: Lax attaches on top-level cross-site GET nav and not on cross-site POST; None without Secure is rejected at set time; __Host- with a Domain attribute is rejected at set time. Expanding a cell in place, rather than opening a panel, is the split-attention requirement. Reduced motion: render the full grid with all decisions and reasons visible as static text.

drills.prompt: Three deployments. For each, choose a CSRF defense and justify: (1) SPA + API on the same site, cookie session; (2) SPA on app.example.com, API on api.partner.com (cross-site), cookie session; (3) SPA with an Authorization: Bearer header held in memory, API cross-site.
drills.answerSketch: (1) SameSite=Lax + __Host- prefix + Origin header check; add a synchronizer token if any state change is reachable by GET or if untrusted subdomains exist. (2) The cookie must be SameSite=None; Secure; Partitioned, which throws away SameSite protection entirely — so a synchronizer token or a strict Origin allowlist becomes mandatory, and the honest recommendation is to move the API onto the same site or a BFF. (3) No classic CSRF: the browser never attaches the header. State the residual: the token is now script-reachable, which trades a CSRF problem for a storage/blast-radius problem — see the token-storage module.

drills.prompt: A stateless double-submit implementation: on login the server sets csrf=<random> with HttpOnly absent and Domain=.example.com; the SPA reads document.cookie and copies the value into an X-CSRF-Token header; the server compares header to cookie. Name the attack that defeats this and the one-line change that fixes it.
drills.answerSketch: Any subdomain the attacker controls (a stale CNAME, a marketing microsite, a compromised docs host) can set csrf=known on .example.com, then submit a cross-site form with the matching header value — cookie and header agree, so the check passes. Fix: bind the token to the session — the cookie value must be an HMAC over the session id under a server key (signed double-submit), so a value the attacker planted does not verify. Setting __Host-csrf (no Domain, Path=/, Secure) also blocks the subdomain from setting it and is the cheaper half of the fix.

drills.prompt: Your session cookie is __Host-session; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax and everything works. The requirement changes: a customer wants to embed your app as a widget inside their own site in an iframe, logged in. What breaks first, what attribute changes, and what must you now add back?
drills.answerSketch: Breaks first: the cookie is not sent in a third-party frame under Lax, so the widget renders logged-out. You must move to SameSite=None; Secure; Partitioned — which (a) forfeits all SameSite CSRF protection, so a synchronizer token or Origin allowlist becomes mandatory; (b) under CHIPS partitioning gives the widget a per-embedder cookie jar, so the session does not carry over from your own site and the user must authenticate inside the frame; (c) requires frame-ancestors listing the customer's origin, reopening clickjacking considerations; (d) Safari and Firefox may block it entirely, pushing you toward a popup-based or redirect-based auth instead. The correct senior answer notices that partitioning changes the product behaviour, not just the header.

drills.prompt: Fill in: The ____ prefix requires Secure, requires Path=/, and forbids a Domain attribute. SameSite=None is ignored unless ____ is also set. A cookie with no SameSite attribute is treated as ____ by Chrome and Firefox. SameSite is evaluated at the ____ boundary, not the ____ boundary. Cookies ignore the ____ component of the origin entirely.
drills.answerSketch: __Host- / Secure / Lax / site (scheme + eTLD+1) / origin / port

drills.prompt: Your API rejects any request whose Origin header is not https://app.example.com, and requires Content-Type: application/json. A colleague says the synchronizer token is now dead weight. Agree or disagree, with the residual risk that decides it.
drills.answerSketch: Largely agree for browser-originated CSRF: the Origin check plus a preflight-forcing Content-Type is a real defense. Residual risks that decide it: (1) any endpoint that also accepts form-encoded bodies or a GET; (2) clients that omit Origin (some old webviews, non-browser clients) — the check must reject on missing Origin, not allow it; (3) a same-site subdomain XSS sends a valid Origin, so the Origin check never defends against that, while a session-bound synchronizer token also does not — only fixing the XSS does. The correct answer states that CSRF tokens and Origin checks are alternatives, and that neither defends against XSS.

failureModes: "SameSite=Lax is on by default, so CSRF is solved" — ignoring top-level GET navigations, subdomains, and non-conforming clients.
"HttpOnly protects us from XSS."
Believing cookies are origin-scoped and therefore protected by the same-origin policy.
Implementing unsigned double-submit and not being able to name the subdomain attack.
Setting SameSite=None to 'fix' a bug without noticing the CSRF protection just went away.
Checking Referer instead of Origin.
interviewProbes: Set the attributes on our session cookie and defend each one. Why __Host-?
We have SameSite=Lax. Under what circumstances do I still need a CSRF token?
A partner wants to embed us in an iframe with the user logged in. Walk me through everything that changes.

sec-token-storage.title: Where Do You Store the Token
objectives: Reframe the storage question as a blast-radius question and answer it in under two minutes under pressure.
State, for each storage option, exactly what an attacker gains and for how long.
Explain why in-memory storage is not the safe default it appears to be once a refresh mechanism exists.
Judge when the honest answer is 'the browser holds no token at all'.
claims: Every browser-accessible store — localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, a module-scope variable, a Zustand store — is readable by any script running in the origin, so the storage question is not about which API is 'secure' but about the blast radius of script execution.

An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie is the only option that script cannot read; that is the entire security difference, and it is why 'localStorage' is scored as a wrong answer — it turns a transient XSS into a persistent, exfiltrable, long-lived credential.

A cookie does not make you XSS-proof: an attacker with script execution can issue authenticated same-origin requests from the victim's page for as long as the page lives, so cookies remove exfiltration, not abuse.

In-memory storage narrows the window to a live XSS on a live page and survives no reload, but it forces a silent-refresh mechanism, and that refresh endpoint is reachable by the same injected script — so an attacker can mint a fresh token and re-establish persistence, which is the trap in 'just keep it in memory'.

localStorage is origin-scoped but shared across every tab and every path of that origin, is synchronous and blocks the main thread, and has no expiry — a token written there lives until code removes it.
A token in localStorage is readable by every third-party script you load, with no XSS required at all: a compromised analytics vendor or a tag added through a tag manager reads it directly.

sessionStorage is not more secure than localStorage against XSS — the injected script runs in the same tab; its per-tab scope is a UX property, and it also creates a distinct multi-tab session bug class.
Encrypting a token before putting it in localStorage provides no protection, because the key or the code that derives it also ships in the bundle.

Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention deletes all script-writable storage — localStorage, IndexedDB, service worker registrations and caches — after seven days of browser use without user interaction on the site, so browser storage is not durable even ignoring security.

A browser-held refresh token must be rotated with reuse detection per the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700); a non-rotating refresh token in the browser is a long-lived bearer credential and is the worst of the options.

The strongest browser answer is to hold no token: a backend-for-frontend keeps the tokens server-side and hands the SPA an HttpOnly session cookie, trading one deployed component for the elimination of the entire storage question and reintroducing a CSRF surface.

viz.title: Blast radius over time
viz.whatIsDrawn: One horizontal time axis with four stacked lanes: localStorage, in-memory, HttpOnly cookie, BFF session. Marked events on the axis: XSS lands (t0), 400ms of attacker script (t1), page reload (t2), tab closed (t3), user idle 7 days (t4). Inside each lane, a filled bar shows what the attacker still holds at that moment, labelled in place with the concrete capability ('has the raw token, can replay from their own machine' / 'can act only while this page lives' / 'can act from the victim's page only' / 'nothing left'). A ghost bar behind each lane shows the same lane with the refresh endpoint disabled, so the learner sees the refresh mechanism as the thing that changes the shape.
viz.predictPrompt: Your SPA holds the access token only in a module-scope variable — never persisted anywhere — and refreshes it silently from a /refresh endpoint the app can call. An XSS runs for 400 milliseconds before the user navigates away. Rank the four designs by what the attacker walks away with, and name the one where 'in memory' still gives the attacker access for the next 30 days.
controls: Storage design: localStorage / in-memory / HttpOnly cookie / BFF
Toggle: a refresh endpoint is callable from page script
Toggle: refresh-token rotation with reuse detection
Toggle: third-party script present on the page (no XSS)
viz.insight: Storage choice bounds exfiltration, not abuse — and the refresh mechanism you are forced to add to make in-memory tokens usable is exactly what hands persistence back to the attacker. The only designs that genuinely bound the attack are the ones where the credential is not reachable by page script at all, and even those leave the attacker able to act as the user while the page is open.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: (design, refreshReachable, rotationEnabled, timelineEvent) -> {attackerHolds: 'raw-token'|'session-ride'|'nothing', persistsPastReload: bool, actsFromOwnMachine: bool, durationDays: number}. This sim must be unit-tested hard because it IS the pedagogical claim: assert that in-memory + refreshReachable yields persistsPastReload=true, and that HttpOnly cookie yields actsFromOwnMachine=false but session-ride=true. Capability labels live inside the bars. Reduced motion: static 4x5 matrix of lane by event with the same labels, plus the narration text.

drills.prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Where do you store the access token?' You get 90 seconds to commit to a design, then 6 minutes of locked written justification. Constraints: a React SPA on static hosting, an API you control on the same site, a mobile Safari user base, and no appetite for a new deployed service. Commit first, then justify.
drills.answerSketch: Model answer decomposed into criteria: (1) Reframes the question as blast radius before naming a store; (2) explicitly rejects localStorage and gives the reason (persistence + third-party script readability, not vibes); (3) names the chosen design and its refresh mechanism together, because the two cannot be evaluated separately; (4) states what the choice does NOT protect — an XSS can still ride the session from the victim's page under every option; (5) prices the rejected BFF honestly (a stateful component, a CSRF surface back, an ops cost) rather than dismissing it; (6) names a concrete trigger that would change the decision, e.g. 'the moment we need cross-site embedding or a third-party API we do not control, I move to a BFF'. Anchor answers at three levels: weak = 'HttpOnly cookie, that's the secure one'; solid = criteria 1-4; strong = all six, plus the Safari ITP point as a durability (not security) argument.

drills.prompt: You designed a BFF. The requirement changes: the company will not deploy or operate any server of its own — the app must be static files calling a third-party API you do not control, which issues bearer tokens only. What breaks first, and what is the best remaining design?
drills.answerSketch: Breaks first: there is nowhere to hold the token out of script's reach, so HttpOnly is off the table and the entire storage question comes back. Best remaining: access token in memory only, short lifetime (5-15 min), refresh token with rotation and reuse detection if the provider supports it (if it does not, that is a procurement finding), a strict nonce-based CSP with Trusted Types to make XSS as hard as possible since XSS is now the whole threat model, no third-party scripts in the app origin at all, and single-flight refresh via navigator.locks. State plainly that the residual risk is higher and that the compensating control is XSS prevention, not storage.

drills.prompt: Code review (Shiki-rendered): a login handler does localStorage.setItem('auth', JSON.stringify({accessToken, refreshToken, user})); an axios interceptor reads it on every request; a logout handler does localStorage.removeItem('auth'). The team also loads a session-replay script and a tag manager. List every distinct security problem, ranked.
drills.answerSketch: 1) The refresh token — a long-lived credential — is in script-readable persistent storage; an XSS or any malicious third-party script gets indefinite account access replayable from the attacker's machine. 2) The session-replay script and every tag published through the tag manager can read it today, with no XSS required; this is an active data-exposure issue, not a hypothetical. 3) Logout only clears the client; the tokens remain valid server-side until expiry, so a copied token still works. 4) The user object in storage tempts client-side authorization decisions that the API may not enforce. 5) No expiry means a shared/kiosk device keeps a live session forever. 6) Safari ITP will silently delete it after 7 idle days, producing a mystery-logout bug the team will 'fix' by extending token lifetimes — making problem 1 worse.

drills.prompt: Which statement is true? (a) sessionStorage is safer than localStorage against XSS because it is per-tab. (b) Encrypting the token in localStorage with AES-GCM protects it from XSS. (c) An HttpOnly cookie prevents an XSS from making authenticated requests. (d) None of the above. Give the rationale for the one you pick and for the strongest distractor.
drills.answerSketch: (d). (a) is false: the injected script runs in that same tab, so it reads sessionStorage trivially; per-tab scope is a UX property. (b) is false: the key ships in the bundle or is derivable by the same script. (c) is the strongest distractor and is false in a specific way — HttpOnly stops the read, not the ride; the attacker calls fetch('/api/transfer', {credentials:'same-origin'}) from the victim's page and the browser attaches the cookie for them.

drills.prompt: Rank these five mitigations by how much they actually reduce the risk of an XSS on a token-holding SPA: (1) move the token from localStorage to memory, (2) shorten access-token lifetime from 24h to 10 minutes, (3) adopt a strict nonce CSP with Trusted Types, (4) add refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, (5) bind the token to a device key. Justify the ordering.
drills.answerSketch: Roughly (3) > (4) ≈ (2) > (1) > (5) for a typical team. (3) attacks the cause and reduces the probability of the whole class; (4) converts silent long-term persistence into a detectable, auto-revoked event; (2) bounds the value of a stolen access token but does nothing for a stolen refresh token; (1) helps only if the refresh path is not script-callable, which it usually is; (5) (DPoP / device-bound sessions) is genuinely strong but is usually not available end-to-end and does not stop the attacker acting from the victim's page. The point of the drill is that the highest-ranked item is not a storage change at all.

failureModes: "localStorage — it's simpler and everyone does it."
"HttpOnly cookies, so XSS can't hurt us" — conflating exfiltration with abuse.
"sessionStorage, because it's cleared when the tab closes" offered as a security property.
Proposing to encrypt the token client-side.
Choosing in-memory storage and never mentioning the refresh mechanism, which is where the whole risk moved.
Answering with a store and never once saying the words 'blast radius', 'what the attacker gains', or 'for how long'.
interviewProbes: Where do you store the access token, and what exactly does that choice buy you?
I have an XSS on your page. Walk me through what I can do under each of your candidate designs.
You said in-memory. How does the app survive a page refresh, and what did that mechanism just cost you?

sec-oauth-pkce-bff.title: OAuth 2.0, OIDC, PKCE and the BFF
objectives: Design an end-to-end browser auth flow using Authorization Code + PKCE, naming every parameter and what it defends.
Explain precisely why the implicit flow and hidden-iframe silent refresh are dead, in terms of a concrete browser change.
Distinguish OAuth authorization from OIDC authentication and place validation on the correct side of the boundary.
Choose between a public SPA client with rotation and a BFF, pricing both.
claims: OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization and OpenID Connect layers authentication on top of it by returning a signed id_token describing the user; using an opaque access token to identify the user, or treating an id_token as an API credential, are the two standard confusions.

Authorization Code with PKCE is the required flow for public browser clients: the client generates a random code_verifier, sends code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)) with code_challenge_method=S256 to the authorization endpoint, and presents the raw verifier at the token endpoint.

PKCE defends against authorization-code interception and injection; it does not authenticate the client, so a public client's client_id is not a secret and code_challenge_method=plain provides no protection.

The implicit flow (response_type=token) is removed in OAuth 2.1 and prohibited by RFC 9700 because it returns the access token in the URL fragment, where it lands in browser history, in logs, and in anything reading location.

state binds the callback to the browser session that initiated it and defends against CSRF on the redirect; nonce is sent to the authorization endpoint and echoed inside the id_token to defend against id_token replay — they solve different problems and neither substitutes for the other.

Silent refresh via a hidden iframe with prompt=none depends on the user's cookie at the authorization server being available in a third-party context, which Safari and Firefox block by default, so it is not a viable refresh strategy in 2026 regardless of Chrome's behaviour.

Refresh-token rotation issues a new refresh token on every use and invalidates the previous one; presenting an already-used refresh token is treated as evidence of theft and must revoke the entire token family, which is what turns silent persistent compromise into a detectable logout.

The BFF pattern terminates OAuth on a server you control: tokens never enter the browser, the browser holds only a same-site HttpOnly session cookie, and the cost is a stateful component plus a reintroduced CSRF surface that must be defended with SameSite plus an Origin check or a token.

Validating a JWT in browser code is not a security control — the browser is not the resource server and any check it makes can be skipped by the user; signature, iss, aud and exp validation belongs to the API. Reading unverified claims for UI purposes is acceptable only if the API independently enforces them.

The authorization server's redirect_uri must be registered and matched exactly; a wildcard or prefix match on the redirect URI is a standard account-takeover vector because it lets an attacker receive the code.

viz.archetype: sequence diagram with a scrubbable timeline
viz.title: What is in the URL, and who can read it
viz.whatIsDrawn: Four actor lanes — Browser page, Authorization Server, Token endpoint, API — with numbered messages between them. A second, thin channel runs along the top: the current URL bar, redrawn at each step, with any credential material in it highlighted in place. The learner switches flow variants and the same timeline redraws; the ghost baseline of the implicit flow stays faint behind the code+PKCE flow so the fragment-borne token is visibly the difference. Each message is annotated inline with which parameter defends what.
viz.predictPrompt: You use Authorization Code + PKCE with no client secret. An attacker obtains the authorization code from the redirect URL by exploiting an open redirect on your callback path. Can they exchange it for tokens? Now suppose instead that the attacker has script execution on your origin and steals the code the same way. Is the answer the same, and why?
controls: Flow: implicit / code without PKCE / code + PKCE / code + PKCE behind a BFF
Toggle: third-party cookies blocked at the authorization server
Toggle: refresh-token rotation with reuse detection
Attack injection point: steal from URL / steal from page script
viz.insight: PKCE protects the code in transit, not the client. Its guarantee is exactly 'whoever finishes the exchange must be whoever started it' — which an attacker with script on your origin trivially satisfies, because the verifier is in the page. That is why PKCE closes the interception attack and closes nothing about XSS, and why the BFF variant is the only one where the credential never touches the page.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models the flow as a message list with a credential-location field per step: (flow, attackerCapability, thirdPartyCookiesBlocked) -> {steps, attackerObtains, exchangeSucceeds}. Unit-test the claims: implicit puts token in fragment at step N; code+PKCE with URL-only theft yields exchangeSucceeds=false; code+PKCE with script capability yields true; prompt=none silent refresh yields a failure step when thirdPartyCookiesBlocked. Annotations pinned to the message arrows. Reduced motion: static side-by-side sequence diagrams for the four flow variants.

drills.prompt: Order the full Authorization Code + PKCE exchange for a browser SPA, including every parameter, and mark which two steps travel over the front channel (the URL) and which over the back channel.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Generate code_verifier (high-entropy random) and state and nonce; persist them for the session. 2) Compute code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)). 3) FRONT CHANNEL: redirect to /authorize with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, nonce, code_challenge, code_challenge_method=S256. 4) User authenticates and consents at the AS. 5) FRONT CHANNEL: AS redirects back to the exact registered redirect_uri with code and state in the query. 6) Client verifies state matches what it stored, then discards it. 7) BACK CHANNEL: POST to /token with grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri, client_id and code_verifier. 8) AS recomputes SHA256(verifier) and compares to the stored challenge. 9) AS returns access_token, id_token, refresh_token. 10) Client validates the id_token's nonce (and the API validates signature/iss/aud/exp). Common wrong ordering: sending the verifier at step 3.

drills.prompt: An auth integration review. Findings: redirect_uri is registered as https://app.example.com/* ; code_challenge_method is 'plain'; state is set to a constant string 'login'; the id_token is verified in the browser with a JWT library and then the user's role claim drives which API calls the UI makes; the refresh token is stored in localStorage and does not rotate. Rank these by severity and say what each one actually enables.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Wildcard redirect_uri — account takeover: an attacker gets the code delivered to a path they control (an open redirect, an XSS-hosting path, a user-content route). 2) Non-rotating refresh token in localStorage — any script on the origin gets indefinite account access, replayable off-device. 3) Constant state — CSRF on the callback: an attacker can force the victim's browser to complete a login as the attacker's account (session fixation via login CSRF). 4) code_challenge_method=plain — PKCE provides no protection against an attacker who saw the authorize request. 5) Browser-side id_token verification driving authorization — not a vulnerability by itself, but it is evidence the API may not be enforcing; probe whether the API independently checks the role.

drills.prompt: Choose one and defend it in writing (timed, 7 minutes): (a) public SPA client with PKCE, in-memory access token and rotating refresh token; (b) a BFF that holds all tokens and gives the SPA an HttpOnly session cookie. Constraints: a 4-person team, static hosting today, one first-party API, an identity provider you do not control, and a compliance requirement to revoke access within 60 seconds.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) notices the 60-second revocation requirement is decisive — a stateless JWT with a 15-minute lifetime cannot meet it, so either the API checks a revocation list or you need a stateful session, which pushes toward (b); (2) prices the BFF concretely (a deployed service, sticky/shared session state, a CSRF defense you must now build); (3) prices (a) concretely (the refresh endpoint is script-reachable, so an XSS is persistent unless rotation+reuse detection is on, and you depend on the IdP supporting it); (4) states what the browser holds in each design in one sentence; (5) names the migration path between them, because the answer 'start with (a), move to (b) when X' is legitimate if X is named; (6) states the residual risk that remains under the chosen option.

drills.prompt: Your SPA has used hidden-iframe silent refresh with prompt=none for three years. The requirement changes: it must work in Safari and in Firefox with default settings. What breaks, and what are your two viable replacements?
drills.answerSketch: Breaks: the iframe's request to the AS is a third-party context, so the AS session cookie is not sent and prompt=none returns login_required — the user is bounced to a full-page login on every token expiry. Replacements: (1) refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection, held in memory, refreshed via a back-channel POST from the app (no third-party cookie involved); (2) a BFF that holds the refresh token and refreshes server-side, with the browser holding a first-party HttpOnly session cookie. Note that a same-site AS (auth.example.com under your own eTLD+1) makes the cookie first-party-ish for SameSite purposes but does NOT help under Safari's storage partitioning for a genuinely different site.

drills.prompt: Fill in: ____ binds the authorization callback to the session that started it; ____ binds the id_token to the authorization request. code_challenge = ____(SHA256(code_verifier)) with code_challenge_method=____. The ____ flow is removed in OAuth 2.1 because it returns the token in the URL ____. Presenting a refresh token that was already used must trigger revocation of the whole ____.
drills.answerSketch: state / nonce / BASE64URL / S256 / implicit / fragment / token family

failureModes: "We use JWTs, so we're stateless and secure" — treating the format as a security property.
Verifying the JWT in the browser and calling that authentication.
Using state and nonce interchangeably, or omitting nonce entirely with OIDC.
Proposing implicit flow or hidden-iframe silent refresh in 2026.
Storing the refresh token in localStorage because 'the access token is short-lived anyway'.
Registering a wildcard or prefix redirect_uri for developer convenience.
Describing the BFF as strictly better without naming the CSRF surface it brings back.
interviewProbes: Draw the auth flow for this SPA. Which parts travel in the URL, and who else can read them?
What exactly does PKCE protect against, and what does it not protect against?
The access token expires while the user is mid-form. Walk me through the next 500 milliseconds.

sec-session-authz.title: Session Lifecycle and Authorization in the UI
objectives: Design logout, revocation and idle timeout as three distinct mechanisms with distinct scopes.
Design correct multi-tab session behaviour, including a single-flight token refresh.
Model UI authorization from a server-supplied permission set and defend why the client check is UX only.
Diagnose the refresh stampede and other cross-tab race conditions.
claims: Logout has three independent scopes — clear local application state, invalidate the server session or refresh-token family, and end the identity provider's own session via OIDC RP-Initiated Logout at the end_session_endpoint — and doing only the first means the next 'Sign in' click silently re-authenticates the same user.

A stateless JWT access token cannot be revoked before it expires; the only real options are a short lifetime (typically 5-15 minutes), a revocation list the API checks on every request, or a stateful session — and a stated revocation requirement of under a minute forces one of the latter two.

BroadcastChannel is the correct primitive for same-origin cross-tab session messaging; the storage event is a fallback that fires only in other tabs, only for localStorage writes, and never in the tab that performed the write.

When an access token expires while several tabs are polling, every tab attempts a refresh with the same refresh token; under rotation with reuse detection the first succeeds and the rest present an already-used token, which the authorization server treats as theft and responds to by revoking the family — logging the user out of every tab.

The fix for the refresh stampede is single-flight refresh: one shared in-flight promise within a tab, plus a cross-tab mutex, with all pending requests queued behind it and replayed once with the new token.

navigator.locks.request() provides an origin-scoped cross-tab mutex with automatic release on tab crash, and is supported across all current major browsers, making it the simplest correct way to serialise refresh without leader-election bookkeeping.

Idle timeout is measured from the last real user interaction and must be enforced server-side; a client-side timer is a UX affordance that a paused debugger or a modified client defeats. Absolute session lifetime is a separate control and both should exist.

Client-side route guards, disabled buttons and hidden menu items are UX, not security: the client's copy of the user's permissions is attacker-controllable, so the API must re-make every authorization decision on every request.

RBAC assigns permissions to named roles; ABAC evaluates attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment at decision time and is what you need as soon as the rule involves the specific record (ownership, tenant, region, time).

The UI should render from a server-supplied permission list rather than from role names, so that a policy change does not require a frontend deploy; and it must still handle a 403 gracefully on an action it did render, because the permission set can go stale mid-session.

viz.title: Three tabs, one refresh token
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three tab lanes plus one authorization-server lane on a shared time axis. A token-expiry line crosses all three lanes. Each tab emits request markers; when a request meets the expiry line it spawns a refresh attempt drawn as an arrow into the AS lane. The AS lane holds a visible token-family state cell (active / rotated / revoked). With the lock enabled, a lock-held band is drawn across the lanes and the queued requests visibly stack behind it. The user-visible outcome ('all tabs logged out' / 'seamless') is stamped inside the lane where it happens.
viz.predictPrompt: Three tabs of your app share a session. The access token expires at the same moment in all three while each is polling. Your authorization server uses refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, exactly as the security BCP recommends. What does the user see thirty seconds later — and which tab is responsible?
controls: Toggle: refresh-token rotation with reuse detection
Toggle: BroadcastChannel propagation of the new token
viz.insight: Rotation with reuse detection is the correct security control and is also the thing that turns an ordinary multi-tab race into a full logout. Every hardening measure has a concurrency consequence, and the cross-tab mutex is not a nicety — it is the piece that makes the security control shippable.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes an injected clock and a seeded RNG for jitter — no Date.now, no Math.random — and returns an ordered event log plus a final familyState and userVisibleOutcome. The unit test asserts the claim directly: tabs>1 && rotation && !lock => familyState 'revoked'; with lock => 'rotated' and outcome 'seamless'. All labels pinned inside lanes; at most seven at a time. Reduced motion: static event-log table with the same outcome stamps, plus the live-region narration.

drills.prompt: Review this axios/fetch refresh interceptor (Shiki-rendered): on a 401 it calls POST /refresh, stores the new token, and retries the original request. There is no queue and no lock. Name four distinct failure modes, at least one of which is user-visible and at least one of which is a security control misfiring.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Concurrent 401s inside one tab each trigger their own refresh — N refreshes, and with rotation N-1 of them fail. 2) Across tabs, the same race revokes the token family (security control misfiring into a mass logout). 3) The retry can loop infinitely if /refresh itself returns 401 — needs a retry guard and a hard failure path to login. 4) In-flight requests that started before the refresh are not queued, so they retry with a token that may already be rotated. 5) The new token is not broadcast, so other tabs keep using the stale one. Fix: one shared refresh promise per tab, navigator.locks around it, a request queue drained after resolution, a BroadcastChannel publish of the new token, and a single-attempt retry policy.

drills.prompt: Order a complete logout for an OIDC SPA with a BFF, and mark which steps are optional and why.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Optimistically disable the UI and cancel in-flight requests / abort controllers. 2) Call the BFF logout endpoint. 3) BFF revokes the refresh token at the AS (revocation endpoint) and destroys its own session record. 4) BFF clears the session cookie with an expired Set-Cookie carrying identical attributes (a cookie set with Domain/Path cannot be cleared without matching them). 5) Clear client state: store reset, IndexedDB caches purged, any personalised query cache dropped. 6) Broadcast the logout on BroadcastChannel so other tabs tear down too. 7) Optionally redirect to the AS end_session_endpoint with id_token_hint and post_logout_redirect_uri to end the IdP session — optional only if single sign-out is not required, and skipping it is exactly why 'Sign in' instantly logs the same user back in. 8) Navigate to a public route.

drills.prompt: Today: stateless JWTs with a 15-minute lifetime, no revocation list. The requirement changes: when an admin deactivates a user, that user's UI must stop working within 60 seconds. What breaks first, and give three designs at different cost points.
drills.answerSketch: Breaks first: nothing at all — the deactivated user keeps working for up to 15 minutes, because nothing consults the deactivation. Options: (1) cheapest — drop access-token lifetime to under 60s, which multiplies refresh traffic and makes the stampede/lock work mandatory; (2) middle — the API checks a small, cached revocation set (a Redis deny-list or a per-user 'tokens-valid-after' timestamp) on each request, adding one lookup; (3) strongest — stateful sessions at a BFF, where deactivation deletes the session and the very next request fails. Also mention pushing a logout to open tabs (BroadcastChannel is same-origin only, so this needs a server push channel), and note that a UI-side push is UX, not enforcement.

drills.prompt: The API can expose the user's authorization to the UI in three shapes: (a) a list of role names, (b) a flat list of permission strings, (c) a per-resource capability set returned with each resource. Given a multi-tenant app where a user can edit only documents they own or that their team shares with them, choose and justify — and say what the UI must still handle.
drills.answerSketch: Roles alone (a) cannot express ownership, so the UI would have to reimplement the policy — the classic drift bug. Flat permissions (b) are right for coarse navigation ('can see the Billing section') but still cannot answer 'can I edit THIS document'. The correct shape is (c) for per-record actions — return the allowed actions alongside each resource, which is ABAC evaluated once, server-side, and shipped as data. Use (b) for chrome and (c) for record actions. The UI must still handle a 403 on an action it rendered, because the capability set can go stale between fetch and click, and must never treat the absence of a capability as security.

drills.prompt: Fill in: The ____ event fires only in other tabs and only for localStorage writes; ____ is the correct same-origin cross-tab messaging primitive; ____.request() gives an origin-scoped cross-tab mutex that releases automatically if the tab crashes. Logout must cover three scopes: ____, ____, and ____.
drills.answerSketch: storage / BroadcastChannel / navigator.locks / local client state, server session or refresh-token family, identity-provider session (end_session_endpoint)

failureModes: "Logout removes the token from storage" — leaving the server session and the IdP session alive.
Treating a hidden button or a route guard as the authorization control.
Shipping roles to the frontend and encoding the policy in the UI, then having it drift from the API.
No multi-tab story at all — and then blaming the identity provider when reuse detection logs everyone out.
A client-side idle timer offered as the idle-timeout control.
Claiming JWTs can be revoked without describing the deny-list or stateful mechanism that makes it true.
interviewProbes: An admin revokes a user's access right now. How long until the UI stops working, and what makes that number what it is?
The user has four tabs open and the token expires. Talk me through it.
Where does the 'can this user edit this document' decision live, and how does the button know?

sec-embedding-isolation.title: Embedding: Frames, sandbox, postMessage
objectives: Diagnose clickjacking exposure and choose the correct framing control.
Read an iframe sandbox attribute and state exactly which capabilities remain — including the self-defeating combination.
Diagnose an unsafe postMessage handler and write the correct origin check.
Explain what cross-origin isolation buys and what it costs.
claims: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors supersedes X-Frame-Options; browsers that support CSP ignore X-Frame-Options when frame-ancestors is present, and frame-ancestors cannot be delivered via a <meta> tag — it must be an HTTP header.
frame-ancestors 'none' is the correct default for an authenticated application; a page that must be framed needs an explicit origin allowlist, and 'frame-ancestors *' is equivalent to no protection.

An <iframe sandbox> with no tokens places the frame in a unique opaque origin with scripts, forms, popups, top-level navigation, pointer lock and downloads all disabled; every token added re-enables exactly one capability.

sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" on a frame served from your own origin is self-defeating: the framed script is same-origin with the parent, so it can reach parent.document and simply remove the sandbox attribute — the combination is equivalent to no sandbox at all.
postMessage with targetOrigin "*" delivers the message to whatever origin currently occupies the target window, which may not be the one you loaded; always pass the exact expected origin.

A message receiver must validate event.origin against an exact-match allowlist and confirm event.source is the window it expects; a substring check such as event.origin.includes('example.com') is defeated by https://example.com.evil.net and by https://notexample.com.

rel="noopener" prevents an opened page from using window.opener to navigate or inspect the opener; modern browsers imply it for target="_blank", but it must still be set explicitly for window.open and for older embedded webviews. rel="noreferrer" additionally suppresses the Referer header.
