Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin severs the window.opener relationship with cross-origin openers; combined with Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp or credentialless it produces cross-origin isolation, which is required for SharedArrayBuffer and high-resolution timers and which breaks any third-party embed that does not send Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy.

Untrusted user-authored HTML should be rendered on a different hostname inside a sandboxed frame without allow-same-origin, because any same-origin rendering surface shares the cookie jar, the DOM and the storage of the authenticated application.
Framing protections do not stop an attacker who can already run script in your origin; they defend against a hostile outer document, which is a different threat than XSS.

viz.title: What can this frame reach?
viz.whatIsDrawn: A nested box diagram: outer document containing an iframe, with the iframe's origin shown as a labelled chip. Capability arrows are drawn from the inner frame outward — read parent DOM, read cookies, navigate top, submit form, open popup, postMessage — and each arrow renders solid (allowed) or severed (blocked) with the deciding token pinned to it. Toggling a sandbox token flips exactly the arrows it governs. A separate small panel INSIDE the outer box shows the framing decision (frame-ancestors / XFO) as a gate on whether the outer document could load the inner page at all.
viz.predictPrompt: A page embeds untrusted user HTML using <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" src="/usercontent/42"> where /usercontent is served from the same origin as the app. Write the one line of attacker JavaScript inside that frame that fully escapes the sandbox, and say what it reaches.
controls: Sandbox tokens: allow-scripts, allow-same-origin, allow-forms, allow-popups, allow-top-navigation, allow-modals
Frame content origin: same origin / separate hostname / opaque (srcdoc)
Framing header on the inner page: none / X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors
viz.insight: allow-same-origin is not one capability among many — it is the token that hands the frame the ability to delete its own restrictions. Sandbox isolates by origin, so the only way to sandbox untrusted content that also needs scripts is to serve it from a hostname that is not yours.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: (sandboxTokens, contentOrigin, framingHeader, coop) -> per-capability {allowed, decidingToken, note}. Unit-test the headline claim: allow-scripts + allow-same-origin + sameOrigin content => canRemoveOwnSandbox true; same tokens with a separate hostname => false. Arrow labels are pinned to the arrows inside the nested boxes. Cap visible labels at seven by grouping the rarely-toggled tokens. Reduced motion: static three-configuration comparison (no sandbox / naive sandbox / correct cross-origin sandbox).

drills.prompt: A payment widget's message receiver (Shiki-rendered): window.addEventListener('message', (e) => { if (e.origin.indexOf('pay.vendor.com') > -1) { applyResult(JSON.parse(e.data)); } }). Find three defects and write the corrected handler.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Substring match — https://pay.vendor.com.evil.net and https://notpay.vendor.com both pass. Use exact equality against a constant, scheme included: e.origin === 'https://pay.vendor.com'. 2) No event.source check — any window, including an attacker's popup, can post to this listener; verify e.source === iframeEl.contentWindow. 3) JSON.parse on unvalidated data feeding applyResult — validate the shape and treat every field as untrusted (a price or a status field arriving from a frame is not authoritative; confirm server-side). Bonus: the listener is never removed, and it should also check e.data's expected message type before parsing.

drills.prompt: Your app sets frame-ancestors 'none' and everything is fine. The requirement changes: an enterprise customer must embed your dashboard inside their intranet portal, logged in. Name everything that changes, in order, and the new attack you have just accepted.
drills.answerSketch: 1) frame-ancestors must list the customer's exact origin (and every origin they actually use — a portal often has several). 2) The session cookie is now third-party: SameSite=None; Secure; Partitioned, which under CHIPS gives a per-embedder cookie jar and means the user must authenticate inside the frame; Safari/Firefox may block it entirely, pushing you to a popup-based auth or an embedded token exchange. 3) SameSite CSRF protection is gone, so an Origin allowlist or synchronizer token becomes mandatory. 4) COOP: same-origin will sever popup-based auth flows and needs review. 5) New accepted attack: the outer document can position, resize and overlay your frame, so any irreversible action inside it is clickjackable by the very customer you allowlisted — high-value actions need in-frame confirmation that cannot be driven by a single click, or must be moved to a popup.

drills.prompt: A page sends both X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://partner.example. A modern browser is asked to frame it from https://partner.example. Does it load? Give the rule.
drills.answerSketch: Yes. When both are present, browsers that support frame-ancestors ignore X-Frame-Options entirely — frame-ancestors is authoritative. Keeping XFO alongside is harmless legacy coverage but must not be relied on to be the stricter of the two, and inconsistent values are a common source of 'it works in one browser' bugs.

drills.prompt: Order the steps to enable cross-origin isolation (COOP+COEP) on an existing app that embeds a maps widget, an analytics pixel and self-hosted fonts.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Ship Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy-Report-Only: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy-Report-Only: credentialless and collect reports. 2) Enumerate every cross-origin subresource and check whether it sends Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy. 3) Self-host or proxy anything that does not (fonts are usually easy; the maps widget usually is not). 4) Prefer COEP: credentialless over require-corp so no-cors subresources load without credentials rather than being blocked outright. 5) Verify auth popups still work — COOP: same-origin severs window.opener, so any postMessage-based popup flow must be reworked or use same-origin-allow-popups. 6) Confirm self.crossOriginIsolated is true. 7) Move both headers to enforcing.

drills.prompt: Fill in: ____ supersedes X-Frame-Options and cannot be set in a <meta> tag. The sandbox token combination ____ + ____ on same-origin content is equivalent to no sandbox. postMessage's second argument should be ____, never ____. On receive, check ____ with exact equality and confirm ____.
drills.answerSketch: frame-ancestors / allow-scripts + allow-same-origin / the exact expected origin / "*" / event.origin / event.source is the expected window

failureModes: "X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN handles it" with no frame-ancestors, and no awareness of the precedence rule.
Origin checks written with includes/indexOf/startsWith instead of exact equality.
postMessage with targetOrigin '*' because 'it's only our own iframe'.
sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" on same-origin untrusted content, believing it isolates.
Trusting data arriving over postMessage as authoritative rather than confirming it server-side.
Enabling COEP: require-corp and breaking every third-party embed, then reverting.
interviewProbes: How do you stop your app being framed, and what if a customer needs to frame it?
Here's our postMessage handler. Tell me what's wrong with it.
We need to render user-supplied HTML. Where does it go?

sec-supply-chain.title: Supply Chain: Third-Party Code and Secrets
objectives: Judge the real risk a given third-party include carries, in terms of what it can reach.
State what Subresource Integrity does and does not defend, and decide whether to use it.
Judge build-pipeline controls — lockfiles, npm ci, install scripts, release cooldown — by the attack each one blocks.
Explain why no secret can exist in a browser bundle, and how a 'public' key must be constrained instead.
claims: Any third-party script included with a plain <script src> executes with the full privileges of your origin: it can read the DOM, read every non-HttpOnly cookie, read all web storage, and issue authenticated same-origin requests. There is no sandboxed script tag.

Subresource Integrity (integrity="sha384-..." plus crossorigin="anonymous") makes the browser refuse a resource whose bytes differ from the pinned hash; it defends against a compromised or hijacked CDN, and it pins bytes, not intent.
SRI does not defend against a compromised upstream release: if the vendor's own build is malicious and you update the hash to match, SRI verifies the attack faithfully.

SRI is incompatible with any script the vendor mutates in place at a stable URL — which describes most analytics and tag-manager loaders — so the highest-risk includes are precisely the ones SRI cannot cover.

A tag manager is a remote-code-execution channel granted to whoever holds the tag-manager account; containing it means isolating it on a separate origin in an iframe, or refusing it unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval in CSP, or explicitly accepting that the marketing account is now a production credential.

npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile pins and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree; npm install may resolve new versions and rewrite the lockfile, so only a committed lockfile plus npm ci in CI makes a build reproducible.

A lockfile pins versions and integrity hashes but does not stop a malicious lifecycle script inside a pinned version from running at install time; --ignore-scripts (or the equivalent config) is a separate control with its own breakage cost.

npm's minimum release age / cooldown setting (npm 11.6+, 2025) delays installing packages published within the last N days, which specifically blocks the short window in which a compromised publish is live before it is caught — the pattern behind the 2025 chalk/debug and Shai-Hulud incidents.

Any value referenced through Vite's import.meta.env.VITE_* is inlined into the client bundle at build time and is public; a server-side secret placed in a VITE_-prefixed variable is published, and the framework will not warn you.

A publishable key (a Stripe publishable key, a Firebase web config, a Maps API key) is not a secret but must be constrained server-side by allowed origins/referrers, per-key scopes and rate limits, because it will be extracted from the bundle.
A leaked credential must be rotated, not merely removed from the code — it remains in git history, in build artifacts, in source maps published to production, and in CI logs.

viz.title: Blast radius of one bad include
viz.whatIsDrawn: Your origin drawn as a boundary box containing the app; outside it, nodes for each third party (CDN library, analytics, tag manager, npm dependency, font host) with an edge into the box labelled by how it enters (script tag, bundled at build, injected by another tag). The learner marks one node compromised; the propagation is animated along edges into the origin and then out to the assets it can reach (DOM, cookies, storage, API), drawn as reach-arrows inside the boundary. A gate icon sits on each edge showing which control (SRI / CSP / lockfile / cooldown) applies there, and gates that do not apply are drawn hollow.
viz.predictPrompt: Your CSP is script-src 'self' https://cdn.vendor.com and vendor.js is loaded with a correct, matching SRI hash. The vendor's own build pipeline is compromised and they publish malicious code at the same URL. On your site: (a) nothing happens, SRI blocks it; (b) the script is blocked and the feature it powers breaks; (c) the malicious script runs. Pick one — and then say what happens next week when your team updates the hash.
controls: Compromise injection point: CDN host / vendor release / npm transitive dep / tag-manager account
Toggle controls: SRI, strict CSP, lockfile + npm ci, install-script blocking, release cooldown
Toggle: token stored in localStorage vs HttpOnly cookie
Step the propagation one hop at a time
viz.insight: SRI does not make third-party code safe — it converts a silent compromise into a visible outage. Deciding whether you can tolerate that outage is the actual security decision, and it is why teams quietly remove SRI. The controls that address a malicious upstream release are entirely different ones: cooldown, pinning, vendoring, and not granting the code your origin in the first place.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: (compromisePoint, controlsEnabled, tokenStorage) -> {blocked: bool, blockedBy, reaches: string[], userVisible: 'outage'|'silent-compromise'|'none'}. Unit-test the headline: compromisePoint='cdn-host' && SRI => blocked with userVisible 'outage'; compromisePoint='vendor-release' && SRI => not blocked. Reach arrows and gate labels are drawn inside the boundary box. Reduced motion: a static 4x2 grid of compromise point by controls-on/off with the outcome text.

drills.prompt: Timed, 6 minutes. Your team is deciding whether to put SRI on all third-party scripts. Commit to yes or no, then justify against: a CDN compromise, a malicious vendor release, vendor-initiated hotfixes, and your on-call rotation.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) states what SRI defends (byte-level tampering in transit / at the CDN) and what it does not (a malicious upstream release); (2) names the failure mode explicitly — SRI turns a vendor's routine in-place update into a hard outage, which is an availability trade, not a free win; (3) distinguishes versioned-immutable URLs (SRI is nearly free) from mutable loader URLs (SRI is unusable) and applies the decision per-include rather than globally; (4) proposes the actual alternative for mutable loaders — self-host and vendor the file, or isolate it on another origin; (5) accounts for on-call: an SRI break at 3am looks like a total outage with a confusing console message, so it needs a runbook and monitoring; (6) states the decision rule rather than a preference.

drills.prompt: A .env file committed alongside a Vite app: VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com; VITE_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_...; VITE_SENTRY_DSN=https://...; VITE_ADMIN_API_TOKEN=sk_live_...; DATABASE_URL=postgres://... . Classify each line as safe, safe-but-must-be-constrained, or an incident, and say what you do in the next ten minutes for the incident.
drills.answerSketch: VITE_API_URL — safe (public by nature). VITE_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY — safe by design but confirm it is a publishable key and that origin restrictions exist. VITE_SENTRY_DSN — public by design, but rate-limit and enable inbound filters; a DSN in the bundle invites report spoofing. VITE_ADMIN_API_TOKEN — incident: the VITE_ prefix inlined a secret key into every built bundle served to every user. Next ten minutes: revoke and rotate the key at the provider first (not delete the line first), audit provider logs for use from unexpected origins, then remove the variable, then purge from history and rebuild/redeploy, and add a CI check that fails on any VITE_-prefixed name matching secret patterns. DATABASE_URL — not exposed by Vite (no prefix) but must not be in a frontend repo at all.

drills.prompt: You have budget for exactly three supply-chain controls this quarter. Choose from: SRI on all includes, npm ci in CI with a committed lockfile, install-script blocking, a minimum-release-age cooldown, dependency-count reduction, a strict CSP without unsafe-inline, moving the tag manager to a separate origin, provenance/attestation verification. Rank your three and say which attack each one blocks.
drills.answerSketch: A defensible top three: (1) strict CSP without unsafe-inline — reduces the value of any injection and constrains what a compromised script can load next; (2) npm ci + committed lockfile + release cooldown as one build-integrity change — blocks the dominant real-world attack, a freshly published compromised version being pulled into a build; (3) moving the tag manager off the app origin — removes a standing RCE channel held by non-engineers. Weaker choices to justify against: SRI (does not stop the release-compromise attack and adds outage risk), install-script blocking (real but breaks native deps and is often reverted), provenance (good but coverage is still partial). The graded skill is naming the attack each control blocks, not the ranking itself.

drills.prompt: Your app currently loads zero third-party scripts. The requirement changes: legal requires a consent-management platform, and marketing requires a tag manager, both before the next release. What breaks first in your security posture, and what is the containment design?
drills.answerSketch: Breaks first: your strict CSP — both vendors want unsafe-inline and often unsafe-eval, and both are mutable loaders so SRI is unavailable. Containment: put the tag manager and everything it loads on a separate hostname inside an iframe with a narrow postMessage contract, so tags never execute in the app origin; keep the CMP loader in the app origin only if it can accept a nonce, and pin its version. If the tag manager must be in-origin, then it must not be able to reach credentials — which means no token in web storage, HttpOnly session cookies only — and the marketing account needs the same access controls as production deploy access, including review of new tags. Write down which of those you accepted.

drills.prompt: Fill in: ____ installs exactly the lockfile and fails on drift; ____ may resolve new versions. SRI requires the attributes ____ and ____. A variable named ____ in a Vite app is inlined into the client bundle. A leaked key must be ____, not just deleted.
drills.answerSketch: npm ci / npm install / integrity / crossorigin="anonymous" / VITE_* / rotated

failureModes: "We pin exact versions, so we're safe from supply-chain attacks."
Believing SRI protects against a malicious vendor release.
Putting a server secret behind a VITE_ / NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix and assuming the framework hides it.
"It's a public key, so it doesn't matter" with no origin restriction or rate limit.
Adding a tag manager without noticing it is an RCE channel and without touching CSP.
Deleting a leaked key from the repo without rotating it.
Describing dependency risk only as 'we run npm audit'.
interviewProbes: This page loads six third-party scripts. What can the worst one do?
Would you put SRI on that? What breaks when the vendor ships a hotfix?
Where do you put the API key the frontend needs?

sec-privacy-pii.title: PII, Telemetry and Consent as Architecture
objectives: Design the data-egress surface of a frontend deliberately, naming every channel by which user data leaves the origin.
Apply data minimisation as an API-shape decision rather than a UI decision.
Design consent so that it gates script execution, not just script behaviour.
Design for erasure and export obligations that reach client-side caches.
claims: Data minimisation is a client architecture decision: a field never fetched cannot leak through a session replay, an error report, a screenshot or a client-side cache, so a /me endpoint that returns the full user record makes every downstream privacy control harder and permanent.

Error reporters and session-replay tools capture the DOM, network payloads and full URLs by default, which means PII most often leaves an application through the observability path rather than the authentication path.

Identifiers, tokens and reset codes must never appear in a URL path or query string, because URLs are recorded in browser history, in server access logs, in cross-origin Referer headers, and in every analytics tool that captures page paths.

Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the modern browser default: it sends the full URL same-origin, only the origin cross-origin over HTTPS, and nothing when downgrading to HTTP — so it stops cross-origin URL leakage but not your own logs and same-origin analytics.

Redaction must happen where the payload is constructed, before it crosses the origin boundary; masking in a vendor dashboard is not redaction, because the raw data has already been transmitted and persisted by a third party.

Under GDPR, consent for non-essential processing must be obtained before the processing occurs, which means a non-essential tag must not be present in the initial HTML at all; a banner that loads analytics and then honours the choice afterwards is a common and material audit finding.

Consent state must be readable synchronously at application bootstrap and propagated across tabs, or a second tab loads trackers the user has just rejected — which makes consent a store-level and loader-level concern, not a banner component's local state.

Erasure and data-portability obligations extend to data the app mirrors into IndexedDB, caches and localStorage; a client-side store therefore needs a documented schema, an owner for each field, and a tested wipe path.

navigator.sendBeacon and fetch with keepalive fire during pagehide, after React has unmounted and after any consent context may have been torn down, so the consent check has to live in the transport layer rather than in the component tree.

Pseudonymised identifiers are still personal data when they can be linked back to an individual, so replacing an email with a stable user id in analytics reduces exposure but does not remove the obligation.

Client-side masking of a displayed value (showing only the last four digits) protects against shoulder-surfing and screen capture but not against anyone reading the network response, so masking must be paired with an API that does not return the full value in the first place.

viz.title: Every way a field leaves the page
viz.whatIsDrawn: The origin as a boundary box containing a simplified screen with one highlighted field (say, a customer email). Egress channels radiate outward as labelled edges: analytics event, error report, session replay, cross-origin Referer, same-origin access log, third-party font/CDN request, client-side cache write into IndexedDB. The learner injects the field at one point in the app and each edge lights or stays dark, with the deciding control pinned on the edge (Referrer-Policy, consent gate, redaction hook, API shape). A ghost overlay shows the same map with the field never fetched at all, so the learner can compare 'controlled everywhere' against 'not present'.
viz.predictPrompt: A password-reset page is at https://app.example.com/reset?token=abc123. Referrer-Policy is the browser default (strict-origin-when-cross-origin). The page loads a webfont from a third-party host and reports errors to a third-party error tracker. Does the reset token reach the font host? Does it reach the error tracker? Name every place it does end up.
controls: Field injection point: URL / rendered DOM / API response body / form input
Toggle each control: Referrer-Policy strict, redaction at transport, consent gate, field removed from the API
Step outward one egress channel at a time
viz.insight: Controls attenuate egress channel by channel and every one of them can be misconfigured; not fetching the field closes all of them at once. Privacy work that starts at the API's response shape is cheap and permanent, and privacy work that starts at the vendor dashboard is expensive and always partial.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: (injectionPoint, controls, channelSet) -> per-channel {leaks: bool, decidingControl, note}. Unit-test the specific claim in the predict prompt: with strict-origin-when-cross-origin, the font host receives origin only (leaks=false) while the same-origin access log and browser history both leak=true, and the error tracker leaks unless a beforeSend URL scrubber is configured. Edge labels are pinned to the edges inside the map. Reduced motion: static map with all channel outcomes labelled, plus narration.

drills.prompt: Review this instrumentation (Shiki-rendered): analytics.track('checkout_completed', { userEmail: user.email, cardLast4: card.last4, url: window.location.href }); and, elsewhere, Sentry.init({ dsn, integrations: [replayIntegration()] }) with default options. Name every distinct privacy defect and the fix for each, in the order you would ship them.
drills.answerSketch: 1) Email sent to a third-party analytics vendor as an event property — replace with a pseudonymous, non-reversible-for-the-vendor id, and note it is still personal data. 2) window.location.href captured wholesale — any id or token in the URL now sits in the analytics vendor; scrub the URL at the transport and, better, stop putting ids in URLs. 3) Session replay with defaults records the DOM including form fields — enable masking of all text and inputs by default and allowlist what may be recorded, rather than blocklisting what may not. 4) Sentry with defaults attaches request bodies and breadcrumbs containing headers; add a beforeSend scrubber that runs before transmission. 5) None of this is behind a consent gate. Ship order: consent gate and transport scrubber first (they stop the bleeding for everyone), then the event-payload fixes, then the API-shape change that removes the field from the client entirely.

drills.prompt: Your app caches the user's document list and profile in IndexedDB for offline reads. Legal now requires that a deletion request purge all personal data within 30 days, including anything on the user's device, and that you be able to enumerate what you hold. What breaks first, and what do you build?
drills.answerSketch: Breaks first: you cannot enumerate or purge what you never modelled — an untyped cache with ad-hoc keys has no owner per field and no way to answer 'what do we hold'. Build: (1) a documented schema per object store with a classification tag per field (personal / pseudonymous / non-personal) and a schemaVersion; (2) a single repository module that is the only writer, so a wipe path exists and is testable; (3) a server-signalled purge — on next authenticated load, if the server reports the account deleted or a purge epoch newer than the local one, the client wipes before rendering; (4) a purge on logout as the common case; (5) an export path so the portability obligation is satisfied from the same schema; (6) a test that asserts the wipe removes every store, since a forgotten store is the actual failure. Note honestly that a device that never comes back online cannot be purged, and that this is why caching less is the real control.

drills.prompt: Order the bootstrap sequence for a consent-gated analytics setup that is correct on a second tab opened one second after the user rejects in the first tab.
drills.answerSketch: 1) The HTML contains no non-essential tag — only the consent module. 2) At bootstrap, read persisted consent synchronously from a first-party cookie or localStorage before any tag decision. 3) Subscribe to a BroadcastChannel consent topic so live changes propagate to other tabs. 4) If consent is absent, render the banner and load nothing. 5) On acceptance, persist, broadcast, and only then dynamically import and initialise the tags. 6) On rejection or withdrawal, persist, broadcast, and tear down: stop the transport, drop queued events, and clear vendor cookies/storage. 7) The transport layer itself re-checks consent immediately before every send, including sendBeacon on pagehide, because that fires after the React tree is gone. The graded ordering error is loading the tag before step 5.

drills.prompt: Product wants a 'share this page' link on an internal report page whose URL is /reports/2026-q3?customer=acme&contact=jane.doe@acme.com. Triage: what must change before this ships, what is merely advisable, and what is out of scope for the frontend?
drills.answerSketch: Must change: the email must leave the URL entirely (history, logs, Referer, analytics, and now a link users will paste into chat tools); use an opaque report id resolved server-side. Must change: the share link must not grant access by possession unless that is a deliberate, expiring, revocable capability — otherwise sharing the URL shares the data. Advisable: set Referrer-Policy explicitly rather than relying on the default; scrub URLs at the analytics transport; add a copy-link affordance that produces the opaque URL so users are not copying the address bar. Out of scope for the frontend: the server-side authorization check on the report id, and the retention policy — but the frontend must not be the thing enforcing them.

drills.prompt: Timed, 6 minutes. Session replay would materially speed up debugging a checkout funnel that handles names, addresses and partial card data. Argue for or against enabling it, and specify the exact configuration you would require if it ships.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: (1) states the default posture — replay records the DOM, so the default is mask-everything and allowlist, never blocklist; (2) names the network-payload capture separately from the DOM capture, since they are configured separately and the payload is usually the bigger leak; (3) requires a consent gate and states which lawful basis is being claimed; (4) names the vendor-side controls that do NOT count — dashboard masking is post-transmission; (5) prices the alternative honestly (structured events plus a reproduction harness are slower to debug but carry no PII), rather than pretending the debugging value is zero; (6) states a bounded decision, e.g. 'enabled on non-checkout routes with allowlist masking, disabled on any route rendering payment or address fields', and the review that would revisit it.

failureModes: "We mask it in the logging dashboard" — treating post-transmission masking as redaction.
Loading analytics on page load and then 'respecting' the consent choice afterwards.
Putting user ids, emails or reset tokens in query strings.
Treating consent as a banner component's local state, with no cross-tab propagation and no synchronous bootstrap read.
Forgetting IndexedDB and localStorage entirely when asked about the right to erasure.
Enabling session replay with default settings on a page containing payment or address fields.
Assuming a pseudonymous id is not personal data.
interviewProbes: Name every way a customer's email address can leave this page.
Where does redaction happen in your telemetry pipeline, and why there?
A user asks us to delete their data. What does the frontend have to do?

ops-error-capture.title: Client Error Capture: The Surfaces You Are Missing
objectives: Enumerate every surface a client error can escape through, and name the exact handler that catches each one
Diagnose an error that arrives as "Script error." with no stack and state the two-part fix
Decide what a React error boundary does and does not catch, and wire React 19's root-level error callbacks so swallowed crashes are still reported
claims: window.onerror and window.addEventListener('error') catch uncaught synchronous exceptions but never catch a rejected promise; an unhandled rejection fires the separate 'unhandledrejection' event instead.
A failed ,

An exception thrown by a cross-origin script reaches window.onerror as the literal message "Script error." with no file, line or stack, unless the script tag carries crossorigin="anonymous" and the server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

A React error boundary catches errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods and in child constructors; it does not catch errors thrown in event handlers, in async callbacks, or by the boundary component itself.

React 19's createRoot accepts onUncaughtError, onCaughtError and onRecoverableError options, which are the supported way to report crashes an error boundary swallowed and hydration mismatches React silently recovered from.

'unhandledrejection' fires when a rejected promise reaches the end of a microtask checkpoint with no handler; attaching .catch() later fires 'rejectionhandled' but the error report has already been sent.
An exception thrown inside a Web Worker does not reach the main thread's window.onerror; the worker needs its own error handler and must post a serialized error back to the page.
error.cause (ES2022) is the standard channel for preserving the original error when re-throwing, so a reporter that serializes only error.stack silently loses the causal chain.

viz.title: Where the Error Escapes
viz.whatIsDrawn: One page frame containing six labeled emission sites (throw in render, throw in a click handler, throw in a setTimeout callback, rejected promise, 404, throw from a cross-origin script). Firing a site sends a single token upward through four candidate catch layers drawn as horizontal bands inside the frame — error boundary, capture-phase window listener, window.onerror, unhandledrejection — and the band that actually catches it lights up with its handler name annotated inline on the band; anything that reaches the top exits through a band labeled UNREPORTED. A dimmed ghost band across the whole frame shows the naive mental model ("onerror catches everything") for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Your reporter registers window.onerror and nothing else. Which of these five reach it: (a) a throw inside a click handler, (b) a throw inside a .then() callback, (c) an that 404s, (d) a throw during render inside an error boundary, (e) a throw inside a setTimeout callback?
controls: Toggle crossorigin="anonymous" on the script tag
Step the token one layer at a time
viz.insight: Uncaught exceptions and rejected promises travel on two entirely different rails, and an error boundary is a third; a reporter wired to only one rail loses whole classes of failure without ever looking broken.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure routing table: (emissionSite, config) -> orderedLayers[] + caughtBy | 'UNREPORTED'. No timers in the sim; the viz drives stepping. Unit-test every (site, config) pair against the claim list — this table IS the teaching content. prefers-reduced-motion renders the full routing table statically with all six paths drawn at once. Live region announces "click handler throw: not caught by boundary, caught by window.onerror".

drills.prompt: Here is a 14-line telemetry bootstrap: it calls window.onerror = report inside a useEffect in <App/>. Select every class of error this setup silently drops.
drills.answerSketch: Rejected promises (needs unhandledrejection); resource load failures (needs capture-phase listener); everything thrown before <App/> mounts, including the initial bundle's own top-level errors; errors a boundary caught (needs onCaughtError); worker errors. Also: assigning window.onerror clobbers any other handler.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the bundle now ships from cdn.example.com instead of the app origin. Which field of your existing error reports goes blank first, and what two independent changes restore it?
drills.answerSketch: Message collapses to "Script error." and stack/file/line are empty. Fix requires BOTH crossorigin="anonymous" on the <script> tag AND Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the CDN response; either alone does nothing.

drills.prompt: Order these by the sequence an exception thrown during React render actually passes through: window 'error' listener, nearest error boundary getDerivedStateFromError, componentDidCatch, root onCaughtError, UNREPORTED exit.
drills.answerSketch: getDerivedStateFromError -> componentDidCatch -> root onCaughtError; the window 'error' listener does NOT fire in production because React catches the throw (it re-throws only in development).

drills.prompt: To observe a failed load globally you must write window.addEventListener('error', handler, ____) because resource error events do not ____.
drills.answerSketch: true (capture phase); bubble.

drills.prompt: Your error dashboard shows zero events this week; support has 40 reports of a blank screen after clicking Export. Pick the single most likely cause and justify it in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: An error boundary is rendering a fallback and swallowing the throw, with no onCaughtError wired — the app 'handled' the crash so nothing was ever reported. Distractors: quota exhaustion, ad blocker, sampling.

failureModes: Says window.onerror catches everything, including promise rejections and failed resource loads
Assumes an error boundary reports to the error tracker automatically, and never wires onCaughtError — so every caught crash is invisible
Blames a browser extension or the CDN for "Script error." instead of naming crossorigin + Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Installs the global handler inside a component effect, so it exists only while that component is mounted and misses every startup error
Cannot explain why a worker's errors never appear
interviewProbes: Your error dashboard is quiet but users report white screens. Walk me through everything that could be swallowing errors.
Why does "Script error." happen, and what exactly do you change to fix it?
Where in a React app do you install error handlers, and why not in a component?
What does an error boundary not catch, and what do you do about those?

ops-error-pipeline.title: Symbolication, Grouping and the Noise Budget
objectives: Design an error pipeline that turns raw minified events into a small number of owned, actionable issues
Choose a sampling policy that reduces cost without deleting the rare fatal errors you are paying to find
Specify the build-time contract between bundle, source map and release that makes stack traces resolve to the right line
claims: A minified file is linked to its source map either by the //# sourceMappingURL comment or by a build-injected //# debugId=<uuid> that also appears as debug_id inside the map; debug IDs survive CDN path changes and file renames, URL-based matching does not.
Source maps for a private app must be uploaded to the error backend at build time and removed from the deploy artifact — a publicly served .map file reconstructs the entire original source.

Every event must carry a release identifier (typically the git SHA) that also tags the uploaded maps, or a stack frame from an older bundle resolves against newer sources and confidently points at the wrong line of code.

Errors are grouped by a fingerprint derived from the normalized stack trace, not from the message; IDs, URLs and timestamps must be stripped before fingerprinting or a single bug appears as thousands of distinct issues.

Sampling must be applied per fingerprint (keep the first N per group per window), not uniformly at random, because uniform sampling discards a rare fatal error at exactly the same rate as one noisy loop.

Browser-extension frames (chrome-extension://, moz-extension://) and injected third-party scripts are the largest source of unactionable client errors and must be dropped in the SDK before the request is sent, so they never consume quota.
An error backend that has exhausted its quota drops events silently, which means the rate limit itself has to be a monitored metric — otherwise the first outage after you hit the cap is invisible.

"ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications" and "Non-Error promise rejection captured" are known benign-by-default noise classes; suppressing them is a documented decision with an owner, not a fix.

viz.title: The Noise Funnel
viz.whatIsDrawn: 10,000 raw error events enter at the top and pass through six labeled stages drawn as narrowing bands — extension denylist, PII scrub, fingerprint normalization, group/dedupe, sample, quota — with the surviving count printed inside each band and the reason for each drop annotated on the band itself. The output is a stacked bar of distinct issues, each segment sized by event count and shaded actionable vs unactionable. A dimmed ghost outline behind the funnel shows the same 10,000 events with every stage disabled (3,400 distinct issues, mostly extension noise).
viz.predictPrompt: To cut cost you add uniform 10% sampling. You have twelve distinct bugs this week; one of them is a crash that hit exactly six sessions. What is the probability that rare crash appears in your dashboard at all, and which bugs are unaffected?
controls: Switch sampling mode: uniform random vs first-N-per-group
Step the funnel stage by stage
viz.insight: Uniform sampling lowers your bill by deleting precisely the rare errors you were paying to discover; sample per group so every distinct bug survives at least once.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes a seeded event corpus (fixed fixture, seeded RNG injected) and a config, returns per-stage counts plus the grouped issue list. Unit-test the headline claim numerically: assert that at 10% uniform sampling a 6-event group is missed with p ≈ 0.53, and that first-N-per-group keeps 12/12 groups. Reduced-motion: static funnel with all counts printed.

drills.prompt: A crash affects 6 sessions per week and emits one event per session. Under uniform 10% sampling, what is the probability you see it at least once this week? Give a percentage within 5 points.
drills.answerSketch: 1 - 0.9^6 = 0.469, about 47%. So more than half the weeks it is completely invisible — while a 50,000-event noisy loop is never at risk.

drills.prompt: Your issue list has 2,140 issues, most named `Failed to fetch https://api.example.com/orders/8f21c…`. Name the pipeline defect and the one-line fix.
drills.answerSketch: Grouping is fingerprinting on the raw message, which embeds a unique order id. Normalize dynamic segments out of the message (or fingerprint on the normalized stack trace only) before grouping.

drills.prompt: Order these pipeline stages so that quota is protected and no PII ever leaves the browser: send, per-group sample, fingerprint, scrub, extension denylist, dedupe.
drills.answerSketch: denylist -> scrub -> fingerprint -> dedupe -> per-group sample -> send. Scrub must precede anything that persists or transmits; denylist first because it is the cheapest and largest reduction.

drills.prompt: Sentry-style tooling injects `//# ______=<uuid>` into the minified bundle and a matching `______` field into the .map, so the two can be paired without relying on the file's ____.
drills.answerSketch: debugId; debug_id; URL/path.

drills.prompt: Legal wants every error retained for compliance. Your quota is 100k events/month; you currently generate 4M. You have five minutes to choose a policy and defend it.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer separates the two goals: a cheap high-volume aggregate counter (count by fingerprint, no payload) satisfies 'we know it happened', while full-payload capture is reserved for first-N-per-group. Denylist extension noise first (usually 40–70% of volume) before negotiating retention at all.

failureModes: Uploads source maps to the CDN next to the bundle and considers it done, making private source public
Groups on error.message, producing a dashboard where every issue has a count of 1
Cuts cost with a uniform sampleRate and never realizes rare fatal errors vanished
Uses the release name "production" for every deploy, so stack traces resolve against whatever build uploaded last
Filters extension noise in the dashboard UI, after it has already consumed the quota
interviewProbes: Your stack traces are minified in production. Walk me through the build-to-dashboard contract that fixes that.
You have 4M errors a month and budget for 100k. What do you drop, and in what order?
Two engineers say the same bug is two different issues. What is wrong with your pipeline?

ops-rum-vitals.title: RUM: Field Vitals, Attribution, and the Data You Never Collected
objectives: Diagnose a p75 regression by separating a genuine code regression from a traffic-mix shift
Specify when each vital is final and where it must be flushed so the numbers are not systematically optimistic
Name the dimensions a vitals beacon must carry for a regression to be investigable at all
claims: Core Web Vitals are judged at the 75th percentile of page views over a rolling 28-day window, with 'good' at LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms and CLS <= 0.1; a mean or median can look healthy while the p75 fails.

LCP and CLS are not final at load: LCP stops being updated at the first user interaction, and CLS accumulates for the entire page lifetime, so any metric read at the load event is systematically too optimistic.

The only reliable flush point is the visibilitychange event transitioning to 'hidden' (with pagehide as a companion); unload and beforeunload frequently never fire on mobile, and listening for them disqualifies the page from the back/forward cache.

A page restored from the back/forward cache does not re-run navigation timing; the web-vitals library emits a synthetic navigation on pageshow with event.persisted, and ignoring it under-counts your fastest visits and skews the whole distribution.

INP attribution depends on the Long Animation Frames API (long-animation-frame entries, Chrome 123+): without it you know an interaction took 480 ms but not whether the time went to input delay, script in the handler, or presentation delay.

RUM is survivorship-biased: sessions that crashed, were abandoned before the beacon fired, or ran in a browser without PerformanceObserver are absent from the data, so a segment with no data is a finding rather than an empty cell.

A vitals beacon must carry dimensions — device class, country, effective connection type, route, and whether the visit was a cold or warm load — or a p75 regression is uninvestigable: the aggregate moved and nothing indicates which cohort moved.
A p75 can shift entirely because of traffic mix, with no code change at all, so cohort-level comparison is what distinguishes a regression from a mix shift.

viz.title: What Actually Moved the p75
viz.whatIsDrawn: A histogram of LCP samples along the x-axis, stacked into two shaded cohorts (fast desktop, slow mobile), with a solid vertical p75 marker and a dashed 2.5 s threshold line drawn through the bars. Last week's distribution sits behind as a dimmed ghost outline with its own faint p75 marker, so the delta is read inside the chart. The current p75 value and each cohort's share are annotated on the bars themselves, not in a side panel.
viz.predictPrompt: Mobile is 40% of your traffic at p75 LCP 4.0 s; desktop is 60% at 1.6 s; your global p75 is 3.1 s. A marketing campaign shifts mobile to 55% of traffic. No code changed. Does the global p75 move, and is the move small (under 0.2 s) or large?
controls: Per-cohort improvement slider (shift one cohort's distribution)
Toggle 'exclude sessions that never flushed' to expose survivorship bias
viz.insight: The p75 is a property of your traffic mix as much as of your code — segment before you celebrate a win or open an incident, because the same number moves for both reasons.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds two fixed lognormal-ish cohort sample arrays (pre-generated fixture, seeded — no Math.random at runtime) and a pure percentile function; the config is (mobileShare, cohortShift, excludeUnflushed). Unit-test that mixing two static cohorts reproduces the exact p75 quoted in the predict prompt, and that the mix-only change moves p75 by the amount the prose claims. Reduced-motion: render both distributions side by side, statically, with both p75 markers.

drills.prompt: Review this reporter: it computes vitals inside window.addEventListener('load', ...) and sends them with fetch() on beforeunload. List three separate defects and what each one does to the numbers.
drills.answerSketch: (1) Reading at load freezes LCP/CLS before they are final — LCP too low, CLS far too low. (2) beforeunload frequently does not fire on mobile, losing the sessions most likely to be slow. (3) Registering beforeunload disqualifies bfcache eligibility, which itself degrades real navigation speed and removes the fast restores from the dataset.

drills.prompt: Given: desktop 60% at p75 1.6 s, mobile 40% at p75 4.0 s, global p75 3.1 s. Mobile share rises to 55%. Estimate the new global p75 and state whether you would open an incident.
drills.answerSketch: It moves materially worse (roughly 3.6–3.9 s depending on tail shape) with zero code change. Do not open a code incident: both cohort p75s are unchanged. Correct action is to report the mix shift and, separately, decide whether mobile's 4.0 s is now the priority.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes from 'report vitals' to 'alert within 30 minutes on a p75 LCP regression'. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The 28-day window is unusable for alerting, and short windows have too few samples per cohort for a stable percentile. You need a minimum-sample-size gate per window, cohort-level series rather than one global series, and a change-detection method robust to weekday/mix effects — otherwise the alert fires on noise every day and gets muted in a week.

drills.prompt: Vitals must be flushed when the document's visibility state becomes '______'; a bfcache restore is detected by checking event.______ on the pageshow event.
drills.answerSketch: hidden; persisted.

drills.prompt: Your CFO asks why RUM runs at 100% sampling while errors are sampled at 10%. Defend or change the policy in writing, with numbers.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer prices it: vitals beacons are small and fixed-size per page view, and percentile estimates need volume per cohort, so head sampling directly costs you the ability to segment small cohorts. A defensible compromise is 100% for the vitals beacon (cheap, aggregate-only) and sampling only the heavy attribution payload (LoAF entries, element selectors).

failureModes: Reports LCP and CLS at the load event and shows numbers that are quietly far too good
Uses averages, or a p50, because 'p75 is what Google uses but we track our own'
Alerts on an unsegmented global p75 and spends a week chasing a marketing campaign
Uses beforeunload/unload to flush, losing mobile sessions and bfcache eligibility at once
Expects their own RUM to match CrUX exactly, and treats the gap as a bug rather than a different population and window
interviewProbes: Your LCP p75 went from 2.3 s to 3.1 s overnight. How do you find out whether you caused it?
When is LCP final? When is CLS final? Where do you send the beacon and why there?
Your dashboard shows no data for Android in Brazil. What does that tell you?

ops-slo.title: Frontend SLOs and Burn-Rate Alerting
objectives: Judge whether a proposed SLI is actually measurable, aggregable and user-centric
Choose between static-threshold and multi-window burn-rate alerting, and justify the thresholds numerically
Identify the blind spot in any SLI computed only from client beacons
claims: An SLI requires an explicit denominator: '99.5% of route transitions complete within 1 s' is measurable; 'the app is fast' is not.
An error budget is the complement of the target over the window — a 99.9% monthly target permits roughly 43 minutes of failure per 30 days — and spending budget is permitted, not a failure.
Threshold-count SLIs ('fraction of page views with LCP <= 2.5 s') aggregate correctly across shards and time windows; percentile SLIs do not, because a percentile of percentiles is not a percentile.

Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting pages on fast burn (about 2% of a 30-day budget consumed in 1 hour, a 14.4x rate) and files a ticket on slow burn (about 10% consumed over 3 days, roughly 1x); one static threshold either pages on noise or misses a slow bleed entirely.
An SLI computed from client beacons cannot observe total failure: if the app never loads, no beacon is sent and the SLI looks perfect, so availability needs a server-side or synthetic denominator.
Bots, uptime checkers and your own synthetic monitors must be excluded from a user-facing SLO, or the number is partly measuring your monitoring.
An SLO with no agreed consequence is decoration; the contract is what the team does when the budget is exhausted (feature freeze, reliability work), agreed in advance of the first breach.
Alerts should fire on the SLI — a symptom users feel — not on every dependency; the dashboard explains why, the page says that someone is being harmed.

viz.title: Burn Rate vs the Static Threshold
viz.whatIsDrawn: A 30-day error-budget burndown drawn as a descending line from 100% to 0%, with an injected incident visible as a change of slope; the remaining-budget percentage is annotated on the line at the incident. Two alert lanes run underneath, labeled inline — 'static 5-min threshold' and 'multi-window burn rate' — each lighting up at the moment it would fire, or staying dark. A dimmed ghost line shows an ordinary month's burn for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Your alert fires when the 5-minute error rate exceeds 1%. A 0.4% error rate persists continuously for nine days. Does the alert ever fire, and how much of a 99.9% monthly error budget is left at the end?
controls: Toggle alert strategy: static / burn-rate / both
viz.insight: A static threshold is blind to duration; burn rate is the same alarm expressed in units of error budget, which is the only unit proportional to how much users were actually harmed.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is pure arithmetic over an injected clock: (targetSLO, window, incidentRate, incidentDuration, strategy) -> budgetRemainingSeries[] + firedAt[]. Unit-test the predict-prompt case exactly: 0.4% for 9 of 30 days = 0.12% of the window against a 0.1% budget = 120% consumed, static alert never fires. Reduced-motion: static chart with both alert lanes and the final budget figure labeled.

drills.prompt: Convert to allowed downtime per 30-day month: 99.9%, 99.95%, 99.99%. Then state how long a single incident may last before it consumes the entire 99.9% budget.
drills.answerSketch: 99.9% ≈ 43m 12s; 99.95% ≈ 21m 36s; 99.99% ≈ 4m 19s. One incident may last 43 minutes at 100% failure — or over 7 hours at 10% failure, which is the point of measuring burn rather than duration.

drills.prompt: A team defines their availability SLI as 'fraction of client-reported page loads with no fatal error'. Give the specific outage this SLI reports as 100% healthy.
drills.answerSketch: Any failure that prevents the JS from running at all — a bad deploy, a broken entry chunk, a CDN or DNS failure, a CSP that blocks the bundle. Nothing loads, so nothing reports, and the denominator shrinks with the numerator. Needs an edge/server-side request count as denominator.

drills.prompt: Leadership tightens the SLO from 99.9% to 99.95%. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Alerting, before engineering. The budget halves to ~21 minutes, so the burn-rate thresholds must be recomputed, and the minimum sample size needed to distinguish 99.95% from 99.9% within a short window roughly quadruples — low-traffic routes become statistically unalertable. Also every existing planned-maintenance and deploy-blip allowance now has to come out of a much smaller budget.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of writing a frontend SLO: choose the alert burn rates, pick the SLI, pick the target, define the user journey, define the denominator, agree the budget policy, choose the window.
drills.answerSketch: user journey -> SLI -> denominator -> target -> window -> burn-rate alerts -> budget policy. The journey comes first because the SLI has to be something the user experiences; the policy comes last because it is a negotiation about the number, not an input to it.

drills.prompt: Pick 99.9% or 99.99% for a checkout flow and defend the choice with the cost of the extra nine.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer prices the nine: 99.99% is ~4 minutes/month, which is shorter than a human can be paged and respond, so it requires automated rollback, multi-region static hosting, and a deploy process that cannot cause a 5-minute blip — plus it becomes unmeasurable on low-traffic routes. Defensible answer often sets a tighter SLO on a narrow critical journey and a looser one elsewhere.

failureModes: Picks 99.99% because it sounds serious, without noticing it is under 5 minutes a month
Defines the SLI as a p99 latency and then cannot aggregate it across shards or windows
Computes availability entirely from client beacons and cannot see a failed deploy
Treats budget consumption as a failure to be punished, so teams hide incidents
Alerts on CPU, dependency health and every subsystem, and pages nobody when users are actually broken
interviewProbes: Write an SLO for the checkout page. What is the denominator?
Why is a p99 latency a bad SLI and a threshold count a good one?
Your error rate is 0.3% for a week and nothing paged. Is that fine?

ops-tracing.title: Tracing Across the Client Boundary
objectives: Explain how a trace started at a click is propagated into and correlated with server spans
Explain the CORS and latency cost that trace propagation imposes on cross-origin requests
Explain why the browser can only head-sample, and what that forces the collector to do
claims: W3C Trace Context defines traceparent as version-traceId-parentId-flags, with a 32-hex trace id and a 16-hex span id; the client can generate the trace id at the moment of the click, before any request exists.

traceparent is not a CORS-safelisted request header, so adding it to a cross-origin request converts a simple request into a preflighted one — an extra OPTIONS round trip per request unless Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the preflight.

tracestate carries vendor state and must be forwarded unmodified; the baggage header carries user-defined context and is both a data-exfiltration risk and a header-size risk if it is populated from client state without an allow-list.

Server-Timing is the only standard mechanism for exposing server-side timings to client JavaScript, and reading it for a cross-origin response requires the Timing-Allow-Origin header, otherwise the PerformanceResourceTiming fields are zeroed.

The sampling decision must be made once at the root of the trace and propagated in the traceparent sampled flag, or the client retains a span whose server-side counterpart was dropped and every trace is half-missing.

Head sampling decides at trace start and is cheap but keeps mostly uninteresting traces; tail sampling decides after the trace completes and can keep the slow and failed ones, but requires buffering at a collector — a browser can only head-sample.

A useful client span is anchored to a user-visible event (interaction start through the paint that answers it), not to fetch start, because fetch-anchored spans hide input delay, queueing and render — the parts the user actually felt.

A full OpenTelemetry browser SDK costs tens of kilobytes gzipped and patches globals; under a strict bundle budget, a hand-rolled propagator that only injects traceparent and emits one span per interaction is frequently the correct trade.

viz.title: One Click, Two Systems
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three stacked swimlanes — browser main thread, network, server — sharing one time axis, with a single trace id printed once at the left. Spans are bars: click, handler script, fetch, an optional preflight OPTIONS bar drawn in a hatched fill, then server spans reconstructed from Server-Timing, then response handling and paint. Durations are labeled on the bars themselves. A dimmed ghost row shows the same interaction with no propagation, where all server work is one opaque grey block labeled 'unknown 240 ms'.
viz.predictPrompt: You add a traceparent header to every API call from the browser to api.example.com. Nothing on the server changes. Median API latency in your RUM rises by about 90 ms. What did you actually change?
controls: Toggle Timing-Allow-Origin (server spans visible or opaque)
viz.insight: Propagating a trace changes the CORS class of the request: observability is not free at the network layer, and the first thing your instrumentation measures may be its own overhead.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure span-layout function: (config) -> spans[] with start/duration, plus derived totals; the preflight bar is inserted by a rule, not by a timer. Unit-test that enabling propagation without Access-Control-Max-Age adds exactly one RTT per request and that enabling max-age adds it only to the first. Reduced-motion: full static timeline with both the propagated and non-propagated rows shown together.

drills.prompt: traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01. The 32-hex segment is the ____, the 16-hex segment is the ____, and the trailing 01 is the ____ flag.
drills.answerSketch: trace id; parent (span) id; sampled.

drills.prompt: Your traces all show a client span and nothing from the server, even though the backend is instrumented. The header is being sent and the backend team confirms it arrives. Name the most likely cause.
drills.answerSketch: The sampled flag is being sent as 00 (or regenerated per request), so the server drops the span while the client keeps its own. Second candidate: a new trace id is generated per request, so client and server spans exist but never join into one trace.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes to 'only keep traces for interactions slower than 1 s'. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The browser cannot do this — the decision must be made at trace start, before the duration is known, and the server span is created from that decision. Either send everything and tail-sample at the collector (cost moves to ingest), or make a heuristic head decision (route, prior p95, user segment) and accept bias.

drills.prompt: Your CDN serves the API from a different origin. PerformanceResourceTiming reports 0 for requestStart, responseStart and transferSize. Which single header fixes it, and why is it not a CORS header in the usual sense?
drills.answerSketch: Timing-Allow-Origin. It governs exposure of timing detail to JS, independently of Access-Control-Allow-Origin, which governs whether the response body is readable — a response can be fully readable and still have opaque timings.

drills.prompt: You have a 5 kB gzipped budget for observability on the landing route. Argue for full OpenTelemetry-JS or a hand-rolled propagator, and say what you give up.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer names what OTel buys (auto-instrumentation of fetch/XHR/document-load, a standard exporter, ecosystem context propagation) and what it costs (tens of kB, global patching, and instrumentation of things you do not care about), then proposes the narrow build: generate an id, inject one header, emit one span per interaction, ship server spans via Server-Timing — with the explicit loss being uninstrumented third-party calls and no automatic resource spans.

failureModes: Generates a new trace id per request, producing thousands of single-span traces that correlate nothing
Puts a user email or auth token into the baggage header
Blames the backend for a latency jump their own preflight caused
Believes the browser can decide to keep only slow traces
Anchors the client span at fetch start, so the trace shows a fast API and a user who waited 900 ms
interviewProbes: Trace a click through to a database query. What does the browser have to send, and when is the id created?
Adding tracing made every cross-origin call slower. Why?
How would you keep only the interesting traces? Where does that decision have to happen?

ops-event-taxonomy.title: Event Taxonomy, Schema Governance and PII
objectives: Judge whether a proposed event set is queryable and durable, or will splinter into unusable metrics
Classify every property for PII at definition time and decide what must never leave the browser
Choose a governance mechanism that survives team growth rather than one that decays into a wiki page
claims: An event name should encode object plus past-tense action (checkout_completed) drawn from a closed, reviewed object list; free-form naming reliably produces 'Checkout Complete', 'checkout-completed' and 'completed_checkout' as three unrelated metrics.
Values belong in properties, not in names: video_played {quality: '1080p'} stays queryable, while video_played_1080p creates a new metric per value and breaks every aggregate.

A schema registry that fails the build on an unregistered event or a changed property type is the only governance that survives a growing team; a naming convention documented on a wiki decays within a quarter.
Event schemas need explicit versioning and additive-only evolution, because changing the type or meaning of an existing property silently corrupts every historical query that already ran against it.

Every property must carry a PII classification at definition time (none / pseudonymous / personal), because reliable scrubbing is only possible against a declared schema — a regex deny-list over free-form JSON eventually leaks.

URLs and page titles are the most common accidental PII carrier (order ids, email addresses in query strings, password-reset tokens), so paths must be templated to /orders/:id before they leave the browser.
Where consent is required, the consent state must gate the SDK's queue, not just its network call — otherwise the data is merely delayed until consent, which is collection, not abstention.

An impression or exposure event needs its trigger rule written into the schema (for example, 50% visible for at least 1 s via IntersectionObserver), or two teams will count 'seen' differently and neither number can be compared.

viz.title: The Metric That Splintered
viz.whatIsDrawn: A 12-month conversion funnel rendered as four connected stages, with the event-name tree that feeds it drawn directly beneath, each node annotated inline with its first-seen date and a lint marker (duplicate, value-in-name, unregistered, unclassified-PII). As the timeline is scrubbed, teams introduce name variants and the funnel's stages visibly change height. The governed version is a dimmed ghost funnel drawn behind, so the divergence between the real number and the reported number is read inside the chart.
viz.predictPrompt: Three teams independently ship checkout_completed, 'Checkout Completed' and checkout_complete over six months. Today you rebuild the conversion funnel over 12 months of history, querying one of those names. Does the chart show an obvious gap, an obvious drop, or a smooth line?
controls: Toggle 'value in event name' for the video events
viz.insight: Bad taxonomy does not produce missing data — it produces a smooth, plausible, confidently wrong chart, which is the failure mode nobody notices in review.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds a fixed synthetic event log (fixture, no RNG at runtime) and a pure query function: (selectedName, governanceOn, timeRange) -> funnelCounts + lintFindings. Unit-test that the ungoverned query returns a monotone series while the true total is materially higher — the pedagogical claim is that the chart looks fine. Reduced-motion: both funnels rendered side by side with the delta labeled.

drills.prompt: A PM sends 14 tracking requests ('track when they see the banner', 'track 1080p plays', 'track how long they stayed', 'track their plan tier'…). Sort each into: new event, property on an existing event, derivable at query time, or refuse.
drills.answerSketch: Most are properties or derivable. Session duration is derivable from existing events, not an event. Plan tier is user context, not an event property to be duplicated on every event. 'Sees the banner' is a new event but requires a visibility trigger rule. Refusals: anything that duplicates an existing event under a new name.

drills.prompt: Here is an event payload: {event:'purchase', email:'a@b.com', url:'/reset?token=abc123', price:'49.99', ts:1718...}. Name four separate defects.
drills.answerSketch: Raw email is personal data with no classification; the URL carries a reset token and is untemplated; price is a string, so it will not aggregate and will break the moment someone sums it; the event name is a bare noun with no action and no version.

drills.prompt: An impression counts when the element has been at least ____% visible for at least ____, measured with ____Observer.
drills.answerSketch: 50; 1 second; Intersection. (Exact numbers are a policy choice — the claim is that the rule must be written down, and this is the common default.)

drills.prompt: Legal now requires per-user deletion on request. What breaks first in an event pipeline that was designed without it?
drills.answerSketch: You cannot find the user's rows: events keyed by a rotating anonymous id, or with identity smeared through free-form properties and URLs, make deletion impossible to prove. You need one stable pseudonymous id per event, no identity in free-form fields, and a documented mapping — retrofitting this over historical data is usually impossible, so history gets deleted wholesale.

drills.prompt: Argue for or against failing the build on a schema violation, given that it will block a hotfix at 2am.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer separates severity: block on unregistered events and type changes (silent corruption, unrecoverable), warn on style violations, and provide an explicit escape hatch that registers the event as provisional with an owner and an expiry, so 2am is unblocked without permanently defeating the gate.

failureModes: Encodes values into event names, creating a metric per value
Says 'we'll scrub PII in the pipeline' — after the data has already left the device
Never versions the schema, then changes a property's type and corrupts a year of history
Counts impressions on component mount rather than on visibility
Relies on a naming convention in a Notion page as the governance mechanism
interviewProbes: Design the event taxonomy for a checkout flow. What is an event and what is a property?
How do you stop 40 engineers from inventing 200 event names?
Where does PII most often leak in analytics, and what stops it?

ops-telemetry-sdk.title: Designing the Analytics SDK
objectives: Design a queue-batch-flush pipeline that does not lose the events emitted immediately before the page disappears
Choose a transport per situation and state its hard limits and failure behaviour
Budget the SDK's own bundle, main-thread and INP cost as a product constraint
claims: navigator.sendBeacon() queues a POST that survives page unload, but gives you no response, no custom headers and a body limited in practice to 64 KiB — so it cannot be used for anything you must retry on failure.
fetch(url, {keepalive: true}) permits methods and headers sendBeacon cannot, but all in-flight keepalive request bodies share a 64 KiB budget; exceeding it makes requests fail rather than queue.
Events must be flushed on visibilitychange to 'hidden', not only on a timer, because a mobile tab can be frozen or killed without any further JavaScript running.

A durable queue in IndexedDB survives reloads and crashes and enables retry, but every queued event must carry both the time it occurred and the time it was sent, or offline events silently land on the wrong day.
Batching trades freshness for cost and must be bounded on both axes — flush at N events or T seconds, whichever comes first — so a quiet session is not lost and a burst does not produce 200 requests.

A substantial share of requests to well-known analytics hostnames is blocked by content blockers, so serving the collector from a first-party path is the difference between measuring your users and measuring only the users who do not block trackers.

The SDK's own cost is a product decision: it belongs in the bundle budget, must not block first paint, and its serialization work should run in requestIdleCallback or a worker so it does not add to INP.
Sampling must be deterministic per session (hash a stable session id) rather than per event, or a sampled session produces a funnel with holes and every conversion rate computed from it is wrong.

viz.title: Where the Events Go Missing
viz.whatIsDrawn: A single session timeline: event emissions as ticks along the top, a queue box beneath that visibly fills, and flush attempts as arrows leaving the queue toward a server lane. Injectable interruptions (tab hidden, network offline, tab killed, blocker installed) appear as vertical markers on the timeline, and any event still in the queue when the session ends is drawn struck through inside the queue box with the reason labeled on it. A dimmed ghost row above shows the naive one-request-per-event transport for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Your SDK batches and flushes every 10 seconds using plain fetch(). A user completes a purchase and closes the tab 2 seconds later. The batch holds 6 events including purchase_completed. How many of those 6 arrive at your server?
controls: Flush policy: timer / size / visibilitychange / all three
Inject interruption: hide, offline, kill, blocker
viz.insight: The events with the highest business value are emitted moments before the page goes away, so the flush trigger and the transport — not the schema — decide whether you have a funnel at all.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: pure reducer over a scripted event/interruption tape with an injected clock — (policy, transport, interruptions) -> delivered[] | lost[] with a reason per lost event. No real network, no Date.now. Unit-test the six headline cases including 'plain fetch at tab kill loses the whole batch' and 'sendBeacon over 64 KiB returns false'. Reduced-motion: static timeline with delivered/lost columns enumerated.

drills.prompt: Order the flush pipeline so no event is lost at tab kill and no PII is persisted: enqueue in memory, scrub, serialize batch, persist to IndexedDB, sendBeacon, remove from durable queue on next successful send.
drills.answerSketch: scrub -> enqueue in memory -> persist to IndexedDB -> serialize batch -> sendBeacon -> remove on next session's confirmed send. Scrub before anything persists. Removal cannot happen on beacon return (there is no return value you can trust); it happens when a later, response-bearing send confirms receipt.

drills.prompt: Review: window.addEventListener('beforeunload', () => fetch('/collect', {method:'POST', body})). Give three defects.
drills.answerSketch: beforeunload often never fires on mobile; a plain fetch is cancelled when the document goes away (needs keepalive or sendBeacon); registering beforeunload disqualifies the page from bfcache, degrading real navigation performance to collect data.

drills.prompt: Events average 350 bytes of JSON. How many fit in one sendBeacon call, and what does your SDK have to do when a batch would exceed that?
drills.answerSketch: 64 KiB / 350 B ≈ 187 events. The SDK must chunk the batch and be aware the 64 KiB budget is shared across in-flight keepalive bodies, so several large concurrent beacons can fail even though each is individually under the limit. It must also cap queue growth so an offline session does not build an unsendable batch.

drills.prompt: The requirement becomes: a purchase event must never be lost, even if the user is offline for three days. What changes?
drills.answerSketch: Durable IndexedDB queue with a bounded size and eviction policy; separate occurredAt from sentAt so analytics does not attribute the purchase to Thursday; a client-generated idempotency/dedupe key because retries will duplicate; a transport that reports success (so plain sendBeacon is insufficient for the confirm step); and quota handling, since IndexedDB can be evicted.

drills.prompt: Complete: document.addEventListener('______', () => { if (document.visibilityState === '______') navigator.______(url, blob); });
drills.answerSketch: visibilitychange; hidden; sendBeacon.

drills.prompt: Defend routing analytics through a first-party path on your own domain instead of the vendor's hostname.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer names the win (recovers blocked traffic, avoids third-party cookie loss, same-origin means no preflight) and the costs honestly: you now own the endpoint's availability, abuse and cost; you become responsible for the data leaving your origin; it can be read as circumventing user intent, which is a policy decision, not an engineering one; and your own CDN/WAF now sees the payloads.

failureModes: Sends one HTTP request per event and calls batching a later optimization
Flushes on beforeunload/unload
Retries a sendBeacon call, not realizing there is no way to know whether it failed
Ignores the SDK's own bundle size and its serialization cost on the main thread, then reports a worsening INP
Samples per event rather than per session, producing funnels whose steps do not nest
interviewProbes: Design an analytics SDK. Start with what happens when the user closes the tab.
What are the actual limits of sendBeacon and keepalive fetch?
A third of your events never arrive. Give me four independent explanations.
How much of the bundle may your telemetry own, and how would you enforce it?

ops-feature-flags.title: Feature Flags: Kill Switches, Rollout and Where to Evaluate
objectives: Classify a flag by type and lifetime, and judge which system should own it
Judge where a given flag must be evaluated — bundle default, client SDK, or edge — from its flicker, caching and secrecy constraints
Judge the correctness cost of flag debt rather than treating it as tidiness
claims: Flags are not one thing: release flags (short-lived, deleted after rollout), operational kill switches (long-lived, must evaluate with the network degraded), experiment flags (sticky assignment, exposure logged) and permission flags (which belong to authorization, not to a flag system) have different owners and different lifetimes.
A kill switch that requires a network fetch to evaluate is useless during the incident it exists for; it needs a safe default compiled into the bundle plus a cached last-known value.

Client-side evaluation means the flag payload arrives after first paint, so any flag that changes above-the-fold UI produces a visible flash of the wrong variant unless the value is bootstrapped into the HTML or resolved at the edge.

Evaluating at the edge or server and injecting the result yields zero flicker and keeps targeting rules off the client, but makes the HTML response uncacheable unless it is varied on a bucketing cookie or header.

Bucketing must be a pure function of hash(flagKey + salt + stableUserId) so the same user resolves to the same variant everywhere without stored state; Math.random() re-rolls the user on every page load.
Percentage rollouts must be monotonic — a user included at 10% must remain included at 25% — which a hashed-bucket threshold gives for free and re-randomized assignment does not.

Every flag is a live branch: n flags on one screen means up to 2^n reachable states, of which only a handful are ever tested, which makes flag debt a correctness problem rather than a cleanliness problem.
A flag needs an owner, a created date and an expiry recorded at creation, with a stale-flag report that fails CI after expiry — this is the only mechanism that reliably gets flags removed.

viz.title: The Rollout That Re-Rolled
viz.whatIsDrawn: 200 user dots arranged around a ring, each colored by variant, with the current rollout threshold drawn as an arc and its percentage labeled on the arc itself. The learner steps the rollout 5% -> 25% -> 50% and the dots that change are outlined. The previous step's assignment persists as a dimmed ghost ring behind, so 'who changed' is visible directly. A toggle switches the assignment function between hashed bucketing (dots only ever join treatment) and per-load randomness (dots churn in both directions at every step).
viz.predictPrompt: You increase a flag from 10% to 20%, evaluated as Math.random() < rate on every page load. Of the users who saw the new UI during the 10% phase, roughly what fraction will see the OLD UI on their very next visit?
controls: Stable user id vs per-load id
viz.insight: A rollout percentage only means something if assignment is a deterministic hash; otherwise you are re-randomizing your entire user base on every page load and no one has a consistent product.
