viz.buildNotes: sim.ts implements a real 32-bit hash (fixed, e.g. a small murmur3) over (flagKey|salt|userId) -> [0,1), with the user id list a fixed fixture. Unit-test monotonicity explicitly: assert that the treatment set at 10% is a strict subset of the set at 25% for the hashed function, and that it is not for the random one. Reduced-motion: three static rings for 5/25/50% side by side, with changed dots marked.

drills.prompt: A kill switch is implemented as: on app start, fetch('/flags').then(setFlags); if flags.paymentsEnabled === false, hide the payments UI. Give two reasons this fails during the incident it was built for.
drills.answerSketch: If the flag service or network is degraded — which correlates with the incident — the fetch fails and the code falls through to the default, which here is 'enabled'. And it only evaluates at app start, so an already-open session never sees the switch flip. Needs a safe default in the bundle, a cached last-known value, and a push/poll path to flip a live session.

drills.prompt: Classify each by flag type and lifetime: (a) hide the new dashboard until launch day, (b) disable third-party chat when it is down, (c) show variant B to 50% for an experiment, (d) enterprise customers get SSO, (e) a debug overlay for the team, (f) a 2% canary of a new checkout renderer.
drills.answerSketch: a release (delete after launch); b operational kill switch (permanent); c experiment (sticky + exposure logged, delete at conclusion); d NOT a flag — entitlement/authorization, must be enforced server-side; e internal, gate on identity not percentage; f release/canary with monotonic hashed bucketing and an automated rollback trigger.

drills.prompt: The flag must now also control a server-rendered header on a CDN-cached page. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Cacheability. The HTML now has two variants, so either the cache key includes a bucketing cookie/header (fragmenting the cache and halving hit rate) or evaluation moves to the edge worker. Also client and edge must use the identical hash and salt, or a user sees variant A in the header and variant B in the app.

drills.prompt: Deterministic bucketing hashes the concatenation of ____, ____ and ____, then compares the normalized result against the rollout fraction.
drills.answerSketch: flag key; a per-flag salt; a stable user (or device) id.

drills.prompt: A logged-out marketing page must stay fully CDN-cached and must run a flag that changes the hero image. Argue for client evaluation or edge evaluation and name what you sacrifice.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer refuses the false choice at first: the cheapest correct option is to ship both hero variants in the HTML and choose with a synchronous inline script before paint, at the cost of a little extra HTML. Edge evaluation is correct if variants are large or targeting must stay secret, at the cost of a cache split. Client evaluation is the wrong answer here because the hero is the LCP element.

failureModes: Buckets with Math.random(), so users flicker between variants across page loads
Hides the body with an anti-flicker style until the flag SDK loads, destroying LCP for 100% of users to serve 10%
Treats entitlements and permissions as feature flags, putting authorization decisions on the client
Has 300 live flags, no owners and no expiry, and cannot say which are actually on
Builds a kill switch that cannot be evaluated when the network is degraded
interviewProbes: How do you roll a risky change out to 1% of users and then to 100%?
Where do you evaluate the flag, and what does that decision cost you?
You have 300 flags. What do you do on Monday?
Design a kill switch for a payment provider outage.

ops-experiments.title: A/B Testing Architecture: Assignment, Exposure and SRM
objectives: Diagnose a sample-ratio mismatch from stage counts and name the frontend defect that caused it
Distinguish assignment from exposure and explain how conflating them biases the result
Identify the frontend-specific ways an experiment harms users outside its primary metric
claims: Assignment (which bucket a user is in) and exposure (that the user actually reached the changed surface) are distinct events; analyzing on assignment dilutes the measured effect with users who never saw the variant.
Each experiment must use its own salt in the bucketing hash, or users in the treatment of experiment A are correlated with the treatment of experiment B and the two results contaminate each other.

A sample ratio mismatch — an observed split materially different from the designed split, conventionally flagged at a chi-square p-value below about 0.001 — invalidates the experiment; it is a bug report, not a result to interpret.

The common frontend causes of SRM are a variant-specific JavaScript error that stops the exposure beacon, redirect-based variants that lose users during the redirect, a treatment slow enough that more users abandon before logging, and bot filtering applied after assignment instead of before.

Rendering the variant client-side after paint produces a flash of original content; the classic fix of hiding the page until the experiment SDK loads converts a cosmetic bug into an LCP regression for every user, including the control group.

Guardrail metrics — JS error rate, LCP and INP, bounce rate, revenue per session — must be evaluated on every experiment regardless of hypothesis, because most damage from experiments is collateral rather than in the metric under test.

Checking results continuously and stopping the moment p < 0.05 inflates the false-positive rate far above 5%; either fix the sample size in advance or use a sequential method that is valid under peeking.
Novelty and primacy effects plus strong day-of-week seasonality mean a result must survive at least one full weekly cycle before it can be trusted.

viz.title: Diagnosing a Sample Ratio Mismatch
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two parallel counter columns (control, treatment) descending through four stages — assigned, exposure logged, interacted, converted — with the observed ratio printed between the columns at every stage and the first stage where the ratio departs from 50/50 marked in place with the deviation labeled. Injectable defects appear as annotations on the stage where they act. A dimmed ghost pair shows a healthy experiment's ratios for direct comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Your treatment shows a 6% conversion lift. The split is 50.0% control / 47.8% treatment. Should you ship, and in which direction is the missing 2.2% most likely to bias the result?
controls: Inject defect: variant-only JS error / redirect variant / slower treatment / post-assignment bot filter
Toggle exposure logging vs assignment-only analysis
viz.insight: A sample ratio mismatch almost always removes the WORST users from one arm — those who errored, waited, or bounced — so it manufactures precisely the lift you were hoping to see.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts generates stage counts from a fixed seeded population plus a defect model, and computes the chi-square statistic itself. Unit-test that the injected 'variant-only error' produces both an SRM and a spurious positive lift, since that pairing IS the claim. Reduced-motion: static two-column table with the deviation stage highlighted and the chi-square p-value printed.

drills.prompt: Stage counts — assigned 100,000 / 100,000; exposure logged 92,400 / 88,100; converted 4,100 / 4,520. Where does the ratio first break, and what class of frontend bug produces exactly this shape?
drills.answerSketch: It breaks at exposure, not at assignment, so bucketing is fine and something is killing the treatment beacon. Classic cause: a JS error in the variant that throws before the exposure event is sent — which removes the users who had the worst experience, inflating treatment conversion. Check the error tracker filtered by variant before touching the stats.

drills.prompt: A 50/50 experiment observed 5,012 vs 4,790 users. Is this an SRM? Show the reasoning at the level you would on a whiteboard.
drills.answerSketch: n = 9,802, expected 4,901 each, deviation 111. SD = sqrt(n*0.25) ≈ 49.5, so z ≈ 2.24, p ≈ 0.025 — above the ~0.001 alarm threshold, so it is not conclusive evidence of an SRM, but it is worth a second look given SRM's severity. The reasoning (compare the deviation to sqrt(n)/2) matters more than the exact p.

drills.prompt: The experiment must now run on a logged-out page served entirely from the CDN edge cache. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: There is no stable user id and no uncached HTML. You need an edge-assigned bucketing cookie set on first response, the cache key varied on that cookie (halving hit rate, or two pre-rendered variants at the edge), and identical hash+salt on client and edge. Exposure logging still has to happen client-side, and bot traffic at the edge must be excluded before assignment, not after.

drills.prompt: Order the experiment launch checklist: SRM check, define primary metric, choose salt, power/sample-size calculation, A/A validation, wire exposure logging, define guardrails, analyze.
drills.answerSketch: define primary metric -> power/sample size -> choose salt -> wire exposure logging -> define guardrails -> A/A validation -> SRM check -> analyze. SRM is checked before results are looked at, and the A/A run validates the pipeline before any real hypothesis rides on it.

drills.prompt: After three days the treatment shows a 6% lift with p = 0.03, all guardrails green, no SRM. The launch is Friday. Defend shipping or waiting.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer names peeking (a p of 0.03 obtained by watching daily is not a 3% false-positive rate), novelty effect, and the absence of a full weekly cycle — three days may be entirely weekdays. It also names the asymmetry: if the change is cheap to reverse and guardrails are green, shipping behind a flag with continued measurement is a legitimate risk-managed choice; claiming a validated 6% lift is not.

failureModes: Interprets the result of an experiment that has an SRM, usually as a win
Logs exposure at assignment time, so the effect is diluted by users who never saw the variant
Reuses one hash across every experiment, correlating treatment groups
Peeks daily and stops at the first p < 0.05
Ships an anti-flicker snippet that hides the body and never measures its LCP cost on the control group
Cannot name a single guardrail metric
interviewProbes: Design the A/B system for a page that is served from the CDN edge.
Your split is 50.0/47.8 and the treatment wins. What do you do?
What is the difference between assignment and exposure, and why does it matter?
How do you keep the variant from flashing, without wrecking LCP?

ops-resilience.title: Client Resilience: Retry, Timeout, Circuit Break, Fall Back
objectives: Design a request policy that specifies, per endpoint, what may be retried, for how long, and what happens when it stops
Explain why unjittered retries schedule a second outage at the moment of recovery
Choose an honest fallback rather than a spinner, and state the staleness contract to the user
claims: Only idempotent operations may be retried blindly; a non-idempotent POST requires a client-generated idempotency key sent identically on every attempt so the server can deduplicate.

Retries need exponential backoff with jitter — full jitter picks a random delay in [0, base * 2^n] — because a fixed or purely exponential backoff synchronizes every client and turns a blip into a self-inflicted thundering herd at recovery.

A retry budget (for example, retries capped at 10% of total requests) stops retries from multiplying load exactly when the dependency is already failing; unbounded per-request retries are how a partial outage becomes a total one.

A request with no explicit timeout has an effective timeout of minutes; AbortSignal.timeout(ms), combined with a user cancellation via AbortSignal.any(), is the standard bound, and the value should be set by the user's patience, not by the server's p99.
A Retry-After header on a 429 or 503 (delay-seconds or an HTTP-date) overrides your own backoff, and ignoring it is what gets a client rate-limited or blocked outright.

A circuit breaker moves closed -> open past a failure threshold, serves the fallback immediately while open, and admits a single trial request in half-open; its primary value is sparing the user a queue of doomed requests, not sparing the server.
4xx responses other than 408, 425 and 429 must not be retried: they will fail identically, and retrying them disguises a client bug as a flaky network.
A fallback must be honest about staleness — rendering cached data with no indication that it is stale is worse than an error state for anything transactional.

viz.title: The Retry Storm
viz.whatIsDrawn: Top lane: offered request rate against a server capacity line over 60 seconds, with the outage window shaded and the recovery moment marked. Bottom: a circuit-breaker state machine (closed / open / half-open) whose active state is highlighted in step with the timeline, with the trigger condition labeled on each transition arrow. A dimmed ghost curve shows the baseline offered load with retries disabled, so the amplification is read inside the chart.
viz.predictPrompt: 800 clients are calling a failing endpoint. Each retries 3 times with a fixed 1-second backoff. The dependency recovers at t=20s. What is the peak request rate in the second after recovery relative to normal, and why does the service fail again immediately?
controls: Backoff: fixed / exponential / exponential with full jitter
Circuit breaker on/off with failure threshold
viz.insight: Retries without jitter and without a budget do not recover the system — they schedule a second, larger outage for the exact moment it comes back.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a discrete-time simulator with an injected clock and a seeded RNG for jitter: (clients, policy, outageWindow) -> loadPerTick[] + breakerState[]. Unit-test the pedagogical claim directly — assert peak post-recovery load with fixed backoff exceeds capacity and that full jitter keeps it under, using a fixed seed. Reduced-motion: static small-multiples of the three backoff policies with peak values labeled.

drills.prompt: Complete full jitter: const delay = Math.random() * Math.min(______, base * 2 ** ______);
drills.answerSketch: maxDelay (a cap); attempt. Full jitter is uniform over [0, capped exponential), not exponential ± a small wobble.

drills.prompt: A fetch wrapper retries any rejected promise or any non-2xx response, 3 times, 500 ms apart, for every request in the app. Name four distinct hazards.
drills.answerSketch: Retries non-idempotent POSTs, so a payment can be submitted three times; retries 4xx that will never succeed, hiding client bugs and burning rate limit; fixed backoff synchronizes clients; no overall deadline, so the user waits 1.5 s plus three request timeouts with no feedback and no cancellation.

drills.prompt: The endpoint changes from GET /balance to POST /transfer. What breaks first in your existing retry policy?
drills.answerSketch: Blind retry becomes a correctness hazard — a timeout does not tell you whether the transfer executed. You need a client-generated idempotency key created once per user intent (not per attempt), server-side dedupe, and a UI that can express 'we are not sure yet' rather than optimistically retrying.

drills.prompt: Order a circuit breaker's transitions and their triggers: half-open -> closed, closed -> open, open -> half-open, half-open -> open.
drills.answerSketch: closed -> open on failure threshold; open -> half-open after the cooldown elapses; half-open -> closed when the single trial succeeds; half-open -> open when the trial fails (restarting the cooldown, usually longer).

drills.prompt: The account balance endpoint is down. Argue for showing the cached balance from 40 minutes ago versus showing an error, and write the exact UI copy you would ship.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer distinguishes informational from transactional: a stale balance is acceptable only if it is explicitly timestamped and every action that depends on freshness is disabled. Copy must state the age, not merely 'offline'. Silent stale data on a number people act on is the failure mode being trained against.

failureModes: Retries everything, including 4xx and non-idempotent POSTs
Uses a fixed or unjittered backoff and re-kills the service at recovery
Sets a 30-second timeout because 'the backend p99 is 20 seconds', ignoring that the user left at 5
Creates the circuit breaker inside a component so a new instance is created on every mount and it never trips
Calls a spinner a fallback, or shows stale data with no indication of age
Ignores Retry-After and gets the client blocked
interviewProbes: The orders API is down. What does your app do, second by second?
Which requests do you retry, and which do you refuse to retry?
800 tabs are polling a service that just recovered. What happens?
What is your timeout, and how did you choose the number?

ops-build-chunking.title: From Module Graph to Hashed Chunks
objectives: Explain how entry points and dynamic imports determine chunk boundaries, and what silently defeats a split
Explain why a chunking strategy is really a cache-invalidation strategy, in kilobytes re-downloaded
Explain the conditions under which tree shaking actually removes code
claims: A production build is a graph problem: entry points and dynamic import() boundaries define chunks, and every static import is pulled into its importer's chunk, so one stray top-level import of a heavy module silently cancels a code split.

Tree shaking removes an export only when the bundler can prove it is unused and free of side effects; a missing or incorrect sideEffects field in package.json, or a module-level call with observable effects, keeps the whole module in the bundle.

A content hash is computed from a chunk's emitted output, so a chunk's hash changes whenever module ids or import paths inside it change — which is how one dependency bump can invalidate chunks whose source never changed.

The single-vendor-chunk strategy maximizes invalidation: any dependency change rewrites the largest file the user had cached. Grouping by change frequency — framework, stable libraries, application code — caches far better.

Over-splitting has a real cost too: each additional chunk adds a request and a preload hint, and below roughly 20 kB the loss of compression context and per-request overhead outweighs the caching benefit.
Vite emits <link rel="modulepreload"> for a dynamic chunk's static dependencies so a lazy route loads in one round trip; removing those hints to 'reduce requests' reintroduces the import waterfall.

Bundle size must be measured compressed (gzip or brotli) and as a per-route delta rather than a project total, and enforced in CI with a tool such as size-limit — a budget checked by hand is a budget already exceeded.
Source maps, license banners and polyfill injection are build outputs with their own cost, and shipping a legacy polyfill bundle to modern browsers can double parse cost for the majority of users.

viz.title: The Hash Cascade
viz.whatIsDrawn: Left: the module graph with one entry and two dynamic-import boundaries drawn as dashed cut lines. Right: the emitted chunk files, each labeled with name, content hash and compressed size. Far right: a returning user's cache column, each row marked HIT or MISS with the kilobytes re-downloaded totaled at the bottom. Editing a module lights the affected nodes on the left and flips the corresponding hashes and cache rows on the right. The previous build's hashes remain as dimmed ghost text under each new hash.
viz.predictPrompt: You change one line in a 2 kB utility that three routes import. Your build emits vendor.[hash].js (180 kB), app.[hash].js (60 kB) and three route chunks. Under a single-vendor-chunk config, how many kilobytes must a returning user re-download — and is the answer different if the util lives in node_modules?
controls: Pick the edited module: leaf util / shared dep / route component / framework dependency
Chunking strategy: single vendor / by change frequency / per route
viz.insight: Your chunking strategy is your cache-invalidation strategy: you are choosing, in advance, how many kilobytes a returning user re-downloads the next time you touch one line.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models a fixed module graph with declared sizes and a deterministic fake hash (content -> stable id, no randomness): (editedModule, strategy, stableIds) -> chunks[] with hashes, plus cacheDelta in kB. Unit-test the headline numbers so the prose and the sim cannot drift. Reduced-motion: two static builds side by side with changed hashes marked and the kB delta labeled.

drills.prompt: App code 60 kB, deps 180 kB (of which the framework is 130 kB and rarely changes). You bump one small dependency. Compute the returning user's re-download under (a) one vendor chunk, (b) framework / other-deps / app split.
drills.answerSketch: (a) 180 kB — the whole vendor chunk's hash changes. (b) roughly the 50 kB other-deps chunk, with the 130 kB framework chunk still a cache hit. The app chunk may also change if module ids shift, which is what deterministic ids prevent.

drills.prompt: routes.tsx begins with `import { Chart } from './charts'` and then lazily loads the analytics route with `lazy(() => import('./routes/analytics'))`, which also imports Chart. The initial bundle is 90 kB larger than expected. Explain and fix.
drills.answerSketch: The static top-level import pulls charts into the entry chunk, so the lazy boundary no longer excludes it — the dynamic import is still lazy but its heaviest dependency already shipped. Fix: remove the static import (import the type only, with `import type`), or move the eager usage behind the same boundary.

drills.prompt: A package advertises that it is safe to tree shake by setting `"______": false` in package.json; a bundler cannot drop a module when it contains a top-level ______.
drills.answerSketch: sideEffects; side effect (a top-level call, assignment to a global, or a CSS import).

drills.prompt: The requirement becomes a hard 120 kB gzipped budget for landing plus roadmap. Which chunk do you attack first, and what is the risk of the obvious move?
drills.answerSketch: Attack whatever is largest AND on the critical path — usually a graph/visualization or date/i18n library. The obvious move (lazy-loading it) helps only if it is genuinely not needed for first paint; if it renders above the fold, you have converted bytes into a waterfall and a layout shift. Measure the delta compressed, per route, and gate it in CI.

drills.prompt: Six proposed build changes; mark each as helps caching, hurts caching, or no effect: deterministic module ids; one chunk per component; hashing filenames; bumping a dep weekly; splitting framework from other deps; inlining all CSS into JS.
drills.answerSketch: Deterministic ids: helps. Chunk per component: hurts (request overhead, worse compression). Hashed filenames: enables long-term caching, no effect alone on invalidation scope. Weekly dep bumps: hurts, proportional to how deps are grouped. Framework split: helps. Inlining CSS into JS: hurts — style changes now invalidate JS chunks and block render.

failureModes: Hand-writes manualChunks for everything and creates worse caching than the default
Believes tree shaking removes unused code from any library regardless of side effects
Measures uncompressed bundle size, or measures project total instead of per-route delta
Creates a chunk per component and regresses load time via request overhead
Deletes modulepreload links to 'reduce requests' and reintroduces the waterfall
interviewProbes: Walk me from a module graph to the files on the CDN.
You bump one dependency. What does a returning user re-download, and why?
How would you decide where to put a code-split boundary?
How do you keep the bundle from growing over a year?

ops-deploy-assets.title: Immutable Assets, Atomic Deploys and the Stale Chunk
objectives: Diagnose the failure a deploy causes for sessions that were already open
Specify cache headers and a deploy sequence that make releases atomic and rollbacks instant
Design a chunk-load recovery path that cannot become a reload loop
claims: Hashed asset files should be served with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, while the entry HTML must be no-cache so it revalidates on every navigation; caching the HTML is what pins users to an old release.
The immutable directive additionally tells the browser not to revalidate on an explicit reload, which removes a conditional request per asset — a measurable win on high-latency connections.

A deploy is not atomic by default: publishing new HTML before every new asset is uploaded, or deleting old assets at cutover, produces 404s. Upload assets first, flip the HTML last, and never delete old assets as part of a deploy.

A user whose tab was opened before a deploy still holds release N's HTML, so any import() they trigger afterwards requests a release-N chunk; if that file has been deleted the dynamic import rejects with a 'Failed to fetch dynamically imported module' error and the route simply never renders.

Old chunks must be retained for at least the length of a realistic session — commonly every release from the last 30 days — which makes asset retention, not the deploy mechanism, the actual fix for the stale-chunk problem.

Recovery needs an explicit handler: Vite dispatches a vite:preloadError event when a preload fails, and route-level dynamic imports should catch the rejection and reload once, guarded by a sessionStorage flag so a genuinely broken deploy cannot cause an infinite reload loop.

Rolling back static assets means re-pointing the HTML at a previous release, which only works if that release's assets still exist; re-running the build produces different hashes and is a new deploy, not a rollback.

Canarying a static SPA happens at the edge — a cookie or header selects which index.html is served — and the bucket must be sticky, or a user alternates releases and loads a chunk graph that does not match their HTML.

viz.title: The Tab That Was Left Open
viz.whatIsDrawn: A horizontal time axis with three release bars along the top and an asset-store lane beneath showing each release's chunk files, with deleted files drawn as tombstones at the moment of deletion. Below that, one user session lane: a marker for which release's HTML they hold, and their chunk requests drawn as arrows that either land on a live file or on a tombstone, with the resulting user-visible symptom labeled at the arrowhead. A dimmed ghost session that started after the deploy runs alongside and succeeds throughout.
viz.predictPrompt: You deploy at 14:00 and your host deletes the previous deploy's assets. A user loaded the app at 13:40 and clicks 'Settings' — a lazily imported route — at 14:05. What does that user see, and does an error reach your error tracker?
controls: Retention policy: delete on deploy / keep last N releases / keep 30 days
viz.insight: A deploy does not break the app for new visitors — it breaks it for the people already using it, and the fix is asset retention plus a guarded reload, not a faster or cleverer build.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: pure function over an injected clock — (deploySchedule, retentionPolicy, sessionStart, requestTimes, recoveryEnabled) -> per-request outcome {served | 404 | reloaded | reload-loop}. Unit-test the reload-loop case explicitly: recovery enabled + asset genuinely missing on the new release must terminate after one reload because of the sessionStorage guard. Reduced-motion: static timeline with each request outcome tabulated.

drills.prompt: Here is the cache header table: /index.html -> public, max-age=31536000, immutable; /assets/*.js -> no-cache. Describe the two symptoms users report.
drills.answerSketch: It is exactly inverted. Users are pinned to whatever HTML they first fetched for up to a year, so they never receive any deploy (including security fixes) until they hard-reload; and every hashed asset is revalidated on every load, adding a conditional request per file for no benefit since the filename already changes on content change.

drills.prompt: Order a safe static deploy: invalidate the HTML at the CDN, upload new hashed assets, verify assets are reachable from every edge, publish the new index.html, retain previous assets.
drills.answerSketch: upload new hashed assets -> verify reachable from edges -> publish new index.html -> invalidate the HTML at the CDN -> retain previous assets (i.e. never delete). Assets first, HTML last, and retention is the standing policy rather than a step.

drills.prompt: Complete the guarded recovery: window.addEventListener('vite:preloadError', () => { if (!sessionStorage.getItem('______')) { sessionStorage.setItem('______','1'); location.______(); } });
drills.answerSketch: A reload-guard key (same key in both places); reload(). The guard is what prevents an infinite loop when the new release is genuinely broken; it should also be cleared on a successful load.

drills.prompt: The requirement becomes: roll back a bad release in under 60 seconds. What breaks first in a pipeline whose rollback is 'revert the commit and redeploy'?
drills.answerSketch: Time and identity. A rebuild takes minutes and produces different content hashes, so it is a new release, not the old one — any bug caused by an environment or dependency resolution difference will not be reverted. A real rollback re-points the HTML at a retained previous release's asset set, which requires that those assets were never deleted and that the HTML pointer is a cheap, separately deployable artifact.

drills.prompt: A new release is live and a user is 12 fields into a form on the old one. Argue for an immediate reload versus a dismissible 'new version available' prompt, and say when each is wrong.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer makes it conditional on severity and on data loss: an immediate reload is correct for a security fix or a release that cannot function against the new API, and is otherwise hostile because it destroys unsaved work. The prompt is the default, but it needs a deadline and a forced path for breaking API changes — and either way the lazy-route recovery reload must still exist for the stale-chunk case, which is a different problem from 'a newer version exists'.

failureModes: Proposes a service worker as the fix for stale chunks, adding a second, harder cache-invalidation problem
Reloads on any chunk load error with no guard, producing an infinite reload loop when the new release is broken
Sets immutable on index.html
Assumes the CDN purge is instantaneous and global
Believes reverting the commit and rebuilding is a rollback
Never realizes the failure is invisible in the error tracker because the rejection is swallowed by a Suspense boundary
interviewProbes: What cache headers do you put on index.html and on the hashed bundles, and why the difference?
A user had the tab open when you deployed. Walk me through what happens when they click a lazy route.
How do you roll back a static site in 60 seconds?
How would you canary a single-page app that ships as static files?

ops-testing-strategy.title: What to Test, at Which Level, and What to Assert
objectives: Judge which level a given test belongs at, and which proposed tests should not exist
Judge an assertion by whether it fails when behaviour changes and passes when only structure changes
Judge how a mock will drift from the real contract, and choose the mechanism that catches the drift
claims: The testing trophy weights integration tests most heavily because most real defects live in the composition of units; unit tests written against implementation detail break on every refactor without ever catching a bug.
A test should assert only what a user can observe — rendered text, accessible roles, navigation, and the network requests actually made — never internal state, prop names or render counts.

Testing Library's query priority (getByRole, then getByLabelText, then getByText, with getByTestId last) is an accessibility check in disguise: a control findable only by test id is also unfindable by a screen reader user.

findBy* awaits, getBy* throws immediately and queryBy* returns null, so asserting that something is absent requires queryBy — using getBy for a negative assertion produces a test that cannot fail correctly.

MSW intercepts at the network layer, so one set of handlers serves unit tests, Storybook and local development; mocking the fetch function or the API client module instead couples the test to the transport and hides serialization and error-shape bugs.

Every mock is a copy of a contract and will drift from it; the drift is caught by generating handlers and types from the provider's schema in CI, or by consumer-driven contract tests — never by team discipline.
Coverage percentage measures which lines executed, not which behaviours were verified: a suite of snapshot tests can reach 90% coverage while asserting nothing anyone cares about.
Loading, empty, error and stale states are the least-tested and most-often-broken paths, so every component that fetches needs a test for each — they are the states nobody designed a mock for.

viz.title: The Refactor Test
viz.whatIsDrawn: A small component tree on the left with six tests attached at their levels (unit on a hook, integration on the form, e2e on the flow), each drawn as a badge on the node it targets. Applying a change highlights the affected nodes and flips each test badge to pass or fail in place. Behind each badge sits a dimmed ghost marker showing what the test SHOULD have done for that change, so false greens and false reds are visible as a mismatch between the two.
viz.predictPrompt: Two changes, applied separately: (1) you refactor a component's internal state from useState to useReducer with identical behaviour; (2) the backend renames a JSON field from `total_cents` to `totalCents` and nobody touches the test fixtures. For each, which tests should fail, and which actually do?
controls: Pick the change: internal refactor / API field rename / button label change / route rename
Mock source: hand-written fixtures vs schema-generated handlers
viz.insight: A good suite fails exactly when behaviour changes; hand-written mocks invert that — they make the suite pass precisely at the moment the contract broke.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure impact table: (change, mockSource, enabledLevels) -> per-test {actual, ideal}. The teaching content is the table itself, so unit-test every cell against the claims — especially that the API rename is green everywhere under hand-written mocks and red under schema-generated ones. Reduced-motion: render the full matrix statically.

drills.prompt: Ten proposed tests for a checkout form (validation message on empty email; useReducer returns the right state; the submit button calls onSubmit; a full purchase through Stripe test mode; the loading spinner appears; a snapshot of the whole form; the API is called with the right body; the error banner on a 500; the total recomputes on quantity change; the component renders without crashing). Keep, move level, or cut each.
drills.answerSketch: Cut: reducer state (implementation), whole-form snapshot (asserts nothing, changes constantly), renders-without-crashing (subsumed). Move to e2e/rare: the full Stripe flow (one happy path only, it is slow and flaky). Keep as integration: validation message, request body, 500 error banner, total recomputation, loading state. 'Submit calls onSubmit' is implementation unless onSubmit is the component's public contract.

drills.prompt: expect(mockSetState).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2); expect(wrapper.find('SubmitButton').props().disabled).toBe(true). Name what is wrong and rewrite both assertions.
drills.answerSketch: Both assert implementation: render counts and prop values. Rewrite as user-observable: expect(screen.getByRole('button', {name:/submit/i})).toBeDisabled(), and delete the render-count assertion entirely — if render count matters it is a performance concern with a different tool.

drills.prompt: To assert an element is absent use ______ByRole; to wait for one that appears asynchronously use ______ByRole; the query of last resort is ______.
drills.answerSketch: query; find; getByTestId.

drills.prompt: The backend team starts deploying independently, several times a day. What breaks first in a suite built entirely on hand-written MSW fixtures?
drills.answerSketch: Nothing breaks — that is the problem. The suite stays green while production breaks, because the fixtures encode last quarter's contract. The fix is to generate handlers and types from the published schema in CI (so a schema change fails the build), or consumer-driven contract tests verified against the provider; a nightly smoke test against a real staging API is the weaker fallback.

drills.prompt: You inherit 400 snapshot tests. Coverage is 88%. Argue for deleting them and say what you would put in their place, in the order you would do it.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer notes snapshots detect change, not correctness, so they train the team to press -u; the coverage number will drop and that must be pre-negotiated with whoever watches it. Replacement order: characterize the top user journeys with integration tests first, keep a very small number of narrow snapshots for genuinely serialization-shaped output, and delete the rest in one commit rather than by attrition.

failureModes: Argues for the pyramid and a 90% unit-coverage target as the strategy
Asserts on state, props and render counts, then complains the tests break on every refactor
Mocks the API client module rather than the network, hiding serialization and error-shape bugs
Never tests the error or empty path
Treats coverage percentage as the definition of done
Cannot say how their mocks would ever be shown to be wrong
interviewProbes: How do you test this component? Now tell me what you would deliberately not test.
Your tests are green and production is broken because the API changed a field. Why did no test catch it?
Why is getByTestId the last resort?
You have 88% coverage and weekly production bugs. What is going on?

ops-ci-gates.title: E2E, Visual, A11y and Perf Gates That Stay Green
objectives: Design a gate set bounded by total wall time and by the false-positive rate the team will tolerate
Design flake control that produces signal rather than hiding failures behind retries
Decide which quality checks should block a pull request and which should only report
claims: Playwright's web-first assertions such as expect(locator).toBeVisible() retry until their timeout, so any waitForTimeout in a suite is a flake waiting for a slower CI machine.
Parallel E2E requires isolation, not ordering: each test needs its own seeded data and its own storageState, and any shared mutable fixture both serializes the suite and makes it flaky.
Capturing a trace on first retry is what makes a flake diagnosable after the fact; retries without traces simply delete the evidence.

Retrying is not flake control: flakes must be tracked as a per-test flake rate, quarantined out of the blocking suite once they exceed a threshold, and then fixed or deleted — a suite that passes on the third attempt carries no signal.

The dominant cost of visual regression testing is triage, not compute: font loading, cross-OS antialiasing, animation timing and unfrozen dates generate diffs that are all false. Pinning a container image, disabling animations and freezing the clock removes most of them; raising the pixel-difference threshold instead removes the sensitivity you were paying for.

Automated accessibility checks such as axe-core reliably detect only a minority of WCAG failures — roughly a third — because contrast, names and roles are machine-checkable while meaningful labels, sensible focus order and keyboard traps largely are not; the CI gate is a floor, not a pass.

Lighthouse in CI has genuine run-to-run variance, so it belongs on a fixed device profile with a median across runs and generous thresholds; the deterministic performance gate is a compressed bundle-size budget that fails the pull request on a byte delta.

A gate that can be bypassed with a label will be bypassed, so the checks worth blocking on are the fast, deterministic ones that name an obvious next action; everything else should report rather than block.

viz.title: The Gate Budget
viz.whatIsDrawn: A pull-request pipeline drawn as parallel horizontal lanes — typecheck, unit, integration, e2e shard 1-4, visual, axe, Lighthouse, size-limit — each bar scaled to its duration with its name and per-gate false-positive rate labeled on the bar. A vertical 'developer patience' line sits at 10 minutes. To the right, a counter shows expected red-but-correct builds per week for the chosen configuration. The all-blocking configuration remains behind as a dimmed ghost set of lanes.
viz.predictPrompt: You have five blocking gates and each fails spuriously on 2% of correct pull requests. What fraction of correct pull requests gets at least one red build — and what do engineers start doing about it by month two?
controls: Set each gate to block / report / off
viz.insight: A gate's value is signal multiplied by trust: at a 2% false-positive rate across five gates, roughly one in ten honest pull requests turns red, and the team's response is to stop reading the results — after which the gates protect nothing.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is pure probability plus a critical-path duration calculation over a lane fixture: (config) -> {wallClockMinutes, pFalseRed, expectedRedBuildsPerWeek}. Seeded only for illustrative sampling; the headline numbers are closed-form. Unit-test 1-(0.98^5) ≈ 0.096 and the shard-count critical path. Reduced-motion: static lane chart with all figures labeled.

drills.prompt: Five blocking gates, each 2% false-positive. Compute the probability a correct PR gets at least one red. Then compute it for eight gates at 1%.
drills.answerSketch: 1 - 0.98^5 = 9.6%. Eight at 1%: 1 - 0.99^8 = 7.7%. The lesson is that gate count multiplies as fast as flake rate does, so adding a 'cheap' extra gate is never free.

drills.prompt: A Playwright spec starts with a shared beforeAll login writing to a module-level variable, uses await page.waitForTimeout(2000) after clicking Save, and asserts on the first row of a table seeded by a previous test. Name every source of flake.
drills.answerSketch: Shared mutable auth state prevents parallel isolation and leaks between tests; the fixed 2 s wait is a race that fails on a slow runner and wastes 2 s when fast; depending on another test's seeded data creates an ordering dependency; asserting on 'the first row' depends on an unspecified sort. Fixes: per-test storageState, web-first assertions, per-test seeded data, a locator scoped by content rather than position.

drills.prompt: Classify each as block / report / delete: typecheck, unit tests, full E2E suite on every PR, visual diff of every page, axe on three key routes, Lighthouse performance score, size-limit on the two main routes, a nightly cross-browser run.
drills.answerSketch: Block: typecheck, unit, size-limit, axe on key routes (fast, deterministic, actionable). Report or partial: E2E — block on a small smoke subset, run the full suite post-merge or nightly. Report: Lighthouse (variance). Delete or heavily narrow: whole-page visual diffs — keep component-level diffs on a pinned container image. Nightly cross-browser: report, with an owner for triage.

drills.prompt: The suite must complete in 8 minutes. What goes first, and what must NOT go?
drills.answerSketch: Move the full E2E suite off the PR path (keep a smoke subset), shard what remains, and move whole-page visual diffs to a scheduled run. What must not go: typecheck and size-limit — they are seconds long, fully deterministic, and size-limit is the only non-flaky performance gate you have. Cutting the deterministic gates to save time is optimizing the wrong axis.

drills.prompt: The checkout E2E is your most valuable test and flakes about one run in twelve. Argue for quarantining it or for keeping it blocking, and state what you commit to either way.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answer refuses to leave it as-is: at 1 in 12 it is already training people to hit re-run, so its blocking status is nominal. Either quarantine it with a named owner and a dated deadline to fix the underlying race, or keep it blocking and stop the line until it is fixed. The unacceptable option is retries: it would hide the very race most likely to be a real intermittent product bug in checkout.

failureModes: Sets retries: 3 and declares the flake fixed
Screenshots whole pages, then raises the pixel threshold every time it flakes until the gate detects nothing
Claims axe-core passing in CI means the application is accessible
Blocks pull requests on a Lighthouse score, then disables the gate a month later when nobody trusts it
Adds gates without ever measuring the compound false-positive rate or the wall-clock cost
Quarantines flaky tests with no owner and no deadline, so the quarantine becomes a graveyard
interviewProbes: Design the CI gates for this app. What blocks a merge and what does not?
Your E2E suite is flaky. Walk me through what you do — and do not say retries.
Is visual regression testing worth it? Defend your answer with the triage cost.
How do you stop performance regressing over a year, given Lighthouse is noisy in CI?

rt-transports.title: Choosing a Real-Time Transport
objectives: Map a concrete requirement (direction, message cadence, payload size, ordering need, device class) onto SSE, WebSocket, WebTransport, WebRTC data channel, or plain polling.
Quantify what each transport costs in connection count, proxy/CDN compatibility, and radio wake-ups rather than in abstract 'latency'.
Defend the boring choice — SSE or interval polling — when the requirement is one-directional and low-rate.
claims: SSE is one-directional server-to-client over ordinary HTTP; the client still sends data with normal HTTP requests, so a feed with a low client send rate does not need a WebSocket.

SSE reconnects automatically and resumes by sending the client's last event id back in the `Last-Event-ID` request header, which the server must honour; WebSocket has no built-in reconnect and no built-in replay.

Over HTTP/1.1 an SSE stream permanently occupies one of the browser's ~6 connections per origin and can starve other requests; over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 streams multiplex over one connection and that limit effectively disappears.

A WebSocket upgrades an HTTP/1.1 request and then leaves HTTP semantics behind: no response caching, no automatic retry, no per-message status codes, and no ability to set custom request headers from the browser.

WebTransport runs over HTTP/3 (QUIC) and offers both reliable ordered streams and unreliable datagrams; it became Baseline when Safari 26.4 shipped in March 2026, but server/CDN support and networks that block UDP are the real adoption constraints, and it still gives you no reconnect or replay for free.

WebRTC data channels are peer-to-peer and can be configured unreliable and unordered, but they require a signalling server plus STUN and usually TURN; TURN relays real bandwidth you pay for, so peer-to-peer is not free infrastructure.

Battery cost on cellular tracks radio wake-ups, not bytes: a 200-byte message every second keeps the radio in a high-power state far longer than one 200 KB transfer, which is why coalescing messages beats compressing them on mobile.
Long polling is still a correct answer when updates are rare and infrequent; its real cost is a held server connection per client, not client complexity.
failureModes: Defaults to WebSocket for a notification feed that is server-to-client only and updates a few times a minute, then has to hand-build reconnect and replay that SSE provides.
Says WebTransport 'replaces WebSocket' without mentioning server support, UDP-blocking corporate networks, or that it has no reconnect/replay either.
Calls WebRTC 'serverless' and forgets signalling and TURN bandwidth costs.
Compares transports on latency alone and never mentions connection count, proxy idle timeouts, or radio behaviour.
interviewProbes: Design the update channel for a live sports scoreboard with 2 million concurrent viewers. Which transport, and what does the client do when it drops?
When would you pick SSE over WebSocket in 2026, and what would make you change your mind?
Your product must work inside a bank's corporate network. How does that change the transport shortlist?

viz.title: Transport Chooser with Live Cost Meter
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame. On the left, a four-leaf decision tree (direction -> cadence -> reliability need -> topology); the selected leaf lights up. Anchored immediately beside that leaf, inside the same frame, two horizontal meters: bytes/minute on the wire and radio wake-ups/minute, each with a ghost bar showing the previously selected transport for comparison. Network-profile constraints strike out unreachable leaves in place.
viz.predictPrompt: A dashboard pushes one update per second to 10,000 viewers, server-to-client only. You switch from SSE over HTTP/2 to WebSocket. Does the client's radio wake-up rate go up, down, or stay the same — and what do you lose?
controls: network profile: wifi / 4G / corporate proxy blocking UDP
viz.insight: Direction and cadence decide the transport; cadence — not the transport — decides battery cost. The cheapest transport that satisfies direction wins, and switching away from SSE costs you reconnect and Last-Event-ID replay for nothing.
viz.buildNotes: Meters are hand-rolled SVG rects. The cost model lives in a pure sim.ts with a documented cellular radio tail-time constant and a seeded RNG; unit-test asserts the SSE-vs-WebSocket wake-up equivalence at equal cadence, because that IS the pedagogical claim. The corporate-proxy profile must visibly disable the WebTransport leaf rather than merely slowing it. Reduced motion renders the final meter state with all annotations pre-placed.

drills.prompt: Six one-line requirements (order-status feed; multiplayer cursor sharing; CI log tail; voice-chat side channel; stock ticker for 500k viewers; admin dashboard refreshed every 30s). Pick the transport for each.
drills.answerSketch: SSE; WebSocket (or WebTransport if server supports it); SSE; WebRTC data channel; SSE over HTTP/2 behind a CDN; polling. Grading is on the transport choice; the one-line reason is self-scored.

drills.prompt: Your SSE feed works well. The requirement now adds: the client must publish its cursor position 30 times a second. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Not the SSE stream — the client's 30 POSTs/second. You need a client-to-server channel; that is the first requirement that actually forces WebSocket or WebTransport, and it also forces coalescing.

drills.prompt: 50 peers in a room, each sending 20 updates/second, naive broadcast to everyone. Inbound messages per second at one client? Now with a server snapshot at 10 Hz?
drills.answerSketch: Naive: 49 x 20 = 980 msg/s inbound. Snapshot: 10 msg/s inbound, each carrying 49 positions. Message count falls ~98x; bytes fall far less.

drills.prompt: Which single property of SSE most often makes it the better choice than WebSocket for a notification feed, and why is it not simply 'it is simpler'?
drills.answerSketch: Automatic reconnect with Last-Event-ID replay: it is the only one of the four transports with a resume protocol built into the platform.

drills.prompt: Defend shipping long polling in 2026 for a specific product you describe. State the requirement that makes it correct and the requirement that would kill it.
drills.answerSketch: Correct when updates are rare, infrastructure is HTTP-only, and per-client held connections are affordable. Killed by high cadence or high concurrency, where held connections dominate server memory.

rt-ws-connection.title: WebSocket Connection Management: Heartbeats, Half-Open Sockets, Backoff
objectives: Design a reconnect controller with jittered backoff, a stability window, and heartbeat-driven liveness detection.
Detect a half-open socket that the browser will never report as closed.
Authenticate a WebSocket from a browser given that custom headers are impossible.
claims: RFC 6455 ping/pong control frames are not exposed to browser JavaScript, so a browser client can only detect a dead connection with an application-level heartbeat message plus a response timer.
A connection dropped by a NAT timeout or a mobile network handoff can leave the socket half-open: `readyState` stays OPEN, `onclose` never fires, and `send()` silently buffers instead of throwing.

Close code 1006 means the connection closed abnormally with no close frame and is generated locally by the browser — it is what a network drop looks like; 1000 is a normal close, 1001 is 'going away', and 4000-4999 are reserved for application-defined codes.

Plain exponential backoff synchronizes every client that dropped at the same instant; adding full jitter (delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))) is what actually decorrelates them and prevents the reconnect storm.

The backoff attempt counter must reset only after the new connection has stayed open for a stability window (about 10 seconds), because resetting it on `open` makes a socket that dies immediately reconnect in a tight loop forever.

Browsers cannot set custom headers — including `Authorization` — on a WebSocket handshake, so auth uses a short-lived single-use ticket fetched over HTTPS and passed via the subprotocol header or query string, re-fetched on every reconnect attempt.

Intermediaries commonly close an idle WebSocket after about 60 seconds of silence (the default idle timeout for AWS ALB and for nginx's proxy read timeout), so the heartbeat interval must be shorter than the shortest idle timeout anywhere in the path.

`navigator.onLine === true` only means the device has a network interface with a route; it is true on captive portals and dead uplinks, so it is a useful hint for when to attempt a reconnect and never a source of truth for connection state.
failureModes: Reconnects on a fixed 1-second interval, or uses exponential backoff with no jitter, and only discovers the problem during a real incident.
Trusts `onclose` to detect every disconnect, so the UI shows 'connected' on a socket that has been dead for twenty minutes.
Resets the backoff counter in `onopen` instead of after a stability window.
Puts a long-lived JWT in the WebSocket query string, where it ends up in proxy access logs, and never rotates it.
interviewProbes: Your users report the app 'silently stops updating' on mobile but the connection indicator stays green. Walk me through how you'd diagnose and fix it.
Your WebSocket server restarts and 50,000 clients reconnect. What happens, and what would you have built beforehand?
How do you authenticate a WebSocket from a browser, and how do you rotate that credential?

viz.title: Half-Open Socket and the Reconnect Storm
viz.whatIsDrawn: Top half: one client's socket state machine (CONNECTING / OPEN / CLOSING / CLOSED) with an app-level ALIVE / SUSPECT / DEAD overlay, and a timeline directly beneath the state boxes showing heartbeat sends as ticks and expected replies as hollow ticks that fill or stay empty. Bottom half: a 200-client density strip showing reconnect attempts per 100 ms bucket after a server restart, with a ghost strip behind it from the previously selected jitter mode. All labels anchored on the lanes.
viz.predictPrompt: 200 clients are dropped simultaneously at t=0. Backoff is exponential, base 500 ms, cap 30 s, no jitter. Is the server's worst instantaneous load on the 1st reconnect attempt, the 3rd, or the 6th — and does the load spread out over time?
controls: fault injection: clean close (1000) / abrupt drop (1006) / half-open blackhole
viz.insight: Backoff spreads reconnects in time but not in phase — every attempt is an equally tall spike until you add jitter. And without an application-level heartbeat, the client never learns it is disconnected at all.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes an injected clock and a seeded RNG. Unit tests assert (a) with jitter=none, max clients-per-bucket equals N at every attempt, (b) full jitter reduces peak bucket occupancy by more than 10x, and (c) in half-open mode the state machine reaches SUSPECT only via heartbeat timeout and never via a close event. Reduced motion renders both completed density strips statically with the peak buckets annotated.

drills.prompt: Complete the full-jitter delay computation and the stability-window reset in a reconnect controller (two blanks).
drills.answerSketch: `const delay = Math.random() * Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)` and reset `attempt = 0` inside a timer that fires only after the socket has been OPEN for the stability window, cleared on close.

drills.prompt: A 25-line reconnect implementation with three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) fixed 1000 ms retry with no backoff or jitter; (2) `attempt = 0` inside `onopen`; (3) no heartbeat, so a half-open socket is never detected.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of a correct reconnect: detect liveness loss, tear down, wait, re-authenticate, reconnect, resume, resume UI.
drills.answerSketch: Heartbeat reply timeout -> mark SUSPECT and stop sending -> close and null the socket -> compute jittered delay -> fetch a fresh ticket over HTTPS -> open with ticket -> send resume cursor -> apply replay -> start the stability timer -> flip the UI to connected.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: must survive a corporate proxy with a 30-second idle timeout, and must not drain battery when the tab is backgrounded. What breaks first, and what is the minimum change?
drills.answerSketch: A 45 s heartbeat breaks first — the proxy kills the socket before the heartbeat proves it dead. Drop below 30 s. Then handle background: on `visibilitychange` to hidden, stop the heartbeat and let the socket close; on visible, reconnect and resume. Do not simply lengthen the interval.

drills.prompt: Your heartbeat is every 25 seconds. Support reports battery complaints on mobile. Defend keeping it or changing it, in writing, in 4 minutes.
drills.answerSketch: Strong answers separate the two costs: heartbeat cadence versus keeping the socket open at all while backgrounded. The defensible move is to suspend the connection when hidden rather than to lengthen the heartbeat past the proxy timeout.

rt-delivery.title: Gaps, Replay, Ordering and Idempotency
objectives: Design a resume protocol using sequence numbers or opaque cursors, including the mandatory full-resync fallback.
Make a client tolerant of duplicates and reordering without unbounded memory growth.
State which delivery guarantee a design provides and where idempotency has to live.
claims: A reconnecting client must tell the server where it left off; the two workable shapes are a monotonic per-stream sequence number and an opaque server cursor, and the opaque cursor is safer because it lets the server change its internal ordering without breaking deployed clients.

Servers can only retain a bounded replay buffer — last N messages or last T seconds — and when a client's cursor falls outside it the correct response is an explicit gap signal that forces a full state resync, never a silent partial replay.

Gap detection requires per-stream monotonic sequence numbers: if an arriving message's seq is not lastSeq + 1, messages were lost or reordered and the client must stop applying optimistically and resync.

At-least-once is the only guarantee a reconnecting client gets cheaply, so duplicates are normal traffic; 'exactly-once' on the client means exactly-once EFFECTS achieved by idempotent application, not exactly-once delivery.
A client-generated idempotency key is created once per user intent and reused on every retry of that intent; a key generated per HTTP attempt provides no protection at all.

Deduplication needs a bounded structure — an LRU or ring buffer of recent ids sized to the replay window — because an unbounded Set of seen message ids is a slow memory leak in a tab that stays open for days.

Ordering guarantees are per-stream, not global: two entities are ordered relative to each other only if the server assigns their messages sequence numbers in the same stream, so sharding a socket by topic silently discards cross-topic ordering.
Client wall-clock timestamps must never be used to order events; client clocks drift and can move backwards, so ordering uses a server-assigned sequence or a per-entity version number.
failureModes: Says 'we use exactly-once delivery' and cannot say what the client does when the same message arrives twice.
Resumes with a client-side timestamp instead of a server-issued cursor.
Assumes the server can replay from any point in history and never designs the full-resync path, so the bug only appears for users who were offline over a weekend.
Generates the idempotency key inside the retry loop, so every retry looks like a new intent.
interviewProbes: A user's laptop sleeps for two hours. They wake it. Walk me through exactly what the client and server exchange before the UI is correct again.
Your chat shows duplicate messages, but only for users on flaky mobile networks. Where is the bug and what is the fix?
How would you decide the size of the server's replay buffer?

viz.title: Replay Window and the Gap
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame, two horizontal lanes. Top: the server's message sequence 1..N as small numbered boxes, with the retained replay window drawn as a bracket under the lane. Bottom: the client's applied sequence, with the disconnect drawn as a shaded interval spanning both lanes. On reconnect, either the missing boxes fill in from the bracket, or a RESYNC marker is drawn in place at the point where the cursor fell outside the window. A duplicate-injection toggle draws repeated boxes that the dedupe buffer greys out inline.
viz.predictPrompt: The server retains the last 1,000 messages per stream. Client A disconnects for 20 seconds during a burst of 4,000 messages/minute. Client B disconnects for 20 minutes during a quiet period of 5 messages/minute. Which one resumes cleanly?
controls: retention policy: last N messages vs last T seconds
viz.insight: Whether a client can resume depends on the message RATE during its absence, not the LENGTH of its absence — so a message-count replay window fails the short disconnect and survives the long one. Every resume design needs an explicitly tested full-resync path.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure reducer over an event list with an injected clock and seeded RNG. Two unit tests encode the predictPrompt scenarios directly (short-burst disconnect -> RESYNC, long-quiet disconnect -> clean replay) so the counter-intuitive result can never drift from the animation. A third test asserts the dedupe buffer never exceeds its bound under a duplicate flood.

drills.prompt: Fill in the gap-detection condition and the dedupe insert in an onMessage handler (two blanks).
drills.answerSketch: `if (msg.seq !== lastSeq + 1) { requestResync(); return; }` and a bounded LRU insert keyed on `msg.id` that evicts the oldest entry when it reaches capacity.

drills.prompt: Order the resume handshake, including the branch where the cursor is too old.
drills.answerSketch: Reconnect -> send last cursor -> server compares against retention window -> if inside: stream buffered messages then live -> client verifies contiguity and dedupes -> if outside: server sends GAP -> client discards local stream state -> fetches a snapshot with a new cursor -> resumes live from that cursor.

drills.prompt: Design the resume protocol for a collaborative task board: name the cursor, the retention policy, the gap signal, and the resync payload.
drills.answerSketch: Opaque per-board cursor; retention as max(500 messages, 60 s) per board; explicit `{type:'gap'}` frame; resync payload is a board snapshot plus the cursor it was taken at, applied as a replace-not-merge before live messages resume.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds multi-tab: one user, three tabs, three sockets, three independent cursors. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Nothing about delivery breaks — each socket resumes independently. What breaks is anything derived from 'the user saw this': read receipts, unread counts and per-user dedupe, because each tab dedupes separately. Shared state belongs in one place (a leader tab or a shared worker), not per socket.

drills.prompt: A stream averages 40 msg/s per room. You want any client that reconnects within 60 seconds to resume without a resync. How big is the replay buffer per room, and what does that cost for 5,000 active rooms at 300 bytes per message?
drills.answerSketch: 2,400 messages/room -> ~720 KB/room -> ~3.6 GB across 5,000 rooms. The estimate is the point: message-count windows have a memory price that scales with room count, which is why time-based windows with a hard count cap are common.

rt-backpressure.title: Client Backpressure: Batching, Coalescing and the Render Budget
objectives: Diagnose whether a stalling real-time UI is bound by parsing, by state updates, by rendering, or by an unbounded queue.
Distinguish batching from coalescing and pick the one the workload actually needs.
Identify the hidden-tab failure mode in any frame-driven flush loop.
claims: The standard WebSocket API provides no receive-side backpressure: messages are delivered to `onmessage` as fast as they arrive and the only lever is how quickly the handler returns. WebSocketStream, which does expose stream backpressure, is Chromium-only and non-standard.

`ws.bufferedAmount` is the only send-side signal available; if it grows across successive ticks the client is producing faster than the socket drains, and the correct response is to coalesce or shed, not to keep calling `send()`.
Batching (accumulate N messages or T milliseconds, then apply once) bounds how many times you render; coalescing (keep only the newest value per key) bounds how much work there is to do at all.

Applying every inbound message as its own React state update turns a 500 msg/s stream into 500 renders per second; buffering into a ref and flushing once per animation frame caps renders at the display refresh rate no matter how fast messages arrive.

An unbounded inbound queue turns a slow consumer into an out-of-memory crash, so every queue needs a bound plus a stated drop policy: drop-oldest for telemetry and positions, drop-newest for ordered mutations, and never-drop for user intents — which means those belong in durable storage, not a memory queue.

Per-message compression (permessage-deflate) trades CPU and per-connection memory for bandwidth; on a high-frequency stream of small messages, coalescing before send reduces both, so it is the change to try first.

`requestAnimationFrame` does not fire in a hidden tab, so a flush loop built only on rAF lets the buffer grow unbounded while backgrounded; a hidden tab needs an explicit cap, a timer-based drain, or a suspend-and-resync on return.
Moving parsing to a Web Worker only helps if parsing is the bottleneck; if the cost is React reconciliation, the worker adds a structured-clone hop and makes it slower.
failureModes: Claims 'we handle backpressure' and points at `bufferedAmount` with no policy for what happens when it grows.
Throttles at the network layer, so positions arrive less often but every stale one is still applied in order and the cursor visibly lags.
Never considers the hidden tab; the buffer grows for forty minutes and the tab janks or dies when the user returns.
Reaches for a Web Worker before profiling, and moves the wrong stage of the pipeline off the main thread.
interviewProbes: Your collaborative canvas is smooth with 5 users and unusable with 40. Walk me through the diagnosis in order.
What is the difference between throttling, batching and coalescing here, and which one fixes a laggy remote cursor?
A user leaves the tab in the background for an hour on a busy document. What happens when they come back, and what would you have built?

viz.title: Queue Depth Under a Slow Consumer
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame: a producer arrow labelled with arrival rate feeds a queue drawn as a vertical bar with a hard bound line; a consumer arrow labelled with flush rate drains it. A queue-depth sparkline runs directly beneath the bar with a ghost trace of the previously selected policy. Drop counts and current depth are labelled inside the frame on the bar itself. A visibility band across the top shades the hidden-tab intervals.
viz.predictPrompt: Messages arrive at 400/s. Your consumer flushes in a rAF callback at 60fps and each flush can apply any number of buffered messages. Is the queue stable? Now the tab is hidden for 5 minutes at the same rate — what is the depth on return, and what does the first visible frame do?
viz.insight: Batching bounds the number of renders; only coalescing bounds the amount of work. And a hidden tab silently converts a stable batching system into an unbounded one, because rAF stops firing while messages do not.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure discrete-time queue with an injected clock and seeded RNG; the visibility state is an input, not a browser read. Unit tests assert: batch-per-frame is stable while visible at 400/s, depth after 5 hidden minutes equals rate x duration under batching, and depth stays at O(number of keys) under coalescing regardless of visibility. Reduced motion renders the final sparkline with the hidden interval shaded and the peak annotated.

drills.prompt: A 30-line message pipeline with three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) `setState` called inside `onmessage` per message; (2) the buffer array is never bounded; (3) the flush is rAF-only with no hidden-tab handling.

drills.prompt: Complete a coalescing buffer: one blank for the data structure, one for the flush.
drills.answerSketch: `const pending = new Map<PeerId, Position>()` with `pending.set(id, pos)` overwriting, and a flush that drains the Map into a single state update then clears it.

drills.prompt: Given a profile showing 90% of main-thread time in commit and layout, which change helps most: a Web Worker for JSON parsing, permessage-deflate, coalescing by key, or a larger batch window?
drills.answerSketch: Coalescing by key — the cost is rendering redundant intermediate values, and neither a worker nor compression removes any of that work.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: every inbound message is now a user mutation that must be applied in order and cannot be dropped. What breaks first in your coalescing pipeline?
drills.answerSketch: Coalescing itself is now illegal — you cannot discard intermediate values. The queue must become bounded-and-durable (spill to IndexedDB) or the connection must be suspended and resynced; dropping is no longer an option, so backpressure has to move upstream.

drills.prompt: 40 peers each emit 30 position updates/second. Under apply-each, batch-per-frame, and coalesce-by-key, how many state updates per second and how many distinct values applied per second?
drills.answerSketch: Apply-each: 1,200 updates/s, 1,200 values. Batch-per-frame: 60 updates/s, still 1,200 values. Coalesce: 60 updates/s, at most 40 values per flush = 2,400/s worst case but only 40 distinct positions rendered — the render cost is bounded by peer count, not by rate.

rt-presence.title: Presence, Typing Indicators and Live Cursors
objectives: Design a presence system whose correctness comes from TTL expiry rather than from goodbye messages.
Choose a fan-out strategy given room size and update rate, and state what it buys.
Design typing and cursor channels that survive a crashed client and a hidden tab.
claims: Presence is soft state with a TTL: the server marks a peer offline when its heartbeat lapses, so 'X went offline' is always late by up to one heartbeat interval plus the timeout, and the UI must be designed to tolerate that lag rather than to hide it.

Naive presence fan-out is quadratic in room size: 50 peers each sending 20 updates/second produce roughly 1,000 inbound messages per second at every client, which is a client-side problem long before it is a server-side one.

Server-side aggregation into periodic snapshots (one message containing all peers' current state, at 10-20 Hz) collapses message count and render count, but barely reduces bandwidth, because the snapshot carries every peer's value.

Typing indicators should be a debounced 'started typing' signal plus a server-side expiry of 3-5 seconds, never a per-keystroke stream and never dependent on a 'stopped typing' message that a crashed or backgrounded client will never send.

Live cursor positions are the canonical coalescing case: only the newest position per peer has value, so the outbound and inbound buffers hold one entry per peer and older positions are overwritten rather than queued.
Interpolating a remote cursor between samples over roughly 100 ms makes 10 Hz updates look continuous, which lets you cut send rate by three to five times with no perceived loss of smoothness.
Presence must travel on an ephemeral channel that is never persisted and never included in reconnect replay; replaying stale presence makes users who left reappear.

A hidden tab, a sleeping laptop and a killed app all disconnect without sending anything, so an honest roster is maintained by `visibilitychange` and `pagehide` hints combined with a server TTL — `beforeunload` is not reliable on mobile and cannot be the mechanism.
failureModes: Sends a message per keystroke for the typing indicator.
Relies on an explicit 'user left' message and ships ghost users that linger for hours.
Broadcasts every cursor move to every peer and blames the framework when the room reaches 40 people.
Stores presence in the same durable store as documents, then replays it after reconnect and resurrects departed users.
interviewProbes: Design presence and live cursors for a design tool. How many messages per second at a client in a 30-person file, and what did you do about it?
A user force-quits the app. How long until everyone else sees them leave, and what determines that number?
Why is a typing indicator not just a boolean you set and clear?

viz.title: Presence Fan-Out and the Ghost User
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame. A ring of N peer nodes with fan-out edges that light for a single tick; an inbound-messages-per-second and inbound-bytes-per-second readout anchored at the centre of the ring, each with a ghost value from the previously selected strategy. Below the ring, inside the same frame, a roster strip listing each peer with its last-heartbeat age as a small bar; a peer whose bar crosses the TTL line flips to a 'ghost' style in place.
viz.predictPrompt: A room has 30 users, each sending 20 cursor updates/second. Strategy A broadcasts every update to every peer. Strategy B has the server aggregate and send one snapshot of all 30 cursors at 10 Hz. Compute each client's inbound message rate and inbound bytes/second under each — which drops more, messages or bytes?
controls: strategy: broadcast / server snapshot at Hz / client-coalesced
kill a peer without a disconnect message
viz.insight: Server snapshot aggregation buys you message count and render count, not bandwidth. And presence correctness comes from TTL expiry — never from a goodbye message, which the clients that matter most will never send.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts computes fan-out arithmetic and roster expiry from an injected clock; unit tests pin the exact numbers used in predictPrompt (580 msg/s vs 10 msg/s inbound; bytes ratio under 3x) so the meter cannot contradict the claim. The ring uses at most 7 labels — peer count, two rates, TTL line, ghost marker, strategy name, tick counter. Reduced motion draws one settled tick with all edges shown at once and the roster in its expired state.

drills.prompt: Design the presence channel for a 100-person live document: message shapes, heartbeat interval, TTL, fan-out strategy, and what happens on reconnect.
drills.answerSketch: Ephemeral channel separate from document updates; client heartbeat every 10 s carrying cursor + status; server TTL 25 s; server snapshot at 10 Hz with per-peer coalescing; on reconnect the client sends a fresh join and receives a full roster snapshot — no presence replay.

drills.prompt: 60 peers, 15 updates/second each, 60-byte payloads. Inbound msg/s and KB/s per client under naive broadcast vs a 12 Hz server snapshot?
drills.answerSketch: Broadcast: 59 x 15 = 885 msg/s, ~53 KB/s. Snapshot: 12 msg/s, each ~3.6 KB, ~43 KB/s. Messages fall ~74x; bytes fall about 20%.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: presence must be accurate within 2 seconds of a user closing their laptop lid. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The TTL. A 25 s TTL cannot detect a lid close in 2 s, and a lid close sends nothing. You must shorten the heartbeat below 2 s (multiplying fan-out cost) or accept that only an explicit, reliable disconnect path — which a lid close is not — can meet it. The honest answer is that the requirement is not satisfiable cheaply and the UI should show 'last seen' instead.

drills.prompt: A typing-indicator implementation with three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) emits on every `keydown` with no debounce; (2) clears the indicator only on an explicit 'stopped' message; (3) presence state is written into the same store that is replayed on reconnect.

drills.prompt: Your PM wants cursors to feel 'as smooth as Figma'. Defend, in writing and in 4 minutes, sending at 10 Hz with interpolation rather than 60 Hz.
drills.answerSketch: Perceived smoothness comes from interpolation on the receiving side, not send rate; 10 Hz plus ~100 ms interpolation is visually indistinguishable while cutting fan-out six-fold, and the saved budget goes to lower cursor latency for the local user.

rt-collab-model.title: Collaborative Editing: You Choose a Library, Not an Algorithm
objectives: State precisely what convergence guarantees and what it does not, and separate it from intent preservation.
Select between last-write-wins, a sequence CRDT, and server-ordered OT from the constraints of a given product.
Name the real cost of a CRDT (metadata and document growth) and what still needs a server.
claims: Both OT and CRDTs guarantee convergence — replicas that have seen the same set of operations display the same document — but neither guarantees that the converged result is what either user intended.
OT requires a central server to order and transform operations; a CRDT converges without one, which is why a CRDT is the default whenever the topology includes offline peers or peer-to-peer sync.

CRDTs pay for that with metadata: deleted characters leave tombstones and every insert carries an identity, so document size grows with edit history rather than with current content — libraries mitigate this with compaction and columnar encoding, they do not eliminate it.

Last-write-wins is itself a CRDT (an LWW register) and is the right choice for independent scalar fields such as a title or a status; a sequence CRDT is only needed where two users concurrently edit the SAME text or list.

The real 2026 decision is between libraries and their ecosystems, not between algorithms: Yjs has by far the largest ecosystem of editor bindings and network/persistence providers, Automerge offers a git-like document history and change model, and Loro is the newest with the strongest large-document performance — all three are MIT-licensed and all three converge correctly.
