Rich text needs more than a sequence CRDT: formatting spans that survive concurrent edits require a marker-based model (the Peritext approach), which is a property of the library's rich-text type rather than something you can layer on top.

A CRDT removes the need for a server to resolve conflicts but not the need for a server: you still need persistence, authorization, a presence relay, and a way for a new client to load a document without replaying its entire history.
Writing your own CRDT or OT engine is a multi-year correctness problem with no user-visible payoff; the defensible interview answer is a named library plus the single constraint that selects it.
failureModes: Explains transformation functions or RGA internals at length and never states the actual decision or the constraint driving it.
Says 'CRDTs solve conflicts' — they guarantee convergence, not intent preservation, and the difference is the whole subject.
Uses a text CRDT for a form in which each field has exactly one owner, paying tombstone costs for nothing.
Ignores document growth and ships a document that takes eight seconds to load after a year of edits.
interviewProbes: Two users edit the same paragraph while partitioned. After the merge, what is guaranteed and what is not?
When would you use last-write-wins on a field in a product that already ships a CRDT document?
You picked Yjs. What does your server still have to do, and what does it no longer have to do?

viz.title: Three Peers, One Scripted Divergence
viz.whatIsDrawn: Three horizontal peer lanes (A, B, C), each showing the same short string as boxed characters. A partition is drawn as a shaded band across the lanes. Each applied operation is annotated inline on the affected character box. At merge, the three lanes are shown holding an identical string, and directly beneath, a fourth ghost lane shows what a naive last-write-wins-per-document merge would have produced. A tombstone counter sits inside the frame beside the lanes.
viz.predictPrompt: Peers A and B are partitioned. A inserts 'X' at position 3; B deletes the character that was at position 3. When the partition heals, do they converge — and is the converged result what either user intended?
controls: scrub the scripted operation list step by step
compare model: sequence CRDT vs last-write-wins whole document
viz.insight: Convergence is guaranteed; intent is not. The tombstone counter is the price of that guarantee, and the LWW ghost lane is what you get instead if you refuse to pay it.
viz.buildNotes: The operation script is fixed and hand-authored. This is explicitly NOT a general CRDT engine and must never grow into one — sim.ts encodes the scripted op list and the expected converged string as a unit-tested fixture, so the animation cannot contradict the claim. No algorithm internals (identifiers, transformation functions, causal ordering machinery) are shown or explained; the tombstone counter is the only internal exposed, because cost is the thing being taught. Reduced motion shows the pre-merge and post-merge states side by side with the LWW ghost.

drills.prompt: Six product surfaces (doc body; doc title; a kanban card's column; a shared spreadsheet cell; a comment thread; a user's 'is archived' flag). For each, choose LWW field, sequence CRDT, or server-authoritative.
drills.answerSketch: Body: sequence CRDT. Title: LWW field. Column: LWW field (or server-authoritative if capacity limits exist). Cell: LWW field unless cells are concurrently text-edited. Comment thread: append-only set, no sequence CRDT needed. Archived flag: server-authoritative if it gates permissions.

drills.prompt: Your product is a note editor with offline support and no peer-to-peer. Choose Yjs, Automerge, or server-ordered OT, and defend it in writing in 5 minutes. Name the constraint that decides it and the one that would flip it.
drills.answerSketch: Offline editing rules out plain OT (no server to order operations while offline). Between Yjs and Automerge, editor-binding ecosystem and document size favour Yjs; a requirement for per-change history and time-travel flips it to Automerge.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: documents must load in under 500 ms after two years of daily editing by ten people. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Document growth from tombstones and per-insert metadata. The fix is not a different algorithm but a loading strategy: periodic snapshots plus a bounded tail of updates, and library-level compaction — which also means you can no longer assume the full history is always available.

drills.prompt: A candidate says 'we use a CRDT so we don't need a server'. Which of the following does the CRDT actually remove, and which four does it not?
drills.answerSketch: It removes central conflict resolution and central operation ordering. It does not remove persistence, authorization, presence relay, or initial document loading.

rt-sw-lifecycle.title: Service Worker Lifecycle and the Update Trap
objectives: Diagnose which service worker controls which tab after an arbitrary sequence of deploys, reloads and tab closes.
Implement the user-consented update flow correctly, including the reload on controllerchange.
Recognise the stale-chunk failure that follows every deploy of a lazily-code-split SPA.
claims: A new service worker that finds an existing controlled page enters the `waiting` state and stays there until every tab controlled by the old worker is closed; a reload is not enough, because the old worker keeps controlling the page across a navigation.

`skipWaiting()` activates the new worker immediately, which means a page whose JavaScript came from the old build is suddenly served by the new worker's caches; it is only safe if you also reload the page, and it is dangerous when called unconditionally in `install`.

The correct update flow is: detect `registration.waiting` (or `updatefound` followed by the installing worker reaching `installed`), surface 'a new version is available', and only on the user's click post a SKIP_WAITING message and reload on the next `controllerchange` event.

The browser bypasses the HTTP cache when it fetches the service worker script for an update check and caps its freshness at 24 hours regardless of `Cache-Control`, which bounds a bad worker's blast radius but does not remove it — serve the script with `Cache-Control: max-age=0` anyway.

A registration is checked for updates on navigation and roughly every 24 hours, so a long-lived single-page app that never navigates can go days without noticing a deploy; call `registration.update()` on an interval or on `visibilitychange`.

After a deploy, the old page's lazily-loaded chunks may no longer exist on the server, so a dynamic `import()` rejects at runtime — every route-level lazy import needs a catch that offers a reload rather than rendering a blank screen.

The `install` event's `waitUntil` promise gates activation: if precaching fails on a single asset, the whole worker fails to install and the previous worker keeps serving, which is the safe outcome but only if the failure is reported.

`clients.claim()` lets a newly activated worker take control of pages that are already open but uncontrolled; without it the very first page load of a user's first session is never controlled by the worker at all.
failureModes: Calls `self.skipWaiting()` at the top of the install handler because a tutorial said so, then spends a week debugging mixed-version behaviour.
Believes a hard refresh updates the service worker.
Never handles a rejected dynamic import, so every deploy produces white screens for users with a tab open.
Assumes the first visit is controlled by the worker and is surprised that nothing was cached.
interviewProbes: You deploy at 10am. At 3pm a user reports they are still on the old version, and they insist they refreshed. Explain what happened.
Walk me through your 'new version available' flow, event by event.
What breaks for a user who has had your SPA open for six hours when you deploy?

viz.title: Two Tabs, Two Workers
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame containing the registration state machine (installing -> installed/waiting -> activating -> activated -> redundant) drawn once, with two tab tokens placed on the worker that currently controls each of them. Deploy, reload, hard reload, close-tab and skipWaiting are labelled edges. A ghost pair of tokens shows where the tabs would sit under the alternative skipWaiting policy. Version labels sit inside the state boxes, not in a legend.
viz.predictPrompt: Tab 1 is open on v1. You deploy v2. The user opens Tab 2 (new tab, same origin) and then hard-refreshes Tab 1. Which worker controls Tab 1, and which controls Tab 2?
controls: reload tab / hard reload tab / close tab / open new tab
viz.insight: Waiting is not a bug — it is the guarantee that a single page never mixes two builds. skipWaiting trades that guarantee away, and you have to hand it back by reloading.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models registration state plus a set of client records with a controlling worker id; the browser is never consulted. Unit tests pin the predictPrompt answer (both tabs on v1 after a hard reload) and assert that under on-user-click, controllerchange fires exactly once per accepted update. Reduced motion renders the final placement with the transition edges numbered in order.

drills.prompt: Order the events of a correct, user-consented update from deploy to the user running the new build.
drills.answerSketch: registration.update() -> updatefound -> installing worker -> install/waitUntil resolves -> state 'installed' with an existing controller -> show 'new version available' -> user clicks -> postMessage SKIP_WAITING -> worker calls skipWaiting -> activate -> controllerchange fires -> location.reload().

drills.prompt: A service worker registration module plus sw.js containing three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) `self.skipWaiting()` called unconditionally inside `install`; (2) no `controllerchange` listener, so the page never reloads onto the new worker; (3) no catch on the lazy route import, producing a blank screen on stale chunks.

drills.prompt: Fill in the two blanks that detect an available update and reload exactly once after the user accepts.
drills.answerSketch: `if (registration.waiting) showUpdatePrompt()` plus `let reloading = false; navigator.serviceWorker.addEventListener('controllerchange', () => { if (reloading) return; reloading = true; location.reload(); })`.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: the app is a kiosk that is never closed and never navigates, and must pick up deploys within 15 minutes. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The 24-hour automatic update check and the waiting state both break it: no navigation means no update check, and no tab close means the new worker never activates. You need a periodic registration.update() plus an automated accept-and-reload path — which is exactly the case where skipWaiting-plus-reload is correct.

rt-caching.title: Cache Strategy Per Asset Class
objectives: Assign a caching strategy per asset class and justify each from the asset's mutability and freshness requirement.
Predict what a given cache configuration does on the day of a deploy.
Identify what must never enter Cache Storage.
claims: Cache strategy is chosen per asset class, not per app: content-hashed static assets are cache-first indefinitely, HTML and navigation requests are network-first with a cached fallback, and API GETs are stale-while-revalidate only where a few-seconds-old value is acceptable.
Cache-first on a URL that is not content-hashed is how an app becomes permanently stale; immutability must be guaranteed by the filename, never by the strategy.
Only safe, idempotent GET requests belong in the Cache API; a POST cannot be cached, and an offline POST belongs in a durable outbox rather than in any cache.

The service worker Cache Storage is not the HTTP cache: your code can store a response that carried `Cache-Control: no-store`, which means a worker can serve content the server explicitly told the browser not to retain — authenticated responses on shared devices are the failure this causes.

Every deploy must write to a new named cache and delete the old ones in `activate`; without that cleanup Cache Storage grows monotonically and eventually contributes to eviction of the entire origin's storage.
Navigation preload starts the network request for a navigation in parallel with the service worker's startup, removing worker boot time from the critical path of a network-first navigation.
A stale-while-revalidate response must be rendered as stale — with an age or a refresh affordance — or the user cannot distinguish fresh data from a value cached a week ago.

Cache-first HTML plus network-first API produces 'the shell loads instantly and then shows an error' when offline; that is usually better than a blank page, but it is a design decision that has to be made deliberately, not discovered in production.
failureModes: Applies one strategy — nearly always cache-first — to everything and cannot say what happens on deploy day.
Caches an authenticated API response and serves it to the next user of a shared device.
Never cleans up old caches, then blames the browser for evicting the origin.
Claims stale-while-revalidate makes the app 'offline capable' when the revalidate half never surfaces to the user.
interviewProbes: Give me the caching strategy for each asset class in a typical SPA, and tell me what happens to each one on the day of a deploy.
Where would you refuse to use the service worker cache at all?
A user says the app has been showing last week's data for days. Where do you look?

viz.title: Four Requests, Four Strategies, One Deploy
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame: a fetch-handler router drawn as a single decision column. Four labelled request tokens (hashed app.a1b2.js, index.html, GET /api/feed, POST /api/message) flow through it into one of four strategy boxes, each showing an inline cache-hit / network-hit / queued indicator and the version served. A deploy event re-runs all four; the previous run is retained as a ghost row directly beneath for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: You deploy a new build. index.html is cache-first and your JS filenames are content-hashed. The user opens the app while fully online. Which version do they get, and how many reloads until they get the new one?
viz.insight: The HTML is the version pointer. Caching it aggressively pins the entire app to a past deploy no matter how carefully everything downstream is hashed — and 'online' does not save you.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure router over a fixture manifest of two builds, with an injected clock. Unit tests assert that cache-first HTML serves the old build indefinitely under any number of online reloads, and that network-first HTML plus hashed assets converges to the new build in exactly one reload. Reduced motion draws both runs as a static two-row matrix with the divergent cell highlighted.

drills.prompt: Seven asset classes (hashed JS/CSS; index.html; a font file; user avatars; GET /api/settings; GET /api/live-prices; POST /api/order). Assign a strategy to each.
drills.answerSketch: Cache-first; network-first with cached fallback; cache-first; cache-first with a size-bounded runtime cache; stale-while-revalidate; network-only; never cached — durable outbox.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: this is a clinical tool on a shared workstation, and no patient data may persist on the device. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Every runtime cache holding authenticated API responses. Cache Storage survives logout and is readable by the next user; the fix is network-only for authenticated data plus an explicit cache purge on sign-out, and it removes most of the offline story you had.

drills.prompt: Which of these is true about a response with `Cache-Control: no-store` in a service worker context?
drills.answerSketch: Your fetch handler can still put it into Cache Storage — the directive constrains the HTTP cache, not your code. That is why authenticated-response caching is a policy decision you must make explicitly.

drills.prompt: Defend making index.html cache-first with a background revalidate, for a product where you describe the constraints. Then state the failure mode you are accepting.
drills.answerSketch: Defensible for an app-shell product with an aggressive in-app update prompt; the accepted failure is that a user who ignores the prompt runs an arbitrarily old build, which means every API must remain backward-compatible indefinitely.

rt-idb.title: IndexedDB: Schemas, Versions, Transactions and Quota
objectives: Design a migration ladder that is correct for a user arriving from any previous version, in any number of open tabs.
Write transactions that do not die from an accidental await.
Reason about quota, persistence and eviction as product risks, not implementation details.
claims: An IndexedDB schema can only change inside a `versionchange` transaction triggered by opening the database with a higher version number; object stores and indexes cannot be created at any other time.
Migrations must be a ladder of sequential, idempotent steps keyed on `event.oldVersion`, because a returning user can arrive at v5 directly from v1 without ever having run v2, v3 or v4.

If another tab holds the database open at the old version, the upgrade fires `blocked` and stalls indefinitely; every tab must listen for `versionchange` on its connection and close it so the upgrading tab can proceed.

An IndexedDB transaction auto-commits as soon as its request queue drains and control returns to the event loop, so awaiting a `fetch` or any non-IDB promise mid-transaction kills it with a TransactionInactiveError.

Values are stored with the structured clone algorithm: Blob, File, Map, Set, Date, ArrayBuffer and typed arrays survive, while functions, DOM nodes, class prototypes and symbol-keyed properties do not.

`navigator.storage.estimate()` reports usage and quota, but both are deliberately imprecise and the quota is a single origin-wide budget shared across IndexedDB, Cache Storage and other script-writable storage — it is not a per-store limit.

Quota shape differs by engine: Chromium allows an origin up to roughly 60% of total disk, Firefox gives best-effort storage about 10% of disk (up to ~10 GB) with a per-eTLD+1 group cap, and Safari is far smaller and prompts the user to extend — so a design that assumes gigabytes is only true on Chromium.

`navigator.storage.persist()` moves an origin from best-effort to persistent so it is exempt from eviction under storage pressure; Chromium grants it silently from engagement signals such as being installed or holding notification permission, while Firefox prompts the user.

Safari deletes all script-writable storage — IndexedDB, Cache Storage and service worker registrations — after seven days without user interaction with the site, and only a Home Screen web app is exempt, so months of local-only data can vanish from an ordinary browser tab.
failureModes: Awaits a network call inside a transaction and concludes IndexedDB is 'flaky'.
Writes migrations as an if/else-if chain on the new version, or deletes and recreates the database on every upgrade, silently destroying user data.
Never handles `blocked`, so on the day of a schema change every multi-tab user gets a permanent hang with no error.
Assumes local-only data is permanent, ships no export, and loses a user's history to Safari's seven-day eviction.
interviewProbes: A user returns after a year, on version 1 of your schema, with three tabs restored. Walk me through what happens.
How much data can you store, and what makes that number wrong?
Your writes intermittently fail with TransactionInactiveError. What is the code doing?

viz.title: Upgrading a Database Someone Else Has Open
viz.whatIsDrawn: A vertical version ladder v1 to v5, each rung labelled with its migration step. Two tab tokens sit at their current version on the ladder. Opening at a higher version draws the upgrade path actually executed, highlighting the rungs that run and dimming those skipped. A blocked upgrade draws a stall marker anchored on the rung where it halted, with the blocking tab's token ringed. A quota bar runs alongside the ladder inside the same frame.
viz.predictPrompt: A user last opened your app when it shipped v2. Today they open it at v5, with two tabs restored at once. Which migration steps run, in which tab, and what does the second tab experience?
controls: set the user's stored version (v1 to v4)
toggle: does the older tab listen for versionchange?
viz.insight: Migrations run as a jump from an arbitrary old version, so every step must be written to run in any sequence — and a single tab that refuses to close its connection deadlocks the upgrade for the whole user.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models connections, versions and the blocked path as pure state with an injected clock; no real IndexedDB is touched. Unit tests assert that opening at v5 from v2 executes exactly steps 3, 4, 5 in order, and that with the versionchange listener absent the second tab's open request never resolves. Reduced motion renders the executed rungs highlighted with an ordered numbering and the stall marker in place.

drills.prompt: Complete the upgrade handler so it is correct for any oldVersion (two blanks: the ladder guard and the versionchange listener).
drills.answerSketch: Sequential `if (oldVersion < 2) {...}` `if (oldVersion < 3) {...}` blocks with no else, and `db.onversionchange = () => db.close()` registered on every opened connection.

drills.prompt: A 30-line IndexedDB repository module with three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) `await fetch(...)` between two store operations inside one transaction; (2) `if/else if` migration chain keyed on the new version; (3) no `blocked` handler and no `onversionchange` listener.

drills.prompt: Order the steps for shipping a schema change safely to users who may have several tabs open.
drills.answerSketch: Add the migration step to the ladder -> bump the version constant -> ensure every connection registers onversionchange -> handle blocked with a user-facing 'close other tabs' prompt -> write the migration to be idempotent and to leave old stores readable -> ship -> keep the previous read path until the version is fully rolled out.

drills.prompt: Design the object stores and indexes for a spaced-repetition app storing claims, review history, and an outbox. Name the keys and the indexes and justify each index by the query it serves.
drills.answerSketch: `claims` keyed by claimId; `reviews` keyed by autoincrement with an index on [claimId, reviewedAt] for history and an index on `due` for the daily queue; `outbox` keyed by autoincrement with an index on status. Indexes exist only where a range query needs them.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: users must be able to keep six months of review history, and a meaningful share of them use Safari without installing the app. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Not quota — eviction. Safari clears script-writable storage after seven idle days, so history disappears for anyone who takes a break. The mitigations are a nudged export snapshot, a merge-aware import, an install prompt, and being explicit in the UI that data is local.

rt-outbox.title: The Offline Outbox: Durable Mutations, Retry and Background Sync
objectives: Design a durable outbox of user intents with idempotency, a retry classification, and a dead-letter path.
Layer Background Sync as an enhancement over triggers that work everywhere.
Model dependencies between queued mutations so one failure cannot block the rest.
claims: An outbox stores durable user INTENTS in IndexedDB, not serialized HTTP requests, because the endpoint, auth scheme and payload shape may all change between enqueue and the eventual successful send.
Every outbox entry carries a client-generated idempotency key created once at enqueue time and reused on every retry, so a request that timed out after the server committed it does not apply twice.

The Background Sync API is Chromium-only — neither Safari nor Firefox has ever implemented it — so it must be a progressive enhancement layered over a flush triggered by the `online` event, `visibilitychange`, and application start.

Retry policy has to classify failures: network errors and 5xx retry with jittered backoff; 408, 425 and 429 retry with respect for `Retry-After`; other 4xx are permanent and must not be retried; and 409 usually means a conflict to resolve rather than an operation to repeat.
A poison entry that fails forever will block a strictly ordered queue indefinitely, so an outbox needs an attempt cap, a dead-letter state, and a way for the user to see and discard the stuck item.

Ordering only needs to hold between dependent mutations — 'create doc' before 'rename doc' — while independent mutations can be sent in parallel; modelling that dependency explicitly is exactly what stops one stuck entry from blocking everything.

The outbox and the optimistic pending layer are the same data viewed twice: pending entries are what the UI renders as 'not yet sent', so they must be read back from durable storage on boot or a reload erases work the UI already confirmed.
A Background Sync attempt runs in the service worker with no page: it cannot see your in-memory auth token or your Zustand store, so every input the retry needs must already be in IndexedDB.
failureModes: Queues `Request` objects and finds the whole queue unusable after an auth scheme change.
Assumes Background Sync is available everywhere and ships an app that never flushes on iOS.
Retries 400-class errors forever, burning battery and filling server logs.
Keeps the outbox in memory, so a refresh silently drops the queue while the UI still shows the items as saved.
interviewProbes: Design offline sending for a field-service app used in basements. What is stored, what triggers a flush, and what happens after 20 failed attempts?
One queued mutation returns 422 forever. What do the other 39 queued mutations do?
How does your retry behave differently on iOS Safari versus Chrome on Android?

viz.title: The Queue That Cannot Drain
viz.whatIsDrawn: One frame. The outbox is a vertical list of entries, each showing its attempt count, next-retry countdown, and state (pending / in-flight / dead-lettered), with dependency arrows drawn between entries that must stay ordered. A network band runs across the top. A ghost column immediately to the right shows the same queue under the alternative flush policy at the same instant, so the number of entries delivered is directly comparable.
viz.predictPrompt: Entry #2 in a strictly FIFO outbox is a rename of a document whose create (#1) already succeeded, but #2 returns 422 on every attempt. Entries #3 through #40 are unrelated likes on other documents. With strict FIFO, how many of the 40 entries reach the server in the next hour?
controls: inject a failure type per entry: 500 / 422 / 409 / timeout
flush policy: strict FIFO / dependency-ordered / fully parallel
viz.insight: A durable ordered queue with no dead-letter path turns one permanently failing mutation into total sync failure — and the fix is modelling dependencies, not loosening ordering everywhere.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure queue machine with an injected clock and seeded RNG for jitter. Unit tests pin the predictPrompt answer (exactly one entry delivered under strict FIFO) and assert that dependency-ordered flushing delivers 39 with the same fault injected. A third test asserts an entry is dead-lettered at exactly the configured attempt cap and never retried afterwards.

drills.prompt: Design the outbox for a notes app: the record shape, the flush triggers, the retry classification, the dependency model, and the dead-letter UX.
drills.answerSketch: Record {id, intentType, payload, idempotencyKey, dependsOn, attempts, nextAttemptAt, state}. Triggers: app start, online event, visibilitychange to visible, plus Background Sync where available. Classification as in the claims. Dependencies by entity id. Dead-letter surfaces as a per-item error with retry and discard, never as a global banner.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: the app must also flush while fully closed on iOS. What breaks first, and what is the honest answer?
drills.answerSketch: Background Sync does not exist on iOS, and a closed web app gets no execution. The honest answer is that it cannot be done on the open web on iOS; you flush at next launch, communicate 'pending' clearly, and if the requirement is truly hard you need a native or Home Screen app with push-triggered wake, which is itself best-effort.

drills.prompt: A 35-line outbox flush implementation with three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) idempotency key generated inside the retry loop; (2) all non-2xx responses retried, including 400 and 403; (3) the auth token read from an in-memory module that is undefined when the flush runs in the service worker.

drills.prompt: A user is offline for 6 hours generating 4 mutations/minute at 800 bytes each. How large is the outbox, and what does the flush look like when they reconnect?
drills.answerSketch: 1,440 entries, ~1.2 MB — trivially within quota. The problem is the flush: 1,440 sequential requests. You need bounded concurrency (say 6) plus server-side batching, or the reconnect becomes a self-inflicted burst.

drills.prompt: Defend either strict global ordering or dependency-only ordering for a collaborative task app, in writing, in 5 minutes. Name what each one costs you.
drills.answerSketch: Strict ordering is simpler to reason about and to debug, and costs you total-blockage on any poison entry. Dependency ordering costs you an explicit dependency model and harder debugging, and buys partial progress. The deciding constraint is whether unrelated mutations are common.

rt-conflict-ux.title: Conflict Resolution and Honest Offline UI
objectives: Choose a conflict policy per field rather than per application, and make conflicts detectable in the first place.
Design an offline and staleness UI that tells the truth without a global banner.
Decide when to disable an affordance offline and when to accept and queue the input.
claims: The choice between silent merge, last-write-wins and prompting the user is a product decision made per field, not a global technical setting: a document body deserves a merge, a 'published' toggle deserves a prompt.

Detecting a conflict at all requires the client to send back a version it read — an ETag with `If-Match`, or a per-record version number — because a plain PUT of the whole record cannot distinguish 'I changed this' from 'I am overwriting someone else's change'.

A conflict prompt must show what differs, not that something differs; 'this record was modified by someone else' with an OK button forces the user to guess, and users choose whichever button ends the dialog.

`navigator.onLine` is false only when the operating system reports no network at all; it is true on captive portals and on connections with a dead uplink, so an honest connection indicator must be driven by the outcomes of real requests or heartbeats.

Staleness should be labelled with an age at the point of use — 'updated 4m ago' next to the value — rather than behind a global banner, because the user reads the value long after they have stopped noticing the banner.

Disabling an affordance offline is only correct when the action genuinely cannot be queued; for queueable actions, accept the input and show a 'will send when online' state, because a disabled button with no explanation is indistinguishable from a bug.

Preserving the losing side of a conflict — as a duplicate, a version, or an undo — converts a data-loss incident into an inconvenience, and is almost always cheaper to build than getting the merge right.
A pending state and a failed state must be visually distinct and both must be addressable; collapsing them into one 'not saved' style is how users learn to ignore both.
failureModes: Ships last-write-wins across the whole record and calls it conflict resolution.
Uses `navigator.onLine` for the offline indicator and gets bug reports from hotel wifi and captive portals.
Shows a modal conflict dialog with no diff and two equally weighted buttons.
Greys out the entire interface when offline, including actions that could have been queued perfectly well.
interviewProbes: Two users edit the same record, one of them offline. Design what each of them sees, including the moment the conflict is discovered.
How do you know you are actually offline? Why is `navigator.onLine` not enough?
Which actions in your app would you disable offline, and which would you accept and queue?

viz.title: The Same Screen in Six Truth States
viz.whatIsDrawn: One product screen rendered six times in a 3x2 grid inside a single frame: fresh-online, stale-online, offline-queued, send-failed, conflict-detected, and merged. Each cell carries inline callouts pointing at the exact element that changes — the age label, the badge, the button state, the diff affordance — with at most seven callouts across the whole grid. The fresh-online rendering is repeated as a faint ghost behind each other cell so the delta is visible without looking away.
viz.predictPrompt: A user edits a record offline while a colleague edits the same record online. The user reconnects and your client sends a full PUT with no version header. What does the server do, what does the user see, and at what moment does anyone learn a change was lost?
viz.insight: A conflict you cannot detect becomes silent data loss; a conflict you can detect becomes a UX problem — and the UX problem is by far the cheaper one to have.
viz.buildNotes: This visual is a static composition with a stepped callout reveal — deliberately one animated channel, because the content is comparative rather than dynamic. The six states are rendered from one component driven by a state prop so they cannot drift apart. sim.ts here is the conflict-detection predicate (given clientVersion, serverVersion, and granularity, does this write conflict?), unit-tested against the six cases. Reduced motion shows all callouts at once.

drills.prompt: Six fields on one record (body text; title; assignee; due date; 'published' boolean; a running comment thread). Assign a conflict policy: silent merge, LWW, prompt, or append-only.
drills.answerSketch: Body: merge. Title: LWW. Assignee: prompt (it has real-world consequences). Due date: LWW or prompt depending on whether it triggers notifications. Published: prompt — never silently flip. Comments: append-only, never conflicts.

drills.prompt: A save handler and a connection indicator with three defects. Select the offending lines.
drills.answerSketch: (1) full-record PUT with no If-Match or version field; (2) `navigator.onLine` used as the sole source of connection state; (3) a global 'unsaved changes' banner with no per-item state, so the user cannot tell which item failed.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: the app is used by two people editing the same record simultaneously, on purpose, all day. What breaks first in a prompt-on-conflict design?
drills.answerSketch: The prompt itself — it fires constantly and users click through it, which is worse than LWW because it trains dismissal. At that collaboration frequency the field must move to a merge model (a sequence CRDT for text, per-field ownership elsewhere), not to a better dialog.

drills.prompt: Design the connection-truth mechanism for an app that must never lie about being online: signals, state machine, and what the UI shows in each state.
drills.answerSketch: States: online-confirmed, degraded (requests failing or heartbeat late), offline-confirmed. Driven by request outcomes and heartbeat replies, with navigator.onLine and the online event only as hints to re-probe. UI shows per-value ages in degraded, and per-item queued state in offline.

drills.prompt: Your PM asks for a single global 'You are offline' banner instead of per-item states, because it is much cheaper. Defend or refuse it in writing, in 4 minutes.
drills.answerSketch: A banner answers 'is the app online', but users need 'is THIS value current' and 'did MY change save'. Cheapest honest compromise: keep the banner, add an age label at the point of use and a per-item pending state for anything queued.

rt-push.title: Web Push and the Permission Moment
objectives: Judge when Web Push is the right mechanism and when a socket or a poll is.
Design a permission request whose timing accounts for the fact that a denial is permanent.
State the platform constraints that decide whether push is available at all.
claims: Web Push requires a service worker, a PushSubscription obtained with your VAPID public key, and a push service endpoint owned by the browser vendor; your server never contacts the device directly, it posts an encrypted payload to that endpoint.
Chromium requires `userVisibleOnly: true`, which means every push you send must produce a visible notification — silent push for background data sync is not available on the open web.

On iOS and iPadOS, push is only available to a web app added to the Home Screen; a site open in a Safari tab cannot subscribe, and `Notification.requestPermission()` must be called from a user gesture.

Safari 18.4 introduced Declarative Web Push, where the push payload itself declares the notification and no service worker push handler is required — the Home Screen requirement still applies, and since iOS 26 any site added to the Home Screen opens as a web app by default, which widens the eligible population.

The permission prompt is effectively one-shot per origin: a denial is sticky and cannot be re-prompted from JavaScript, which is why the browser prompt must be preceded by an in-page explanation the user can decline for free.

Browsers penalise sites that ask on page load — Chrome and Firefox both suppress the prompt for users who habitually dismiss it — so prompt timing is a deliverability concern and not merely a courtesy.

Subscriptions expire and rotate: the service worker must handle `pushsubscriptionchange` and re-subscribe, and the server must delete endpoints that return 404 or 410 or it accumulates dead subscriptions and wasted sends.

Push is not a real-time transport: delivery is best-effort, can be delayed by minutes on a sleeping device, and is throttled by the operating system — anything that must arrive in order or on time belongs on a socket, with push used only to say 'come back'.
failureModes: Calls `Notification.requestPermission()` on page load and permanently loses the permission for that user with no way to ask again.
Plans to use silent push to trigger background data sync on the open web.
Assumes iOS web push works from a Safari tab and ships a feature that is invisible to every iOS user.
Never handles 410 Gone and grows a table of dead endpoints that inflates delivery metrics.
interviewProbes: When would you use Web Push rather than keeping a socket open, and what do you give up?
Design the permission request flow. What happens if the user says no?
What does your push implementation do differently for an iOS user?

viz.title: The Permission Funnel
viz.whatIsDrawn: A five-stage funnel drawn as nested horizontal bars in one frame — eligible, prompted, granted, subscribed, still-subscribed-at-30-days — with the absolute count and the drop labelled inline on each bar. A ghost funnel sits directly behind it showing the previously selected prompt strategy. The platform selector greys out stages that are structurally unreachable (iOS-in-tab greys out 'eligible' entirely, with the reason labelled on the bar).
viz.predictPrompt: You move the permission prompt from page load to after the user's first meaningful action. Grant rate rises from 12% to 40%. Does the absolute number of subscribed users go up? What else has to be true for this to be a win?
controls: prompt timing: on-load / after-first-action / in-page double opt-in
platform: Chrome desktop / Chrome Android / iOS Home Screen / iOS Safari tab
viz.insight: A permission you cannot re-request makes prompt timing an irreversible one-shot decision — so optimise the 30-day stage, not the grant rate, because a high grant rate on a tiny prompted pool can still be fewer subscribers.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure funnel model with documented, cited-as-illustrative conversion constants and a seeded RNG; the module prose must state plainly that these are illustrative shapes, not measured industry figures — inventing precise conversion numbers would be a wrong claim. Unit tests assert the counter-intuitive case: a strategy with a higher grant rate can produce fewer absolute subscribers. iOS-in-tab must yield a structurally zero funnel, not a small one.

drills.prompt: Five notification needs (a chat message while the tab is open; a chat message while the app is closed; a background data refresh; a build-finished alert; a 'your document was shared' alert). For each: socket, push, poll, or not possible on the web.
drills.answerSketch: Socket; push; not possible on the open web (userVisibleOnly forbids silent push, and Periodic Background Sync is Chromium-only and unreliable); push; push.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: 60% of your users are on iPhones and must receive notifications. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Eligibility, before any prompt-timing work matters. iOS push requires the app on the Home Screen, so the project becomes an install-prompt and onboarding problem — and a large fraction of users will never install, which has to be stated as a cap rather than engineered around.

drills.prompt: Defend an in-page double opt-in — an interstitial the user can decline without touching the browser prompt — against the objection that it adds friction and lowers volume. Written, 4 minutes.
drills.answerSketch: The browser denial is permanent, so a soft decline preserves the option to ask later; volume lost today is recoverable, a denial is not. Only defensible if you actually re-ask later at a better moment.

drills.prompt: 1,000,000 monthly users. 30% are on iOS in a Safari tab, 5% of the rest install to Home Screen. On-load prompting reaches 100% of eligible users at a 10% grant rate; after-action prompting reaches 25% at a 40% grant rate. Compute subscribers under each.
drills.answerSketch: Eligible: 700,000 non-iOS plus 15,000 installed iOS = 715,000. On-load: 71,500. After-action: 715,000 x 0.25 x 0.40 = 71,500. Identical — which is the point: the grant rate alone tells you nothing, and the 30-day retention stage is what separates them.

rt-local-first.title: Local-First Sync Engine Architecture
objectives: Judge whether a given product or a given slice of a product should be local-first at all.
Name the four consequences of moving the network out of the read path: partial replication, server-side authorization, rejection handling, and on-device schema migration.
Choose between an off-the-shelf sync engine and a hand-built one, with the constraint that decides it.
claims: In a local-first architecture the local store is the source of truth for reads and writes, and the network is a background replication process, so every UI query is synchronous against local data and no screen has a loading state tied to the network.

A sync engine replaces per-screen data fetching with two generic mechanisms — a subscription to a subset of server state and a durable stream of local mutations — which is why adopting one removes endpoints rather than adding them.

Partial replication is the hard part: a client cannot hold all data, so the engine needs a declarative statement of which subset this user syncs, and that statement is also where authorization is expressed.

Authorization cannot be enforced on the client in a local-first app: the server must validate every mutation independently, because the client's write already 'succeeded' locally before the server ever saw it.
Because the server can reject a mutation the client already applied, a rollback path and a user-facing story for it are mandatory parts of the architecture rather than edge cases.
Rejecting an old mutation requires rebasing, not reverting: later accepted mutations must be replayed on top of the corrected state, or the user loses work they were never told was at risk.

Not everything should be local-first: server-authoritative data under contention — prices, inventory, permissions, anything another actor changes — should stay request/response, and mixing the two models per domain is the normal outcome.

The category has real off-the-shelf options in 2026 — Replicache/Zero, ElectricSQL, PowerSync, LiveStore, Convex, and CRDT libraries plus a provider — and building your own means owning the migration of a schema that already lives on devices you cannot reach.
Migrating a local-first schema is a distributed migration: old builds keep running on devices you cannot update, so the sync protocol has to be tolerant of both older and newer peers, indefinitely.
failureModes: Describes local-first as 'cache everything' with no mutation log, no rejection path, and no partial-replication story.
Puts authorization into the sync query and assumes a client cannot lie about what it is subscribed to.
Applies local-first to a checkout or seat-selection flow where the outcome is server-owned and contended.
Treats schema change as a server deploy and forgets that the schema now lives on users' devices.
interviewProbes: Design the data layer for a Linear-style issue tracker that must be instant and work offline. Where does the network appear?
The server rejects a mutation the user made four minutes and twenty edits ago. What does your client do?
Which parts of this product would you refuse to make local-first, and why?

viz.title: Where the Read Goes
viz.whatIsDrawn: One architecture frame with four stacked layers — UI, local store, sync engine, server — and two traced paths drawn directly on it: a READ that terminates at the local store and never crosses the network boundary, and a WRITE that runs UI -> local store -> mutation log -> server -> confirm-or-reject -> local store. A faint ghost overlay shows the same two traces in a conventional fetch-per-screen architecture, where the read crosses the boundary. Layer contents are labelled inside each band; the rejection branch is drawn as a returning arrow annotated 'rebase', not 'revert'.
viz.predictPrompt: The server rejects a mutation the user made four minutes ago, after which they made twenty more edits that the server accepted. What must the client be able to do, and what does the user see?
controls: trace: a read / a write / a rejection
viz.insight: Local-first is one move — take the network out of the read path — and everything hard about it (partial replication, server-side authorization, rejection and rebase, on-device schema migration) is a direct consequence of that single move.
viz.buildNotes: The traced path and a small contents badge on the local store are the only two animated channels; the layer diagram itself is static. sim.ts holds the mutation-log rebase reducer, unit-tested with the predictPrompt scenario: rejecting mutation #1 of 21 must preserve the other 20 and produce a state that differs from both a naive revert and a naive server-snapshot replace. Reduced motion renders both traces simultaneously with numbered steps.

drills.prompt: Six product surfaces in one B2B app (issue list and editing; billing and invoices; team permissions admin; a full-text search across all org data; user preferences; a live availability calendar with double-booking risk). For each: local-first, request/response, or hybrid.
drills.answerSketch: Issues: local-first. Billing: request/response. Permissions admin: request/response (server-authoritative, and it is the authorization source). Full-text search: hybrid — local index over the replicated subset, server search beyond it. Preferences: local-first. Calendar: request/response for booking, local-first for viewing.

drills.prompt: Choose between adopting an off-the-shelf sync engine and building a bespoke outbox-plus-subscription layer for a product you describe. Written, 6 minutes. Name the constraint that decides it and the one that would flip it.
drills.answerSketch: Deciding constraints are usually partial-replication complexity and existing backend shape: an off-the-shelf engine wins when your data model fits its replication primitives; a bespoke layer wins when your authorization or data shape does not, and you accept owning on-device migration forever.

drills.prompt: The requirement adds: an organization can have 40 GB of issue history, and users search all of it. What breaks first in your local-first design?
drills.answerSketch: Partial replication. The device cannot hold the data, so the sync subset must become explicitly scoped (recent, assigned, subscribed) and search splits into a local index over the subset plus a server search for everything else — which reintroduces a loading state and therefore a UX decision about where the boundary is visible.

drills.prompt: Design the sync subset definition and the mutation validation path for a multi-tenant issue tracker. Say where authorization is enforced and what a malicious client can and cannot do.
drills.answerSketch: Subset declared server-side per user (org membership plus subscribed projects), evaluated on the server on every subscription refresh — never trusted from the client. Every mutation revalidated server-side against the same rules. A malicious client can fabricate local state and send invalid mutations; it cannot obtain data outside its server-evaluated subset or have an invalid mutation accepted.

cs-autocomplete.title: Case: Autocomplete / Typeahead
objectives: Design a typeahead whose rendered list is provably never stale with respect to the current input value.
Choose and defend a caching strategy with an explicit key, eviction policy and behaviour on backspace.
Wire the combobox ARIA pattern so that keyboard navigation never moves DOM focus out of the input.
claims: A trailing-edge debounce of roughly 150 ms delays every request by the window; it is a cost control on request volume and does nothing for correctness.

Out-of-order responses, not slow responses, are the defining correctness bug of a typeahead: a two-character query resolving after a five-character query overwrites the list with results the user is no longer asking for.

AbortController cancels the in-flight request but does not by itself order responses; correctness requires either aborting the previous request or discarding any response whose query string does not equal the current input value.
Suggestions cache cleanly by exact query string, and a prefix trie additionally lets 'rea' reuse the results for 're' as an instant provisional list while the network request is in flight.

The correct ARIA pattern is role=combobox on the input with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at a role=listbox, and aria-activedescendant naming the highlighted option — DOM focus must remain in the input or typing stops working.
Between compositionstart and compositionend, input events fire for intermediate characters, so querying on them produces meaningless requests for every CJK user.
The perceived-instant budget for a typeahead is roughly 100 ms from keystroke to painted list; past about one second users stop trusting suggestions and press Enter instead.

Rendering the list is itself a main-thread cost: recomputing match highlighting for ten results on every keystroke at eight keystrokes per second is enough to breach the 200 ms INP budget on a mid-tier phone if done with a fresh regex per item per render.

viz.title: The Stale-Response Race
viz.whatIsDrawn: A horizontal time axis with one lane per in-flight request, each drawn as a bar from send to arrival under seeded jittered latency, labelled with its query string at the bar's left edge. Beneath it, a single strip showing what the list currently displays, coloured by which query it reflects; every interval where that colour disagrees with the current input value is hatched and labelled 'stale' inline. A ghost lane above shows the same keystroke sequence with cancellation enabled.
viz.predictPrompt: The user types 'react' at eight characters per second. Latency is uniform between 120 and 600 ms. With a 150 ms trailing debounce and no cancellation, how many times does the visible list show results for a query that is no longer in the box — and does raising the debounce to 400 ms eliminate it?
controls: latency spread with a seeded RNG
toggle abort-previous vs discard-stale vs neither
viz.insight: Debounce is a cost control, not a correctness control: because latency variance exceeds any sane debounce window, only cancellation or a response-versus-current-query comparison makes the list correct.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {keystrokes, seed, debounceMs, strategy} and an injected clock, and emits a list of {t, requestId, query, sentAt, arrivesAt, rendered}. Unit test asserts staleRenderCount === 0 for all 200 seeds when strategy is 'discard' or 'abort', and asserts it is strictly greater than zero for 'none' at debounce values from 0 to 500 ms — the test IS the pedagogical claim.

drills.prompt: This handler debounces at 300 ms, calls fetch, and sets state in .then(). AbortController is present but the .catch() also calls setState with the last known good results. Name the user-visible symptom and the smallest correct fix.
drills.answerSketch: Aborted requests reject, the catch resurrects stale results, so the list flickers back to an older query after the correct one has rendered. Smallest fix: rethrow or return early when err.name === 'AbortError'; better, compare the response's query against a latestQuery ref before any setState.

drills.prompt: Complete the guard that makes this handler correct without any AbortController: `const res = await fetch(url); if (______) return; setResults(await res.json());`
drills.answerSketch: `query !== latestQueryRef.current` — the response is discarded unless it corresponds to what is currently in the input.

drills.prompt: The requirement changes: suggestions must still work for previously seen queries when the device is offline. What breaks first, and what changes on your canvas?
drills.answerSketch: The in-memory cache dies on reload, so a durable store node appears; cache key and eviction policy must now be explicit and bounded; the UI needs a distinct 'showing cached results' state; and the discard-stale guard now has two result sources to reconcile, so cached results must be marked provisional and never overwrite a fresh response for the same query.

drills.prompt: Order the steps that must happen when the user presses ArrowDown while the listbox is open, for a correct combobox.
drills.answerSketch: preventDefault -> compute next option index with wraparound -> set aria-activedescendant on the input to that option's id -> apply the visual highlight class to that option -> scroll the option into view within the listbox -> do NOT call .focus() on the option.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4-minute timer then locked: ship a 5,000-entry trie bundled with the client, or call the server on every debounced keystroke? Justify and name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the bundle byte cost of the trie; names the freshness cost (a bundled dictionary is stale until the next deploy); names the p75 latency saved; names coverage (a trie only helps head queries); states a flip condition such as 'flip to server-only once the head-query hit rate falls below ~40% or the trie exceeds ~30 KB gzipped'.

drills.prompt: Why must the query be suppressed between compositionstart and compositionend, and what is the correct trigger instead?
drills.answerSketch: Intermediate composition characters fire input events, so a CJK user issues requests for phonetic fragments that are not words. Trigger the query on compositionend, and on input only when event.isComposing is false.

failureModes: Says 'debounce it' and considers the race handled.
Uses AbortController but still calls setState from the rejection path, resurrecting stale data.
Moves DOM focus into the listbox on ArrowDown, so the user can no longer type.
Proposes caching without ever stating the key, the eviction policy, or what happens when the user backspaces into a prefix already in the cache.
Proposes building a client-side trie over the full 50-million-item corpus.
Never states a latency budget, so 'instant' is never falsifiable.
interviewProbes: Your debounce is 300 ms and p99 latency is 900 ms. Walk me through exactly what the user sees.
How would you cache this? What's the key, what's the eviction, and what happens when they type 'reac' then backspace to 'rea'?
The PM wants results to update while the user holds backspace. What changes?
A screen reader user tabs into this. Narrate what they hear.

cs-feed.title: Case: News Feed
objectives: Design pagination for a ranked, mutating feed such that no item is duplicated or skipped across page boundaries.
Model feed entities so that the same post cannot diverge between the feed and its detail view.
Specify optimistic reaction updates that survive rapid double-toggles and network failures.
claims: Offset pagination over a mutating ranked list duplicates items when rows are inserted above the cursor and skips items when rows are deleted; cursor pagination keyed on a stable sort tuple such as (score, id) does neither.
A ranked feed is not append-only — the server may re-rank between page requests — so the client must dedupe by item id across pages rather than trusting page boundaries to be disjoint.
Feed items must be normalized into an entity cache keyed by id, so that liking a post in the feed and opening its detail view cannot produce two different like counts.
An optimistic reaction needs a per-entity pending-mutation counter rather than a boolean, or two rapid toggles resolve to the wrong final state when the responses arrive out of order.
'New posts available' is architecturally different from auto-prepending: prepending content above the viewport shifts the reading position unless the scroll offset is compensated in the same frame.
Every media element in a feed must reserve its box via width/height attributes or aspect-ratio before load, or layout shift is guaranteed; the CLS threshold is 0.1 at p75 per page load.

Impression and read-state events are high-volume and low-value individually, so they must be batched and flushed with navigator.sendBeacon or fetch with keepalive on visibilitychange, not sent per card.

Triggering the next page fetch when a sentinel enters the viewport is too late at fast scroll speeds; the IntersectionObserver rootMargin must be expressed as the distance the user scrolls during one round trip, not as a fixed pixel guess.

viz.title: Why Page 3 Shows You Page 2
viz.whatIsDrawn: A vertical server-side list on the left with items being inserted at the head and deleted at random positions over time. On the right, the client's assembled feed as pages arrive. Duplicated items are outlined and labelled 'seen twice' inline; skipped items are drawn as a gap with a labelled hole marker. A ghost column shows the same event stream under cursor pagination.
viz.predictPrompt: The feed re-ranks every 30 seconds. The user pages with ?offset=40&limit=20. Between fetching page 2 and page 3, two new posts are inserted at the top. How many items does the user see twice, how many do they never see — and does the answer change if the two posts were deleted instead of inserted?
viz.insight: Offset paging over a mutating list produces duplicates on insert and holes on delete — the direction of the bug depends on the mutation — while a cursor makes the page boundary a property of the data rather than of a count.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts: seeded event stream of inserts/deletes applied to a ranked list, with a pure pager(strategy) producing the client's assembled sequence. Unit test asserts duplicates === 0 and holes === 0 for the cursor strategy across all seeds and all insert/delete mixes, and asserts duplicates > 0 under insert-heavy offset paging.

drills.prompt: React logs 'Encountered two children with the same key' after the user scrolls to page 4 of a ranked feed. The keys are post ids and the API is correct. Explain the root cause and the fix.
drills.answerSketch: Offset paging over a re-ranked list returned the same post on two pages. Fix: cursor pagination on a stable sort tuple, plus an id-keyed dedupe when merging pages — the dedupe alone hides duplicates but still leaves holes on delete.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of an optimistic 'like' that is correct under two rapid toggles and a server failure on the first one.
drills.answerSketch: Increment pending counter for that post id -> apply optimistic delta to the normalized entity -> issue mutation with a client-generated id -> on response, decrement pending counter and reconcile the entity against the server's authoritative count -> if pending counter is still greater than zero, do not overwrite the optimistic value -> on failure with pending back to zero, revert to the last server value and surface a retry.

drills.prompt: New requirement: after a hard reload, the user must land exactly where they were, with the same items. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The scroll offset alone is meaningless without the items, so the loaded cursor set must be persisted; the ranked feed may have changed, so restoring by cursor may not reproduce the same list; and variable item heights mean the offset does not map to the same item. Realistic answer: persist the cursor of the topmost visible item and restore by item id, not by pixel offset.

drills.prompt: Users flick-scroll at up to 4,000 px/s. Your next-page request takes 350 ms at p75. What rootMargin do you set on the sentinel, and what does that cost you?
drills.answerSketch: About 1,400 px of lead, so rootMargin around '0px 0px 1500px 0px'. Cost: you prefetch a page for many users who stop scrolling, which is bandwidth and server load — worth stating as the trade-off, with a flip condition on data cost.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: normalize feed items into an entity cache, or keep them page-shaped as the server returned them. Justify with a flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the cross-view consistency problem; names the memory and complexity cost of normalization; names what happens to a like when the same post appears in two feeds; attaches a number (entity count, duplicate rate); flip condition such as 'stay page-shaped if no entity ever appears in two places and there are no mutations'.

drills.prompt: This feed sends a POST per card as it scrolls into view to record impressions. At 60 cards per session that is 60 requests. Name three separate problems and the standard fix.
drills.answerSketch: Connection contention with the page-fetch requests; battery and radio cost on mobile; and losing the tail of the batch when the tab closes. Fix: buffer impressions in memory and flush on a timer plus on visibilitychange using sendBeacon or keepalive fetch.

failureModes: Uses page numbers or offsets and does not notice that the list mutates underneath them.
Stores isLiked as a boolean and reverts to the wrong state on a rapid double-tap.
Auto-prepends new posts and destroys the user's reading position.
Fires an analytics POST per card impression.
Renders images with no reserved box and then blames CLS on 'the CDN'.
Keeps the feed page-shaped and cannot explain how a like stays consistent with the post's detail page.
interviewProbes: Someone posts while I'm on page 2. What do I see on page 3?
I double-tap the like button. Network is 800 ms. What's the final state, and how do you know?
This feed has been open for an hour on a phone. What's the memory doing?

cs-chat.title: Case: Chat
objectives: Choose a transport for a chat product and defend the read path and the write path separately.
Design reconnection so that no message is silently lost or duplicated across a disconnect.
Specify the send lifecycle so that a retried message can never be delivered twice.
claims: SSE is a server-to-client stream that reconnects automatically and resumes with the Last-Event-ID header; a WebSocket is duplex but you must implement reconnection, heartbeats and backfill yourself.

Sending over ordinary HTTP POST while receiving over SSE is a legitimate and often superior chat architecture, because the write path then gets status codes, retries, idempotency and HTTP caching semantics for free.
Message ordering must come from a server-assigned sequence number, never from a client timestamp, because client clocks skew by seconds and users will watch their own message jump position.
A client-generated idempotency key per composed message is what makes retry-after-timeout safe; without it a flaky network reliably produces duplicate messages.

After a reconnect the client must backfill from its last acknowledged sequence, not refetch the last N messages, or it will produce a silent hole in the middle of the conversation whenever more than N messages arrived while it was away.
An optimistic sent message needs three visible states — pending, acknowledged, failed — and the failed state must keep the text editable and retryable rather than dropping it.
With N tabs open the naive design opens N connections; electing one leader tab with the Web Locks API and fanning out over BroadcastChannel collapses it to one.
Unread counts must be derived from a server-held read cursor rather than a client-side counter, or they desynchronise the moment the user reads on a second device.

viz.title: The Silent Hole
viz.whatIsDrawn: A vertical message-sequence axis with server-assigned sequence numbers on the left. A connection bar runs alongside it and goes dark for a configurable interval. On reconnect, the client's resulting view is drawn to the right with missing sequences rendered as a labelled gap and repeated sequences as a labelled overlap, both annotated inside the message column. A ghost column shows the same disconnect handled by sequence-based backfill.
viz.predictPrompt: A mobile tab is backgrounded for four minutes and the socket dies with no close event. On resume the client refetches the last 50 messages. 63 messages arrived while it was away. What exactly does the user see — and would a heartbeat have prevented it?
viz.insight: Reconnect failures are silent: a heartbeat detects the dead socket but does not repair the gap, and only a sequence-anchored backfill can prove no message was lost.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {rate, seed, disconnectMs, strategy, heartbeat} with an injected clock and returns the client's observed sequence set. Unit test asserts observedSet === serverSet exactly for the backfill-from-lastSeq strategy across all seeds, and asserts a non-empty gap whenever messagesDuringOutage > N under refetch-last-N.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: WebSocket for both directions, or SSE for reads plus HTTP POST for writes? Justify with a flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: treats read and write paths separately; names what you lose by giving up HTTP semantics on the write path; names the reconnect story for each; attaches a number (client write rate, connection count, message size); flip condition such as 'flip to WebSocket once client writes exceed a few per second per user, once binary frames matter, or once per-message HTTP overhead dominates'.

drills.prompt: Order the send lifecycle for a message that times out, is retried, and turns out to have succeeded the first time.
drills.answerSketch: Generate client message id (idempotency key) -> render optimistically as pending -> POST with the key -> no response before timeout -> keep the message pending, do not remove it -> retry the POST with the SAME key -> server recognises the key and returns the original message with its assigned sequence -> reconcile the optimistic message with the server message by client id -> mark acknowledged.

drills.prompt: New requirement: messages composed while offline must send in order when connectivity returns. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: In-memory optimistic state dies on reload, so a durable outbox appears on the canvas; ordering now needs a client sequence within the outbox as well as the server sequence; idempotency keys become mandatory rather than nice; and the UI needs a fourth state, 'queued', distinct from pending.

drills.prompt: Complete the leader election so exactly one tab holds the connection: `navigator.locks.request('chat-socket', ______, async () => { openSocket(); await ______; });`
drills.answerSketch: `{ mode: 'exclusive' }` and a promise that never resolves while this tab is alive (e.g. `new Promise(() => {})`) — releasing the lock is what hands leadership to another tab on close.

drills.prompt: Messages sometimes appear out of order for one user and in order for everyone else. The server assigns sequence numbers correctly. What is the client doing wrong?
drills.answerSketch: Sorting or inserting by createdAt, which is a client timestamp on the optimistic message and a server timestamp on the acknowledged one; the user's own clock is skewed. Sort by server sequence, and place pending messages at the tail by convention rather than by time.

drills.prompt: Why must unread counts be derived from a server-held read cursor rather than decremented locally?
drills.answerSketch: Because reading on device B must clear the badge on device A, and a local counter has no way to learn about that read. The cursor makes 'unread' a derived value from a single source of truth.

failureModes: Says 'use WebSockets' without ever separating the read path from the write path.
Refetches the last N messages on reconnect and never notices the hole.
Sorts by client timestamp and cannot explain why one user's messages jump.
Opens one socket per tab and calls the resulting load 'a backend problem'.
Retries a failed send with no idempotency key and ships duplicate messages.
Tracks unread with a local counter that desyncs the moment a second device exists.
interviewProbes: I lock my phone for four minutes and come back. Walk me through every request and what I see.
I hit send, the spinner spins, I hit send again. How many messages exist?
I have this open in three tabs. How many connections do you have, and how do you know?

cs-dashboard.title: Case: Analytics Dashboard
objectives: Orchestrate a dozen independent queries under one shared time range without letting the slowest one gate the page.
Decide the client/server boundary for aggregation and downsampling from a pixel-count argument.
Make a hand-rolled SVG chart accessible without pretending an aria-label is sufficient.
claims: A dashboard is N independent queries sharing one time range, and the shared range belongs in the URL so that any dashboard state is linkable, restorable and shareable.
Per-widget loading and error states beat a single page-level spinner, because one slow or failing widget must not block the other eleven from painting.
Widgets should mount and query on viewport intersection; firing twenty queries on mount saturates the connection — six per origin on HTTP/1.1, and bandwidth-bound rather than count-bound on HTTP/2.
Downsampling belongs on the server once the series exceeds the chart's pixel width: rendering 50,000 points into an 800 px wide SVG creates 50,000 nodes for at most 800 distinguishable columns.
Hand-rolled SVG charts are viable because the drawing is trivial; the real work is the scale functions, the axis tick algorithm, and the accessible equivalent.
A chart is not accessible because it has an aria-label; it needs either a semantic table equivalent or a role=img with a description naming shape, extremes and trend.
Cross-filtering creates a dependency graph between queries, so without request deduplication and cancellation, changing a filter twice quickly leaves the older result rendering last.
Timezone is a correctness requirement rather than a formatting one: daily-active-users bucketed in UTC and displayed in local time will not sum to the headline figure.

viz.title: Batching Wins the Wrong Race
viz.whatIsDrawn: Twelve widget rows, each with a request bar from issue to response under seeded latency. A vertical marker labelled 'first useful widget' and a second labelled 'all widgets complete' sit inside the waterfall. A ghost set of bars behind shows the currently unselected strategy for direct comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Twelve widgets, each a 300 ms server query, over HTTP/2. You batch all twelve into one request that the server answers in 700 ms. Does time-to-first-painted-widget improve or get worse?
viz.insight: Batching optimises total completion time and pessimises first-paint time; dashboards are judged on the latter, so the right answer is usually to batch only the queries that are already fast and let slow ones stream independently.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {widgetCount, latencyDist, seed, strategy, connectionLimit} and returns per-widget {issuedAt, paintedAt} plus the two markers. Unit test asserts firstPaint(batch) > firstPaint(eager) for every seed where at least one query is faster than the batch, and asserts allComplete(batch) < allComplete(eager) under a constrained connection limit.

drills.prompt: A user selects a 2-year range on a metric sampled every minute. The chart is 900 px wide on a 2x display. How many raw points exist, how many can be distinguished, and where do you downsample?
drills.answerSketch: About 1,051,200 raw points; at most about 1,800 device pixels of horizontal resolution. Downsample server-side to roughly 1,800 buckets (or use a shape-preserving algorithm like LTTB), because transferring a million points to discard 99.8% of them is the actual cost.

drills.prompt: New requirement: clicking a bar in one widget filters all other widgets. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Every widget's query key gains a dimension, so the cache must be keyed on it; rapid clicks create the out-of-order response race, so cancellation and a current-filter comparison become mandatory; and the filter must join the time range in the URL or the filtered view is not shareable.

drills.prompt: This SVG line chart has role='img' and aria-label='Revenue over time'. A screen reader user says they cannot use the dashboard. Name three specific things missing.
drills.answerSketch: No values are exposed — no table equivalent and no described extremes or trend; the interactive tooltip is pointer-only with no keyboard path along the data points; and no live region announces that the chart updated after the time range changed.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: one batched request for all widgets, or one request per widget? Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: distinguishes first-paint from completion; names the connection/bandwidth constraint; names error isolation (one batch fails together); names cancellation granularity; flip condition such as 'batch once per-request overhead exceeds the per-query work — many tiny queries — and never batch a slow query with fast ones'.

drills.prompt: The interviewer says 'it should load fast'. Write the three NFRs for a dashboard that make that checkable, and say which one you would optimise first.
drills.answerSketch: Time to first painted widget under ~1 s at p75; LCP at or under 2.5 s at p75; INP at or under 200 ms at p75 while changing the range. Optimise first-painted-widget first, because it is the one users perceive and the one batching quietly ruins.

drills.prompt: Why does bucketing DAU in UTC while displaying local dates produce a number that does not match the headline?
drills.answerSketch: A user's local day boundary is offset from the UTC bucket boundary, so events near midnight land in a neighbouring bucket; summing local-labelled UTC buckets double-counts or drops the edges. The bucket timezone must be part of the query, not part of the formatting.

failureModes: Wraps the whole dashboard in one Suspense boundary so the slowest widget gates all twelve.
Sends a million points to the browser and then optimises the chart's render loop.
Keeps the time range in component state, so the dashboard cannot be linked or restored.
Adds aria-label to an SVG and declares the chart accessible.
Batches everything because batching sounds like an optimisation, and regresses first paint.
Cannot say where aggregation happens or why.
interviewProbes: One widget's query takes eight seconds. What do the other eleven do?
I change the range from 7 days to 2 years. Talk me through every byte that moves.
I'm using a screen reader. Get me the revenue number for last Tuesday.

cs-uploader.title: Case: Resumable File Uploader
objectives: Design an upload that survives network loss, tab backgrounding and a browser restart, and say precisely which of those three you cannot fully solve.
Derive a chunk size from a failure-rate argument rather than from a round number.
Report progress from acknowledged bytes and explain why the naive source is wrong.
claims: Resumability requires the server to expose the current byte offset for an upload resource, so the client asks 'where were we?' and appends, rather than starting over.

The IETF draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload work — the successor to tus — models this as a temporary upload resource with an Upload-Offset header and a boolean Upload-Complete; it is an Internet-Draft, not a shipped browser API, so the client is code you write.

fetch() exposes no upload progress events; XMLHttpRequest.upload.onprogress still does, and streaming request bodies via duplex:'half' are not universally available, which makes uploads the one remaining place where XHR is the correct choice in 2026.
Chunk size trades per-request overhead against how much work is lost on a failure: on a lossy mobile link chunks of roughly 1-5 MB win, and on a stable connection larger chunks win.
Progress must be computed from bytes the server has acknowledged, not from bytes handed to the socket, or the bar reaches 100% and then hangs while the last buffered megabytes are still in flight.
Hashing a file to detect a resumed-but-changed file must be chunked and run in a worker, because hashing a 2 GB file on the main thread freezes the tab for tens of seconds.

File and Blob handles do not survive a page reload, so resuming after a reload requires re-prompting for the file — or holding a FileSystemFileHandle from the File System Access API, which Safari does not support.

Parallel chunk uploads raise throughput but make progress non-monotonic and complicate the resume offset, so a single ordered stream is the correct default and parallelism is an optimisation you must defend.

viz.title: When Restart Never Finishes
viz.whatIsDrawn: The file drawn as a horizontal byte bar segmented into chunks, filling left to right. Below it a network lane with seeded outage blocks. On failure, the restart strategy resets the bar to zero with an inline 'lost' label showing the wasted bytes; the chunk strategy resets only the current segment. Cumulative wasted bytes and elapsed time are printed inside the bar's right edge. A ghost bar shows the alternative strategy running on the same seed.
viz.predictPrompt: A 500 MB upload at 10 MB/s over a link that drops for 5 seconds roughly once a minute. Compare whole-file restart against 5 MB chunks. Does the whole-file upload ever finish?
controls: strategy: restart / sequential chunks / parallel chunks
