viz.insight: Once mean-time-between-failures is shorter than the transfer time, restart-on-failure has unbounded expected completion time; chunking is what makes the expectation finite, and chunk size only tunes the constant.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {fileBytes, bandwidth, mtbf, outageMs, chunkBytes, strategy, seed} with an injected clock and a seeded RNG, returning {completedAt|never, wastedBytes, attempts}. Unit test asserts that for mtbf < fileBytes/bandwidth the restart strategy fails to complete within a 100x horizon for a majority of seeds, while sequential chunks complete for all seeds.

drills.prompt: 1 GB file, 8 MB/s, outages of 4 s occurring on average every 90 s. Estimate total time for 8 MB chunks and explain in one sentence why the whole-file strategy has no useful estimate.
drills.answerSketch: Transfer time is about 128 s of pure throughput; roughly 1-2 outages are expected, each costing ~4 s plus at most one chunk (~1 s) of rework, so on the order of 135-145 s. Whole-file has no useful estimate because expected completion is a geometric process over 'did we finish before the next drop', and with 128 s > 90 s the probability of success per attempt is low.

drills.prompt: The progress bar reaches 100% and then sits there for eight seconds before the success callback fires. The code uses xhr.upload.onprogress and reports e.loaded / e.total. What is wrong?
drills.answerSketch: onprogress reports bytes handed to the OS socket buffer, not bytes the server has received and committed. Progress must come from the acknowledged offset returned by the server after each chunk; the last chunk's socket buffer is what creates the dead time.

drills.prompt: Order the resume handshake after the user returns to a half-finished upload in the same tab.
drills.answerSketch: Look up the stored upload resource URL -> HEAD the upload resource to read the current offset -> verify the local file still matches (size plus a chunked hash of the first and last chunk) -> slice the file from that offset -> append the next chunk with Upload-Offset set to the server's reported value -> on each 2xx, persist the new offset before starting the next chunk.

drills.prompt: New requirement: uploads must survive the user closing and reopening the browser. What breaks first, and what is the honest limit?
drills.answerSketch: The File handle is gone, so the bytes are unreachable even though the server-side offset survives. Honest limit: you can persist the upload resource URL and offset in IndexedDB and resume once the user re-selects the same file; only File System Access API handles (no Safari) let you re-acquire the file without a prompt.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: sequential chunks or three parallel chunk streams? Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names throughput gain versus resume complexity; names non-monotonic progress as a UX cost; names how the server tracks a non-contiguous offset; attaches a number (measured link utilisation of a single stream); flip condition such as 'go parallel only when a single stream demonstrably fails to saturate the link — typically high-bandwidth high-latency paths'.

drills.prompt: Complete the chunk append: `await fetch(uploadUrl, { method: 'PATCH', headers: { 'Upload-Offset': String(______), 'Upload-Complete': ______ }, body: file.slice(offset, offset + chunkSize) })`
drills.answerSketch: `offset` (the server-reported offset, not a locally incremented counter) and `?0` / `?1` as a Structured Fields boolean — false for every chunk except the last.

failureModes: Proposes 'retry the upload' with no offset concept and cannot explain why a 2 GB upload on a train never completes.
Reports progress from onprogress bytes-sent and ships a bar that hangs at 100%.
Hashes the whole file on the main thread to detect changes and freezes the tab.
Claims the upload will resume after a page reload without addressing that the File handle is gone.
Picks 5 MB because it is a round number, with no failure-rate argument.
Goes parallel first and then cannot describe how the server reconciles a non-contiguous offset.
interviewProbes: I'm on a train. Walk me through what happens in the next ten minutes.
My progress bar says 100%. Is my file uploaded?
I close the tab and come back. What do you have, and what do you need from me?

cs-ai-assistant.title: Case: AI Chat Assistant
objectives: Design token streaming from the transport up to the render, and locate the cost that kills long transcripts.
Specify abort semantics that stop server-side generation, not just client-side reading.
Model tool calls as a state machine that a failed tool cannot be mistaken for an answer.
claims: Token streaming rides SSE (Content-Type: text/event-stream) because it is one-way with built-in reconnect semantics, but the request that starts it is normally a POST, so EventSource — which is GET-only — is replaced by fetch plus a ReadableStream and a manual SSE frame parser.

Modern streaming protocols such as the AI SDK data stream protocol frame content as typed start/delta/end parts with per-block ids over SSE, so the client is reassembling identified blocks rather than concatenating one undifferentiated string.

Rendering streamed markdown requires either an incremental-safe parser or a 'close the open fences' pass, because naively re-parsing the partial buffer on every token makes code blocks and lists flicker open and shut.
Re-rendering the whole transcript on every token is O(tokens x transcript) work; isolating the streaming message so only its own subtree re-renders is what makes long conversations viable.
Streaming improves perceived latency without changing completion time, so the metric that matters is time-to-first-token, with a visible cursor or skeleton inside roughly 400 ms.

Abort must cancel the server's generation, not merely stop reading the stream, or the user keeps paying for tokens they cancelled — an AbortSignal on the fetch plus a server that observes request cancellation.

Tool calls need their own state machine — proposed, running, result, error — kept visually distinct from assistant text, because a failed tool call rendered as prose reads as a confident wrong answer.

Auto-scroll must be sticky-only-if-at-bottom, or the user can never read back during generation; and the growing streaming message should sit outside the virtualized window as a live tail, because its height changes every frame.

viz.title: Render Scope, Not Render Frequency
viz.whatIsDrawn: A token arrival lane along the top with tokens landing at a configurable rate. Beneath it, a per-frame main-thread work bar whose height is the size of the rendered subtree that frame, with the 200 ms INP ceiling drawn as a horizontal rule labelled inline. A ghost work bar shows the isolated-tail strategy on the same token stream. Transcript length is shown as a slider-driven count printed inside the work lane.
viz.predictPrompt: A 1,200-token answer streams at 40 tokens/second into a transcript that already holds 60 messages. With a naive re-render of the whole transcript per token, what happens to INP by the end — and is batching renders to 60 fps enough to fix it?
controls: strategy: per-token full re-render / frame-batched full re-render / isolated tail
viz.insight: Frame batching bounds how often you render but not how much you render; when each render is O(transcript), only narrowing the render scope to the streaming message brings the per-frame cost under the INP ceiling.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {tokensPerSec, transcriptNodes, strategy, seed} with an injected clock and returns per-frame work units and a computed INP proxy. Unit test asserts that frame-batching leaves peak per-frame work unchanged relative to per-token rendering at equal transcript size, and that the isolated-tail strategy makes peak per-frame work independent of transcript length — that independence IS the claim.

drills.prompt: The assistant's code blocks flash between rendered and unrendered while a response streams. The markdown library is correct and the tokens are correct. Explain the cause and two fixes.
drills.answerSketch: The partial buffer contains an unterminated ``` fence, so the parser alternates between treating the tail as code and as prose as each token arrives. Fixes: append a synthetic closing fence before parsing the in-flight buffer, or use an incremental parser that keeps block state across chunks.

drills.prompt: New requirement: the transcript must be searchable with jump-to-match while a response is still streaming. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The virtualized window means most matches are not in the DOM, so search must run against the message model rather than the DOM; jumping to a match must scroll a windowed list to an item whose height may be unmeasured; and the sticky-scroll rule must be suspended while the user is at a match, or generation drags them back to the bottom.

drills.prompt: Order what must happen when the user clicks Stop mid-generation.
drills.answerSketch: Call abort() on the AbortController -> the fetch rejects and the reader is released -> the server observes request cancellation and stops generation -> the partial assistant message is kept and marked 'stopped' rather than discarded -> the pending tool call, if any, transitions to cancelled rather than error -> the composer is re-enabled and the partial text remains part of the transcript for the next turn's context.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: SSE-over-fetch, WebSocket, or chunked polling for token delivery? Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names that the stream is one-way; names reconnect/resume semantics; names proxy and infrastructure behaviour with long-lived responses; names the write path separately; flip condition such as 'flip to WebSocket once the client must send during generation — live interruption, voice, or collaborative sessions'.

drills.prompt: Complete the sticky-scroll predicate: `const atBottom = el.scrollHeight - el.scrollTop - el.clientHeight < ______; if (atBottom) el.scrollTop = el.scrollHeight;`
drills.answerSketch: A small threshold in pixels (commonly 32-64) — an exact equality check fails because of subpixel layout and because the streaming message grows between the measurement and the write.

drills.prompt: Which metric should the NFR for this feature target, and why is the obvious alternative wrong?
drills.answerSketch: Time-to-first-token (target roughly 400 ms at p75), because streaming does not change total generation time and users judge the wait by when something appears. Targeting total response time optimises something the model, not the frontend, controls.

failureModes: Uses EventSource and then discovers the endpoint needs a POST body.
Concatenates deltas into one string and re-parses the whole markdown buffer on every token.
Calls setState on the transcript root per token and blames React for the jank.
Stops reading the stream on Stop and leaves the server generating (and billing).
Renders a failed tool call as assistant prose, so the user reads an error as an answer.
Auto-scrolls unconditionally, making it impossible to read earlier output during generation.
Virtualizes the transcript including the streaming message, producing a scrollbar that thrashes every frame.
interviewProbes: It's token 900 of a long answer and the page is janky. Where is the time going?
I hit Stop. What is the server doing one second later?
I scroll up to read something while it's still writing. What happens?

cs-maps.title: Case: Maps UI (independent partner to Autocomplete)
objectives: Transfer the stale-response discipline from a one-dimensional text key to a two-dimensional viewport key.
Choose a marker rendering strategy from a node-count argument and defend the clustering stability requirement.
Ship a synchronized semantic list as a first-class equivalent to the canvas, not as a fallback.
claims: Map tiles form a quadtree pyramid with 4^z tiles at zoom level z, so the number of tiles a client requests is bounded by viewport area, never by world size.
Panning emits a continuous stream of viewport changes, which is the typeahead race with a two-dimensional key: responses must be discarded unless their viewport key still matches the current one.

Fifty thousand markers cannot be DOM nodes; the viable options are canvas or WebGL rendering, server-side clustering, or a viewport-and-zoom-bounded query, and the choice follows from how much interactivity each marker needs.

Clusters must be computed deterministically from position and zoom so that the same cluster does not appear and disappear as the user nudges the map, which is the single most common visual defect in map UIs.
Coupling typed query text with the current viewport means the cache key is the pair; omitting the viewport from the key returns results from the wrong city with no error.

A map canvas is entirely invisible to assistive technology, so a synchronized semantic list of visible results sharing the same selection state is the required equivalent — an aria-label on the canvas is not one.
Geolocation must be requested on a user gesture with a stated reason, and a watchPosition left running is a battery and privacy cost that no requirement asked for.

viz.title: The Same Race, With a 2D Key
viz.whatIsDrawn: A pan path drawn across a tile grid on the left, with each tile request as a bar on a timeline to the right, labelled with its (z, x, y) key. Tiles rendered at rest that belong to an abandoned viewport are hatched and labelled inline. A ghost timeline shows the same pan with viewport-key discarding enabled.
viz.predictPrompt: The user pans continuously for three seconds across four tile-grid widths, with 250 ms tile latency and a 200 ms debounce but no cancellation. How many tiles rendered at rest belong to a viewport the user has already left?
viz.insight: The typeahead race is not about text: any continuous input stream keyed by a value needs a response-versus-current-key comparison, and the only thing that changes is the shape of the key.
viz.buildNotes: Reuses the request-timeline-with-race sim with a tuple key instead of a string key; the sim module is shared with cs-autocomplete and parameterised by a key equality function. Unit test: staleRenders === 0 for all seeds when discardStale is on, for both key types.

drills.prompt: A 1200x800 viewport at zoom 14 with 256 px tiles, on a 2x display. How many tiles per frame at rest, and how many distinct tiles does a 3-second pan across four viewport widths touch?
drills.answerSketch: About ceil(2400/256) x ceil(1600/256) ≈ 10 x 7 = 70 tiles at rest; a four-width pan touches roughly 4-5 times that in the pan direction, so on the order of 250-350 distinct tiles — which is why cancellation and an LRU tile cache both matter.

drills.prompt: A user types 'Springfield' with the map over Illinois, then pans to Massachusetts and types it again. They get the Illinois results instantly with no loading state. What is wrong?
drills.answerSketch: The cache key is the query string only, so the viewport is not part of the key and a cache hit returns the wrong city's results. Key must be (query, viewportBounds-at-some-quantisation) — and quantising the bounds is what keeps the hit rate usable.

drills.prompt: New requirement: every marker must be individually clickable, hoverable and keyboard-focusable. Which rendering strategy survives, and what does it cost?
drills.answerSketch: Canvas/WebGL survives only with hit-testing plus a parallel semantic list for keyboard and screen reader access; DOM markers survive only under aggressive viewport-bounded querying and clustering. Cost is either a hand-built hit-test and focus model, or a hard cap on visible marker count.

drills.prompt: Build the canvas for a map with a search box, viewport-bounded results, clustering, and a synchronized accessible list. Label every edge with what flows and when.
drills.answerSketch: View (canvas) and view (semantic list) both read from one client store holding {viewport, query, selectedId, results}. A server-cache layer owns results keyed by (query, quantised bounds), fed by HTTP on debounced viewport-or-query change with discard-by-key. Tile fetches go direct to CDN. Forbidden: two sources of truth for selectedId; forbidden: the list deriving from DOM state of the canvas.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: cluster on the server or on the client? Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the marker count that forces the decision; names cluster stability across zoom; names the extra round trip on every zoom change if server-side; names the memory cost of holding all points if client-side; flip condition such as 'client-side while the full point set fits in memory and is bounded — say under ~50k — server-side above that'.

failureModes: Debounces the pan and considers the tile race handled.
Caches search results by query string only and serves the wrong city.
Renders markers as absolutely positioned divs and discovers the limit at about two thousand.
Adds an aria-label to the canvas and calls the map accessible.
Uses non-deterministic clustering, so markers flicker on every nudge.
Requests geolocation on page load.
interviewProbes: I pan fast across the city. What tiles are on screen when I stop, and are they the right ones?
There are 40,000 restaurants in view. What am I looking at?
I'm blind. How do I use this?

cs-notifications.title: Case: Notification Center (independent partner to Chat)
objectives: Derive an unread badge from a durable read cursor rather than a client counter.
Manufacture exactly-once delivery on the client from an at-least-once push channel.
Coordinate multiple tabs and a service-worker push channel so one event produces one toast.
claims: A notification centre is a push stream plus a durable read cursor, and the badge count must be derivable from that cursor so reading on one device clears it on every other.

Every push system delivers at least once, so the same event will arrive twice — once by push and once in the reconnect backfill — and deduplication by stable server id is where exactly-once is manufactured.
Grouping ('3 people liked your post') is a client-side collapse over a stable grouping key, and the collapse must be idempotent so that a redelivered event does not inflate the count.
With multiple tabs, exactly one should own the connection and the toast; a Web Locks-elected leader fanning out over BroadcastChannel prevents N toasts for one event.

Web Push (the Push API plus a service worker) is a separate channel with separate permission and lifecycle rules from in-app notifications, and the two channels must dedupe against each other by the same id.
Requesting notification permission on page load is the most reliable way to be permanently denied; the request must follow a user action that makes the value obvious.

A toast that steals focus breaks keyboard and screen reader users; announce through an aria-live=polite region and leave focus alone unless the notification is an interruption the user must act on now.
Notification ordering is a display concern, not a delivery concern: sort by the server's event time, and treat arrival order as meaningless.

viz.title: At-Least-Once, Times Two Tabs
viz.whatIsDrawn: A server event lane at the top with five events. Below it, two tab lanes, each with its own connection bar that drops and reconnects, and a toast column showing every toast raised, labelled with the event id. Duplicate toasts are outlined and counted inline. A ghost pair of lanes shows the same events under leader election plus id dedupe.
viz.predictPrompt: Two tabs are open. The connection drops for 30 seconds while five notifications are generated. On reconnect both tabs backfill. With no leader election and no id dedupe, how many toasts does the user see for those five events — and how many more if a service-worker push channel is also active?
viz.insight: Duplicate delivery multiplies across every independent receiver — tabs and channels alike — so dedupe must happen against a shared, durable seen-id set, not per connection.
viz.buildNotes: Reuses the reconnect-backfill-ladder sim with an added receiver dimension. Unit test asserts toastCount === eventCount for any tab count and any channel mix when both leader election and shared dedupe are on, and asserts toastCount === eventCount x receiverCount when both are off.

drills.prompt: Users report the bell badge showing 3 unread on desktop after they have read everything on mobile. The client decrements a counter on click. Explain and fix.
drills.answerSketch: The counter is client-local, so a read on device B is invisible to device A. Fix: the server holds a read cursor (last-read event id or timestamp); the badge is a derived count of events after the cursor; reading advances the cursor on the server and the change propagates on the push channel.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when a notification arrives while three tabs are open and one is hidden.
drills.answerSketch: Leader tab receives the event -> checks the shared seen-id set and inserts if new -> writes the notification into the durable store -> broadcasts over BroadcastChannel -> every tab updates its list and badge from the store -> only the visible, focused tab (or the leader, by policy) raises the toast -> the aria-live region announces politely without moving focus.

drills.prompt: New requirement: notifications must arrive when the app is closed. What appears on the canvas, and what new duplication problem do you inherit?
drills.answerSketch: A service worker plus Push API node, with its own subscription lifecycle and permission gate. Duplication: the same event now arrives via push and via the in-app stream when the app reopens, so the seen-id set must be shared between the service worker and the page — which means it lives in IndexedDB, not in memory.

drills.prompt: Why must the grouping collapse ('3 people liked your post') be idempotent, and what breaks if it is not?
drills.answerSketch: Because a redelivered event would be counted again, inflating the group to 4 with three real actors. Idempotent means the collapse is a fold over a set of unique event ids, not an increment on arrival.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: every tab holds its own SSE connection, or one leader tab fans out over BroadcastChannel. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the server connection cost per user; names the failure mode when the leader tab is closed or frozen; names the added complexity of lock-based election; attaches a number (average tabs per user); flip condition such as 'skip the leader when average tabs per user is near one, or when connection cost is negligible against the reliability cost of a frozen leader'.

failureModes: Decrements a local unread counter and cannot explain cross-device reads.
Opens one connection per tab and produces N toasts per event.
Requests notification permission on page load.
Deduplicates in memory, so a reload or a service worker delivery re-toasts everything.
Moves focus to the toast, trapping keyboard users.
Sorts by arrival order and shows notifications out of chronological sequence after a backfill.
interviewProbes: I read everything on my phone. What does my laptop's bell say?
I have four tabs open. How many times do I hear the ding?
The tab was closed when the event fired. Then I open it. What do I see?

cs-datagrid.title: Case: Data Grid at Scale (independent partner to Analytics Dashboard)
objectives: Window both axes and justify column virtualization from a node-count argument.
Handle variable row heights with a measured-offset index rather than a constant multiplier.
Make a virtualized grid navigable by screen reader by describing the full dataset, not the rendered window.
claims: A 100,000-row by 40-column grid is four million cells, so windowing must apply to both axes: column virtualization is what bounds the node count per row, and it is the node count that costs.
Frozen or pinned columns break naive windowing and must render in a separate layer whose vertical scroll is synchronized with the main body, not as duplicated rows inside it.

Variable row heights require a measured-offset index — a prefix sum or binary-searchable offset cache keyed by row id — because index multiplied by a constant row height is wrong the moment one row wraps.

role=grid with aria-rowcount and aria-colcount describing the FULL dataset, plus aria-rowindex on each rendered row, is what makes a virtualized grid navigable; without it the screen reader truthfully reports only the thirty rendered rows.
An ARIA grid has exactly one tab stop for the whole grid, with arrow keys moving a roving tabindex between cells; making every cell tabbable is the most common keyboard regression in data grids.
Sorting and filtering must move to the server once the dataset exceeds what you are willing to hold in memory, and that boundary should be stated as a number rather than as a feeling.
Sort, filter, column set and page belong in the URL, because a grid view that cannot be linked is a grid view that will be screenshotted instead.
Cell-level memoization matters more than row-level: editing one cell must not re-render its forty siblings, which is the difference between a 2 ms and a 40 ms keystroke.

viz.title: Rows Are Not the Problem
viz.whatIsDrawn: The full dataset drawn as a large rectangle with the rendered window as a bright inset. Live DOM node count and an estimated memory figure are printed inside the window itself. Toggling between row-only and two-axis windowing redraws the inset and the node count in place. A ghost inset shows the alternative strategy's window for direct comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: You virtualize rows only, rendering 30 of 100,000 rows, each with 40 columns. Scrolling vertically is smooth but horizontal scrolling still janks. How many DOM nodes are live, and why does row virtualization not help horizontal scroll?
controls: strategy: none / rows only / both axes
viz.insight: Row virtualization bounds how many rows exist; only column virtualization bounds how many nodes each row contains — and horizontal scroll pays that per-row cost on every frame.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is pure: given {rows, cols, windowRows, windowCols, nodesPerCell, frozenCols} it returns live node count, estimated bytes, and per-frame layout cost proxy. Unit test asserts node count is independent of total rows under both-axes windowing and linear in columns under row-only windowing.

drills.prompt: 100,000 rows, 40 columns, ~3 DOM nodes per cell. Compute live nodes for: no virtualization, row-only virtualization at 30 visible rows, and both-axis virtualization at 30 rows by 12 visible columns.
drills.answerSketch: No virtualization: ~12,000,000 nodes (impossible). Row-only: 30 x 40 x 3 = 3,600 nodes. Both axes: 30 x 12 x 3 = 1,080 nodes. The row-only number is survivable but it is 3.3x the work on every horizontal scroll frame, and it scales with column count without bound.

drills.prompt: A virtualized grid is announced by a screen reader as 'table, 30 rows, 40 columns' for a 100,000-row dataset, and pressing Tab walks through every visible cell one at a time. Name both defects and their fixes.
drills.answerSketch: aria-rowcount is missing (or set from the rendered window), so the full size is misreported — set aria-rowcount to the true total and aria-rowindex on each rendered row. And every cell is tabbable — an ARIA grid must have one tab stop with a roving tabindex driven by arrow keys.

drills.prompt: New requirement: rows can wrap to two or three lines depending on content. What breaks first in a grid built on a constant row height?
drills.answerSketch: Scroll offset to row index mapping breaks, so the window renders the wrong rows; the scrollbar length is wrong; and jumping to a row id becomes impossible. Fix: measure rows as they render, cache heights by row id, keep a prefix-sum offset index, and binary-search it for the scroll position — accepting that the scrollbar corrects as measurements land.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: client-side sort and filter, or server-side? Name the row count at which you flip.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names memory held on the client; names the latency of a round trip against the latency of an in-memory sort; names correctness under concurrent server-side mutation; attaches a number; flip condition such as 'client-side up to roughly 10,000-50,000 rows depending on row width, server-side above, and always server-side if the dataset mutates while the user is looking at it'.

drills.prompt: Complete the copy handler so a spreadsheet receives a real table: `e.clipboardData.setData('text/plain', tsv); e.clipboardData.setData('______', html);`
drills.answerSketch: `text/html` — spreadsheets read the HTML flavour to reconstruct cell boundaries and types; TSV alone loses types and any cell containing a tab or newline.

drills.prompt: Build the canvas for a grid over a 2-million-row server dataset with sort, filter, column pinning and CSV export. Label every edge.
drills.answerSketch: View reads a windowed slice from a server-cache layer keyed by (sort, filter, cursor). Client store owns view state: selection, pinned columns, roving focus cell — mirrored to the URL. HTTP transport fetches slices on scroll-window change with cancellation. Export is a separate streamed request that must not go through the cache layer. Forbidden: the view holding the full dataset; forbidden: two sources of truth for sort.

failureModes: Virtualizes rows, declares victory, and cannot explain why horizontal scroll janks.
Uses index times rowHeight and ships a grid that renders the wrong rows once anything wraps.
Makes every cell tabbable.
Sets aria-rowcount from the rendered window, so the grid claims to have 30 rows.
Keeps sort and filter in component state, so no view is shareable.
Cannot name the row count at which sorting moves to the server.
interviewProbes: Scroll me to row 74,000. What happens between the scroll event and the paint?
One row has a long comment that wraps to three lines. What breaks?
I'm on a screen reader. How many rows does this grid have?

cs-video.title: Case: Video Streaming Page (independent partner to Resumable Uploader)
objectives: Explain adaptive bitrate as a control loop over throughput and buffer level, and say which input dominates.
Branch a player correctly across MSE and Managed Media Source without pretending one API covers everything.
Build custom playback controls that a keyboard and screen reader user can actually operate.
claims: Adaptive bitrate streaming splits the video into short segments encoded at several bitrates, described by a manifest (HLS m3u8 or DASH mpd), and the client — not the server — chooses each next segment's quality.

Media Source Extensions is how JavaScript feeds those segments into a video element; Safari on iPhone exposes Managed Media Source instead (from iOS 17.1), which hands buffering and network decisions back to the browser, so the same player must branch on which API exists.
MediaSource is not Baseline, and iOS specifically required Managed Media Source before browser-based ABR was possible on iPhone at all — which is why 'just use MSE' is an incomplete answer.
The ABR decision is a control loop over measured throughput and current buffer level; optimising on throughput alone makes quality oscillate, and buffer-level rules are what damp it.

Startup latency is dominated by manifest fetch plus the first segment, so starting at a low bitrate and stepping up trades initial quality for time-to-first-frame — a decision that should be stated, not defaulted.

Autoplay is only permitted muted (or with sufficient media engagement), and video.play() returns a promise that rejects when it is blocked; ignoring that rejection is the standard cause of a silently dead play button.

Captions require a track element with kind=captions, and custom div-based control bars are the most common accessibility regression on video pages because they have no roles, no keyboard handling and no state announcement.

Preloading the next item's manifest costs almost nothing and preloading its first segment costs real bytes, so the second must be justified by a measured continue-watching rate rather than by symmetry with the first.

viz.title: Buffer Is a Low-Pass Filter
viz.whatIsDrawn: A bandwidth trace across the top with a configurable dip. Below it, the buffer level as a filled area with the target buffer drawn as an inline rule. Below that, the selected bitrate as a step function, with each switch marked and counted inline. A ghost step function shows the throughput-only rule against the same bandwidth trace.
viz.predictPrompt: Bandwidth drops from 6 Mbps to 1.2 Mbps for eight seconds, then recovers. With a 12-second buffer and a throughput-only ABR rule, how many quality switches occur — and does a LARGER buffer increase or decrease the number of switches?
controls: bandwidth trace with a configurable dip (seeded)
viz.insight: Buffer is not just rebuffer insurance — it is the low-pass filter on the quality-selection loop, so a larger buffer reduces switching by letting the player ignore transient dips entirely.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts takes {bandwidthTrace, seed, bufferTarget, rule, segmentSec, ladder} with an injected clock and returns per-segment {chosenBitrate, bufferLevel, rebuffered}. Unit test asserts switchCount decreases monotonically with bufferTarget for the buffer-based rule on a fixed dip trace, and asserts the throughput-only rule rebuffers on at least one seed where the buffer-based rule does not.

drills.prompt: 4-second segments, a ladder of 400k/1.2M/3M/6M bps, a 12-second buffer target, and a 4-second startup budget. How many segments must land before playback starts, and which ladder rung do you start on?
drills.answerSketch: One segment is enough to start (4 s of media), but you need manifest plus init segment plus segment 1 inside the 4 s budget. Start at 400k or 1.2M — the lowest rung whose segment reliably fetches in under about 1.5 s at the measured throughput — and step up once two consecutive segments arrive faster than real time.

drills.prompt: A custom control bar built from divs: play/pause, a seek bar, a volume slider, and a fullscreen button. List every accessibility defect and the minimum fix for each.
drills.answerSketch: No roles or names on the buttons (use button elements with accessible names); the seek bar has no role=slider with aria-valuenow/valuemin/valuemax and no keyboard handling; state changes (play/pause, buffering) are never announced; focus is invisible; and there is no captions control or track element. Minimum fix is real buttons, a real slider role with arrow-key handling, and a polite live region for state.

drills.prompt: New requirement: the page must also work on iPhone. What changes in your player?
drills.answerSketch: MediaSource may not exist; branch on ManagedMediaSource. Under MMS the browser controls buffering, so your buffer-based ABR rule loses authority and you must respect the browser's streaming signals rather than fighting them; and native HLS via a plain source URL becomes a legitimate fallback path with a different control surface.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: start playback at the lowest bitrate, or probe bandwidth first and start at the estimated rung. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names time-to-first-frame as the metric; names the perceived-quality cost of a visibly low first few seconds; names how long a probe costs; attaches a number; flip condition such as 'probe when a prior session's throughput estimate is cached and recent, start low when it is a cold session on an unknown network'.

drills.prompt: Complete the autoplay guard: `try { await video.play(); } catch (err) { if (err.name === '______') { showUnmutedPlayButton(); } }`
drills.answerSketch: `NotAllowedError` — the rejection when autoplay policy blocks playback; treating it as a generic failure is why the button appears to do nothing.

drills.prompt: Why does a throughput-only ABR rule oscillate on a link with variable latency even when average bandwidth is stable?
drills.answerSketch: Because per-segment throughput estimates are noisy at short segment durations, so the rule chases noise: it steps up on a fast segment and down on a slow one. Buffer level is a smoothed integral of the same signal, which is why mixing it in damps the loop.

failureModes: Says 'use HLS' and cannot describe who decides the bitrate.
Assumes MSE exists everywhere and ships a player that is blank on iPhone.
Writes a throughput-only ABR rule and then adds hysteresis constants until the oscillation stops, without knowing why.
Ignores the rejected play() promise, producing a play button that silently does nothing.
Builds div-based controls with no roles, no keyboard, no captions.
Preloads the next episode's first segment for every user to save 300 ms for the 12% who continue.
interviewProbes: My bandwidth halves for ten seconds. Walk me through every decision the player makes.
I'm on an iPhone. What code path am I on?
Turn on captions using only the keyboard. Narrate it.

cs-collab-editor.title: Case: Google-Docs-Style Collaborative Editor (independent partner to AI Chat Assistant)
objectives: Choose between OT and a CRDT from the topology of the system, not from which one is fashionable.
Explain why convergence does not imply intent preservation and show the concrete failure.
Keep the local caret and the local undo stack correct while remote operations rewrite the document underneath them.
claims: Operational transformation requires a central server to transform operations into a canonical order; CRDTs converge without one, which is why CRDT libraries dominate new builds while OT survives inside centralized products that already have the server.

Yjs, Automerge and Loro are all production-grade and MIT-licensed in 2026, and they differ on the axes that matter to a frontend: document size and memory (Yjs and Loro are far leaner than pre-2.0 Automerge), built-in version history (Automerge's strength), and native movable-tree support (Loro's).

Convergence is not intent preservation: two replicas can agree exactly on the final document and still show a result neither user wanted, because concurrent insertions at the same position interleave character by character.

A remote operation must not move the local caret, so the caret has to be stored as a relative position or anchor that survives remote inserts, never as a numeric offset into a string that just changed.
Presence — cursors, selections, who is in the room — is ephemeral, high-frequency state and belongs on a separate awareness channel that is never persisted with the document.
Undo in a collaborative document must be scoped to the local user's own operations, or Ctrl+Z deletes a colleague's paragraph, which is the single most reported bug in naive collaborative editors.
A document loads as a snapshot plus a tail of updates, so without periodic snapshotting the update log grows without bound and cold load time degrades forever.

The real product benefit of a CRDT is that offline edits merge on reconnect with no conflict dialog; the real cost is document overhead from tombstones and metadata, which is why deleted content still occupies space.

viz.title: Converged, and Still Wrong
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two document lanes side by side, each showing its local text with the caret marked. An operation stream runs between them, steppable. After sync, both lanes show the identical converged text, with the interleaved characters highlighted inline and labelled 'both users typed this at the same position'. A ghost lane shows the result if the same two edits had been applied sequentially.
viz.predictPrompt: Two users, temporarily offline from each other, both type a five-word sentence at exactly the same position. When they sync, both documents converge to the same text. Do either of them end up with a readable document?
controls: step operations one at a time
choose concurrent edit positions (same / adjacent / distant)
viz.insight: CRDTs guarantee that everyone sees the same thing, not that the thing is what anyone meant — interleaving at a shared position is a convergence success and a product failure at the same time.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts implements a minimal, well-documented list CRDT purely for teaching, with an injected id generator instead of random ids so runs are reproducible. Unit tests assert convergence (both replicas equal for every interleaving of the op stream) AND assert the specific interleaved output for the same-position case — the second test is the pedagogical claim and must not be 'fixed'.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 5 minutes then locked: OT with a central server, or a CRDT. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the topology requirement (does a central authority exist and is it acceptable?); names document size and memory overhead from tombstones; names offline merge behaviour; names ecosystem and binding availability for your editor; flip condition such as 'CRDT when peers must merge without a server or offline editing is a product requirement; OT when a central server already exists, document size is tightly constrained, and you need exact server-side authority over content'.

drills.prompt: A user reports that their cursor 'jumps backwards' when a colleague types earlier in the document. The document content is correct. What is the bug?
drills.answerSketch: The caret is stored as a numeric offset. A remote insert before that offset shifts the text but not the stored number, so the rendered caret lands earlier in the content. Fix: store the caret as a relative position anchored to a character identity, and map it to a DOM range at render time.

drills.prompt: New requirement: a user must be able to work offline for a week and then merge. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: The awareness channel is meaningless offline, so presence must degrade rather than error; the local update log grows, so it needs its own durable store and a compaction strategy; and undo scoping gets harder because a week of local operations must remain undoable after a merge that reordered the world around them. Snapshot-plus-tail loading becomes mandatory rather than an optimisation.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when a collaborative document is opened cold.
drills.answerSketch: Fetch the latest snapshot -> hydrate the CRDT document from it -> render the editor from the document model -> connect the awareness channel and publish local presence -> subscribe to the update stream from the snapshot's version vector -> apply the tail of updates -> map the restored caret anchor to a DOM range -> enable input.

drills.prompt: Why must undo be scoped to the local user's operations, and what is the correct behaviour when a local operation's target has since been deleted by someone else?
drills.answerSketch: Global undo would revert other people's work, which no user expects from Ctrl+Z. When the target is gone, the undo becomes a no-op (or restores only the surviving portion) rather than resurrecting deleted content, because resurrecting it would itself be an unrequested edit.

drills.prompt: A document has had 400,000 operations applied over two years. Without snapshotting, estimate the cold-load cost and say what snapshot interval you would choose.
drills.answerSketch: Cold load is O(operations) to apply the log — hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of CPU plus the full log transfer, growing forever. Snapshot on a size or op-count threshold (e.g. every 10,000 ops or 1 MB of updates) so cold load is bounded at snapshot plus tail; keep the log for history if history is a product feature.

failureModes: Says 'use a CRDT, they handle conflicts' and cannot describe a case where the merged result is wrong.
Stores the caret as an integer offset and ships jumping cursors.
Persists presence with the document, so the document accumulates cursor positions forever.
Implements global undo and lets one user erase another's paragraph.
Never snapshots, so cold load degrades linearly forever.
Cannot say what a tombstone is or why a document with all its text deleted is not small.
interviewProbes: We both type at the same spot at the same time. What do we each see afterwards?
My colleague types at the top of the document. Where is my cursor?
I hit Ctrl+Z. What exactly gets undone, and what if that text is gone?

cs-rte.title: Case: Rich Text Editor
objectives: Design an editor around its own document model and treat contenteditable as an input and render surface only.
Intercept input at beforeinput and map inputType to model operations.
Sanitize paste against a schema allowlist and preserve IME composition.
claims: document.execCommand is deprecated and produces browser-divergent HTML, so a modern editor keeps its own document model and never asks the browser to mutate content on its behalf.

The beforeinput event carries an inputType — insertText, deleteContentBackward, formatBold, insertFromPaste — that names the user's intent before the DOM changes, which is the correct interception point for a model-driven editor.

Selection must be modelled in the editor's own coordinates and mapped to a DOM Range at render time; reading the DOM selection as the source of truth breaks as soon as a render reorders or replaces nodes.
Undo must be a model-level stack with adjacent typing coalesced into single entries, because once you intercept beforeinput the browser's native undo no longer matches what happened.
Pasted HTML must be mapped into the schema through an allowlist, never a denylist, because paste is the primary XSS vector in an editor and denylists are open-ended.

Composition must be allowed to complete: intercepting or re-rendering between compositionstart and compositionend destroys CJK input, so the model applies the composed result at compositionend rather than per keystroke.
A toolbar button must call preventDefault on mousedown, or the editable region loses focus and the selection collapses before the command runs.

The document model should be a tree with a declared schema (which nodes may contain which), because a schema is what makes paste normalisation, undo and collaborative merging all definable instead of ad hoc.

viz.title: The DOM Is an Output
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two synchronized panes: the editor's model tree on the left and the resulting DOM on the right, with the caret marked in both. An input event stream at the bottom is stepped one event at a time, and each step highlights the model node changed and the DOM node re-rendered, connected by a leader line drawn between the panes. A ghost DOM pane shows what a DOM-as-truth editor produces from the same events, diverging visibly after the third step.
viz.predictPrompt: The user selects a word and clicks the Bold toolbar button, implemented with a plain onClick handler. By the time the handler runs, what has already happened to the selection — and would the same bug appear if the button were a div?
controls: inject a paste event with hostile HTML
viz.insight: The DOM is an output of the editor, never its state — every editor bug that is hard to reproduce comes from somewhere in the code treating it as input.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds a small schema-validated document model plus a reducer over beforeinput-shaped events; no DOM in the sim. Unit tests assert that applying the same event sequence always yields the same model, that paste normalisation drops every non-allowlisted node, and that composition events produce exactly one model operation.

drills.prompt: A toolbar Bold button uses onClick and calls document.execCommand('bold'). Two separate bugs are present. Name both and give the minimum fix for each.
drills.answerSketch: First: mousedown moves focus out of the editable region and collapses the selection before click fires — fix with preventDefault on mousedown. Second: execCommand is deprecated and emits browser-divergent markup outside your schema — fix by dispatching a model operation and re-rendering.

drills.prompt: Order the handling of a paste of external HTML into a schema-driven editor.
drills.answerSketch: beforeinput fires with inputType 'insertFromPaste' -> preventDefault -> read text/html from the clipboard -> parse in an inert document (DOMParser or a detached template) -> walk the tree against the schema allowlist, dropping or unwrapping disallowed nodes and stripping all event handler and style attributes not on the allowlist -> convert the surviving tree into model nodes -> apply as one undoable model operation -> re-render and restore the mapped selection.

drills.prompt: Complete the composition guard: `editor.addEventListener('beforeinput', e => { if (______) return; applyOperation(fromInputType(e)); });`
drills.answerSketch: `e.isComposing` — intermediate composition events must reach the browser untouched, with the model updated once at compositionend.

drills.prompt: New requirement: the editor must support inline comments anchored to a text range that survive editing around them. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Character-offset anchors break on every edit before the range, so anchors must become model positions tied to node identity; undo must restore anchors as well as text; and the schema needs a mark type that can span partial text nodes, which changes normalisation. This is also the point at which the model becomes shareable with a CRDT.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: build on contenteditable with your own model, or render the text yourself onto a non-editable surface with a synthetic caret. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names IME and mobile keyboard support as the decisive reason contenteditable usually wins; names accessibility (screen readers understand contenteditable); names the control you gain from a synthetic caret; attaches a number or scope; flip condition such as 'go synthetic only when the content is not natural language — a code editor or a formula field — where IME and dictation matter far less'.

drills.prompt: Why is a denylist the wrong approach to sanitizing pasted HTML, given that you can enumerate the dangerous elements?
drills.answerSketch: Because the attack surface is open-ended — new attributes, new elements, nested contexts, and encoding tricks all bypass an enumeration — while an allowlist fails closed: anything you did not explicitly permit simply does not survive the paste.

failureModes: Builds on execCommand and then patches per-browser markup differences forever.
Reads window.getSelection() as the source of truth and breaks on every re-render.
Intercepts input during IME composition and ships an editor unusable in Japanese, Chinese and Korean.
Sanitizes paste with a regex over an HTML string.
Relies on native undo after intercepting beforeinput, so Ctrl+Z does something unrelated to what the user did.
Cannot state a schema, so paste, undo and serialization each behave differently.
interviewProbes: I paste a table from Word. Walk me through what happens.
I'm typing in Japanese. What does your beforeinput handler do?
I hit Ctrl+Z after typing a sentence. How many operations does that undo, and why that many?

cs-spreadsheet.title: Case: Spreadsheet (independent partner to Rich Text Editor)
objectives: Model formulas as a dependency DAG and recompute only the transitive dependents.
Separate the data model from the rendered window so formulas can reference cells that are not on screen.
Keep recalculation off the main thread and define what the UI shows while it is stale.
claims: Formulas form a directed acyclic graph over cells, so an edit recomputes only the transitive dependents in topological order — recalculation cost is a property of the dependency graph, not of sheet size.
Circular references must be detected at edit time with cycle detection on the DAG and surfaced as a cell error, rather than discovered at evaluation time as a stack overflow.

A large recalculation on the main thread blocks input, so the evaluator must be a pure module that can run in a worker, with the UI showing last-known values marked stale rather than blocking or blanking.
The rendered grid is a window over a model that must be complete: formulas routinely reference cells far outside the viewport, so the data model cannot be derived from what is rendered.

Cell editing is a mode — the same arrow key means 'move' in navigation mode and 'move the text caret' in edit mode — and the ARIA grid pattern requires exactly one tab stop for the entire grid with a roving tabindex.
Copying a range must transform relative references and preserve absolute ones, which is a model operation over the formula AST, not a string copy.
Sparse storage keyed by cell address beats a dense two-dimensional array, because real sheets are overwhelmingly empty and a dense array pays for every empty cell.

Volatile functions (NOW, RAND) and whole-column references are the two constructs that turn a sparse recalculation into a full-sheet recalculation, which is why they must be modelled explicitly in the dependency graph.

viz.title: Recalc Follows the Graph, Not the Sheet
viz.whatIsDrawn: A grid with filled cells shown as nodes and formula dependencies as edges. Editing a cell marks it dirty and the dirty set propagates along edges step by step, with the count of recomputed cells printed inline next to the edited cell. A ghost overlay shows the full-sheet recompute for comparison, with its own count.
viz.predictPrompt: A sheet has 20,000 filled cells. You edit one cell that three other cells depend on, and those feed a SUM over a 10,000-cell range. How many cells must be recomputed — and is the answer closer to 4, to 10,004, or to 20,000?
controls: toggle a volatile function in the sheet
edit different cells in the graph
viz.insight: Sparse recalculation is the whole optimisation, and exactly two constructs — volatile functions and whole-column references — destroy it by making everything depend on everything.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts holds a sparse cell map, a dependency graph, topological ordering, and cycle detection, all pure. Unit tests assert the recomputed set equals the exact transitive closure for hand-authored graphs, that a cycle is detected at insertion time rather than at evaluation, and that adding one volatile cell makes the recomputed set equal the full filled set.

drills.prompt: A sheet has 20,000 filled cells. Edit A1, which feeds B1:B3, which feed a SUM in C1. Then add NOW() in D1. Give the recomputed cell count before and after adding D1, and explain the difference in one sentence.
drills.answerSketch: Before: 5 cells (A1 plus B1:B3 plus C1). After adding a volatile function, every recalculation must re-evaluate D1 and everything depending on it — and if anything aggregates broadly, the closure approaches the full 20,000. Volatile functions are unconditionally dirty on every recalc.

drills.prompt: A user types =B1 into A1 and =A1 into B1. The tab freezes and then the page crashes. What is missing, and where exactly does it belong?
drills.answerSketch: Cycle detection at edit time. The check belongs in the model operation that inserts or updates a formula's dependency edges — before the edge is committed — not in the evaluator, where it manifests as unbounded recursion.

drills.prompt: New requirement: sheets can reach 500,000 filled cells and recalculation must never drop a frame. What changes?
drills.answerSketch: The evaluator moves to a worker, which forces the model to be transferable or mirrored; the UI must render last-known values marked stale with a visible recalculating state; recalculation must be chunked and cancellable so a new edit supersedes an in-flight recalc; and the sparse store's addressing must be efficient to serialize.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when a user pastes a 3x3 range containing relative and absolute references into a new location.
drills.answerSketch: Read the clipboard payload (prefer the internal model flavour, fall back to text/html then TSV) -> parse each formula to an AST -> offset every relative reference by the paste delta, leave absolutes untouched -> validate the resulting dependency edges for cycles -> apply all nine cell writes as one undoable operation -> mark the dirty set -> recompute the transitive closure in topological order -> render.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: recalculate synchronously on the main thread, or asynchronously in a worker with stale values on screen. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names the dirty-set size at which main-thread recalc exceeds a frame budget; names the correctness risk of showing stale values; names cancellation of superseded recalcs; attaches a number (cells recomputed per frame budget); flip condition such as 'synchronous while the transitive closure is small enough to finish inside ~8 ms, worker above that, with a hard rule that a visible stale marker is mandatory in worker mode'.

drills.prompt: Why must the data model be independent of the rendered window, when a virtualized grid renders only 30 rows?
drills.answerSketch: Because a visible formula can reference any cell in the sheet, including cells that are far off screen and have never been rendered. A model derived from rendered rows would evaluate references to undefined cells — silently producing zeros instead of errors.

failureModes: Recomputes the whole sheet on every keystroke and then optimises the formula parser.
Detects cycles in the evaluator via a recursion depth limit rather than in the graph at edit time.
Derives the data model from the virtualized window, so off-screen references evaluate as empty.
Makes every cell a tab stop.
Uses a dense two-dimensional array and pays for a million empty cells.
Copies formulas as strings and breaks every relative reference.
interviewProbes: I edit one cell in a 20,000-cell sheet. What runs?
I put =A1 in B1 and =B1 in A1. What happens?
I scroll to row 9,000 and there's a formula referencing row 3. How does that work?

cs-infinite-scroll.title: Case: Infinite-Scroll Social Feed
objectives: Bound DOM nodes and memory in a list the user can scroll forever.
Restore scroll position on back-navigation in a way that survives variable item heights.
Distinguish what content-visibility gives you from what only windowing gives you.
claims: Windowed rendering with variable item heights requires measured heights cached by item id; estimating and correcting is legitimate but makes the scrollbar jump as measurements land, which must be a stated trade rather than a surprise.
Removing items above the viewport shifts content unless the scroll offset is compensated in the same frame; browser scroll anchoring helps only when the removed node is not itself the anchor.

content-visibility: auto skips rendering work for offscreen elements but keeps every DOM node alive, so it lowers layout and paint cost without bounding memory and is not a substitute for windowing at ten thousand items.

Scroll restoration on back-navigation requires persisting both the scroll position and enough loaded pages to make that position meaningful; restoring an offset without the items lands the user at the top of a short list.
Infinite scroll makes the footer unreachable and hurts deep-linking and crawling, so an accessible escape hatch — a Load More control, or paginated URLs — is a requirement rather than a nicety.
A recycled DOM node that currently holds focus silently moves focus to body, stranding keyboard users mid-list; recycling must check for contained focus and restore it deliberately.

A feed left open for an hour must have a memory ceiling: unbounded page accumulation is the leak, and dropping far-offscreen pages while retaining their measured heights is what makes the ceiling possible without breaking the scrollbar.
Restoring by item id rather than by pixel offset is what survives a re-ranked feed, because the same pixel offset points at different content after a re-rank.

viz.title: Nodes vs Work
viz.whatIsDrawn: A tall list column with the rendered window marked as a bright band and the retained-but-offscreen region shaded. Live DOM node count, retained page count and an estimated memory figure are printed inside the column. A per-frame work bar runs alongside. Toggling strategies redraws both the node count and the work bar in place, with a ghost of the previous strategy retained for comparison.
viz.predictPrompt: Ten thousand feed items, roughly six DOM nodes each. You apply content-visibility: auto to every item and scrolling gets dramatically smoother. Which number does NOT change — and what symptom is still there after twenty minutes of scrolling?
controls: strategy: naive / content-visibility / windowed / windowed with page eviction
viz.insight: content-visibility bounds the work per frame; only windowing bounds the node count, and only eviction bounds memory — three different problems that look identical while you are scrolling.
viz.buildNotes: Reuses the two-axis-window sim collapsed to one axis, extended with a retention policy. Unit test asserts node count is constant under windowing regardless of items loaded, that content-visibility leaves node count linear in items, and that retained memory is bounded only when eviction is on.

drills.prompt: A feed drops far-offscreen pages to save memory. Users report that the scrollbar 'jumps' and the page scrolls itself when they scroll up fast. Name the cause and the fix.
drills.answerSketch: Removing items above the viewport reduces total scroll height, so the browser's scroll offset now points at different content. Fix: replace removed pages with a spacer of exactly their measured height (keeping the height cache), or adjust scrollTop by the removed height in the same frame before paint.

drills.prompt: New requirement: back-navigation from a post detail must return to the exact item, in a feed that may have re-ranked. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Pixel offsets become meaningless after a re-rank, so restoration must key on the item id of the previously topmost visible item; that item may no longer exist, so a fallback is needed; and enough pages must be re-fetched or retained for that item to be present at all, which forces a decision about whether restoration refetches or reuses a persisted cache.

drills.prompt: Ten thousand items, ~6 DOM nodes each, ~1.5 KB of per-node engine overhead. Compute retained nodes and rough memory under naive rendering, content-visibility, and a 60-item window.
drills.answerSketch: Naive and content-visibility: 60,000 nodes, on the order of 90 MB — identical, because content-visibility changes work, not node count. Windowed at 60 items: 360 nodes, well under 1 MB. The point is that two of the three numbers are the same.

drills.prompt: Order what must happen when a windowed list recycles the DOM node that currently contains focus.
drills.answerSketch: Detect that the node about to be recycled contains document.activeElement -> record the logical focus target (item id plus which control) -> perform the recycle -> after render, look for the equivalent control in the new position -> if it exists, restore focus to it; if the item is gone, move focus to a stable ancestor and announce the change politely -> never leave focus on body.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: infinite scroll, or a Load More button. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names discoverability of the footer and deep-linking or crawling; names the keyboard and screen-reader experience of a list with no end; names engagement as the actual reason infinite scroll exists; names the memory ceiling either way; flip condition such as 'infinite scroll when the content is a browsing surface with no destination below it, Load More whenever anything below the list must remain reachable'.

drills.prompt: Why does the browser's native scroll anchoring not save you when you evict pages above the viewport?
drills.answerSketch: Scroll anchoring picks an anchor node near the viewport and preserves its position when content above it changes — but if the eviction removes the region containing or preceding the anchor, or replaces it with content of different height, the anchor is lost or relocated and the compensation is wrong.

failureModes: Applies content-visibility, sees a smooth scroll, and declares the memory problem solved.
Restores scroll by pixel offset into a re-ranked feed and lands the user somewhere arbitrary.
Recycles nodes without checking for contained focus and strands keyboard users.
Never evicts pages, so an hour of scrolling exhausts memory on a mid-tier phone.
Uses a constant estimated item height and ships a scrollbar that lies.
Ships infinite scroll over a page that has a footer users need.
interviewProbes: I scroll for twenty minutes. What's the memory doing?
I tap a post, read it, and hit back. Where am I?
I'm navigating with a keyboard and the item I'm on gets recycled. Where's my focus?

cs-email.title: Case: Email Client (independent partner to Infinite-Scroll Feed)
objectives: Decide what is synced locally and what is fetched on demand, from a storage estimate.
Render untrusted email HTML without letting it reach into the host document.
Design a keyboard-first three-pane interface where single-key shortcuts never fire in the composer.
claims: A three-pane client is master-detail with independent scroll containers and independent data lifetimes, so selecting a message must not cause the list pane to refetch or lose its scroll position.
A mailbox is synced rather than paged: a durable local store holding message headers, with bodies fetched on demand, is what makes instant search and offline reading possible at all.

Search over a locally synced index is instant and works offline, while search that round-trips is a materially different product — so which one you are building must be settled as a requirement, not discovered later.
Storage scales on what you sync: headers are on the order of 1 KB each and bodies are tens of KB, so syncing bodies is a 40x storage decision, not a detail.

Untrusted email HTML must render inside a sandboxed iframe without allow-same-origin, with remote content blocked by default; sanitizing into the host document is insufficient because CSS and layout attacks survive sanitization.

Keyboard-first is a hard requirement for this product class, which means a roving tabindex over the message list and single-key shortcuts that are suppressed whenever focus is inside a text field or the composer.
Drafts must be persisted on an interval and on visibilitychange rather than only on blur, because tab closes and mobile app switches do not reliably fire anything else.
A bulk action over 200 messages must be one idempotent request with a single undo affordance, not 200 requests with 200 possible partial failures.

viz.title: Sync the Index, Fetch the Payload
viz.whatIsDrawn: A horizontal storage bar for the local store, split into header bytes and body bytes, with the current total printed inside the bar. A slider for mailbox size and a toggle for what is synced redraw it in place. Alongside, a search latency indicator shows local-index versus round-trip search on the same mailbox size. A ghost bar shows the headers-only strategy against the current one.
viz.predictPrompt: A mailbox has 80,000 messages averaging 40 KB of body and 1 KB of headers. You want instant offline search over all of them. How much must you store locally — and does storing bodies change the answer by roughly 40x?
controls: sync policy: headers only / headers plus recent bodies / everything
viz.insight: Search scales on headers and storage dies on bodies, so the sync boundary is the single decision that determines whether this product fits in a browser's quota at all.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure storage model over {messageCount, headerBytes, bodyBytes, policy, retentionDays} returning bytes and an estimated index size, plus a search-latency proxy. Unit test asserts headers-only storage stays under a typical origin quota for mailbox sizes up to 500k while full-body sync exceeds it well before that — the crossing point is the claim.

drills.prompt: 80,000 messages, 1 KB headers and 40 KB bodies. Compute local storage for headers-only, headers plus 90 days of bodies (assume 15% of messages), and everything. Say which policies are viable in a browser.
drills.answerSketch: Headers only: ~80 MB. Headers plus 90 days of bodies: ~80 MB + 12,000 x 40 KB ≈ 560 MB. Everything: ~3.2 GB. Only the first is comfortably viable; the second is borderline and requires quota monitoring and eviction; the third is not a browser product.

drills.prompt: An email body is rendered by sanitizing the HTML and injecting it into the app's DOM. Name three attacks or defects that survive sanitization.
drills.answerSketch: CSS from the email can restyle or overlay the host UI (position: fixed overlays, clickjacking the reply button); remote images act as tracking pixels and leak read status and IP; and layout from the email can break out of its container or blow up the page height. All three are contained by a sandboxed iframe without allow-same-origin plus blocked remote content.

drills.prompt: New requirement: full-text search must work offline across the whole mailbox, including bodies. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Storage — full bodies exceed quota. The resolution is to store an inverted index over body text rather than the bodies themselves (a fraction of the size), accept that search results show snippets fetched on demand, and add quota monitoring with an eviction policy for the body cache.

drills.prompt: Complete the shortcut guard so 'e' archives only outside text entry: `if (______) return; if (e.key === 'e') archive();`
drills.answerSketch: A check that the event target is not an input, textarea or contenteditable — e.g. `e.target.closest('input, textarea, [contenteditable]')` — because otherwise typing 'e' in the composer archives the thread.

drills.prompt: Order what happens when the user selects 200 messages and hits Archive.
drills.answerSketch: Generate one client operation id -> optimistically remove the 200 from the visible list and adjust counts -> issue ONE request carrying the id set and the operation id -> show a single undo affordance with a timeout -> on success, commit and drop the undo -> on failure, restore all 200 and surface one error -> on undo, send the inverse operation with its own id, not 200 individual restores.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: local synced search, or server search. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names storage and initial sync cost; names offline capability as a product decision; names index freshness for messages that arrive while offline; names result quality (server can rank better); flip condition such as 'local when offline use is a requirement and mailboxes are bounded, server when mailboxes are unbounded or ranking quality is the product'.

failureModes: Syncs full bodies and hits the storage quota at 20,000 messages.
Renders email HTML into the app document after 'sanitizing' it.
Loads remote images by default and ships read-tracking to every sender.
Binds single-key shortcuts globally, so typing in the composer archives threads.
Refetches the list pane every time the selected message changes.
Fires 200 requests for a bulk archive and has no coherent undo.
interviewProbes: I'm on a plane. What can I do and what can't I?
An email contains a full-page fixed-position div. What does my inbox look like?
I select two hundred messages and hit archive, then immediately hit undo. Walk me through it.

cs-pdp-checkout.title: Case: E-commerce PDP + Checkout
objectives: Apply two different rendering strategies within one application and justify each from its caching and privacy profile.
Make a payment submission safe to retry, and explain why a disabled button is not a solution.
Make a multi-step checkout resumable after a reload or a device switch.
claims: A product detail page is public, cacheable and SEO-critical while a checkout is private, uncacheable and write-heavy, so one application must apply two different rendering strategies rather than one compromise.
The LCP element on a PDP is almost always the hero image, so preloading it with fetchpriority=high and never lazy-loading it is the single highest-leverage performance change available.
Price and stock must come from a live source even when the page shell is statically cached, which means a cached shell with a small dynamic hole rather than an uncached page.
A payment submission must carry a client-generated idempotency key that is stable across retries of the same intent and different for a new intent, or a retry after a timeout double-charges.
A timeout is not a failure, it is an unknown outcome — the request may have committed — and only an idempotency key converts that unknown into a safe retry.

Disabling the Buy button prevents a second click in one tab and does nothing about a second tab, a back-navigation resubmit, or a client-side retry, so it is a UX affordance and never a correctness mechanism.
Checkout state held only in component state is lost on reload, so the flow must be resumable from a server-held cart or order-draft id with the current step reflected in the URL.

Client-side form validation is a latency optimisation and never a guarantee: price, stock and address validity must be re-checked server-side at submission because the client's copy can be stale or forged.
Payment SDKs are frequently larger than the entire application shell, so they must load only on the checkout route and be measured against an explicit byte budget.

viz.title: A Timeout Is Not a Failure
viz.whatIsDrawn: A vertical submit sequence: client, network, server, payment processor. An injected fault drops the response AFTER the server has committed. The user's retry is drawn as a second pass down the same ladder, with the resulting charge count printed inline at the processor node. A ghost ladder alongside shows the same fault with an idempotency key, where the second pass short-circuits at the server and the charge count stays at one.
viz.predictPrompt: The payment POST times out on the client after the server has already charged the card. The user clicks Buy again. With a disabled-button guard but no idempotency key, how many charges exist — and does the button guard change the answer at all?
controls: fault injection point: before commit / after commit / after response sent
toggle a second tab performing the same submit
viz.insight: Every guard on the client protects against one specific sequence of clicks; only a key that the server recognises protects against the failure the network actually produces.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts models {commitPoint, faultPoint, retryCount, idempotencyKey, tabs} and returns charge count and observed client state, with an injected clock. Unit test asserts charges === 1 for every fault point and every tab count when the key is present, and asserts charges > 1 for at least one fault point when it is absent regardless of client-side guards.

drills.prompt: Checkout works in testing. In production, roughly 0.3% of orders are duplicated, clustered on mobile networks. The Buy button is disabled on click and re-enabled on response. Explain the mechanism precisely.
drills.answerSketch: On a flaky mobile link the response is lost after the server committed. The client times out or the user backgrounds and returns, the button re-enables (or the page reloads), and the resubmission creates a second order. The disabled state never spanned the failure. Fix: an idempotency key generated when the intent is formed — not per click — that the server stores and matches.

drills.prompt: New requirement: a user must be able to start checkout on a phone and finish it on a laptop. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: All client-held checkout state — form values, selected shipping, applied promo — is device-local, so the draft must move server-side behind an order-draft id; the step must be in the URL or derivable from the draft; and the idempotency key must be bound to the draft rather than to a browser session, or the second device generates a new key for the same intent.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: server-render the PDP with a client-side island for price and stock, or client-render the whole page. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names SEO and LCP as the reason to server-render; names the freshness requirement on price and stock as the reason for the island; names cache hit rate on the shell; attaches a number (LCP target, cache TTL); flip condition such as 'client-render only when the page is behind auth and not indexed, where the caching and SEO arguments both disappear'.

drills.prompt: A payment SDK is 180 KB gzipped and your app shell budget is 120 KB gzipped. Where does the SDK load, and what is the observable consequence of getting this wrong?
drills.answerSketch: On the checkout route only, ideally deferred until the user reaches the payment step, and never in the shared shell. Getting it wrong means every PDP visitor — the overwhelming majority, who never check out — pays 180 KB, which shows up directly in LCP and INP on the highest-traffic page on the site.

drills.prompt: Order the steps of a correct payment submission including the failure path.
drills.answerSketch: Create the order draft server-side and receive its id -> generate an idempotency key bound to that draft and persist it locally -> validate client-side for latency -> POST with the key -> server re-validates price, stock and address authoritatively -> server checks the key: if seen, return the original result; if new, commit and store the key with the result -> client receives a terminal status and clears the key -> on timeout, retry the SAME key rather than generating a new one.

drills.prompt: For 'design our product page', sort into In Scope / Deferred / Out of Scope and mark the two with architectural blast radius: reviews, size selector, stock indicator, recommendations, AR try-on, wishlist, guest checkout, saved cards, promo codes, address autocomplete.
drills.answerSketch: Blast radius: 'stock indicator must be live' (forces a dynamic hole in an otherwise cacheable page) and 'guest checkout' (determines whether identity exists before the write path, changing draft ownership and idempotency scoping). The rest are features on an existing architecture.

failureModes: Uses one rendering strategy for the whole app and either loses SEO on the PDP or caches private checkout data.
Lazy-loads the hero image and reports a 4-second LCP as a CDN problem.
Prevents double-submission with a disabled button and ships duplicate orders.
Generates a fresh idempotency key on every click, which is the same as having none.
Loads the payment SDK in the shared shell.
Treats client-side validation as authoritative and lets a stale price through.
interviewProbes: My connection dies right after I hit Buy. What do I see, and how many times was I charged?
The price changed while I was on the page. What happens when I check out?
Your LCP is 4 seconds on mobile. Where is the time?

cs-kanban.title: Case: Kanban Board (independent partner to PDP + Checkout)
objectives: Encode ordering so that concurrent reorders converge instead of fighting.
Design an optimistic drag whose rejection is legible rather than a silent snap-back.
