Provide a keyboard equivalent for reordering that is a real path, not a token one.
claims: Card order must be stored as a sortable rank per card rather than an integer position, or moving one card rewrites the position of every sibling and every concurrent move conflicts.

Fractional ranks between adjacent keys exhaust floating-point precision after a few dozen insertions at the same spot, so a string-based rank with a midpoint algorithm, or a periodic rebalance, is required rather than optional.

Expressing a move as 'set this card's rank to K' makes concurrent moves converge under last-writer-wins on a single field; expressing it as 'insert at index 3' makes two concurrent moves produce different orders on each client.
A drag is an optimistic mutation: the card must render at the destination immediately, and a server rejection must animate it back with a stated reason rather than silently snapping.

Drag and drop must have a keyboard equivalent — a move mode entered from the card, arrow keys to reposition, and an aria-live announcement of the new position — because pointer-only reordering excludes keyboard and screen reader users entirely.
During a drag, only the dragged element should move, and it should move via transform on its own layer so the drag does not trigger layout on the rest of the board.

Board data is small enough to hold entirely in memory, so the interesting problems here are write conflicts and ordering rather than data volume — which is exactly why this case is about the write path.
A rejected move must restore not just the card's position but the ranks of anything the client optimistically renumbered, which is an argument for never renumbering siblings in the first place.

viz.title: Rank, Not Index
viz.whatIsDrawn: Two client boards side by side over a shared server lane. Both perform a move at the same moment; each operation is drawn descending into the server lane and back. The resulting order on each client is printed beneath its board, before and after refresh, with any divergence outlined and labelled inline. A ghost pair shows the same two operations encoded as ranks instead of indices.
viz.predictPrompt: Two users both looking at [A, B, C] simultaneously drag C to the top. With integer positions the server applies both operations. What order does each user see before refresh, and after? Now answer the same question with fractional ranks.
controls: encoding: integer index / fractional rank / string rank
concurrent operation pair (same card / adjacent cards / distant)
server ordering of the two operations
viz.insight: Encoding a move as an absolute rank makes concurrent reorders converge by construction; encoding it as an index makes each client's result depend on an ordering neither client can observe.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts applies a pair of concurrent move operations under each encoding and returns each client's pre-refresh and post-refresh order. Unit test asserts post-refresh orders are identical across clients for rank encodings under every server ordering, and asserts they differ for index encoding under at least one ordering.

drills.prompt: Users repeatedly drag cards to the position between the same two cards. With JavaScript number midpoints, roughly how many insertions before ranks collide, and what do you do about it?
drills.answerSketch: Doubles give about 52 bits of mantissa, so repeated midpointing between the same two values exhausts precision after roughly 50 insertions. Options: string ranks with a base-62 midpoint algorithm (unbounded, keys grow slowly in length), or detect collision and rebalance the affected column — and the rebalance is a write that must be conflict-safe itself.

drills.prompt: Dragging a card sometimes causes the whole board to stutter, and the effect is worse on boards with many columns. The drag uses left/top updates on mousemove. Explain and fix.
drills.answerSketch: Updating left/top triggers layout on every mousemove, and layout cost scales with board size. Fix: use transform: translate3d on the dragged element, promote it to its own layer, and update it in a rAF-batched handler so nothing else in the board recalculates.

drills.prompt: New requirement: a card cannot be moved into a column that is at its WIP limit, and the limit is enforced server-side. What changes in your optimistic drag?
drills.answerSketch: The optimistic move can now be rejected for a business reason, so the rejection path must be legible: animate back with an explanation, not a snap. The client should also apply the known limit optimistically to prevent the drop where it can, while accepting that the server remains authoritative because another user may have filled the last slot in the meantime.

drills.prompt: Order the keyboard reorder path for a screen reader user moving a card from column 1 position 3 to column 2 position 1.
drills.answerSketch: Focus the card via the list's roving tabindex -> activate move mode (e.g. Space) and announce 'move mode, card X, column 1 position 3' -> ArrowRight moves to column 2, announced -> ArrowUp twice to position 1, each announced -> Space or Enter commits and announces the final position -> Escape at any point cancels and restores the original position with an announcement -> focus stays on the card throughout.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: fractional numeric ranks with rebalancing, or string ranks with a midpoint algorithm. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names precision exhaustion as the concrete failure; names the cost of a rebalance write as a conflict source; names key length growth for strings; attaches a number (insertions before collision); flip condition such as 'numeric with rebalance is fine when repeated same-position insertion is rare — a personal board — string ranks when many users insert at the same point, because rebalancing becomes a contended write'.

drills.prompt: Why does 'insert at index 3' fail to converge while 'set rank to K' succeeds, even though both are just one field?
drills.answerSketch: An index is relative to a list state the client observed and the server may no longer have; the same index means a different position after any other move. A rank is an absolute value in a total order that does not depend on what else changed, so applying two rank writes in either order yields the same final ordering.

failureModes: Stores integer positions and rewrites every sibling on every move.
Uses numeric midpoints with no rebalance and ships an ordering that silently breaks after fifty insertions at one spot.
Snaps a rejected card back with no explanation.
Animates the drag with left/top and blames React for the stutter.
Ships drag and drop with no keyboard path and calls it a known limitation.
Cannot explain what happens when two users move the same card at once.
interviewProbes: Two of us drag the same card to the top at the same time. What do we each see?
I've dragged fifty cards into the same gap. Still working?
Move a card between columns using only the keyboard. Narrate what a screen reader says.

cs-widget.title: Case: Embeddable Third-Party Widget
objectives: Choose an isolation strategy from what the widget must overlay, and state precisely what each strategy does and does not isolate.
Design a loader that costs the host page a few kilobytes rather than the whole widget.
Communicate across an origin boundary without opening a hole in either page.
claims: You do not control the host page: its CSS, its global objects, its Content Security Policy, its network conditions and its other third-party scripts are all hostile inputs your widget must survive.

Shadow DOM blocks selectors but not inheritance, so a host rule like `* { box-sizing: content-box }` does not reach into a shadow root while inherited properties such as font-size and any custom property do — which is why shadow DOM is partial isolation, not isolation.

An iframe is the only full style and script isolation available, and its cost is layout: the parent cannot read the child's content height cross-origin, so the child must measure itself with ResizeObserver and postMessage the height out.
The loader script must be tiny and cached aggressively, bootstrapping the real bundle asynchronously, so the host's measured page weight cost is a few kilobytes rather than the widget's full size.
Cross-origin postMessage requires an explicit targetOrigin when sending and an origin check when receiving; using '*' on either side is a security bug, not a convenience.
A host page's CSP can block your inline styles, your inline scripts and your CDN origin, so you must publish the exact directives customers need and design to avoid requiring unsafe-inline.

Third-party cookies and storage are partitioned or blocked in modern browsers, so a widget cannot rely on cross-site state and identity must be passed in by the host or scoped to a first-party mechanism.

The widget must fail to nothing rather than to a broken host page: wrap the entry point in a boundary, never mutate host globals or built-in prototypes, and never let an exception escape into the host's error handling.

viz.title: Selectors Stop; Inheritance Doesn't
viz.whatIsDrawn: A host page rectangle containing the widget's boundary drawn as a solid, dashed or dotted line depending on the chosen strategy. Three host declarations are drawn as arrows aimed at the boundary; each either bounces off with an inline 'blocked' label or passes through with an inline 'inherited' label, annotated at the crossing point itself. The widget's rendered appearance updates in place to show the actual consequence.
viz.predictPrompt: Your widget uses shadow DOM. The host page sets `* { box-sizing: content-box }`, `html { font-size: 10px }`, and `:root { --primary: hotpink }`. Which of these three change how your widget renders?
controls: isolation strategy: namespaced classes / shadow DOM / iframe
toggle each of several host declarations
toggle a host CSP that blocks inline styles
viz.insight: Shadow DOM blocks selector matching and nothing else — inherited properties and custom properties cross it freely — so a widget that must look identical everywhere either resets every inherited property explicitly or lives in an iframe.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure table mapping (strategy, declaration kind) -> crosses/blocked, derived from spec behaviour and verified against a small manual browser matrix documented in the module. Unit test locks the table so a future refactor cannot silently teach the wrong thing.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: iframe or shadow DOM for a support-chat widget that opens a panel over the host page. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names that the panel must overlay host content, which an iframe can do only if the iframe itself is positioned and resized by the loader; names full isolation as the iframe's advantage; names inheritance leakage as shadow DOM's risk; names the height-messaging complexity; flip condition such as 'iframe whenever the widget handles credentials or untrusted content, shadow DOM when visual integration with the host matters more than isolation and no secrets are handled'.

drills.prompt: A widget receives configuration via postMessage with `window.addEventListener('message', e => applyConfig(e.data))`. Name the vulnerability and the fix.
drills.answerSketch: No origin check, so any page — or any other frame or extension able to post to this window — can inject configuration. Fix: verify e.origin against an allowlist of expected host origins before touching e.data, and validate the payload shape; on the sending side, always pass an explicit targetOrigin instead of '*'.

drills.prompt: New requirement: a customer's CSP is `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com`. What in your widget breaks?
drills.answerSketch: Inline styles injected by your bundle are blocked (no style-src permitting them), your fonts and images from other origins are blocked, any XHR/fetch to your API is blocked by default-src, and any inline bootstrap snippet is blocked. You must publish required directives (connect-src for your API, style-src or a nonce strategy, img-src, font-src) and ship styles as external files or adopted stylesheets rather than inline tags.

drills.prompt: Order what the loader script does from the host's script tag to a rendered widget.
drills.answerSketch: Parse its own data attributes for configuration -> create the container element and attach the isolation boundary -> asynchronously import the real bundle from the CDN with an integrity hash -> on load, initialise inside a try/catch so failures never escape -> establish the postMessage channel with explicit origins -> report the measured height to the parent via ResizeObserver -> render. On import failure, remove the container and stay silent rather than leaving a broken shell.

drills.prompt: Your widget is 140 KB gzipped and is embedded on 400 customer pages, most of whose visitors never interact with it. What do you ship in the loader, and what is the measured host cost?
drills.answerSketch: Ship a loader of roughly 2-4 KB gzipped that renders only a launcher affordance, and defer the 140 KB until the user opens the widget (or until requestIdleCallback on high-intent pages). Host cost becomes a few kilobytes plus one cached request rather than 140 KB on every page load, which is the difference between being kept and being removed.

drills.prompt: Why can a parent page not simply read `iframe.contentDocument.body.scrollHeight` to size a cross-origin widget?
drills.answerSketch: The same-origin policy blocks access to the child document entirely, so contentDocument is null. The child must measure itself and postMessage the height, which is why auto-resizing iframes always involve a message protocol and why that protocol needs origin checks on both ends.

failureModes: Assumes shadow DOM gives full isolation and ships a widget that inherits a 10 px root font size.
Injects a global into window and collides with the host's own code.
Uses postMessage with '*' and no origin check.
Ships the full bundle in the loader, so every host page pays for a widget most visitors never open.
Requires unsafe-inline and is rejected by every security-conscious customer.
Lets an exception escape into the host page's error handler and gets blamed for the host's outage.
interviewProbes: The host page sets a 10 px root font size. What does your widget look like?
The customer's CSP blocks your CDN. What do they see?
Your bundle fails to load. What's on the page?

cs-design-system.title: Case: The Design System Itself (independent partner to Embeddable Widget)
objectives: Treat the API surface and the release process as the design, not as process overhead.
Judge a component API by its escape hatches and its prop count.
Define what constitutes a breaking change for a library whose output is DOM and CSS.
claims: A design system is a library shipped into applications you do not control, so its API surface and its release process are the design; the components are the easy part.
Tokens must be a build-time contract expressed as CSS custom properties or generated constants, so theming and dark mode require no JavaScript re-render and no second bundle.

A component API is judged by its escape hatches — className and style passthrough, forwarded refs, and slot-style composition — because the absence of an escape hatch is what causes a consumer to fork the component.
Compound components sharing context beat a thirty-prop monolith, because uncontrolled prop growth is the specific mechanism by which design systems become unusable.

Semantic versioning for a design system is a promise about rendered DOM structure and CSS as much as about props: changing an element's tag or a class name breaks every consumer who styled around it, whether or not you consider that supported.

Tree-shaking requires side-effect-free modules declared with `"sideEffects": false` and per-component entry points; a barrel file that re-exports everything makes every consumer pay for all of it unless their bundler can prove otherwise.

Adoption must be measured with a usage scan across consumer repositories rather than assumed, and a codemod shipped alongside a breaking change is what converts a migration from a negotiation into a command.

Centralising accessibility — the focus ring, the dialog focus trap, the ARIA wiring, the reduced-motion handling — is the strongest argument for a design system's existence, because it is the work that never gets done correctly in forty separate places.

viz.title: Your DOM Is Public API
viz.whatIsDrawn: One library component at the centre with forty consumer applications drawn as surrounding tiles. A change is selected from a list (rename a class, change a wrapper tag, add a required prop, change a token value, reorder DOM children) and the tiles that break light up with the breaking mechanism labelled inside each tile. A ghost ring shows the same change against a version of the component that exposed proper escape hatches.
viz.predictPrompt: You rename an internal wrapper div to a span inside Button. No props change, no visual change in your own Storybook. How many of your forty consumer apps can this break, and through exactly what mechanism?
controls: toggle whether consumers use descendant selectors or only tokens
viz.insight: A design system's public API includes every element it renders and every class it emits, whether or not that was the intent — which is why the honest way to keep DOM private is to make the supported surface good enough that nobody needs to reach past it.
viz.buildNotes: sim.ts is a pure model over {change, consumerProfiles} returning which profiles break and why, with the profile mix drawn from a documented survey of real consumer patterns. No RNG. Unit test locks the breakage table for each change type.

drills.prompt: A design system publishes an index file re-exporting 120 components and reports that consumers' bundles include the whole library. `"sideEffects"` is unset and the package ships CommonJS only. Name every contributing cause.
drills.answerSketch: No `"sideEffects": false`, so bundlers cannot prove modules are safe to drop; CommonJS has no static analysis for tree-shaking, so an ESM build is required; a single barrel entry point defeats per-component splitting; and CSS side-effect imports inside component modules are themselves side effects that pin the module.

drills.prompt: Forced choice, 4 minutes then locked: a Dialog with twenty props, or a compound Dialog with Dialog.Trigger, Dialog.Content, Dialog.Title and Dialog.Close. Name your flip condition.
drills.answerSketch: Criteria: names prop growth as the failure mode of the monolith; names the discoverability and type-safety cost of compound components; names composition needs (arbitrary content, custom triggers); names the accessibility wiring that must not become the consumer's job either way; flip condition such as 'monolith when the component has exactly one shape and no slot needs arbitrary content — a Spinner, a Badge — compound the moment consumers need to place their own content inside it'.

drills.prompt: New requirement: the system must support a second brand with different spacing scale and border radii, not just different colours. What breaks first?
drills.answerSketch: Any token consumed as a hard-coded value at build time; any component with spacing or radius baked into its styles rather than referenced from a token; and any consumer that overrode a value by targeting your class names. It forces spacing and radius into the token contract and forces a real answer to whether theming is per-tree (CSS custom properties on a scope) or per-build.

drills.prompt: Order the steps for shipping a breaking change to Button across forty consumer apps.
drills.answerSketch: Scan consumer repos to measure actual usage of the affected surface -> introduce the new API alongside the old in a minor release -> deprecate the old with a build-time or runtime warning naming the replacement -> publish a codemod and run it against the top consumers to validate it -> announce with a migration window and the measured blast radius -> ship the major that removes the old API -> keep a patch line on the previous major for the tail.

drills.prompt: Why is changing a rendered element's tag from div to span a breaking change even though no prop changed?
drills.answerSketch: Because consumers style and query the rendered DOM: descendant CSS selectors, test selectors, and layout assumptions (span is inline by default, so a flex or block layout can collapse). The rendered DOM is observable behaviour, and observable behaviour is what semver governs.

drills.prompt: Your library is 240 KB gzipped in total across 120 components. A consumer imports Button and Dialog. Estimate what they should ship and name the two things that most commonly stop that from happening.
drills.answerSketch: Ideally a few kilobytes — Button, Dialog, their shared primitives and tokens. The two blockers are a barrel entry point combined with a missing sideEffects declaration, and CSS imported as a module side effect inside every component so the whole stylesheet is pulled in regardless.

failureModes: Treats the rendered DOM as private and ships tag changes in patch releases.
Grows a component to thirty props rather than making it composable, then wonders why teams fork it.
Ships CommonJS with a barrel export and reports that tree-shaking 'does not work'.
Bakes spacing and radius into components and discovers theming means a second build.
Announces a breaking change with no codemod and no usage measurement.
Cannot say who actually uses the system or which components are dead.
interviewProbes: I'm a consumer and I need this Button to have one extra element inside it. What do I do?
You changed a class name in a patch. Who broke?
How do you know which of your components nobody uses?
